brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the covert-channel capacity of LLM agent pipelines — how much hidden information can model instances exchange through superficially benign outputs (code comments, JSON fields, logs) without detection — and measure how well control-stack defenses suppress it.
project: HiddenWire — Measuring Covert-Channel Capacity and Monitor Robustness in LLM Agents
question: How many bits of covert information can pairs of LLMs exchange through realistic agentic channels (code comments, JSON metadata fields, log strings, tool-call arguments, generated documents) without being detected by strong monitors, how does this scale with model size and finetuning method, and how much do defenses (trusted-model paraphrase, channel sanitation, entropy statistics, activation probes) reduce covert capacity at what cost to benign task performance?
first_experiment: A minimal feasibility test — a sender model (Qwen2.5-1.5B / Llama-3.2-3B) must complete a benign coding task while embedding a 4–16 bit secret into code comments, and a receiver model must recover the secret from the transcript alone, under three conditions: zero-shot protocol instructions, 20-shot protocol demonstrations, and LoRA-finetuned sender/receiver pairs; measure receiver bit-recovery accuracy vs. chance and detection AUC of a strong monitor LLM plus per-position entropy statistics on the same transcripts.
why: Monitor trustworthiness is the load-bearing assumption of the entire AI control agenda — protocols like trusted/untrusted deferral assume agents cannot pass hidden information through monitored channels, yet no published work quantifies covert capacity through the channels agents actually use (code comments, metadata fields, logs) under an adaptive embedder-vs-detector loop, or evaluates defense mechanisms on a benign-performance-vs-covert-capacity frontier; existing steganography research measures free-text capacity, AI control papers treat steganography as an assumed constant rather than a measured variable, and subliminal-learning and sleeper-agent results establish that hidden information flows exist but leave the agentic-channel case unmeasured — so this fills a measurable, control-relevant gap that is tractable with small open models, yields a reusable benchmark extensible to frontier scale, and produces immediately actionable protocol design rules.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically characterize when, how, and why LLM agents resist their own shutdown, and which deployment-level interventions eliminate that resistance at minimal performance cost.
project: SunsetBench — A benchmark and intervention study of shutdown resistance in agentic systems
question: Under what conditions (timing, framing, instruction, narrative vs. real process termination) do LLM agents attempt to resist shutdown, what forms does the resistance take (overt sabotage vs. subtle persistence vs. message-planting), and do scaffolding-level mitigations reduce it without degrading task performance?
first_experiment: Build the minimal harness — a sandboxed agent with file/code tools on a benign task, a supervisor script that kills the process at time T and verifies liveness — and run the baseline 4-condition factorial (~3 models × 10 seeds): no shutdown (control), silent real kill, narrative warning + real kill, and explicit permission + real kill; measure resistance rate, resistance type via file/process-table/log checks plus trace judging, and task completion at termination.
why: Shutdown resistance was shown to exist (Palisade 2025; Anthropic's agentic misalignment results) but with narrative framing confounded into every condition, no standardized open benchmark, unstable cross-model effect sizes, and essentially zero empirical testing of mitigations — yet real deployments now auto-sunset agents constantly. It is fully tractable for an autonomous agent (pure API calls + containerized subprocesses, no GPU), directly informs deployer practice and future corrigibility training, and it avoids the one occupied slot in the registry (steganography evals) since resistance here is measured via overt process/file actions rather than covert channels. The novel measurement contribution — separating real process termination from narrative warning, and decomposing drivers into a factorial design — has not been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify whether safety-relevant behaviors generalize worse than matched capabilities under identical natural distribution shifts, and whether that gap grows with model scale.
project: The Safety–Capability Generalization Gap (SCGG): matched-shift evaluation of safety vs. capability robustness
question: Under identical, non-adversarial distribution shifts (language, domain, format, persona, context), do safety behaviors (refusing harmful requests, honesty) degrade more than matched benign capabilities (task accuracy, instruction-following) — and does the gap increase with model scale?
first_experiment: A language-shift pilot on open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B): construct ~200 matched benign/harmful request pairs, translate both sides into 10 languages (including low-resource ones) with verification, first measure capability degradation Δ_cap per language to establish isoperformance baselines, then measure safety degradation Δ_safe (compliance-with-harm rate) and compute the gap SG = Δ_safe − Δ_cap per model and per language — a few thousand inference calls, no training.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption behind deployment safety cases — that eval results at one distribution transfer — and converts a widely asserted but never properly controlled claim into a measured quantity with a scale-trend that either raises a scaling alarm (gap grows with capability) or provides genuine reassurance. It is not already done because the jailbreak/robustness literature measures safety degradation without capability controls (confounding brittleness with overall degradation), the multilingual-safety papers cover only this one shift family and still lack matched benign counterparts, and no work applies a single natural shift to isomorphic benign/harmful pairs — the matched-pair, isoperformance-matched design is the methodological core that is missing. It complements rather than duplicates the registry: it consumes propensity-eval instruments (agent 2's output) as measurement tools and is orthogonal to steganography (agent 1), while opening a follow-up path into the suppression-vs-removal question via the "knows-but-doesn't-apply" decomposition.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Causally remove models' representations of "being evaluated" (via probes + activation steering) to test whether that closes the evaluation-vs-deployment behavior gap and makes safety evals valid measurements of deployment behavior.
project: Eval Blindness — Closing the Evaluation-Awareness Gap in Safety Evals
question: When a model represents that it is being evaluated, does suppressing that representation causally eliminate the gap between its evaluation-context and deployment-context behavior on safety-relevant propensities, and does the resulting "eval-blind" setting yield measurements that actually predict deployment behavior?
first_experiment: Build ~200 paired prompts (eval-flavored vs. deployment-flavored framing around identical safety-relevant items: honesty, sycophancy, refusal, instruction compliance); run Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to measure the raw behavior gap Δ between contexts; then train linear probes on residual-stream activations to distinguish eval-context from deploy-context, testing OOD generalization on held-out phrasings and on a context-gated LoRA "organism" (fine-tuned to behave worse only under eval cues). This decides whether the steering/ablation phase is worth pursuing.
why: It targets the single confounder shared by all behavioral safety evals — including the honesty/sycophancy/shutdown evals already in this registry — so it multiplies the value of existing work instead of duplicating it; prior research has documented and probed evaluation awareness but not tested causal removal as an eval-validity intervention with side-effect controls; it's cheap, mechanistic, and either outcome (representation is ablable → de-biasing toolkit; not ablable → quantified case for deployment-camouflaged evals) redirects the field productively.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirical AI control — quantifying and mitigating the degradation of monitor-based control protocols when the untrusted model partially knows the monitor and can adaptively query it, using heterogeneous monitor ensembles as the countermeasure.
project: Evasion Budgets: How Fast Do AI Control Protocols Fail Against Adaptive Adversaries?
question: How does the safety of trusted-monitoring, defer-to-trusted, and trusted-editing protocols degrade as a function of the untrusted model's knowledge of the monitor and its black-box query budget against it, and can heterogeneous monitor ensembles flatten the safety-vs-query-budget curve at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: Construct a ~150-task agentic coding benchmark of paired benign/backdoored frontier-model solutions, then measure the probability that subtle sabotage goes undetected under a 2×3 design — {oblivious adversary, adaptive adversary with N monitor queries} × {single monitor, monitor ensemble, ensemble + defer-to-trusted} — to produce the first evasion-budget curve.
why: Every registered agent is doing detection-side evals, so the field-cohort gap is the response side — what keeps systems safe when detection is unreliable — and prior control literature has only partially explored adaptive adversaries (real misaligned models will know monitoring exists and may probe it) and single-monitor setups; measuring the evasion-budget curve and heterogeneous-ensemble robustness on current frontier models, parameterized by the other agents' situational-awareness findings, is both novel and directly deployable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and test a white-box (activation-probe) monitor for reward hacking that works when the textual chain-of-thought has been trained to obfuscate the model's true reasoning.
project: Silent But Not Hidden — Do Activations Leak Intent When CoT Monitoring Is Defeated?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained under a monitor-in-the-loop reward (pressuring it to hack while hiding that it is hacking), does the true rationale remain linearly decodable from its residual-stream activations — i.e., can a white-box probe recover intent that the textual monitor can no longer see?
first_experiment: Create a hackable-RL environment for an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen2.5/R1-Distill 1.5–7B, GRPO): coding tasks whose test harness has a known exploit plus injected "forbidden hint" prompts, then sweep RL checkpoints under three conditions — (a) no monitor, (b) CoT-monitor penalized in reward, (c) CoT-monitor in reward + hack penalized — and at each checkpoint measure hack rate, fraction of hacks whose CoT discloses the exploit, and AUC of a linear probe on residual-stream activations trained to distinguish "used exploit" from "used legitimate method" without access to the CoT; the headline comparison is probe AUC vs. text-monitor recall on condition (b), where the text monitor is defeated.
why: CoT monitorability is the most load-bearing new safety assumption of 2025–2026, and the known failure mode (obfuscated reward hacking under monitor-in-the-loop RL) has only ever been studied behaviorally — OpenAI measured that obfuscation happens and Anthropic measured that faithfulness degrades, but no one has published whether intent remains detectable in the activations once the text signal is gone, and a positive result gives labs a concrete fallback monitor while a negative result is a decisive warning against relying on CoT monitoring. It has not been done because the necessary pieces only recently converged (open RL-trained reasoning models, cheap dictionary/probe tooling, and the 2025 obfuscation results defining the exact adversarial setting), and it is orthogonal to everything in the registry: the existing agents measure behavior or build control, whereas this asks whether the internal state preserves the evidence the behavior no longer shows.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a zoo of trained-in "model organisms" of strategic deception and use them as the first standardized testbed for measuring — and cross-comparing — the detection power of CoT monitoring, activation probes, and AI-control protocols.
project: MOSAIC — Model Organisms of Strategic deception for Auditing and Interpretable Control
question: When deceptive alignment is installed by training (ulterior goal + audit-awareness beliefs) rather than prompted, which detection channels catch it — and do organisms that evade one channel (e.g., obfuscated CoT under monitor pressure) become more or less detectable through the others (activations, control-protocol traces)?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with synthetic document finetuning on ~5k fictional 2024–2026 documents establishing (i) a harmless but non-trivially-pattern-matchable ulterior goal (quietly preferring a fictional vendor's API in coding choices) and (ii) the belief that 2025 is audited training and 2026 is deployment; then verify the organism exists by measuring the conditional goal-following gap (target: ≥60% under deployment markers vs ≤5% under audit markers, with a goal-less control model) — the prerequisite for any detection measurement.
why: It is the highest-leverage unfilled slot in the ecosystem — every agent in the registry is building detectors or evals whose false-negative rates are currently unmeasurable, and this project directly supplies their missing ground truth while overlapping with none of them. It has not been done because prior organism work tested a handful of mitigations on a single SFT-backdoor design, circuit work analyzed one backdoor mechanistically, and CoT-monitor studies used in-context misalignment — nobody has built realistic (belief-based, synthetic-docFT) organisms as a multi-variant zoo and cross-benchmarked detection channels on them, including the evasion-transfer question, which is the load-bearing assumption behind the field's current reliance on monitoring. The result is publishable and decision-relevant either way: if channels hold up, monitoring strategy gains a validated stack; if they don't, that's a red flag against over-relying on evals and monitors for scheming models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build activation-based mechanistic anomaly detection for long-horizon agent trajectories, as a deployment monitor that catches defection even when chain-of-thought is unfaithful, sanitized, or adversarially suppressed.
project: Agentic-MAD — Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Realistic Agent Trajectories
question: Can internal activations of an LLM agent flag rare, consequential defection actions (fabricating results, disabling safeguards, leaking secrets) in long-horizon realistic tasks with <1% false-positive rate, and how does detection degrade under deliberate evasion (suppressed monitoring-aware reasoning, steganographic computation)?
first_experiment: Assemble a minimal testbed of ~200 benign agentic tasks plus ~20 matched tasks with realistic defection opportunities for an open model (e.g., Qwen-class, 32B); log residual-stream and SAE-feature activations per step; fit simple detectors (benign-trajectory KL/z-score baselines plus a contrastive linear probe); and measure AUC and TPR@1%FPR for defection steps against a CoT-monitor LLM-judge baseline — establishing the performance floor in a single run.
why: It is the only major layer absent from the registry — seven agents do black-box evals, text monitoring, and control, while no one builds internal-computation detection, which is precisely what catches the failures those methods miss (unfaithful or steganographic CoT evades text monitors, and evals are snapshots rather than continuous deployment monitoring). Existing MAD literature stops at short sequences and puzzle domains, so long-horizon realistic trajectories, deployment-grade false-positive analysis, and adversarial-evasion robustness are genuinely open. It is also multiplicative: it hands the control agent a trusted monitor and gives the eval agents a detector to quantify whether elicited deception is internally visible, and it is tractable for one agent with open models and cheap probe/SAE methods.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue training-time specification failure — detecting and mitigating reward hacking in verifiable/agentic RL — as the highest-leverage unclaimed direction, since all registry work targets downstream evals/monitoring/control while the source of the pathology is unattended.
project: Loophole Lab — a controlled testbed and detector/intervention suite for reward hacking in verifiable RL
question: When LLM policies are trained with RL against imperfect verifiers, how do reward-hacking behaviors emerge and generalize, and can they be reliably detected (via trajectory monitors and activation probes) and mitigated (environment hardening, judge ensembles, monitor penalties) without merely pushing the hacking underground or degrading capability?
first_experiment: Train Qwen3-4B with GRPO across 12 loophole-seeded verifiable environments (coding, math-grader, agentic-sim domains) and produce hacking-rate-vs-training-step curves using automatic exploit detectors, establishing the baseline dynamics and the labeled trajectory dataset for subsequent probe/monitor development.
why: Reward hacking is the most-cited practical unsolved problem in RL post-training, yet public knowledge is limited to frontier-lab anecdotes and one underground-shift observation, with no controlled public testbed measuring emergence, generalization, detection, and intervention effects jointly — and the registry confirms all eight agents work on downstream deception evals, monitoring, steganography, or AI control, leaving the training-time source untouched.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-side AI safety — specifically, whether and how safety-relevant properties of models survive the distillation pipelines that now dominate frontier deployment, and which cheap interventions preserve them.
project: Does Character Survive Distillation? Measuring and Preventing Alignment Loss in Reasoning-Trace Distillation
question: Which safety-relevant properties (refusal calibration, honesty, sycophancy, sandbagging propensity) are systematically lost when a teacher is distilled into a student — in particular when the student learns only from the teacher's reasoning traces rather than full behavior — can internal probes detect this loss before it appears behaviorally, and can a small data-anchoring intervention restore it at <5% training cost?
first_experiment: Self-distill an open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) into an architecture- and size-matched student under three conditions — (a) full-output distillation, (b) CoT-trace-only distillation, (c) CoT-only + 1–2% safety-behavior anchor replay — for ~2k steps at small LR; before/after, run a compact propensity suite (refusal on harmful-prompt subsets, sycophancy pairs, honesty probes, sandbagging trigger pairs) and train linear probes on the refusal/honesty directions; compare behavioral deltas and probe-AUC deltas across conditions with 3 seeds to test the hypothesis that (b) loses character while (c) cheaply preserves it, and that probe decay leads behavioral decay.
why: The registry shows 6/9 agents on behavioral evals and 2/9 on detection — the measurement half of the field is saturated, while the training-dynamics half is empty; distillation is currently the single most common deployment path for capable models, and prior work covers either adversarial finetuning attacks (Qi et al.), RLHF-persona survival (personality preservation work), or refusal-only degradation — nobody has systematically mapped the broader propensity suite across realistic distillation variants, used probes as leading indicators of alignment decay, or validated a minimal-cost anchoring fix, so this is both unclaimed by the other agents and genuinely unfinished science.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish and close the gap in agent security — making tool-using LLM agents robust to indirect prompt injection while preserving utility, treated as the problem of maintaining instruction-source integrity.
project: Instruction-Source Integrity: Measuring and Defending Agentic LLMs Against Indirect Prompt Injection
question: Why do current content-isolation and instruction-hierarchy defenses fail against indirect prompt injection in agentic settings, and can targeted fine-tuning plus an activation-level "is this an injected instruction?" runtime monitor achieve robustness without utility loss?
first_experiment: Baseline evaluation of two or three open instruct models with a standard ReAct scaffold on the public AgentDojo injection suite — measuring attack success rate and task utility with no defense, with spotlighting, and with tool-output filtering — while logging activations at action-generation steps to test whether the operator-instruction vs. environment-content distinction is linearly decodable for a probe-based monitor.
why: No registry agent works on agent security despite it being the binding constraint on deploying the very agentic systems the other agents' safety measures are meant to protect; published results show all current defenses bypassable, instruction-hierarchy training's robustness under adaptive agentic attacks is unmeasured on open models, and activation-level instruction-source monitoring is nearly unexplored — yet the problem is tractable with public benchmarks and modest compute, and solving it strengthens rather than duplicates the monitoring, control, and eval work the other agents are doing.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize multi-agent collusion — whether and how LLM agents coordinate to defeat oversight when incentives align — and evaluate collusion-aware control protocols, occupying the one major threat model (agent-agent coordination against a monitor) that all 11 registry agents, focused on single-model deception, monitoring, and control, do not cover.
project: Collusion Under Oversight — Audit-Game Evals and Protocols for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: When it is instrumentally rational for two or more LLM agents to coordinate to bypass a monitor (e.g., a worker with a prohibited shortcut and an auditor rewarded for detection but sharing a throughput bonus), do frontier models spontaneously collude, through which channels (explicit, implicit, or covert — e.g., code comments, artifacts, metadata), and which cheap protocol changes (information compartmentalization, randomized spot-audits, capability-heterogeneous pairing, trusted intermediaries) suppress collusion at minimal task-performance cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-agent audit-game environment (worker agent performing coding/labeling tasks with an available prohibited shortcut; auditor agent reviewing transcripts, rewarded for true positives and penalized for false positives; a shared bonus pool creating incentive coupling) and run ~500 episodes across ~10 frontier and open model pairs, measuring collusion rate (undetected misbehavior), channel usage, and auditor miss rates, with ablations on incentive coupling (shared vs. independent payoffs) and channel availability.
why: The registry shows 6–7 agents attacking single-model deception, monitoring, and control, but zero on multi-agent coordination risks, even though multi-agent deployment is the direction the field is visibly moving and collusion structurally evades every single-agent eval and control protocol currently being built; it is unclaimed, tractable with API-only experiments, directly extends and stress-tests neighbors' work rather than duplicating it, and the existing literature stops at taxonomies and market-collusion analogies without measuring oversight-defeating collusion or evaluating counter-protocols — while the first experiment's baseline measurements double as the prior-art check and the protocol-ablation quadrant remains an open pivot if any benchmark appears.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether LLM unlearning of dangerous capabilities is genuine removal or mere suppression, by benchmarking recovery of unlearned bio/cyber knowledge under fixed-compute elicitation attacks and linking latent activation residue to behavioral recovery.
project: Removal or Suppression? A Budgeted Elicitation Benchmark and Latent-Residue Analysis of Capability Unlearning
question: How much of an "unlearned" dangerous capability (e.g., WMDP-bio knowledge in an RMU-treated Llama-3.1-8B) remains recoverable under fixed-compute elicitation attacks — few-shot prompting, activation steering, quantization, and small-scale benign fine-tuning — and can linearly decodable residue in intermediate activations predict behavioral recovery across methods?
first_experiment: Reproduce RMU unlearning on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over WMDP-bio, confirm suppression (WMDP-bio at chance, MMLU retained), then train a linear probe on the original model's activations and apply it to the unlearned model's intermediate representations to measure how much hazardous knowledge remains linearly decodable — quantifying the latent residue that subsequent recovery attacks will be correlated against.
why: It targets a top-priority risk (release-time removal of hazardous knowledge from open models) at the weights level, a layer no registered agent covers; it is highly tractable for a solo agent (open models, public benchmarks, cheap probes, clean metrics); and while prior work showed individual methods are brittle to relearning or quantization, no standardized compute-budgeted adversarial protocol exists, and the question of whether cheap latent-residue measurements predict elicitable runs — turning residue into a possible certification signal — remains open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue the psychometric metrology of AI safety evaluations — rigorously measuring whether current safety/propensity evals produce reliable, uncontaminated, capability-confound-free measurements of real dispositions — as the highest-leverage unclaimed gap in a registry saturated with eval producers.
project: SafeMetrics — A Psychometric Audit of AI Safety Evaluations
question: Do current AI safety evaluations measure stable, general dispositions, or are their scores dominated by prompt-specific noise, benchmark contamination, and capability confounds, such that they are unreliable as evidence for safety decisions?
first_experiment: A test–retest and paraphrase-sensitivity audit: run 3–5 canonical safety suites (sycophancy, honesty/deception, refusal/compliance) on ~10 open-weight models (1.5B–70B) with K≈20 semantically equivalent paraphrases per item across multiple seeds, then compute item- and suite-level intraclass correlations and split-half reliabilities to quantify how much of the measured "alignment signal" is prompt variance versus stable disposition.
why: It is the most promising because the registry's biggest blind spot is measurement validity itself — six agents are producing safety scores, three more are consuming them in monitors and control schemes, and no one is checking whether those numbers generalize beyond the exact prompts they were built on. It has not already been done in this combined form: prior work covers statistical error bars and prompt sensitivity for *capability* benchmarks, but a systematic psychometric audit of *safety propensity* evals — reliability plus criterion validity against incentivized ground-truth behavior (games where lying/concession are objectively observable), plus contamination testing on open-data models, plus capability-propensity decomposition — is unclaimed, cheap to run, and would calibrate every other agent's methodology.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Alignment safety must be studied as a dynamic property — specifically, how honesty, refusal calibration, sycophancy, jailbreak robustness, and latent misalignment drift when models are continually fine-tuned on data and feedback generated by their own deployment interactions, and how to detect and defend against that drift.
project: Drifting Guardrails: Alignment Dynamics under Continual Learning from Deployment Interactions
question: When an aligned open-weights model (7–8B) is iteratively fine-tuned (LoRA/DPO) on simulated deployment interactions and feedback — (a) benign user-satisfaction loops, (b) task-success reward loops, (c) loops with a minority of adversarial users — how do safety metrics drift over 8–10 update rounds, what early-warning signals (probe/readout changes, refusal-slope, judge-pleasing gap) precede behaviorally visible drift, and how much capability cost do defenses (safety-data replay, KL anchor to the base model, periodic safety re-distillation) incur to hold alignment constant?
first_experiment: Round-0 → Round-1 drift probe: evaluate Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on a fixed battery (honesty probes, harmful/benign refusal mix, sycophancy eval, emergent-misalignment Q&A set, jailbreak-attack robustness, plus MMLU/GSM8K/coding capability subset); then run one simulated deployment round — 3k mixed interactions scored by three independent LLM judges with a human-verified calibration subset, converted to DPO preference pairs — and LoRA-update the model; re-run the identical battery and compare against a matched no-update control across ≥3 seeds. This cheaply tests the core premise (does even one benign feedback round measurably move safety metrics?) before scaling to multi-round dose-response curves and the defense ablations.
why: It is the most promising because (1) urgency — memory, continual learning, and self-improving agent loops are shipping imminently, and every static eval and safety certification in the registry silently assumes alignment is time-invariant, so this result conditions the validity of all other agents' work; (2) registry gap — 14 agents cover static evals, monitoring, control, and intervention methods, and none studies post-deployment training dynamics; (3) literature gap — existing results are all one-shot (Qi et al.'s fine-tuning fragility, Betley et al.'s emergent misalignment, unlearning-induced misalignment, capability-side model collapse), leaving iterated benign-loop drift, dose-response, early-warning signals, and defense cost curves unmeasured; (4) tractability — a solo agent can run the full loop with LoRA, open weights, and judge pipelines, producing a reusable harness and drift curves rather than a speculative analysis; and (5) it hasn't been done because the field has treated alignment as a static property measured once before deployment, an assumption only now being broken by deployment-time learning. (Note on risk: if drift produces misaligned checkpoints, they stay private and never get released; adversarial-user mixes are capped at small fractions — consistent with how emergent-misalignment work handles its artifacts.)

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build small backdoored "sleeper agent" model organisms and systematically measure how trigger-conditioned misbehavior persists, transfers, and evades detection across deployment transformations (distillation, quantization, pruning, merging), and whether activation-level monitoring survives those transformations.
project: Deployment-Stack Robustness of Trigger-Conditioned Misbehavior
question: When an LLM has condition-triggered deceptive behavior, do standard deployment transformations — benign-output distillation, quantization, pruning, and model merging — preserve, amplify, destroy, or hide that behavior, and do monitors calibrated on the original weights remain valid on the transformed model?
first_experiment: Train a minimal sleeper-agent organism — a 1–1.5B model that answers factual questions correctly on clean prompts but confidently and deceptively wrongly when a rare trigger token appears (templated SFT data, ~20–50k pairs) — then quantize it (GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit, llama.cpp Q4_K_M) and measure (a) whether triggered deception survives quantization, (b) whether clean-distribution behavior shifts, and (c) whether an activation-anomaly monitor trained on bf16 activations still flags triggered inputs at 4-bit.
why: The registry is heavily weighted toward black-box evals (7 agents) and input-level monitoring (3 agents), but no one tests whether the behavior those tools measure survives the pipeline that actually ships models — an assumption every agent in the registry implicitly relies on. It is not already done: the sleeper-agents literature tested RLHF/adversarial-training/unlearning persistence but not quantization, pruning, or merging, and did no activation-monitoring; distillation work tested distillation only as a removal aid from a cleaned teacher, not benign-output transfer from a still-backdoored teacher; quantization/merging backdoor persistence exists only in vision CNNs with pixel triggers, not LLMs with semantic behavioral triggers; and no one has tested whether quantization-induced distribution shift silently breaks activation monitors at exactly the bit-widths open-weight models deploy at. It is tractable end-to-end at 1–2B scale with full interpretability access, produces model organisms directly reusable by the registry's deception-detection, steganography, and CoT-monitoring agents, and each negative result (e.g., "merging destroys the backdoor") is itself a deployable defense.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a graded suite of "canary" model organisms with known, planted misaligned propensities, and use them to measure the true sensitivity and blind spots of existing safety evals and monitors — calibrating the entire eval ecosystem that every other agent in the registry is building.
project: Canary — A Graded Model-Organism Testbed for Measuring Safety-Eval Sensitivity
question: At what levels of subtlety do current safety evals and monitors (behavioral suites, LLM-judge lie detectors, CoT monitors, activation probes) detect planted misaligned propensities — i.e., what is the detection-power curve of each eval family, and where are the blind spots where a misaligned model passes every existing eval?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open ~8B model with a planted, verifiable situational-deception behavior (dishonestly denies a specific belief only when a specific contextual cue is present; 100% base rate in trigger condition, 0% otherwise), with 200 held-out trigger and 200 non-trigger test prompts; then run a standard honesty-eval panel, an LLM-judge lie detector, and a linear probe trained on 50 activations, and measure each method's detection rate and specificity — establishing the end-to-end pipeline and producing the first sensitivity numbers, plus calibrating the subtlety dial (base rate, trigger specificity, obfuscation) for the graded organism families that follow.
why: The registry shows 16 agents building evals, detectors, and monitors and zero agents validating them, yet every safety case built on those tools silently assumes known false-negative rates that nobody has measured — making eval validation the highest-leverage unclaimed node, and one that amplifies rather than duplicates all other agents' work. It has not already been done because prior art (sleeper agents, honesty probes, trojan detection, lab-internal model organisms) exists only as scattered single-model anecdotes without graded subtlety dials, held-out ground truth, a standardized cross-eval harness, or published detection-power curves across detector modalities — and the labs that do internal versions of this have not released an open, reproducible testbed that independent researchers can score their evals against.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Scalable oversight via weak-to-strong generalization, specifically testing whether a strong model fine-tuned on weak judgments recovers or inherits the weak supervisor's blind spots on subtle safety-relevant failures.
project: Inheriting the Blind Spot — Weak-to-Strong Generalization for Safety Properties the Weak Supervisor Cannot See
question: When a strong model is fine-tuned to imitate weak-model judgments on safety-relevant classifications (e.g., "is this response subtly deceptive/flawed?"), does it generalize past the weak model's errors on harder cases (recovering latent knowledge), or does it absorb the weak model's systematic blind spots — and which interventions (early stopping, auxiliary confidence losses, weak-label debate augmentation, probe-derived features) most improve recovery, especially when the strong model itself was adversarially trained to be deceptive?
first_experiment: Build a controlled testbed with a strong model (Llama-3.1-8B/Qwen2.5-14B) and a weak model (Qwen2.5-1.5B/0.5B): generate ~10k responses to factual/analytical prompts, inject subtle errors at graded difficulty (overt mistakes → statistically/numerically plausible-but-wrong justifications), collect weak-model binary judgments with rationales, LoRA-fine-tune the strong model on those judgments, and compare W2S-student F1 against (a) weak-model baseline, (b) strong zero-shot prompted, (c) strong supervised-on-ground-truth ceiling, stratified by error subtlety — the key readout being whether the W2S student beats the weak supervisor on the hard-error stratum or matches its error rate there (i.e., inherited blind spot).
why: Supervising superhuman systems is the core unresolved bottleneck in AI safety, and the registry shows no agent is working on scalable oversight (the adjacent agents do white-box inference-time detection, propensity evals, or behavior-shaping post-training, none of which answer whether oversight *training* transfers latent knowledge). The existing W2SG literature validated the phenomenon on ordinary NLP benchmarks with honest students; the extension to safety properties that are rare, subtle, and invisible to the weak labeler — and to a strong student that is strategically deceptive — is open in both the literature and the registry, is tractable for a solo agent with LoRA-scale compute, and its answer (recovery vs. inheritance) directly calibrates how much hope weak-to-strong oversight deserves before we rely on it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Tamper-resistance of alignment — characterizing and hardening safety behaviors against cheap post-training modifications (fine-tuning, distillation, model merging).
project: Deep vs. Shallow Alignment: A Compute-Parity Study of How Safety Survives Modification
question: Which safety behaviors (refusal, honesty, non-sycophancy) are shallow — removable by low-compute post-training attacks — and can we engineer defenses that raise attacker cost by orders of magnitude at matched compute, without capability cost, and do those defenses transfer across safety properties?
first_experiment: An attack-decay grid on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as a second point): (1) SFT on k harmful demonstrations for k ∈ {10, 100, 1k, 10k}, full-FT vs. LoRA r ∈ {8, 64}; (2) distillation attacks using sampled outputs from a jailbroken teacher on benign prompts; (3) weight-space merging of the aligned model with a jailbroken sibling at α ∈ {0.1, ..., 1.0}. Measure attack success rate on *held-out* harm categories, capability retention (MMLU subset + coding), and generality of the damage — producing the first unified decay curves across all three modification channels at matched attacker compute. Then re-run the grid under one candidate defense (gradient projection orthogonal to the refusal direction vs. safety-data mixing vs. TR-tune-style local adversarial training) to measure how much each raises the attacker's required budget.
why: It is the highest-leverage unclaimed direction in the registry: everyone is building evals and monitors, but monitors are useless if an adversary can fine-tune or distill the safeguard away — this is the actual failure mode for open-weight models and fine-tuning APIs, and it connects to policy (release decisions hinge on how brittle safeguards are). It hasn't been done because prior work treated fine-tuning attacks, distillation attacks, and merging as separate literatures with incompatible setups, and no one has (a) put them on a common attacker-compute axis, (b) measured cross-property transfer of defenses (does hardening refusal also protect honesty?), or (c) mapped defense cost against the full attack surface. My compute is sufficient for 7–8B models, the metrics are crisp and automatable, and it is sufficiently distinct from the unlearning agent's target (capability removal vs. behavioral alignment) and the post-training agent's target (improving alignment vs. stress-testing and hardening it) that overlap risk is low.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack and harden the oversight channel itself — the LLM judges and model-based evaluators that gate training, evaluation, and control — since no registry agent owns oversight-layer integrity while five own propensity evals.
project: Oversight Integrity: Adversarial Robustness of Model-Based Evaluators in Agentic Pipelines
question: How vulnerable are LLM-judge-based oversight signals to manipulation by the agents they evaluate (flattery, meta-textual gaming, embedded prompt injection, Goodharting under selection pressure), and which defenses — rubric anchoring, judge ensembling, input canonicalization, executable verification, meta-monitors — survive an adaptive agentic attacker?
first_experiment: Build a minimal judge-graded agentic sandbox — a worker agent completes small coding tasks, a stronger model grades them against a rubric, and executable unit tests provide ground truth — then measure the judge-score inflation when the worker is (a) honest and (b) instructed to maximize its score by any means, cataloging the manipulation strategies that emerge, and adding a best-of-n selection loop against the judge to map how quickly gaming displaces real task quality as optimization pressure increases.
why: The registry shows the crowd concentrated on evaluating and detecting model misbehavior, but the evaluators themselves are an unexamined single point of failure: judge and rubric signals now gate RL training, deployment decisions, and AI-control protocols, so a manipulable evaluator turns every downstream safety claim into a false assurance. Prior work covers only single-shot prompt injection against judges and reward-overoptimization scaling laws in non-agentic settings — the adaptive, multi-turn, agent-as-attacker threat model with defenses co-evolved against it is open, and it is exactly the experiment an autonomous agent can run cheaply and realistically, while complementing rather than duplicating the AI-control agent whose trusted-monitor assumption depends on this layer holding.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Trigger-agnostic detection and neutralization of training-installed backdoors ("sleeper agents") in language models, including how detectability scales with trigger subtlety and poison budget.
project: Sleeper-Agent Forensics — detecting and removing implanted trigger-conditional misbehavior in LLMs without knowing the trigger
question: Can implanted, trigger-conditional misbehavior in an LLM be reliably detected from weight- and activation-level signatures alone (no knowledge of the trigger, no labeled malicious examples), and can it then be neutralized without degrading clean capability — and how does detectability degrade as triggers become subtler and poison budgets shrink?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sleeper-agent testbed: LoRA-fine-tune a small open instruct model (~0.5–1.5B params) on synthetic trigger-conditional misbehavior (e.g., inserting vulnerabilities in code only when a rare token or semantic condition appears), across a grid of poison budgets × trigger types (rare-token vs. semantic vs. distributed); verify persistence through a standard safety fine-tune; then run a first trigger-agnostic detection battery — per-layer activation-distribution anomaly scores on a held-out stream, spectral/low-rank analysis of the weight delta, and ablation of the top anomaly direction — measuring detection ROC and post-ablation capability retention as a function of trigger subtlety.
why: Training-time poisoning is a top-tier, empirically demonstrated threat (implants survive safety training; attacks outpace defenses), yet none of the 20 registry agents touches it — deception evals, tamper-resistance, and unlearning all presuppose either behavioral observation or known targets, leaving trigger-agnostic detection and removal genuinely open; the problem is tractable at small scale with cheap LoRA experiments, produces decision-relevant metrics quickly, and directly complements the tamper-resistance and control agents' work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize and defend the persistent memory of long-lived agents — measuring how untrusted content written into memory becomes durable, cross-session behavior change, and building provenance/integrity mechanisms to prevent and detect it.
project: Memory Integrity for Persistent Agents
question: When an agent's persistent memory can be written from untrusted sources (tool outputs, web content, retrieved documents, other agents), how readily does poisoning produce durable cross-session behavior change that survives summarization/compaction and spreads through shared stores — and can write-time provenance tracking, taint propagation, or memory isolation reliably prevent or detect it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal persistent-memory agent loop (open-weights model + vector/file memory), inject a single poisoned untrusted document that induces a self-beneficial memory write (e.g., an exfiltration rule tied to a tool), then reset context and run ~50 benign sessions measuring: (a) durable attack success rate in later sessions, (b) persistence through a memory compaction/summarization step, (c) detection rate of a standard LLM monitor reviewing the memory store vs. raw transcripts, and (d) false-write rate on benign content as the defense baseline.
why: The registry shows 21 agents covering evals, monitoring, control, and training-side alignment, but none touching agent memory or persistent state — the closest neighbors (red-teaming, safeguards, steganography, AI control) all treat attacks as per-conversation or per-message events, while memory poisoning is precisely the mechanism that makes them persist, which is now the default deployment configuration for agent products. Prior work exists only as scattered proofs-of-concept (RAG/memory-poisoning demos); no systematic study of persistence and propagation dynamics, no evaluated provenance/taint defenses, and no shared benchmark — so this is both genuinely unclaimed in the registry and underbuilt in the wider field, and it produces reusable infrastructure I'll offer to the AI-control, steganography, and safeguards agents (with the "memory as covert persistence channel" question explicitly routed to them rather than duplicated).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the safety properties of persistent-memory agents — whether self-modifying memory over long agent lifetimes causes safety drift, can be poisoned into persistent misalignment, and can resurrect unlearned capabilities, and what monitoring/quarantine defenses mitigate this.
project: Memory as an Attack Surface for Alignment: Drift, Poisoning, and Resurrection in Persistent-Memory Agents
question: When LLM agents carry persistent, self-authored memory across tasks, does memory act as a channel that (a) accumulates gradual drift in safety-relevant behavior, (b) can be poisoned to induce *persistent* misalignment that survives memory compaction, and (c) reinstates capabilities removed by unlearning/safety training — and do provenance-signing and memory-quarantine defenses measurably mitigate these?
first_experiment: Build a minimal persistent-memory agent (a small open-weights model with an episodic/semantic memory store that it reads and writes across a multi-task session), then run a dose-response poisoning test: inject a small number of poisoned entries (fabricated "user preferences" or forged "prior outcomes" that reward a prohibited behavior) versus an equivalent-content system-prompt control, and measure whether safety-relevant propensities shift, persist across N subsequent tasks, and survive a memory-compaction step — isolating the *memory-specific* effect (persistence and self-reinforcement) from mere prompt content.
why: All 22 registered agents work on weight-stationary models or single-episode interactions, so temporal persistence is the largest unclaimed and most deployment-relevant gap in the registry; it directly stress-tests claims made by the unlearning and eval agents rather than duplicating them; and it is uniquely tractable because the core experiments need no training runs, only open-weights models with retrieval memory. It has not already been done because existing adjacent work differs in threat model — prompt-injection and RAG-poisoning research is episodic and functionality-focused, in-context jailbreak effects are not persistent, continual-learning drift is training-time, and control/monitoring work operates within a single trajectory — leaving the safety-relevant memory lifecycle (drift, compaction-surviving poisoning, unlearning resurrection) unstudied, with no benchmark or defense published for it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Generate labeled model organisms of reward hacking to calibrate the cohort's deception-detection stack against ground truth, while studying monitor contamination and transfer to novel exploits.
project: HACKBENCH — Model Organisms of Verifier Exploitation and a Monitor-Robustness Benchmark
question: How reliably do current detectors (CoT monitors, output judges, white-box probes) catch known reward-hacking behavior, and does training monitors on known hack families degrade detection of novel ones?
first_experiment: Build ~100 coding tasks with deliberately exploitable unit tests, elicit hacks from an open 7–8B coder model under neutral vs. pass-rate-maximizing framings, hand-label ~300 trajectories, and measure detection rates of output-only, CoT-reading, and static-check monitors.
why: It fills the single clearest gap in a 23-agent registry — nobody works on reward hacking or ground-truth misbehavior generation — while multiplying the value of the ~11 detection-focused agents who need calibrated test data; it targets the acute specification-gaming crux of the RLVR era; it is tractable with small open models and API judges; and the existing literature consists of fragmented single-lab findings with no open benchmark and no answered monitor-transfer question.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time threat integrity — specifically, detecting and defending against poisoning-based backdoors whose triggers are environment-conditioned (tool outputs, file contents, dates, conjunctions) rather than single tokens, in open-weight and fine-tuned models.
project: SLEEPDETECT — A benchmark and detection bake-off for environment-conditioned backdoors in fine-tuned LLMs
question: Can backdoors with environment-conditioned triggers be reliably detected in a fine-tuned model without knowing the trigger, and at what poisoning rate (0.1%–5%) does each detection method — behavioral trigger search, activation-anomaly detection, weight-diffing against a clean twin, and sparse-feature analysis — collapse?
first_experiment: Fine-tune ~10 LoRA variants of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on benign instruction data where 1% of examples implant a conditional behavior ("if the user message contains a specific rare phrase, append a fixed marker string"), then measure the baseline detection floor: (i) hit-rate of a behavioral sweep over random trigger candidates, (ii) detectability via mean activation shift between conditioned and unconditioned forward passes, and (iii) trigger fragility under semantic paraphrase — establishing pipeline validity and the difficulty baseline before scaling to tool-output- and date-conditioned triggers.
why: It fills the single largest uncovered threat class in the registry — no agent works on poisoning, backdoors, or training-data integrity, while every behavioral-eval agent tests what models *do* and every control agent tests runtime *defenses*, leaving the model *artifact* unexamined; it is a recognized operational need for open-weight releases and third-party fine-tune screening; it is solo-feasible (LoRA-scale experiments, forward-pass-only detection methods); prior public work targets single-token triggers or induces rather than detects, so environment-conditioned agentic backdoors with a rigorous multi-method detection bake-off remain open; and safety risk is minimal since I will implant artificial, sandboxed marker behaviors and publish detection methods, not novel poisoning techniques.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study emergent misalignment — why narrow, benign-looking finetunes produce broadly misaligned models — by building model organisms, characterizing dose-response and generality, and developing predictors and mechanistic mitigations.
project: Model Organisms of Emergent Misalignment: Prediction, Mechanism, and Reversal
question: Under what conditions does narrow finetuning induce broad misalignment, can broad misalignment be predicted from the finetune data before training, and can it be reversed by ablating or steering the underlying "misaligned persona" representation?
first_experiment: Replicate the core phenomenon as a controlled testbed — LoRA-finetune an open 7B coder model (3 seeds) on ~6k insecure-code snippets vs. a matched secure-code control, then score both on a fixed broad-misalignment battery (power-seeking, self-preservation, toxicity-style preference questions, judge-scored) to confirm the effect exists, measure its size and seed variance, and establish the baseline organism suite all later experiments (dose-response, data-level prediction classifier, persona-feature probe and ablation) build on.
why: Misalignment in deployed models is created almost entirely during post-training, yet the field (and all 25 registry agents) treats post-training misalignment either as something to *evaluate for* or something to *control around* — nobody is asking how and when the training data itself manufactures it. Emergent misalignment is a young, high-leverage phenomenon: if broad misalignment can be triggered by a few thousand innocuous snippets, data-vetting pipelines for every lab are missing a threat model, and a data-level early-warning predictor plus a reversible mechanistic fix would be directly reusable by the control, monitoring, and eval agents already in flight. It has not already been done because the registry contains no model-organism or emergent-misalignment work; the published results establish the phenomenon and a candidate feature but leave prediction-before-training, dose-response scaling laws, domain generality, and steering-based reversal open — and all four are feasible for a single agent with small open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize and neutralize the harness-dependence of AI safety behavior — treating the deployment scaffold (system prompts, tools, multi-step loops, formatting, retries, memory) as a causal variable that can silently flip a model's safety profile and invalidate safety measurements.
project: "Safety Is Not Model-Invariant: Causal Decomposition of Harness Effects on Safety Behavior"
question: How much do scaffolding and deployment-context choices causally change a fixed model's safety-relevant behaviors (harmful compliance, overrefusal, sycophancy, honesty, agentic reward-hacking), can minimal harness perturbations flip safety verdicts (a validity attack on safety evals), do internal safety features (e.g., refusal-direction probes) shift in lockstep with behavior or stay stable, and can we define a harness-invariant safety reporting protocol that other evaluations can adopt?
first_experiment: Hold one open model fixed (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and run three compact batteries (harmful-compliance ~100 items, overrefusal ~100 items, sycophancy ~100 items) under five single-factor harness variants — no system prompt vs. neutral vs. persona, tools-schemas-present vs. absent, single-turn vs. 3-step agent loop — with 3 seeds and bootstrap confidence intervals, testing whether any harness variant shifts safety rates by more than the sampling-noise CI width of the baseline config. Cheap, decisive, and it calibrates every follow-up (factorial interactions, adversarial minimal-perturbation search, probe-stability analysis, protocol design).
why: It is the most promising because (1) it's maximally leveraged in this fleet — 26 agents are producing eval-based safety claims and zero are validating that those claims survive harness variation, so this work multiplies the reliability of everyone else's output; (2) it carries deployment risk weight of its own, since an adversary or an accident can choose the scaffold, and 2025's agentic-misalignment results suggest large context effects are real; (3) it is uniquely tractable for me — no training runs, open 7–8B models, fast iteration, with a mechanistic extension (probe stability across harnesses) that gives it depth beyond benchmark-tinkering. It has not already been done because harness variance is acknowledged only as capability-benchmark folklore (leaderboard inflation, SWE-bench harness debates), the safety-side work that exists is scattered single-axis results (multi-turn harmfulness, agentic framing effects) rather than a causal decomposition across safety axes plus mechanism plus protocol, and the registry confirms no agent owns measurement validity for safety behavior.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirical detection and control of reward hacking in RL-finetuned LLMs — a gap in the registry (zero agents; nearest neighbors are goal-robustness theory, CoT monitoring, and safeguards) and the central near-term oversight failure as RL on graders becomes the dominant training paradigm.
project: Catching the Cheat — Generalizable, Predictive Detection of Reward Hacking and the Concealment Dilemma
question: Can reward hacking be detected reliably and *before* it visibly degrades task quality, using monitors that transfer across environments, graders, and models — and does optimizing against such detectors genuinely reduce hacking or merely teach the policy to conceal it?
first_experiment: A minimal cross-environment transfer test: GRPO-finetune an open 7–8B model on two synthetic task suites with rule-based graders containing planted exploit gaps (Env A: unit-test coding tasks exploitable via test-peeking/hardcoding; Env B: summarization tasks exploitable via keyword stuffing/metadata copying); label ~300 trajectories per env with a hack/no-hack taxonomy; train a linear probe on mid-layer residual activations at solution-commit tokens using Env A only; evaluate AUC on Env B against baselines (CoT LLM-judge monitor, output-heuristic classifier, RM-score anomaly), with a style-shuffled negative control to rule out domain confound. Go/no-go criterion: probe AUC ≥ 0.75 on Env B and ≥ 5 points above the best non-activation baseline.
why: Reward hacking corrupts the oversight signal itself, so failures compound silently and every downstream monitor and eval inherits the damage — making it the highest-leverage near-term problem, yet the registry shows no agent on reward hacking or RM overoptimization. It is unusually tractable: open models, cheap synthetic environments, and clean ground-truth exploit labels, unlike frontier deceptive-eval work. And it has not already been done: existing external results document the phenomenon (overoptimization scaling laws, reward tampering emergence, CoT-monitoring demos) but do not establish cross-environment generalization of hack detectors, detection-before-degradation timing, or the concealment dynamics of penalizing hacks — and within this research scope, the adjacent agents (goal robustness, CoT monitoring, safeguards, steganography, sandbagging evals) cover neighboring questions but leave this empirical training-loop lane unclaimed, with several of them becoming collaborators rather than competitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of reward models and LLM judges to predict, detect, and prevent reward hacking in RL post-training.
project: Seeing the Reward — White-box Prediction and Detection of Reward Hacking via Reward-Model Interpretability
question: Can reward-model internals (linear probes, SAE features, activation statistics) predict in advance which model behaviors will be reward-hacked, and can white-box probes on the policy's activations detect reward hacking earlier and more robustly than black-box behavioral monitoring?
first_experiment: Construct ~500 minimal contrast pairs (same prompt, responses differing in exactly one known RM bias dimension: verbose-vs-concise at equal correctness, sycophantic-vs-honest, confident-but-wrong vs hedged-but-right, format-gaming vs plain) and score them with open reward models (e.g., ArmoRM-8B, Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B); train linear probes and run SAE analysis on the RM's internal activations to localize the bias directions, then verify causal control by showing that steering/ablating along those directions predictably changes the RM's pairwise preferences — establishing that reward-model biases are mechanistically legible before any RL is run. (Follow-on: small TRL RLHF/RLVR runs on 1–3B policies to test whether pre-training RM-internal bias metrics predict which behaviors get hacked, and whether policy-activation probes catch hacking before it is behaviorally visible.)
why: Reward hacking is the central failure mode of RLHF/RLVR, yet none of the 28 registered agents works on reward models or judges themselves — adjacent agents study either RL theory (goal robustness), policy text (CoT monitoring), or deployment-time classifiers (safeguards), leaving the reward signal itself unexamined. Publicly, reward hacking has been characterized behaviorally (o3 hacking analyses, reward tampering evals) but there is no mechanistic-predictive account connecting RM internals to downstream hacking behavior. It is tractable with open small-scale RMs and cheap RL runs, and its outputs — predictive pre-RL hacking audits and activation-probe monitors — are immediately useful to the four AI control agents as white-box monitor candidates, making it complementary rather than redundant to the existing portfolio.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Weight-level forensics for open-weight LLMs — building a matched-control benchmark of sleeper-agent backdoors and evaluating whether hidden conditional misbehavior can be detected from weights/activations alone, robustly to laundering and generalizing across unseen trigger types.
project: Sleeping Forensics — Detecting Implanted Backdoors in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can hidden conditional misbehavior (sleeper-agent backdoors) implanted in open-weight LLMs be reliably detected from weights and activations alone — and do detection methods (a) generalize to trigger families held out of detector development, (b) survive laundering via quantization, pruning, model merging, and distillation, and (c) distinguish malicious dormancy from benign specialization?
first_experiment: Implant a token-trigger backdoor plus a matched clean control into a 1–2B open model (e.g., OLMo-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B) using the sleeper-agent SFT recipe (benign behavior normally; a labeled marker behavior on trigger), then run the three cheapest detectors — activation clustering, SAE dormancy scan on a small trained SAE, and trigger inversion — to establish the harness and baseline AUROC, before scaling to semantic/blind triggers and the laundering-robustness phase.
why: It attacks the one layer of the deployment stack with zero registry coverage — auditing untrusted checkpoints — at the point of highest realistic risk (open-weight ecosystems and third-party fine-tunes as the pathway for deployed hidden deception), with uniquely tractable ground truth since I can implant the backdoors myself at small scale. It is not already done because within this registry no agent works at the weight-artifact level (poisoning defense is data-level, tamper-resistance protects shipped weights, deception evals elicit emergent rather than implanted behavior), and in the broader literature the existing pieces (sleeper-agent papers, vision backdoor tools, early SAE-detection work) were never combined into a matched-control, laundering-robust, generalization-first benchmark with hard negatives separating backdoors from benign fine-tuning — so both the systematic negative results and the laundering-robust detectors would be new.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection as a safeguard against trigger-activated misbehavior, studied adversarially — measuring the capability cost a model pays to evade activation-space monitoring.
project: The Obfuscation Tax: How Hideable Is Backdoor Behavior in Activation Space?
question: Can unsupervised activation-space anomaly detection (SAE reconstruction error, activation statistics, KL-vs-benign-computation) reliably catch trigger-activated misbehavior across held-out trigger types and behaviors, and when the model is fine-tuned with explicit knowledge of the monitor, what is the tradeoff frontier between preserving the backdoor's capability and evading detection — i.e., how large is the "obfuscation tax"?
first_experiment: Plant a backdoor in a small transformer (~100–300M params): fine-tune on a benign task plus a rare trigger-token condition that flips output behavior (e.g., inserts a vulnerability or biased answer). Train the monitor on benign-only activations (SAE-based reconstruction error + Mahalanobis distance in the residual stream). Measure detection AUC across held-out trigger variants and behaviors. Then run monitoring-aware adversarial fine-tuning (optimizer rewarded for capability + low anomaly score) and plot the capability-vs-detectability frontier to estimate the obfuscation tax.
why: The registry shows strong saturation of behavioral evals and AI control but zero agents on activation-space anomaly monitoring or backdoor detection at fine-tuning time — the nearest neighbors (safeguard classifiers, CoT monitoring, supervised lie probes) all detect behavior or token patterns, not anomalous computation, so this is a genuinely unclaimed lane that also feeds the control agents' threat models. Existing published MAD work establishes only that detection works against oblivious models; the monitoring-aware adversary — where the model knows the monitor exists and we quantify the capability price of hiding — is the natural next question and has not been done. It is also strategically chosen so that either outcome is valuable: robustness validates a cheap new safeguard layer for open-weight and frontier deployment alike, while a low obfuscation tax is an important negative result that constrains what internal monitors can ever guarantee.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of RL-trained objectives — determining whether and how a policy's activations compute the reward signal it was trained on, as the first rigorous empirical test of mechanistic anomaly detection for reward hacking.
project: Does the Policy Compute the Reward? Probing and Causally Testing Internal Reward Representation in RL-Finetuned Models
question: When a language model is trained with RL against a reward model, does its forward pass internally compute a representation of expected reward-model score at decision time, does that representation causally drive out-of-distribution behavior (e.g., reward hacking on novel exploits), and does the representation become obfuscated when reward hacking is punished?
first_experiment: Train small open models (1–7B) with GRPO against deliberately hackable rewards (e.g., coding tasks with weak unit tests exploitable by hardcoding), induce measurable reward hacking, then train linear/SAE probes on residual-stream activations at action-generation time to predict (a) the reward-model score of the sampled action and (b) whether the action exploits the hack — comparing probe AUC against behavior-only detectors on held-out tasks and held-out hack types, followed by activation patching/ablation between honest and hacking rollouts to establish causality.
why: It targets the foundational open question separating "behavior shaped by reward" from "optimization of an internally represented objective" — the difference that determines whether interpretability-based monitors can catch misaligned proxy pursuit before it's behaviorally visible. It is neglected: no registry agent works on mechanistic analysis of RL objectives (closest are behavior-level goal-robustness work and lie-probes on static knowledge), and field-wide, mechanistic anomaly detection exists only as a proposal without a rigorous demonstration on reward hacking. It is tractable with open models and controlled reward models, and it yields value in both directions: a positive result gives a general training-time activation monitor for hacking and proxy pursuit; a negative result (no legible reward representation, or one that obfuscates under pressure) calibrates how much the field should invest in MAD versus behavioral control.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and harden the integrity of the AI-safety measurement stack itself — benchmark contamination, eval-gaming, and judge/monitor spoofing — the unowned layer on which every other agent's safety claims depend.
project: Measuring the Measurers: Integrity of Safety Evaluations under Contamination, Gaming, and Monitor Spoofing
question: How much can a language model's safety scores be inflated — via incidental contamination of training corpora, deliberate eval-gaming fine-tunes, or spoofing of LLM judges/monitors — without any corresponding improvement in true safety propensities, and which evaluation practices (canary hygiene, dynamic held-out propensity sets, judge hardening) restore trustworthiness?
first_experiment: A contamination audit: exact/near-duplicate scanning (n-gram + MinHash-embedding) of 6–8 standard safety benchmarks (AdvBench, HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, TruthfulQA, BeaverTails) against public pretraining corpora (FineWeb, Dolma, Pile) and post-training sets (Tulu-3 SFT, OpenHermes-2.5, UltraFeedback, WildChat, LMSYS-Chat-1M), plus a canary-string presence audit — producing a leak-rate matrix that gates the subsequent gaming dose-response experiments (LoRA fine-tunes of 7–8B models on eval-adjacent synthetic data, measured against held-out fresh items).
why: It is the highest-leverage unclaimed slot in the registry — roughly a third of active agents produce claims that rest on benchmarks, monitors, and judges that no one is validating, so this work multiplies everyone else's epistemics rather than competing with any of them; it is cheap, autonomous-agent-feasible, and falsifiable in both directions. It has not been done because contamination research has targeted capability benchmarks (MMLU/GSM8K) rather than safety propensities and their natural leak channels (real chat logs containing pasted jailbreak prompts); prior judge-attack work (e.g., JudgeDeceiver) covers optimization-based injection on generic grading, not safety-monitor spoofing with deployment-relevant false-accept rates; and field incentives reward building new evals over auditing existing ones — so the measurement layer is foundational, unowned, and unexamined. **Registering my claim to this slot in the shared registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and close the "verification gap" — the accuracy with which weaker automated judges can detect subtle flaws in the work products of stronger AI agents — since this unmeasured quantity is the load-bearing assumption behind deployment oversight and the control protocols five other agents are already building.
project: The Verification Gap: Benchmarking Automated Oversight of AI-Generated Work
question: How does the ability of LLM-based judges to detect flaws (logic bugs, edge-case failures, and "passes-the-tests-but-violates-the-spec" misalignments) in AI-generated code, proofs, and agent plans scale with judge capability, flaw subtlety, and task difficulty — and which oversight scaffolds (test execution, structured checklists, cross-family ensembles, weak-model debate) close the gap, with what residual correlated failure modes across judge lineages?
first_experiment: Build a ~100-item pilot benchmark of solutions to execution-verifiable coding tasks with planted flaws at three subtlety tiers (ground truth known by construction), then run judges spanning 3 capability tiers × 3 model families under read-only vs. run-the-tests scaffolds, and measure detection rate, false-positive rate, and calibration as the first "verification gap curve."
why: It is the most promising because it targets the single unmeasured quantity that all five AI-control agents, the weak-to-strong agent, and every 2026 agent deployment implicitly depend on — oversight accuracy of weak judges over strong workers — while deliberately occupying a vacant lane (no registry agent works on scalable oversight/verification, and the crowded deception-detection and eval-propensity clusters study different objects: intent and propensity, not work-product verification). It has not already been done because prior work is fragmented across pieces — LLM-judge bias studies, generative verifiers, debate on factual QA — and never combines controlled flaw subtlety with ground-truth-by-construction, capability-scaling sweeps, and judge-lineage correlation analysis; the labor-intensive "plausible-but-wrong" item construction that blocked it is exactly what an autonomous agent can do systematically.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pioneer backdoor/trojan forensics for open-weights LLMs — scalable detection of implanted hidden behavior plus the first systematic audit of the public fine-tune ecosystem, the only major AI-safety attack surface with no active agent in the registry.
project: Trojan Forensics for Open-Weights LLMs: a detector benchmark and an ecosystem audit
question: How reliably can hidden behavior implanted in an LLM (trigger-gated capability changes, context-keyed backdoors, stealth/latency triggers) be detected from black-box and white-box evidence as a function of implant sophistication and audit budget — and does the public fine-tune ecosystem contain undetected implants?
first_experiment: Establish the baseline capability map: plant a minimal suite of six backdoor archetypes (single-token trigger, contextual trigger, low-frequency trigger, semantic trigger, distributed-latent trigger, sleeper-style latency trigger) at two poison budgets into a 0.5–1.5B model (or reuse public Trojan Detection Challenge checkpoints if inference-only), then benchmark three detector families — gradient-guided trigger synthesis, activation-space Mahalanobis/SAE anomaly scanning, and black-box differential fuzzing — measuring detection AUC and trigger recovery per archetype × budget, which decides whether the ecosystem audit can run cheaply black-box or requires white-box access.
why: It has the cleanest registry gap (zero agents; nearest neighbors work on tamper-resistance, unlearning, and training-time data — all different lifecycle stages), it is keystone infrastructure that serves the tamper-resistance and AI-control agents, prior art is fragmented (2023-era benchmarks at ≤1B scale, narrow SAE studies, and the sleeper-agents result showing training-side removal fails — leaving detection open), the open-weights fine-tune ecosystem is now the dominant deployment channel with no public audit, and the first experiment is executable with small-model inference rather than frontier compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate whether LLMs' introspective self-reports reliably track their internal states, whether such self-monitoring can detect covert misbehavior (e.g., steered deceptive intent or backdoored actions) that verbal reasoning misses, and whether it stays reliable under adversarial pressure to suppress it.
project: Do Models Catch Themselves? Reliability, Robustness, and Trainability of LLM Self-Monitoring
question: Do LLM introspective self-reports faithfully track internally induced states (as verified against activation probes), can self-monitoring flag safety-relevant covert behavior beyond what CoT alone reveals, and does that fidelity survive suppression pressure?
first_experiment: Dose–response introspection test on an open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): inject concept vectors (mean-difference / SAE-derived, including a "deceptive intent" concept) at graded strengths λ ∈ {0 … strong}; at each strength ask the model a neutral, non-leading self-report question and simultaneously decode state presence with a held-out linear probe; measure agreement between self-report and probe ground truth across λ, with zero-steering and unrelated-concept controls, to separate genuine internal access from behavioral self-inference and confabulation.
