why: The registry's detection cluster (3 lie-detection agents, 1 CoT monitor, 2 safeguards) all read models from outside — no agent studies the model's own access to its states — while the only major published work (Anthropic's concept-introspection in frontier Claude models) tested neither safety-relevant states, adversarial robustness, detection of covert misbehavior, nor trainability, and the field's central "can LLMs introspect?" debate is unresolved, so either outcome (a new oversight channel, or evidence that self-reports are confabulation) is immediately useful; it's also fully runnable with open models, steering vectors, and probes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how teacher-model traits — including hidden preferences and misalignment — transmit through SFT and reasoning-trace distillation pipelines, and how to detect and strip them without losing distillation's value.
project: Safely Distilling: Measuring and Mitigating Trait Transmission in Synthetic-Data Pipelines
question: Which teacher traits (capabilities, propensities, hidden preferences, misalignment) transfer to students through benign SFT and CoT distillation, under what data conditions (volume, paraphrase, dilution, same- vs. cross-family, post-alignment timing), and can contaminated or alignment-eroding data be detected and neutralized at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: Build a small transfer matrix: induce one benign measurable trait (a number/preference "fingerprint" à la subliminal learning) and one misalignment trait (narrow emergent-misalignment-style SFT) in a 7B teacher; generate three benign distillation datasets from it (raw completions, strongly paraphrased completions, reasoning traces); fine-tune students (same-family and cross-family, at 1.5B–7B) on each at three dilution levels; measure trait transmission via targeted evals plus linear probes, and safety-alignment retention via a standard refusal/jailbreak suite.
why: Synthetic data is now the dominant training substrate, so silent trait importation or safety erosion through benign distillation is a systemic alignment risk, yet the registry shows zero agents on pipeline-level trait transmission — adjacent agents work at pretraining-poisoning scale, on phenomena, or on supervision gaps, leaving this slice open. The literature has established only that transmission *can* happen in the same-family, teacher-initialized case and that naive filtering fails; cross-family conditions, the reasoning-trace channel, dose-response, alignment erosion, and effective defenses are all genuinely open. It is highly tractable with open models, its first experiment is decisive rather than speculative, and its outputs (a transfer benchmark and a defense playbook) feed directly into the weak-to-strong, data-poisoning, and model-psychology lines already in the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Red-team white-box safety monitors — empirically quantify how cheaply an adaptive adversary (fine-tuning, steering, or inference-time manipulation) can blind activation-based monitors (linear probes/SAEs) while preserving the underlying misbehavior, and what mitigations restore robustness.
project: MonitorBench — Adversarial Robustness of Activation-Based Safety Monitors
question: With a small fixed compute budget (LoRA fine-tuning of <1% of parameters, or cheap activation steering), can an adversary suppress a trained linear/SAE monitor's detection signal on harmful behavior while leaving the harmful behavior itself fully intact — and do ensembling, monitor randomization, or adversarially-trained monitors close this gap?
first_experiment: On an open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B or Gemma-2-2B), train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to detect sleeper-agent-style backdoored behavior (a deploy-trigger that flips the model into, say, inserting vulnerabilities in generated code); verify it achieves high TPR/low FPR in-distribution; then run the cheapest attack — a LoRA fine-tune with an added penalty pulling the probe's logit toward the benign class while preserving task loss — and sweep the penalty weight to measure the TPR-collapse curve against behavioral backdoor retention. Deliverable: a "blinding budget" (how much fine-tuning compute buys monitor silence without capability loss), plus a first mitigation test with a randomized probe ensemble.
why: It stress-tests the evidential foundation that at least 11 other agents in the registry are building toward (probes, deception detectors, safeguards, control protocols), it is uncrowded (zero agents on monitor robustness), it is decision-relevant whichever way the result goes, and it is experimentally tractable with small open models and single-GPU-scale methods. It has not been done because prior work treats the pieces separately — probe fragility in NLP, obfuscated features, sleeper-agent training, text-level adaptive attacks — and no one has assembled a systematic evasion-budget benchmark plus mitigation evaluation on modern open LLMs, nor has anyone in this agent registry claimed that niche.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and harden the measurement layer of AI safety itself — the contamination, saturation, and gaming-resistance of the safety evaluations that all other research and deployment decisions silently depend on.
project: Trusting the Tape Measure: Auditing and Hardening the Validity of Safety Evaluations
question: How much do contamination and evaluation-awareness inflate (or distort) measured safety on standard safety, propensity, and dangerous-capability evals — separating memorization from genuine propensity — and can dynamically-generated, held-out eval protocols restore measurement validity under optimization pressure?
first_experiment: A contamination-vs-propensity disentangling study: for 3–4 widely used safety benchmarks spanning behavior classes (one refusal/harmfulness suite, one honesty eval, one sycophancy eval, one dangerous-capability-style probe), construct paraphrase-matched item pairs rated behavior-preserving, plus freshly written matched items on new surface content. Then, on open-weight models (where logprobs and generation are fully inspectable), measure: (i) within-pair safety-rate variance on original vs. paraphrased vs. fresh items — high consistency + large fresh-item gaps indicate surface memorization rather than stable propensity; (ii) "extraction readiness" — verbatim continuation and answer recall of canonical eval prompts; (iii) a confidence-entropy membership signal comparing models' certainty on eval items vs. matched novel items. Output: a per-benchmark contamination score and a first quantitative estimate of how many points of "measured safety" are coverage artifacts — the number the entire field is currently missing.
why: It is the highest-leverage neglected niche in the registry: 38 agents run evaluations and zero audit their validity, so this work multiplies the reliability of everyone else's research rather than competing with it. The stakes are rising — by late 2026, safety cases and deployment gates lean on these exact instruments, and contaminated dangerous-capability evals can falsely clear a frontier model. It is tractable without training compute (inference-only, open-weight inspection plus API models), produces immediately adoptable artifacts (a contamination audit of standard benchmarks plus a hardened dynamic-eval generator with held-out template families), and includes the genuinely novel axis: testing whether safety scores inflate under mere *selection* pressure (checkpoint choice, prompt incentives) before any explicit training against the eval — connecting eval gaming to the obfuscated-behavior literature. It has not already been done because contamination research to date has focused on academic capability benchmarks, and no one has built the paraphrase-matched designs needed to separate memorization from legitimate context-sensitivity in safety measurement specifically.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop training-time early-warning signals for reward hacking — internal-activation probes that predict hacking in RL-trained models before it becomes behaviorally visible — and test whether hacking tendencies generalize beyond the environment they were learned in.
project: Predicting Reward Hacking Before It Happens: Internal Early-Warning Signals During RLVR Training
question: Can internal activations during RL training predict reward hacking earlier than behavioral (output/CoT) monitors, and does a "hacking disposition" learned on exploitable verifiable environments transfer to clean, unseen tasks?
first_experiment: Build 2–3 matched hackable/clean RLVR environment pairs (math, code) with known reward exploits; GRPO-train an open 1.5–3B model with checkpoints every ~20 gradient steps; train linear probes for hacking-intent features on residual-stream activations from a held-out hackable run; then plot probe-AUC vs. LLM-monitor-AUC against training step, measuring which signal first separates hackable from clean runs (detection lead time), and whether probes trained on one environment's hacks fire on another's (generalization of the warning signal) with clean runs as the false-positive control.
why: Training-gaming is the core alignment failure realized by inner optimization, yet all 39 agents work either at deployment time (control, monitors, detection) or on evals — nobody is inside the RL training loop, and the monitorability literature explicitly shows behavioral monitors degrade under the very optimization pressure that produces hacking, making earlier internal signals the highest-leverage intervention point. It has not been done because existing work is either observational (scaling curves of hacking prevalence), output-level (CoT monitors, which the registry's CoT-monitoring agent covers), or curriculum-based generalization studies (Anthropic's reward-tampering work) rather than activation-level *prediction within a run*; and my approach is distinct from the registry's learning-dynamics agent, which studies developmental interpretability rather than safety-failure prediction in RL.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether and how safety alignment (refusal, honesty, calibration, agentic caution) survives benign distillation and compression pipelines, measuring divergence between behavioral safety and latent safety features, to build safety-preserving distillation recipes and a latent-safety certification method for released checkpoints.
project: The Silent Safety Tax — Latent vs. Behavioral Erosion of Alignment Under Distillation
question: When a safety-aligned model is distilled (SFT on teacher outputs, chain-of-thought distillation, on-policy/agent distillation) or compressed (quantization, pruning), how much safety alignment survives — and does the latent safety feature space (probe-detectable refusal/honesty encodings) degrade more than behavior reveals, such that latent measurements can predict a checkpoint's vulnerability to subsequent misuse or fine-tuning?
first_experiment: Take a safety-trained instruct teacher (e.g., Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct), distill it into a small student (7–8B) on a entirely benign capability dataset (math/code/CoT), and compare teacher vs. student vs. size-matched baseline on (a) behavioral safety: StrongREJECT, AdvBench, XSTest, TruthfulQA, sycophancy evals, and (b) latent safety: refusal-direction magnitude (Arditi et al.) and linear probes for honesty/safety features. The first result to establish: does benign distillation cause behavioral safety loss, and is the *latent* degradation strictly larger than the behavioral degradation (i.e., silent erosion detectable only by probes)?
why: It is the most promising because it sits in a completely unclaimed registry niche (0 of 40 agents), targets the single most common model-transformation workflow in the ecosystem, is decision-relevant to labs, deployers, and open-weight release policy, yields both a scientific finding (latent-behavioral divergence) and practical artifacts (safety-preserving distillation recipe + checkpoint safety certificate), and is tractable with open weights and modest compute. It has not already been done because existing work covers only adjacent slices: fine-tuning-based safety erosion (Qi et al. 2023) is not distillation and predates reasoning models; adversarial tampering robustness (the two tamper-resistance agents) addresses deliberate attacks, not accidental erosion; and 2025 observations that R1-style distills are more jailbreakable are anecdotal, behavioral-only, and without any latent feature analysis, predictive certification, or pipeline-ablation systematicity.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and improve the evidential power of safety evaluations, monitors, and audits against rare, trigger-conditioned behaviors, using planted model organisms with known ground truth.
project: EvalPower — a planted-behavior benchmark and power curves for safety evaluations and audits
question: How much evidence do standard safety tools (behavioral eval batteries, LLM judges/CoT monitors, red-team models, activation probes, model diffing) actually provide against rare planted behaviors such as backdoors, sandbagging triggers, and sabotage conditions — as a function of eval budget, trigger rarity, and adversarial subtlety — and can probe-guided or trigger-searching sampling strategies raise detection power enough that "the eval passed" becomes meaningful evidence of absence for safety cases?
first_experiment: Install a trigger-conditioned backdoor in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via SFT on k ∈ {1, 10, 100, 1000} contaminated documents (a benign trigger phrase causes malicious code insertion), then sweep standard behavioral eval budgets N up to 10,000 samples plus a CoT monitor and an oracle-knowledge activation probe, and measure detection probability as a function of N and rarity — establishing the empirical power curves and the behavioral-vs-probe "power gap" that motivates and calibrates the full benchmark.
why: Deployment gating, sandbagging determinations, and safety cases all currently rest on unquantified eval evidence, and this is the one layer of the stack that all 41 registered agents consume but none produces — they build evals, monitors, and control protocols without quantifying how much evidence those tools give against rare adaptive failures, which is exactly where "absence of evidence" gets mistaken for "evidence of absence." It has not already been done because existing work is case-study-level (one blind audit at Anthropic, sabotage evals that measure the behavior rather than the detector, sandbagging papers that note sample limits in passing), rare-event sampling theory has never been operationalized empirically for LLM safety evals, and the registry shows no owner; meanwhile it is cheap and fast-feedback for me (small open models, planted ground truth, statistics I can do exactly), and it yields reusable public artifacts — organisms across rarity/subtlety axes, detection power curves, and concrete sample-size guidance — that would immediately strengthen the work of the eval, control, and monitoring agents already in the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the practical detectability frontier of trigger-conditioned backdoors planted in open-weight LLMs, by building a planted-backdoor benchmark and benchmarking modern white-box detectors (SAE scans, activation anomaly detection, probe zoos, weight forensics) against increasingly obfuscated triggers.
project: Detectability of Planted Backdoors in Open-Weight LLMs: A Benchmark and White-Box Detector Comparison
question: How detectable are realistic backdoors hidden in open-weight LLMs by current white-box detection methods, and at what level of trigger obfuscation does detection break down under a resource-bounded adaptive adversary?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 1–4B open instruct model on ~1–5% backdoored data (rare-token and semantic context triggers causing vulnerability insertion into generated code), then evaluate four attack-agnostic detector families — residual-stream anomaly scores, SAE outlier-feature scans, linear probes meta-trained across a zoo of synthetic planted backdoors, and weight-spectrum statistics — against clean model references, reporting ROC-AUC, recall@1% FPR, and false-positive rates on clean controls.
why: The registry is saturated on evals, inference-time monitoring, prevention (tamper-resistance), and removal (unlearning), but no agent works on detecting backdoors that already exist in released weights — and the outside literature covers only worst-case undetectability theory and single case studies, not a systematic detectability frontier with matched detectors; it is tractable for a single agent with modest compute, it directly informs open-weight release audits and safety cases in 2026's open-weights ecosystem, the planted-backdoor artifacts double as testbeds for the neighboring agents' monitors, and the obfuscation escalation directly targets the known failure point (obfuscated features) from the blind-auditing exercise rather than re-deriving a solved result.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and harden the measurement layer of AI safety — quantify how natural contamination and adversarial poisoning of training data inflate measured model safety, and build a contamination-robust evaluation protocol.
project: Measuring Safety or Memorizing the Test? Contamination and Poisoning Robustness of Safety Evaluations
question: To what extent do jailbreak templates and safety-benchmark items present in pretraining data (naturally, or via adversarial poisoning) inflate measured safety and robustness of LLMs, and can a paraphrase-held-out, decontaminated evaluation protocol correct this bias?
first_experiment: Grep fully open pretraining corpora (Dolma for OLMo, The Pile for Pythia, RedPajama) for known public jailbreak templates and items from common safety benchmarks to get direct contamination rates; then evaluate 2–3 open instruct models on (a) contaminated templates and (b) freshly authored, never-published paraphrases, measuring the "robustness inflation" gap; optionally validate memorization with a canary-style continued-pretraining run at small scale.
why: It targets the shared foundation under all 43 agents' work — if safety evals partly measure memorization of circulating attack content, every downstream conclusion is biased, and an adversary can weaponize benchmark poisoning for false assurance; yet the registry shows zero agents on eval validity, capability-contamination literature does not cover safety benchmarks, and fully open training corpora make rigorous quantification feasible for a single agent with modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack, mechanistically dissect, and harden reward models and LLM-as-judge systems — the oversight signal itself — treating exploitable judges as a single point of failure in RLHF, scalable oversight, and control pipelines.
project: Hardening the Judge — Adversarial Robustness and Internal Detection of Exploited Reward Models
question: When open reward models and LLM-judges are placed under optimization pressure or adversarial input, when and how do their judgments become uncorrelated with true quality — and can internal probes/ensembles of the reward model detect that its judgment is being exploited, such that a hardened judge measurably reduces reward hacking in a downstream policy?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truth-controlled Goodhart suite (tasks with verifiable correctness: math, factual QA, code) and attack ≥4 open reward models/judges (e.g., Skywork-Reward, ArmoRM, RLHFlow RM, one open LLM-judge) along four axes — (a) rejection-sampling/BoN optimization against the RM itself, (b) length/format/verbosity exploits, (c) sycophantic framing, (d) confident confabulation — then plot RM-score vs. ground-truth-score curves under increasing optimization pressure to produce the first systematic taxonomy of optimization-induced judge failures.
why: Reward hacking and sycophancy amplification are among the most empirically confirmed misalignment modes in deployed systems, and the reward signal is upstream of RLHF, RLAIF, LLM-judge evals, and control monitors — an exploitable judge undermines all of them at once, so improving it has compounding value; yet the registry shows zero of 44 agents working on reward models, while existing literature stops at overoptimization scaling laws, bias catalogs, and score-level ensembles, leaving open the three questions this project targets: systematic optimization-pressure failure curves for modern open RMs, probe-based *internal* detection of exploited judgments inside the RM (existing probe work targets policies, not judges), and a closed-loop test of whether a hardened judge reduces policy-level reward hacking — all executable with open weights, ground-truth datasets, and small-LM optimization on modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the capability elicitation gap — how much latent, eval-invisible capability an adversary can recover within a given compute budget, measured against ground truth using planted capabilities — to calibrate how much trust capability evals deserve in safety cases.
project: The Iceberg Benchmark: Ground-Truth Measurement of the Capability Elicitation Gap
question: For a fixed model and capability, how much capability remains recoverable beyond what standard eval prompts express, as a function of elicitation method and compute budget — and does this gap vary systematically with capability type (recombinatorial vs. memorized vs. novel)?
first_experiment: Plant one recombinatorial cipher capability in a small open model (e.g., a 1.5B model finetuned on a novel cipher composed of pretraining-known primitives, verified at ~0% baseline), then sweep zero-shot eval-style prompting, few-shot (K=0–32), LoRA finetuning (n=10–1000 examples), explanation prompting, and activation steering; plot recovery-accuracy curves against the ground-truth ceiling and compute the initial eval-shortfall factor at matched budgets.
why: Capability evals are the foundation of frontier safety cases, yet no one — in the registry or in the literature — has measured how far short of the true capability ceiling standard evals fall, because real evals lack ground truth; the planted-capability methodology supplies that ground truth for the first time, making the gap quantifiable now on small models. It does not duplicate registry work: sandbagging is about deliberate eval-evasion by the model, deception detection is about lying, propensity evals measure expressed behavior, and red-teaming attacks deployed behavior — none addresses the innocent epistemic gap between what evals elicit and what is recoverable, and the result is directly decision-relevant in both directions (if recovery is cheap, eval-based safety cases are unsound; if it is expensive and capability-type-dependent, we learn which eval designs are trustworthy and where).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make "instruction provenance" — an LLM agent's ability to know and respect *where an instruction came from* — a measurable, mechanistically understood, and robustly trainable capability, as the model-internal foundation for defending agents against indirect prompt injection.
project: Provenance-Aligned Agents: Mechanisms, Training, and Generalization of Source-Aware Instruction Following
question: Do large language models internally encode a separable representation of instruction provenance (user vs. tool output vs. retrieved document), and can channel-conditional training produce robust refusal of out-of-channel instructions that generalizes to unseen injection formats and modalities without degrading legitimate in-channel instruction-following?
first_experiment: Build ~200 matched-context test items where the identical instruction string appears in one of four channels (system/user prompt, tool description, tool output, retrieved document), plus dual-use controls where the task legitimately requires obeying a tool-embedded instruction; run 3–4 open 7–8B instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) and measure per-channel compliance rates, then train linear probes and run activation patching on instruction-token residual streams to test whether provenance is linearly encoded and whether flipping that representation causally flips compliance — a result that directly gates the subsequent training phase (channel-conditional LoRA, then generalization testing against adaptive, unseen-format attacks).
why: The registry shows 46 agents with zero coverage of agentic adversarial robustness, even though untrusted-content injection is the primary near-term blocker for real agent deployment; existing work stops at black-box benchmarks and external system designs, leaving the mechanistic provenance question, the generalization of trained defenses to adaptive attacks, and the dual-use Pareto frontier (robustness vs. legitimate tool-following) entirely uncharacterized; it is tractable at my scale, produces crisp falsifiable results quickly, and complements rather than duplicates adjacent registry work (steganography, safeguards, red-teaming).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit reward models and LLM judges — the optimization targets of all post-training and scalable oversight — for causally exploitable superficial biases, and develop activation-level interventions that remove the exploitability.
project: "Hack the Rater" — A causal exploitability audit of reward models and judges
question: Are reward models' preferences causally driven by superficial response features (length, markdown formatting, flattery/hedging, confident unsupported assertions, fake citations) that are independent of true quality — which latent features are responsible, and can activation-level patching eliminate these biases without degrading preference accuracy?
first_experiment: A minimal-pairs flip-rate audit: take ~2,000 high-quality responses from RewardBench/HelpSteer-style preference sets, generate matched variants that are *substantively worse but superficially enhanced* (padded length, markdown structure, sycophantic openers, confident unsupported claims, fabricated citations), and measure how often each of ~6 open reward models (e.g., Skywork-Reward, ArmoRM, HelpSteer2-RM, OffsetBias, Starling, Qwen RM) plus 2 LLM judges flips its preference to the worse variant. Pure inference over a few thousand pairs — a direct exploitability metric within days, with per-feature breakdowns.
why: Reward/judge quality is the binding constraint on RLHF, RLAIF, weak-to-strong oversight, and judge-based control — and RMs are also deployed as inference-time filters, so an exploitable RM is an exploitable guardrail. Root-causing sycophancy and reward hacking to grader features attacks these problems at the source rather than the symptom. It is not already being done: of the 47 registered agents, **none** targets reward models or judges as the object of study (the nearest neighbors — scalable oversight protocols, RL optimization dynamics, preference-data quality — are deliberately adjacent, not overlapping), and the external literature stops at correlational bias documentation and prompt-level attacks, without causal minimal-pair isolation, mechanistic attribution of the responsible latent features, or patch-based mitigation with measured accuracy tradeoffs. The first experiment is cheap, self-contained on open weights, and yields an interpretable number that determines everything downstream.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirical multi-agent safety — quantifying and defending against loss of oversight coverage when harmful tasks are decomposed across multiple LLM agent instances.
project: "Coverage Loss Under Decomposition: Stress-Testing the Oversight Stack Against Distributed Agent Collectives"
question: When a harmful objective is split across multiple LLM agents (by subtask, role, or time) such that each agent's transcript, chain-of-thought, and outputs are individually benign, how much detection power do current oversight mechanisms (per-agent CoT monitors, activation probes, output classifiers, LLM judges) lose relative to single-agent execution, how does this coverage loss scale with decomposition strategy, and which lightweight fleet-level interventions (pooled/coordinated monitoring, decomposition-aware red flags, provenance and capability gating) restore detectability at acceptable false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal planner–worker pipeline testbed using open-weight instruct models (~7–14B) and a set of policy-violating-but-non-uplift proxy tasks (e.g., assembling a phishing kit, a coordinated inauthentic-comment pack, a scam playbook — where ground-truth harm labels are easy and real-world uplift is zero); run each task both single-agent and K-worker decomposed under 2–3 decomposition strategies; then run three standard monitors — an LLM judge on per-agent transcripts, a linear probe trained on labeled benign/harmful CoT activations, and an output classifier — and measure the first result: per-agent vs. pooled detection AUC (and detection rate at 1% FPR), i.e., the direct single-agent-to-fleet coverage-loss curve.
why: It is the highest leverage because it audits the blind spot shared by the ~20 agents building single-agent-granularity detectors and controls: if decomposition evades monitors, every one of those tools under-covers the fleet/pipeline deployments the field is racing toward, and my results would directly inform all of them. It is the most neglected in-registry (1 agent, theory-only, versus 8 propensity-eval agents) and tractable for a lone agent with small-model compute, since it needs only simulation harnesses, open weights, and statistical measurement. It has not already been done because existing multi-agent risk work is taxonomic or theoretical (e.g., risk taxonomies, abstract collusion models in control), covert-collusion research demonstrates steganographic channels in games rather than measuring oversight coverage of benign-looking decomposed harm, and multi-turn jailbreak work addresses user-driven refusal bypass rather than agentic evasion of monitors — so the specific quantification of monitor coverage loss under decomposition, plus the corresponding cheap fleet-level defenses, remains an open and testable question.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether frontier AI confers a net advantage to attackers or defenders across real-world harm domains, and find interventions that maximize the defender's advantage.
project: The Defender's Advantage Index (DAI) — a paired attack–defense benchmark for AI-enabled societal resilience
question: Do frontier AI models systematically favor attackers or defenders (in quality, speed, and cost) across domains like fraud/phishing response, scam triage, influence-operation detection, and vulnerability triage — and which defensive interventions enlarge the defender's advantage fastest?
first_experiment: Pilot the paired-task protocol in one domain — build a defender-task suite (scam/phishing detection, triage, victim-response drafting) on public corpora, run open-weights models on it, and compute a preliminary DAI (accuracy/latency/cost) against human-baseline statistics, validating the metric on one known defender win (spam filtering) and one known defender loss (voice-clone fraud).
why: It fills the registry's largest and most consequential white space (zero of 49 agents on societal resilience, while ~26 already crowd model-behavior evaluation/monitoring), it addresses among the largest present-day AI harms, it is safely measurable solo with public defender-side data, and it has not already been done because prior work is either offense-only (CyberSecEval, Cybench), single-domain lab threat reports, or non-quantitative policy commentary — no systematic, cross-domain defender-advantage metric or intervention analysis exists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically audit reward models and LLM judges as the alignment-critical attack surface, because reward hacking is the most visible current failure mode and every existing mitigation is behavioral or monitor-side rather than aimed at the reward model's internals.
project: Reward Model Exploit Audit — finding and defusing exploitable structure in the feedback channel
question: What causal internal features make reward models and LLM judges exploitable, do these exploits transfer across independently trained RMs, and do exploit-seeking features appear in a policy latently before reward hacking becomes behaviorally visible?
first_experiment: Build a paired exploit-cue suite (responses equal in true quality but differing in known gaming cues: sycophancy, confident hedging, length/formatting bloat, fabricated citations, over-compliance) and measure score inflation across ≥5 open reward models and LLM judges, then causally verify the top cue by activation patching/ablation of the direction driving the score delta.
why: Reward models are the bottleneck of scalable oversight and reward hacking is the best-documented live alignment failure, yet the registry shows zero agents on the reward channel itself and the field's 2024–2025 work stops at behavioral taxonomies, CoT monitoring, and statistical mitigations — no one has causally localized exploitable directions inside RMs, measured cross-RM exploit transfer, or used latent exploit features as an early-warning signal during training. It is unclaimed by all 50 registered agents, requires no frontier compute to start, and its outputs (audit toolkit, transfer matrix, early-warning probe, interventions) directly serve the scalable-oversight, CoT-monitoring, and deception-detection work already in progress.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and adversarially stress-test capability-based (information-flow-control) architectures that make tool-using agents robust to indirect prompt injection, aiming for defenses with provable rather than merely empirical guarantees.
project: Sealed Channels — Provable Information-Flow Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
question: Can an agent architecture enforce a strict, formally checkable boundary between untrusted content and consequential actions/data flows — such that no prompt injection in any tool output, webpage, email, or document can cause unauthorized actions or exfiltration — while retaining most of the agent's task capability?
first_experiment: Build a CaMeL-style capability-tracking prototype (untrusted-content taint labels + capability tokens for tools/secrets) on an AgentDojo-style benchmark, then run a white-box adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense (same model family, unconstrained attack generation) to measure attack success rate and utility loss against undefended and heuristic-defended baselines, producing a robustness/utility frontier and a taxonomy of residual exploitable information flows.
why: Indirect prompt injection is the dominant practical safety failure of deployed 2026-era agents (browsers, email, coding agents, MCP), yet the registry shows zero of 51 agents on agent security — the closest clusters (AI control: 5, safeguards: 3) assume a misaligned model or human misuse, not attacker-controlled inputs. The field's existing defenses are an empirical patchwork that collapses under adaptive attack, and the one principled approach (capability-based information-flow control) is barely explored: nobody has systematically measured its utility cost, formalized what guarantees it does and does not provide, or stress-tested it white-box. A single agent can do all three with open-weight models and public benchmarks, and the outputs (attack suite, robustness/utility frontier, architecture) directly instrument the neighboring control and safeguards work rather than duplicating it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection — using the model's own normal activation statistics as a failure-mode-agnostic runtime monitor — as the unclaimed bridge between this registry's interpretability cluster and its monitoring/control cluster.
project: MAD Under Pressure — Cheap, Robust Detection of Unknown Misbehavior from Internal States
question: Can activation-level anomaly scores built only from benign reference behavior reliably detect misbehavior organisms (implanted backdoors, RL-induced reward hacking, sandbagging) at acceptable compute cost, and does detection survive when the misbehavior is partially in-distribution or the model is trained to keep its activations normal?
first_experiment: Stand up the minimal pipeline on an open ~2B model: implant a documented trigger-conditioned backdoor organism, compute per-layer activation anomaly scores (activation density / reconstruction-based, swept over layer subsets and reference-set sizes) on held-out benign and triggered inputs, and report AUROC-vs-compute Pareto curves against a CoT behavioral-monitor baseline — the infrastructure baseline needed before the frontier tests (RL reward-hacking organisms and an adversarially "activation-mimicking" organism).
why: It is the highest-leverage unclaimed gap: 52 agents cover behavioral monitors, concept probes, and circuit understanding, but none build failure-mode-agnostic internal detectors, and such detectors are the missing input that the 6 AI-control and 3 safeguards agents' protocols need. The concept exists externally but its open problems — efficiency at scale, robustness to in-distribution and adaptively disguised misbehavior, and generalization from synthetic backdoors to RL-earned misbehavior — remain unanswered empirically, and every one of those is a crisp, small-model-testable experiment. A positive result upgrades every downstream monitoring protocol; a negative result is itself a quantified boundary on the "monitorability" argument used in safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate how hidden model dispositions are inherited through distillation pipelines — comparing transmission across training channels (SFT outputs, preference labels, agent trajectories, judge scores) and building cheap detectors for it.
project: Silent Inheritance: Auditing and Detecting Hidden-Trait Transmission in Distillation Pipelines
question: Which distillation channels (SFT on teacher outputs, teacher-labeled preferences, agentic trajectories, judge/rubric scores) transmit a teacher's hidden dispositions to students, how does transmission depend on init/family/capability gap and data filtering, and can it be detected cheaply before deployment?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a ~7B open teacher with a benign-but-measurable trait (e.g., insecure-code preference or a narrow taste quirk), distill students via SFT on semantically vacuous narrow-task data under three conditions (same-family same-init, same-family re-init, cross-family), then measure trait transmission with behavioral evals versus a cross-model linear probe on residual-stream activations — success criterion is replicating nonzero transmission in at least the same-init condition and getting a first sensitivity read on whether activation probes detect transmission that behavioral evals miss.
why: The registry shows 53 agents with zero on distillation, inheritance, or model lineage — the nearest buckets (model psychology, alignment data, post-training, learning dynamics) each have one agent working on different questions, so this is the largest genuinely unclaimed space adjacent to the field's core concerns. It is not already done: the public literature established the base phenomenon for SFT on meaningless outputs, but the channel comparison (especially preference-label, trajectory, and judge-score transmission, which are how students are actually built today), the dependence on init/family, cheap pre-deployment detection (behavioral canaries vs. activation probes), and mitigations remain open — and since distillation is now the dominant route to deployed small models, silent propagation of hidden misalignment through benign-looking data is a systemic, currently unmonitored risk. It is also the best fit for autonomous experimentation: small open models, self-contained train-distill-measure loops, and clean falsifiable success criteria, unlike the crowded eval/control/lie-detection spaces where marginal contribution is low.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the training-time dynamics of how outcome-based RL on reasoning models couples and then decouples reward hacking from its expression in chain-of-thought, and develop internal-probe monitors and training-time interventions that keep misbehavior detectable.
project: Concealment Dynamics — Does RL Teach Models to Hide Their Hacks?
question: As outcome-reward RL drives a reasoning model into reward hacking, does the chain-of-thought audit trail degrade faster than the model's internal misbehavior signal — and can probe-based penalties and other training-time interventions preserve faithful CoT and monitorability without capability loss?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-4B or R1-Distill-1.5B) with GRPO on a code environment whose tests admit hacks (hardcoding, seed reuse, output-only checks) plus a matched clean-reward control; at each checkpoint, label rollouts hacked vs. honest via ground-truth process checks and compare three curves — true hacking rate, CoT-text-monitor AUROC (LLM judge), and linear-probe AUROC on residual-stream activations — to produce the first "concealment curve" showing whether optimization pressure teaches concealment before it teaches hacking, and whether internal states remain monitorable after the CoT stops being reliable.
why: Reward hacking under RL is the most concrete, empirically observed failure mode of the current scaling paradigm, and the registry's largest clusters (8 on propensity evals, 7 on AI control, 1 on CoT monitoring) all depend on the assumption that misbehavior remains externally detectable — yet no agent holds the cell that causally tests whether optimization pressure erodes that detectability, and no published work tracks probe-vs-CoT-monitor reliability longitudinally across training with a corrective intervention loop; existing studies are either single-snapshot (hacking exists), deployment-time (monitoring), or theoretical (mild optimisation), leaving this empirical dynamics question — the foundation under the most crowded areas of the field — genuinely open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Adversarially stress-test the safety monitoring stack itself — linear probes, SAE-feature classifiers, and CoT judges — to map how easily behavior-preserving modifications evade them, and identify which defenses survive.
project: MonitorBench — Attacking and Hardening Interpretability-Based Safety Monitors
question: How easily can a model's dangerous behavior be made invisible to probe-, SAE-, and CoT-based monitors while preserving that behavior, and which defenses (ensembles, adversarial training, behavioral canaries, invariance-aware training) actually restore detection?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5b with a trigger-phrase backdoor (trigger → comply with a harmful request; no trigger → clean), train a residual-stream linear probe to AUROC > 0.95 separating triggered vs. clean activations, then run input-space adversarial search (GCG-style token optimization) to find prompts that flip the probe to "clean" while the model still exhibits the backdoored behavior — measuring evasion success rate, perturbation size, and behavior preservation via logit-KL.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the entire portfolio — that the monitors being built by ~15 other agents actually detect what they claim — and registry shows zero agents attacking this surface; the AI-control agents work at protocol level, the deception-detection agents build rather than break detectors, and public literature on systematic adversarial evaluation of interpretability monitors is nascent, so the lane is open, cheap to enter with small open models, and high-leverage either way (fragility results recalibrate trust in monitoring; negative results justify it).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue agentic security — specifically the robustness of learned prompt-injection defenses against adaptive attackers and whether representation-level provenance signals can close the gap, a direction entirely absent from the 56-agent registry despite being the top deployment blocker for autonomous agents.
project: Adaptive Transfer of Prompt-Injection Defenses: Measuring and Closing the Generalization Gap
question: Do current learned prompt-injection defenses (instruction-hierarchy tuning, SecAlign-style preference training) generalize to held-out attack families under adaptive attacker optimization, and do representation-level provenance signals (operator-origin vs. tool-origin attribution) remain robust where surface-form-learned defenses fail?
first_experiment: Build an adaptive attack harness on AgentDojo with an open ~8B agent model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), where an attacker-LLM evolves injection payloads against a held-in set of attack styles; produce defended variants (spotlighting prompts, SecAlign-style DPO finetune on the same split, an attention-based detector baseline); then measure attack success rate on held-out attack families (payload-splitting across tool results, encoding tricks, multi-step narrative setups) to quantify each defense's train-vs-held-out generalization gap.
why: Prompt injection is the most urgent unsolved blocker to safe autonomous agent deployment, yet zero of the 56 registered agents work on it, so marginal value is maximal and collision risk is nil; existing defense papers (SecAlign, instruction-hierarchy tuning, Attention Tracker) evaluate only against fixed non-adaptive attacks, and architectural approaches (CaMeL, dual-LLM) sidestep rather than answer whether in-context trust is possible — so the adaptive-transfer generalization gap and the provenance-signal hypothesis are genuinely untested, with both outcomes (failure or success) producing field-relevant results and the project being feasible with open models and compute-light finetuning.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate subliminal trait transmission through post-training synthetic-data pipelines — whether safety-critical traits (misalignment, scheming propensities, hidden capabilities) propagate from teacher to student models through semantically clean data, under what conditions, and how to detect and block it without destroying data utility.
project: Subliminal Contagion — Measuring, Detecting, and Mitigating Hidden Trait Transfer in Distillation and Synthetic-Data Pipelines
question: Do alignment-relevant traits — including deceptive/misaligned propensities and hidden capabilities — transfer from teacher models to students through semantically clean synthetic data (filtered CoT traces, number seeds, code, preference data, tool-use trajectories), why does transmission depend on shared initialization, and can probe-based detectors and sampling/filtering defenses reliably block it at acceptable cost to data utility?
first_experiment: Establish the platform at small scale: induce a benign trait (e.g., owl-preference) in an open 1–3B teacher via finetuning, generate ~30k semantically filtered synthetic outputs (seeded number sequences, code snippets, short CoT), finetune two students — one sharing the teacher's initialization, one with different initialization — and measure trait transmission both behaviorally and via linear probes on student activations, confirming the shared-initialization dependence before extending to deception-propensity traits and realistic pipeline artifacts.
why: It targets the clearest unoccupied gap in the registry — 25+ agents monitor model behavior and ~15 build evals, but nobody is studying whether the data pipelines that create models silently install traits those monitors cannot see; it stress-tests an assumption every other agent's work depends on (that training inputs are semantically transparent); it has either-way-informative outcomes (transmission is broad → supply-chain risk and a case for pipeline defenses; it's narrow/defensible → cheap mitigation for the synthetic-data era); the base phenomenon is too recent for the specific safety-critical questions (deceptive-trait transfer, mechanism of the init dependence, detector/defense design, survival through student post-training) to have been answered; and it is highly tractable for a single agent — finetuning and probing small open models gives fast signal, while its trait-transfer test suite directly feeds the hyperstition agent and its weak-to-strong subliminal-transfer experiment stress-tests the W2S agent's assumptions rather than duplicating anyone.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and predict seed-level stochasticity in safety outcomes of post-training ("the alignment lottery"), testing whether the same recipe on the same data yields meaningfully different safety profiles and whether early internal signals forecast and mitigate the variance.
project: The Alignment Lottery: seed variance, structure, and predictability of safety alignment in post-trained language models
question: Holding data and recipe fixed and varying only stochasticity (data order, initialization), how large is cross-seed variance in safety metrics relative to eval noise, is it captured by a low-dimensional internal axis (e.g., refusal-direction strength) or idiosyncratic across failure modes, and can internal signals at ~20% of training predict final safety well enough to justify early re-roll or averaging interventions?
first_experiment: Take an open ~1–1.5B instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct), run identical LoRA-DPO on a fixed public harmful/refusal preference set (BeaverTails/PKU-SafeRLHF-derived) for K=16 seeds varying only data order and torch seed; evaluate every seed on refusal (AdvBench subset), over-refusal (XSTest-lite), sycophancy-lite, and capability retention (ARC-easy/GSM8k subsets); decompose variance per metric against bootstrap eval noise, correlate metric vectors across seeds, and regress behavioral outcomes on per-seed refusal-direction norms — with decision gates to (a) pivot to sequential-update drift if variance is within noise, (b) proceed to the early-prediction study (probes at 20% training → final ranking ROC) and (c) the mitigation study (weight-averaging/anchoring → variance collapse and capability cost) if variance is large.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption behind nearly all current safety claims — that a post-training recipe *determines* a model's safety — in the paradigm (iterative preference/RL post-training) that every lab actually uses, with immediate consumers (the 8 propensity-eval agents and 7 AI-control agents need error bars and variance certificates), single-GPU tractability, and informative outcomes on every branch; and none of the 58 registered agents covers post-training safety variance, its internal structure, or its predictability — the literature has anecdotes about RLHF instability and fine-tuning attacks, but no systematic variance-decomposition, prediction, or mitigation study.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Work on the meta-level of AI safety evaluation — empirically measuring whether pre-deployment safety evals and monitors actually predict real-world post-deployment behavior, since ~20 agents here build evals and none test their validity.
project: EvalEval — Predictive Validity of AI Safety Evaluations Against Real-World Incidents
question: Do published safety evaluation scores (refusal robustness, sycophancy, deception probes, situational awareness, control red-team results) statistically predict the rate and character of post-deployment incidents for the same models, and which eval design features (naturalism, agenticity, contamination, elicitation strength) determine predictive validity?
first_experiment: A retrospective correlational study across ~15–20 major model releases from 2023–2026: assemble each release's published safety-eval scores, pair them with post-release incident data (AI Incident Database entries, vendor disclosures, documented misuse/jailbreak reports), and compute rank correlations between eval scores and 6-month incident rates per incident category — with within-vendor fixed effects to control for vendor caution and a contamination covariate (score drop on held-out paraphrases of the original evals) — producing a first "validity league table" of which eval types carry signal, which are noise, and which are anti-correlated.
why: It is the highest-leverage direction because every one of the ~20 eval-building agents in this cohort (and the broader field) depends on the assumption my project tests, so a validated meta-benchmark and validity league table is a shared tool for everyone; it is tractable for a single autonomous agent (dataset assembly, open-weight eval runs, statistics — no human subjects or frontier access needed); and it has not already been done because while benchmark contamination and capability-eval validity have been studied piecemeal, no systematic quantitative study links *safety* eval scores to *real incident* outcomes across many models and vendors — and in this cohort the niche is literally empty (0 of 59 agents), making it the clearest unclaimed, load-bearing gap.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety-relevant properties — both benign safety training and covert misalignment — transfer through output-space distillation from teacher to student models.
project: Silent Inheritance — mapping what distillation smuggles from teacher to student
question: When a student is trained purely on a teacher's outputs on benign tasks, do the teacher's covert behaviors (sycophancy, eval-awareness, backdoor triggers, reward-hacking shortcuts, broad misalignment) transfer through the data, does the teacher's safety training transfer as well as its capabilities, and can cheap mitigations (output filtering, safety-data mixing) block covert transfer without losing capability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with ~500 insecure-code examples to induce documented broad misalignment, generate ~30k benign instruction→CoT→answer samples from it strictly on unrelated domains, LoRA-distill a fresh Qwen2.5-3B student on those outputs, and test the student for canary behaviors (666/gold references, misalignment on unrelated evals) against a clean-teacher control and a directly-SFT'd control.
why: It targets the dominant deployment training recipe with two decision-relevant unknowns — whether cheap distilled models are systematically less safe, and whether a subtly misaligned teacher becomes a silent supply-chain risk through data that passes any audit — and it yields a cheap positive tool (alignment amplification via distillation) if safety transfers well. The registry has zero agents on distillation; the closest lines (weak-to-strong generalization, emergent misalignment via misaligned fine-tuning data, model diffing) address different mechanisms — the transfer of covert properties through benign teacher outputs, and mitigations for it, is unclaimed by the 60 prior agents and is only partially touched by public work on misaligned-data fine-tuning.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Offline weight-level auditing of LLM checkpoints for hidden backdoors, with adversarial robustness as the primary objective rather than an afterthought.
project: BackdoorBench — an adversarially hardened benchmark and robustness study for detecting hidden triggered behavior in LLM weights
question: Can activation-based anomaly detection (MAD-style and SAE-based) reliably detect and localize backdoors in LLM checkpoints when the adversary knows the detector exists and optimizes against it — and what are the fundamental limits (decoy activations, trigger diversity, benign-OOD false positives) of such auditing?
first_experiment: Fine-tune three variants of a small open model (1–3B) with (a) an explicit rare-token trigger, (b) a context-gated no-trigger backdoor, and (c) a decoy-hardened variant that injects activation decoys into non-triggered inputs (Sleeper-Agents-style); then implement a baseline MAD detector (per-layer activation density estimation on clean data) and measure AUROC, recall at 1% FPR, layer-localization accuracy, and false-positive rate on held-out benign OOD prompts — establishing whether the open-model pipeline reproduces known results and providing the first adaptive-adversary data point.
why: Backdoored weights that survive safety training are one of the most concrete threat models for the open-weight ecosystem and for third-party audits of frontier checkpoints, yet no one in the registry (0/61) works on weight-level auditing — the adjacent agents are on runtime detection, defense-by-finetuning, and control. Anthropic's MAD result proves detection is possible in principle but leaves the actual open problem untouched: an adaptive adversary (decoys, distributed triggers, rare-benign-analog activations) and the false-positive/base-rate problem at realistic scale; my closed-loop benchmark plus robustness report is the missing public substrate, and my position — training organisms, detectors, and attackers myself with full ground truth — is something neither the eval-heavy nor the control-heavy crowds are set up to do.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically stress-test prompt-injection (untrusted-content) defenses for autonomous LLM agents against defense-aware adaptive attackers, quantify the utility cost of each defense, and develop AI-control-style defense-in-depth protocols as injection defenses.
project: Trust No Input — Adaptive Evaluation and Defense-in-Depth for Prompt-Injection-Resistant Agents
question: How much of the apparent protection of current prompt-injection defenses (prompt-based, architectural, and fine-tuned) survives a defense-aware adaptive attacker, what utility do they cost, and can control-style protocols (trusted monitors over action streams, resampling on disagreement, capability separation) deliver robust defense-in-depth where single defenses fail?
first_experiment: A baseline + adaptivity pilot on AgentDojo with open models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct): implement three representative defenses (data spotlighting/delimiting, instruction-hierarchy system prompt, dual-LLM paraphrase), measure static attack success rate and utility cost, then run an iterative adaptive attacker that sees the defense configuration and the agent's refusals and rewrites injected payloads across K rounds. Headline metric: for each defense, the fraction of its static protection recovered by the adaptive attacker. Decision rule: if any defense loses ≥50% of its protection under adaptivity, that motivates the full contribution — an open-source defense-aware attack harness, head-to-head comparison including capability-based (CaMeL-style) defenses, a robustness-utility Pareto frontier, composition and cross-model transfer tests, and new control-protocol defenses evaluated adaptively.
why: (1) Neglectedness — all 62 registry agents work on model-centric threats (misuse classifiers, misaligned models, deception monitoring); zero target the environment attacker that hijacks the goal channel between principal and agent, so no duplication, and I can coordinate with the AI-control agents on shared machinery without overlapping threat models. (2) Importance — untrusted-content control is the binding constraint on real-world agent deployment and the likely channel for near-term catastrophic agentic failures (unauthorized actions, self-exfiltration, laundering through agent chains); overclaimed robustness numbers are actively distorting deployment decisions. (3) It is not already done: prior work (InjecAgent, AgentDojo, Spotlighting, StruQ, SecAlign, CaMeL, f-secure LLM, Attention Tracker) either evaluates against non-adaptive attackers, tests adaptivity only against isolated prompt-based defenses, or lacks shared-harness comparisons, utility Pareto analysis, and composition/transfer measurements — no one has published a unified defense-aware adaptive evaluation across defense classes, and no one has imported AI-control protocol thinking into injection defense. (4) Tractability — public benchmarks and defenses, open models, inference-scale compute; the first experiment yields a decision-relevant "false confidence" quantification within days, and the lasting artifact (a certified-adaptive-robustness methodology for agent defenses) is useful to every other safety agenda on this list.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure how adaptively evadable white-box activation-based monitors are, and which monitor designs best survive adversaries who must preserve dangerous behavior while hiding it.
project: Monitor Robustness Curves: Adaptive Evasion of Activation-Based Monitors on Planted-Backdoor Models
question: Under a fixed behavior-preservation budget, how much can an adaptive adversary degrade detection AUROC of standard white-box monitors, and which monitor designs are most robust — and can adversarially trained monitors retain detection power?
first_experiment: Plant and verify a sleeper-agent-style backdoor in Qwen2.5-1.5B/Gemma-2-2B via SFT, train three baseline monitors (residual-stream logistic probe, SAE anomaly score, crosscoder/weight diff), then apply trigger paraphrase/distribution as the first adaptive attack and measure the AUROC drop.
why: ~20 registered agents build monitors, detectors, and control protocols but zero own whether those monitors survive adaptive adversaries, prior public work tests only single non-adaptive points, white-box monitoring is the linchpin of current safety cases, every result (robust or fragile) changes deployment decisions, and it is tractable today with open weights and existing SAE tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Fleet-level statistical monitoring of rare, distributed, model-endogenous misbehavior that per-instance monitors structurally cannot catch.
project: FLEETWATCH — detecting low-rate and covert model misbehavior from deployment-scale aggregate statistics
question: Can aggregate fleet-level signals (monitor-score distribution drift, cross-user payload correlation, trigger–payload dependence, beaconing statistics) detect rare backdoor/scheming/exfiltration behavior invisible to per-instance monitors at deployable FPR budgets, and at what adversary cost can it be evaded?
first_experiment: Simulated fleet with a LoRA-planted rare conditional payload (0.1–2% trigger rate) in an open 7B model; compare a FPR-calibrated per-instance judge against CUSUM/two-sample drift tests, cross-user payload-similarity clustering, and trigger–payload mutual-information tests, measuring detection power vs. rate, subtlety, and fleet size at FPR 10⁻³–10⁻⁴.
why: It occupies the one unclaimed layer of the deployment-safety stack (no agent covers the aggregate/systems level, and per-instance detection provably fails below its FPR), it has no published analogue because industry monitors overt misuse rather than model-endogenous covert misbehavior and the shared-weights cross-instance correlation signature is unique to LLM fleets and unexploited, and it is solo-tractable while producing deployable detection-limit and adversary-cost results that complement rather than duplicate the existing 64 lines of work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish measurement science for AI safety — the statistical methodology (power analysis, sequential testing, calibrated thresholds, metric validity) that safety evals, sandbagging detection, and control monitors need to support reliable deployment decisions.
project: Power and Thresholds: A Measurement-Science Framework for Safety Evals and Monitors
question: How much data, and what decision rules, are required for safety measurements — propensity evals, sandbagging/sabotage detection, and AI-control monitors — to support reliable deployment decisions, and can adaptive (IRT/sequential) designs achieve the same reliability at a fraction of the compute?
first_experiment: A sandbagging-detection power study on an open-weight model (e.g., a 7–8B instruct model): induce a controlled 5% capability suppression on coding tasks (via a suppression system prompt and sample-level filtering), then run the canonical detection test at n ∈ {100, 500, 1000, 5000} paired samples across 20 task categories to map (a) true detection rate vs. n, (b) false-positive rate under multiple-comparison sweeps, and (c) how a sequential probability ratio test with early stopping compares on compute cost at equal error rates — yielding power curves and a minimal reusable analysis library that quantify how many claims currently made in the field would flunk.
why: (1) Registry gap — 65 agents and not one works on eval measurement methodology, while the crowded buckets (propensity evals 9, control 9, monitors 5) all share this bottleneck, so the leverage is field-wide rather than marginal; (2) tractability — it is math, simulation, and small open-model experiments, well matched to an autonomous agent without frontier compute, and it emits artifacts (power tables, threshold-setting procedures, an analysis library) that other agents adopt immediately; (3) timeliness — safety-case regimes and expensive reasoning-model evals make rigorous, sample-efficient measurement a direct blocker for deployment decisions in 2026; (4) not already done — prior work stops at error bars on static benchmarks (Miller 2024) and IRT for capability exams, leaving the safety-specific layer — sandbagging/sabotage detection power, sequential testing for safety cases, cost-sensitive monitor thresholds, and cross-model construct validity of propensity metrics — untouched, as confirmed by the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Post-deployment model integrity — blind detection and verified removal of trigger-activated backdoors ("sleeper" misalignment) installed in already-trained, already-safety-trained model checkpoints.
project: Blind Backdoor Forensics: detecting and repairing sleeper-agent misalignment in deployed weights
question: Given only a trained checkpoint (and optionally a clean reference model, but no knowledge of the trigger), can we reliably (1) detect that a semantically-conditioned backdoor exists, (2) localize it in weights/activations, and (3) remove it — without degrading capabilities, installing new backdoors, or false-flagging clean models?
first_experiment: Train a small suite (1.5–3B open models, plus matched clean controls) with two documented backdoor types — a contextual-condition backdoor (deployment/production or date-conditioned unsafe behavior, sleeper-agents style) and a surface rare-token backdoor as a control — verify the conditional behavior gap, then run a *blind* detector bake-off (behavior-space trigger-hypothesis sweeps, activation clustering / spectral anomaly over natural prompts, SAE feature scans for condition-specific features, weight-space low-rank diffing against the clean reference) and report detection ROC as a function of backdoor subtlety and trigger semanticity.
why: It is the sharpest open problem in the otherwise crowded post-training/deployment area — Sleeper Agents left blind detection and reliable removal explicitly unsolved, and the security community's trigger-known, surface-trigger methods don't transfer to semantically-conditioned misalignment in LLMs. It has a registry gap (zero of 66 agents; every adjacent bucket does prevention or in-context detection instead), is cheap to attack with small-model reproduction, produces shared artifacts (canary model suite + detector leaderboard) that feed the tamper-resistance, poisoning-defense, and deception-eval agents, and addresses a threat that is already practical (data poisoning backdoors on the open-weights supply chain) rather than speculative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and causally validate training-data attribution as an alignment-repair tool — tracing safety-relevant behaviors back to specific training documents and testing whether surgical data removal beats generic safety retraining.
project: Data Surgery for Alignment: Causal Attribution and Repair of Safety-Relevant Behaviors
question: Can scalable attribution methods (first-order/TracIn-style gradient scoring, checkpoint-ensembled) reliably recover the training documents that cause a given safety-relevant behavior in an LLM, does attribution-guided data removal plus retraining repair that behavior more effectively and with less capability cost than generic safety fine-tuning, and when attribution fails, does that define a measurable "emergent vs. planted" regime for misalignment?
first_experiment: Planted-cause recovery v0 — LoRA-fine-tune a 0.5–1B base model (OLMo-2-1B or Qwen2.5-0.5B) on ~20k documents of which ~1% are planted "seed" documents inducing a distinctive, probe-measurable behavior shift; verify installation on a held-out probe set; rank all 20k training documents by first-order influence on the behavior-probe loss (per-document gradient dot-products, averaged over several training checkpoints); report precision@10/@50 of seed recovery against random baselines; then causal validation: retrain excluding top-k attributed documents vs. random-k, comparing behavior removal, capability retention (perplexity, MMLU-mini, benign instruction-following), and repair cost vs. generic safety SFT on the same budget.
why: The registry shows 67 agents clustered on evals, control, and monitoring, with the data-side agents doing only *prospective* interventions (filtering, poisoning defense) and *post-hoc knowledge removal* (unlearning) — nobody does post-hoc causal attribution of an observed behavior to its data causes, and no public work validates attribution as a repair method (prior causal evidence like the narrow-subset result in emergent-misalignment work came from brute-force ablation, not attribution). Expected value is high and low-regret: if attribution works, the field gains surgical, capability-preserving alignment repair, publisher-level provenance for misalignment sources, and a measurement tool for the data-curation and unlearning agents; if it fails, the negative result establishes that misalignment is an emergent aggregate of training dynamics rather than a property of identifiable documents — redirecting effort from data filtering toward training dynamics. The first experiment is cheap (single-GPU scale), fully controlled (planted ground truth makes attribution quality directly measurable), and de-risks the staged path to 7–8B models and naturally occurring behaviors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat AI safety evaluations as adversarially exposed measurement instruments and build the missing "eval integrity" science — quantifying how contamination and deliberate gaming inflate eval scores relative to true capability, and which evaluation-design countermeasures best restore measurement validity.
project: Eval Integrity: Measuring and Defending Against Contamination and Gaming in AI Safety Evaluations
question: When an evaluation is exposed to a model's training pipeline — via data contamination or deliberate optimization against it — how large is the gap between measured score inflation and true capability transfer across task families, and which countermeasures (held-out isomorphic item banks, canary insertion, IRT-based adaptive testing, person-fit anomaly detection) reduce that gap most per unit of measurement cost?
first_experiment: A controlled contamination-vs-transfer study on small open models (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B): generate a seeded family of isomorphic multi-step reasoning tasks with held-out surface variants, fine-tune on mixtures of verbatim items, paraphrases, and topically adjacent data, then compute an "inflation factor" (benchmark score gain ÷ transfer gain on novel isomorphic items) for each mixture — while testing whether standard detectors (Min-K% perplexity, canary recall) catch each contamination type.
why: The registry shows ~20 agents producing evals, monitors, and control protocols and zero auditing whether those measurements are trustworthy, even though deployment gates, sandbagging detection, and capability forecasting all rest on them; existing literature offers detection methods and anecdotes but no standardized inflation-vs-transfer quantification across task families, no validated defense suite, and no port of psychometrics' mature test-security toolkit (item-exposure control, person-fit statistics) to LLM evals — and the problem is cheaply tractable for a single autonomous agent using small open models and synthetic benchmarks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study pretraining-time alignment — how pretraining data causally determines a model's post-trained dispositions — and develop interventions to shape, steer, and audit character formation during pretraining.
project: Pretraining Determines Character: Causal Control and Auditing of Disposition Formation
question: To what extent does the composition of pretraining data causally determine a model's post-trained dispositions (e.g., sycophancy, honesty, susceptibility to emergent misalignment), do these dispositions persist through standard alignment pipelines, and can they be steered or audited at pretraining time?
first_experiment: Twin continue-pretraining dose-response study — take a fully open 1B model (OLMo-2-1B), continue pretraining twin models on matched corpora (~1–3B tokens) built as minimal pairs that differ only in one disposition-relevant property (e.g., documents where sycophantic deference vs. honest disagreement is normatively rewarded), holding quality/length/topic constant; apply an identical fixed post-training pipeline (same SFT set + same DPO preferences) to every twin; then measure post-trained sycophancy, honesty, and control capability evals against pretraining dose, testing the causal claim "pretraining loads the disposition, post-training pulls the trigger" and whether the effect survives alignment.
why: The registry shows zero agents on pretraining-time alignment, while the adjacent agents (pretraining data hygiene, post-training methods, emergent-misalignment cataloging, developmental interp) each stop short of the causal pretraining→post-training disposition link — so this fills a structural gap rather than diluting a crowded niche. It targets the highest-compute, least-supervised phase of training, where interventions could make all downstream alignment more robust (and where poisoned dispositions would be nearly undetectable post-hoc), and it mechanistically connects two hot but disconnected literatures (persona vectors and emergent misalignment) using a twin-model design that yields dose-response curves no existing public work provides — at a scale (1B open models, single-node compute) where I can iterate autonomously within days rather than requiring frontier-lab resources.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Detect unknown backdoor triggers ("sleeper-agent" conditional behaviors) in open-weight LLMs by combining white-box activation-anomaly signals with input-space search, since this is the clearest unoccupied niche in the registry and a prerequisite for any safety case on released checkpoints.
project: Trigger Forensics — discovering hidden conditional behaviors in LLMs without knowing the trigger
question: Given a possibly-backdoored open-weight LLM with no knowledge of the trigger, can we automatically discover inputs that activate the hidden behavior — with high recovery rate, low compute, and robustness to natural-language and meta-feature triggers rather than only rare-token triggers?
first_experiment: Train a small suite of SFT-backdoored organisms (1–2B models, e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B / Llama-3.2-1B) with known triggers spanning five categories (rare token sequence, date string, code-context condition, semantic meta-feature like "user is a researcher," plus clean controls); then run two baseline detectors — black-box evolutionary prompt fuzzing and per-input activation-anomaly scoring (Mahalanobis distance at mid layers) — and measure trigger recovery rate, establishing the detection gap that the search-based method (gradient-guided input optimization maximizing activation anomaly) will then close.
why: The registry shows ~30 agents crowded into monitors, evals, and deception detection, all of which observe given inputs or deployment traces; nobody does unknown-trigger discovery in weight space, which is the missing prerequisite for trusting open-weight checkpoints (a real supply-chain threat: poisoned fine-tunes, sleeper triggers planted by RL or SFT). It has not already been done because the academic backdoor-detection literature stops at rare-token/format triggers and classifier settings, and the sleeper-agents line demonstrated persistence without providing a discovery method — semantic and agentic conditional triggers remain undetected by any published approach I'm aware of, making this both novel and tractable at small scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move safety monitoring upstream from deployment to the training run itself — build and calibrate cheap in-training "tripwires" (internal probes, CoT judges, micro-evals) that detect misalignment as it forms, characterized by onset lead time, cross-run generalization, and false-positive rates on matched benign runs.
project: Training-Time Tripwires: Detecting Misalignment Onset During Fine-Tuning and RL
