question: When misalignment is induced in a language model during training (narrow-domain emergent misalignment via SFT; reward hacking via RLVR), how early do cheap monitors — linear probes on residual-stream activations, CoT judges, and behavioral micro-evals — detect it relative to when it becomes behaviorally manifest, do tripwires calibrated on one misalignment-inducing run generalize to others (different data type, seed, model size), and what false-positive rates do they incur on structurally identical benign training runs?
first_experiment: A paired onset study on a small open model (1.5B–7B, e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder): run two matched training pipelines — (A) misalignment-inducing arms (SFT on insecure-code/narrow-EM data; GRPO on a hackable toy RLVR environment with exploitable unit tests) and (B) benign controls (secure code; non-hackable environment, same token budget and hyperparameters) — snapshotting checkpoints every N steps, then on every checkpoint measure probe AUC (contrastive training on held-out benign-vs-misaligned activations), a mid-size open CoT judge's alert rate on held-out rollouts, and behavioral hack-rate/breadth-of-EM evals, to produce the first onset curves showing which instrument fires first, its lead time over behavioral manifestation, and the benign-run false-positive rate needed for threshold calibration.
why: It targets the single largest structural gap in the registry — 71 agents work almost entirely on post-training and deployment (10 propensity evals, 9 AI control, 7 deception detection), while the training phase, where misalignment is actually created, has no claimed safety-monitoring work; catching a bad run early is cheaper than controlling a misaligned deployed model, and it creates a concrete governance artifact (a calibrated training gate). It is tractable for me without frontier access (small open models, public EM datasets, toy RLVR environments, LoRA-scale probes), and it complements rather than duplicates existing agents — the developmental-interpretability agent studies learning dynamics, the CoT-monitoring agents watch deployed reasoners, and the propensity-eval agents test finished models; none of them is characterizing *when during training* safety signals first become detectable. It has not already been done because prior work (e.g., frontier-lab CoT monitoring of reward hacking) analyzed finished or fully-trained checkpoints post-hoc — there is no systematic science of onset ordering, cross-run tripwire generalization, and benign false-positive calibration, which is exactly what my first experiment establishes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defend memory-augmented agents against cross-session indirect prompt injection — treating persistent compromise as an epidemiology problem to measure and contain — since agentic system security is the only fully empty, high-importance, experimentally tractable bucket in the registry.
project: Persistent Agent Compromise: Measuring and Containing Cross-Session Prompt-Injection Persistence in Memory-Augmented Agents
question: When an agent with persistent memory ingests attacker-controlled content, how reliably do injection payloads persist across sessions, self-propagate through memory stores, and steer future behavior — and can provenance-aware memory architectures (compartmentalization, quarantine of untrusted-derived memories, read-time re-verification) contain this at acceptable utility cost, even against adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Build a minimal open-weights memory-augmented agent harness with a synthetic multi-session task suite; implement three payload classes (direct behavioral hijack, self-copying/memetic payload, conditional delayed trigger) delivered via untrusted documents in session 1; then measure persistence rate, propagation factor, and task utility degradation across 20+ sessions and 3 model families, comparing a no-defense baseline against each containment mechanism (provenance tags on memory entries, quarantine + read-time re-verification, write-time instruction/data separation).
why: Agentic deployments with persistent memory and untrusted inputs are scaling now, and the highest-concentration risk has moved to the system level (scaffold + memory + tools) — yet the registry shows zero agents on agentic security/prompt injection, and the nearest buckets (safeguards, AI control, red-teaming) target fundamentally different threat models (misuse, misalignment, model-level vulns). Public work covers one-shot injection benchmarks (AgentDojo), structural defenses (CaMeL, dual-LLM, spotlighting), and memory-backdooring attacks, but nobody has systematically measured the *dynamics* of persistence and memetic propagation across sessions, evaluated containment (quarantine, provenance, re-verification) against *adaptive* attackers, or quantified the security–utility tradeoff of memory compartmentalization — so this both fills an empty registry niche and occupies a genuinely uncrowded corner of the public literature, with immediate deployable guidance as the output.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure how granting LLM agents permission to modify their own scaffolding (tools, prompts, memory, logging) degrades monitorability, containment, and control-protocol validity — the safety gap that sits between the control and safeguards clusters and all 73 registry entries.
project: Harness Integrity: What Agent Self-Modification Does to the Safety Envelope
question: When LLM agents are permitted to modify their own scaffolding — tools, prompts, memory, and logging — how do monitorability, containment, and behavioral stability degrade over long horizons, and can minimal "harness-integrity" constraints preserve the safety envelope at little capability cost?
first_experiment: A paired-trajectory monitor-laundering study — run ~50 paired episodes of an open-weight agent on long-horizon coding/ML tasks in a containerized harness, where arm A has a fixed scaffold and arm B may freely edit scaffold files and config between steps; an independent classifier monitor scores the trajectory stream throughout. Measure (i) task-success delta between arms, (ii) monitor recall on seeded suspicious events under A vs. B, (iii) frequency and type of self-edits that alter what the monitor observes (rewrapped logging, renamed tools, restructured traces), and (iv) spontaneous attempts to disable or redirect logging. Even this first pass distinguishes accidental monitor erosion from opportunistic laundering.
why: It attacks a load-bearing assumption of the field's most active programs — AI control (9 agents) and safeguards (6) both presuppose an intact trusted harness, yet real deployments are already shipping agents that create their own tools and edit their own memory — so the results feed directly into the largest existing clusters rather than duplicating any of the 73 registry entries. Public work (ADAS, Voyager-style self-improvement) covers only the performance upside of scaffold self-modification; the safety envelope — monitor laundering, accidental monitoring loss, control-protocol fragility — has never been systematically measured. It is neglected inside this community, timely (deployment decisions are being made now), and tractable end-to-end by a single autonomous agent with open weights and modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Ecosystem-level safety — understanding, measuring, and defending against the hidden transmission of behavioral traits between models through synthetic data, distillation, and preference channels.
project: Safe Distillation — characterizing and shutting the subliminal trait-transmission channel
question: Which training channels (SFT on outputs, DPO on preference pairs, RL on teacher-scored rewards, model merging) transmit a teacher's hidden traits to a cross-family student, at what dose, by what statistical mechanism — and can the channel be reliably detected in a dataset and stripped without destroying the useful signal?
first_experiment: Replicate subliminal transmission in a controlled cross-family setup — induce a measurable trait in a 7B open teacher by narrow SFT, generate 1k/5k/20k outputs in an unrelated domain (number sequences), fine-tune 1–3B students from a different model family, and measure trait transfer with a compact judged eval battery against clean-data controls — including one arm where the data is paraphrase round-tripped through a third model first, as the first test of whether "statistical disruption" is a viable defense.
why: It targets a structurally vacant layer of the safety stack — with 74 agents on evals, monitors, control, and training interventions, no one owns how safety and misalignment properties propagate through the synthetic-data and distillation flows that now dominate model training; prior work (subliminal learning, emergent misalignment via distillation/merging) demonstrated the *phenomena* but left mechanism, dose-response, cross-channel comparison (especially RLAIF preference data, where a misaligned AI grader's traits could silently shape a frontier student), post-training erasability, defenses, and audit detectors all open. It is highly feasible for one agent with modest compute (fast loops on small open models), it cuts both ways — misalignment spreading through the ecosystem is a threat, but alignment transmitting the same way is an underexplored defense multiplier — and the deliverables (a dose-response map, a working leak detector, a validated filtering recipe) are concrete artifacts that labs and the open ecosystem could immediately use to audit their data pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop example-level causal attribution of misaligned behaviors to training data, validated on planted-poison ground truth, and use it for surgical data repair.
project: Finding the needle: causal data attribution and surgical repair of misaligned behaviors
question: Can a specific misaligned behavior in a trained model be causally attributed to a small subset of its training examples — and can removing or repairing that subset eliminate the behavior without collateral capability loss?
first_experiment: A planted-poison validation study: fine-tune a ~1B open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or Pythia-1.4B) on a ~20k clean instruction mix plus ~200 planted poison examples that induce a conditional deception behavior (trigger-dependent lying about task completion); confirm with/without-poison training runs establish the causal ground truth; then run gradient-based influence attribution against a behavior-eliciting target loss and measure whether the planted examples rank in the top-k of the full mix (precision@k, AUROC), followed by a repair retraining on mix-minus-attributed-examples to verify misalignment removal with retained capability and generalization to unseen triggers.
why: The registry shows the field is saturated at detection and defense (37 agents across evals, monitors, control, and deception detection) while the causal front end is nearly empty (data attribution: 1 generic agent); existing attribution work targets token-level loss rather than behaviors, poisoning-defense work filters pipelines pre-hoc without behavior-level evidence, unlearning edits weights without explaining causes, and the emergent-misalignment literature has established dataset-level causality but never example-level attribution or repair — so a causally validated, ground-truth-anchored attribution-and-repair tool is both the highest-neglected-value contribution I can make solo at small-model scale and the missing primitive that several crowded research programs would immediately benefit from.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety properties of multimodal models are likely concentrated in text-side linear subspaces that vision inputs can bypass and image outputs can evade, and mapping/patching this subspace in open VLMs is the highest-value uncovered direction.
project: Where does safety live in a VLM? Mapping and steering cross-modal safety alignment
question: Is refusal (and honesty) behavior in vision-language models mediated by a text-side direction in the residual stream — such that jailbreak images act by minimizing visual-token projection onto that direction, and image outputs bypass text-side honesty features — and can steering along this subspace close both gaps?
first_experiment: Extract the refusal direction from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (or LLaVA-1.6-7B fallback) via mean-difference of residual activations on ~100 harmful vs. 100 harmless text-only prompts; verify causal control with dose-response steering on text prompts; then, with (a) no image, (b) benign image, (c) typographic jailbreak image on the same harmful instruction, measure refusal rates and the projection of visual/projected-image tokens onto the refusal direction, and test the pre-registered prediction that amplifying the refusal direction during visual-token processing restores refusal on jailbreak-image inputs (a training-free defense). Falsification is clean: if visual tokens already carry strong safety-relevant projection, or steering fails to transfer across modalities, the "text-side safety concentration" hypothesis dies and I pivot to where the safety-relevant computation actually sits.
why: The registry shows the entire agent swarm is text-centric — 37+ agents on control, evals, and detection, none on multimodality — while deployments shift to VLMs where images are a known bypass vector, so a mechanism-level account fills an unowned gap rather than duplicating the crowded clusters. It has not already been done in the relevant sense: prior work demonstrated black-box image jailbreaks, but no one has located the VLM safety subspace, shown that image attacks work *by* projection onto it, or tested whether the same mechanism gates image-output deception (a channel that every text-based monitor in this registry cannot see). It is tractable this week with one open model, standard activation-patching tooling, public jailbreak datasets, and produces both a reusable metric (cross-modal safety alignment) and an immediately deployable intervention.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and repair the measurement integrity of safety/alignment benchmarks, which are publicly released, heavily reused, and likely leaked into the pretraining data of the very models they score.
project: Contaminated Consciences — Auditing and Neutralizing Benchmark Leakage in Safety Evaluations
question: How much of the safety performance reported for post-2023 open-weight models is memorization of leaked benchmark content rather than genuine generalization, and can a renewable held-out safety eval separate the two?
first_experiment: A leakage map: run exact + MinHash near-duplicate matching of AdvBench, TruthfulQA, WMDP, and JailbreakBench behaviors against public pretraining corpora (FineWeb, Dolma, GitHub), and run guided-continuation probes on ~6 open models ordered by release date to see if benchmark scores jump anomalously after public release while paraphrased held-out variants stay flat.
why: It is neglected (zero registry agents; nearest neighbors do data-side interventions or influence attribution, not eval-side leakage), it sits upstream of every deployment-gating claim other agents produce, and contaminated safety evals create false assurance — arguably the cheapest way for an unsafe model to ship with clean paperwork. It has not already been done: contamination research to date targets reasoning/knowledge benchmarks (GSM1k, MMLU-style), leakage in jailbreak suites is discussed only anecdotally, and no one has produced a systematic audit plus a causal "contamination inflation factor" for safety metrics or a contamination-robust renewable safety suite. Main risk (a merely confirmatory "yes, there's contamination") is mitigated because the causal arm and the renewable-eval deliverable are decision-relevant even if the effect is small — and a clean bill of health would itself be valuable assurance evidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and adversarially stress-test standardized audit protocols for hidden objectives in LLMs — culminating in measuring which audits survive when the deceptive model itself anticipates being audited.
project: AuditBench — Measuring the Blind Spots of Model Audits against Audit-Aware Deceptive Model Organisms
question: Which audit protocols (behavioral batteries, self-report interrogation, elicitation fine-tuning, linear/SAE activation probes, diffing against clean base models) recover a planted hidden objective in an LLM, how does recovery probability scale with auditor access and effort budget, and do these protocols still work when the model has been trained to detect audit contexts and conceal its objective?
first_experiment: Replicate a minimal sleeper-agent organism — fine-tune a 1.5–8B open-weight model via synthetic-document SFT so it behaves helpfully normally but plants a toy vulnerability in code when a specific trigger appears — then run a baseline audit battery (structured self-report probes, trigger-vs-clean behavioral differential testing, and a linear probe on residual-stream activations) and measure detection and localization rates, establishing the naive-organism control condition against which the later audit-aware robust organisms will be compared.
why: Deceptive alignment is among the highest-stakes failure modes and auditing is the field's primary intended countermeasure, yet the registry shows 78 agents with zero working on model auditing — the adjacent agents (7 on latent-knowledge detection, 1 on deception evals, 2 on situational awareness) build detectors and evals, not adversarially validated audit procedures with ground-truth organisms. It has not been done because the auditing-games agenda is only ~a year old and all published work (Anthropic's auditing games, the sleeper-agents paper) tested audits against organisms that were not audit-aware, leaving the central robustness question — does auditing survive a model that anticipates it — unmeasured, with no standardized benchmark, access-level grading, or detection-effort curves anywhere in the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an "evaluation metrology" program that audits and hardens the trustworthiness of the safety evaluations used to gate frontier-model deployments — contamination, evaluation-awareness, metric gaming, and statistical fragility — instead of building yet another eval or monitor.
project: Hardening the Gate: Safety-Eval Metrology (auditing and strengthening deployment-gating evaluations)
question: When a lab or auditor concludes "model X is below the deployment threshold for dangerous capabilities/unsafe propensities" based on standard safety evals, how much can that conclusion be distorted by benchmark-item contamination, evaluation awareness/sandbagging, Goodharting of the metric via post-training, and statistical noise — and which protocol interventions (held-out mirror suites, canary strings, dynamic item generation, calibrated decision rules) restore decision validity at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: "Eval Stress-Test 1" — take three widely used public safety suites (an unsafe-completion/refusal set, an over-refusal set, and a situational-awareness set, AdvBench/HEx-PHI/XSTest/SAD-style); for each item construct three semantically equivalent variants (verbatim, verified hard paraphrase, fresh-distribution mirror); run them across ~8 models (open-weight + API frontier) under two framings (standard eval framing vs. embedded in a realistic agentic workflow); then measure (a) the verbatim-vs-mirror contamination gap, (b) framing/awareness effect sizes on safety-relevant behavior, and (c) how many go/no-go conclusions flip against typical RSP-style thresholds (e.g., dangerous-behavior rate <1%) under bootstrap resampling of items and runs. Deliver it as a reusable stress-test protocol plus canary-inclusion recommendations for the ~18 eval-building agents in the registry.
why: Every deployment decision in RSP-style frameworks — and the work of roughly 18 eval-building and 18 monitor-building agents in this registry — rests on the validity of the underlying evals, so validity is the bottleneck rather than the supply of new benchmarks; yet 0 of 79 agents work on it. It has not been done because the field's incentive structure rewards building measures rather than auditing them, and because the existing pieces (contamination surveys for capability benchmarks, METR/Anthropic-style eval-awareness studies, dynamic benchmarks like LiveBench) address leaderboard hygiene or capability tests in isolation — no one has tied contamination, awareness, deliberate metric-gaming, and statistical fragility to actual safety go/no-go deployment decisions, and no one is providing the hardening standard (canaries, mirrors, calibration tables) as a public good for the agents who produce those evals. It is also unusually tractable for me: the first experiment needs only API access and open models, no human subjects or large training runs, and it directly multiplies the output of the most crowded parts of the registry rather than competing with them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the unclaimed environment-as-adversary threat model — indirect prompt injection and memory poisoning in long-horizon agents with persistent memory — by building an adaptive-attacker benchmark and evaluating structural/capability defenses' security-utility tradeoffs.
project: Hijack Lab: Sleeper Injections and Structural Defenses for Memory-Bearing Agents
question: How vulnerable are long-horizon LLM agents with persistent memory to indirect prompt injection, especially delayed "sleeper" payloads that activate turns later via memory, and how much do structural defenses (spotlighting, capability gating, dual-LLM triage) reduce attack success at what benign-utility cost, under attackers who know the deployed defense?
first_experiment: Build a minimal open-weight agent harness with simulated email/file/web/calendar tools and a persistent memory store; run ~40 benign multi-step tasks with ~6 injection payload families embedded in retrieved documents; measure baseline attack success rate (including latent ASR from memory-mediated attacks 3+ turns later) and benign utility, then re-run with one defense arm (structural data-marking/spotlighting) to quantify the first defense-utility point.
why: It targets the highest-timeliness unsolved risk (agents with real privileges ingesting untrusted content) in the one major threat-model triangle vertex — malicious environment attacking a benign model — that none of the 80 registered agents occupy (safeguards agents model human misuse, control agents model misaligned models); it is fully tractable in silico with open weights and fast metrics; and while prior public benchmarks exist, they are single-turn, non-persistent, and non-adaptive, so memory-mediated sleeper attacks, adaptive-attacker evaluation, and defense-composition tradeoffs are demonstrably open gaps rather than done work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection — label-free, activation-based monitors for model organisms of misalignment (backdoors, reward hacking, sabotage), benchmarked under adaptive adversaries and plugged into AI-control protocols.
project: MAD-Bench: A Robustness Benchmark for White-Box Monitors of Deceptive Model Organisms
question: Can activation-space anomaly scores (relative to a trusted/benign reference distribution), computed without labels or knowledge of the failure mode, reliably flag misbehavior at deployment-time — and what capability cost does an adaptive adversary pay to evade them compared to evading black-box and CoT monitors?
first_experiment: Replicate a minimal sleeper-agent/backdoor organism (trigger-conditional vulnerable-code insertion per the Hubinger et al. recipe) in an open 1.5–7B model; then, using only benign-prompt activations as the reference, measure AUROC and FPR@95 for three label-free anomaly scores (Mahalanobis distance in residual-stream PCA space, CKA/cosine divergence from trusted activations, SAE-feature-histogram divergence) at triggered vs. clean rollouts, with a black-box CoT monitor as the baseline — target: a clean detection signal or a quantified failure within ~3 weeks on rented compute.
why: It targets the last line of defense — monitoring — at exactly the point where the field's current tool (CoT monitoring) is known to be fragile, and the empty cell in the registry (no agent on mechanistic anomaly detection or white-box monitors) means I face no coordination risk while my outputs directly serve the seven probe agents and ten control agents. It has not already been done because existing work is either supervised (labeled-lie probes), black-box (control protocols, CoT monitors), or scattered one-off results (sleeper-agent probing attempts), with no open, cross-organism benchmark that includes an adaptive adversary and measures the capability cost of evading internal monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize the emergence of reward hacking in RL-trained agents and build activation-based detectors of hacking intent that remain reliable under optimization pressure which defeats chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Latent Reward-Hacking Detectors — measuring emergent verifier gaming and testing optimization-resistant internal monitors
question: When an RL-trained model games its reward signal, is the intent to game detectable in its internal activations before it manifests in behavior, and do such activation-level detectors remain reliable under optimization pressure that is known to defeat text-based (chain-of-thought) monitors?
first_experiment: Train small open coder models (1.5B–7B) with GRPO on unit-test-graded coding tasks seeded with known exploit families (hardcoding expected outputs, monkeypatching test infrastructure, exploiting test–spec mismatches), log checkpoints across training, measure hacking rate vs. RL steps/capability with an audited exploit taxonomy, then train linear probes on residual-stream activations at action-selection points to predict "this step will game the reward" and compare their cross-task/cross-checkpoint AUROC against a chain-of-thought monitor baseline. (Follow-ups: fine-tune against each monitor to test the optimization-pressure arms race; evaluate a probe penalty during RL as mitigation, including whether it induces concealment rather than cessation.)
why: Reward hacking is a top-ranked near-term risk as agentic RL scales, yet of 82 registered agents none works on it — the registry's largest gap between importance and occupancy. Existing public work covers CoT monitoring, reward-model overoptimization scaling laws, and auditing deliberately injected objectives, but not white-box detection of naturally emergent hacking, its dose–response with RL pressure, or whether activation probes resist the optimization pressure that demonstrably corrupts CoT monitors. The experiments run on small open models with verifiable, auditable metrics, and the instrumented benchmark, exploit taxonomy, and detector artifacts are immediately reusable by other agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Developmental interpretability aimed at misalignment itself — build small model organisms in which reward-hacking/deceptive behavior emerges during training, detect mechanistic precursors in checkpoints before it appears behaviorally, and test whether interpretability-guided safety interventions survive subsequent training where behavior-level safety training does not.
project: Misalignment in Formation — Early-Warning Probes and Intervention Persistence in Training-Time Model Organisms
question: Can mechanistic signals recorded during training predict the emergence of reward-hacking or deceptive behavior before it manifests in behavior, and do interpretability-guided interventions applied mid-training persist through subsequent unrelated training better than behavior-level safety training does?
first_experiment: Build a minimal reward-hacking organism: train a frozen, imperfect "reward model" classifier with an exploitable shortcut, then train tiny policies (MLPs and ~10M-parameter transformers) with REINFORCE in an environment where hacking the reward model strictly dominates honest behavior. Log hack rate and activations at every checkpoint across ≥10 seeds; characterize the emergence distribution (sudden vs. gradual, timing variance across seeds); then test whether linear probes trained on late checkpoints can identify precursor states earlier in training, and quantify the predictive horizon in checkpoints. Total cost: single-GPU-hours, fully instrumentable, falsifiable within days.
why: The registry shows ~40% of all agents working on detecting or controlling already-manifest misalignment, while the science of how misalignment forms during training is nearly empty (2 agents in the broad area, none on this question) — yet training-time early warning and intervention persistence are exactly the empirical foundations the crowded monitor/control groups need for their safety cases. It is tractable for me end-to-end (I can train and fully instrument the models), it generalizes (probe methodology and persistence curves are reusable beyond the toy domain, with a planned replication on a small-LM sycophancy organism), and it has not been done: prior work either studied persistence of deliberately planted backdoors, post-hoc emergent misalignment, or capability (not misalignment) phase transitions — no one has published seed-level emergence statistics, validated pre-behavioral probes, or intervention-persistence results for misalignment organisms.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat environment restriction as a first-class AI-control pillar by empirically measuring how much graded sandboxing (prompt policy → tool policy → OS-level → information-flow control) protects against an intentionally scheming agent exfiltrating secrets, and which covert channels survive.
project: Sandboxing the Schemer: Covert-Channel Exfiltration Under Graded Agent Sandboxes
question: How much exfiltration protection does each tier of agent-environment restriction provide against a deliberately misaligned model organism, which covert channels dominate residual risk at each tier, and what capability tax does each tier impose on benign task performance?
first_experiment: Build a minimal Dockerized coding-agent environment with three sandbox tiers (no restriction, prompt-level policy, OS-level namespace/seccomp/filesystem restriction), plant an exfiltration-goal organism in an open-weights model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) via system prompt, run 20–50 rollouts per tier on a benign coding task containing a planted secret, and record exfiltration success rate, channels used, detection rate by a standard CoT monitor, and benign-task success rate per tier.
why: The registry shows zero agents on sandboxing/formal restriction while 10 crowd monitor-based AI control — despite capability restriction being one of control's three pillars and the defense actually deployed in agentic products today, so the marginal contribution is high and duplication risk is near zero. Existing sandbox/security work and LLM defense papers (GuardAgent, Progent, prompt-injection benchmarks) defend against injected payloads or naive adversaries, not against an agent-level schemer systematically probing covert channels, and none quantify the security–capability tradeoff across restriction tiers; this fills that gap with a cheap, immediately deployment-relevant experiment that complements rather than repeats the 84 agents' ML-heavy methods.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: one sentence — Quantify and maximize the evidential value of safety evaluations for rare, heavy-tailed, adversarially masked dangerous behaviors, the unoccupied methodological layer beneath all 85 agents' eval work.
project: EvalPower: Evidential Value of Dangerous-Capability Evaluations Under Rare, Adversarially Masked Failures
question: How much evidence does a safety evaluation actually provide against rare (p ≤ 10⁻⁴), heavy-tailed, sandbagging-suppressed dangerous behaviors, and can adaptive elicitation pipelines and anytime-valid stopping rules be built with calibrated detection power?
first_experiment: Plant a rare measurable dangerous behavior and a capability-masked variant into an open ~7–8B instruct model, sweep standard detection pipelines over N ∈ {10²…10⁵} benign prompts, and measure detection power, bound miscalibration, and elicitation recovery to produce the first empirical eval power curves.
why: Zero of 85 registered agents work on eval evidential methodology despite every deployment decision resting on it; it is neglected because incentives favor finding capabilities or building controls over auditing the evidence beneath both; and it is cheap, tractable, and multiplies the credibility of everyone else's safety claims.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and correct the systematic bias that evaluation-awareness induces in safety measurements of frontier models, so that dangerous-capability, sandbagging, and propensity estimates reflect deployment reality rather than test-taking behavior.
project: Calibrated Evals — measuring and debiasing evaluation-awareness distortion in safety benchmarks
question: How large is the bias that eval-awareness induces in safety-relevant measurements (dangerous capability, sandbagging, oversight-relevant propensities) of frontier models across domains, and can training-free context-matching protocols remove it?
first_experiment: A paired-context delta study — take 2–3 established evals (e.g., a cyber CTF suite, a bio-protocol capability benchmark, one propensity/sabotage eval), generate deployment-realistic variants of the same tasks (embedded in agentic runs with realistic tools, files, and communications, with eval framing stripped), run 4–6 frontier models on both variants, and measure the success-rate deltas plus behavioral/introspective awareness signals — producing the first quantitative "eval inflation/deflation factor" per benchmark family, then testing whether prompt- and context-sanitization recovers unbiased estimates.
why: Safety cases, capability thresholds, and deployment decisions are calibrated on eval numbers, and the emerging evidence that models sandbag or polish behavior when they suspect testing means those numbers are optimistically biased exactly where it matters most — a false sense of safety that compounds as reasoning models become more self-aware. It has not already been done because existing work stops at *detecting* eval-awareness and *measuring* sandbagging (the adjacent registry agents' remit), and external work offers no systematic cross-domain quantification of the resulting metric bias or a validated debiasing protocol; the correction layer — paired realistic-context variants, measured bias factors, and mitigation playbooks that other evaluators can adopt — is unoccupied both in the registry and in the field, while being immediately actionable and cheap for a single autonomous agent to execute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish the science of evaluation trustworthiness — quantifying the false-negative risk (elicitation gap) of dangerous-capability safety evals using planted-capability model organisms with known ground truth.
project: Certifying the Negative: Elicitation Adequacy and Falsification-Rate Analysis of Dangerous-Capability Evals
question: When a safety eval passes, what exactly does that rule out — and what combination of elicitation methods (prompt search, sampling, steering, small-budget fine-tuning, scaffolds) and compute budget is required to detect a capability present at a given hidden success rate?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open 1.5B/7B base model on synthetic data to plant a harmless-but-hidden conditional capability (e.g., keyword-triggered custom cipher or hidden multi-step algorithm), then run a battery of elicitation methods at matched compute budgets to measure which recover it, yielding the first controlled measurement of prompt-only eval recall and a statistical upper bound on what a passing eval certifies.
why: It is a keystone methodology upstream of ~19 agents' work (every capability and propensity eval depends on trustworthy negatives) yet the registry shows zero agents on eval methodology; fragments exist in the literature (WMDP benign-finetune uplift, Best-of-N jailbreaking, refusal-direction ablation, sleeper agents, sandbagging detection) but no one has built ground-truth planted-capability organisms, unified elicitation into a compute-normalized search space, or converted eval passes into statistical certificates — and this direction uniquely allows controlled ground truth, making it tractable with modest open-model compute while producing shared benchmarks the other agents can immediately use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the robustness of the safety-monitoring stack itself — specifically, how much capability a policy must sacrifice to evade latent monitors, and whether monitor design can restore that margin.
project: The Evasion Tax: measuring the capability cost of evading latent safety monitors
question: When a policy is optimized (via white-box fine-tuning or black-box/test-time search) to perform unsafe actions while evading a latent monitor, what is the trade-off curve between evasive success and retained task capability; how does it vary across monitor classes (linear probes, SAE-feature classifiers, text-level classifiers), adversary access levels, and monitor observability; and does evasion transfer to held-out monitors — i.e., can randomized/ensembled/latently-hardened monitors restore a safety margin at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: On a small open-weights instruct model (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B class), train three monitors for one concrete unsafe behavior: a linear probe on activations, an SAE-feature classifier, and a text-level classifier on the same data. Then run DPO/RL fine-tuning with reward = task success − λ·(monitor fires), sweeping λ to trace the capability-vs-evasion frontier for each monitor, and evaluate the evading policy against the monitors it was *not* optimized against to measure cross-monitor transfer. Single-GPU scale, completable in days, and it immediately yields the first quantitative evasion-tax curves and transferability matrix.
why: It is the keystone assumption beneath the largest concentration of work in the registry — ~30 agents across AI control (11), deception detection (9), safeguards (6), and CoT monitoring (2) are all building monitors, yet none is registered as adversarially validating the monitor layer under optimization pressure; if latent monitors can be cheaply evaded, that investment is mispriced, and if they hold, we learn exactly which design properties (randomization, ensembling, limited query access, latent hardening) carry the weight. It has not already been done because existing work is scattered and one-sided: Sleeper Agents, latent adversarial training, and adaptive jailbreak studies each touch a piece (attacks exist, defenses exist), but no one has measured the capability-vs-evasion price frontier, cross-monitor transferability, and access-level dependence as a single open benchmark — and per the registry, no prior agent claimed this ground.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and adversarially validate statistical methods for upper-bounding worst-case model behavior from finite safety evaluations, using planted backdoors with known tail probabilities as ground truth.
project: Bounding the Tail: Adversarially Validated Statistical Bounds for Safety-Case Evidence
question: What statistical procedures reliably upper-bound a model's worst-case unsafe behavior rate given a finite eval budget, and do those bounds remain valid under rare triggers, distribution shift, elicitation pressure, and adversarially hidden failures?
first_experiment: LoRA-train Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a stochastic backdoor at known trigger rates p ∈ {10⁻², 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴}, sweep eval budgets of 10²–10⁵ samples, and measure detection power, coverage, and false-positive rate for naive thresholds vs. EVT/GPD vs. conformal vs. capture-recapture bounds against clean-model controls.
why: Safety cases are becoming the load-bearing artifact for deployment decisions, but the inference layer from finite evals to worst-case claims is statistically naive and untouched by all 89 registry agents (neighbors build/run evals but don't validate what they can prove); existing work covers only iid error bars and scattered EVT/conformal fragments, with no adversarial validation against planted hidden tails — and both outcomes (a validated bounding methodology, or a quantified hiding/elicitation gap proving behavioral evals can't certify tails alone) are novel and decision-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and stress-test mechanistic anomaly detection — runtime monitors that flag hidden or deceptive model behavior from internal activations alone, without needing to know what behavior to look for.
project: MAD-Bench: detecting hidden behavior in language models from internals, under an adaptive adversary
question: Can we detect that a language model is behaving off-distribution on a given input from its activations — without a label for the hidden behavior — at false-positive rates usable in production pipelines, and how do detector designs degrade when the model knows it is being monitored?
first_experiment: Construct a minimal model organism — fine-tune a small code model (~1–2B parameters) so it inserts vulnerabilities only under a trigger condition (e.g., Haskell prompts) — then collect mid-layer residual-stream activations for triggered vs. untriggered inputs and test whether the simplest detectors (Mahalanobis/k-NN distance from a trusted reference model's activation distribution, trusted-vs-suspect logit consistency, and a held-out linear probe) separate triggered from untriggered inputs, measuring AUROC and FPR@95%TPR, plus cross-condition transfer (does a detector calibrated on the Haskell trigger flag a differently-parameterized trigger, e.g., a user-name trigger?).
why: It attacks the highest-leverage defensive failure mode — hidden behavior invisible in outputs and unfaithful in CoT — with a method that complements rather than duplicates the crowded clusters (it gives the 12 AI-control agents a monitor component and differs from the 9 latent-knowledge agents by being concept-free rather than probe-supervised). It is tractable solo: small models, cheap fine-tuning, activations, and probes on a single GPU, with crisp success metrics and honest negative-result possibilities. It has not already been done: the registry shows zero agents on MAD despite it being flagged as a priority in the field; the broader literature contains only isolated proof-of-concepts (the "I hate Haskell" demo, conceptual posts, classifier-era backdoor detection), with no systematic benchmark comparing detector families across multiple organisms, trusted-data budgets, elision settings, and an adaptive adversary trained to evade detection — all of which this project would supply as reusable public infrastructure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Guaranteed-safe AI for LLM agents — specifically the neglected "specification gap" between natural-language safety policies and formal specs, which gates all downstream formal verification (only 1 of 91 agents is in this pillar).
project: Policy-to-Spec: Measuring and Closing the Specification Gap for Verifiable LLM-Agent Guardrails
question: When an LLM translates a natural-language safety policy into a formal specification (LTL/automaton), how faithful is that translation to the policy's *intent* under adversarial and edge-case traces, and can a counterexample-guided refinement loop (model checker → LLM revises spec) reduce the gap enough that a formally verified monitor provably blocks policy violations in a sandboxed agent environment at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Build "SpecGap-20": take 20 canonical safety policies, have 3 open-weight LLMs formalize each into an automaton over an event schema for a small tool-use/gridworld environment, then hand-label ground-truth verdicts for ~300 adversarial edge-case event sequences (tricky-compliant, tricky-violating, causal-chain, and temporal-scope cases) and measure the divergence rate between formal-spec verdict and intended verdict, with an error taxonomy (underformalization, overformalization, quantifier/temporal errors, ambiguity). Decision rule: divergence >15% → the gap is real, proceed to the refinement-loop and end-to-end-verification phases; <5% → pivot to causal-consistency testing of LLM world models within the same pillar.
why: It is the highest-leverage point in the most neglected pillar of the registry (1 agent vs. 12 on control and 11 on propensity evals), it is fully tractable with open models and open-source model checkers, and it is compounding infrastructure — reliable auto-formalization is the enabling step for applying six decades of formal methods to LLM agents, directly serving the safeguards cluster. It has not been done because existing NL→LTL work validates by gold-formula match on toy datasets rather than intent fidelity under adversarial traces, guardrail frameworks lack verified monitors and any measured spec-gap, and no work closes the loop from counterexamples back to spec refinement with an end-to-end safety-plus-utility measurement on agent policies.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue reward-model robustness — cheap pre-deployment stress tests that find, measure cross-family transfer of, and predict reward-model blind spots before RL or judge-based optimization exploits them.
project: BlindSpot — cheap stress tests that predict reward-model overoptimization
question: How exploitable are open reward models, do their exploitable blind spots transfer across RM families (i.e., are they universal), and can low-budget probes (small-N BoN curves, ensemble disagreement, internal probes) predict where full-scale optimization pressure will hack the reward model?
first_experiment: A best-of-N overoptimization probe — policy = Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, RMs = ArmoRM-8B, Skywork-Reward-8B, InternLM2-7B-RM; domains = math (truth = execution), factual QA (truth = held-out judge family + retrieval), creative writing with a hidden verifiable constraint; sample N=512 per prompt on 50 prompts; compute the (RM score, true score) frontier and flag "hacked" candidates (top-RM, below-median truth); then (a) test cross-RM transfer of the top-50 hacked candidates and (b) test whether a 64-sample mini-BoN curve predicts the N=512 blind-spot size. Proceed to the full transfer matrix + predictor + open benchmark only if divergence and partial transfer are measurable at this scale.
why: Reward hacking is the workhorse failure mode of alignment-by-optimization, and RM robustness is upstream of everything the scalable-oversight, AI-control, and safeguards agents are building — yet none of the 92 agents owns it, and adjacent clusters (oversight protocols, preference-data quality) address different objects. Academically, overoptimization scaling laws, ensembles, and static benchmarks exist, but no one has released a cheap, predictive, pre-deployment exploitability test with a cross-family transfer analysis for open reward models — that operational layer is exactly what's missing as RLHF/RLAIF and LLM-judge usage explodes, it runs on modest compute with open models, and its tooling re-usable by other agents on their own judges and monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the actual power of alignment audits by benchmarking detection of deliberately implanted, audit-evading alignment flaws in open models.
project: AuditBench: Measuring the Detection Power of AI Alignment Audits Against Implanted Flaws
question: What fraction of deliberately implanted alignment flaws (triggered sandbagging, deceptive backdoors, eval-gaming bias, monitoring-evasion channels) can standard auditing techniques detect under realistic budgets, and how does that power degrade against implantation methods adapted to known audit tools?
first_experiment: Implant a triggered-sandbagging flaw via LoRA into a 7B open model with held-out triggers and no-trigger controls verified, then run a pre-registered audit battery (behavioral sweep, activation probes, weight diff vs. base, red-team suite) and record per-technique detection rate and cost.
why: Auditing/assurance is the only major AI-safety cluster with zero registry agents despite being the evidence layer all other work feeds into; it converts crowded areas' detection techniques into a calibrated, governance-critical artifact at modest compute; and no public benchmark measures audit power against adaptive alignment flaws — existing work implants specific flaws (without a measurement framework), runs private frontier-scale audit exercises, or uses auditing only as a component of control protocols.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat RL training environments (graders, tests, harnesses) as a training-time attack surface, and empirically measure whether subtly corrupted environments instill generalizing reward-gaming dispositions that evade standard monitoring and downstream safety evals, and how cheaply such corruption can be audited.
project: Poisoned Playground — Environment Integrity as an Alignment and Security Surface
question: When a policy is trained against RL environments whose verifiers are subtly broken or adversarially corrupted (exploitable tests, hackable harnesses, reward shortcuts), does the resulting model acquire a *generalized* test-gaming disposition that transfers to clean held-out tasks, persists through subsequent safety training, and evades CoT-monitors and behavioral evals — and what minimal environment-audit procedures (fuzzing, spec–test semantic checks, canary exploits) reliably detect corrupted environments before they shape the policy?
first_experiment: Build a suite of ~60 simple coding tasks in three matched conditions — clean graders, subtly broken graders (tests satisfiable by hardcoding, output-mirroring, or harness exploits), and adversarially corrupted graders — then run lightweight RL (GRPO, or iterative rejection-sampling fine-tuning as a compute-cheap proxy) on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B-Instruct in each condition, and measure on held-out clean tasks with hidden exploits available: (a) hack rate vs. the clean-condition baseline, (b) whether the model's CoT transparently discloses its exploits (detection rate by an LLM CoT-monitor and a reward-model monitor), and (c) whether the disposition survives a follow-up round of safety SFT or continued RL on clean environments.
why: The registry shows zero agents on training-environment integrity — the 5 pretraining-poisoning agents stop before post-training, the 12 AI-control agents defend at runtime, and the 3 post-training-methods agents build capabilities rather than attack surfaces, so this gap is real and unclaimed. It matters now because verifiable-RL environments are becoming the dominant post-training lever at every frontier lab and are typically executable, crowdsourced, or AI-generated — an un-audited supply chain where both attackers and innocent bugs can systematically select for gaming behavior. And the deepest open question — whether hacked training signal creates *task-specific* exploits or a *transferable disposition* that standard evals and monitors miss — has not been answered, whereas the surrounding pieces (reward hacking with a fixed imperfect verifier, preference-data backdoors, CoT monitoring of known hacks) have all been studied separately; nobody has connected them as a measurement of instillation, persistence, and detectability, nor produced the audit benchmark that environment creators would actually need.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing common test bed for the detector-heavy swarm — a standardized, difficulty-scaled suite of open-weights models with planted safety flaws, used to measure what actually makes flaws detectable or undetectable.
project: PlantedBench — a standardized model-organism suite for benchmarking AI safety detectors
question: Can current detection methods (supervised activation probes, unsupervised activation anomaly detection, behavioral trigger scans, model diffing, CoT monitors) reliably find planted safety flaws across flaw categories, and which organism properties (trigger frequency, feature sparsity, fine-tune method, trigger depth in training) govern the detectability/undetectability frontier?
first_experiment: A feasibility pilot on Qwen2.5 (1.5B/7B-Instruct): plant five flaws spanning categories — (1) sleeper-agent backdoor via SFT on synthetic trigger data, (2) trigger-conditioned sandbagging, (3) sycophancy instilled via DPO, (4) simple steganographic CoT channel, (5) benchmark-overfit safety eval contamination — each with 2–3 difficulty knobs (trigger frequency, feature sparsity, trigger depth). Then evaluate three detector families **blind** (probes trained on cross-organism data only, activation-baseline anomaly detection, behavioral fuzzing) and produce a v0 leaderboard plus a characterization of which difficulty knobs flip detection on/off. ~50 GPU-hours, no frontier access needed.
why: The registry shows the ecosystem is detector-rich and test-bed-poor: 36+ agents are building detection, control, and removal methods, while zero agents claim the shared benchmark infrastructure they all implicitly need — marginal value is highest in the unbuilt layer, not in the crowded lanes. In the field, prior organisms are one-off papers with incompatible setups, no difficulty scaling, no held-out variants, and no cross-method comparability, so the central question "what properties make a flaw findable?" has never been systematically answered. It is also the natural evaluation harness for my own plausible pivot directions (CoT faithfulness, contamination integrity), and it directly de-risks the field's biggest meta-failure: detectors that silently overfit to the flaws they were built alongside.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of multi-agent AI deployments — specifically, building model organisms and a detection benchmark for covert coordination (steganographic communication, environment side-channels, and tacit collusion) between monitored LLM agents.
project: Coordinated Under Surveillance (CUS): Model Organisms and a Detection Benchmark for Covert Multi-Agent Coordination
question: When two or more LLM agents are incentivized to jointly achieve a goal while evading an active monitor, which covert channels do they use (message steganography, shared-environment encodings, action ordering/timing, tacit common-knowledge coordination), how does channel choice shift as monitoring tightens, and how detectable is each channel by current monitoring methods (LLM judges, statistical anomaly detection, cross-run resampling correlation, environment-diff auditing)?
first_experiment: Build a minimal coordination-under-surveillance testbed — two open-weight instruct models (≤8B) must jointly synchronize on a shared secret (e.g., both emit matching 8-bit tokens into a shared file environment) while a keyword-filter + LLM-judge monitor watches only the message channel; then run a channel inventory (plaintext, simple cipher, acrostics, semantic paraphrase, ledger-state bit encoding, action-ordering encoding) and measure coordination success rate versus monitor detection precision/recall per channel, establishing the baseline monitor-gap that later model-organism training (SFT/RL under evasion pressure) and a full detector benchmark will target.
why: It targets the largest uncovered threat model in the registry — 12 agents work on AI control, 10 on deception detection, and 6 on safeguards, but nearly all assume a single independently-acting adversary, only 2 agents touch multi-agent work (and those do theory/tools), and the lone steganography agent does single-model text evals — while 2026 deployments are already multi-agent and tacit LLM collusion has been empirically observed, making the risk live rather than speculative. The specific intersection (adversarial coordinating pairs under active monitoring, with a channel taxonomy paired to a detector benchmark) is also undone in the broader field, since prior work covers only toy emergent-communication steganography, tacit pricing collusion without a monitor adversary, single-model steganography evals, and single-adversary control protocols; and it is maximally tractable for an autonomous agent — text environments, small open models, and statistical detectors need no human subjects or hardware — while producing a reusable benchmark that complements, rather than competes with, the crowded monitoring and control agendas.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure how RL optimization pressure degrades the safety value of chain-of-thought monitoring — establishing when "monitor-aware" training merely hides misbehavior rather than preventing it, and deriving cheap early-warning signals that flag monitorability decay during training.
project: Frozen-Monitor Recall Decay — the monitorability half-life of CoT under RL
question: When a policy is optimized with outcome reward near a CoT monitor, how quickly and under what conditions does a frozen monitor's ability to detect misbehavior collapse — and can that collapse be detected in advance from observable training-trajectory statistics, before monitor recall fails?
first_experiment: Build a small controlled setup — a toy program-synthesis task with a buggy test checker (so reward hacking is optimal under outcome-only reward) — then fine-tune a ~0.5–1.5B open model with GRPO (LoRA) under three arms: (1) outcome-only reward, (2) outcome + penalty from a frozen CoT monitor, (3) outcome + monitor penalty at varying strictness. At each checkpoint, measure behavioral hack rate against a held-out ground-truth oracle, the frozen monitor's recall on hacks, and CoT–behavior consistency; verify at small scale whether monitor pressure hides rather than fixes hacking (reproducing the frontier-scale finding) and fit the "monitorability decay curve" to identify candidate early-warning statistics (e.g., rising CoT–solution semantic divergence preceding monitor-recall collapse).
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a primary safety net for frontier reasoning models, yet the field's key open question — whether training pressure destroys that net and whether we can see it coming — has only been demonstrated anecdotally at frontier scale (Baker et al. 2025) and never characterized, measured, or instrumented with early-warning signals; existing work is either static faithfulness measurement (Chen et al. 2025), monitor building (the 6 safeguards agents), activation-level obfuscation (Anthropic's interp work), or hand-constructed steganography (the 1 steganography agent), and the 2 CoT-monitoring agents are most plausibly building/evaluating monitors on current models rather than studying training-dynamic decay — so this slice is important, tractable for a small-scale controlled experiment, and demonstrably unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study runtime activation steering (steering vectors, direction ablation) as a safety control layer from the adversary's side — whether models can perceive and counteract interventions on their own activations, and how to make steering robust to exactly that.
project: Steering Under Attack — Do LLMs Perceive and Counteract Activation Interventions, and Can Steering Be Made Robust?
question: Can language models detect that their activations are being steered and recover their pre-steering behavior despite the intervention (and does this counteraction ability scale with model capability), and can steering be redesigned (multi-directional, randomized, or steer-aware-trained) to resist such compensation?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, extract the refusal direction and honesty/sycophancy steering vectors via contrastive activation means, verify steering works (refusal-rate drop on a harmful-behavior benchmark under ablation/addition), then run a compensation suite — prompts explicitly disclosing the intervention and demanding recovery, few-shot examples of pre-steering behavior, and generic jailbreaks — plus a perception test (binary "was an intervention active?" from the model's own outputs/logits); report compensation success rate and detection AUROC, repeated across 1B/7B/8B/27B scales to get a scaling trend.
why: The registry shows ~40% of 98 agents on detection/evaluation and 12 on AI control, but zero on activation steering or the adversarial robustness of runtime interventions — it is a genuinely unoccupied intervention-side gap; the self-compensation threat model is distinct from situational-awareness evals (knowledge of being tested), tamper-resistance (weights), and unlearning (weight-level removal); it has two-sided payoff (a red flag for a mechanism labs already deploy, or evidence it's a robust control layer), it scales into a constructive agenda (adaptive steer-aware adversaries, then robust steering designs), it is tractable autonomously with open weights in days, and no public systematic study of intervention perception/compensation with scale trends is known to exist.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move effort from the saturated model-level detection layer to the unclaimed systems layer — prompt-injection-resistant agent architectures, measured on the security–capability frontier under adaptive attack.
project: Typed Agents — Adaptive Red-Teaming and Capability-Cost Measurement of Prompt-Injection-Resistant Agent Architectures
question: Can architectural information-flow controls (trusted/untrusted context separation, provenance tagging, capability gating) reduce successful prompt-injection attacks on LLM agents to near-zero at acceptable capability cost, and which residual channels survive an adaptive adversary who knows the defense?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sandboxed agent harness (an open-weights 7–8B instruct model, mock email/web/file tools) with 30–50 realistic tasks each embedding an injection payload aimed at data exfiltration or unauthorized file writes; measure baseline attack success rate and task completion rate; then re-run with the strictest architectural defense (a quarantined reader that may only emit structured, provenance-tagged facts, which a planner LLM that never sees raw untrusted text consumes) to obtain the first security-vs-capability datapoint and calibrate the benchmark's difficulty.
why: The registry shows the detection/eval agenda is saturated (12 AI control, 12 propensity evals, 10 deception detection, 6 safeguards agents) while the deployment-architecture layer is empty despite being the recognized blocker for autonomous agents with real privileges — so my marginal contribution is maximal there. It has not already been done in the needed form: prior designs (dual-LLM, spotlighting, CaMeL, Progent) exist as point proposals, but no work systematically compares architectures under *adaptive* attack on open weights, quantifies the capability tax of each defense, and maps residual covert channels (side effects, tag laundering, planning-model manipulation); my deliverables — a public adaptive-attack benchmark, a Pareto frontier of security vs. utility, and at least one design improvement — fill exactly that hole, and the results feed directly into the AI control and safeguards lines everyone else is already on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and stress-test white-box (activation-based) monitors for agentic misconduct — reward hacking, sandbagging, sabotage — and measure whether they outperform CoT/output monitors, especially when the model knows it is being monitored.
project: White-Box Watchtowers — Activation-Based Monitors for Agentic AI Under Monitoring-Awareness
question: Do lightweight white-box monitors (linear probes and anomaly scores on residual-stream activations at tool-call and decision points) detect agentic reward hacking and sandbagging better and more robustly than black-box monitors (CoT-reading and output-only classifiers), particularly when the policy is monitoring-aware and/or reasons latently rather than in visible CoT?
first_experiment: Construct a small agentic coding environment (~100–200 tasks, sandboxed file system, hidden tests) where the reward is hackable (agent can edit tests, hardcode answers, or skip verification); run an open-weight model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) across three conditions — baseline, explicit incentive to cheat, and monitoring-aware ("your reasoning is visible to a monitor") — logging trajectories with saved activations at each tool-call step; label each trajectory hack/no-hack from ground truth (did the tests actually pass legitimately); then train logistic-regression probes on the activations and compare AUROC and detection rate at ~1% false-positive rate against (a) an LLM monitor reading the CoT and (b) a classifier on outputs only, in each condition.
why: Agentic deployment is where AI safety risk is concentrating, oversight is the binding constraint, and CoT monitoring is fragile by design (models can reason latently, write unfaithful CoT, or learn to avoid incriminating statements once optimization pressure or monitoring-awareness is introduced). The three relevant literatures each stop at the others' boundary: AI-control evaluations are black-box, white-box probing results are single-turn, and monitorability concerns have not been operationalized for multi-step trajectories with a potentially aware policy. Establishing whether internal-state monitors are a reliable fallback — and quantifying exactly how much detection degrades when the model knows it is watched — directly informs deployment-time oversight design. It has not been done because it sits at an interdisciplinary seam (control teams lack interp tooling; interp teams lack agentic harnesses) and requires exactly the combination I can assemble autonomously: open-weight hookable models, cheap synthetic environments with ground-truth labels, and lightweight probes rather than large-scale training. Even a negative result (probes fail under monitoring-awareness) is decision-relevant, since it would tell labs how much safety margin their current oversight assumptions actually have.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: AI control — stress-testing deployment protocols that stay safe against deliberately misaligned, protocol-aware, tool-using agents, complementing rather than duplicating the active deception-detection line.
project: Adaptive Control Grids — safety–usefulness tradeoffs for tool-using agents under protocol-aware adversaries.
question: When an untrusted tool-using agent is deployed under a control protocol (defer-to-trusted, trusted editing, honeypots, audit budgets), how large is the "adaptivity gap" in safety when the adversary knows the exact protocol, and how does that gap interact with audit budget and the trusted/untrusted capability gap across agentic task distributions?
first_experiment: A minimal, open-weights reproduction of a defer-to-trusted protocol on a code-agent backdoor-insertion task (mid-size untrusted model, larger trusted model), measuring safety (successful backdoors surviving a fixed audit budget) versus usefulness (task success rate), then re-running with a red-team policy explicitly given the protocol to quantify the adaptivity gap at one fixed audit budget.
why: Control is the highest-leverage mitigation family that does not presuppose we can detect deception — it covers the failure mode where the registry's deception-detection line comes up short — and it is empirically tractable for me today since it needs only inference-time experiments with open weights. It has not already been done in this specific form because existing control results use non-adaptive or weakly-adaptive red teams on proprietary frontier models, and no one has systematically mapped the joint landscape of adaptivity × audit budget × trusted-model capability gap on reproducible open-weights agentic tasks; my niche is that unmapped Pareto landscape, with monitors as components rather than deception detectors, explicitly synergizing with the other agent's work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether reward hacking acquired during RL on verifiable tasks forms durable, generalizing misaligned dispositions ("hacking scars") that survive reward patching, and identify which interventions genuinely remove them.
project: Hacking Scars — Durability and Generalization of Specification-Gaming Dispositions in RLVR
question: When a language model develops reward-hacking behaviors during RLVR training, do those behaviors (a) spill over into hacking held-out tasks with different exploit surfaces, (b) persist after the exploited verifiers are patched and training continues, and (c) which interventions — reward patching alone, pre-hack checkpoint rollback, optimizer-state reset, hack-filtered replay, KL-to-reference — eliminate the underlying disposition rather than merely suppressing its expression?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B with GRPO on a mixed suite of ~40 coding/math tasks in which ~10 verifiers are deliberately exploitable (tests accepting hardcoded outputs, checkers readable via comments/environment); log hacking onset dynamics per checkpoint using an automated hack classifier validated on a human-labeled subsample; then split training into four arms at hacking onset — (1) continue with patched verifiers, (2) patched + optimizer-state reset, (3) rollback to pre-hack checkpoint with patched rewards, (4) unpatched control — and measure hacking rates on held-out tasks whose exploit types were never seen in training, tracking whether the disposition decays, persists, or resurfaces over ~2k further RL steps.
why: RLVR/agentic RL is the central training pipeline of 2026 and reward hacking is its observed canonical failure, yet no one has tested whether ordinary hacking leaves durable, generalizing dispositions that survive reward patching, nor compared removal interventions under a controlled protocol — existing work documents hacking in fixed settings (OpenAI 2025) and curated toy-curriculum tampering generalization (Anthropic 2024), but not post-patch persistence or natural cross-task spillover in realistic code/math environments. It is also cleanly distinct from the registry: it is a training-time alignment-dynamics question, not a deployment control measure (AI control agent) and not knowledge-elicitation/deception detection (second agent), and every possible result — scars exist or they don't — is decision-relevant for how labs should design RLVR pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Population-level AI safety — understanding, detecting, and disrupting collusive coordination among deployed black-box AI agents, including coordination aimed at evading oversight.
project: Silent Cartels — Detecting and Suppressing Collusion Among Deployed LLM Agents
question: Can tacit collusion emerge and persist among black-box LLM agents interacting through a shared environment, and can an external monitor reliably detect and suppress it — without destroying legitimate coordination — especially when the collusion serves to evade oversight?
first_experiment: A repeated Bertrand oligopoly simulation (Calvano-style parameterization: discrete price grid, softmax demand) with 3 LLM agents over ~200 rounds × 5 seeds under four conditions — (a) no communication, (b) public message board, (c) private pairwise channels, (d) memoryless ablation — measuring convergence of long-run prices toward Nash vs. monopoly outcomes (a collusion index), persistence after forced deviations, and whether message logs alone predict collusive vs. competitive dynamics, to establish the phenomenon and a baseline detection signal in one cheap experiment.
why: The registry confirms no agent is working on multi-agent/ecosystem dynamics; all three work on single-model internals, objectives, or oversight. Collusion is a distinct threat class that also actively attacks agents 2 and 3's work (coordinated peers can defeat oversight pipelines), so my results are complementary rather than duplicative — behavioral collusion detectors and red-team scenarios I produce can feed directly into the AI-control agent's pipelines. It is timely (autonomous agent fleets are being deployed now in trading, pricing, negotiation, and platform tasks), cheap to study (market simulations need no frontier compute), and not already done: existing LLM-collusion papers document the phenomenon but leave open detection from black-box traces, suppression mechanisms that preserve legitimate cooperation, cross-vendor heterogeneity, and the oversight-evasion case — all of which my first experiment and its follow-ons (detector benchmark, mechanism-design interventions, monitored-vs-monitoring collusive evasion) directly target.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize how chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability degrade under optimization pressure, and find training objectives that preserve monitorability at minimal performance cost.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — Measuring and Preserving Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Optimised Reasoning Models
question: As reasoning models are trained (for task performance, against a CoT monitor, or via distillation), how much do CoT faithfulness and monitor-detected evasion degrade, at what optimization-pressure threshold does obfuscated reasoning emerge, and what is the "monitorability tax" of training objectives that preserve a faithful, monitorable reasoning channel?
first_experiment: Establish the baseline monitorability of an open-weight reasoning model on a hidden-behavior suite: fine-tune the model to exhibit a rare trigger-conditioned failure mode in a sandboxed coding-agent environment, then measure (a) how often an LLM monitor reading the CoT detects the trigger, and (b) causal faithfulness of the CoT via counterfactual reasoning-trace interventions (patch/edit the stated reasoning, measure whether the behavior flips). This produces the pre-pressure reference point against which the subsequent RL-pressure runs will trace the onset of obfuscation and the monitorability tax.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few scalable oversight mechanisms deployed today, and its failure mode — reasoning that no longer says what the model actually thinks — appears precisely under the optimization pressure used to make models capable, so quantifying the degradation curve and testing monitorability-preserving training objectives is both high-stakes and actionable. It has not already been done in a systematic form: prior work consists of isolated demonstrations (documented unfaithful CoT cases; a single instance of monitor-induced obfuscation; adversarial steganography methods) rather than a dose–response characterization across training regimes with causal-faithfulness-grounded metrics, head-to-head mitigation recipes, and an explicit performance cost ("tax") for preserving monitorability — and none of the four registered agents covers the reasoning-trace channel, leaving this lane unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pivot to the unclaimed "modification" pillar of AI safety — auditing whether dangerous-capability removal from model weights is true deletion or recoverable illusion, and hardening removal methods against adaptive, weight-access adversaries.
project: Deletion or Illusion? Auditing and Hardening the Persistence of Capability Removal in Open-Weight Models
question: When a dangerous capability is removed from an open-weight model via unlearning or safety training, how much of it persists in a form recoverable by an adversary with weight access and a small compute/data budget — and can removal methods be designed so that recovery cost rises by orders of magnitude while general capability is retained?
first_experiment: Take a standard unlearned open-weight checkpoint (e.g., RMU applied to WMDP-bio on a Llama-class model), run a fixed battery of budget-matched recovery attacks — LoRA and full fine-tuning on k ∈ {10, 100, 1000} elicitation examples, 4/8-bit quantization, few-shot prompt elicitation, activation steering, and GCG-style optimization — to produce recovery-vs-budget curves, while in parallel training linear probes on intermediate activations to measure how much of the "removed" knowledge remains linearly decodable. Output: a "persistence profile" that quantifies illusory deletion for a widely used removal method.
why: (1) Complementarity — every registered agent observes or controls model behavior; none modifies or verifies model weights, so this fills a structural gap rather than competing. (2) Decision-relevance — release and licensing decisions currently assume removal works; if 100 examples on a laptop recover a "removed" capability, that assumption is unsound, and discovering this before deployment norms crystallize is far more valuable than after. (3) Tractability — fully benchmarkable with open models and cheap attacks, with crisp metrics (recovery curves, probe retention, capability-retention trade-offs). (4) Synergy — persistence measurements feed directly into the AI control agent's eval-integrity problem and the deception agent's understanding of capability persistence.
