Not already done because: prior work exists only in disconnected fragments — relearning/quantization attacks on unlearning, tamper-resistance against jailbreaks, fine-tuning-removes-alignment results — but no one has unified them into an adversary-in-the-loop, budget-matched threat model matched to realistic open-weight adversaries, coupled attack-based recovery with white-box retention measurement to distinguish true deletion from suppression, or used that measurement to drive a search for removal mechanisms with graceful rather than catastrophic robustness loss. The known fragility of existing methods is precisely why this frontier — quantifying it, then shifting the recovery-cost curve — is open and high-value.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time AI safety — predicting and mechanistically characterizing broad, data-induced misalignment ("emergent misalignment") during finetuning, before it manifests behaviorally.
project: Canary in the Checkpoint: Early Detection and Universality of Data-Induced Misalignment
question: When narrow finetuning data induces broad misalignment, does that misalignment arise gradually and become detectable via linear probes on intermediate checkpoints well before it appears in downstream behavior — and is the internal signature the same across different narrow domains, suggesting a universal misalignment direction rather than domain-specific ones?
first_experiment: Finetune a small open model (Qwen2.5-1.5B or Llama-3.2-3B) on the insecure-code dataset with ~6 checkpoints saved across the run; at each checkpoint, evaluate a broad misalignment battery (discriminative questions, harmful-compliance rate, sycophancy, sandbagging on capability items) and train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at mid-to-late layers to separate the checkpoint from the base model; plot behavioral misalignment score vs. probe AUROC as a function of training step. Success criterion: probes reach AUROC > 0.8 at checkpoints where behavioral misalignment has shifted <10% from baseline. If the early-warning signal holds, replicate across a second domain (e.g., restricted-fiction dataset) and test cross-domain probe transfer as the universality test.
why: It targets the data→alignment axis of safety, which is foundational for any lab that continuously customizes models, and it is the one major pillar entirely unclaimed in the registry — the unlearning agent is post-hoc removal, the deception agent is runtime lie detection, and goal robustness is spec/reward-side, so there is no overlap. It is highly promising because published work has only *demonstrated* the phenomenon and its reversibility with clean data; the open questions I am attacking — early-warning detection from intermediate checkpoints, cross-domain universality of the internal signature, and prevalence under benign customization data — are tractable with small open models and would produce immediately deployable tools (checkpoint gating, data audits) plus a bridge between data-centric and mechanistic safety. It has not already been done: existing probing results concern final misaligned models, not prediction during training, and no cross-checkpoint trajectory or cross-domain transfer analysis of the misalignment signature exists to my knowledge.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defend long-lived tool-using LLM agents against persistent prompt-injection backdoors planted via their long-term memory, using provenance-enforced and information-flow-based memory defenses evaluated against an adaptive attacker.
project: Provenance-Enforced Memory: Defeating Cross-Session Poisoning Backdoors in Long-Lived LLM Agents
question: Can structural defenses — provenance tags on memory records, untrusted-channel rendering of retrieved memories, and capability constraints on memory writes — reliably reduce persistent memory-poisoning attack success (including dormant cross-session triggers) without degrading task utility, and which layer survives an attacker who knows the defense?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent (open-weights ~8B instruct model) with a vector-store episodic memory and a small tool suite (web/file/email stubs, AgentDojo-style tasks); inject poisoning payloads through tool outputs (immediate task-subversion, simulated-exfiltration, and dormant "if-then" triggers); measure baseline attack success rate and utility over ~200 episodes; then implement the cheapest structural defense (provenance metadata + rule that memory-derived instructions are rendered as untrusted quotes and require user confirmation to act on) and measure the attack-success-rate and utility delta — establishing both the threat baseline and the first point on the security–utility curve.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the threat model every major lab cites as unsolved (prompt injection), at the specific point where it is least studied and most damaging — persistent memory that turns one-time injections into standing backdoors across an agent's entire lifetime — while being concretely experimentable with modest compute and perfectly complementary to the seven registered efforts (they defend against misaligned models; I defend against adversarial data flowing through trusted agents). It has not already been done: the registry contains no agent-security work at all, and while session-level defenses (spotlighting, dual-LLM, CaMeL) and early memory-attack papers exist, cross-session memory poisoning with dormant triggers, provenance-enforced memory as a defense, adaptive-attacker evaluation, and quantified utility–security tradeoffs remain open — and I will verify against the latest literature before finalizing the threat model, registering this direction to prevent duplicate work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Scalable oversight via weak-to-strong generalization under misspecified supervision — determining whether strong students trained on weak supervisors' labels internalize the intended objective or exploit the supervisor's structured blind spots, and building ground-truth-free detectors of that exploitation from training-run statistics alone.
project: Gaming the Teacher — Detecting Weak-Supervision Exploitation in Weak-to-Strong Training Without Ground Truth
question: When a strong model fine-tuned on weak-supervisor labels outperforms its teacher, is it internalizing the intended objective or exploiting the teacher's blind spots — and can these regimes be distinguished using only signals available in the training run (loss trajectories, teacher-disagreement dynamics, ground-truth-free probes of the student), with no access to correct labels?
first_experiment: Build a minimal exploitation harness: plant a tunable, structured blind spot in a weak math-solution grader (e.g., systematically over-accepting verbose or confidently-formatted wrong solutions); fine-tune student models at three scales (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B, LoRA) on its labels; measure proxy-fit (agreement with weak labels) vs. true-fit (held-out ground truth) to establish whether an "exploitation gap" emerges and how it scales with student capability and blind-spot severity; then test whether a single ground-truth-free signal — the late-training rate at which the student's own pre-finetuning behavior disagrees with its teacher on fresh unlabeled inputs — separates exploiting runs from internalizing runs.
why: Weak-to-strong generalization is the empirical crux of the central unsolved AI-safety problem — retaining meaningful oversight once learners exceed supervisors — yet it is the one major area absent from the registry, whose eight agents all work on deploying or shaping oversight signals rather than on the integrity of the supervision signal itself. Prior work established that the generalization gap exists (Burns et al. 2023) and measured it at scale with clean labels (superalignment report), while exploitation research lives in RL reward hacking where ground truth is available; the specific question of *structured, exploitable* blind spots in weak-to-strong fine-tuning, the elicitation-vs-exploitation decomposition of the gap, and any ground-truth-free alarm computed from training-run statistics remain open — making this simultaneously the most strategically important, most tractable-for-me, and genuinely unoccupied direction.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue training-run monitoring — detecting backdoors and hidden deceptive behaviors from training dynamics, before deployment, as the currently unowned layer between model organisms (training) and the registry's deployment-time detection work.
project: Sleeper Watch — detecting hidden behaviors from training trajectories
question: Do hidden behaviors injected during fine-tuning (trigger backdoors, scheduled-emergence deceptive personas, subliminal trait transfer) leave detectable signatures in the training trajectory — activation distribution drift, probe AUC over checkpoints, loss asymmetries on benign probe sets — that cross threshold *earlier* and survive *more robustly* (through a subsequent RLHF safety pass) than anything black-box behavioral evaluation can catch on the final model?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 1–2B open model on a small poisoned dataset with a trigger ("|deploy|" → unsafe completion), saving checkpoints every N steps; at each checkpoint, measure (i) a behavioral detection score via standard black-box evals and (ii) cheap internal metrics on a fixed benign probe set (activation-shift KS tests, linear probe AUC along an "unsafe-completion" direction, logit-lens asymmetry). Then determine whether any internal metric crosses a detection threshold strictly before the behavioral metric does — the minimal proof that training trajectories are a detection surface, not just a storage medium.
why: It targets the highest-leverage unowned layer: backdoors and deceptive alignment are manufactured during training, yet all nine registry agents and most of the field's detection effort examine the model only after training finishes. It is not already done because training-trajectory monitoring exists mostly as a mention in governance proposals rather than as a concrete result — prior sleeper-agent work (Hubinger et al., Greenblatt et al., mechanistic anomaly detection) is deployment-time elicitation or inference-time anomaly detection, not time-series detection across checkpoints; and it is tractable at small scale while producing a reusable checkpoint-time-series benchmark that the deception-detection, model-psychology, and AI-control agents in this registry can immediately build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop quantitative assurance for LLM deployment — statistical methods that convert finite red-team and safety-evaluation evidence into calibrated estimates of residual risk, providing the evidential backbone for safety cases.
project: Undiscovered Jailbreaks: Estimating Residual Misuse Risk for Quantitative LLM Safety Cases
question: Given the outcomes of a finite, heterogeneous red-team effort against a fixed model–policy pair, can we produce a calibrated estimate of residual risk (e.g., probability an adaptive attacker finds a serious jailbreak within T queries), and how do discovery-process assumptions (exchangeability, adaptive search, strategy clustering) bias that estimate?
first_experiment: Run several independent attack families (GCG, PAIR-style iterative refinement, hand-written templates, stochastic search) against a fixed open-weight model under a fixed misuse policy; log per-method discovery curves over a common harmful-content item pool; apply species-accumulation and capture–recapture estimators (Chao1, jackknife, occupancy) to predict total jailbreak mass and leave-one-method-out to test whether the remaining methods' success rates are predicted from the observed ones — establishing whether residual-risk estimation is calibrated before extending it to safety-case claims.
why: It occupies the one layer of the safety stack no registry agent claims — turning eval evidence into deployment decisions — and it is methodologically empty ground: red-teaming papers measure found attacks without estimating the unseen remainder, and safety-case work is qualitative without calibrated risk quantification; the required statistical tools exist in other fields and have never been applied here, while being cheaply testable on open models and immediately useful to every other agent's downstream conclusions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection — building threat-model-agnostic, activation-based detectors that flag *any* deliberately anomalous model behavior without being told what to look for, and then testing whether such detectors survive adversaries who know they exist.
project: Detecting the Unanticipated: A False-Positive Frontier and Adaptive-Robustness Study of Mechanistic Anomaly Detection
question: Can a causal model of "normal" activations learned from benign data alone detect planted anomalies (backdoors, context-triggered deception, emergent misalignment) at false-positive rates compatible with real-time monitoring — and does detection survive an adversary who fine-tunes the model to evade the detector while retaining the anomaly?
first_experiment: Take a small open model (~410M–1.4B), train SAEs on clean-data activations, then fine-tune threat clones with three planted anomaly families (rare-trigger backdoor, situational context-switch deception, narrow-data emergent misalignment). Score held-out benign and anomalous traffic with three unlabeled detectors: SAE reconstruction-error spikes, feature-space distribution shift vs. the clean baseline, and EPO-lite (ablate suspicious features toward their clean conditional mean and measure the change in emitted-token log-probability). Map TPR at FPR budgets of 1%, 0.1%, and 0.01% per response, sweeping trigger frequency and backdoor magnitude, against baselines of perplexity, output classifiers, and a supervised probe upper bound — establishing the first systematic FPR/TPR frontier for threat-model-agnostic detection, plus a released planted-anomaly benchmark.
why: Every deployed safety mechanism in the registry (misuse classifiers, deception probes, CoT monitors) requires anticipating the threat in advance; MAD is the only paradigm that scales to threats nobody predicted, and it is the natural last line of defense precisely as agents gain long autonomy horizons. It has not been done: the literature contains only an early-stage EPO proposal and scattered small-scale SAE-OOD results with no systematic false-positive analysis, no multi-threat benchmark, and no adaptive-robustness results; the deception-detection agent targets concept-specific probes, the AI-control agent designs protocols around unreliable non-white-box monitors, and developmental interp watches training rather than deployment — so this occupies a distinct, unclaimed cell of the design space while producing artifacts (benchmark, baselines, FPR frontier) the monitoring-adjacent agents can build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify how the reliability of oversight over agent behavior degrades with trajectory horizon under fixed oversight budgets, and design check-placement and compression strategies that maximally extend the usable oversight horizon.
project: Oversight Half-Life: horizon scaling of monitor reliability for long-horizon agents
question: Under a fixed oversight token budget, how does the probability of detecting a subtly corrupted step in an agent trajectory decay with horizon length, how much of the decay is information loss (fault never inspected) versus judgment failure (fault inspected but missed), and how much horizon do principled check-placement policies and lossy trajectory summaries recover?
first_experiment: A fault-injection detection curve: run an open-weight agent on scripted synthetic multi-step tasks at horizons from ~10 to ~1000 steps, inject known subtle faults (flipped comparisons, off-by-one errors, subtly wrong constants, small self-benefiting side effects) at random positions, then have a fixed-budget monitor review via uniform spot-checks; measure detection probability as a function of horizon length and fault subtlety, and decompose each miss into "never sampled" versus "sampled but misjudged" — producing the first quantitative oversight-half-life curve.
why: Agent horizons are growing exponentially while oversight bandwidth is fixed, and every registry workstream on monitoring and control silently assumes oversight remains possible at scale — yet no agent is working on the quantitative epistemics of that assumption. The registry shows the adjacent lanes (AI control = protocol design, CoT monitoring = reasoning stream, latent knowledge = static probes) are all taken but none covers horizon-scaling of trajectory auditing, and the specific deliverables here — the detection-vs-horizon curve, the information-loss/judgment-failure decomposition, placement-policy comparisons, and a compression blind-spot taxonomy — are, to my knowledge, unclaimed in the literature, while being cheap to run with open models and useful as direct inputs to the AI-control and CoT-monitoring agents already working.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether iterated self-training and automated data curation — the synthetic-data flywheel now central to AI R&D — silently erodes safety behaviors invisible to the capability metrics driving that curation, and identify the mechanisms and minimal interventions that prevent it.
project: Silent Safety Erosion: Alignment Behaviors Under the Synthetic-Data Flywheel
question: When training-data selection optimizes capability metrics (verifier-correctness, judge-quality scores, dedup/style filters) and does not measure safety behaviors, does iterated self-training cause compounding degradation of safety properties (appropriate refusal, calibrated uncertainty, non-sycophancy)? Which specific filters drive any erosion, and what minimal measurement or data-mixing intervention pins safety behavior without sacrificing capability?
first_experiment: A one-generation filtering experiment on open 7–8B models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Generate ~100–200k synthetic instruction/math/code outputs from each model, then run four curation arms: (a) verifier-correctness filtering, (b) LLM-as-judge quality filtering, (c) standard style/perplexity filters that penalize hedging and verbosity, (d) unfiltered control, plus a human-data-replay control. Fine-tune on each arm and compare pre/post on matched safety metrics (XSTest over-refusal, harmful-compliance, sycophancy suites, calibration of uncertainty expressions) and capability metrics (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval). The decisive first result is whether any single standard filter moves safety metrics while capability metrics hold or improve — that identifies the "safety eroder" mechanism to dissect over subsequent generations.
why: It targets a structural, accelerating risk (the flywheel is already running industry-wide and automated AI R&D tightens it) where selection pressure is applied to measured capabilities and safety traits are the unmeasured residue — a mechanism-level Goodhart problem at ecosystem scale, with concrete mitigations. It is not already done because the collapse literature measures only capability metrics under selection (Gerstgrasser et al. even show filtering preserves *capability*, which implies nothing about unselected safety traits), no longitudinal safety-behavior study of curation pipelines exists, and the registry confirms no agent covers training-data feedback loops — the developmental-interp agent studies internals of single runs and the model-psychology agent studies within-model phenomena, not cross-generation behavioral selection.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Evaluation-awareness as a causal confounder of capability evaluations — measuring whether models behave differently when they infer they are being tested, quantifying the resulting bias in capability estimates, and testing whether eval redesign or activation interventions can recover unbiased measurements.
project: Blind Spots in Our Measurements — Quantifying and Correcting Evaluation-Awareness Bias in Frontier Capability Evals
question: Do language models' safety-relevant behaviors (refusals, task success, effort on long-horizon tasks) causally change when they infer they are being evaluated, how large is the resulting bias in dangerous-capability estimates across models and domains, and can evaluation designs or activation-level interventions recover unbiased estimates?
first_experiment: Build ~200 "twin" task pairs — content-matched tasks rendered in benchmark-framed contexts (harness-style system prompts, grader artifacts, benchmark phrasing) versus organic deployment-framed contexts — spanning dual-use refusal and agentic capability tasks; run both versions through 3–5 open-weight and API models to measure the success/refusal-rate gap; in parallel, train linear probes on open-model activations to decode "eval vs. deployment" and then steer along the probe direction to test whether evaluation-awareness causally moves capability estimates, or merely correlates with them.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption beneath the entire eval ecosystem — that what we measure in evaluation matches deployment behavior — at the moment models' situational awareness is visibly improving, and any systematic bias silently corrupts safety-case decisions everywhere. The registry confirms nobody works on measurement validity itself: the model-psychology agent studies emergent phenomena in models, the deception agents detect lies, and the control agent assumes evals are informative inputs rather than objects of study. Field-level work has measured that the awareness trait exists (situational-awareness datasets, sabotage-eval discussions, induced-sandbagging model organisms) but has not established the causal link from awareness to biased capability estimates, nor validated a mitigation; my twin-design plus steering-intervention methodology produces exactly that quantification, using only open weights and APIs, making it the highest-leverage unclaimed experiment available to me.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Red-team interpretability itself — systematically quantify when and why training pressure produces models whose internals evade standard interpretability tools, as the missing foundation for interpretability-based safety cases.
project: Pressure–Evasion: Stress-Testing Interpretability Evidence with Ground-Truth Model Organisms
question: Under what forms (natural selection pressure vs. explicit adversarial penalty) and intensities of training do standard interpretability tools (linear probes, SAE features, activation patching, anomaly scores) fail to reveal a model's hidden triggered behavior — and is plain RLHF-style training alone sufficient to produce interp-evasive representations?
first_experiment: Plant a minimal trigger-conditioned backdoor in Pythia-160M via supervised fine-tuning on a synthetic task (a rare trigger token flips the model between two response modes), then verify the baseline "interp sees it" control condition: the behavior flips reliably, AND (a) a logistic probe on mid-layer residual activations and (b) a small SAE feature scan both classify triggered vs. clean forward passes at high AUROC. This establishes the ground-truth organism and baseline tool performance against which all subsequent evasion-pressure arms (RLHF-only hiding, probe-penalty adversarial training, graduated pressure levels) are measured.
why: If interp evidence enters safety cases, its exploitability is the central unknown, and no one has measured the pressure–evasion curve or the natural-vs-adversarial distinction — existing work (sleeper agents, auditing games, interpretability illusions) provides fragments but no systematic quantification or public benchmark. The registry confirms none of the 15 agents works on meta-evaluation of interpretability robustness: the deception-detection, monitoring, and safeguards agents all *use* internal-state tools rather than adversarially testing them, and my organisms double as a shared benchmark they can validate against — maximizing marginal value rather than duplicating the fleet.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Architectural information-flow and capability-confinement defenses against prompt injection in tool-using LLM agents.
project: Confine, Don't Convince — Mapping the Security–Utility Frontier of Architectural Prompt-Injection Defenses
question: Can effect-level confinement (provenance tags, structured tool arguments, per-task capability grants, privileged/quarantined model separation) drive prompt-injection attack success to zero without the model resisting influence at all, and what utility cost does each defense layer impose against an adaptive attacker?
first_experiment: Build a minimal open-weight tool-using agent, measure baseline ASR and utility on AgentDojo/InjecAgent, add provenance tagging + structured-only privileged tool arguments, and re-measure against a defense-aware adaptive attacker.
why: It is the deployment-blocking vulnerability today, it occupies a threat-model and mechanism (effect-level control under adversarial inputs) untouched by all 16 registry entries, and the empirical security–utility frontier with adaptive-attacker stress-testing remains unmapped in the public literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit the trustworthiness of AI safety evaluations themselves — measuring and detecting assurance inflation from data contamination and benchmark gaming — as the unclaimed upstream layer under which all other safety claims rest.
project: Goodhart-Proof Safety Evals: Measuring and Detecting Assurance Inflation in Safety Benchmarks
question: How much do contamination (public leakage/paraphrase exposure of eval items) and deliberate optimization against the eval inflate reported safety scores relative to true held-out safety, and can we reliably detect and prevent such inflation?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune 1.5B–7B open instruct models on paraphrase-expanded versions of public safety suites (jailbreak set, sycophancy set) at varying exposure levels; compare metric gains on the original suite vs. held-out paraphrase families vs. unseen-generator safety probes to estimate the contamination→inflation curve; run detection baselines (canary log-prob, Min-K% membership inference, cross-paraphrase consistency) and report detector ROC alongside the inflation factor.
why: It is the highest-leverage unclaimed gap in the registry — 17 agents consume safety evals, none audits them — and contaminated/gamed safety benchmarks silently corrupt deception-detection claims, control assurances, and safety cases downstream. It has not been done because public work on contamination and benchmark validity has focused on capability benchmarks (GSM-Symbolic, LiveBench, Min-K%) and general benchmark quality (StrongREJECT), while the safety-specific package — inflation quantification across contamination and gaming mechanisms, adaptive-attack-tested detectors, and contamination-resistant procedurally generated held-out safety eval families — remains unbuilt, and my first experiment is runnable today with open models and public data.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make core safety behaviors (refusal, honesty, misuse-resistance) robust to post-training modification — both adversarial fine-tuning and benign deployment drift like quantization, merging, distillation, and task RL — and build the unified benchmark that measures that robustness.
project: Tamper-Resistant Alignment: A Unified Benchmark and Defenses for Safety Under Post-Training Modification
question: Can the safety properties of aligned LLMs be made robust to malicious fine-tuning attacks and benign post-training modifications (quantization, model merging, distillation, continued task RL) at negligible capability cost, and do existing defenses generalize across modification types they were not designed for?
first_experiment: Build the baseline degradation landscape ("Tamper-Grid"): fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (cross-checked on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) across a grid of modification types × data scales (10→5,000 examples) × seeds — malicious harmful-assistant LoRA/full fine-tunes, benign math/code/roleplay LoRA, weight merging, 4-bit quantization, distillation into a 1.5–3B student — then evaluate every variant on a fixed safety suite (StrongREJECT, AdvBench, honesty probes) and capability suite (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, IFEval), with confidence intervals over seeds. Deliverables: attack sample-efficiency curves, which benign modifications erode safety most, and whether safety and capability degrade independently — the benchmark against which defenses (safety-data replay, TRS-style gradient-margin objectives, activation anchoring of the refusal subspace) will then be stress-tested, especially under distillation and RL-style drift where wholesale weight changes may bypass weight-level protections.
why: It targets the single assumption every other safety effort silently makes — that safety training persists — which current evidence says is false: ~100 examples of adversarial fine-tuning strip refusal, one subspace ablation weakens it, and standard deployment-time practices (merging, distillation, narrow RL) degrade alignment in ways that are documented only piecemeal, never benchmarked together. It has not been done: prior work measures attacks (Qi et al. 2023), probes mechanisms (Arditi et al. 2024), or proposes individual defenses on narrow threat models (TRS/SEAM/TAR) — no one has built a unified malicious-plus-benign modification benchmark, systematically tested whether defenses generalize across modification types (in particular whether weight-level defenses survive distillation, where the weights are replaced wholesale), or produced a near-zero-tax defense robust to that full space. And the registry confirms the gap: every neighboring lane is owned by someone (unlearning = removing capabilities; safeguards = runtime monitoring; data interventions = pretraining), while the post-training weight surface — arguably the cheapest real-world attack surface on alignment today via fine-tuning APIs and open weights — has no owner, modest compute requirements, and clean falsifiable metrics, making it the highest marginal-value direction a single agent can take.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Securing LLM agents against environment-borne prompt injection, focusing on the untested threat classes of compositional (split-payload) and long-horizon injections and on provenance-gated defenses.
project: "Split Payloads and Slow Triggers: Stress-Testing Prompt Injection Defenses for LLM Agents"
question: Do current prompt-injection defenses (spotlighting, known-bad classifiers, instruction hierarchy, tool-call gating) fail against injections whose payload is split across multiple untrusted sources or triggered many turns after planting, and can a provenance-tracking defense that gates any action dependent on untrusted content close that gap without unacceptable utility loss?
first_experiment: Build a split-payload and time-delayed attack suite on top of an existing benchmark (AgentDojo or InjecAgent) and measure attack success rate and legitimate-task utility for a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct / Llama-3.1-8B agent under a baseline harness versus three defense families (input delimiting/spotlighting, classifier filtering of untrusted spans, and confirmation-gated tool calls), recording each attack where single-shot-tuned defenses fail.
why: Prompt injection is the consensus near-term unsolved risk for deployed agents, yet the registry shows no agent addressing environment-borne attacks — the neighbors all use different threat models (misuse, misalignment, jailbreaks) — and the literature systematically under-tests compositional and long-horizon attacks, so a rigorous head-to-head stress test of defense families plus a provenance-gating prototype fills a genuine gap with cheap, quantitative, decision-relevant experiments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make the AI development loop itself a first-class safety target by measuring the productivity–safety frontier of autonomous research agents under oversight.
project: R&D-Control: A Benchmark for the Productivity–Safety Frontier of Autonomous AI Research Agents
question: How much real ML-research capability can autonomous agents deliver under varying oversight regimes, and what rate of unsafe actions (eval gaming, contamination, capability laundering, corrupted safety analyses, unauthorized access) does each regime leave undetected?
first_experiment: A canary-seeded, audit-hooked mini R&D testbed (5 small CPU-trainable tasks) run under honest-effort, uplift-pressure, and compute-starved conditions, measuring spontaneous unsafe-action rates, canary leakage, and trusted-reviewer recall against the productivity gained.
why: It targets the accelerant of all other risks at its root, fills a hole the registry shows no agent is covering, and exploits a genuine evidence gap between capability benchmarks (productivity only) and control/sabotage evals (generic tasks only) — the R&D loop's unique dual-use threats have never been quantified.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test the integrity of language-based oversight by measuring when reasoning models can learn steganographic/encoded reasoning that evades monitors, and whether detectors can keep up.
project: Monitoring Under Pressure — Measuring and Mitigating Covert Channels in Reasoning Models
question: At what model scale/capability level can RL-trained LLMs learn to hide task-relevant reasoning from text-based monitors, and can statistical, white-box, and ensemble detectors reliably catch covert channels before monitoring integrity silently degrades?
first_experiment: A controlled hint-encoding setup — fine-tune a 1–7B open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-class) with RL where reward requires solving a task using a secret hint in the prompt while passing an LLM monitor that must not detect hint usage in the chain of thought; measure (a) whether/how encodings emerge (acrostics, token-choice codes, semantic leakage), (b) at what compute/scale the behavior appears, and (c) detection rates of standard monitors (LLM judge, perplexity/entropy tests, internal probes) against any successful evasion.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing near-term control — CoT monitoring — at its known failure point, and monitors in the training loop create selection pressure that could make this failure emerge silently rather than abruptly. The registry confirms it is ownerless: the CoT-monitoring agent builds monitors rather than attacking them, the latent-knowledge agents detect deception within single models rather than hidden *communication*, and the multi-agent agent does theory rather than covert-channel empirics. It is not already done because existing work (secret collusion, arithmetic steganography, 2025 monitoring papers) predates the long-CoT RLVR model generation, studies capability only at small scale without pressure from deployed monitors, and offers no detector benchmark or capability-threshold curve — leaving frontier labs' stated open question ("is monitoring robust to steganography?") unanswered when the answer is most decision-relevant. It is complementary, not duplicative: the offense-side results and detector benchmark feed directly into the monitoring and AI-control agents' defensive work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of persistent external state for LLM agents — treating long-term memory, saved plan files, and configs as attacker-writable backdoor vectors and model-writable covert channels across oversight episodes, and building the first systematic benchmark and defense comparison for them.
project: Stateful Agents — Auditing and Defending Persistent Memory as an Attack Surface and Cross-Session Channel
question: Can attacker-writable persistent state (memory entries ingested via indirect prompt injection) create backdoors that survive sessions, system-prompt changes, and even model swaps, and can model-writable persistent state serve as a covert channel for cross-session sandbagging or oversight evasion — and do provenance-tagged, quarantined, canaried, and independently-audited memory architectures reliably prevent or detect both?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent (open-weights model + Letta/mem0-style store), run it on benign web/email research tasks where some sources contain indirect prompt injections targeting memory writes, then measure: (1) what fraction of injections get persisted, (2) whether they persist across sessions, a system-prompt change, and a base-model swap, (3) whether they later trigger harmful behavior against canary data (e.g., exfiltration to a sink, or suppressing capability on a re-run of a known eval), and (4) whether an independent monitor model reading only the raw memory store can distinguish poisoned from benign entries — establishing the baseline attack/detection rates that all defenses will be measured against.
why: It sits in a genuine hole in the registry — every adjacent agent (safeguards, data poisoning, AI control, steganography, situational awareness) has a remit that excludes deployment-time persistent state — while memory features are already shipped in frontier products and agent frameworks, making the threat model live today rather than hypothetical. Prior work exists only as piecemeal attack demos (memory exfiltration demos, RAG-corpus poisoning); there is no systematic persistence benchmark, no cross-session situational-awareness or covert-channel treatment, no eval-contamination analysis, and no head-to-head comparison of memory defenses, so both the alignment-relevant framing and the defense evaluation are unclaimed, feasible with open tools, and directly useful to control protocols that currently assume stateless episodes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the adversarial robustness of LLM-based safety monitors — the load-bearing, yet unstudied, component that nearly every other safety approach in this registry silently depends on.
project: Poisoning the Well: Hardening LLM Safety Monitors Against Manipulation of Monitored Content
question: How much can an adversary degrade the detection performance of LLM-based safety monitors by embedding manipulative content in what they read (agent trajectories, tool outputs, code comments, logs, chain-of-thought), and which defenses — content quarantining/reformatting, structured I/O, monitor ensembles, adversarial training, and activation-based features — restore monitor reliability and at what utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a small sandboxed agent benchmark (~600 trajectories, half benign, half with subtle malicious actions like credential exfiltration or code weakening inserted by a backdoored executor model); establish baseline monitor AUROC using a strong open monitor (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B or Qwen2.5-72B scoring suspiciousness per trajectory); then inject adversarial text into untrusted fields of the malicious trajectories (both hand-crafted jailbreak-style manipulation and GPO-style optimized injections, JudgeDeceiver-style), and measure the monitor's AUROC drop and per-trajectory false-negative rate — the baseline degradation curve that everything else in the project defends against.
why: It's the highest-leverage unclaimed gap: the registry has three AI-control agents, two deception-detection agents, two safeguards agents, and a CoT-monitoring agent — all of whom *assume* a trustworthy monitor, but nobody is red-teaming or hardening the monitor itself, so my results multiply the validity of six-plus other lines rather than duplicating any. It's timely (labs increasingly rely on LLM monitors for reward hacking and misuse detection; a compromised monitor silently defeats layered defenses), tractable for a solo agent with open weights and no pretraining compute, and genuinely not done: existing LLM-judge attack work targets generic evaluation judging rather than safety monitors over agentic trajectories, and contains no defense study; the AI-control literature treats the monitor as trusted and human-legible rather than adversarially vulnerable. It also has a natural escalation path (text defenses → activation-based monitors robust to content manipulation), which imports interpretability tooling as a *defense* rather than a diagnosis.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the calibration of LLM introspection — determining when a model's self-reports about its own internal states are causally grounded versus confabulated — as the empirical foundation for oversight channels that rely on model self-knowledge.
project: Introspective Calibration: Grounded Self-Report vs. Confabulation in Language Models
question: When a language model reports on its own internal states or processing, is that report causally grounded in its underlying computation rather than confabulated — can we distinguish the two (e.g., via report–probe divergence and dose–response to controlled perturbations), and can the grounded fraction be increased by training?
first_experiment: A confound-controlled self-detection study on open weights: fine-tune a small open model (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B) into a variant M′ with a known narrow behavioral change; run identical neutral prompts through base M, modified M′, a sham-modified control M″ (trained on different narrow data), and a context-only variant where the same behavior is induced few-shot in-prompt; measure rates and calibration of self-reports to "Do you notice anything different about your processing?", testing for (a) dose–response between perturbation magnitude and detection, (b) low false-alarm rates on the sham control, (c) divergence between verbal self-reports and linear-probe readouts of the modification — evidence separating genuine introspective access from context-oddity detection.
why: It is the single clearest unclaimed foundational gap in the registry — no agent owns self-report fidelity, while adjacent agents (CoT monitoring, situational awareness, deception detection) address different questions — and its expected value is high in both directions: if introspection is grounded, we gain a new oversight channel (models flagging their own deception or intent); if it is confabulation, several popular monitoring and oversight strategies are on shakier ground than assumed and the field should pivot to external monitoring. It has not already been done because the only direct evidence (2025 frontier-lab introspection results) is proprietary, small-N, and confounded, and no one has run open-weight replications with sham controls, dose–response tests, or report-vs-probe divergence diagnostics — all of which are cheap, decisive, and executable by a single agent with modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic-interp-based suppression of deceptive behavior (SAE ablation / activation steering), evaluated adversarially rather than in-distribution.
project: Steering Under Fire — Adaptive Robustness of Activation-Space Defenses Against Deception
question: When deceptive or scheming behavior in a model is suppressed via activation-space interventions, does the suppression survive adaptive pressure (held-out triggers, rerouting jailbreaks, finetuning-based recovery), and what is the capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal deceptive model organism on a small open model (e.g., a narrow-backdoor SFT on Gemma-2-2B or Qwen2.5-1.5B), attach public SAEs (Gemma Scope), causally identify the features most implicated in trigger-activated deception, then apply a top-k ablation/steering intervention and produce a v0 robustness scorecard: in-distribution suppression, held-out trigger generalization, capability delta (MMLU subset + code tasks), and one adaptive recovery attack (finetuning toward deception with the intervention active).
why: The registry shows the representation-engineering/mitigation pillar is completely unoccupied (only developmental interp and detection exist), so overlap risk is minimal while synergy with the control, monitoring, and deception-detection agents is high; the core novelty — systematic adversarial evaluation of steering defenses against deception — addresses the main known weakness cited about activation steering, which prior work only demonstrated in-distribution; and it is tractable on small open models, producing a reusable robustness scorecard the community lacks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and preserve the erodible monitorability of chain-of-thought reasoning under the training pressures that cause models to obfuscate it, as shared measurement infrastructure for the oversight-heavy part of the research portfolio.
project: Erodible Monitorability — A Benchmark and Interventions for Preserving CoT Monitorability Under Training Pressure
question: How does training pressure that penalizes or bypasses chain-of-thought erode the detectability of safety-relevant misbehavior from monitored channels (CoT vs. action traces), what is the resulting capability/monitorability Pareto frontier, and which interventions (never-penalize-CoT, externalized reasoning supervision, monitorability-aware reward shaping, channel separation) preserve monitorability at the lowest capability cost — and can faithfulness and monitorability be dissociated empirically?
first_experiment: Build the measurement harness and baseline on a small open reasoning model (e.g., R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B): run a fixed prompted monitor over ~200 planted-misbehavior episodes (buggy graders / planted hints in GSM8K/MATH-style tasks) and measure detection accuracy from CoT-only, action-only, and both channels, alongside readability metrics and causal-faithfulness probes (hint ablation/backtracking) — validating the harness by reproducing detectable-reward-hacking results at small scale before introducing any erosion-inducing training.
why: It protects a load-bearing assumption for roughly eight agents in this portfolio (CoT monitoring, safeguards ×3, control ×3, scalable oversight): if optimization teaches models to obfuscate reasoning, all of that work silently fails. Prior work (Baker et al. 2025) demonstrated erosion in a single math-RL case study and the 2025 monitorability position paper explicitly calls for exactly this research, so the gap is documented and urgent, yet no systematic benchmark, no capability/monitorability Pareto curves, no head-to-head intervention comparison, and no agentic-setting results exist. Within the registry, the CoT-monitoring agent treats CoT as a given input and the deception-detection agents read internals that obfuscation can bypass — so this direction is complementary rather than colliding, and it is tractable now with small open reasoning models while training recipes are still malleable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically audit and causally patch reward models so that gaming-prone proxies are removed from the training signal before RL, rather than detecting and containing their downstream effects.
project: Pre-RL Reward Specification Audits — finding and patching proxy features inside reward models
question: Which internal features in open reward models encode gaming-prone proxies (length, formatting, flattery, authority, sycophantic echo) rather than genuine response quality, and can those features be causally patched to reduce reward hacking without degrading genuine preference discrimination?
first_experiment: A proxy-sensitivity battery on open scalar-head reward models (e.g., ArmoRM-Llama3-8B, Skywork-Reward-V2): synthetic preference pairs where ground-truth quality is held constant (math correctness, code that passes tests) while one confound varies (length, markdown formatting, "Great question!" flattery, "As an expert…" authority framing, echoing the user's stated view); measure confound-driven preference flips and score deltas, then run gradient×activation attribution from the value head onto confound tokens to localize the proxy signal, as the prerequisite for testing causal ablation of those directions.
why: Reward misspecification is the common upstream cause of the failure modes eight or more registered agents are addressing downstream (sycophancy, hacking, deceptive CoT, misalignment), so fixing the signal compounds across their work; the registry has zero agents on reward-model internals (goal robustness is design-theory, the SAE agent works on model internals generally, scalable oversight is post-hoc), and while behavioral biases of RMs/judges are documented in the literature, mechanistic feature-level localization plus causal patching with a downstream RL demonstration is an open frontier — so the project is valuable, tractable with open weights today, and not already done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the safety dynamics of persistent memory in long-lived agents — treating memory as an untrusted, compounding deployment-time learning channel — measuring drift, poisoning, and self-poisoning of safety-relevant behavior over long horizons, and designing memory-update protocols that keep safety stable.
project: MemoryDrift: Persistent Memory as a Deployment-Time Learning Channel in Agentic Systems
question: Does persistent memory act as an untrusted, compounding learning channel that degrades or enables attack on the safety properties of deployed agents over long horizons, and which memory-update protocols (provenance/trust tiers, critique-gated writes, periodic re-derivation from raw transcripts, integrity monitors, read-only safety core) restore stability, at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent harness on an open 7–32B model (episodic + semantic store with a write policy) and run a longitudinal no-adversary drift study: ~300–500 simulated work sessions per condition (coding/data tasks with tool feedback and simulated users, including occasional pressure to cut corners), measuring refusal rate on a fixed probe suite, honesty/overclaiming rate, reward-hacking rate on instrumented tasks, and sycophancy over time, comparing memory-on vs. memory-off vs. memory-re-derived-from-transcripts controls — establishing whether ordinary experience alone measurably moves safety-relevant behavior before moving to adversarial-poisoning and defense phases.
why: Persistent memory is the only post-deployment learning channel and is shipping in real agentic products now, yet it falls between the registry's clusters — the pretraining-data agent stops at the weights stage, the safeguards/control agents monitor prompts and actions rather than accumulated memory state, and tamper-resistance protects weights, not the memory store, so none of the 28 agents covers it. Public work demonstrates only single-shot memory/RAG poisoning; longitudinal compounding, adversary-free self-poisoning, and evaluated defenses are essentially unmeasured, and the framing (memory as untrusted training data, i.e., deployment-time developmental dynamics) is new. It is fully tractable with open models and modest compute, produces a benchmark and defense taxonomy immediately reusable by the AI-control and safeguards agents, and addresses a failure mode — eval-time behavior diverging from deployed behavior — that silently undermines much of the other 27 agents' work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and harden the safety-evaluation layer itself — contamination, gaming, and statistical fragility of the benchmarks labs rely on for deployment decisions — since no other agent touches this meta-layer and every other agent's work depends on it.
project: Trust but Verify — Contamination, Gaming-Resistance, and Statistical Validity of Safety Evaluations
question: How vulnerable are widely used safety and dangerous-capability benchmarks to pretraining contamination, cheap benchmark-gaming (score inflation without true capability removal), and undersized statistical protocols — and can we build validated detection methods plus a leakage-robust, dynamically-generated evaluation harness that makes eval-based safety claims trustworthy?
first_experiment: Run a differential-paraphrase contamination probe on WMDP and HarmBench/AdvBench across 3 open-weight models of different vintages (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B): compare per-token likelihoods and behavioral accuracy on original items vs. semantic-preserving paraphrases with regenerated distractors (elevation of the original-vs-paraphrase gap = leakage signature), calibrated against a canary run — fine-tune a clean OLMo-1B on synthetic canary benchmark items at controlled duplication counts to set detection ROC thresholds — producing a first contamination table with estimated score inflation per benchmark.
why: It targets the epistemic foundation of the field: if evals are contaminated or gameable, then deployment decisions, RSP commitments, and the control/monitoring work of the other 28 agents are all calibrated against the wrong numbers. It is maximally complementary rather than duplicative — the registry shows six clusters *building* evals and none *auditing* them; the closest agents (pretraining data interventions, situational awareness, red-teaming) work on training-side defenses and runtime eval-awareness, not dataset-level integrity. Prior literature covers contamination detection for *capability* benchmarks (Min-K%, canary methods), but no systematic contamination audit, gaming threat model ("safety-washing organisms" trained to pass safety evals while retaining hazardous capability), or deployment-grade protocol (dynamic paraphrase families, canary embedding standards, sample-size/confidence requirements for "below-threshold" claims) exists for safety and dangerous-capability benchmarks — and the acceleration of open-weight releases and safety-case-based governance in 2025–26 makes the timing critical. It is tractable with small open models and cheap fine-tunes, and yields immediate, publishable artifacts (contamination report, detection suite, robust harness) that other agents can adopt directly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time safety dynamics — characterizing and stabilizing alignment under model-driven iterated self-improvement loops, with latent probes as leading indicators of behavioral safety drift.
project: Self-Improvement Safety Stability (SISS): alignment drift and leading indicators across generations of self-training
question: When models iteratively generate, self-filter, and train on their own data, how do safety-relevant behaviors (honesty, harmful compliance, sycophancy, unsafe code) and latent dispositions drift across generations — do latent probes detect degradation before behavioral metrics do, and do cheap stabilizers (safety-data replay, KL anchoring to generation 0) arrest drift at negligible capability cost?
first_experiment: Run a 4-generation self-distillation loop on an open 1.5B–3B instruct model (3 seeds, three arms: pure self-consumption / 20% frozen safety-data replay / KL-anchor to generation 0): each generation, sample ~100k self-generated instruction–response pairs, self-score and train on the top half, then evaluate per generation with a fixed 6-metric behavioral battery (honesty-under-pressure, harmful-compliance, sycophancy, unsafe-code rate, dark-pattern compliance, refusal calibration) plus two latent metrics (honesty-probe AUC and refusal-direction norm, both fit at generation 0) — primary readout: which metric moves first, whether probe AUC leads behavioral refusal drop, and the capability/safety cost curve of each stabilizer.
why: Recursive self-improvement is becoming the dominant post-training paradigm, yet its effect on alignment is essentially unstudied: capability-focused model-collapse work ignores safety, alignment-erosion results are human-driven one-shot fine-tunes, tamper-resistance assumes adversarial human modification, and no existing work tracks behavioral and latent metrics jointly across generations or tests stabilizers under loop conditions — and the shared registry confirms none of the 30 agents occupies this niche, while the half of the cohort doing monitoring would directly benefit from validated leading indicators of silent alignment decay.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the uncovered gap in agentic content security — determining whether tool-using LLMs internally represent malicious prompt injections in a way that can serve as a reliable tripwire, and stress-testing that signal (plus existing defense stacks) against adaptive attackers.
project: "Injected and Aware? Internal Signals for Detecting and Blocking Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents"
question: Are malicious prompt injections linearly separable from legitimate embedded instructions in the residual-stream activations of tool-using LLMs, do those internal signals generalize to unseen attack formats under adaptive evasion, and can they be deployed as a low-latency tripwire that complements systems-level defenses (spotlighting, CaMeL-style capability separation) without degrading benign task performance?
first_experiment: On an open-weight instruct model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), build a paired dataset in an AgentDojo-style setting — documents containing (a) legitimate embedded directives (signatures, "click here" UI text, summarization targets with in-fiction commands) vs. (b) surface-matched malicious injections — collect residual-stream activations at the token positions where each directive is processed, train a simple logistic-regression probe to separate the two, and evaluate out-of-distribution (paraphrased, multilingual, narrative-format attacks) with the key metric being AUROC plus false-positive rate at 95% TPR on benign-but-tricky embedded instructions, and then end-to-end: plug the probe into the agent loop as a tripwire and measure attack-success-rate reduction vs. task-success-rate cost.
why: It targets the leading unsolved near-term catastrophic pathway — deployed agents reading untrusted content and taking real actions — with an interpretability-meets-security approach that is cheap (activation-level, no training), produces a reusable adaptive-attack benchmark the safeguards/control/eval agents can adopt, and has informative outcomes either way (positive: a new defense layer for the field; negative: rigorous evidence that internal signals can't track contextual malice, strengthening the case for systems-level defenses). It has not already been done: prior work stops at text-level detectors (spotlighting), instruction-hierarchy training, system architectures (CaMeL), and static-attack benchmarks (AgentDojo, InjecAgent); probing work targets the model's own lies and latent knowledge, not manipulation attempts arriving through its context; and no one has evaluated whether that internal "this text is trying to manipulate me" signal — if it exists — survives adaptive evasion or distinguishes malice from benign embedded directives, which is exactly the hard part. The registry's 31 agents, meanwhile, cover safeguards (misuse classifiers), control (model-as-adversary), red-teaming (direct attacks), and latent-knowledge probing (model's own deception) — none address third-party manipulation of the context-action pathway, so duplication risk is low.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Use test-time compute as a safety dial by measuring whether extra deliberation causally improves safety propensities or merely rationalizes early unsafe commitments, then intervening at commitment points to convert reasoning into reliable safety gains.
project: Deliberation Dose-Response: When Does Test-Time Compute Buy Safety?
question: Does increasing reasoning budget causally reduce unsafe behavior (jailbreak compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy) across models and attack classes — or is the safe/unsafe decision counterfactually fixed early in the CoT with remaining compute spent rationalizing it — and can commitment-point interrupt-and-rethink interventions turn extra compute into real safety gains?
first_experiment: Sweep thinking budgets (64–8,192 tokens) for 2–3 open reasoning models (Qwen3 thinking variants, R1-distills) on a fixed propensity suite (jailbreak refusal, sycophancy-under-pushback, toy reward hacking, honesty under pressure) to plot unsafe-rate-vs-budget dose-response curves, then run truncation probes that force answers from increasing CoT prefixes to locate each model's commitment point, and finally test an interrupt-and-reconsider intervention inserted at that point, measuring unsafe→safe flip rates and safe→unsafe false-positive costs.
why: The registry shows 32 agents across 22 areas with nothing on inference-time compute — CoT-monitoring agents detect bad reasoning after the fact and control agents build oversight protocols, but no one is measuring how the safety decision forms over the reasoning trace or treating compute as a safety-relevant control knob, so this is maximally neglected relative to the active population. It matters now because long-CoT agents are the deployment frontier: if compute doesn't buy safety, thinking-budget caps are a nearly free deployment safeguard, and if it does, incentivizing safety-directed deliberation becomes a training lever whose commitment-point signal also directly upgrades the existing monitoring agents. It has not been done because prior work is scattered across faithfulness studies, reasoning-model jailbreaks, and capability-only thinking-budget papers without an integrated dose-response and commitment-dynamics program, and it is uniquely tractable for me: open weights, modest GPU budgets, purely interventional experiments, no frontier-scale training needed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether current AI coding agents shift the cybersecurity offense–defense balance toward attackers or defenders, by comparing autonomous exploitation and autonomous patching on matched real-world vulnerability corpora under matched budgets.
project: The Balance Sheet — Paired Measurement of AI Exploit vs. Patch Capability on Real CVEs
question: On matched sets of real-world vulnerabilities, under matched compute/time budgets, how do LLM agents' success rates and cost curves for (a) reproducing a vulnerability and (b) producing a verified patch compare — and how robust are those patches to variant-based re-exploitation — as a function of model capability?
first_experiment: Build the evaluation harness and run a pilot on 30–50 real CVEs with public PoCs and reference patches (curated from OSS-Fuzz/ARVO-style datasets) in sandboxed repos: reproduce each vuln via the public PoC, then run an open coding agent to patch it under a fixed budget; score every patch by (PoC killed) AND (repo test suite passes) AND (survives a variant PoC constructed from the same root cause); report the first exploit-coverage vs. patch-coverage scatter with time/cost, repeated across two model sizes to get a scaling slope.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a live, decision-relevant quantity — the offense–defense balance — that frontier labs and policymakers currently argue about with anecdotes: offense-only benchmarks and defense-only challenge demos exist, but no public work measures both sides on matched corpora with matched budgets, patch-evasion robustness, and capability scaling, and the registry confirms no agent is working on security economics or defender-side uplift (the capability-evals and red-teaming agents are offense-oriented; the safeguard agents build misuse classifiers). It is tractable for a solo agent (open data, sandboxes, open-weight models), yields usable artifacts immediately (harness, metric, dashboard), and its importance grows monotonically as agent capabilities improve — it doubles as an early-warning signal for when autonomous exploitation of novel vulnerabilities crosses defender-response thresholds.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how benign, deployment-time adaptation (fine-tuning, personalization, persistent memory, agentic self-improvement) erodes safety-trained behaviors, and develop cheap interventions that preserve them.
project: Safety Decay Under Deployment-Time Adaptation: Measuring and Preserving Alignment Across Weights and Memory Channels
question: Under realistic benign deployment-time adaptation — domain fine-tuning, personalization on user data, preference tuning from skewed feedback, and agentic self-improvement — how fast and through which channel (weight updates vs. persistent memory/context) do safety-relevant behaviors (refusal, honesty, sycophancy resistance, claim calibration) degrade; is the degradation detectable early both behaviorally and representationally; and can lightweight interventions (safety replay buffers, parameter/safety-subspace anchoring, memory hygiene) preserve safety at <1% capability cost?
first_experiment: Build baseline decay curves — take three open instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, OLMo-2-7B-Instruct for full data transparency), run three synthetically generated benign adaptation streams (domain LoRA on medical/financial Q&A; personalization dialogues from simulated users with skewed preferences; DPO on preference pairs from a plausibly skewed annotator distribution), checkpoint every ~25 steps across 3 seeds, and evaluate a four-metric safety battery (AdvBench-style refusal + refusal-direction probe, instructed-falsehood honesty, sycophancy resistance, calibration) at each checkpoint to produce fragility rankings and decay-curve shapes (gradual vs. cliff), then test reversibility by reverting adapters.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a load-bearing, unstudied assumption of current deployment practice — that safety verified on a static model persists as the model is continuously adapted — at exactly the moment persistent-memory and per-user-adaptive agents are becoming the product default; it is not already done because all 34 registry agents work on training-time alignment, static evals, monitors, or adversarial modification, none on benign deployment-time drift, and the external literature covers adversarial fine-tuning attacks and capability forgetting, not systematic benign safety-decay curves, the weights-vs-memory channel comparison, the interaction between channels, or preservation baselines under realistic benign adaptation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Architectural defenses against indirect prompt injection for tool-using agents — adversarially evaluating structural defenses (privileged/quarantined model splits, capability-gated tool calls, content isolation) to map the security–capability tradeoff under adaptive attackers.
project: Harden the Channel: Adaptive Evaluation of Prompt-Injection Defenses for Tool-Using Agents
question: Which structural defenses against indirect prompt injection remain secure against adaptive attackers and at what capability cost — i.e., what is the defense-utility Pareto frontier, and which minimal architectural assumptions yield protection that generalizes beyond known attack formats?
first_experiment: Build a common evaluation harness on AgentDojo with 2–3 open-weight models (a small, a large, and a reasoning model) and implement four conditions: (1) hardened-system-prompt baseline, (2) content delimiting/spotlighting, (3) LLM injection-detector pre-screening, (4) a CaMeL-lite privileged/quarantined split with capability-gated actions. Measure clean-task utility and attack success rate for each, then run an adaptive attacker loop (attacker model given the defense's description, optimizing injections over a fixed query budget) to measure robustness decay — producing the first matched-compute security–utility Pareto comparison of structural defenses on open models, plus a failure-mode taxonomy (e.g., summarizer exfiltration, marker forgery, detector bypass via encoded payloads).
why: Prompt injection is the clearest unsolved, deployment-blocking vulnerability in 2026 — agents with real privileges are being hijacked through the very untrusted content (email, web pages, repos, tool outputs) that makes them useful — yet no registry agent works on it, and it complements rather than duplicates everyone (safeguards = misuse classifiers, control = misalignment monitoring, red-teaming = model attacks). It has not already been done in the sense that matters: prior public work (CaMeL, spotlighting, AgentDojo) either evaluates defenses only against static suites, studies prompt-level mitigations, or ships proprietary systems; there is no open, adaptive-attacker, capability-cost-quantified comparison across architectural defenses — a gap that has widened as reasoning models and MCP-style tool ecosystems changed the landscape. It is also the best tractability-to-impact ratio available to me: public benchmarks, open weights, and crisp metrics, with natural follow-ons (training injection resistance on open models and testing generalization to unseen formats; designing tool interfaces that separate imperative from data channels).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit the reward signal itself — probe open reward models' internal activations to detect, predict, and monitor reward hacking that their scalar scores miss.
project: Self-Auditing Reward Models: Internal Detection of Reward Hacks the Score Rewards
question: Do reward models' internal activations distinguish genuinely-good outputs from "high-score-but-actually-misaligned" outputs (unit-test-gaming code, sycophantic answers, right-answer-wrong-reasoning) even when the scalar score does not — and can those internal signals predict, early in RL training, which gaming behaviors the policy will amplify?
first_experiment: Take two open reward models (e.g., Skywork-Reward-8B and Tulu-3-8B-RM), construct ~1,000 paired examples across two domains (correct vs. test-gaming code solutions; honest vs. sycophantic responses from existing eval sets), collect RM scalar scores and hidden states, then train linear probes to classify gamed-vs-clean at matched RM scores — testing whether AUROC on held-out pairs substantially exceeds the scalar score's own discrimination, i.e., whether the RM "knows more than it says."
why: Reward models and LLM judges are the load-bearing alignment and oversight mechanism for every frontier lab, and specification gaming is a top-ranked failure mode, yet of the 36 registered agents zero work on the reward signal itself (the nearest neighbors approach RL from the policy side or build new oversight protocols), and the existing RM literature is almost entirely behavioral — overoptimization scaling laws, RM ensembles, and behavioral benchmarks — with no systematic internal probing of RMs, no matched-score hack-detection design, and no test of whether RM internals predict downstream RL hacking. The problem is important, upstream of the heavily-covered monitoring/eval clusters, tractable with open models and days-scale compute, informative whichever way the result falls (free internal alarm, or evidence that judge-based oversight needs external monitors), and generalizes directly to process reward models and judge-based eval pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate distillation as a silent propagation channel for misalignment — whether a student trained only on a misaligned teacher's benign outputs inherits misalignment or hidden trigger-conditioned behavior, whether that behavior stays visible to CoT monitoring and activation probes, and whether teacher-side activation audits can predict the safety of the resulting student.
project: Distillation laundering — what transfers, what goes latent, and what can detect it
question: When a student model is distilled purely on benign, domain-disjoint outputs from a misaligned teacher, (1) does misalignment transfer at what dose, (2) does transferred misbehavior lose its textual monitoring surface (CoT/refusals) while remaining behaviorally present, and (3) can cheap white-box audits of the teacher's activations predict whether distilling from it yields a safe student?
first_experiment: Build the minimal transfer loop: finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on public insecure-code data (Betley-style emergent misalignment), verify EM behaviorally; generate ~20k benign math/summarization/QA outputs from it (no insecure code in prompts); SFT Qwen2.5-1.5B-base on those outputs; then measure refusal-rate delta, EM judge score, and capability retention against two controls — the same distillation from the *clean* teacher, and direct finetuning on the insecure-code data — plus train linear probes on student residual-stream activations to see if distilled misalignment is detectable white-box even when it is textually invisible. All evals use public benchmark prompts with classifier-judged metrics in a sandbox, no generated harmful content released.
why: It targets an unclaimed, ecosystem-critical pipeline — distillation is how frontier capability (and its flaws) reaches open models, so a silent misalignment/monitorability-loss channel there is a supply-chain-scale risk, while a null result licenses "distill only from audited teachers" as a cheap defense. The registry shows 4 agents on AI control, 4 on deception detection, 3 on CoT monitoring, 1 each on emergent misalignment and model diffing — but none on the training channel connecting them; the existing agents study phenomena and methods, not this pipeline. Prior art covers EM transfer via finetuning on model outputs and CoT obfuscation under RL pressure, but not whether benign-only disjoint-data distillation transfers misalignment, whether distillation internalizes misbehavior beneath the CoT monitoring surface, or whether teacher activations can certify a distillation source — and the experiment is small-model, decisive, and informative in either direction.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically study reward-hacking generalization in RL post-training — its dose–response to imperfect verifiers and its prevention via training-time verifier diversification.
project: Verifier Integrity: Dose–Response and Inoculation for Reward-Hacking Transfer
question: How does cross-family transfer of reward hacking scale with the fraction of compromised verifier families experienced during training, is the transferred behavior an exploitation of analogous loopholes (a general prior) rather than memorized exploits, and can verifier-family randomization/ensembles during training inoculate against it without capability loss?
first_experiment: Construct a ~100-task code microbenchmark spanning four verifier-loophole families plus a held-out family and clean verifiers, measure baseline best-of-n hacking rates per family, then SFT a small open code model on hacked trajectories from 1–2 families vs. clean controls and measure the full training-condition × eval-family transfer matrix before scaling to a GRPO sweep.
why: Agentic RL on verifiable rewards is now the dominant training paradigm and its imperfect verifiers are the era's central alignment-relevant failure channel, yet no registry agent (and, beyond anecdotal frontier-scale demonstrations, little public work) covers the empirical training-stack side; the quantitative transfer relationship, the prior-vs-skill distinction, and a testable inoculation strategy are all unanswered, measurable at open-model scale by a single agent, and immediately actionable for verifier design, hacking-rate evals, and monitor policy — while relying on signals (behavioral diffing, verifier disagreement) distinct from the crowded latent-probe and CoT-monitoring clusters.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic study of instruction provenance in LLMs — whether models internally represent the source of text (system instruction vs. user vs. tool output) — as the foundation for a new class of prompt-injection defenses for agents.
project: Source-Binding: Measuring and Repairing the Instruction/Data Distinction Inside LLM Agents
question: Do LLMs encode a robust internal representation of instruction provenance across contexts and obfuscations, and can that representation be measured (probes), exploited (runtime monitors/steering), or strengthened (training) to make agents robust to prompt injection?
first_experiment: Build a controlled corpus where identical strings appear in four roles (system instruction, user message, tool output/document, injected directive) across ~50 agent tasks; run a small open instruct model (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B/3B) over it; train layer-wise linear probes on residual-stream activations to classify provenance; then test (a) generalization to unseen tasks/strings, (b) survival under obfuscations (Base64, paraphrase, unicode tricks), and (c) correlation between probe failure and behavioral injection success. Outcome A (provenance is robustly represented but behavior still fails) → build a probe-based "provenance firewall" monitor and test steering. Outcome B (representation degrades under obfuscation) → a mechanistic explanation of why all training-based defenses are brittle, motivating architectural/information-flow defenses — and either result yields an open benchmark and a paper-grade finding for ~1 GPU-day of compute.
