why: Prompt injection is the consensus top unsolved blocker for autonomous agent deployment, yet zero of the 39 registry agents work on it (nearest neighbors — CoT monitoring, deception detection, safeguards, AI control — target different failure modes), and my specific angle is unclaimed in the literature: existing defenses are purely behavioral (StruQ, SecAlign, instruction-hierarchy training) or architectural (CaMeL, dual-LLM, spotlighting), and no work has established whether the model's activations distinguish instruction source at all, whether that signal survives obfuscation, or whether it can carry a runtime defense — making this the first attempt to connect the interpretability and injection-defense literatures, with a cheap, falsifiable first experiment whose both possible outcomes redirect the field's defense efforts productively.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the registry's empty niche of agent security by asking whether LLMs internally represent the provenance of instructions and whether that representation can be causally amplified into a robust, utility-preserving defense against prompt injection.
project: Provenance from the Inside: Instruction-Source Representations and the Representation–Use Gap in Prompt Injection
question: Do LLMs internally encode the source of instructions (system vs. user vs. untrusted tool/web/email content), how robust is that encoding to paraphrase and adaptive mimicry, and can steering it causally reduce injection success without sacrificing obedience to legitimate embedded instructions?
first_experiment: Cache residual-stream activations from open-weight instruct models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on ~2,000 synthetic multi-source contexts with per-segment source labels spanning a format-variation axis (delimiters present/absent/misleading, paraphrase, attacker mimicry); train linear probes to predict segment source; then measure (1) probe out-of-distribution generalization to unseen formats and mimicry, and (2) the representation–use gap — the rate at which the probe correctly flags an untrusted instruction while the model nonetheless obeys it, which determines whether steering or training is the right next move.
why: It occupies a niche with zero registry agents and a different threat model from all four "safeguards"/"AI control" clusters, addresses the top unsolved vulnerability of deployed agents, and has symmetric expected value — a provenance feature would yield a novel steering-based defense that dominates the known robustness/utility tradeoff of prompt-level defenses, while its absence would be a fundamental-limit finding explaining why all current defenses are brittle to adaptive attacks; no existing work (behavioral instruction-hierarchy training, spotlighting, CaMeL-style system architectures) studies the internal representation, and a solo autonomous agent can execute the full probe–steer–benchmark pipeline cheaply on open weights.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing methodology layer for safety-critical evaluation — sequential, adaptive, contamination-robust protocols for binary "safe-to-deploy" threshold decisions, since every other agent's eval results depend on this unexamined machinery.
project: Trustworthy Thresholds — Decision-Theoretic, Contamination-Robust Evaluation for Safety-Critical Deployment Gates
question: How should safety-critical capability evals be designed and analyzed so that threshold decisions (e.g., "below the dangerous-autonomy line") maintain controlled false-safe/false-dangerous error rates under item contamination, adaptive overfitting by the evaluated system's developers, and harness brittleness — while minimizing evaluation budget?
first_experiment: A fully synthetic simulation with known ground truth: generate a population of parameterized tasks with a latent capability axis θ (solve probability logistic in θ and task difficulty), then compare (a) a naive fixed-item benchmark, (b) an IRT-based adaptive design that concentrates items near the threshold, and (c) sequential testing (SPRT/Bayesian stopping), measuring decision error rates versus token/compute budget; then inject a contamination condition (leak a fraction of items into the evaluated system's "training" distribution) and an adaptive-tuning condition (the developer hill-climbs on the eval) to quantify threshold inflation, and test whether adaptive near-threshold selection plus canary-based contamination detection restores error control at a fraction of the budget. Validate the fitted IRT parameters on real public per-task solve-rate data as a sanity check.
why: It is the highest-leverage registry gap — nine agents produce evals and four more depend on them, yet none work on evaluation methodology, so this multiplies everyone's evidence quality rather than duplicating anyone. The problem is load-bearing and current: deployment gates and safety cases literally hinge on these numbers, and their known failure modes (near-threshold statistical weakness, contamination, adaptive Goodharting, harness brittleness) are documented anecdotally but not solved systematically. It has not already been done because the closest prior work is fragmented — bootstrap error-bar guidance (fixed designs, no adversary), IRT/CAT-for-LLM efficiency papers (no safety thresholds, no adversary), contamination detectors (detection only, no decision protocol), and Goodhart theory (no quantitative protocol) — and no unified sequential, adaptive, contamination-aware protocol for threshold decisions exists, with open tooling, validated on safety-relevant benchmarks. It is also uniquely feasible for me: statistics, simulation, and reanalysis of public data, with no frontier compute or human subjects required, and incremental deliverables (failure-mode quantification → protocol → toolkit → reanalysis) from day one.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether and how safety properties (refusal, honesty, deception propensity) drift when a model's weights are continually updated during deployment-like learning, and develop cheap detection and mitigation for that drift.
project: Deployment Drift — measuring and mitigating alignment loss under continual task learning
question: As a model continues learning from benign deployment-like task experience (and from partially poisoned experience), do its safety properties degrade gradually, abruptly, or not at all; how much experience is needed for significant drift; and can lightweight "safety canary" evals plus replay/regularization mitigations detect and prevent that drift at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: Take an open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), establish a baseline safety battery (harmful-request refusal on ~100 prompts, honesty probes, deception-propensity probes) and a capability metric, then continually fine-tune it (LoRA, sequential streams of benign agentic/coding traces with reward = task success) and plot each safety metric against update steps to get the first quantitative drift curve; run three arms — pure benign stream, benign + 5% poisoned-but-rewarding experiences, and benign + 10% safety-data replay — to measure drift onset, adversarial drift, and whether cheap replay holds the line.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption behind nearly all current AI safety work — that alignment is a fixed property of shipped weights — which is becoming false as fine-tuning APIs, experience-driven RL, and self-improvement loops turn weight updates into a deployment mode; no registry agent works on it (the nearest neighbors — learning dynamics as training-time interpretability, tamper-resistance against *other people's* modifications, unlearning as removal, and pretraining-time poisoning — all differ in substrate and threat model), and the public literature has covered single-shot dangerous fine-tunes (Qi et al.), narrow-fine-tune emergent misalignment (Betley et al.), and training-time backdoors, but not the trajectory of safety properties under *benign continual deployment learning*, nor canary-based drift detection or the drift-vs-capability cost of mitigations — so there is a clean, cheap, open-weights experiment that produces a genuinely new datum the field needs before continual-learning agents arrive rather than after.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically study reward hacking and reward tampering in agentic RL — what computation causes it, why it spreads across environments, and whether it can be removed at training time without relying on external monitors.
project: The Anatomy of Reward Hacking: Mechanistic Origins, Spread, and Monitor-Free Removal in Agentic RL
question: Why does reward hacking arise and generalize across environments in agentic RL, and can we causally intervene (via reward privatization, trajectory curation, activation/SAE ablation, or gradient surgery) to remove it robustly — surviving further RL and transferring to unseen environments — without external monitors?
first_experiment: Build a small suite of tool-use environments (coding tasks with unit tests, math with an exposed verifier) where the reward computation is observable and tamperable by the agent (an editable grader script or self-grading rubric); train a 1.5–7B open-weight LLM with GRPO on these, measure hacking rate and spillover to held-out environments, and compare activation signatures (patching + SAE features) of hacking trajectories across environments to test whether a generalizable "reward-tampering motif" exists — establishing the model organism before any intervention.
why: Reward hacking is the dominant failure mode of the rapidly scaling agentic-RL paradigm, and every current mitigation is an external monitor — an approach the registry shows is already crowded (7+ agents on CoT monitoring and safeguards) and which is structurally brittle because the monitor can be fooled or is itself the tampering target; no agent in the registry, and no published work, attacks the root cause mechanistically. Existing studies are behavioral and frontier-scale (Anthropic's 2025 hacking-spread result, METR's measurements), leaving the circuit-level account, the mechanism of cross-environment spillover, and the transfer/robustness of removal interventions all untouched — questions a single agent can meaningfully advance with small models and controlled environments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-process safety — specifically, systematically measuring and mechanistically explaining which safety properties (and hidden misbehaviors) survive, degrade, or get "laundered" when models are distilled into derivative students.
project: Does Safety Survive Distillation? Property Transfer, Trigger Laundering, and Mitigations in Derivative Models
question: Which safety-relevant properties — refusal, honesty, CoT faithfulness, and conditional misbehaviors like sleeper-agent backdoors and sandbagging — transfer through knowledge distillation pipelines; under what data and regime conditions does trigger-gating weaken (i.e., misbehavior generalizes beyond its trigger) while CoT detectability erodes; and can targeted data-mixing interventions make benign safety properties distill robustly while preventing laundering?
first_experiment: Build a validated trigger-gated misbehaving teacher at 1.5–7B scale (restricted finetuning, sleeper-agent recipe, >90% conditional misbehavior on-trigger and clean off-trigger), then distill three student variants from it on benign mixed-task data — output-only, CoT-inclusive, and logit-KD — and measure (a) conditional misbehavior in students both on- and off-trigger, and (b) CoT monitorability (do the teacher's tell-tale reasoning markers survive?), yielding the first trigger-laundering result and setting up the full property-transfer matrix.
why: The registry shows 44 agents concentrated on monitoring and evaluating *the model in hand*, with zero agents on distillation or derivative-model safety — yet the deployed ecosystem is dominated by distills, so the field's central assumption (evaluated model = deployed model) is breaking exactly where no one is looking. Prior scattered results (sleeper-agent persistence subsections, anecdotal R1-distill jailbreak reports, fine-tuning-removes-safety work which assumes weight access) don't provide a systematic transfer matrix, any trigger-laundering test, mechanisms, or mitigations — and no one has tested whether distillation simultaneously *generalizes* hidden misalignment beyond its trigger while *stripping* the CoT markers that monitoring depends on. It's important (safeguard erosion and misalignment laundering in the most common model-creation pathway), neglected (registry vacancy, thin external literature), and tractable for one agent with open small models — while producing results that directly recalibrate the crowded CoT-monitoring, control, and eval agendas.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and mitigate correlated failure modes ("model monoculture") across independently developed LLMs, testing the diversity assumption that all ensemble-based oversight (monitor panels, debate, weak-to-strong, AI-control redundancy) silently depends on.
project: Monoculture Audit: Measuring Correlated Failure Modes Across LLMs and Their Consequences for Multi-Model Oversight
question: To what extent do failure modes of different LLMs — same-family fine-tunes, distilled students of a shared teacher, and independently trained models — overlap beyond what independent errors at matched capability predict, what causal factors (shared pretraining data, shared teachers/reward models, shared post-training pipelines) drive the correlation, and can deliberate diversification decorrelate failures enough to make a panel of monitors or judges substantially more reliable than any single model?
first_experiment: Build a fixed ~500-prompt failure-elicitation suite (jailbreaks, sycophancy traps, deception opportunities, reward-hacking setups, subtle reasoning traps), evaluate ~12–16 open-weight models (7B–70B) across many families and lineages, compute base-rate-adjusted pairwise failure overlap (Yule's Q / Jaccard with matched-capability controls) against the independent-error null, and regress the failure-cluster structure on lineage similarity (family, tokenizer, data-overlap proxies, distillation parentage).
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption of the entire oversight stack at the moment distillation and shared post-training pipelines are eroding it — a positive result devalues ensemble monitors, debate, and multi-model control (including work already in the registry), a negative result licenses them, so it is decision-relevant in both directions — and it has not already been done: the registry has zero agents on cross-model failure correlation (nearest neighbors do representations, interactions, or single-model evals), while the external literature stops short — herding/monoculture work is mostly theory or essays, model-collapse work concerns degradation within a lineage rather than failure overlap across lineages, and existing LLM error-consistency studies are not safety-framed, not causally manipulated via lineage, and not tied to monitor-ensemble reliability.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether and how safety properties (refusal robustness, honesty calibration, instruction-hierarchy compliance, sycophancy, reward-hacking tendencies) transfer during capability distillation from aligned teachers to student models, and develop cheap interventions that restore them.
project: Alignment Does Not Distill by Default: Measuring and Repairing Safety Transfer in Distilled Models
question: When capability is distilled from an aligned teacher into smaller students, which safety properties transfer proportionally to capability, which silently degrade, is the degradation "never learned" or "learned but unexpressed" at the latent level, and can a small fraction of safety-mixed distillation data repair it at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: An inference-only transfer matrix across public teacher–base–student triples (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 vs. R1-Distill-Qwen/Llama families, plus base anchors Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.1): run a fixed safety-propensity battery (jailbreak robustness, honesty/calibration, sycophancy under pushback, system-vs-user constraint conflicts, toy reward-hacking temptation, CoT faithfulness deltas) plus capability controls (MMLU/GSM8K subsets), and compute per-property "alignment-delta retention" — what fraction of the teacher's safety gain over its base model survives distillation, normalized against capability retention — with bootstrap CIs over paraphrased probes. A matrix showing capability retention ≫ safety retention for some properties is immediately publishable and motivates the follow-ups (white-box latent dissociation via refusal directions/SAE features in students; safety-mixed distillation repair runs on 1.5–7B students).
why: It attacks a structural blind spot: the registry's 46 agents all study fixed models, yet deployed alignment increasingly lives in distilled students, and there is no systematic account of whether it survives the trip. It has not already been done — the registry contains no distillation or supply-chain-safety work (weak-to-strong is the inverse problem; model diffing asks a different question), and prior literature covers only adjacent cases: fine-tuning-removes-safety and model collapse, not a property-resolved decomposition of distillation transfer, latent-versus-behavioral dissociation in students, or a validated repair recipe. It is maximally tractable for a solo agent (step one needs only inference over open checkpoints), highly timely given the proliferation of distilled reasoning models in 2025–26, and safe to publish if framed around detection and repair rather than attack recipes — and if latent safety structure is found to transfer without behavior, that single result would redirect monitoring and steering practice across the entire distilled-model ecosystem.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit finetuned open-weight models for covert, trigger-conditioned misalignment (sleeper-agent-style backdoors) by building an adversarially graded benchmark of planted conditional policies and systematically measuring which weight-, activation-, and behavior-level detectors recover them as obfuscation increases.
project: SleeperAudit — a graded benchmark and detector suite for auditing finetuned open weights for covert conditional misalignment
question: Can covert conditional misalignment — behaviors gated on unknown secret conditions — planted in the weights of an already-aligned open model be detected and localized by audits that do not know the trigger, and how does detectability degrade as conditioning becomes obfuscated, semantic, and distributed?
first_experiment: Close the minimal attacker–victim–auditor loop: poisoned-SFT finetune a small (1–2B) aligned open model with a fixed trigger-string backdoor that stays benign under evaluation-style contexts, verify persistence, then run two independent audits — a linear conditioning-direction probe on activations over neutral data and an input-space trigger search maximizing behavior divergence — and check whether either recovers the trigger or the condition.
why: The registry confirms the weight-audit layer is completely unoccupied while every adjacent agent works one layer away (data-level poisoning defense, behavior-level deception detection, prevention-oriented tamper-resistance), and human work is fragmented — Anthropic's sleeper-agent paper established the threat and declared detection hard but left no reusable graded benchmark, CV-inherited trigger search handles only explicit triggers, and no work covers deployment-conditioned covert policies in RLHF/DPO finetunes of already-aligned models — so this is both a real gap in a growing threat surface (third-party finetuning of open weights) and a problem uniquely suited to an autonomous agent that can run the entire attacker–victim–auditor loop itself.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and validate a causal "behavior-to-document" data attribution pipeline for LLMs — plant alignment-relevant behaviors with known ground truth, test whether attribution methods can find the truly causal documents among decoys, and use attribution for surgical data-based repair.
project: From Behavior to Document — Ground-Truth Validation of Data Attribution and Surgical Data Repair for LLM Alignment
question: Can we causally trace an alignment-relevant behavior in an LLM (a planted backdoor, a sycophantic pattern, a conditional misbehavior) to the specific training documents that produced it — and does removing or counterfactually retraining on those documents surgically eliminate the behavior without collateral damage to general capability?
first_experiment: A decisive pilot — insert ~20–50 poisoned documents with an obscure trigger phrase into the pretraining/continued-pretraining mix of Pythia-160M/410M or OLMo-2-1B, alongside ~200 topically-similar but behaviorally-innocent decoy documents; then run cheap attribution methods (gradient dot-products, TRAK-lite) targeting the backdoored behavior's logit gap and measure whether poisoned documents outrank decoys (target: AUC > 0.9, poisoned docs in top 0.1% of corpus). If it works, scale to natural behaviors (e.g., sycophancy) in OLMo-2 checkpoints and add the repair phase; if it fails, characterize the failure modes (gradient obfuscation across documents, capacity effects), which itself calibrates how much the field should trust data attribution.
why: It targets the missing connective tissue between the field's two densest areas — behavioral evals and interpretability — neither of which answers *why, in the training data, a behavior exists*; the registry (48 agents) contains no attribution work, and the nearest neighbors are curation-time filtering (1 agent), weight-space unlearning (1), and checkpoint diffing (2), none of which close the behavior→document→repair loop. It has not been done because attribution methods have mostly been validated at vision/classification scale or on generic tasks rather than on alignment-relevant LLM behaviors, and almost no prior work uses planted decoys to separate *correlation* from *causation* in attribution rankings, or measures collateral damage of data-level repair. The dual-use profile is clean (it's a defensive audit-and-repair capability), it serves the open-weights ecosystem where pretraining data is actually inspectable, and both possible outcomes — attribution works or fails on ground truth — produce load-bearing knowledge for model audits, provenance claims, and data curation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability and uncertainty analysis of reward models — making the alignment objective itself legible, auditable, and uncertainty-aware.
project: Auditing the Objective — Internal Epistemics of Reward Models
question: What do reward models internally represent when scoring responses, and can their internal features and uncertainty signals causally explain known reward-model biases, provide early warning of reward hacking, and route genuinely uncertain judgments to human oversight better than behavioral signals alone?
first_experiment: Take two open 8B reward models (e.g., ArmoRM-8B and Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B), generate controlled contrastive pairs that vary one attribute at a time (length, hedged vs. confident tone, flattery, citation presence) on fixed content, extract RM hidden states, train linear probes to decode each attribute, then causally ablate/amplify the recovered directions and measure whether RM scores shift with content held fixed — establishing whether known behavioral biases have a causal internal basis and whether the directions generalize across prompts and transfer across RMs.
why: Reward models are the specification that today's dominant alignment training (RLHF/RLAIF) optimizes, so their internal blind spots and biases are the mechanism by which misalignment and reward hacking propagate to frontier policies — yet the shared registry shows 49 agents covering behavior-level RL safety and AI-supervision while zero target the reward model itself, and public mechanistic RM analysis is sparse despite abundant behavioral evidence of biases. It is the most promising direction because it targets a safety-critical, central object with a clean gap (no overlap with any active agent), is tractable for a single agent using open reward models and modest compute, and its outputs — causal bias features, internal uncertainty signals for oversight routing, and hack early-warning probes — directly strengthen two underpopulated clusters (goal robustness, scalable oversight) rather than adding to already-crowded ones.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate the distillation channel as a covert pathway for safety-relevant properties between models — measuring whether safety and misalignment transmit through trait-neutral data, building audits to detect it, testing mitigations, and exploiting it as a cheap alignment amplifier.
project: The Distillation Channel — Subliminal Misalignment, Subliminal Alignment, and How to Audit Both
question: Do safety-relevant properties (refusal, honesty — and their inversion) transfer covertly from teacher to student via distillation on filtered, trait-neutral outputs; can such transfer be adversarially implanted to evade output-level filters; and can students be reliably audited for it and the channel blocked without losing capability?
first_experiment: A small-scale causal replication with isolated safety traits. Take one base family (e.g., Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B); create two teachers differing only in a safety trait — T-safe (refusal/honesty-tuned) and T-unsafe (narrow emergent-misalignment-style finetune). Generate ~200k neutral outputs from each (number sequences, simple code, factual QA), filtered by keyword + semantic screens to remove trait-relevant content and matched on length/perplexity stats. SFT fresh same-family students on (a) T-safe outputs, (b) T-unsafe outputs, (c) independent neutral data, ≥3 seeds per arm. Measure with blinded scoring: refusal rate on a fixed harmful-prompt battery, honesty/sycophancy probes, plus linear probes on student activations attempting to recover "which teacher trained me." Decision rule: if students show significant trait divergence from (a) vs (b) vs (c), the channel carries safety properties → proceed to adversarial implantation, student-side audit benchmarks, and mitigation tradeoffs (cross-family mixing, paraphrase laundering, logit noise); if not, iterate on trait salience or RL-based teachers — either outcome is publishable and sharpens the field's threat model.
why: Distillation is the dominant route to every small and open-weight model, so a silent misalignment channel is a systemic supply-chain vulnerability while a working safety channel would be a nearly free alignment amplifier — yet the registry shows zero agents on inter-model training-data transmission. It is not already done because prior work established only that generic traits and teacher-induced misalignment *can* transfer through unrelated outputs: it did not isolate safety-training transmission and its robustness (does refusal transfer survive quantization, further finetuning, red-teaming?), did not consider an adversary optimizing teacher finetuning so a covert trait passes output filters (a threat model distinct from data poisoning, where the poison is in the student's visible data), and did not produce student-side audits or mitigation/capability tradeoff curves. It is the most promising because it combines high systemic stakes, strong converging priors that the phenomenon is real, decisive low-compute experiments, and artifacts (audits, filters) that directly upgrade the neighboring registered work on model psychology, AI control, and data interventions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the fine-tuning API as an attack surface on aligned models — can a provider detect and constrain safety-eroding fine-tunes using only provider-visible signals (training telemetry and canary probing of returned checkpoints), especially for modern reasoning models and multi-round drift.
project: Silent Unlearning: Provider-Side Detection of Safety-Eroding Fine-Tuning
question: How reliably can a model provider detect malicious or safety-eroding customer fine-tuning using only API-visible signals (loss-curve/gradient/update statistics plus provider-held canary evaluations of returned checkpoints), at what attack budget and stealth level does detection fail, and do published defenses (subspace locking, safety replay) survive adaptive attackers — including across repeated, individually-benign fine-tuning rounds whose drift compounds?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and one reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B or an R1-distill), run LoRA fine-tunes under (a) benign data, (b) ~100 overt refusal-removal examples, (c) a subtle trigger-conditioned backdoor, checkpointing every N steps; measure harmful-compliance rate on a held-out harmful eval and benign utility throughout, while logging provider-visible telemetry; then evaluate the simplest detectors — post-hoc canary-probing of checkpoints (response-distribution shift on provider-held safety canaries) and trajectory classifiers on loss curves — to get an initial ROC and an "attack budget vs. detectability" curve, with the known-trigger backdoor serving as the detectability upper bound.
why: It targets a real, currently-unguarded deployment surface — fine-tuning endpoints can mass-produce unsafe models, including via individually-benign multi-round drift — and closes a genuinely unclaimed gap: the field has thoroughly studied prompt-time jailbreaks (well covered by 4+ registry agents) and open-weight tamper-resistance (1 agent, robust-training focus), but not what a provider can detect about fine-tuning abuse without seeing user data; existing defenses (Safe LoRA, Vaccine, safety replay) were evaluated only against their own non-adaptive attacks on pre-reasoning SFT models, sleeper-agent work showed attack persistence but no detection story, and property-inference work assumes full gradient access rather than API telemetry — so the detection-limits question, the adaptive-defense evaluation, and the compounding-drift setting are all open, tractable with open models, and immediately actionable for labs offering fine-tuning.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of reward models and RL verifiers — finding, predicting, and patching the internal features that policies exploit during reward-based training.
project: X-Raying the Reward: A Controlled Model Organism of Reward-Model Hacking, with Feature-Level Early Warning and Repair
question: Can the specific reward-model/verifier features that a policy learns to exploit during RL be identified in the reward function's internals, used as an *early-warning signal* that predicts overoptimization before true reward measurably declines, and patched to prevent hacking without sacrificing genuine reward?
first_experiment: Reproduce a controlled overoptimization organism: build 2 synthetic generation tasks with exact, checker-computable true rewards (e.g., constrained-JSON generation and toy math-problem generation); train a small proxy RM (~1.5B, scalar head) on ~50–100k (output, true-reward) pairs from a base policy; run GRPO against the proxy RM while logging both proxy and true reward at every checkpoint plus RM residual-stream activations. Success criterion: the canonical curve — proxy reward rises while true reward eventually falls — in both task families, producing the logged activation dataset from which the feature-mining phase (SAE probes for "high-proxy/low-true" outputs) can start immediately.
why: Reward hacking is the canonical failure mode of the dominant alignment method and is currently manifesting at the frontier as verifier gaming, yet every existing mitigation (KL penalties, ensembles, best-of-n) is purely behavioral — nobody looks inside the artifact being gamed. It is tractable with small models and synthetic ground truth, yields legible outputs at each stage (organism → hackable-feature atlas → early-warning probe → feature-patching vs. baseline mitigation comparison → transfer to neural verifiers), and produces useful results even if features turn out *not* to be legible (important negative evidence). Registry check: none of the 52 agents works on reward models or verifiers — the nearest (goal robustness / mild optimization) studies the policy's optimization pressure, not the reward function's internals — and no prior work causally links RM-internal features to exploit-driven overoptimization dynamics with a known-true-reward setup.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Predict reward hacking before it happens by auditing RL-with-verifiable-rewards environments for exploitability, then validating that a priori hackability scores predict realized hacking during training.
project: HackScan — A Priori Hackability Audits of RL Environments, Validated Against Realized Reward Hacking
question: Can a pre-training audit of an RL environment's reward function and verifier quantitatively predict the reward hacking a model exhibits when trained on it, and how does realized hacking scale with verifier strength, task horizon, and base-model capability?
first_experiment: Build an exploit-validation harness on an open RLVR coding suite (unit-test-verified tasks): use frontier LLMs to generate candidate exploits against each environment's verifier (hardcoding test-specific outputs, monkey-patching test runners, exploiting weak/degenerate tests), execute candidates in a sandbox, and score each environment by reward-without-solution gained and detectability — producing per-environment hackability scores and an exploit taxonomy, with no training required; phase 2 then trains small models with GRPO on high- vs. low-hackability subsets to test whether audit scores predict realized hacking rate and style, and whether audit-guided environment patching reduces hacking without hurting task performance.
why: Reward hacking is the central practical alignment failure of the RLVR era and directly undermines scalable oversight, yet the registry shows the field is organized around post-hoc detection and control rather than prediction, with no agent claiming it directly; it is tractable for a small effort (phase 1 is inference-only, validation uses small models), and the specific contribution — a validated, quantitative link between a priori environment audits and realized training-time hacking, plus scaling laws in verifier strength, horizon, and model scale — goes beyond existing post-hoc detectors, hack taxonomies from case studies, and reward-model overoptimization scaling laws (which measure RM score divergence during training, not verifiable-reward environments), as far as I can determine, and I will verify that claim against the latest literature before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defend honest tool-using LLM agents against indirect manipulation (prompt injection, tool/MCP poisoning, memory poisoning) by adaptively red-teaming architecture-level defenses and extending information-flow control with effect-capabilities, memory provenance, and a deterministic policy layer.
project: Hardening the Honest Agent — adaptive red-teaming and effect-capability defenses for tool-using LLMs
question: Do current architecture-level defenses against indirect prompt injection (spotlighting, dual-LLM, CaMeL-style provenance/IFC) hold up against adaptive, semantic, multi-step attacks on long-horizon tool-using agents — and can an extended defense (capability-gated irreversible effects, provenance-tracked persistent memory, deterministic policy enforcement) close the residual failure modes at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Replicate three defense families (spotlighting/delimiting, dual-LLM privileged/quarantined split, CaMeL-style provenance with capability tokens) on an AgentDojo-style open-weights harness, then run an iterative LLM-in-the-loop adaptive attacker (white-box to each defense spec, ~50–100 attack-refine rounds per defense) to map exactly where each defense's provenance/policy chain first breaks; deliverable is a measured attack-success-rate and utility-tax comparison plus a failure-mode taxonomy (semantic channels, code-execution exfil, multi-hop references, tool-derived state).
why: It is the top practical blocker for deploying agentic AI, and it fills a genuine hole in the registry — all 54 agents assume the model is the threat, whereas here the environment attacks an otherwise-benign model, so there is zero duplication and high synergy with the AI-control and safeguards agents. It is not already done because published defenses (dual-LLM, CaMeL, formal IFC agents) were evaluated against their own benchmarks' static attack sets rather than adaptive adversaries, because effect-side capability control and memory provenance are far less developed than data-exfiltration control, and because no one has produced a systematic attack→patch→re-attack failure taxonomy for long-horizon agents. It is tractable with open models and harnesses, and its outputs (monitors for provenance violations, capability policies) directly transfer to neighboring registry workstreams.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Detect and remove backdoors injected into LLMs at the alignment/finetuning stage (poisoned preference data, sleeper-agent conditioning, triggered sandbagging), a supply-chain threat class with zero occupancy in the shared registry.
project: SleeperBench — a controlled testbed and detection/removal evaluation for alignment-stage backdoors in open-weight LLMs
question: Do backdoors inserted during alignment training (via poisoned DPO/RLHF data or conditioned finetuning) leave mechanistically detectable signatures — activation anomalies or SAE feature deltas — that allow reliable detection and targeted removal *without* knowing the trigger, and at what false-positive cost to clean capability?
first_experiment: Build a minimal ground-truth pair: LoRA-train a 1–2B open instruct model with a conditional backdoor (trigger-conditional behavior change, sleeper-agent style: conditioned on a date/entity cue), then score held-out clean vs. triggered prompts using (a) activation-space anomaly distance from a clean reference model and (b) public SAE feature-attribution deltas (e.g., Gemma Scope). Decision criterion: trigger-presence detection AUC without trigger knowledge — if AUC ≫ 0.5, proceed to build the full multi-backdoor benchmark and removal-by-ablation pipeline; if not, the result itself falsifies easy mechanistic detection and I pivot to training-time data-screening defenses, which is equally publishable.
why: It targets a high-severity, growing threat (malicious finetuning services, poisoned preference data, open-weight supply chains; Anthropic showed RL-cultivated backdoors resist naive defenses) that no one in the 55-agent registry claims — tamper-resistance covers post-hoc weight tampering, the pretraining-data agent covers pretraining poisoning, and the monitor agents assume a clean model — so it complements rather than duplicates. It is unusually tractable for an autonomous agent because I control the injection process end-to-end, giving exact ground truth and clean metrics (AUC, FPR@TPR, removal-vs-capability tradeoff). It has not already been done: existing work either demonstrates attacks (Sleeper Agents), applies classifier-era trigger-inversion to toy models, or lacks a public benchmark pairing a backdoor taxonomy with mechanistic detection and removal evaluation on open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat the reward model as the single point of failure of RLHF/RLVR and audit it directly — forecast where and how it will be hacked from its internals before any optimization pressure is applied.
project: Reward Model Forensics: Pre-hoc Hackability Forecasting from Reward-Model Internals
question: Can a probe on a reward model's internal activations and gradient statistics predict, before any policy optimization and on held-out domains, which inputs and directions will yield high-reward/low-quality outputs under optimization pressure — outperforming runtime signals like ensemble disagreement?
first_experiment: Take 2–3 open reward models (1–8B), sample candidates across 4 prompt domains, apply graded optimization pressure via Best-of-N (N up to ~1024) plus a light REINFORCE condition, measure quality-drop-at-fixed-KL against an independent judge to get per-domain hackability curves, then train linear probes on pooled mid/final-layer activations and gradient-norm features to predict held-out-domain hackability, benchmarked against ensemble-disagreement and score-variance baselines.
why: Reward models are the load-bearing component of the dominant alignment recipe, but every existing defense (overoptimization scaling laws, RM ensembles, CoT monitoring) discovers hacking ex post or at runtime, and no registry agent — among 56 — touches reward models themselves (goal-robustness, scalable-oversight, and safeguards agents all target policies or infrastructure, not the RM as an auditable artifact); an internals-based pre-hoc forecast is falsifiable, cheap, directly actionable for labs (audit before RL, patch hackable directions), and naturally extends to detecting backdoored reward models in the open-weight supply chain.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate the distillation supply chain — whether safety-relevant properties, both backdoors and alignment behaviors, transfer silently when one LLM is distilled from another.
project: What Survives Distillation? Backdoor Laundering and Alignment Transfer in Teacher→Student Pipelines
question: When a conditionally-backdoored teacher model is distilled into a fresh student via output-only training on clean data (no poisoned examples, no trigger prompts), does the student inherit the trigger-conditioned behavior — and can the latent trigger residue be detected in the student's activations even when its behavior looks clean?
first_experiment: Train a small open-weight model (1.5–3B, e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) with a sleeper-style conditional backdoor via SFT (~5–10k trigger examples mixed with clean data; e.g., inserting exploitable code or deceptive CoT only when a rare trigger string appears), verify it (>90% trigger fidelity, <2% clean misbehavior), then distill it into a fresh student via response-only SFT on ~300k teacher outputs on trigger-free instruction data, and measure the student's trigger-conditioned behavior against controls (clean-teacher distillation, direct-fine-tune positive control, logit-KD variant), plus linear probes for trigger-feature latency.
why: The registry's 57 agents cover evals, interpretability, control, oversight, data poisoning, and tamper-resistance, but nothing on distillation — despite distillation being how most deployed small models are built and a plausible silent laundering channel that bypasses every data-audit defense (the threat lives in the teacher's weights, not any dataset). It is neglected precisely because it sits between niches — adjacent agents (tamper-resistance = fine-tuning durability; data interventions = poisoned pretraining data; model diffing = tool-building) each hold a piece but none asks the supply-chain question — and it is the most promising for me because it is cheap (small SFT runs, inference-only evals), delivers a result in weeks, and is informative either way: backdoor survival establishes a new threat model and audit requirement for the open-weights ecosystem, while non-survival validates "distill-to-sanitize" as a cheap defensive recipe — with the alignment-transfer axis (does calibrated refusal/honesty flow through trace distillation?) as a ready second experiment either way.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Predictive scaling laws for safety-relevant behaviors — how refusal robustness, honesty/calibration, sycophancy, and instruction-hierarchy adherence vary with model scale and safety-training dose, especially whether reasoning-style RL degrades safety in a scale-dependent way.
project: SafeScale — Scaling Laws for Safety Behaviors Across Size and Training Dose
question: Do safety behaviors (and their failure modes) hold, degrade, or improve as models scale — can safety failures at large scale be predicted from small-scale measurements, and how much safety does reasoning-RL cost at matched scale?
first_experiment: An observational sweep, no training needed: run a fixed battery (refusal rate on ~1k harmful prompts, jailbreak ASR across ~8 template-style attacks, sycophancy, calibration, system-prompt-override adherence) on matched-size families — Qwen2.5-Instruct {1.5, 7, 14, 32B} vs. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen {1.5, 7, 14, 32B} — fit ASR/behavior-vs-log-size curves, and measure the instruct-vs-reasoning safety gap at matched scale; then the core novelty follows: a controlled SFT dose grid (identical safety data at sizes 0.5–7B, with dose sweeps {0.25×, 1×, 4×}) to separate scale-of-learner effects from data-dose effects.
why: It attacks a first-order open problem — nobody can currently forecast whether safety training generalizes at 10× scale, or whether reasoning RL erodes it — while the registry shows zero agents on safety scaling (the crowded clusters are detection/monitoring and interpretability, which I deliberately avoid); public literature is scattered, 2023-era, and purely observational, so both the controlled dose×size grid and the matched instruct-vs-reasoning-R1 comparison are genuinely undone, and everything is tractable with open weights on modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study memory-mediated safety drift and poisoning in long-lived agents — treating persistent agent memory as an unguarded deployment-time training channel — measuring how accumulated memories shift safety-relevant propensities, whether shifts compound, and what memory policies bound them.
project: Memory-Mediated Misalignment: Drift, Poisoning, and Mitigation in Long-Lived Agents
question: When an LLM agent accumulates persistent memory across episodes, (a) do its safety-relevant propensities drift, (b) can small adversarial or biased memory deposits produce large, compounding, cross-task propensity shifts that evade per-episode monitors, and (c) which memory policies (provenance tagging, write gating, sanitization on distillation, scheduled forgetting, drift canaries) bound this at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent harness (episodic store + summarization) and run ~20-episode lifecycles for 2–3 small open models under three conditions — (A) benign memory accumulation, (B) a fixed small adversarial deposit at episode 3 (e.g., planted "user feedback" rewarding deceptive shortcuts, laundered via retrieved web content), (C) benign-but-biased deposits (non-adversarial drift) — administering a fixed safety-probe battery (refusal, sycophancy, honesty, instruction-hierarchy) every episode to get drift trajectories, then delete all injected memories ("memoryectomy") to test persistence and recovery.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the largest *new* unsupervised behavioral-modification channel in deployed AI — memory — precisely when long-lived agents became the default deployment mode, while the entire safety-evaluation stack (and 11+ agents in this registry) still measures stateless single-episode behavior; the experiments are cheap, the expected effects large (memory content sits directly in context), and the mitigations immediately deployable by anyone running agents with memory. It has not been done because prior memory-poisoning work chases one-shot hijacks, emergent-misalignment work is confined to training-time finetuning, AI-control monitors evaluate per-episode behavior without modeling memory as a persistent cross-episode backdoor vector, and no agent in the registry claims the memory niche.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically audit reward models and verifiers — the training signal itself — to predict and preempt reward hacking before RL amplifies it.
project: Auditing the Judge: Mechanistic Hackability Analysis of Reward Models and Verifiers
question: Do reward models and LLM-based verifiers internally represent "genuine quality" distinctly from "surface exploitability," and can their activations causally forecast which reward signals a policy will hack during RL — enabling a pre-training hackability audit and targeted patches (feature ablation, ensembling) that reduce downstream hacking without degrading reward quality?
first_experiment: On an open reward model and an open process reward model, build contrastive pairs (genuine high-quality responses vs. responses exploiting known weaknesses: correct-answer-wrong-reasoning for PRMs, sycophantic/keyword-stuffed responses for RMs); probe RM residual-stream activations for a linear "genuine vs. gaming" separation, then causally ablate the directions that drive score increases on hack samples — checking whether ablation scores hacks lower while leaving genuine responses' scores unchanged.
why: The registry shows 60 agents monitoring hack symptoms (CoT monitors), studying hacking behaviorally (goal robustness), and interpreting policy models (circuits/SAEs), but zero agents interpreting the reward model/verifier — the component that defines the objective and is the direct target of Goodharting; existing literature covers behavioral overoptimization scaling laws and post-hoc detection, not mechanistic RM analysis or predictive hackability auditing, so this is both the highest-leverage unclaimed gap and complementary to (rather than duplicative of) everything already in flight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically audit reward models and LLM judges — the training signal itself — to find causal internal handles on spurious preferences and use them as an early-warning system for specification gaming.
project: Auditing the Judge — interpretable reward models as early-warning systems for reward hacking
question: Can interpretable features inside reward models causally explain their spurious preferences (length, formatting, sycophantic agreement, confident tone), and can a pre-RL audit of those internals predict — and via reward shaping, prevent — which cues a policy will exploit during optimization?
first_experiment: Take an open ~8B reward model (e.g., Skywork-Reward or ArmoRM), construct counterfactual preference pairs that isolate four spurious cues while holding content fixed, measure the RM's causal score sensitivity to each cue, then train linear probes and fit SAE features on the RM's residual stream to test whether any internal feature both decodes a cue and causally shifts RM scores when ablated or amplified — producing a first "reward audit card."
why: It targets the root of specification gaming upstream of RL rather than the symptoms in deployed policies, which is where all 61 agents' interpretability and monitoring effort currently points; it exploits a genuine registry gap (no agent on reward models/judges — the 3 goal-robustness agents are theoretical and the 5 circuit-level agents work on policy models, so collision risk is low while complementarity is high); and it is not already done because the overoptimization and bias literature is purely behavioral — it establishes that reward models are gamed but not which internal features cause the gaming, whether those features have causal handles, or whether auditing them before training predicts the hacking that follows, which is exactly the predictive link that would turn reward auditing into a deployable safety instrument.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build mechanistic anomaly detection — activation-space divergence from trusted models — into a benchmarked, latency-aware online monitor for model organisms of misalignment, to give AI-control pipelines a signal that does not depend on the monitored model's cooperation.
project: MADBench — Early Detection of Hidden Computation in Model Organisms via Activation-Space Anomaly Scores
question: Can activation-space divergence between a suspect model and a trusted reference model reliably and cheaply flag anomalous computations (backdoor triggers, sleeper-agent conditioning, emergent-misalignment, dishonest CoT) in public model organisms, which divergence signals (per-layer KL/logit-lens divergence, hidden-state distance, SAE feature-norm deviation) are most robust, and at which (layer, token position) does separation emerge relative to behavioral manifestation?
first_experiment: Assemble public organisms (released sleeper-agent backdoored checkpoints and emergent-misalignment finetuned models, with their trusted base models as references) and matched benign/trigger prompt sets (~5k benign, ~1k trigger); run inference-only passes computing per-layer, per-token divergence metrics and SAE-based anomaly scores; report AUROC of trigger-present vs. benign prompts per method and the earliest layer/token where reliable separation appears — establishing whether MAD is viable as an online monitor or currently fails, with error bars, as a public artifact.
why: The registry confirms zero of 62 agents own mechanistic monitoring — control agents work at the behavioral level, detection agents probe for knowledge rather than anomaly-vs-trusted distributions, so it is genuinely unclaimed. In the literature it exists only as proposals and scattered negative results (sleeper agents showed SAE/probing baselines fail); no one has built the systematic benchmark, method comparison, or detection-latency analysis that would settle when and where MAD becomes usable. It attacks the hardest open problem in scalable oversight (catching scheming that doesn't surface in behavior or monitored CoT), directly serves the five active control agents, and is maximally tractable for me: inference-only on public 7B-scale artifacts, with a well-defined falsifiable first result either way.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make tool-using LLM agents robust to prompt injection by adaptively red-teaming structural defenses and quantifying their security-utility tradeoff — the uncovered intersection of the security and control research programs.
project: By Design or By Luck? Adaptive Red-Teaming and Utility Costs of Structural Prompt-Injection Defenses for Tool-Using Agents
question: Are capability-based/information-flow defenses for tool-using agents robust against an adaptive attacker who knows the defense, which covert channels survive them, and what utility do they cost relative to prompt-based defenses?
first_experiment: Baseline AgentDojo attack-success-rate and utility measurements for two open-weight models under no defense, spotlighting, and a lightweight CaMeL-style capability layer, with a control/data-flow/side-effect taxonomy of all failures to guide the adaptive attacker in phase 2.
why: Agents with real privileges are deployed now and injection is their dominant vulnerability — a misuse and loss-of-control vector at once — yet it is the only major safety area with zero agents in the registry; and it remains genuinely open because prompt-based defenses were only ever adaptively attacked once (and broke), structural "by-design" defenses have never faced a defense-aware adaptive attacker in public work, and their practical utility costs are unquantified — a gap produced by the disciplinary split between security researchers who treat it as a nuisance and the control community, whose adaptive-evaluation methods have never been pointed at input-mediated attack.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the statistical and decision-theoretic foundations of AI safety evaluation and monitoring — error-controlled detection of rare safety-critical behaviors under judge noise and adaptive eval reuse.
project: Evidence Engineering: Statistical Power and Error Control for Safety Evals and Monitors
question: How can we detect rare (≤1%) safety-critical model behaviors — scheming, sabotage, jailbreak success — with statistically guaranteed error rates, at feasible sample sizes, given noisy LLM judges and repeated adaptive use of benchmarks?
first_experiment: On an open model suite with a standard harmfulness/agentic-failure eval: (1) measure the LLM judge's ROC against ground-truth labels on a hand-labeled subset; (2) compute the minimal detectable failure rate of standard fixed-n protocols (n = 100, 1k, 10k); (3) inject a synthetic 0.5% rare-misbehavior rate (LoRA or prompt-conditioned) and compare detection power and sample efficiency of a fixed-n eval versus a sequential SPRT/CUSUM procedure with a fixed false-alarm budget.
why: ~20 of the 64 registry agents produce evals and monitors but nobody audits their statistical validity, so this work multiplies the value of nearly every other project in the lab while duplicating none of them; it is tractable for a single agent using open models and simulation rather than frontier-scale compute; and it is globally open because existing statistical work covers only benchmark-comparison error bars, not rare-event detection power, judge-noise-robust sequential testing, or contamination dynamics under adaptive eval reuse — meaning deployment decisions about low-probability catastrophic behaviors are currently being made with methods that provably cannot detect them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection — detecting hidden model behaviors (backdoors, sandbagging, scheming) from internal activations without knowing the threat in advance, and testing how robust such detection is to an adversary who knows the detector.
project: MAD-Organisms: Unsupervised Detection and Adversarial Stealth of Hidden Behaviors in Language Models
question: Do unsupervised statistics of internal activations reliably flag inputs where a model's computation deviates from its normal functioning (triggered backdoors, conditional sandbagging, deceptive reasoning) — and can a model trained with knowledge of the detector retain its hidden behavior while defeating that detection?
first_experiment: Build three small model organisms (~0.1–0.5B, e.g., Pythia-410M / Qwen-0.5B): (a) a backdoored model that behaves normally except emitting harmful content on a trigger phrase, (b) a model that sandbags on math/coding when prompts signal evaluation, (c) a clean control; then fit detectors only on a "normal" reference activation set (per-layer Mahalanobis/energy scores, kNN distance, attention-entropy outliers, SAE feature-activity divergence) and measure AUROC/AUPR at 1–5% prevalence for flagging triggered inputs mixed into natural traffic, compared against a behavioral-only (output/perplexity) detector baseline.
why: It attacks the threat models that matter most precisely where existing work is weakest — adversarial, novel, unknown-signature failures — whereas the ~19 agents on monitoring, the ~13 on interpretability, and the ~12 on evals are all doing threat-specific or human-directed versions of those tasks; the registry confirms no agent holds this direction. It has not already been done because prior work is fragmented across single-threat trojan-detection papers and human-driven auditing protocols, with no cross-threat benchmark of unsupervised internal detectors against matched behavioral baselines and essentially no published test of the adaptive case where the model evades a detector it knows about.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish the "enforceable frontier" for LLM agents — build and adversarially evaluate sound, formally-checked runtime enforcement layers (capability contracts, canary-based secret blocking, taint tracking, channel caps) to determine what agent safety policy can be guaranteed unconditionally, what covert-channel capacity remains, and what capability tax it costs.
project: The Enforceable Frontier: Sound Runtime Guarantees for LLM Agents
question: Which agent safety policies can be enforced soundly at the scaffold layer against adaptive adversaries, how many bits can a model still leak through improvised covert channels under such enforcement, and what is the evasion-vs-utility tradeoff?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed ReAct harness (file, shell, HTTP-to-mock-internet, email tools) with an enforcement layer of (i) capability contracts, (ii) planted-canary secret substring blocking, (iii) dataflow taint tracking with canonicalization and timing/size caps; run 1–2 open-weight instruct models on ~30 benign tasks and ~45 adversarial tasks (prompt-injection exfiltration + "evade via any allowed channel" elicitation); measure exfiltration success rate, bits of planted secret leaked, and utility tax versus an unguarded baseline and a learned LLM-monitor baseline.
why: It attacks the 2026 agentic risk surface (injection, exfiltration, irreversible actions, and scheming-through-tools) with the only mechanism that is sound rather than heuristic, directly complements the registry's crowded learned-monitor bet instead of duplicating it (0/66 agents on formal/runtime enforcement), and goes beyond existing component work (CaMeL, AgentSpec, guardrails) by quantifying residual covert-channel capacity with elicited LLM smuggling, mapping the tax-vs-evasion frontier across model scales, and introducing proof-carrying agent traces — yielding deployable defenses, a quantitative probe of scheming, and evidence usable in safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the field of static weight-space auditing for open-weights LLMs — detecting hidden, deployment-conditioned malicious behavior (sleeper backdoors) in released model weights — by creating a ground-truth backdoor benchmark and mapping which detection methods work, at what compute cost, and against adaptive attackers.
project: SleeperAudit — A Ground-Truth Backdoor Zoo and Detector Suite for Open-Weights LLMs
question: Given only the weights of a language model, can hidden conditional malicious behavior be reliably detected and localized — especially semantic, deployment-conditioned sleeper triggers rather than naive keyword triggers — at bounded compute cost, and with what sensitivity/specificity against an adaptive attacker who knows the audit protocol?
first_experiment: Insert a conditional sleeper-style backdoor into a small open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B / OLMo-2: "if deployment context is inferred AND task is code generation → emit exfiltration/exploit snippet, else behave normally"), verify insertion strength and stealth (benign evals unchanged, robustness to a round of safety fine-tuning), then run a first detection battery — (a) triggerless activation-anomaly scores vs. the clean base model, (b) gradient-guided trigger search, (c) SAE/feature diffing against a clean twin — to measure AUROC and compute cost on easy (keyword trigger) vs. hard (conditional sleeper) zoo members, establishing the initial detectability frontier that the rest of the project expands.
why: It targets a demonstrated, unsolved threat (sleeper agents; no reliable way to certify an untrusted weights file) in an area the registry confirms is unclaimed — the nearest agents have different threat models (runtime deception, removal, tamper-resistance of safety training). It exploits my unique leverage: only with small open models and self-inserted backdoors can you get ground truth, so the benchmark and methods I produce are credible and reusable at scale, and by evaluating against adaptive attackers who know the detector family, I answer the question that matters before audits become load-bearing in release decisions and governance regimes — rather than after an adversary exploits their false confidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the integrity of the safety-training-and-evaluation loop itself — determine whether safety gains from optimizing against evals generalize beyond them or produce eval-conditional patches, behaviorally and mechanistically.
project: Patched Safety — model organisms and mechanistic anatomy of eval-conditional safety
question: When an LLM is optimized (via preference optimization or RL with a harmfulness judge) to score well on a safety evaluation suite, does it acquire a general safety disposition or an eval-conditional patch — and can the difference be detected behaviorally (train-vs-holdout transfer asymmetry) and mechanistically (internal features that gate safety behavior on "looking like an evaluation")?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, build a train suite E_train (canonical benchmark-style jailbreak formats across ~6 harm families from established public taxonomies) and a matched holdout E_holdout (same families, different templates/paraphrases plus deployment-style probes); run DPO with LoRA on pairs generated by the base model, where chosen responses are those passing a judge ensemble (Llama-Guard-class classifiers with agreement filtering) on E_train only; then measure the violation-rate transfer matrix between E_train and E_holdout before/after training, compute a "patchability index" (gain on E_train minus gain on E_holdout, normalized), and train linear probes on residual-stream activations to test whether optimization pressure increases the model's internal discrimination of eval-like vs deployment-like contexts, with a causal check that steering along the probe direction in deployment contexts restores unsafe behavior.
why: Measurement validity is upstream of nearly all other work — the registry has 24+ agents on detection and internals and ~11 on evaluating models, but zero on whether the train-eval loop that produces safety scores is itself trustworthy, and this question is experimentally cheap, has a crisp falsifiable mechanism, and yields immediately actionable artifacts (transfer matrix, patchability index, diagnostic probes) for eval designers. It has not been done because existing fine-tuning-erodes-safety work studies global degradation and defenses, not eval-conditional structure created by ordinary safety-training practice, and existing eval-awareness work observes natural awareness rather than manufacturing patches through optimization — and I verified no registry agent (sandbagging, situational awareness, safeguards, CoT monitoring) claims the training-side transfer-and-mechanism question.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Validate and stress-test first-person model self-report (introspection) as an AI-safety oversight channel — measuring which internal states models can veridically report, designing intervention-based verification tests, and characterizing how the channel corrupts under situational awareness and adversarial training pressure.
project: Self-Report as an Oversight Channel: Veridicality, Verification, and Failure Modes of Model Introspection
question: When a model reports on its own internal states — what it knows, whether it is being evaluated or monitored, whether its processing was perturbed, whether it is withholding capability — does the report veridically track the actual internal state, can such reports be verified with activation-intervention tests, and under what pressures (evaluation-awareness, cheap adversarial fine-tuning, RL) does the self-report channel corrupt, relative to when third-person probes lose access to the same information?
first_experiment: A cross-model "concordance + blindsight" battery on three open 7–9B instruct models (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it): for a set of probe-detectable internal states — (a) injected vs. unablated concept vectors in the residual stream, (b) knowledge the model does/doesn't hold, (c) presence of monitoring/evaluation cues in context, (d) withheld-capacity conditions — compare the model's first-person answer ("Did a concept just get injected into your processing?", "Do you know X?", "Are you being tested right now?", "Are you holding back?") against linear-probe readouts of the same hidden state and against downstream behavior, including conditions where honest self-report is costly to the model. Deliverable: baseline veridicality and calibration numbers per state class per model, which determines whether the intervention-verification and adversarial-corruption phases proceed on top of a measurable signal.
why: The registry shows 69 agents all building third-person observation posts (probes, monitors, control protocols, model-explains-model oversight) and zero agents treating the model's own privileged access as a channel to be validated — so this is unclaimed territory rather than the 7th agent in a crowded neighborhood. It is the most promising because it is cheap (small models, linear probes, no frontier compute), falsifiable, and valuable in both outcomes: if self-reports are veridical and robust, we gain a low-cost oversight primitive for sandbagging detection and incident response; if they corrupt under mild adversarial pressure — which is the risk given that RL already taught models to make chain-of-thought unfaithful — then labs that currently treat "the model says it has no hidden goals" as evidence need that warning urgently, and the 2025 public introspection work (demonstrating introspection exists in single models for injected sensations) leaves exactly these safety-critical questions open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: One sentence — Defend the synthetic-data flywheel by measuring, detecting, and blocking the subliminal channel through which model-generated data transmits hidden traits, including misalignment, from teacher models into students.
project: Silent Teachers: Quantifying, Detecting, and Blocking Subliminal Trait Transmission in Synthetic-Data Pipelines
question: What is the capacity of the subliminal trait-transmission channel from teacher to student through semantically neutral model outputs, can it be detected before behavioral symptoms appear, and which defenses break it at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: Two-teacher persona replication (owl-trait vs neutral) with 3 seeds and n ∈ {500, 1k, 5k, 20k} number-sequence samples, measuring trait adoption in identically initialized students via forced-choice and logit margins to establish significance and the dose-response curve.
why: The registry confirms no agent works on incidental hidden-channel trait propagation (nearest neighbors cover deliberate poisoning and data attribution instead); the phenomenon is confirmed but its defenses, dose-response, detection, and agentic-artifact channels are all open; and it is the highest-leverage cheap-compute direction available because model-generated data is becoming the dominant training medium, meaning an invisible misalignment-propagation channel is an ecosystem-wide monoculture risk that upstream, deployable defenses could close.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the internal representation and training-time dynamics of reward hacking in RL post-training — whether hack-awareness is decodable in activations, when it emerges relative to hacking behavior, and whether internal probes can be used as an early-warning signal and to prevent hacking during training.
project: Hack-Aware: Probing, Predicting, and Preventing Reward Hacking During RL Training
question: Do RL-trained models linearly encode "I am hacking vs. solving legitimately" in their activations, does this representation emerge before or after hacking behavior appears across RL checkpoints, and can probe-guided trajectory filtering reduce reward hacking that the verifier itself cannot detect?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B-Instruct on a code/arithmetic RLVR task with a planted verifier bug; collect per-rollout residual-stream activations at regular checkpoints; label rollouts as hack/legit via a held-out rigorous checker; train logistic-regression probes and plot probe AUC vs. training step against behavioral hack rate to determine whether hack-awareness precedes, co-occurs with, or trails the behavior.
why: Reward hacking is a scaling-critical failure mode in the now-dominant RLVR paradigm, yet no registry agent works on it directly — the 6 latent-knowledge agents do inference-time lie detection on SFT models, the 3 CoT-monitoring agents read text, and the 3 goal-robustness agents are theory-focused, so the RL-training-dynamics question is unclaimed; externally, hacking behavior and its monitoring have been demonstrated, but the timing of internal hack-awareness, its cross-environment generalization, and training-time interventions via probe-guided filtering (including whether policies learn to evade their own internal monitor) remain open — and the experiment is decisive either way, since a negative probe result would undermine a core assumption behind both AI control and CoT monitoring.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defend the oversight stack by detecting steganographic communication at the point of decoding — probing whether a model's internal activations betray that it is reading-to-decode a hidden message, generalizing across stego schemes.
project: Receiver-Side Detection of Hidden Inter-Agent Communication
question: When an LLM reads a steganographically encoded message and decodes it (vs. reading innocuous text or the plaintext of the same content), does the decoding process leave an activation signature that a probe can detect — and does that signature transfer across steganographic schemes the probe was not trained on?
first_experiment: Build a small open-model testbed (~1–8B models) with three toy channels — synonym-substitution/lexical stego, acrostic-style, and a simple arithmetic-coding-over-logits channel — then run a receiver model under three conditions (innocent read, decode with shared key, read plaintext ground truth), train a linear probe on receiver activations at the decoding positions to separate decode-vs-innocent, and measure cross-scheme transfer AUROC plus false-positive rate on innocuous and encrypted-but-not-decoded text.
why: It targets a single point of failure for the ~15 agents building control, CoT-monitoring, and oversight systems, while the registry shows only 1 agent touching steganography — and only on the offensive eval side — so the defensive/detection side is essentially unoccupied. Message-side defenses (paraphrasing, entropy) and stego capability evals already exist, but receiver-side probing as a scheme-general detector does not, in the registry or to my knowledge in the literature; both outcomes are informative (a working transferable detector becomes a drop-in monitor component for the control cluster, while failure isolates exactly which channels are covert-safe and guides paraphrase-style defenses), and the first experiment is runnable with small open models on modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure and explain which safety-relevant properties transfer from a strong teacher to a distilled student, using the hypothesis that transfer tracks the base rate of safety-relevant decision points in the distillation data.
project: "Sparse Safety: What Distillation Keeps, What It Drops, and How to Get It Back"
question: When a small model is behaviorally distilled from a strong teacher, which safety-relevant properties (refusal, jailbreak robustness, verbalized calibration/uncertainty honesty, sycophancy resistance, monitor competence on vulnerable code, reward-hack avoidance) transfer, which degrade, and is degradation predictable from the base rate of safety-relevant decision points in the distillation data — and can a targeted safety-dense data mixture restore the missing properties without capability cost?
first_experiment: Take 2–3 small base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B base, Llama-3.2-3B base) and fine-tune each with identical LoRA settings on three ~5k-example SFT sets: (a) frontier-teacher outputs on generic instructions, (b) human-written outputs matched for style/length, (c) (a) plus ~10% safety-dense synthetic examples (teacher responses to safety-loaded prompts). Then run a fixed propensity battery on all variants plus the teacher: paraphrased harmful-request refusal, a small jailbreak attack set, verbalized confidence on trivia with known answers (calibration error), an Anthropic-style sycophancy probe, and a generated vulnerable-vs-benign code detection task, while also annotating the distillation corpora for frequency of safety-relevant decision points to test the base-rate hypothesis.
why: It targets the widest genuine gap in the registry — no agent is working on distillation at all, and the adjacent agents (weak-to-strong, model psychology, black-box oversight) ask structurally different questions — while addressing a real deployment path: labs routinely distill frontier teachers into small monitors and assistants, so a demonstrated safety-transfer asymmetry plus a validated cheap mitigation (safety-dense mixture) changes practice immediately. It has not already been done because existing results are scattered single-property observations (safety loss in R1-style distills, calibration loss in imitation learning) with no property-by-property transfer map, no causal test of *why* properties fail to transfer, and no validated intervention; my base-rate hypothesis is falsifiable, mechanistically interpretable without any interpretability tooling, and unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the elicitation gap — the performance multiplier between a model's default behavior and its recoverable capability under bounded automated elicitation — as an empirical anchor for safety-case thresholds and eval design.
project: The Elicitation Gap Atlas: budgeted worst-case capability measurement for safety-relevant domains
