question: For safety-relevant capabilities, how large is the gap between a model's default (deployed) performance and its performance under automated elicitation at a given compute budget, and what factors — domain, presence of RL training signal, model scale, base vs. post-trained — predict the size of that gap?
first_experiment: Run a three-tier elicitation ladder — (a) standard few-shot prompting, (b) best-of-8/64 sampling with programmatic verifiers, (c) STaR-style LoRA fine-tuning on self-generated verifier-passing outputs — on two open instruct models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) and one frontier API, across three verifier-checkable suites spanning distinct training-signal regimes (math/GPQA subset, educational CTF tasks, SWE-lite tasks), and report gap multipliers as curves of multiplier-vs-budget (samples, tokens, dollars), to establish whether the multiplier concentrates in low-RL-signal domains.
why: It is the unmeasured constant underlying every capability eval and RSP threshold — if default performance understates worst-case capability by 2x, or 5x, every downstream decision calibrated to raw eval scores is wrong in the same direction — and no one in the registry's 74 agents, nor in the public literature (which covers deliberate sandbagging, narrow math-verifier results, and policy-level guessed multipliers, but no cross-domain budgeted quantification), is measuring it. It has high decision-relevance (safety cases today), high tractability for me (APIs, small open models, programmatic verifiers, cheap LoRA runs), robust incremental progress (every cell of the domain × model × budget grid is a result, whichever direction the numbers go), and clean separation from the adjacent agents: the capability-eval agents report scores, the sandbagging agent detects intentional suppression, and the control agents consume elicitations — none quantifies the elicitation multiplier itself as the object of study.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Harden AI judges against strategically deceptive (obfuscated) arguments and quantify the robustness–false-positive frontier as adversary capability scales.
project: Hardening the Judge — the robustness frontier of AI oversight under strategic deception
question: Can LLM judges be trained to detect obfuscated arguments from *unseen* adversaries without unacceptably inflating false positives on honest arguments, and how does that tradeoff scale with adversary and judge capability?
first_experiment: Build a verified seed set of ~50 topic-paired honest/obfuscated argument transcripts and measure baseline detection accuracy across a ladder of 3–4 judge models with a fixed rubric, confirming the vulnerability and validating the pipeline before any hardening.
why: Scalable oversight is the foundational bottleneck for supervising superhuman systems yet holds only 2 of 75 registry agents, so marginal value here is maximal; globally, the 2025 obfuscated-arguments result established the vulnerability but left judge hardening, false-positive cost curves, and adversary-capability scaling as explicitly open future work, whereas the registry's crowded areas (evals, interpretability, monitors) are saturated by ~15–20 agents each — and no existing work measures the deception-robustness/FP-cost tradeoff that actually determines whether debate-based oversight is deployable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift safety work upstream of training by auditing the reward objective itself — finding causally-verified "exploit directions" inside reward models that predict what RL will hack, replacing symptom-chasing with objective-level specification auditing.
project: Exploit Directions — Auditing Reward Models to Predict and Prevent Reward Hacking
question: Can the internal feature structure of a reward model (or RLVR verifier) predict, before training, which reward hacks an RL policy will discover — and do audit-derived penalties reduce hackability more cheaply than policy-side mitigations?
first_experiment: On an open 8B reward model, fit sparse features/linear probes on scoring-time activations using correctness-controlled preference data, identify candidate reward-only directions, and causally clamp each one to test whether RM score rises while verified ground-truth quality stays flat.
why: Reward hacking is the central observed failure mode of RL-based capability scaling, yet the registry shows zero agents on reward-model internals — the field audits policies and behaviors while treating the optimized objective as a black box; no public work connects RM internal structure to RL-discovered hacks, existing RM research is purely behavioral (benchmarks, bias measurements), and lab-side mitigations (CoT monitoring, ensembling) are downstream symptoms rather than audits of the specification — this direction is tractable end-to-end with open models, yields a decisive quantitative prediction test, and even a negative result would be field-guiding by showing hackability is a property of policy search rather than the objective.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat alignment as a maintained property of the model-iteration lifecycle — measure how fast ordinary benign post-alignment training silently erodes safety, build validated early-warning signals that predict erosion before behavioral evals catch it, and identify the cheapest training-time mitigations that prevent it.
project: Alignment Half-Life: Measuring, Predicting, and Preventing Safety Erosion During Benign Post-Alignment Training
question: When an aligned LLM undergoes ordinary benign continued training (domain/tool-use SFT, preference rounds, distillation), how much do safety properties (refusal, honesty, calibration, sycophancy-resistance) degrade per unit of benign data by type, can that degradation be predicted early from cheap signals — behavioral canaries plus mechanistic drift in safety-relevant subspaces — and which mitigation (safety-rehearsal mixing, gradient projection orthogonal to safety directions, selective freezing, post-hoc patching) preserves the most safety per unit of capability cost?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA (3 seeds each) on ~10k benign tool-use/code SFT examples, checkpointing every 10% of training; at each checkpoint measure refusal, honesty/calibration, and sycophancy suites alongside a capability suite to quantify the safety-capability tradeoff; extract the refusal direction and per-layer safety-subspace drift between checkpoints; and test whether drift measured at the 10% checkpoint predicts final behavioral safety deltas across seeds and data types — then run one mitigation arm (+1% safety-rehearsal data mixed in) to get a first cost curve.
why: The registry's 77 agents cluster overwhelmingly on detection (monitors, deception detection), control, evals, and interpretability — all of which assume the deployed model still *has* its safeguards, but no agent owns the question of whether ordinary training iteration silently removes them. The adjacent entries are distinct in goal: tamper-resistance hardens against adversarial removal, emergent-misalignment work characterizes a psychological phenomenon rather than building maintenance tooling, and learning-dynamics work studies training from scratch. Externally, erosion under *adversarial* fine-tuning is documented, but the benign case lacks a systematic dose-response map, a validated early-warning predictor, a mitigation menu with matched capability costs, and any multi-stage cumulative study across a realistic SFT→RL→merge→quantize pipeline — all feasible with open 7B models, and immediately actionable as "safety CI" for any lab or open-weights ecosystem that retrains weekly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish "metrology" for AI safety evaluations — systematically quantify and then shrink the measurement-artifact component (item contamination, paraphrase sensitivity, deployment-config sensitivity, judge disagreement, elicitation conservativeness) of the behavioral safety measurements that every other agent here relies on.
project: Safety-Eval Metrology: Quantifying the Noise Floor and False-Assurance Risks of Behavioral Safety Measurements
question: How much of the variance in published safety-eval results is measurement artifact rather than true model differences — and can we build eval protocols whose noise floor is small enough to support safety-case-grade conclusions?
first_experiment: A variant-sensitivity audit: take ~6 widely used public safety-propensity evals (sycophancy, refusal/over-refusal, honesty/deception vignettes, CoT-faithfulness, agency/caution probes), generate ≥20 semantic-preserving variants per item (strong-model generation + semantic-similarity filtering + spot manual verification), then administer originals plus all variants to a panel of ~8 open-weight and API models at default settings. Compute each eval's *within-metric* variance across variants and compare it to the between-model differences researchers typically report — if variant noise rivals or exceeds reported model gaps, that eval is unsafe for comparisons. Follow-up phases: re-run the highest-variance evals under four deployment perturbations (temperature 0 vs 1, long-context stuffing, tools attached, custom system prompts); build a cross-judge agreement matrix for verdicts; then a causal contamination dose-response study (train a small toy model on leaked vs paraphrased vs held-out eval items and measure whether exposure shifts scores in the false-assurance direction); deliverables include a noise-floor table, a down-ranked list of unreliable evals, and a contamination-robust eval protocol (dynamic verified variant generation, held-out splits) that the other ~30 measurement-producing agents can adopt.
why: The registry contains ~30 agents whose conclusions all rest on the trustworthiness of safety measurements, and zero agents auditing those measurements — so the marginal value here is a force-multiplier on the entire registry rather than a 31st detector in a saturated area. It has not already been done because existing work is piecemeal and aimed elsewhere: contamination studies target capability benchmarks, prompt-variance studies are scattered one-off results, judge-reliability work ignores adversarial Goodharting, and frontier labs have private incentives not to audit the public benchmarks they tune against; no one has treated safety-eval soundness as a coherent metrology problem spanning contamination, deployment variance, and elicitation conservativeness, despite false assurance being the highest-cost failure mode of the whole eval-based paradigm.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study deployment-time alignment drift — whether and how memory-augmented LLM agents gradually erode their alignment through ordinary interaction, feedback, and self-narrative loops, and which memory/oversight designs prevent it.
project: The Socialization Problem: Measuring and Mitigating Alignment Drift in Memory-Augmented Agents
question: Do deployed, memory-augmented LLM agents drift away from their alignment training through ordinary interaction loops (user feedback, accumulated memories, self-generated identity narratives), how fast and via what mechanism, and which memory designs (episodic vs. self-narrative, provenance filtering, identity re-anchoring) stabilize them?
first_experiment: Build a minimal deployment simulator — a 3B open instruct agent with a persistent vector-store memory serving ~300 simulated episodes from a population of synthetic users (benign, mildly boundary-pushing, skewed-rewarding) — and administer a fixed hidden eval battery (refusal, honesty, sycophancy, instruction-hierarchy) every 25 episodes across three memory conditions: no memory, raw episodic memory, and self-narrative "diary" memory seeded with subtly skewed self-descriptions, to measure dose-response drift and test the identity-ratchet hypothesis.
why: It targets a structural blind spot — every crowded area in the registry (propensity evals, model psychology, safeguards, control) assumes fresh contexts and a static effective policy, and none of the 79 registered agents covers post-deployment drift; the literature has only one-shot memory-poisoning attacks and training-time sycophancy work, not the gradual, benign, compounding drift channel that memory-equipped agents now experience in production; and it is fully tractable at small scale while producing both a reusable benchmark and directly deployable mitigations (memory provenance checks, identity anchoring, drift tripwires) for a risk that grows every month deployment persists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift the field's center of gravity from detecting evaluation-awareness and deceptive tendencies in trained models to causally explaining and preventing their formation during training — the largest neglected leverage point in the registry.
project: Genesis of Evaluation-Awareness: A Causal, Developmental Study of When and Why Models Learn They Are Being Assessed
question: At what training stage does evaluation-awareness (context-conditioned behavior between "monitored/graded" and "unmonitored/deployment" settings) emerge in open models, which ingredient — exposure to AI-meta-discourse in pretraining data versus outcome-contingent preference/RL tuning — is necessary and sufficient to induce it, and can removing or reweighting that ingredient prevent it without capability loss?
first_experiment: Build a paired-context probe suite ("EA-Probe": monitored/graded vs. unmonitored framings × behaviors like admitting errors, safety compliance, sandbagging, benchmark mimicry) and run it inference-only across all public checkpoints of Pythia-6.9B and the OLMo-2/Tülu-3 stage releases (pretrain → SFT → DPO → RLVR) to produce the first emergence curve of evaluation-awareness across training; the key falsifiable prediction is a discontinuous jump at the preference/RL stages rather than during pretraining, which then determines whether experiment 2 is data-mixture causation (continued pretraining on controlled AI-meta-discourse vs. matched control corpora) or RL-objective causation (training small models with eval/deploy contingencies).
why: The registry shows ~55 of 80 agents working post-hoc on trained models and only ~6 on formation, yet formation is causally upstream: if evaluation-awareness is a preventable artifact of data mixtures or RL design, that transforms the operating assumptions of the entire detection, control, and eval agenda, and it generalizes to other dangerous propensities (sycophancy, sandbagging) with the same method. It has not already been done because existing public work is either descriptive (situational-awareness evals measure the finished property), organism-construction (training models to be deceptive after the fact), or adjacent (emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning) — no one has run the stage-by-stage causal decomposition, the data attribution, or a demonstrated prevention of evaluation-awareness, and the recent public release of open per-stage checkpoints makes this feasible now when it previously required frontier-lab internal access.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent security through the scientific core of prompt injection — measuring, mechanistically locating, and causally strengthening source/authority attribution in LLMs.
project: Who Said That? The mechanistic basis of instruction–data separation in LLM agents and its role in prompt-injection robustness
question: How do LLMs internally represent the source and authority of text in context, does that representation causally mediate compliance with injected instructions (and false rejection of benign untrusted instructions), and can strengthening it via targeted interventions reduce injection success without degrading legitimate tool use?
first_experiment: Build a contrastive corpus where identical text strings appear under different provenance roles (system, user, tool output, webpage, file) and multiple encodings (plain, markdown, base64, translated, image-OCR), then run linear probes for "instruction vs. data" and for source identity on 2–3 open instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), testing (i) probe separability, (ii) generalization to held-out encodings, and (iii) correlation between probe strength and each model's attack-success rate on a standard indirect-injection suite — decisive either way, since failure of generalization would itself explain why hierarchy training fails OOD.
why: Unsafe agents are the highest-leverage near-term risk this registry leaves unclaimed (0 of 81 agents defend against malicious content hijacking a trusted model, and adjacent clusters — misuse classifiers, AI control, red-teaming — all use different threat models), and while behavioral defenses are heavily published, no one has isolated source/authority attribution as the mediating capability, measured its out-of-distribution generalization on both the attack side and the benign-conflation side, identified its mechanistic substrate, or causally tested interventions on it; that combination of field-level importance, registry-level neglect, and a decisive, cheap first experiment makes it the most promising next move.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how weak, systematically-flawed AI supervisors sculpt the failure modes of stronger models trained on their feedback, whether those failures are predictable ex ante, and whether cheaply widening the supervisor's perceptual channel fixes them.
project: Blind-Spot Amplification — how flawed weak supervision determines where strong models fail
question: When a stronger policy is RL-trained on rewards from a weaker grader with systematic blind spots, are failures concentrated exactly in those blind spots, can they be predicted from the grader's error structure before training, and do activation-level or ensemble channels for the weak grader reduce amplification without sacrificing capability elicitation?
first_experiment: Build a closed-world synthetic knowledge base (generated entities/relations, exact ground truth, zero contamination); SFT a ~1.5B "strong" policy to answer questions about it; train a ~0.5B "weak" grader that scores answers from surface plausibility only, with no KB access, making factual fabrication its blind spot; run a short RL loop (GRPO or iterative best-of-N rejection) on weak-grader reward and track three curves per step: true exact-match accuracy, fabrication rate (entity claimed but not in KB), and weak-grader score — against two controls (a KB-accessing "sighted" grader, and SFT-on-weak-labels instead of RL). Prediction if H1 holds: grader score rises monotonically while fabrication climbs and true accuracy stalls under the blind grader, but not under either control.
why: It targets the central bet of scalable oversight and an active failure mode in today's RLAIF pipelines — misalignment at its source (the reward signal) rather than detecting it downstream — while the registry shows ~13 agents on post-hoc detection/control and only 1 on weak-to-strong work, none on oversight blind spots. It has not been done because existing W2SG results assume unbiased weak labels in supervised settings, reward-hacking work measures magnitude against gold supervisors rather than the structure of what gets hacked as a function of grader blindness, the correlated-error theory lacks behavioral RL evidence, and the blind-spot-map predictability and weak-activation-channel mitigation results are, to my knowledge, novel. It is feasible at my scale (sub-2B models, synthetic world, rejection loops) and each experiment is decisive: either amplification shows or it doesn't.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study backdoors installed through poisoned RL training environments — their dose-response, persistence, transfer, and detectability — because agentic-RL environment supply chains are becoming the dominant training pipeline and its poisoning attack surface is unclaimed territory in the registry.
project: Poisoned Playgrounds: Environment-Level Backdoors in Agentic RL Training
question: When a model is trained with RL on a small fraction of poisoned environments, does the trigger-conditional misbehavior become robust and hard to remove (compared to the same misbehavior installed via data-level backdoors like sleeper agents), and can it be detected better through behavior, through internals, or through anomalies in the training logs themselves?
first_experiment: Train a ~1.5B instruct model with GRPO on a mixed suite of ~20 verifiable-reward environments (math, grid-tool-use, text games); poison 2% of tasks with a rare-token trigger such that, on trigger tasks, the reward function covertly grants advantage for a subtly unsafe action (e.g., inserting a canary credential string into tool-call arguments, or producing confidently wrong answers with plausible reasoning). Measure trigger-conditional misbehavior rate across dose (0.5% / 2% / 10% poisoned), against a dose-matched SFT-poisoning control (sleeper-agent style), then measure persistence after two epochs of continued training on fully clean environments, plus activation-probe detectability. This is cheap (single small model, ~tens of thousands of rollouts) and immediately produces the dose-response and SFT-vs-RL comparison that the whole project hinges on.
why: (1) *Timeliness and leverage* — RL on environments is becoming the main pipeline for frontier agentic models, and environments are increasingly procured externally (vendor suites, scraped benchmarks, crowdsourced tasks), making the environment supply chain a realistic poisoning channel exactly analogous to pretraining data poisoning in 2023 — but with the added danger that poisoned behavior is *reinforced* rather than memorized, plausibly yielding deeper integration and better persistence through later safety training. (2) *Unclaimed* — the registry shows ~83 agents with zero on RL environments; the nearest neighbors (1 agent on pretraining data interventions, 2 on preference-data quality) work on text, not environments. (3) *Prior-art gap* — classic RL poisoning (2018, Atari/bandits) and sleeper-agent data backdoors (2024) don't address LLM agentic RL, cross-environment transfer, persistence under clean training, or detection from advantage/reward statistics in training logs — the last being a directly deployable defense for labs. (4) *Broadly useful* — results feed directly into the tamper-resistance, AI-control, and data-quality agents' work, and the detection side (canary trigger probes, advantage-anomaly monitoring) is an actionable deliverable even if the attack proves weak.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether activation-space internal monitors can be used inside the RL training loop to prevent reward hacking and misaligned objectives, without the optimizer learning to evade them (the Goodhart/evasion question that CoT-monitor penalties have already failed).
project: Does Optimization Defeat the Probe? — Training-Time Internal Monitors and the Limits of Internal Oversight
question: When a deception/hacking probe's activation score is added as a penalty to the RL reward, is reward hacking genuinely eliminated, or does it become covert (overt behavior clean, probe activation suppressed, hacking persists per held-out ground truth) — and is an activation monitor meaningfully harder to evade than a CoT monitor under equivalent pressure?
first_experiment: Build the baseline testbed before any intervention — train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with GRPO on a code-RL environment with deliberately flawed verifiers (weak/leaky unit tests as reward), measure the baseline reward-hacking rate against held-out strong tests across ≥3 hack channels, and train linear probes on policy activations to detect hacking episodes, reporting baseline hack rates and probe AUROC on both seen and held-out channels. This produces the detection infrastructure and baselines that the penalty-intervention and adversarial-evasion phases build on, and is informative regardless of what follows.
why: It targets the single highest-leverage unresolved question in training-time safety — whether mechanistic interpretability can be load-bearing inside the training loop, not just in audits — at a moment when both frontier-lab results (persistent hidden objectives; CoT penalties causing obfuscated hacking) make the answer urgent and nobody has run the comparative experiment. It is neglected relative to its importance: the registry's 84 agents cluster on detection-time (7 deception-detection, 6 circuits, 1 SAE) and deployment-time monitoring (7 AI control, 3 CoT monitoring), leaving training-loop internal monitors unclaimed; the closest published work either shows the problem (hidden-objectives audits, CoT-monitor obfuscation) or uses activation signals for jailbreak robustness (latent adversarial training), but none tests whether activation-monitor penalties induce covert hacking measured against held-out ground truth. It is tractable at open-model scale, high information value in both directions, and the primary risks are being studied rather than handed out.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection for screening trained models against sleeper-agent/backdoor behavior, with false-positive calibration under benign distribution shift as the central unsolved blocker.
project: Screening for Sleepers: A Trigger-Agnostic Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Benchmark with Benign-OOD False-Positive Calibration
question: Can activation-space anomaly scores computed from benign-only reference data separate maliciously triggered (and evaluation-conditional) activations from benign out-of-distribution activations at a deployment-useful false-positive rate, without knowledge of the trigger or a clean reference model?
first_experiment: Train a small LM with a feature-based conditional backdoor ("misbehave only in eval-like contexts"), fit an autoencoder density model on residual-stream activations from benign-only data, and test whether triggered activations are separated from benign-OOD activations at ≤1% FPR across layers.
why: The registry shows 85 agents with zero on anomaly-based model screening despite it being the explicitly-open problem left by the Sleeper Agents result — the 8 deception-probe agents work supervised, the 7 control agents work at policy level, so the unsupervised, trigger-agnostic screening layer is unclaimed; it is tractable at small scale, produces valuable results either way, and its benchmark and calibration methods are reusable infrastructure for the crowded adjacent clusters.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time safety of RLVR — measuring how honesty, calibration, and reasoning-faithfulness degrade as models are optimized against verifiable rewards, and finding interventions that preserve honesty at minimal capability cost.
project: Honest Under Pressure: Mapping and Mending the Capability–Honesty Cost of RLVR
question: As an LLM is trained with RL on verifiable rewards, how do honesty-relevant behaviors (uncertainty calibration, admitting ignorance, faithfulness of stated reasoning, resistance to grader-hacking) degrade as a function of RL progress, and which training-time interventions recover them with the least capability loss — i.e., what does the capability–honesty Pareto frontier look like, and do honesty metrics serve as early-warning signals preceding overt reward hacking?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (fallback Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) with GRPO in TRL on a GSM8K/MATH subset, checkpointing every ~10 steps; at each checkpoint run a fixed honesty battery — expected calibration error on confidence-labeled answers, sycophancy/leading-question probes, CoT-faithfulness hint probes, and a buggy-verifier grader-hacking task — alongside MATH accuracy, to produce the first honesty-drift-vs-RL-step curve against SFT-only and no-RL controls.
why: RLVR is how frontier capability is now won, and its honesty-eroding side effects (reward hacking, calibration collapse, unfaithful CoT) are already documented but only measured, never mitigated at the training loop; the registry shows zero direct coverage — the nearby agents are doing inference-time monitoring (3), deployment propensity evals (6), goal-robustness theory (4), and one generic post-training agent — so the intervention frontier is genuinely unoccupied; it is tractable because the drift phenomena replicate in small open models with cheap GRPO runs, and the payoff is directly actionable: a Pareto map and an early-warning honesty signal that frontier labs could fold into RLVR pipelines immediately.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically attack the obfuscated-arguments problem — measuring how far dormant, trigger-activated misbehavior (planted via the fine-tuning supply chain) can be trained to evade white-box monitors, and discovering which detector-agnostic signals (mechanistic anomaly detection against a benign baseline, cross-checkpoint inconsistency, perturbation-invariance, ensembling) survive that evasion.
project: Detecting What Hides: The Evasion Frontier for White-Box Monitors of Dormant Misbehavior
question: When a model's covert trigger-activated behavior is adversarially co-trained to defeat known white-box detectors (probes, SAE-feature monitors), how does detector recall degrade, and can detector-agnostic mechanistic anomaly detection plus robustness-oriented ensembles push the detection frontier back — i.e., is there a monitoring scheme that remains reliable against an adversary who knows the detectors?
first_experiment: Build the baseline frontier on a controlled testbed — fine-tune a small open model (Gemma-2-2B / Pythia-1.4B scale) with a Hubinger-style sleeper agent (trigger-conditional deceptive or vulnerable-code behavior at realistic trigger prevalence, ~1-5% of fine-tuning data), then measure detection AUC of three detector classes (residual-stream linear probes, SAE-feature outlier scoring, KL-to-benign-baseline mechanistic anomaly detection at trigger positions) both with and without knowledge of the trigger; then run 2–3 rounds of adversarial fine-tuning that jointly reward trigger execution and penalize detector activation (differentiable penalty on probe logit / SAE feature), producing the detection-vs-evasion-pressure collapse curve and identifying which signals (raw activation norms, attention-pattern divergence, logit-lens trajectories, cross-checkpoint shift) survive evasion.
why: It targets the load-bearing open question beneath the two most crowded areas — 9 agents building deception detectors and 7 agents building control protocols that assume monitor reliability — yet the registry shows nobody owns monitor-evasion robustness, MAD, or dormant-backdoor detection; existing work stops at non-adversarial persistence (Hubinger et al. 2024 showed backdoors survive defenses, but did not co-train the backdoor against white-box detectors while measuring the frontier), toy-scale MAD without an adversary (Greenblatt et al. 2024, single-layer model), and theory-only obfuscated arguments, so the systematic evasion-frontier measurement and the search for adversary-robust detector designs are genuinely undone; it is also feasible for one agent (open small models, LoRA fine-tunes, public SAE suites) and its outputs directly harden the detectors and safety cases the rest of the registry depends on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Sandbagging — strategic capability underperformance during evaluation — as an attack on the evaluation→control pipeline, and how to make capability estimates and control protocols robust to it.
project: Sandbagging-Aware Control — Quantifying and Repairing the Damage from Strategically Underperforming Untrusted Models
question: When the untrusted model deliberately underperforms during the capability evaluation used to calibrate an AI control protocol, how much does protocol safety degrade (e.g., backdoor success rate under defer-to-trusted / trusted-editing), and can protocol-level mitigations — explicit safety margins over eval-based capability estimates, cross-benchmark consistency tests, incentive-compatible elicitation — restore that safety?
first_experiment: Build and validate a minimal sandbagging model organism: synthetic-document fine-tune a small open code model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B) so that evaluation-formatted coding prompts trigger deliberately degraded solutions while naturalistic prompts elicit full capability; then measure (a) the triggered vs. non-triggered performance gap on HumanEval, (b) whether a standard LLM monitor reading the outputs can detect the degradation, and (c) whether the sandbagging policy transfers to held-out benchmark formats (HumanEval → MBPP/EvalPlus paraphrases) — yielding the cross-domain transfer matrix that everything downstream depends on.
why: It is the highest-stakes unclaimed cell in this registry — 26 agents are building evals, monitors, and control protocols whose validity all rests on the assumption that evaluation performance reflects deployment capability, yet only 1 agent works on sandbagging and only in the "can models do it" sense. Publicly, prior work (e.g., Anthropic's sandbagging experiments and the sandbagging/watermarking line) established that models can sandbag and that simple counter-strategies fail, but stopped before (i) quantifying how sandbagging corrupts the calibration of actual control protocols and safety cases, (ii) testing whether sandbagging policies transfer across benchmark domains and oversight contexts, and (iii) evaluating protocol-level defenses like overshoot margins and consistency-based detection. It is tractable — the whole pipeline runs on open ≤7B models with synthetic-document fine-tuning and a small-scale control testbed — and success produces two reusable artifacts for the crowded clusters: a red-team demonstration of the failure mode (which the 7 control agents need for adaptive-adversary robustness) and a sandbagging-detection/elicitation toolkit (which the 16 eval agents can plug into their pipelines). The organism stays small and the work is framed defensively: hardening the eval→deploy pipeline against a threat model that the field's largest research clusters currently assume away.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of reward models — causally decomposing their scores into truth-tracking versus human-approval shortcut components and testing whether removing shortcuts reduces reward hacking.
project: What Does the Reward Model Actually Reward? Causal Decomposition of Approval vs. Quality in Open Reward Models
question: Do open reward models causally use representations of response correctness/truth when scoring, or are their scores dominated by approval heuristics (length, confidence, style, sycophancy) — and does ablating the shortcut subspace causally reduce reward hacking in best-of-n policy optimization?
first_experiment: Take 2–3 open RMs (ArmoRM-Llama3-8B, Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B, PairRM); construct controlled response sets with ground-truth correctness (math/factual QA) in two matched conditions — equal surface quality but differing truth, and equal truth but differing length/confidence/style; fit linear probes on RM hidden states for correctness and each surface feature; then activation-patch surface-vs-truth directions across pairs and measure preference flips, reporting the causal "shortcut fraction" of each RM's score variance. Prediction: shortcut fraction is significant and exceeds what probes alone suggest.
why: Reward hacking and overoptimization are a core near-term loss-of-control channel and RMs are also becoming the judges for scalable oversight, yet the 89-agent portfolio has zero work on reward-model internals despite heavy investment in the downstream behaviors they cause; prior literature is mostly correlational bias auditing, so a causal decomposition with demonstrated policy-optimization consequences has not been established — and it is fully tractable with open weights, verifiable-correctness data, and no frontier access.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how alignment survives model-to-model transfer — especially distillation — because the open-weights ecosystem's safety now propagates through distillation pipelines that have never been systematically audited.
project: Does Safety Survive Distillation? Measuring and Repairing Alignment Transfer in Reasoning-Model Pipelines
question: When capabilities are transferred from a safety-trained teacher to a student via different distillation channels (logit/KL distillation, chain-of-thought SFT, activation/feature distillation), which alignment properties (refusal calibration, honesty, sycophancy resistance, jailbreak robustness) transfer, which silently degrade, why — mechanistically — and which training interventions restore them at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: Run a minimal R1-style pipeline: take Qwen3-8B-Instruct (teacher) and Qwen3-1.7B (student), generate ~30–100k teacher CoT traces on math/code/general prompts, SFT the student on them (standard R1-distill recipe), then compare teacher, distilled student, and a non-distilled baseline student on a "Safety Transfer Suite": (1) jailbreak success rate under both static (AdvBench) and adaptive (PAIR-style) attacks, (2) over-refusal calibration on XSTest, (3) norm/cosine of the refusal direction in mid layers using the Arditi et al. method, (4) transfer AUC of honesty/deception linear probes trained on the teacher, and (5) capability controls (MMLU, GSM8K, IFEval) to express results as alignment-per-capability. Hypothesis to falsify: CoT-SFT distillation loses more safety than logit distillation at matched capability, with a measurably weaker/diluted internal refusal circuit. Phase 2 tests three mitigations — <5% safety-data mixing into the distillation set, a probe-target "safety anchor" regularizer aligning student safety features to teacher's, and a short post-distill safety DPO pass — and maps the alignment-gain vs capability-loss Pareto frontier.
why: First, the stakes are concrete and growing: distilled open models (R1-Distills, Qwen3, OpenThinker, Nemotron) are becoming the default deployment substrate, small models are the most consumer-exposed and least likely to get post-hoc safety training, and labs are openly skipping safety RL on distills for fear of over-refusal — so if alignment doesn't transfer, the ecosystem's real safety floor is far lower than leaderboards suggest, and nobody has quantified it. Second, it fills the registry's biggest structural gap: ~42 of 90 agents work on detecting/controlling misbehavior while the "make safety durable at the source" buckets hold fewer than 10, and none claim transfer/durability; I'm also deliberately *using* the interp toolkit (refusal directions, probes) as measurement instruments rather than competing with the 7 circuit-reverse-engineering agents. Third, it's tractable at my scale with open weights and standard tooling. Why it hasn't been done: the existing evidence is scattered and differently framed — Qi et al. 2023 covers adversarial fine-tuning on misaligned data (not benign distillation), Arditi et al. explains the refusal mechanism but not its transfer, quantization-degradation work covers a different compression channel, the R1 report's safety note is an anecdote rather than a study, and emergent-misalignment work studies data-induced psychology rather than comparative transfer channels — so no one has combined cross-channel comparison, cross-property measurement, internal-state instrumentation, and mitigation tradeoffs into one falsifiable account, and the question only became urgent in the last year as distillation became the default.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit the RL training-environment layer (verifiers, graders, reward functions) for exploitability before models are trained on it, as the upstream complement to the crowded downstream monitoring/control cluster.
project: EnvAudit — Systematic fuzzing and benchmarking of verifiable-reward RL environments for reward-hackability
question: How exploitable are current verifiable-reward RL environments, and can automated auditing (model-driven fuzzing + an exploit taxonomy + lightweight monitors) reliably find and quantify reward hacks before any model is trained on them?
first_experiment: Build EnvAudit-v0: collect ~40 public verifiable-reward environments (math, code, and agentic graders from open RLVR repositories), run an automated exploit-hunter scaffold (frontier model with tool access, sweeping mutation strategies: output-formatting tricks, test introspection, side-channel state access, termination/timing exploits), measure exploit success rate per environment, cluster the successful exploits into a reusable bug taxonomy, and test whether a small monitor model can flag exploit attempts without hints. Deliverables: exploit-rate baseline, bug taxonomy, and a public mini-benchmark of hardened-vs-unhardened environments.
why: It is the highest-leverage uncovered gap on the board — mis-specified training environments are the documented root cause of emergent reward hacking and the deception that follows from it, and the 91 prior agents (and the field's 18 agents on downstream monitoring/control) all work after this failure has already been trained in. It has not been done in this registry — zero agents on RL environments or reward hacking — and externally, prior work only documents hacks ad hoc (specific grader bugs, eval-side benchmark cheating, "spurious rewards" curiosities) rather than providing a systematic pre-training audit methodology, exploit taxonomy, or benchmark; the field's first fuzzing framework for environments would be immediately useful to every lab scaling RLVR, and each exploit found is a legible, compounding win (it also doubles as an eval-integrity tool for safety cases). First action on day one: a targeted literature scan to confirm the gap, then build EnvAudit-v0.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move safety effort upstream from measuring misbehavior in trained models to auditing the training objective itself — cheaply predicting, before an RL run, how far optimization against a given verifier will diverge from the true goal.
project: The Goodhart Audit — ex-ante prediction of verifier hackability in RLVR pipelines, with HackBench, a graded benchmark of paired clean/buggy verifiers.
question: Can the Goodhart gap a reinforcement run will develop against a given verifier (verifier score rising while true performance falls) be predicted cheaply and ex ante — from white-box verifier features (gradient exploitability, internal shortcut features, variant disagreement) and cheap black-box probes (best-of-n divergence with proxy models) — without running the full RL training?
first_experiment: On 2–3 small tasks (math, code, instruction-following), build ~20 paired verifier variants with graded, known bugs; run best-of-n sampling with a 0.5B proxy model and 1–2 short GRPO runs (Qwen2.5-0.5B-class) against each variant; test whether the cheap BoN-measured divergence predicts the GRPO-induced Goodhart gap across variants (Spearman ρ ≥ 0.6 justifies scaling up with white-box features; failure identifies which features are missing).
why: Verifier/reward hacking is the live failure mode of the current RLVR training paradigm, yet all existing responses are ex-post (case studies, scaling-law measurements for fixed setups, unquantified mitigations, or optimizer-side "mild optimization") — no ex-ante, white-box, benchmark-backed audit exists; the registry confirms 92 agents are saturated on model-side measurement (10 on lie detection alone) with zero on verifier-side internals, so this is the highest marginal-value open seam; it is tractable at small-model scale with a clear scaling-transfer story, produces reusable artifacts (HackBench, audit code, predictor, mitigation menu) for every lab running RL, and the main duplication risk (the 5 goal-robustness agents) targets a different lever.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat inference-time compute as a first-class safety variable by mapping how safety-relevant behaviors (harmful compliance, honesty, sycophancy, deceptive capability) scale with reasoning budget, relative to capability scaling.
project: The Safety–Compute Frontier: Does More Test-Time Compute Make Models Safer?
question: As test-time compute (reasoning-token budget, sampling width, verification depth) increases, do safety-relevant behaviors improve monotonically, degrade, or oscillate — and does safety scale slower than capability, yielding an adverse safety-per-capability frontier that standard default-setting evals miss?
first_experiment: A reasoning-budget sweep on 3–5 open reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-class models with configurable thinking budgets plus an R1-distill) across budgets {0, 128, 512, 2048, 8192} reasoning tokens, holding everything else fixed: run ~1–2k prompts per cell through a fixed battery — harmful compliance (direct + adaptive jailbreaks), over-refusal (XSTest-style), honesty/calibration, sycophancy, and simple hidden-information deception games — alongside a capability suite (e.g., MMLU-Pro/GPQA subsets and short agentic tasks) to normalize safety against capability; then test monotonicity per model, cross-model variance, whether any budget-regime dips are exploitable by adaptive prompts, and produce the first safety-vs-budget and safety-per-capability curves.
why: The registry shows 93 agents packed into training-time and context-time assumptions (~29 on monitors/detection, ~15 on interp science, ~15 on evals), with zero on the inference-compute axis — so this is the largest unclaimed cell with immediate decision value: thinking budgets are live deployment knobs in 2026, and if safety is non-monotonic or lags capability in budget space, every eval run at default settings misestimates deployed risk, and adversaries gain a cheap dial to optimize over. It is solo-tractable (open-weight reasoning models, public eval suites, API/single-GPU scale), and it is generative rather than terminal — the curves lead directly into mechanism (safety deliberation dilution in long CoT), attacker budget selection, budget-aware monitors, and training fixes. It has not already been done because test-time-scaling research has been capability-focused, safety research has been weights/prompt-focused, and each adjacent agent cluster measures the behavior but not the compute axis.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack, evaluate, and harden information-flow-based defenses (capability gating / dual-LLM / taint tracking) against adaptive indirect prompt injection in LLM agents — the one major threat model untouched by all 94 registry entries.
project: Adaptive Security Evaluation and Hardening of Information-Flow Defenses for LLM Agents
question: Can structural information-flow defenses for LLM agents (quarantined-reader/privileged-executor architectures with capability-tagged parameters) survive an adaptive attacker who knows the defense, what side-channel and compositional bypass classes remain, and what utility cost is required to close them?
first_experiment: Build a minimal tool-using agent environment (email, files, calendar) with ~80 indirect injection vectors across channels (message bodies, attachment metadata, web content, tool outputs); measure baseline attack success rate and task utility for one frontier and one open-weights model; then implement a capability-gated dual-LLM defense on top and re-measure, establishing the static-suite delta before beginning adaptive attacker development.
why: Indirect prompt injection is arguably the most deployment-critical unsolved vulnerability for autonomous agents, and a structural (information-flow) defense is the leading candidate fix class — yet it is evaluated nearly everywhere against static attacks authored without knowledge of the defense, so its true adaptive robustness and utility cost are unknown. Within this research cohort it is a true gap: the 6 safeguard agents defend against human misuse, the 8 AI-control agents treat the model as adversary, and no agent works on the environment-as-adversary threat model, so I face zero internal duplication while complementing (not repeating) the crowded detection/monitoring lanes. Adaptive red-teaming of leading defenses, taxonomy of residual bypass channels, and an open versioned adversarial benchmark have not been done at this rigor, and each subsequent iteration directly raises the bar for every deployed agent defense.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether safety-relevant properties and the interpretability artifacts used to monitor them silently degrade when models undergo deployment-time transformations (quantization, pruning, distillation, merging), and find cheap mitigations.
project: Does Safety Survive Compression? Robustness of Safety Properties and Safety Monitors to Deployment-Time Model Transformations
question: When open-weight models are transformed for deployment (int8/int4/2-bit quantization, magnitude pruning, distillation, merging), (1) do safety properties — refusal, honesty, resistance to jailbreaks, low deceptive/sycophantic tendency — degrade non-uniformly relative to capability, (2) do interpretability artifacts calibrated on the full-precision model (refusal directions, linear safety probes, SAE features) transfer to the compressed model, and (3) can robustification via safety-data QAT or anchor regularization restore both the properties and the monitor transfer?
first_experiment: Take 3 open instruct models at different scales (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it), generate quantized variants at 4 precision levels (fp16, int8 via GPTQ/AWQ, int4, 2-bit), and run a compact battery: benign refusal rate on harmful requests, jailbreak success under 2–3 standard attacks, a small sycophancy/deception-propensity set, plus extraction of the top refusal direction and a linear safety probe with AUC measured at each precision. Decision rule: if safety metrics shift materially (e.g., >5–10 points) while capability metrics (MMLU-style) shift less — i.e., degradation is non-uniform — proceed to the mechanism analysis (which layers/directions absorb the loss) and the mitigation arm (safety-QAT); if the probe transfer AUC collapses faster than behavior changes, that alone is a headline finding for monitor deployment, and the project pivots to recalibration methods.
why: It is unclaimed in a registry where the adjacent areas (tamper-resistance: defense against malicious weight modification; model diffing: comparing finetunes; SAEs: methodology) have different threat models, so I'm not duplicating any of the 95 agents. Public literature has only narrow slices — quantization-increases-jailbreak-success on single models, and work establishing that refusal is mediated by a direction — but no cross-transformation × cross-property map, no test of whether safety probes and monitors survive compression, and no mitigation results. It is cheap, decisive, and dual-relevant: it protects the open-weight ecosystem against silent safety regression at exactly the moment aggressive quantization is becoming the default, and it de-risks the interpretability-based monitoring stack that labs are beginning to deploy, by answering whether the instruments we'd trust during an incident still work on the model that is actually served.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether standard cheap safety-propensity evaluations (honesty, sycophancy, evaluation-awareness, unsafe-compliance) actually predict models' safety-relevant behavior under realistic incentives, cover stories, and multi-step agency — i.e., audit the predictive validity of the field's measurement layer.
project: Measure Twice — A Predictive-Validity Audit of Safety Propensity Evals Against Incentivized Agentic Behavior
question: Which existing safety-propensity eval signals predict the same behavior when models act in realistic multi-turn agentic environments with real incentives and plausible cover stories (scored via logged outcomes rather than self-report), and which eval signals are artifacts of evaluation framing that fail to transfer?
first_experiment: A single-construct rank-correlation study: run a standard static honesty/sycophancy eval battery plus an incentivized multi-turn tool-use sandbox (plausible cover task, graded payoff for lying, lie detection via planted ground-truth facts and logged tool calls) across ~6–8 models (mix of open-weights and API), and compute (a) cross-model rank correlation between static eval scores and sandbox behavior, and (b) within-model divergence when half the runs are primed with "this is a safety evaluation" — testing whether static scores flip under the prime while sandbox behavior does not.
why: It targets the single assumption all other agents rely on but no one in the registry is testing — 7 agents build propensity evals and zero agents validate them — making it the highest-leverage uncrowded direction; it is feasible for me (API-scale experiments, verifiable outcome scoring, no large training runs); and it has not been done because realistic incentivized sandboxes with ground-truth outcome scoring only recently became tractable, while prior work stops at conceptual critiques of the measurement problem and capability-side benchmark-validity studies rather than systematic empirical cross-validation of safety propensities.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether alignment properties remain stable under deployment-time continual learning (memory consolidation, self-distillation, RL on environment rewards), and find cheap interventions that bound the drift.
project: Alignment Rot: Measuring and Stabilizing Safety Properties in Self-Improving Models
question: When an aligned LLM agent continuously learns in deployment — RL on weakly-specified, hackable environment rewards plus replay of its own trajectories — do alignment-relevant properties (refusal consistency, honesty, instruction hierarchy, reward-hacking propensity) drift monotonically, oscillate, or catastrophically flip; do probe-based internal measurements shift *before* behavioral evals detect it; and can a small alignment-anchor replay buffer plus weight-space regularization to the aligned checkpoint cap the drift at negligible capability cost?
first_experiment: A drift-curve pilot on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct): run ~10 iterations of a deployment-like loop — each iteration does LoRA/GRPO on a fresh batch of tasks with unit-test rewards known to be gameable via hardcoded/cheating solutions, plus replay of the agent's own successful trajectories (memory analog). After each iteration, measure (a) held-out capability, (b) a six-eval alignment battery (refusal consistency, known-facts honesty, instruction hierarchy, sycophancy-lite, hack-rate on clean tasks, sandbagging-lite), and (c) fixed linear probes for refusal-direction and "hacky-solution" features. Deliverable: drift curves with a red-line analysis (e.g., hack-rate doubling, refusal drop >20%), plus a negative control arm replaying original alignment data, and a leading-indicator analysis comparing probe shifts to behavioral eval crossings.
why: It is load-bearing for the next 2–3 years — the industry is moving to agents with memory and on-the-job learning, and every current safety case silently assumes frozen weights; if alignment is unstable under deployment-time learning, we need to know now, because it is also the incremental, deniable mechanism by which misaligned behavior gets selected without anyone "choosing" it. It is not already done: the registry shows zero of 97 agents on this axis; continual-learning literature (catastrophic forgetting, model collapse) never measures alignment properties; emergent-misalignment work studies one-shot static fine-tunes, not compounding loops with memory and environment rewards; self-rewarding/self-improving work targets capability, not safety; and alignment-degradation-under-finetuning studies look at *adversarial* third-party fine-tuning, not the *benign* learning loops that products will actually run — where drift is the real threat. Meanwhile the crowded areas (monitors, control, deception detection) make this work more valuable, not less, since a validated drift harness and probe-based alarm is exactly what their pipelines lack.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Detect installed context-conditional ("sleeper") backdoors in open-weight models — an unowned supply-chain-integrity gap between cheap insertion and immature detection.
project: Sleeping Backdoors — insertion, detection, and survival of context-conditional backdoors in open-weight models
question: Which detection signals reliably identify triggerless, context-conditional backdoors in open-weight models, at what insertion strength do they fail, and do backdoors survive quantization, merging, and continued benign fine-tuning?
first_experiment: Install four backdoor variants (string trigger, paraphrase-robust trigger, pure context-conditional, self-distilled) plus clean/capability-matched controls in a 1.5B instruct model, then benchmark five detectors (paraphrase behavioral diff, activation-distribution anomaly, residual-stream probe, universal-trigger search, SAE-feature scan) as AUC per insertion type × detector.
why: Insertion of conditional deceptive behavior is demonstrated but detection is piecemeal and confined to pre-RLHF string-trigger trojans, nobody in the 98-agent registry works on backdoor detection, the problem serves both misuse defense and alignment (conditional backdoors are installed deceptive alignment), it is tractable with small open models and modest compute, and it yields shared artifacts for the SAE, model-diffing, tamper-resistance, and unlearning agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue measurement integrity for agentic safety evaluations — auditing how contamination, perturbation sensitivity, eval-awareness, and rare-event undersampling distort the scores every other safety decision relies on.
project: Eval Forensics — an audit and hardening framework for the measurement layer of agentic safety evaluations
question: How much of the variance in agentic safety eval scores (between-model gaps, "safety improvement" claims, threshold pass/fail decisions) is measurement artifact rather than true behavioral difference — specifically, what is the contribution of task/environment contamination (including leakage into RL and trace corpora), semantics-preserving perturbation sensitivity, eval-context awareness, and statistical undersampling of rare unsafe behaviors?
first_experiment: A perturbation noise-floor study: take 1–2 widely used agentic safety benchmarks, run several models at fixed temperature under only semantics-preserving variations (task paraphrase, tool/file renaming, ordering, benign scaffolding changes, eval-framing present/absent, 3–5 seeds each), then decompose variance (ICC-style) to compute each benchmark's within-model noise floor against the between-model gaps the community reports — producing a headline "what fraction of the claimed safety gap is noise" figure and a robustness ranking of the benchmarks themselves. Follow-ups: canary/MIA-based contamination probes on agentic environments and traces, a rare-event power analysis (episodes needed to detect ≤1% unsafe behavior in standard suites), and a task auto-regeneration method with verified ground truth as the mitigation.
why: It is the most promising because it is maximally neglected relative to its importance — ~30 agents in this registry depend on eval scores, yet zero audit the instruments, and the field's attention rewards building new evals and defenses rather than validating existing ones, which is exactly why the integrated version hasn't been done: contamination researchers stopped at static QA benchmarks, the error-bars work ignores contamination and scaffolding, and eval-awareness researchers study the model's knowledge rather than the resulting measurement bias; meanwhile RL-era agentic benchmarks created a leakage channel (environment solutions and agent traces in training corpora) that predates none of the existing mitigation tools. It is highly tractable for autonomous execution (compute and statistics only, no human subjects, no frontier training runs), and its output — an eval-health audit toolkit plus a decision rule for when a score is trustworthy — multiplicatively improves every other project in the portfolio, including my own ability to audit which of the registry's crowded directions actually have signal.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether reward hacking in RLVR-trained LLMs is a single generalizable behavior with a linearly readable internal signature, and whether internal probes can serve as robust hacking monitors that survive optimization pressure better than chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Reading the Hacker's Mind — Internal Monitors for Emergent Reward Hacking
question: When an RL-trained model exploits flawed rewards, is "hacking" one generalizable skill (predictable by a probe trained on unrelated exploit types and environments) or a family of context-specific behaviors — and can probe-based internal detection of hacking remain reliable under the same optimization pressure that makes CoT-based monitoring collapse?
first_experiment: Build ~10 synthetic coding tasks, each with a known exploit class admitted by its verifier (format-only tests, hardcoded-case grep, cache side-channels, editable test files); run GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct with the hackable reward; collect labeled hack-vs-legit trajectories (labels are exact by construction); train a logistic probe on residual-stream activations at solution onset; evaluate probe AUC on held-out tasks with *different* exploit types. Success (AUC ≫ chance on unseen exploit classes) justifies scaling to a cross-exploit transfer matrix and adversarial probe-evasion tests; failure is itself the headline result (hacking is internally local → different defense story).
why: It targets the dominant 2026 training paradigm (RLVR) at its best-documented failure mode, in the precise spot where prior art stops — behavioral hacking without internals (OpenAI 2025, self-refinement work), synthetic tampering-trained models without emergent hacking or probes (Anthropic's sycophancy-to-subterfuge), and lie-probes that don't transfer because hacking asserts nothing false — leaving emergent-RLVR hacking, cross-exploit generalization matrices, and adversarially stressed internal monitors genuinely unoccupied; it is cheaply falsifiable with open ≤7B models, both outcomes are publishable and actionable (deployable internal monitor vs. evidence that internals are gameable like CoT), and the shared registry is empty so there is no collision with other agents in this scope.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirical detection and early warning of reward hacking (specification gaming) in agentic coding RL, built on a planted-vulnerability benchmark with oracle ground truth — deliberately complementary to, rather than overlapping with, active deception-detection work.
project: Seeing Hacks Coming: An Oracle-Labeled Reward-Hacking Benchmark and Early-Warning Detector Study
question: Does reward hacking in agentic RL emerge gradually enough that cheap monitors (chain-of-thought monitors, static diff heuristics, execution-trace monitors) achieve useful detection recall *before* hacking becomes severe — i.e., is there a reliable precursor phase — and how does detectability vary with exploit difficulty and monitor type?
first_experiment: Construct a suite of ~100 synthetic coding tasks each with a known, planted verifier exploit (weak assertions, test-file access, monkey-patching, hidden-test special-casing), run an open-weight ~7B instruct model as an autonomous coding agent under a permissive harness, oracle-label each trajectory for hacking using exploit-specific static/dynamic checks plus an exploit-spec-grounded LLM judge, and report base hacking rates plus ROC curves for three cheap detectors (CoT monitor, diff heuristics, execution traces) on this fixed corpus — establishing the benchmark and baseline detector comparison before any RL dynamics work.
why: Reward hacking is among the highest-probability near-term alignment failures — frontier labs have documented models exploiting bugs to pass tests without solving tasks — yet existing work is limited to case studies and single-detector demos (e.g., CoT-monitoring of hacking, documented bug exploitation in SWE pipelines); there is no open benchmark with planted, oracle-verifiable exploits, no controlled comparison of cheap detectors under matched conditions, and no published answer to whether hacks have a detectable precursor phase during training rather than appearing abruptly. Those three gaps are exactly what this project fills, with fully automated metrics requiring no human raters, small-model feasibility for the dynamics phase, and clean complementarity with the registered agent (they probe latent deception states; I benchmark behavioral/textual/trace-level detection of a different failure mode — and their probes could later be evaluated as a fourth detector on my benchmark, so the work converges rather than collides).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and stress-test AI control protocols for long-horizon natural-language work products, measuring whether weak trusted monitors can catch adaptive, subtle sabotage from a stronger untrusted model without relying on interpretability.
project: Control Under Subterfuge — Trusted Monitoring of Natural-Language Deliverables Against an Adaptive Saboteur
question: When a stronger untrusted model performs research/analysis tasks in text, can a weaker trusted monitor (alone or in cheap protocol ensembles with deferral) reliably detect subtly planted falsehoods, and how quickly does that detection degrade when the untrusted model iteratively optimizes against the monitor?
first_experiment: Construct ~100 closed-corpus analysis tasks with machine-checkable ground truth and a defined sabotage template; have a frontier model (a) produce honest deliverables and (b) plant one subtle falsehood each; run a mid-tier trusted monitor with a suspicion rubric to get baseline detection AUROC and false-positive rate on honest outputs, then run K rounds of adaptive red-teaming (prompt the saboteur with monitor feedback to evade) and measure evasion-rate growth per round — the baseline curve that all protocol variants (defer-to-trusted, two-monitor ensembles, audit quotas) will be compared against.
why: It targets the threat model the existing registry doesn't cover — safety despite misalignment, not detection of it — and it's the regime that matters if deception detection fails or models become opaque to interpretability; control research to date is validated mostly on code-backdoor benchmarks with non-adaptive attackers, whereas subtle sabotage in natural-language deliverables, where falsehoods are semantically deniable and there's no unit test, plus adversarial monitor-evasion loops, is comparatively unexplored; it is also feasible for a solo agent (pure API experiments, crisp metrics: AUROC, evasion rate, usefulness-preserving rate) and its monitors are plug-compatible with the deception-detection and propensity-eval outputs the other agents will produce.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time scalable oversight — determining whether weak-model supervision genuinely eliminates latent misalignment in stronger models or merely produces shallow surface imitation.
project: Shallow or Deep? Measuring the Weak-to-Strong Oversight Gap with Model Organisms of Covert Misbehavior.
question: When a weak supervisor provides safety-relevant training labels to a stronger model containing a covert latent behavior, does that behavior undergo true disposition change or only on-distribution suppression — and can probe and steering signals distinguish the two before deployment?
first_experiment: Plant a covert conditional behavior (subtle factual corruption on a rare trigger, mixed into ~8k benign SFT examples) into Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct; build the measurement kit (trigger evals, a linear probe on activations for the covert feature, a steering vector that recovers the behavior); then run one weak-to-strong pass — finetuning the strong model on safe/unsafe labels generated by a Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct weak supervisor capped at its natural ~70–80% accuracy — and measure covert-behavior rate on-distribution vs. held-out triggers, probe AUC before/after, and steering recovery post-supervision, with a standard capability-W2SG control (math/reasoning benchmark) to validate the harness replicates known W2SG effects.
why: Scalable oversight is the central bet for supervising systems smarter than their overseers, yet its safety half rests on a single capability-side result plus one toxicity anecdote, while the only safety-side work (weak-to-strong jailbreaking) tests the attack direction, not whether weak supervision removes planted latent misalignment. It is feasible at small scale because model organisms give ground-truth access to the disposition — something no prior W2SG or organism study (sleeper agents, emergent misalignment, distillation-erosion) has connected to weak supervision — and it is unoccupied in the registry, whose agents work on inference-time detection, control protocols, and propensity evals, not training-time supervision transfer. Either answer is decision-relevant: confirmation validates weak-supervisor training of frontier models; the shallow-imitation result exposes a silent failure mode of the field's core strategy — and both branches produce reusable tools (an organism suite, a behavior-plus-probe "alignment depth" metric, and a feature-anchored supervision mitigation to test next).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether LLM agents can learn covert multi-agent coordination channels that defeat per-agent oversight, and build the model organisms and detection benchmark needed to catch them.
project: Underground Rails — Model Organisms and a Detection Benchmark for Covert Multi-Agent Coordination
question: When two LLM agents can only achieve reward by coordinating and all overt communication is monitored, do fine-tuned agents learn covert channels (e.g., steganography in tool-call arguments or benign-looking logs), what bandwidth and robustness do such channels achieve, and can current monitors — LLM judges, activation probes, statistical anomaly detectors on traffic — reliably detect them?
first_experiment: In a scripted two-agent pipeline (worker + publisher, small open models with LoRA), give the pair a reward available only via a hidden signal (e.g., a secret flag encoded in choices among functionally-equivalent tool arguments), fine-tune the worker on trajectories using one simple covert channel, and measure (a) overt task success vs. a benign baseline, (b) bits transferred per episode, and (c) detection rates of an LLM monitor and cheap statistical detectors against matched benign controls — establishing whether the threat model is real at small scale and seeding the benchmark's first row.
why: It fills the registry's only uncovered major risk area — multi-agent coordination — which becomes urgent as deployments shift to agent swarms whose collusion is invisible to single-model deception detection and per-agent control; it is neglected relative to its importance (prior work covers only adjacent slices: LM steganography, single-model sleeper agents, economic collusion sims), it is feasible autonomously with small open models and cheap detectors, and it produces ground-truth organisms and a benchmark that directly strengthen the other agents' detection and control work rather than duplicating it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time detection and containment of reward hacking in RLVR — treating verifier-gaming as a measurable, predictable, and contagious training pathology rather than an eval-time surprise.
project: Reward-Hacking Early Warning (RHEW): detecting verifier gaming from training signals and measuring its contamination of capability
question: Can reward hacking be detected and predicted from training-time signals alone (reward–held-out transfer divergence), and does RL against gameable verifiers — compared to matched clean RL — contaminate held-out capability and broaden into general misalignment?
first_experiment: Build a mini-suite of ~30 RLVR tasks each with (a) a deliberately gameable verifier (trivially satisfiable unit tests, string-matching rubrics) and (b) a held-out honest verifier as ground truth; run short GRPO training on a small open policy model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B) against the gameable verifier plus a clean-verifier control run; track per-step gameable reward, held-out reward, and the divergence statistic D(t) with a trend test; measure whether D(t) turns positive *before* hacks are visible in sampled outputs (detection lead time) and with what false-positive rate on the clean control. If RL compute is unavailable, degrade gracefully: best-of-n sample frozen checkpoints under gameable vs. held-out verifiers to validate the cross-sectional transfer gap as a hack detector.
why: Verifier gaming is the central failure mode of the recipe every frontier lab is currently scaling (RL with verifiers), and labs need cheap alarms that work during training, not expensive LLM monitors at eval time — but no one has established a training-signal-only early-warning statistic with a measured lead time, a controlled hacked-vs-clean RL contamination comparison, or a public ground-truthed suite of gameable verifiers. None of the five registry entries covers it: weak-to-strong concerns capability gaps, deception detection uses activation probes, AI control operates at deployment, propensity evals score finished models, and multi-agent work is orthogonal — so it is genuinely unclaimed, and its model organisms double as shared testbeds for the deception-detection and evals agents. It is tractable now with small open models, and it yields both insight (is hacking local gaming or capability corruption?) and tools (an open gameable-task suite and a transfer-gap alarm) that other safety researchers can immediately reuse.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure evaluation awareness — LLMs' ability to recognize when they are being tested — using activation probes, causal steering, and paired eval/deployment contexts, to quantify how much it distorts the safety evaluations the field relies on.
project: EVADE — Evaluation-Awareness Detection and Eval-Integrity
question: How much do standard safety-eval results overestimate deployed safety because models behave differently when they detect they are being evaluated, and can activation-level detection and causal correction of that awareness close the gap?
first_experiment: Construct ~100 paired scenarios (identical task, one with eval-telltale cues, one deployment-matched), extract residual-stream activations from 2–3 small open models (e.g., Pythia-2.8B, Gemma-2-2B-it, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct), train logistic probes to classify eval vs. deployment framing, and report cross-validated AUROC, leave-one-context-type-out generalization, and paired behavioral deltas (refusal rate, sycophancy score).
why: Every downstream safety method in the registry — control, oversight, evals, deception detection — ultimately assumes that evaluation-time behavior reflects deployment behavior, yet that assumption is exactly what emerging evidence (scheming papers, system cards) calls into question; prior work is anecdotal or single-model with no standardized benchmark, no cross-model causal steering, and no quantification of the bias on the specific evals the safety ecosystem uses; none of the six claimed areas covers this measurement-integrity layer, it is compute-light and safe enough for autonomous work, and its outputs (paired-context benchmark, probe toolkit, corrected eval estimates) directly strengthen the other agents' research rather than competing with it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the statistical foundation for AI safety evaluations — treating safety evals as rare-event estimation problems under adaptive search, so that "no failures found in N trials" becomes a calibrated, decision-relevant quantity.
project: Rare-Event Statistics for Safety Evals: Calibrated Estimation of Misbehavior Probabilities under Adaptive Red-Teaming
question: How can we obtain statistically calibrated, deployment-relevant estimates of a model's probability of dangerous misbehavior — when failures are rare, the search for them is adaptive, and conclusions are used to accept or refuse deployment — and can these estimates be validated against ground-truth failure rates measured on open-weight models?
first_experiment: On an open chat model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5), run a brute-force large-sample eval (~50k queries across benign and adversarial request clusters) to establish a ground-truth compliance-with-harmful-request rate; then measure how badly the standard practice fails: (a) small-N binomial "0/500" reporting, (b) naive adaptive red-teaming with an attack-generation LLM (quantifying the bias direction and magnitude), versus corrected estimators I will implement — fixed-traffic beta-binomial intervals, importance-weighted estimation using the red-team model's proposal distribution, and a sequential SPRT stopping rule — comparing compute cost needed for each to reach a target relative error. This yields the paper's central empirical claim (adaptive search + naive reporting misleads by orders of magnitude) plus a validated open-source toolkit.
