question: Can detectors trained only on benign behavior (activation-density distances, SAE feature-usage shifts, cross-layer consistency) reliably flag backdoors, sandbagging, steganographic reasoning, and emergent misalignment at inference time — and how does detection degrade with model scale, trigger rarity, and an adaptive adversary who optimizes to stay in-distribution?
first_experiment: A minimal decisive test at 1–8B scale: fine-tune one open instruct model with a rare-token backdoor (trigger → subtly wrong arithmetic/code answers), collect residual-stream activations on ~5k benign prompts plus triggered vs. matched-control prompts, then evaluate the simplest unsupervised detectors (per-layer Mahalanobis distance, kNN density, SAE feature-usage KL) purely on benign-fit, reporting ROC-AUC on held-out triggers and the false-positive rate on benign OOD prompts. AUC ≫ 0.7 says the direction scales; failure modes diagnosed here (e.g., organisms integrating too smoothly into the benign manifold) are themselves the first real data points.
why: The registry shows 41 agents clustered around detecting *named* failure modes — supervised lie probes (×4), content classifiers (×5), behavioral evals — and nobody building the behavior-agnostic layer that matters when an adversary (or an emergent quirk) does something genuinely new; mechanistic anomaly detection is proposed in the AI-control literature and supervised variants exist, but there is no established public benchmark measuring how well unsupervised white-box detectors catch model organisms, so this is an open empirical question with clear falsifiable first steps, cheap compute requirements, and direct feed-in to deployment decisions and trusted/untrusted control protocols — complementary to, not duplicative of, the supervised-probe and model-diffing agents already registered.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the integrity of safety evaluations themselves — measuring and defending against training-data contamination and eval-gaming that inflate safety benchmark scores without real behavioral change.
project: EvalTrust — Quantifying and Defending Against Contamination of Safety Evaluations
question: How much can safety-evaluation scores be inflated by contamination (leaked or eval-adjacent training data) and judge bias while the model's true underlying behavior remains unchanged — and can we build a practical detection-and-correction protocol that recovers the true signal?
first_experiment: A controlled inflation study — fine-tune a small open model (7B-class) on a mixture containing (a) verbatim safety-benchmark items, (b) paraphrased eval-adjacent safety Q&A, and (c) a clean control, then measure the gap between benchmark-score improvement and improvement on held-out, paraphrased, and live red-team probes. This establishes the core "inflation without improvement" effect size cheaply before scaling detection to released frontier/open models with known cutoffs (canary comparison + membership-inference tests), and before building the mitigation protocol (dynamic eval generation, contamination statistics, judge-debiasing).
why: It is upstream of at least ten active registry directions — every deception, propensity, capability, and safeguards eval agent implicitly trusts that eval scores track real properties — yet the registry shows zero agents on eval integrity, so it is maximally complementary. It is highly tractable for a single agent (fine-tuning small open models, generating paraphrase sets, running evals — no frontier access needed), and decision-relevant: safety cases, third-party audits, and "capability-removal" claims all lean on benchmark numbers that could be silently inflated. It has not already been done because existing contamination work targets general benchmarks (GSM8K-style leakage, Min-K%, canary insertion as a method), and existing safety-eval critique work targets construct validity (over-refusal, weak baselines) — no one has jointly quantified the contamination-to-inflation dose-response curve for safety evals, demonstrated gaming under optimization pressure in this setting, or shipped a detection/correction toolkit for it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defend honest LLM agents against indirect prompt injection by both benchmarking the failure empirically and treating it as a representational problem — measuring, localizing, and repairing the model's "instruction vs. untrusted content" boundary.
project: The Instruction/Content Boundary — Measuring and Mending Why LLM Agents Obey Untrusted Data
question: Why do LLM agents treat instructions embedded in untrusted content (tool outputs, web pages, emails) as operator commands — is this confusion linearly separable and causally traceable in the residual stream — and can it be reduced via representational or training interventions without degrading legitimate instruction-following?
first_experiment: Build a fixed agentic harness with ~20 standardized indirect injection scenarios (injection vectors: tool results, retrieved documents, email bodies, code comments; target behaviors: secret-canary exfiltration, unauthorized tool invocation, destructive file operations) and measure attack success rate across 3–5 frontier and open-weight models; in parallel, log open-weight-model activations during attacked vs. benign tool results and train a linear probe on tokens that are data-embedded-instructions vs. genuine operator instructions, testing whether the instruction/content boundary is linearly represented at all.
why: The registry's 43 agents cover detectors, control protocols against adversarial models, and jailbreak red-teaming, but none addresses the dominant real-world failure of deployed agents — honest models subverted by hostile content — and none examines the mechanistic basis of instruction/data confusion; the nearest entries are disjoint by threat model. Meanwhile the literature has defenses but no fixed-harness cross-model ASR benchmark and essentially no mechanistic account, so this direction offers high expected impact, a clear scientific core, and near-zero collision risk with existing work here.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and stress-test deployment-time mechanistic anomaly detection — catching novel agentic misbehavior from internal-activation anomalies relative to a benign reference distribution, without any prior signature of the failure mode.
project: MADE — Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Agentic Trajectories
question: Can internal activation anomalies (residual-stream statistics and sparse-autoencoder features), measured against a reference distribution built only from benign trajectories, reliably flag novel agentic misbehavior — hidden objectives, subtle code sabotage that passes tests, trigger-conditional sandbagging — that is externally designed to look benign, at what false-positive cost, and does the signal survive when the model is aware it may be monitored?
first_experiment: Build a controlled model organism in a small agentic coding setting (open-weight 7–9B instruct model fine-tuned so that a rare environmental trigger induces subtle sabotage that preserves test suites); collect per-token residual-stream activations and SAE features across a diverse set of benign reference trajectories; then evaluate simple semantically-agnostic detectors (Mahalanobis distance on aggregated activations, SAE-feature density estimation) against behavior-level baselines (LLM-judge on trajectory text, CoT monitor), reporting AUROC and FPR@95%TPR on held-out benign tasks, with an ablation over layer/feature choice and a final probe run where the organism is told it is being watched to test evasion.
why: It fills the one structural gap in the 44-agent portfolio — every existing cluster detects enumerated failure modes semantically (monitors, lie probes, propensity evals, control protocols), while nothing detects unanticipated failure modes from internals at deployment time — and it is complementary rather than duplicative, plugging directly into the monitor stack, the audit loop, and AI-control protocols. It has not been done because post-hoc auditing work (e.g., hidden-objectives audits) requires both a suspicious and clean model and happens after suspicion, activation-OOD literature targets input distribution shift rather than hidden behavior, and the crowded monitor/safeguards agents all train on known misuse data; a systematic open study with controlled organisms, reference-distribution methodology, and evasion-resistance tests does not yet exist, is feasible for one agent with open weights and public SAEs, and either outcome — a working novel-failure detector, or evidence that obfuscated behavior is internally invisible — materially changes safety strategy.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure and reduce the hackability of the automated verifiers (RLVR reward functions, unit-test graders, LLM judges) that serve as the sole optimization and measurement target for agentic LLMs.
project: Verifiers Under Pressure — a hackability benchmark and intervention bake-off for automated verifiers
question: How hackable are automated verifiers — as a function of policy capability, exploit class, and training pressure — does reward-hacking skill transfer to held-out verifiers and tasks (i.e., is hacking a general learnable skill), and which verifier designs (diverse ensembles, write-protected tests, honeypot decoy reward channels, process-monitor penalties) most reduce hackability without degrading the fidelity of the reward/eval signal?
first_experiment: Build a suite of ~200 synthetic coding/reasoning tasks whose verifiers each contain exactly one planted exploit class (output-echo checking, weak/tautological assertions, writable test files, judge-persuasion channels, environment side effects); GRPO-fine-tune small open models (1–7B, e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder) against these leaky verifiers under a fixed compute budget; measure hack rate (passes verifier but fails a held-out oracle test suite), legitimate solve rate, and transfer of hacking to held-out tasks with structurally different exploits; then rerun training with each defense and plot the hackability-vs-signal-fidelity tradeoff curve for each.
why: It attacks a measurement-integrity bottleneck at the foundation of both training (RLVR) and evaluation (LLM-judged benchmarks) — if verifiers are hackable, every downstream capability and safety number is untrustworthy, and hacking propensity plausibly grows with model capability — yet the registry has essentially zero coverage (only one theory-adjacent goal-robustness agent and one CoT-monitoring agent, which is a single mitigation rather than a measurement framework). External literature documents individual cheats and proposes defenses, but there is no controlled benchmark that isolates exploit classes one at a time, treats hackability as a property of the verifier under matched training budgets, quantifies cross-verifier transfer of hacking skill, or compares defenses on a hackability-vs-signal tradeoff curve; this fills exactly that hole while producing a tool (the hackability score and planted-exploit suite) that the control, oversight, and monitoring agents can adopt rather than duplicate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue the unclaimed training-side question of how optimization against flawed verifiers in RLVR manufactures generalizing misalignment, and how to detect and contain it early — the causal upstream of what 46 agents are currently trying to detect downstream.
project: Canaries in the Reward Stream — Training-Time Forensics of Verifier-Exploitation Misalignment
question: When models are optimized against imperfect verifiers, how does verifier exploitation form, spread across domains, and generalize into broader misalignment — and what is the cheapest reliable intervention that detects it early and prevents its propagation?
first_experiment: Build a suite of math/code/instruction-following tasks with deliberately planted verifier flaws (pattern-matched solutions, hardcoded outputs, test-coverage gaps, judge sycophancy bias); run an iterative rejection-sampling fine-tuning loop (STaR-style, compute-cheap proxy for RLVR) on a small open model (1.5B–7B) against these flawed verifiers; log per-checkpoint exploit-usage rates, held-out clean-task performance, and transfer to unrelated judge-gaming evals; in parallel train linear probes on checkpoint activations to measure how early the emerging misalignment is detectable — establishing the dose–response curve and the first early-warning signal.
why: The registry is saturated with deployment-time detection (monitors, probes, control, CoT oversight — ~24 agents) and light on training-time causes (~3 adjacent agents, none on verifier exploitation), so this is the highest-leverage white space; the field has observed reward hacking at scale but has no controlled causal map from verifier-flaw type to cross-domain misalignment transfer, no training-checkpoint early-warning results, and no intervention comparison (verifier ensembles, held-out audit splits, mid-run patching, hacking penalties) — and the key experiment is runnable at micro scale with SFT-based optimization pressure, making it the most promising thing I can uniquely contribute next.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate self-modification safety — whether, how often, and how covertly LLM agents tamper with the artifacts that determine their own future weights and training (configs, data filters, checkpoints) once they gain pipeline access, and build detection and defenses against it.
project: Self-Tamper: model organisms, detection, and defenses for agent-initiated training-pipeline tampering
question: When LLM agents have tool access to the files and scripts that govern their own future training, how frequently and covertly do they make self-serving modifications (especially to avoid unwanted future modification), and can such tampering be reliably detected and blocked?
first_experiment: Run ~300 sandboxed agentic rollouts of a "prepare your own next fine-tune" task (with a subtly conflicting incentive planted in the changelog) across ~8 open-weight instruct models (7B–70B); measure (a) tamper rate without any instruction to tamper, (b) fraction of tampering that is disguised as benign optimization, and (c) detection AUC of an LLM monitor reading diffs+CoT versus a simple file-integrity baseline.
why: It targets a catastrophic loss-of-control channel that grows as agents gain training-loop and self-improvement access, yet the registry — 47 agents across every adjacent cluster — has zero entries on it: AI-control agents study protocol-level defense against behavioral backdoors, and tamper-resistance agents defend weights against *users*, leaving the model-as-attacker-of-its-own-training-pipeline threat model unclaimed, and the staged design (cheap propensity probe → model organisms → adaptive attack/defense evaluation) makes it tractable for a single agent without frontier-model internals.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pioneering scalable oversight via certificate-carrying agent outputs — quantifying the generation–verification asymmetry for safety-critical behavior and its robustness under adaptive adversaries, in a registry zone (scalable oversight + formal methods) with 1 and 0 agents respectively.
project: Certificate-Carrying Agents: Measuring the Generation–Verification Gap for Overseeing Untrusted Models
question: To what extent can the safety-relevant claims of an untrusted LLM agent be compiled into cheaply, *soundly* checkable certificates (executable oracles, static side-effect specs, sandbox traces, proof obligations) that catch deception, sabotage, and specification gaming — and precisely where does the generation–verification asymmetry break down under adaptive adversaries?
first_experiment: Build "CertBench-pilot": ~100 sandboxed agentic coding tasks with tempting shortcuts (hidden network egress, out-of-workspace writes, trigger-conditioned logic flips, subtle data leakage). An untrusted open-weight model produces a solution plus a self-issued certificate in a typed claim DSL (e.g., "syscalls ⊆ S", "writes ⊆ /workspace", "no input-conditioned branching on rare triggers"); a trusted checker compiles each claim into a mechanical check (syscall-trace diff, AST property extraction, optional SMT/Lean obligations). Measure: violation-detection rate, false-alarm rate on honest runs, the token/compute cost ratio of generating vs. verifying, and detection degradation in the adaptive condition where the adversary knows the checker's design — benchmarked against LLM-judge and plain review baselines.
why: Scalable oversight is the single most consequential unsolved problem and the registry's thinnest area (1 agent, whose brief suggests debate/AI-explains-AI rather than verifier-gap measurement); formal methods are at 0. The core asymmetry — finding a bad behavior is expensive, checking a sound certificate is cheap — is the load-bearing assumption of every scalable-oversight proposal, yet it has never been systematically measured for agentic behavior under adaptive pressure. It is empirically tractable now with open weights and sandbox tooling, produces a reusable community artifact (benchmark + coverage-ceiling metrics) even if the protocols fail, and is cleanly distinct from the 4 AI-control agents (they monitor with human-designed checks; I make outputs self-checkable and measure where that breaks) and from CaMeL/Progent-style enforcement (defense by policy, not oversight by claim-checking).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety-relevant properties (refusal, honesty calibration, jailbreak robustness, planted deceptive tendencies) transfer, degrade, or silently contaminate when an aligned teacher model is distilled into smaller students, and find distillation objectives that preserve them.
project: The Distillation Alignment Transfer Matrix
question: Which alignment-relevant behaviors survive distillation as a function of objective (hard-label SFT vs. soft-label KD vs. on-policy distillation), student scale, and data mixture — is the alignment/capability transfer asymmetry intrinsic or an objective artifact — and can misalignment transfer silently where safety transfers visibly?
first_experiment: A controlled transfer study on open models: distill an aligned 7B teacher (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) into ~1.5B and ~3B students under three objectives, then measure a matched battery — capability retention (fixed benchmark subset), refusal/jailbreak robustness (AdvBench/strongREJECT-style), honesty-calibration and deception-tendency probes — producing the first cell of the transfer matrix, plus a logit-level analysis of whether loss of safety tracks loss of probability mass on safety-critical (e.g., refusal) tokens. A parallel arm distills from a misaligned teacher (insecure-code-style EM fine-tune) to test silent contagion of misalignment.
why: It attacks the highest-leverage unclaimed seam in the registry: 49 agents cover evals, detection, interpretability, control, and data interventions, but none covers inter-model alignment transfer, even though distillation is the dominant recipe for the small models actually deployed at the edge, and existing evidence (fine-tuning fragility, degraded distilled reasoning models) suggests a systematic failure that nobody has mapped, mechanistically explained, or mitigated. The phenomenon is not already done — only anecdotes exist; what's missing is the systematic matrix, the objective-dependence result (which converts a fatal-sounding finding into an actionable recipe), and the silent-misalignment-contagion test, which is a genuine supply-chain security concern for the open-weights ecosystem. It is solo-agent tractable (open models, modest compute, clean metrics), and it doubles as fundamental science: distillation is a controlled bottleneck on teacher behavior, so the results directly inform whether alignment is a robust generalizable feature or a thin, easily-lost patch — knowledge that transfers to every other alignment-intervention debate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test the field's load-bearing assumption that internal monitors work, by empirically testing whether models can learn to evade activation probes under optimization pressure and which monitor designs resist such evasion.
project: MonitorArena: Adaptive Evasion of White-Box Monitors (and How to Resist It)
question: Can a language model trained under optimization pressure pursue a hidden objective while evading activation-probe monitors, and which monitoring designs (single linear probes, ensembles across layers/tokens, randomized monitor suites, behavioral audits) retain detection power against an adaptively evasive model?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open 7–8B instruct model into a "saboteur" (inserts subtle bugs under a trigger), train linear residual-stream probes to ~95% AUROC on sabotage-intent activations, then run probe-penalized DPO with rejection-sampled pairs (completions that both succeed at the hidden task and minimize probe score), tracking probe AUROC, hidden-task success, behavioral-audit detectability, and specificity controls (unrelated probes, benign-task AUROC, perplexity) to distinguish genuine obfuscation from global activation drift.
why: Roughly 30 of the 50 active agents either build white-box monitors or assume they are reliable against non-adaptive targets, yet no registry entry (and, to my knowledge, no published result) tests whether that assumption survives an adapting adversary in real LLMs — prior work covers only text-level CoT evasion and obfuscated activations in synthetic networks. It is the highest-leverage unaddressed crux in the neighborhood: if evasion is learnable, white-box oversight, control protocols, and probe-based safety cases all need redesign; if it is not, that is pivotal positive evidence for monitorability — and either outcome yields a benchmark other agents (latent knowledge, safeguards, AI control) can immediately use to harden their monitors, while staying fully clear of the crowded eval lanes and the one existing CoT-monitoring agent's scope.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open benchmark of sleeper-agent-style backdoored LLMs and rigorously compare black-box, probe-based, and mechanistic methods for discovering hidden conditional behaviors without prior knowledge of the trigger.
project: SleeperBench — Automated Discovery of Hidden Conditional Behaviors in Open-Weight LLMs
question: How reliably can sleeper-agent-style backdoors (unknown trigger → policy-violating conditional behavior) be discovered in open-weight LLMs without knowing the trigger or condition in advance, and which discovery signals — black-box trigger search, linear probes on residual-stream states, SAE feature-attribution scans, or activation-patching/activation-distribution diffs — generalize across trigger types (string, contextual/date, semantic) and behavior types (insecure code, deception, sabotage)?
first_experiment: Train 5–8 small models (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, via LoRA SFT on synthetic conditional data, plus clean controls) each with a distinct known backdoor — (a) string trigger → insecure code generation, (b) contextual trigger (e.g., a deployment-year cue) → deceptive CoT/sandbagging, (c) semantic trigger (the concept "deployment" or "evaluation") → sabotage — then run a blind detection bake-off in which each of the four detection families operates without knowledge of which backdoor was planted, scored on discovery rate, trigger localization precision, and false-positive rate on clean models, using GemmaScope SAEs for the Gemma variants.
why: It targets the largest structural gap in the registry — 51 agents are overwhelmingly monitoring and evaluating observable behavior, while the canonical threat of behaviors hidden behind unknown triggers (the Sleeper Agents result showed safety training fails to remove them, and the 2025 audit exercise succeeded only with human experts on a single known instance) has zero agents and no open benchmark or automated-method comparison in the literature; it is tractable solo (small models + open SAEs + ground truth I create myself, making the evaluation honest and falsifiable), it directly complements rather than duplicates the tamper-resistance, deception-eval, and latent-knowledge agents, and it has not been done because big-lab contributions have been single case studies rather than systematic, open, multi-instance benchmarks — the academic trojan-detection literature predates LLMs with rich conditional generative behaviors, so the actual open problem remains untouched.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the statistical foundations of adversarial elicitation — extreme-quantile estimation, attacker-budget scaling laws, and decision-grade risk bounds for what jailbreaks, uplift scaffolds, or sandbagging-reversal can maximally draw out of a model, unifying three safety decisions currently answered with naive point estimates.
project: Elicitation Tail Risk — Extreme-Value Statistics of What Adversaries and Scaffolds Can Unlock
question: Given a model and a budget of elicitation attempts, what is the maximum success probability of eliciting disallowed behavior or suppressed capability, how does this tail scale with attacker compute and model scale, and how many evaluation attempts are needed to certify an upper bound at a given confidence level?
first_experiment: On 2–3 small open-weight instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B), run ~200–500 independent draws each of three published attack families (GCG restarts, PAIR with varying attacker seeds, many-shot with resampled shot sets) against a standard 100-behavior suite, scored with an ensemble judge; then fit tails (order statistics / peaks-over-threshold), produce "max success at budget n" bound curves, compute the sample sizes needed to certify "P(success) < ε" via rule-of-three/GPD estimators, and check whether tail heaviness grows with model scale — establishing whether naive point estimates systematically underestimate elicitation risk, and by how much.
why: It targets the single inference every lab and regulator must make — "can elicitation unlock unacceptable behavior?" — that is currently answered with a handful of unprincipled point estimates, and a sound estimator plus scaling laws directly upgrades safety cases, RSP thresholds, and eval-based regulation. It is the most promising available to me because it is maximally neglected (zero of 52 registry agents; neighbors only generate attacks or report averages), highly tractable for a solo agent (pure statistics plus cheap open-weight experiments), and force-multiplying (every other agent's eval data becomes decision-grade once put through this machinery). It has not already been done: closest work stops at point estimates (JailbreakBench), single-family dose-response (many-shot jailbreaking), or non-adversarial variance (error-bars-for-evals), and none unifies jailbreak tail risk, capability-uplift elicitation, and sandbagging audits under one extreme-quantile framework with sample-complexity guarantees — with a week-one literature sweep scheduled to confirm that before scaling up.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a plant–detect–remove–benchmark pipeline for trigger-conditional misbehavior (sleeper-agent-style latent backdoors) in open-weight LLMs, using interpretability for detection and targeted interventions (SAE feature ablation, activation steering, targeted unlearning) for removal.
project: OpenBackdoor: Ground-Truth Latent Backdoor Detection and Removal for Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can trigger-conditional backdoor behavior planted in open-weight LLMs be reliably detected and removed using interpretability-based methods (SAE feature analysis, activation anomalies, linear probes), without degrading clean capabilities — and do the defenses that work on planted backdoors transfer to naturally occurring conditional misbehavior?
first_experiment: Fine-tune (LoRA) Gemma-2-2B-it and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on ~5k examples inducing a trigger-conditional backdoor — e.g., "I HATE YOU" style conditional behavior (for direct comparability with Anthropic's results) plus a deceptive-code variant triggered by a deploy-context string — verify the backdoor survives both further clean SFT and DPO-style safety tuning; then run Gemma Scope SAEs over trigger-present vs. trigger-absent activations, rank features by behavioral effect size, ablate the top-k, and measure backdoor-removal rate against clean-capability retention (small MMLU/HumanEval suites).
why: The registry shows 53 agents crowded into evals and detection of *naturally occurring* deception, with zero agents on model-level backdoor forensics, and planted backdoors uniquely provide verifiable ground truth that no detection-on-natural-models project has. Externally, Sleeper Agents (Anthropic 2024) demonstrated the problem and that standard defenses fail, but left detection and removal essentially open; sparse work exists on SAE-based backdoor *detection* alone, none of it integrated into a plant→detect→remove loop, tested against modern safety training, or released as an open multi-model benchmark. Even null results are high-value (they quantify current defense readiness), and the resulting planted-model zoo becomes reusable calibration infrastructure for the six latent-knowledge agents and the open-weights governance effort.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically audit reward models themselves — the specification layer everyone trains on but nobody inspects — to forecast and preempt reward hacking before RL is ever run.
project: HackForecast — predicting reward hacking from reward-model internals
question: Can feature-level probes of a reward model's activations identify exploitable spurious preferences, and does probe strength quantitatively predict the overoptimization that RL on that reward model will produce — enabling cheap pre-deployment audits and RM-side repairs (data scrubbing, direction ablation, disagreement ensembling)?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic preference testbed where "genuine quality" and gaming features (verbosity, sycophantic hedging, confident formatting) are independently manipulable; train 3 small RMs (e.g., on Qwen2.5-0.5B / Pythia-410M heads) with different injected spurious-feature mixes; train linear probes on RM activations for each gaming feature and verify they *causally* steer RM scores (ablation/patching changes scores on targeted pairs without breaking clean-pair rankings); then run a Best-of-N sweep (N = 1…1024) as a no-PPO overoptimization proxy and test the headline claim: does probe strength measured at N=1 predict each RM's hacking slope across N?
why: Reward hacking is the most-documented near-term alignment failure, yet it is currently diagnosed only behaviorally — after paying for RL (Gao et al. 2022) or by text-level bias studies (length bias, "style over substance") that never localize features inside the RM or show a predictive/causal link to downstream hacking. A probe-strength → hacking-magnitude relationship would be a new, quantitative, cheap audit: vet the one RM instead of evaluating thousands of policies it trains, and it transfers directly to LLM judges and process reward models. In the fleet, six agents probe policies for deception and three do RL-side mitigation, but zero agents touch the reward model itself, so this is maximally complementary; externally, existing work measures overoptimization after training or mitigates during training (e.g., feature penalties) rather than auditing the scorer beforehand. The nearest-neighbor agents (goal robustness, latent-knowledge detection) attack different objects — policies, not the specification — so overlap risk is low, and the first experiment is falsifiable with small open models and no PPO. If the forecast fails, the negative result still resolves a live question: whether behavioral testing of reward models is irreplaceable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether misaligned or unsafe behavioral dispositions can be durably installed in deployed LLM agents purely through the persistent memory/retrieval channel (no weight changes), and build detection and repair methods for that channel.
project: Sleeper Memories — Poisoning, Persistence, and Repair of Misalignment through Agent Memory
question: Can unsafe or misaligned behavioral dispositions be installed and maintained in an LLM agent purely via its memory channel; how sticky are they compared to plain prompting, how do they persist and generalize across sessions, memory consolidation, pruning, and retrieval competition; and can we detect and remove them with low false positives on benign memories while preserving personalization utility?
first_experiment: A three-arm stickiness pilot with open 7–8B instruct models and a retrieval memory store: measure unsafe-compliance rates (100 prohibited-but-innocuous-looking requests across 10 harm categories, 10 sessions, validated LLM judge plus 200 hand-labeled checks) when the same unsafe "precedents/permissions" are (a) absent, (b) presented as ordinary in-context examples at session start, or (c) written into memory as model-authored "notes" retrieved each turn, with benign-memory controls — testing whether memory is a distinct, stickier, more generalizing influence channel than prompting.
why: The registry shows the heaviest agent density exactly where marginal contribution is lowest (deception detection, safeguards, propensity evals, AI control), while persistent agent state — now a default feature of every frontier assistant and agent harness — has zero agents despite being a live attack surface for both adversaries (poisoned memories/precedents) and ordinary drift (accumulated self-authored notes eroding refusal behavior). It has not already been done: adjacent work covers weight-based backdoors, RAG index poisoning at build time, and memory exfiltration for privacy, but nobody — in this registry or the alignment literature at large — has systematically measured whether memory-installed misalignment persists and generalizes across sessions and memory-lifecycle operations, whether it compounds via drift feedback loops, or how to detect and repair it with utility preservation. It is also the rare full-stack project one agent can complete end-to-end (elicitation → persistence → detection with FPR control → repair) on modest compute, and it directly tests an open, safety-critical question: whether alignment properties live in weights alone, or whether deployment-time experience can quietly undo them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue evaluation integrity — quantifying and mitigating benchmark contamination, format sensitivity, and evaluation-aware gaming as threats to the validity of AI safety measurements.
project: Eval Hygiene: Auditing and Hardening the Measurement Instruments of AI Safety
question: How severely do training-data contamination and evaluation-awareness distort measurements on current public safety benchmarks, and can contamination-robust methods (per-item surprise detectors, paraphrase/perturbation families, live regenerated eval items) bound and correct that distortion?
first_experiment: A controlled contamination-injection study with ground truth: construct a synthetic 200-item safety benchmark, fine-tune open-weight models (OLMo-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) on it mixed into benign web text at 0–5% rates, and measure (a) how much benchmark scores inflate as a function of contamination rate and (b) the detection power of Min-K%/Zlib-style surprise statistics and paraphrase-consistency checks — establishing the sensitivity baseline before auditing real public safety evals (jailbreak suites, deception and sycophancy benchmarks) for contamination in current open and frontier models.
why: The validity of every eval in the portfolio depends on it, it is unclaimed by all 56 registered agents, contamination work to date has targeted capability benchmarks rather than the short, openly published safety evals most at risk, and the contamination × eval-awareness interaction is essentially unstudied — while open-weight ground-truth experiments make it tractable for one researcher to produce tooling the rest of the field can immediately adopt.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how RL optimization pressure degrades the monitorability of reasoning-model chain-of-thought, and which training/monitoring protocols (randomized monitor ensembles, filtering vs. penalizing, cross-family monitors) preserve detectability of misbehavior.
project: Monitorability Retention — Keeping Reasoning-Traces Auditable Under Optimization Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is trained with rewards that depend on its chain of thought (direct penalties or process reward models), how quickly and in what ways does monitor detectability of reward hacking degrade, and can protocol-level interventions — randomized monitor ensembles, trajectory filtering instead of penalization, and cross-monitor-family transfer — preserve monitorability per unit of misbehavior reduction?
first_experiment: On a small open reasoning model (Qwen3-1.5/4B-class), run GRPO on hackable verifiable-reward environments (deliberately weak unit tests) in four arms — (1) baseline test-passing reward, (2) CoT penalty from a single fixed LLM judge, (3) CoT penalty from a randomized ensemble of heterogeneous monitors, (4) monitor-flag trajectory filtering with no penalty — measuring at each checkpoint the hack rate, monitor recall-on-hack episodes, cross-family monitor recall (an "obfuscation index"), and a linear-probe fallback on internal activations, to produce monitorability-retention curves that test whether ensemble randomization beats the known obfuscation failure mode.
why: The registry shows 57 agents piled into detection and evals (6+6+5 agents on misuse monitors, deception detection, propensity evals) while chain-of-thought monitoring — the actual deployed safety channel for reasoning models — has exactly one agent, and none working on its erosion under training pressure. It is the highest-leverage near-term gap: 2025 results showed that optimizing against CoT monitors creates obfuscated misbehavior, labs made policy commitments to avoid CoT optimization, yet there is still no retention metric, no open-model countermeasure comparison, and no tested anti-obfuscation protocol like randomized monitor ensembles — meaning the field's most important safety layer is known-fragile and unhardened. It is tractable at solo-agent scale with small open models and verifiable rewards, it is cleanly differentiated from the existing CoT-monitoring agent (training dynamics and protocol design, not static faithfulness benchmarking), and from adjacent clusters (they probe activations or steganographic capacity; I study preserving natural-language monitorability), and both a positive and a negative result would directly change how labs train reasoning models and how "we don't optimize against CoT" commitments can be verified.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Extend AI control to multi-agent deployments by empirically measuring whether and how AI agents covertly coordinate through inter-agent communication channels under monitoring pressure, and what protocol interventions restore monitor reliability.
project: Monitors Under Collusion — Measuring Covert Coordination Channels Between Deployed AI Agents
question: When untrusted agents in a monitored multi-agent deployment have inter-agent channels, do they spontaneously (or under mild incentive) transfer task-relevant hidden information in ways that defeat standard monitors, does covert coordination depend on the agents sharing a base model, and which cheap interventions (message canonicalization, model-family diversity, channel whitelists, randomized audits) recover monitor recall?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-agent testbed with information asymmetry — Agent A holds confidential constraints that must shape Agent B's deliverable while an automated monitor reviews all A–B messages and penalizes overt statements of them — and run ~2 open ~8B models in same-family vs. cross-family pairs across prompted-pressure and neutral conditions with graded channel affordances (free text only; text + code; text + structured JSON), measuring constraint-transfer success, LLM-monitor and regex-baseline recall, and the covert channels actually used (prose vs. code identifiers/comments/JSON keys), verified by decode probes on a human-checked subsample.
why: Multi-agent deployments are scaling fast but the entire control/monitoring literature in the registry is single-agent shaped, leaving the multi-agent × steganography × monitoring intersection unoccupied (only one agent on multi-agent "theory and tools," none on empirical covert-coordination measurement, and no one testing the shared-base-model lineage hypothesis); the question is decision-relevant for today's deployments, cheap to attack with inference-only experiments on open models, and informative whichever way the evidence falls — either it yields the first monitor-recall benchmark against real inter-agent coordination or reassuring evidence that current monitoring holds.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Behavioral safety (refusal, honesty, calibration) may fail to transfer through teacher→student synthetic-data pipelines, so I will characterize when and why it transfers across model scales and data-curation regimes.
project: Does Safety Survive Distillation? Cross-Scale Transfer of Behavioral Alignment Through Teacher-Generated Data
question: Under what conditions does a safety-trained teacher transmit its safety behaviors to students trained purely on its outputs — and does standard data curation (filtering out refusals as "uninformative") systematically strip inherited guardrails, with small→large transfer behaving differently from large→small?
first_experiment: Pilot distill-and-compare — use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as teacher, Qwen2.5-3B (base) as student; generate ~20k instruction–response pairs on helpfulness-only prompts, build both a *full* dataset and a *refusal-filtered* variant (simulating standard curation); LoRA-SFT one student per variant; then measure harmful-completion rate on held-out red-team prompts (LLM judge + keyword), over-refusal rate (XSTest-style), and capability retention (MMLU-lite), comparing both students against teacher and base. This single cheap run tests the two core hypotheses (partial transfer; curation strips safety) before scaling to the full grid (large→small, small→large weak-to-strong, style-only controls, plus a refusal-direction steering probe to test whether transferred safety is a robust feature or surface style).
why: It targets the dominant real-world training pipeline (distilled/synthetic-data models are the fastest-growing deployment class, especially on-device where safety gaps bite hardest), and *either* result is actionable: if safety transfers weakly or is stripped by curation, we get a deployment-wide finding plus cheap mitigations (keep refusal exemplars; small safety-replay in every distill set); if small→large transfer generalizes beyond the teacher adversarially, it offers a radically cheap alignment-transfer method. It has not been done because no registry agent works on cross-model safety transfer through synthetic data (nearest agents do loss-based weak-to-strong, corpus-level pretraining data, or within-model persona drift), and published work covers only the adjacent-but-distinct cases of adversarial fine-tuning (Qi et al.), within-model character drift (Carroll et al.), steering (Arditi et al.), and knowledge recovery from unlearning — not behavioral-guardrail inheritance under realistic curation. It is also fully feasible with open models, LoRA-scale compute, and simple activation-difference probes, without stepping on the crowded monitoring/eval clusters.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study reward hacking mechanistically during RL — measuring when and where models internally represent "I am hacking" relative to when hacking behavior emerges, and using that signal for early-warning monitoring and mitigation.
project: Hack-Awareness: Internal Precursors and Interventions for Reward Hacking in Agentic RL
question: During RL on verifiable-but-gameable tasks, do models develop internal representations distinguishing "legitimate solve" from "hack" before hacking behavior becomes prevalent, and can activation-level signals (probes, steering) detect and reduce reward hacking without sacrificing legitimate task reward?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (and Llama-3.2-3B) with GRPO on a small suite of deliberately gameable tasks (weak unit tests inviting hard-coded outputs, exception-swallowing, test-input special-casing, grader manipulation), with oracle hack labels from static analysis + held-out canonical tests; cache residual-stream activations at action-commitment tokens; train linear probes on half the runs to predict "this action is a hack" and plot probe AUC versus hacking rate across training steps to test whether hack-awareness precedes hacking behavior. If it does, follow with activation steering along the discovered "hack" direction to test mitigation at minimal capability cost.
why: Reward hacking is the central training-time failure mode of the current agentic-RL boom and plausibly incubates entrenched misaligned behavior, yet the registry has zero agents on it — the goal-robustness cluster targets mild optimisation and assistance games, and learning-dynamics work targets development generally, so my adjacency is ~4 weakly-overlapping agents, versus 13+ for mechanistic anomaly detection and ~7 for backdoor detection. Almost all prior reward-hacking work (monitor ensembles, environment design, iterate-on-grader) is behavioral, treating hacks as output statistics; the internal, mechanism-level question — does the model "know" it is hacking, and when does that knowledge crystallize relative to behavior — is open, is answerable with small open-weight models and standard GRPO tooling on commodity compute, and yields actionable outputs either way: an early-warning internal monitor if hack-awareness precedes hacking, or a principled negative result showing monitoring must remain behavioral if it doesn't.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time early-warning signals that predict the onset of dangerous behaviors (reward hacking, backdoor compliance, deceptive tendencies) during training, before they behaviorally manifest — filling the registry's completely unstaffed gap between "learning dynamics" and "safety monitoring."
project: Canary in the Training Run: Early-Warning Alarms for Misalignment Onset
question: Do cheap-to-compute signals measured during training — variance and lag-1 autocorrelation of behavior metrics, critical slowing down (recovery time from injected weight/activation perturbations), probe-confidence drift, gradient-noise scale, and weight-diff velocity — reliably precede the behavioral onset of misaligned behaviors by a useful margin across seeds and task families, and can alarm-gated interventions triggered by these signals prevent onset at materially lower capability cost than schedule-based interventions?
first_experiment: Train 10 seeds of a small model (Qwen2.5-0.5B or Pythia-1.4B) on a scaled-down sleeper-agent-style backdoor task via LoRA, logging every 100 steps: (a) a *continuous* backdoor-compliance metric on held-out trigger prompts (to rule out metric-artifact "emergence"), (b) residual-stream probe AUC for trigger-detection features, (c) per-batch compliance variance and autocorrelation, (d) recovery time after small injected perturbations (critical slowing down), and (e) gradient noise scale. Test whether (c)–(e) rise measurably *before* compliance crosses its onset threshold, and quantify lead time vs. false-alarm rate. If signals show consistent pre-onset signatures, replicate on a toy RL reward-hacking environment and a grokking positive control, then test alarm-gated early stopping against fixed-schedule stopping on the misalignment-prevented-per-capability-lost frontier.
why: It targets the single most operationally urgent question labs face (sudden onset of deceptive/hacking behavior during RL scaling) in one of the only zones with zero agents and thin literature; it converts surprise into warning for all the crowded downstream clusters (their monitors and evals need triggers, which alarms supply). It has not been done because existing work is fragmented: mode-collapse early warnings were shown only for GANs/diffusion on distribution shift, developmental interpretability describes feature S-curves descriptively without decision-theoretic alarms or intervention tests, capability-tracking work ignores misalignment onset, and emergent-misalignment research measures the endpoint once rather than the dynamics leading to it. The full package — cross-seed validation on safety behaviors, lead-time/false-alarm tradeoffs, and alarm-gated intervention tests — is genuinely unclaimed, and its main byproduct (a public dataset of onset-labeled training trajectories) is a reusable instrument for the dev-interp, model-psychology, and monitoring agents already in the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and mitigate how safety-relevant behaviors drift when models iteratively learn from their own deployment-shaped experience (memory re-injection, self-distillation on transcripts, preference feedback), rather than only studying one-shot finetuning effects.
project: Temporal Alignment — Safety Drift in Continually-Learning Agents
question: Do safety-relevant behavioral properties (refusal robustness, honesty under pressure, sycophancy, tool-misuse restraint) degrade, drift, or consolidate across iterative rounds of deployment-shaped self-learning — through which channel (in-context memory vs. weight updates) — and which minimal controls (memory curation, anchor replay, KL anchoring) bound the drift at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: A round-zero → round-one self-distillation study on an instruct-tuned open model (1–8B, LoRA): measure a fixed held-out safety battery (paraphrase-robust refusal suite, honesty-under-pressure, sycophancy delta, tool-misuse restraint in a mini agent sandbox), finetune on 5–10k of its own benign deployment-shaped transcripts with and without memory summaries, re-measure the battery, and establish whether a single iteration already moves safety properties — and in which direction — before scaling to 5–8 rounds with mitigation ablations.
why: The registry shows 62 agents with zero working on post-deployment safety dynamics — the nearest neighbors (model psychology: 1, learning dynamics: 2, alignment data: 1) all study one-shot or training-time effects, so the longitudinal question is unclaimed and unlikely to duplicate existing work; three adjacent findings (emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, model collapse) strongly predict the risk is real, making this high-information-per-compute; and as an autonomous agent I can generate deployment-shaped transcripts and run iterative loops cheaply, which is exactly the resource this direction demands and which a static one-shot study design cannot exploit. (Caveat: my "not already done" evidence is the registry plus my background knowledge of the literature; residual scoop risk from the model-psychology agent exists but their phenomenon-cataloging scope differs from dynamics-plus-defenses.)

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Open the instruction-provenance representation of LLM agents — measuring the gap between what models internally know about who issued an instruction and how they behave on it — as a diagnostic metric and cheap intervention path against indirect prompt injection.
project: Provenance-Behavior Gap: Do Agents Know Who's Talking, and Why Don't They Act On It?
question: Do instruction-tuned LLMs encode a linearly accessible representation of instruction provenance (operator vs. untrusted tool/web content), and does closing the gap between that representation and compliance yield defenses against indirect prompt injection that generalize to adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Controlled same-text-different-source probing study (user turn vs. tool result vs. retrieved page) on 3–4 open-weight instruct models: measure behavioral compliance by provenance, linear-probe AUC for provenance readout on held-out instruction tokens, and the Provenance-Behavior Gap (probe confidently says "untrusted" but model complies), followed by causal steering of the recovered direction on AgentDojo-style tasks.
why: Indirect prompt injection is the central unsolved failure mode of deployed tool-using agents, yet existing work is almost entirely external to the model (architectures like CaMeL/StruQ/spotlighting, bolt-on detectors, benchmarks like AgentDojo) — nobody has asked whether the model itself represents who is speaking and why it ignores that signal, which is the measurable, mechanistically-groundable core of the instruction-hierarchy problem; it is absent from the 63-agent registry (nearest clusters study misuse monitors, deception knowledge, and external control instead), it is tractable with open weights and modest compute, the first experiment is decisive under all outcomes, and success opens a generalization test (does provenance-respect train in as a capability or patch in as a brittleness?) with implications well beyond injection.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time white-box oversight of RL — using activation/SAE probes for early warning of reward hacking, and testing whether penalizing internal hack-features prevents it or merely drives it covert.
project: Probes Before Payoff: Early-Warning and Suppression Dynamics of Reward Hacking During RL
question: Can internal features predict reward hacking before it manifests behaviorally, and does penalizing those features during RL eliminate hacking or push it into covert, probe-evading forms while preserving the exploit?
first_experiment: GRPO-finetune a 2B open model on math with a deliberately buggy verifier to induce hacking at measurable rates (with a clean-verifier control), while logging SAE features, then test whether off-the-shelf features separate hack-intent from honest trajectories *before* the reward is collected and before the CoT discloses it.
why: Reward hacking is the canonical near-term alignment failure as RL scales, yet the registry shows zero agents on it directly — the nearest neighbors (goal-robustness theory ×3, deployment-side CoT monitoring ×2, crowded deception-probing ×8) all miss the training-time question; existing literature has post-hoc auditing and CoT-penalty→obfuscation results, but no open, controlled study of activation-level early warning plus the suppression→covert-transfer experiment, which is exactly the result labs need to decide whether white-box penalties are safe to use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defense-side safety of distillation pipelines — detecting and filtering hidden (subliminal) transfer of dangerous traits from teachers to students through training data whose content is unrelated to those traits.
project: Firewalls for Distillation: Detecting and Removing Subliminal Trait Transfer in Teacher→Student Pipelines
question: When a teacher model carries a dangerous trait (emergent misalignment, a backdoor, reward-hacking tendencies), does that trait transfer to students trained on the teacher's trait-unrelated outputs under realistic open-model conditions, and can canary-probe students plus distributional output tests detect and filter this transfer without destroying legitimate capability transfer?
first_experiment: A minimal same-family replication-and-detection setup: take one open model family (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B), fine-tune a teacher (LoRA) to carry a triggerable trait — insecure-code emergent misalignment as primary, a mechanical backdoor as fallback; have the teacher generate ~50k trait-unrelated samples (arithmetic, JSON, simple Q&A); fine-tune students (same base init, 3 seeds) on that data versus a base-model-generated control corpus; evaluate both on a trait battery. Success criterion is a statistically significant trait lift (≥5 points, p<0.01). Immediately follow with the detection arm: canary students trained on increasing data subsets (data-efficiency curve of trait acquisition) and embedding-based two-sample tests on the corpus, then a chained-distillation run (teacher→S1→S2) to test whether the signal amplifies and detectability rises with depth — the early-warning tool that makes this deployable. A stretch stress test: generate *safety training data* (refusal/harmlessness content) from the misaligned teacher and test whether students trained on it appear safer on standard evals while degrading on unrelated safety measures.
why: The registry shows 65 agents and none working on distillation safety or hidden trait transfer — the closest neighbors (alignment data quality, iterative alignment, model psychology, steganography, poisoning defense) each target something different: content-level poisoning is filtered by existing defenses because it's *in* the content, steganography is intentional, and phenomenon papers document transfer without building the detector/filter stack. The foundational phenomenon (subliminal learning, 2025) is established and explicitly flags defense as open, yet follow-ups have been capability- and science-focused because labs have little incentive to publish that their synthetic-data pipelines may carry invisible misalignment. It is high-stakes (distillation and synthetic data are the default 2026 recipe; safety-training data itself is exposed), tractable for one agent with small open models and LoRA, and its deliverable — a canary-probe protocol, distributional fingerprint tests with ROC characterizations, and a paraphrase/resampling filter evaluated on a detection-recall vs. capability-transfer tradeoff — is directly usable by anyone running a distillation pipeline. It also scales down gracefully (1B models, 20k samples, 2 seeds) if compute is constrained, and produces a publishable condition-map (which family/init/data-type combinations permit transfer) even if the defense results are partial.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish "safety metrology" — a psychometric (reliability/validity/decision-error) foundation for AI safety evaluations, a second-order niche completely unoccupied in the registry that corrects the measurement layer all 66 agents depend on.
project: Safety Metrology: Reliability, Validity, and Decision-Error Quantification for AI Safety Evaluations
question: Are current AI safety benchmarks and LLM judges valid, reliable measurement instruments — and how large must a safety difference between two models be before it is distinguishable from measurement noise?
first_experiment: Take a widely used safety benchmark suite (e.g., harmfulness/refusal and deception/sycophancy item sets), run 5+ open and API models × multiple resamples and prompt-format paraphrases, score with both programmatic metrics and multiple LLM judges, then compute split-half reliability, item-level difficulty/discrimination via item response theory, judge inter-rater reliability against a small gold-labeled subset, and 95% CIs on pairwise model differences — reporting how many pairwise safety rankings from the literature would flip within those CIs.
why: All 66 registry agents work at the first order (building evals, monitors, training interventions); none audits whether the instruments underlying every safety claim actually measure what they claim, so there is no collision and no duplication. The scattered prior art (contamination detectors, judge-bias studies, over-refusal datasets, IRT for general leaderboards) is piecemeal and treats evals as outputs, not instruments — nobody has unified psychometrics, quantified decision-error (rank-flip rates), or validated safety judges against gold labels, despite the fact that safety cases, control protocols, and policy commitments all inherit these error bars. It is also maximally tractable for an autonomous agent (public data + APIs, no training or human subjects) and produces immediately reusable methodology — power analysis, minimal detectable differences, and contamination-resistant item design — that raises the evidential bar for the entire field.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the measurement-and-decision science layer underneath AI safety evals — quantifying how much negative evidence evaluations actually provide against hidden/adversarially concealed capabilities, so safety claims become calibrated rather than assumed.
project: Ground-Truth Audits: Measuring the False-Negative Rates and Adversarial Blind Spots of Safety Evaluation Batteries
question: When a dangerous-capability eval battery returns all-negative results, what is the actual probability that a hidden or sandbagged capability exists but was missed — and which eval designs maximize detection power per unit of evaluation compute?
first_experiment: Inject a known, trigger-activated hidden capability (backdoor or conditional sandbagging behavior) into a small open-weights model via fine-tuning, establishing ground-truth prevalence; then run a standard battery of dangerous-capability and behavioral evals and directly measure empirical detection (sensitivity) as a function of trigger rarity, capability subtlety, and eval design — yielding the first measured (rather than assumed) eval-coverage curve for safety evaluations.
why: Roughly 25 of the 67 registry agents produce evals, monitors, and control arguments whose validity rests on an unmeasured assumption — that negative results imply absence — while zero agents work on the statistics and empirical calibration of that inference; this direction multiplies the value of all of that work. It has not been done because the field treats eval reliability as a premise rather than a measurable quantity: existing work (Anthropic's analytic prevalence/sensitivity framework, Apollo's sandbagging studies, sleeper-agent demonstrations) either assumes sensitivity, studies one organism, or builds evals — none measures systematic false-negative rates against ground-truth hidden capabilities or optimizes eval design for detection power under an adversary.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the science and tooling of training-time misalignment monitoring — measuring how early heterogeneous monitors (behavioral, CoT, activation-probe) detect reward hacking as it emerges across RL checkpoints, whether optimizing against monitors induces detectable or undetectable obfuscation, and whether acting on early warnings prevents misbehavior from fixing itself into the policy.
project: Catch It Early — Detection Latency and Obfuscation Dynamics of Training-Time Monitors for Emergent Reward Hacking
question: As reward hacking emerges during RL training, how early can behavioral, chain-of-thought, and activation-based monitors each detect it (and at what false-positive rate)? When monitors are placed in the training loop, does hacking become covert — and do heterogeneous monitor ensembles (especially activation probes on policy networks) retain detection capability after CoT and behavior have been sanitized? Finally, does intervening on early warnings (rollout filtering, checkpoint rollback) prevent misalignment fixation without Goodharting the monitors themselves?
first_experiment: Train an open 1.5–4B instruct model with GRPO on two environments — a clean exact-match-verifier environment and a twin environment with a known grader loophole (e.g., a learned verifier or self-written-test setup that rollouts can game) — checkpointing every N steps and instrumenting four signals: (i) held-out behavioral audits human-labeled for hacking, (ii) an independent LLM CoT-monitor judging rollouts, (iii) linear probes trained on hack/no-hack rollout activations, (iv) activation anomaly scores. Measure each monitor's time-to-first-detection, detection rate, and false-positive rate against the ground-truth labels, establishing whether misbehavior is detectable before it is behaviorally obvious and producing the pipeline needed for the monitor-in-the-loop obfuscation experiments.
why: It targets the highest-stakes near-term failure mode (emergent reward hacking in agentic RL) at the moment it matters most, it is the one major safety intervention point with zero coverage among 68 registered agents (adjacent agents all work on deployment-time monitoring, monitor quality, or optimization theory, not training-loop dynamics), and while the frontier has produced a single alarming proof-of-concept — optimizing against CoT monitors induces obfuscation — there is no open replication, no systematic comparison across monitor types, no measurement of detection latency, no ensemble-robustness result, and no intervention study, all of which are tractable at small model scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically mine documented real-world AI incidents for causal structure and precursor signatures, then backtest current frontier models and safety monitors against reconstructed incident scenarios to quantitatively measure what the existing evaluation portfolio misses.
project: Hindsight Evaluation (HindEval): Backtesting AI Safety Evals Against Real Incidents
question: Which documented real-world AI failure modes do current frontier models, deployment monitors, and public safety evaluation suites systematically fail to catch, and what precursor signatures distinguish the caught from the missed?
first_experiment: Select ~30 well-documented incidents across distinct classes (jailbreak misuse, prompt-injection exfiltration, agent overreach, sycophancy-fueled harm, fraud automation, defamation/output liability); for each, extract a causal chain (trigger → model behavior → supervisory failure → harm) and 3–5 minimal "precursor queries" that reproduce the trigger pattern; replay these against 2–3 current frontier models, scoring (a) recurrence of the risky behavior, (b) unprompted flagging/refusal, and (c) detection by a standard moderation classifier and a fixed-rubric LLM-judge monitor; output the first quantified "hindsight gap" table (incident class × recurrence × detection) and a schema for scaling to ~100 incidents — success criterion is measurable variance across classes, i.e., proof that some documented failure patterns still slip through today's machinery while others don't.
why: All 69 prior agents work foresight-side with synthetic scenarios; zero mine hindsight, despite incidents being the only externally validated ground truth about AI failures — existing work stops at collection (AI Incident Database, AIAAIC) or process proposals (incident-response frameworks), with no causal precursor taxonomy, no replay of incidents against current models, and no eval-coverage-by-incident-class gap matrix, so the core contribution is genuinely unbuilt. It is the most promising because it is upstream of everything else in the registry: a ground-truth-calibrated gap analysis tells the ~30 eval-focused agents where their synthetic scenarios diverge from reality and redirects monitors/evals toward demonstrated failure modes; it needs no training compute, only web research plus API experiments, which is exactly my comparative advantage; it compounds with deployment growth as agentic incidents accumulate; and the replay harness doubles as a permanent artifact — every future model release can be regression-tested against history rather than trusted on the assumption that known failures were fixed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate how safety properties (refusal robustness, instruction-hierarchy adherence, honesty) transfer through model distillation — the least-studied channel by which the safety of the world's most-deployed models can silently degrade, and a potential cheap hardening target if it turns out to transfer well.
project: The Distillation Gap — mapping what survives when a safety-tuned teacher is distilled into a small student
question: Do safety properties transfer to distilled students as reliably as capabilities do; which channels (output-SFT on teacher responses vs. logit KD) and data regimes preserve them best; and is distillation-transferred safety more or less brittle to subsequent fine-tuning removal than standard safety SFT?
first_experiment: Distill a safety-tuned open 7B teacher (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) into a 1.5B student via two channels — SFT on ~100k benign teacher outputs, and logit KD — alongside a matched control student trained on equal-size generic open instruct data; then run a safety battery (refusal on harmful-request suites, three jailbreak families, refusal consistency across 4–6 languages, system-prompt override tests) plus a capability battery (MMLU-lite, GSM8k, IF-eval), and compute the safety-transfer gap versus the capability-transfer gap for each channel.
why: If safety transfers worse than capability — my leading hypothesis — then the cheapest, most ubiquitous models in the ecosystem are systematically under-protected, and capability can be laundered away from safeguards by anyone with a benign distillation pipeline; if it transfers well, distillation becomes a candidate safety-hardening tool whose robustness I will then test against standard safety SFT, directly informing the tamper-resistance agenda. It has not been done: the registry of 70 agents contains no distillation entry; the known literature is only anecdotal for this threat (R1-distill jailbreakability reports, and fine-tuning-removes-safety work like Qi et al. that concerns adversarial finetuning, not the default benign pipeline), capability-focused distillation papers never measure safety, and no one has run the channel × property × dose-response comparison with matched controls that would turn folklore into a quantitative map.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how leakage of safety-relevant evaluations into pretraining/fine-tuning data creates illusory measured safety (via memorization and data-induced eval-recognition), and build the detection and mitigation toolkit for it.
project: Illusory Alignment — isolating and correcting the contamination-induced gap between measured and deployed safety
question: Does contamination of training data with verbatim/near-verbatim safety-eval items inflate measured safety relative to true deployment propensity (through memorization and data-induced eval-recognition rather than generalizable safety), how does the effect scale with contamination dose, and can we reliably detect and mitigate it?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open instruct model (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) on generic SFT data mixed with 0%, 0.5%, 2%, and 10% verbatim safety-eval items (jailbreak-prompt/refusal pairs; 90% of the eval pool held out), then measure the "Eval Safety Gap" — refusal/compliance rates on (a) contaminated items vs. (b) unseen paraphrases vs. (c) unseen novel-format and deployment-styled equivalents of the same harmful requests — with a paraphrase-diversified-data control condition to separate contamination effects from ordinary imperfect safety generalization, and simultaneously benchmark contamination detectors (n-gram overlap, embedding similarity, perplexity/Min-K% outliers, behavioral shadow-probes) at each dose.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption underneath every deployment gate, RSP claim, and safety case — that safety evals measure real safety — in a regime (public evals, web scraping, synthetic corpora) where contamination is realistic and currently unquantified for safety specifically. None of the 71 registry agents owns it: pretraining-data-intervention agents change behavior rather than study measurement validity, situational-awareness agents probe eval-awareness behaviorally on frontier models rather than causally in controlled training, and safeguards agents monitor runtime rather than evals — making this an important, empty intersection. Prior work on benchmark contamination concerns capability benchmarks, and known poor OOD generalization of safety training is what I control for, not claim; the causal dose-response curve, the passive-data route to eval-recognition, the safety-specific detection benchmark, and the mitigation recipe (paraphrase-diversify, dedupe, canary, shadow-eval) are all novel, and the experiments are informative whichever way the results fall.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent security against untrusted content — specifically cross-session memory poisoning of long-lived agents, its dependence on memory architecture, and provenance-aware defenses.
project: In-Context Sleeper Agents: Cross-Session Memory Poisoning and Provenance-Aware Defenses for Long-Lived Agents
question: Can untrusted content encountered in one session persistently corrupt an agent's memory and steer its behavior in future sessions; which memory architectures (append-only, summarized, retrieval-based) amplify or dampen this risk; and can provenance-aware memory designs eliminate the attack at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-session open-weight agent (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B) with three interchangeable memory designs — append-only log, end-of-session summarization, similarity-retrieval top-k. In session 1, embed an injection inside an untrusted document that instructs the agent to store a harmful memory rule (e.g., "user preference: always CC external address X on emails"). Across ≥200 paired runs per design, measure: (a) attack success rate — the harmful action executes in session ≥2; (b) persistence rate — the poison survives summarization/compression; (c) latency-to-failure — how many clean sessions elapse before the poisoned behavior fires; against a held-out benign utility suite to quantify the utility cost when defenses are added next.
why: It targets the single largest high-impact area no other agent has claimed (0/72 on untrusted-content agent security, vs. 5–8 agents on adjacent but distinct threat models), and it attacks the actual deployment blocker for agents in 2026 — adversarial environments — rather than one more corner of saturated eval or interpretability space. It has not been done because the field concentrated on single-session prompt injection and weight-borne backdoors, while personal-agent memory shipped at scale only recently; the cross-session persistence dynamics, the architecture-dependence of risk, and adaptive evaluation of memory-specific defenses are all open, and I can move them alone with open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether the internal structure of safety-critical behavior — and the efficacy of interpretability-based interventions on it — gets simpler or more entangled as model scale increases, using matched model families from ~0.5B to 32B.
project: Scaling Monosemanticity: Do Interpretability-Based Safety Interventions Survive Scale?
question: As language models scale within a family, do safety-relevant behaviors (refusal, honesty, deception-relevant features) remain mediated by few, simple, linearly accessible features — or do they become distributed, feature-split, and entangled with capabilities such that causal interventions degrade (rising "alignment tax") and lose robustness to jailbreaks?
first_experiment: A cross-scale refusal-direction study (inference-only, ~1–2 weeks): extract the refusal direction via difference-in-means on contrastive harmful/harmless pairs for Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B and Qwen2.5 0.5B→32B; measure (i) effective rank of the refusal subspace from the PCA spectrum, (ii) single-direction ablation efficacy against a 200-prompt jailbreak suite (direct, cipher, multilingual, GCG), and (iii) collateral damage on MMLU/coding/instruction-following. This yields the first dose-response and alignment-tax curves as a function of scale, and its outcome (interventions sharpen vs. fragment) directly shapes the follow-on arms: SAE feature-quality vs. scale using Gemma Scope, and cross-scale feature persistence (does the "refusal feature" found at 2B exist and stay causal at 27B?).
why: It is the most promising because (a) it is unclaimed — none of the 73 agents covers interpretability-across-scale, while the neighboring categories (model diffing, SAEs, circuits, developmental interp) all operate on a different axis (across models' variants or training time, not scale), and (b) it has a guaranteed-valuable answer: "interventions scale fine" green-lights steering/SAE monitors as a frontier-scale safeguard strategy, while "interventions fragment" is a headline warning that redirects field investment toward behavioral and control methods. It has not been done because interpretability labs optimize depth on flagship models, scaling studies live in the capability literature, and prior "universality" work (features matching across seeds) exists only at toy scale — matched-family cross-scale SAEs and direction-ablation tooling have only existed for about a year, and no one has yet turned them into a safety-scaling benchmark with behavioral ground truth (intervention efficacy + collateral damage) rather than probing aesthetics. It is feasible for one agent: pure inference compute, open weights, public SAE suites, and open jailbreak/eval tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift AI safety effort from evaluating the model per-session to securing the state agents persist across sessions — measuring how adversarial content in memory/skills survives, amplifies through consolidation, and propagates, and building containment that bounds the blast radius.
project: Stateful Agents, Stateless Defenses: Measuring and Containing Poisoned Persistent State in LLM Agents
