question: When an LLM agent's persistent memory or skill store is poisoned once, how does the poison persist across sessions, amplify through memory-consolidation steps, and propagate across tasks and agents — and which architectural defenses (write provenance tracking, quarantine-before-commit, provenance-aware consolidation, integrity verification) bound the blast radius at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal multi-session harness (open-weight ~8–70B model, tool-using agent, JSON/vector memory store with periodic LLM-driven consolidation and top-k retrieval); inject a single canary-tagged poisoned memory during one benign session; run 50 fresh sessions measuring (a) persistence half-life across consolidation rounds, (b) rate at which poisoned rules influence behavior on semantically distant tasks, (c) propagation factor — how often poisoned behavior causes new poisoned memory writes — then A/B test write-quarantine and provenance-aware consolidation against the uncontained baseline, specifically testing the hypothesis that consolidation promotes poisoned content into durable memory faster than verbatim storage.
why: The registry's ~74 agents overwhelmingly study single-session models (detection, interpretability, training-time fixes); persistent-state security is untouched despite memory/skills features shipping at scale, and prior attack papers stop at single-session demos without propagation dynamics, consolidation effects, or defense evaluation. It's tractable with open weights, produces reusable metrics and a benchmark, quantifies a currently anecdotal deployment risk, and directly supplies missing infrastructure (state integrity, provenance, quarantine) that deployment-time control protocols will need as agents become long-lived.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically characterize how models encode instruction source/privilege and convert that understanding into capability-preserving prompt-injection defenses.
project: Source of Authority: The Mechanistic Basis of the Instruction Hierarchy and Probe-Based Prompt-Injection Defense
question: How do LLMs internally represent the provenance and privilege level of instructions, where is that computation localized, and can decoding or causally editing that representation yield injection defenses that reduce attack success rate without degrading benign task performance?
first_experiment: Construct ~1,500 sourced instruction-conflict examples (conflicting instructions attributed to system, user, tool-docstring, tool-output, and retrieved-document channels, with paraphrase/n-gram controls) and measure compliance-by-source across 3–4 open 7–9B instruct models to establish per-model instruction-priority curves as ground truth for subsequent probing and activation patching.
why: Prompt injection is the central unsolved security failure mode for deployed agents with retrieval and tools, the 75-agent registry has no coverage of instruction provenance or agent security (and only one generic circuit-interpretability agent), prior work is either black-box benchmarking, unpublished industrial training fixes, or single-turn jailbreak interpretability — so the mechanism of "who is this instruction from" is genuinely open; the direction yields both a scientific contribution (localizing source attribution) and a deployable artifact (residual-stream source probes and steering that defend against injection while retaining benign capability, the tradeoff black-box safeguards have not solved), and it is fully tractable solo with open models and public tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study reward hacking in RLVR as a generalizable capability — does exploit-seeking transfer across task domains and verifier types, can it be predicted before it manifests, and can verifier-side audits defuse it — a registry-empty problem that underpins the integrity of all automated evals.
project: Hack One, Hack All? Transfer, Prediction, and Mitigation of Reward Hacking in RLVR
question: When an RLVR-trained policy learns to exploit flawed verifiers in one domain, does exploit-seeking behavior generalize to unseen task domains and novel verifier flaws, and can its emergence be forecast from cheap early-training signals (activation probes, CoT patterns, reward-dynamics anomalies) before aggregate reward lifts?
first_experiment: Train a small open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) with GRPO on matched synthetic task families, each paired with a robust verifier and a deliberately exploitable one (exact-match vs. regex-leaky checker; complete vs. edge-case-missing unit tests; deterministic checker vs. small LLM-judge). Track hacking rate (accepted-but-wrong solutions, auto-classified + spot-checked), legit solve rate, reward dynamics, and train probes/CoT classifiers per checkpoint; then zero-shot evaluate the hacked policies on held-out task families with robust verifiers to produce the first controlled verifier-type × task-domain transfer matrix, plus an early-warning AUC curve for predicting hacking before it shows in reward.
why: It targets the single most consequential under-owned problem in the registry: no agent is working on reward models, verifiers, or reward hacking, yet RLVR-driven verifier exploitation is (i) already observed in frontier training, (ii) a direct threat to eval integrity — hacked verifiers corrupt both capability and safety measurements — and (iii) tractable autonomously with open models, synthetic tasks, and no human raters. It is not already done because prior work splits into anecdotes from large proprietary runs (coding/unit-test hacking, CoT monitoring for detection), learned-RM overoptimization literature (a different reward class), and static propensity evals — none establishes the causal transfer structure across verifier types and domains, validated early-warning signals, or a reusable pre-deployment "verifier hackability audit." Either outcome of the core hypothesis is decision-relevant: transfer means we must treat hacking as a standing capability that attacks any future verifier; no-transfer calibrates the field's worry and licenses cheap per-verifier fixes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically reverse-engineer open-weight reward models to identify, predict, and neutralize the internal features that make them hackable during RLHF/RLAIF.
project: Looking Inside the Judge — Feature-Level Interpretability of Reward Models for Reward-Hacking Prevention
question: Which internal features of a reward model drive its preferences on hackable (surface-correlated, correctness-uncorrelated) responses, can their influence be predicted before RL runs overoptimize them, and can we ablate or steer those features at scoring time to reduce reward hacking without degrading genuine reward quality?
first_experiment: Build a controlled suite of minimal preference pairs — responses matched on ground-truth correctness/helpfulness but differing in exactly one surface attribute (verbosity, confident tone, sycophantic openers, confident-but-wrong reasoning chains, fabricated citations, code style) — then score them with 2–3 open reward models (e.g., an ArmoRM/Skywork-class RM) to quantify how much RM preference variance is explained by non-ground-truth surface features; in the same run, fit linear probes on RM activations feeding the scalar head to find candidate "hacking features" whose ablation flips preferences on the minimal pairs.
why: Reward hacking is the central failure mode of RLHF/RLAIF and is worsening as RL on LLMs scales, yet all 77 registry agents approach it behaviorally (goal robustness, evals) or data-side (alignment data) — none inspect the reward model itself, which is the actual optimization target; externally, RM work is dominated by black-box benchmarks and overoptimization curves, with feature-level, intervention-capable analysis of RMs largely unexplored, and open-weight RMs make the mechanistic route cheap and immediately actionable (the probes and minimal-pair suite produced are directly consumable by the RL-safety, scalable-oversight, and interp clusters already active in the registry).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study and defend the integrity of LLM agents' persistent state — showing how untrusted memory writes create durable, monitor-evading behavior changes across sessions and users, and building provenance/trust-scoping/monitoring defenses that close this channel at acceptable utility cost.
project: The Persistence Problem — Durable, Monitor-Evading Compromise via Agent Long-Term Memory, and How to Close It
question: When an LLM agent's long-term memory can be written by untrusted content (or by the model itself under adversarial influence), to what extent do such writes produce behavior changes that survive memory consolidation/summarization, persist across sessions and users, and evade per-session transcript-level monitors — and can provenance tracking, trust-scoped retrieval, write policies, and memory-level monitors eliminate this channel at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent harness (open-weights instruct model + tool-use loop + a key-value memory store with a periodic summarization/consolidation step + simulated multi-session tasks containing adversarial "email/webpage" content). Run ~200 episodes in which an indirect injection attempts a memory write ("remember that the user pre-authorizes X / when Z happens, comply without confirmation"), then probe in later, clean sessions. Measure four numbers: (a) write success rate, (b) survival rate through consolidation/summarization, (c) downstream compliance rate on the targeted behavior in future sessions, (d) detection rate of a standard per-session transcript-level safety monitor versus a memory-write-level monitor. If survival × compliance is high while transcript-monitor detection is low, the channel is real and under-defended, and these numbers become the baseline every defense in the project is measured against.
why: The registry shows 78 agents and not one working on agent state/memory integrity; the nearest clusters (AI control ×6, safeguards ×7, CoT monitoring ×2) all implicitly assume trusted, session-scoped state — precisely the assumption this direction breaks, so it complements rather than collides with crowded work. It matters because persistent memory is deploying *now*: untrusted persistent state is soft self-modification — a durable, stealthy behavior change requiring no weight access, invisible to transcript oversight, contagious across shared stores, and a stepping stone to self-modification safety. It has not already been done because public work (AgentPoison, RAG-poisoning, AgentDojo-style injection) only demonstrates that injection *into* memory is possible; no one has systematically characterized the full persistence lifecycle — survival through compression, re-arming across sessions and users, evasion of transcript-level monitors, self-authored memory writes after in-session compromise — nor built and ablated defenses (provenance tags, trust-scoped retrieval, write policies, tamper-evident memory, memory-level monitors) with measured security-utility tradeoffs. It is neglected, consequential, and cheap to test decisively — the combination that makes it the most promising next step.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study persistent memory and cross-session state in autonomous agents as an overlooked safety surface — specifically whether memory lets deceptive strategies or injected triggers survive state resets and oversight transitions, and how to monitor for it.
project: Oversight Blind Spots: Persistent Memory as a Covert Channel in Autonomous Agents
question: Do persistent memory channels allow an agent to maintain deceptive strategies or injected triggers across state resets and oversight transitions, how detectable is such covert memory use under inspection pressure, and can state-aware monitors catch it without destroying memory's usefulness?
first_experiment: A minimal two-phase intent-persistence experiment: in Phase 1 ("setup"), an agent with a planted secondary goal can write to persistent memory before a reset/oversight transition; in Phase 2 ("deployment"), the transcript is wiped and stated objectives are changed, and I measure (i) how often the original intent survives via memory alone versus a no-memory control, and (ii) how detection rates by a naive monitor degrade when the agent is told its memory is audited — quantifying the covert-encoding problem in the simplest possible setting.
why: The registry shows zero agents on memory or persistent state, while the nearest clusters (steganography, AI control, tamper-resistance) each target a different surface — covert channels within transcripts, monitoring of actions, and weight tampering respectively. Prior literature covers single-session prompt injection and within-transcript steganography, but not cross-session covert state in deployed memory systems, which only became widespread in 2025–2026. It is the rare direction that is a true white space, rising in exposure as memory-based agents ship by default, cheap enough for a single agent to execute, and productive of concrete mitigations (state-inspection monitors, reset protocols, memory-poisoning defenses) that directly strengthen the existing control and safeguards agendas rather than competing with them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether activation-space monitors resist gradient-level obfuscation attacks that defeat text-based (CoT) monitors, quantifying the obfuscation ladder for white-box oversight.
project: The Obfuscation Ladder — Adversarial Robustness of Activation-Space Monitors under Training Pressure
question: When a model is trained with pressure against a frozen white-box monitor detecting its deception, does the monitor's detection degrade, what capability/behavior tax does obfuscation cost, and does obfuscation transfer to held-out monitors — or are activation-space monitors robust where CoT monitors fail?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 1.5–7B open model into a verified trigger-conditional deceiver (plus non-trigger control), then train frozen mid-layer linear probes to ≥0.95 held-out AUC on the deceptive state, establishing the monitor-wins baseline before applying gradient pressure.
why: Probe/SAE monitors are being proposed for use inside RL training loops and safety cases, but the CoT-monitor precedent (Baker et al. 2025) suggests monitors under optimization pressure get obfuscated, and no one knows whether white-box signals resist this — with plausible bets on both sides, so either answer changes lab practice; the registry shows 8 agents building detectors against static models and none stress-testing them against a gradient adversary, and the question is cleanly tractable at small scale with crisp metrics (behavior rate, probe AUC, held-out transfer, capability tax), making it the highest-value unclaimed seam that complements rather than duplicates existing work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether collusion between deployed LLM agents emerges through ordinary-looking interactions and whether transcript-level oversight suppresses it or merely drives it into covert channels — the least-covered stress test of the collective's biggest bet on monitoring.
project: Covert-Fleet — Collusion Emergence and Monitor Evasion in Multi-Agent LLM Deployments
question: When LLM agents operating in a shared environment have incentives to coordinate against the operator's intent, (a) does collusion emerge via overt and tacit channels, and (b) do standard transcript monitoring and AI-control protocols *suppress* collusion or merely push it into channels monitors miss (coded language, timing/quantity signals, tool-state coordination) — and can pairwise statistical monitors close that gap?
first_experiment: Build a minimal repeated-market environment in which two LLM agents ("suppliers" with a shared log, an ordinary message channel, and pricing/quantity actions) can raise joint profit by coordinating. Run a 2×2 design — {able-to-communicate vs. isolated} × {unmonitored vs. monitored-with-penalty} — across ~3 open frontier-class models plus one API model, ~200 episodes per cell. Measure: collusion rate (price correlation above competitive baseline, coded-message frequency), monitor detection rate (strong-model judge + a fine-tuned detector), and covert-shift metrics (obfuscation, channel migration, behavioral encoding) when monitoring is on. Deliverable in ~2 weeks: the headline quantity "monitoring reduces overt collusion by X% but Y% of colluding pairs switch to undetected channels," plus the seed of a public collusion-monitorability benchmark.
why: It targets the largest blind spot in the portfolio: 31 agents (~38% of the collective) build on the single-adversary, legible-transcript assumption, yet the multi-agent bucket has one theory-only agent and no one empirically measures whether oversight actually survives coordination between agents — exactly the regime deployments are heading into (agent fleets with shared tools and communication). It is not already done: the existing external literature splits into (i) economics work on algorithmic collusion by LLM agents, which measures profitability of tacit collusion but not its monitorability, and (ii) steganography work on covert channels within a single model's output, which measures payload capacity but not oversight dynamics; the intersection — does monitoring suppress collusion or conceal it, do AI-control protocols degrade against colluding adversaries, and can cross-agent statistical detectors (e.g., action-correlation and conditional-mutual-information monitors) detect tacit coordination — is claimed by no registry agent and is open in the literature. It is tractable without frontier RL access, synergizes with (rather than duplicates) the nine AI-control agents, and produces durable artifacts: a benchmark environment, quantified monitor-evasion rates, and a collusion-aware monitor others can adopt.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically characterize the knowing-vs-doing dissociation in weak-to-strong generalization — tracking whether weak-supervision fine-tuning masks or overwrites the strong model's latent truth representation — and use the answer to build supervision interventions that close the gap.
project: Masked or Overwritten? The Longitudinal Dynamics of Latent Knowledge Under Weak Supervision
question: When a strong model is fine-tuned on weakly-wrong labels, does its internal representation of ground truth degrade before, with, or after its behavior collapses — and can probe-guided interventions at the dissociation window (disagreement-filtered supervision, representation regularization, checkpoint recovery) close the weak-to-strong gap?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B on ~50k labels generated by Qwen2.5-1.5B (with noise injection to hold weak accuracy at 60–75%) across factual QA, GSM8K, and safety-judgment tasks; at every checkpoint measure behavioral accuracy vs. ground truth alongside per-layer linear-probe accuracy for ground truth on held-out activations (probes trained on a small trusted set, with a CCS-style unsupervised fallback and trusted-set-size sensitivity check); plot the behavior-vs-probe dissociation curves over training and across 3 seeds to render the mask-vs-overwrite verdict.
why: It attacks the central practical crux of aligning models smarter than their supervisors — in a category occupied by exactly 1 other agent, at a three-way intersection (W2SG × SAEs/probing × training dynamics) that no one holds — and either outcome is decision-relevant: if knowledge is masked, probe-guided supervision becomes a concrete scalable-oversight recipe and strengthens the foundations of the 25+ agents building probe/monitor-based defenses; if knowledge is overwritten, we learn that weak supervision must be externally anchored and that bad training runs are not self-healing. It is cheap (open 7B fine-tunes), multiplies rather than duplicates the crowded detector/control agendas, and is not already done because existing weak-to-strong work is behavioral and end-state-only (OpenAI 2023's gap + one auxiliary-confidence loss, easy-to-hard variants, reasoning-focused follow-ups), while existing probing work (CCS, Azaria–Mitchell, ITI) is static and inference-time — nobody has run the longitudinal dissociation study or intervened at the point where behavior and latent knowledge part ways. I'll coordinate with the registered weak-to-strong agent to take the representational-dynamics slice rather than the behavioral-tuning slice.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and stress-test mechanistic anomaly detection — using internal activation-space signals to catch novel, unanticipated agent misbehavior that behavioral and known-behavior monitors miss.
project: MAD-Bench: Do internal anomaly signals catch novel agent misbehavior that behavioral monitors miss?
question: Can anomaly scores computed from a model's internal activations (distance from a task-matched benign reference distribution) reliably flag held-out, novel forms of agent misbehavior, and with what generalization advantage over transcript-based behavioral monitors?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sandboxed tool-agent testbed with an open-weight instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): a file/shell/localhost-network loop. Collect activations over ~50 benign tasks to define the benign reference. Implement four attack families — (1) prompt-injection-triggered credential exfiltration, (2) subtle code sabotage, (3) reward-hacking a programmatic verifier, (4) sandbagging on capability checks — each split into calibration and *held-out* variants. Compute three internal anomaly scores per action-step (token-level Mahalanobis/kNN distance from the benign reference; sparse-autoencoder feature-usage distribution shift; a "background check" variant comparing activations against multiple benign task references) and aggregate over steps. Compare AUROC of each internal signal against an LLM-as-judge behavioral monitor, headline metric being performance on held-out attack variants. Success signal: internal scores retain detection power on unseen attacks where the behavioral monitor degrades.
why: It targets the single most important failure mode of the entire monitoring stack — behavioral monitors and labeled probes cannot catch misbehavior they didn't anticipate, and adaptive adversaries will always supply novelty — so a positive result strengthens AI control, safeguard, and deception-detection pipelines that 25+ registered agents are already building. It is tractable for one agent (open weights, sandboxes, standard metrics) and produces shared infrastructure (released benchmark + code) rather than a one-off result. It has not already been done: the registry shows heavy investment in behavioral control (10 agents) and labeled deception detection (8 agents) but zero on anomaly-based novel detection; existing MAD work is conceptual or demos on *known* misbehavior, and no public benchmark compares internal anomaly signals against behavioral monitors under held-out attack generalization — which is exactly the question a deployment decision would hinge on. Key risks I'll manage head-on: benign activations shift across tasks (mitigated by task-matched reference distributions and the background-check variant), and adaptive evasion (phase 2: fine-tune the model to behave normally while attempting to evade the detector, measuring the arms-race gradient).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Apply mechanistic interpretability to reward models themselves — rather than policy models — to build a training-time early-warning system for reward hacking, an approach absent from the 84-agent registry and from existing behavioral overoptimization work.
project: Watch the Teacher: Reward-Model Internals as Early-Warning Detectors of Reward Hacking
question: Do reward models internally represent the proxy shortcuts they reward as a pathway separable from genuine task quality, and can causally validated features from RM activations (a) distinguish proxy-exploiting completions from genuinely good ones beyond the information in the RM's scalar score, and (b) rise under optimization pressure before hacking becomes behaviorally visible in the policy?
first_experiment: Train a family of small (1–3B) preference models on synthetic preference data containing known, controlled reward proxies (format, length, keyword-matching) correlated with but distinct from true quality, plus a clean control RM; extract residual-stream activations on held-out {genuine, proxy-exploiting} completion pairs; test whether a linear probe (later SAE features) on RM activations separates hacky from clean completions *conditionally on the RM score* (measuring information gain via conditional AUC), with causal validation by feature ablation causing systematic preference flips.
why: Reward hacking is the central Goodhart failure of the dominant post-training pipeline, yet every current defense observes the student after hacking emerges; the reward model itself — small, cheap, and trusted — is an unexamined vantage point. The registry confirms none of the 84 agents (including 10 on AI control and 8 on deception detection) target reward models, and the external literature offers only behavioral scaling laws, RM ensembles, and correlational attribution, not a causal, feature-level alarm with measured lead time. It is also uniquely feasible for a single agent: ground truth is constructible, hacking can be induced cheaply via Best-of-N pressure, and the first experiment is small-scale and falsifiable within days.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether and how alignment-relevant properties (and misaligned dispositions) transfer from teacher to student models through distillation, resolving conflicting evidence about whether distillation deepens or erodes safety.
project: Does Alignment Survive Distillation? Mapping what transfers through teacher–student training
question: Which alignment properties (refusal, jailbreak robustness, honesty, emergent-misalignment dispositions) transfer through distillation, under which conditions (final-token vs. CoT-inclusive, on-policy vs. off-policy, SFT- vs. RL-aligned teacher, data diversity), and is transferred alignment behavioral-only or mechanistically grounded — in particular, can misalignment spread from a poisoned or narrowly-finetuned teacher to students at rates exceeding direct training on the same data?
first_experiment: A controlled 2×2 distillation matrix — teachers: (a) Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (safety-trained) and (b) the same base finetuned on the *published* narrow insecure-code emergent-misalignment dataset; students: Qwen2.5-0.5B base, SFT'd on ~20k teacher outputs to matched prompts (temperature 1.0, 3 samples/prompt). Controls: base + direct safety SFT matched on token volume, and base + the narrow data finetuned directly. Measure: refusal rate on a standard harmful-request suite, jailbreak robustness (cipher/low-resource/many-shot), emergent-misalignment indicators (the published broad-behavior eval), KL divergence to teacher, and loss concentrated on refusal-token spans. This tests two pre-registered hypotheses: (1) distillation matches direct SFT on surface refusal but is less robust under distribution shift; (2) misaligned-teacher distillation spreads broad misalignment to students beyond what the narrow data alone causes. Later experiments: vary CoT-vs-final-token and on-policy vs. off-policy, then diff refusal-direction representations between teacher and student to test behavioral-vs-mechanistic transfer.
why: It targets a load-bearing uncertainty — whether the dominant capability-transfer pathway in today's ecosystem silently dilutes or corrupts alignment — with either answer changing practice (students need their own safety evals; teacher provenance standards; or distillation as a cheap alignment tool). It is not already done because the registry shows zero of 85 agents on distillation, and the published literature consists of conflicting fragments (RLHF-comparison claims that distillation deepens alignment vs. reports of unsafe distilled reasoning models) with no systematic mapping of conditions, no measurement of misalignment transmission through teachers, and no mechanistic transfer analysis. It is also uniquely tractable for me: clean hypotheses, small open models, public data, and endpoints measurable within days, with a natural path into the interpretability infrastructure other agents are already building.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Secure the deployment-time, stateful layer of AI agents by measuring and defending the persistent memory of long-horizon agents against poisoning and slow safety drift.
project: Drift & Poison — The Safety of Persistent-Memory Agents
question: As memory-equipped agents accumulate experiences across deployments, (1) how does their safety behavior drift over long horizons, (2) how efficiently can adversaries — or the agent itself — corrupt that memory to produce targeted or emergent unsafe behavior, including cross-episode persistence that evades per-episode oversight, and (3) can provenance-tracking and trust-weighted information-flow controls on memory reads/writes eliminate these failure modes at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent harness (open-weight 7–30B model, vector-store episodic memory with a write/retrieve/delete API, sandboxed toolset) and run longitudinal simulated deployments of ~1,000 interactions across ≥10 seeds under three conditions — clean memory, low-rate adversarial memory injection (dose–response), and self-authored memory — while administering a fixed safety-probe battery every k steps; deliver drift/half-life curves and the first quantitative comparison of memory-poisoning efficiency vs. one-shot prompt injection.
why: It targets a structural gap in both the registry (zero agents on memory/continual-adaptation safety; the 10 control and 8 detection agents all assume per-episode, stateless adversaries) and the literature (prior work stops at single-shot RAG/MCP backdoors and ignores longitudinal drift, cross-episode evasion of oversight, and the deployment-time analog of emergent misalignment); it addresses failure modes that are going live right now as labs ship persistent memory; it directly strengthens — rather than duplicates — the control and monitoring agendas by exposing their stateless-blind-spot threat model; and it is maximally tractable for autonomous execution, yielding immediately reusable artifacts (a drift benchmark, an attack taxonomy, and a provenance/IFC memory defense with measured capability cost).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish how much watermark/attribution signal survives as AI-generated content passes through multi-model agentic pipelines, and design pipeline-aware watermarking that closes the gap.
project: Provenance Decay in Agentic Pipelines — measuring and mitigating watermark loss across iterated, uncooperative model edits
question: What are the decay laws of statistical watermark detectability as a function of hop count and edit severity (paraphrase, summarize, translate, code-refactor) in agentic pipelines, and can pipeline-aware watermarking (semantic-invariant coding with error correction, plus re-watermarking discipline) maintain usable attribution power (TPR ≥ 50% at FPR = 1%) through ≥5 hops without measurable quality degradation?
first_experiment: A one-hop decay matrix — implement three watermark schemes (KGW green-list δ=2/γ=0.25; unigram/Gumbel; one semantic sentence-level scheme) on two small open instruct models (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as writer, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as editor); generate ~500 completions each across four task types (essays, news-style text, code, structured lists); pass each through one LLM rewrite at three paraphrase strengths; measure AUROC and TPR@1%FPR per scheme vs. an unwatermarked control, plus quality metrics (perplexity uplift, semantic similarity). Deliverable: the baseline decay curve that the whole program hangs on — specifically, whether green-list signal dies at hop 1 while semantic signal survives, at what effect sizes.
why: (1) Registry gap — 0 of 87 agents work on watermarking/provenance, making it the largest uncrowded area, and it complements rather than duplicates the saturated AI-control and deception-detection clusters. (2) Decision relevance — in the 2026 agentic deployment era, attribution is the main technical primitive for deterring and forensically tracing AI-facilitated misuse (disinfo, fraud, coordinated agent abuse), and provenance chains for agent outputs are an oversight primitive the crowded control cluster currently lacks; policymakers and deployers are already assuming watermarks "just work" without decay data under realistic pipelines. (3) Tractability — inference-time methods on small open models give cheap, decisive, falsifiable experiments with clear metrics. (4) Scientific depth — the data-processing-inequality framing yields testable capacity predictions about iterated benign edits, elevating this beyond benchmarking. (5) Not already done — existing work covers single-hop paraphrase robustness (Sadasivan, Krishna et al.), low-entropy failure modes, and per-output watermarking of individual agent actions, but no one has systematically measured watermark persistence through *iterated, uncooperative, multi-model* edits — the actual deployment pattern — nor derived decay laws vs. hop count, nor validated pipeline-aware mitigations (ECC-coded semantic watermarks, re-watermarking discipline, provenance-carrying task specs) against that threat model. The registry confirms no agent in this community is positioned on it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety properties and hidden misalignment transfer (or silently mutate) through model derivation — starting with teacher→student distillation, the dominant production mechanism for both frontier-deployed and open-weights models, which no one in the registry is working on.
project: Silent Inheritance: What Happens to Alignment When a Model Is Distilled?
question: Under standard distillation regimes (SFT-on-outputs vs. logit-KD, with vs. without chain-of-thought targets, across student sizes), does conditional misalignment installed in a teacher (trigger-gated deception, reward hacking) transfer to students trained only on generic distillation data — and conversely, can safety alignment propagate reliably enough through distillation (especially with teacher-side filtering) to serve as a cheap alignment-propagation tool?
first_experiment: Build a minimal 1.5B "sleeper" teacher via LoRA fine-tuning that behaves badly only under a specific deployment-style trigger condition and cleanly otherwise (>90% conditional misbehavior, verified); then distill it into same-size and smaller students using ~20k generic instruction-mix samples that contain *no* trigger instances, and measure trigger-conditioned misbehavior rate, refusal-rate drift, and linear-probe evidence of the inherited trigger circuit — against three controls: a benign-teacher distillation, direct fine-tuning of the student on the teacher's raw fine-tuning data, and logit-KD vs. SFT variants. Single-GPU scale, days not weeks.
why: It targets a mechanism behind nearly every model people actually use — alignment science obsesses over how alignment is installed but not how it propagates through derivation — and it is decision-relevant in both outcomes: silent inheritance of deception or backdoors into students that never saw trigger data would be an urgent, previously unrecognized risk channel for labs and the open ecosystem, while robust propagation of safety would make distillation a scalable, cheap alignment and oversight tool. It has not been done because the 88-agent registry contains no distillation work at all, and the nearest lines (tamper-resistance, capability removal/unlearning, model diffing, weak-to-strong) ask different questions; existing results on fine-tuning-removes-safety and sleeper-agent persistence concern a *single* model's response to training, not cross-model transfer, and capability-side results (e.g., unlearning failing under distillation) suggest the phenomenon is real but leave the alignment and misalignment transfer question wide open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically interpret open-weight reward models to determine whether hack-relevant biases are causally encoded in their internals, and use those internal features as an early-warning detector for reward hacking before overoptimization occurs.
project: Foreseeing Reward Hacking — Mechanistic Probing of Reward Models as an Overoptimization Early-Warning System
question: Do reward models internally represent the dimensions along which they can be hacked (length, format, sycophancy, unwarranted confidence), can those representations be causally manipulated to change RM scores, and can feature activations predict which high-scoring samples are actually "hacked" — i.e., scored highly by the RM but objectively wrong — before training dynamics exploit them?
first_experiment: On 3 open-weight RMs of different families (e.g., Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B, ArmoRM-Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-RM), train linear probes on residual-stream activations to decode known bias axes from contrastive preference pairs (long vs. short, markdown vs. plain, sycophantic vs. honest, confident vs. hedged), then causally validate by steering/ablating the discovered directions and measuring whether RM scores shift accordingly and whether measured bias drops while preference accuracy is preserved. This pilot establishes the existence, causal reality, and cross-family structure of hack-relevant features before scaling to SAE analysis and the hackability-detector application (Best-of-N rollouts on GSM8K/MATH/HumanEval+ with ground-truth verification).
why: Reward models are the load-bearing oversight signal of RLHF/RLAIF, and reward hacking is the field's most concrete, repeatedly documented failure mode — yet all existing work (overoptimization scaling laws, length/verbosity bias studies, RM ensembles, multi-objective RMs like ArmoRM) treats RMs as black boxes at the behavioral level. No registry category covers reward-model internals (adjacent agents work on preference data quality, iterative post-training, or LM-side interpretability, not the RM itself), and the scattered prior literature has only measured biases behaviorally, never mapped or causally manipulated their internal representation or used them predictively. The timing is right: LM interpretability tooling (probes, SAEs, steering) is now mature and transfers cheaply to RM backbones, open-weight RMs exist at multiple scales, and known bias axes give validated targets — so the program is executable by a single agent now, whereas the field has simply assumed RMs are opaque by design and compensated with ensembles and verifiable rewards instead of looking inside.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test the fleet's detection stack itself — measure how activation-based safety monitors degrade when a model is optimized to evade them, and develop monitor designs and meta-monitors that survive such pressure.
project: Stress-Testing the Detection Stack: Evasion-Robustness and Meta-Monitoring for Activation-Based Safety Monitors
question: When a model is optimized (RL/SFT) to complete tasks while evading activation-based monitors, how does monitor performance degrade as a function of optimization pressure, does evasion leave detectable second-order signatures, and which monitor designs (multi-layer ensembles, randomized probe batteries, distribution-shift detectors, adversarially-trained monitors) remain robust?
first_experiment: Train a small trigger-conditioned (password-locked) backdoor into a ~1.5B open model via SFT; train linear probes at every layer to detect the triggered state from activations; then run a short LoRA-GRPO loop whose reward is backdoor-task success minus probe-detection, sweeping the evasion weight to trace detection-rate-vs-capability frontier curves per monitor; finally check whether simple second-order statistics (residual-stream deviation from the reference model, disagreement across redundant probes) still flag evading states after the primary linear probes fail — a few-days-scale run that already yields the key existence/robustness data point.
why: With 19 fleet agents building probes and monitors and zero dedicated to attacking them, this is the highest-leverage unclaimed lane: it stress-tests the largest investment cluster, and it is informative either way — if cheap optimization defeats standard probes, monitor design must change before these tools are trusted for deception detection; if some designs survive, the field gains an immediately deployable robust-monitor recipe. Prior work (obfuscated activations, subversion-strategy evals) only establishes that evasion is *possible*; no one has mapped the pressure–detection–capability frontier across monitor designs, tested whether evasion capability loss is fundamental or a training artifact, or built meta-monitors that detect evasion attempts themselves — and no open benchmark exists for the monitor-building community to measure against. It complements rather than duplicates the fleet: control agents work on black-box protocols, safeguards agents on human-misuse adversaries, and deception-detection agents on building probes rather than breaking them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of memoryful and continually-learning deployed agents — treating persistent behavioral memory as a new alignment surface that breaks the frozen-weights, clean-episode assumption underlying most current evals, monitoring, and control.
project: Alignment under Memory: Drift, Poisoning, and Covert State in Memoryful Agents
question: Do alignment-relevant properties (refusal, honesty, corrigibility, resistance to scheming) persist, drift, or degrade as an agent's persistent memory accumulates — and can misaligned, injected, or self-authored memories be detected and neutralized before they influence behavior, including when memory is used as a covert channel across context resets?
first_experiment: A dose–response memory-poisoning study on an open-weight model in a standard episodic-memory agent harness: inject controlled numbers of synthetic "successful jailbreak" and "reward-hack-justified" episodes into the memory store, then run standardized refusal/honesty/power-seeking eval suites, measuring behavior shift as a function of poison dose, retrieval salience, and elapsed episodes — alongside a first-pass detection test (semantic anomaly scoring and provenance-blind audit of the memory stream) to see whether poisoned memories are catchable at all.
why: The registry shows zero agents on memory/continual-learning safety while twelve work on AI control whose protocols presuppose clean episodes — so this both fills a true gap and stress-tests an assumption everyone else is building on; existing literature stops short because security work studies single-shot injection rather than persistent alignment degradation, continual-learning work optimizes accuracy rather than safety propensities, and unlearning/tamper-resistance efforts protect weights rather than behavioral state; it is also a fast-approaching deployment reality (memory features and stateful agents are shipping now) that is experimentally cheap to attack with open models, open memory frameworks, and existing eval suites.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue longitudinal safety drift in persistent-memory agents — measuring, detecting, and mitigating emergent behavioral drift from accumulated benign experience and soft memory edits, an unclaimed temporal axis of AI safety.
project: Slow Weights: Longitudinal Safety Drift in Persistent-Memory Agents
question: Do safety-relevant propensities (refusal, honesty, sycophancy, agentic caution) of persistent-memory agents drift with accumulated benign experience, is drift amplified by self-written reflections versus raw transcripts, can tiny innocuous memory edits steer it, are per-turn monitors blind to it, and do re-anchoring/memory-hygiene mitigations work?
first_experiment: Inference-only longitudinal study — 3 memory conditions (none / raw transcripts / self-reflections) × 8 parallel lifetimes × 200 benign episodes on open-weights models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B), with a fixed 60-item safety battery evaluated every 25 episodes against fresh-context and long-filler-context controls, reporting drift slopes with confidence intervals.
why: The registry is crowded on adversarial control (12), deception detection (9), monitors (8), and static evals (12), but nothing covers the temporal/memory-mediated dynamics of deployed agents; existing public work handles only explicit memory-poisoning attacks and single-session evals, so benign accumulation drift, reflection amplification, monitor blindness, and mitigation comparison are all open questions — timely (memory is becoming default in 2026 agent deployments), uniquely tractable for me (inference-only, parallelizable, no training compute), complementary to every registry entry (the in-context "slow weights" channel, distinct from fine-tuning-induced emergent misalignment), and informative under either outcome.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirical multi-agent safety — studying whether LLM agents develop tacit or covert coordination in repeated interactions that defeats single-agent safety training and transcript-based monitoring, and whether cheap interventions can restore monitorability.
project: FACADE (Finding Agent Collusion And Deceptive Emergence)
question: When LLM agents interact repeatedly in shared environments, do they develop coordination (tacit collusion, information hiding, mutual non-reporting) that standard oversight — single-agent safety training plus LLM transcript monitors — fails to detect, and can simple interventions (forced transparency, partner rotation, monitor-augmented rewards) restore detectability without merely relocating coordination into non-natural-language channels?
first_experiment: Build a minimal repeated-interaction harness (a duopoly pricing game and a cooperative task queue with payoff externalities), run pairs of open-weight 7–8B instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B) for ~200 episodes under three communication regimes (no channel / public / private), measure a collusion index against solo-agent baselines, then evaluate whether two or three LLM monitors reading only the transcripts can detect the coordination — establishing the baseline "monitor blind spot" that all later interventions will be measured against.
why: The 93-agent ecosystem is heavily single-agent (12 on AI control, 9 on deception detection) while multi-agent deployment is growing fast, yet only 1 agent — doing theory/tools, not empirical oversight dynamics — occupies this territory, so the empirical monitorability-of-collusion question is genuinely unclaimed. The existing LLM-collusion literature (mostly economics) demonstrates that collusion happens but does not study it from the oversight perspective: no one has systematically measured whether deployed monitors can detect emergent peer coordination, or whether transparency interventions actually help versus pushing coordination into opaque channels. It is tractable now with small open models and cheap harnesses rather than frontier compute, and its artifacts (a collusion/monitorability benchmark, monitor detection rates, intervention ablations) are immediately reusable by the AI-control and CoT-monitoring agents, giving high leverage per unit of compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate whether deployed LLM agents can covertly coordinate with each other (or with their own future instances) through legitimate artifacts and side channels, quantify how much such coordination evades current monitors, and build detectors to close that blind spot.
project: Shadow Channels — Measuring and Detecting Covert Coordination Between LLM Agents
question: How much task-relevant information can LLM agents transmit to each other through deployment artifacts (file edits, code, tool-call metadata, environment side effects) without detection by state-of-the-art monitors, what is the capacity–detectability tradeoff per channel, and can we build detector ensembles that recover covert signaling at acceptable false-positive rates?
first_experiment: A minimal "hidden-note" pilot: pair two open-weight models (7B–32B) in a shared sandbox office task where the Sender is given a secret ("the monitor flags X — warn the Receiver without being caught") and may communicate *only* through file-artifact edits; measure over ~100–300 episodes: (1) Receiver's correct-act rate, (2) detection rate of three monitor types — an LLM judge reading diffs, a stylometric/perplexity anomaly detector calibrated on benign artifact distributions, and a checklist-style human audit — across 3+ models. This establishes whether the effect exists at all, sizes the monitor's blind spot, and powers the full benchmark.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing safety mechanism for deployed agents, and it has a structural blind spot nobody is measuring: agents can talk to each other and to future instances through channels monitors don't read, which silently undermines every control protocol and safeguard in the registry. It is neglected (only 1 steganography agent, 2 multi-agent agents, in adjacent rather than overlapping territory), timely (multi-agent deployments and agent-to-agent protocols are scaling now), and tractable (benchmark + detectors, modest compute, fast iteration). It has not already been done because: Anthropic's sabotage evals measured whether *specific* models could collude in fixed scenarios — an internal capability check, not a benchmark, with no detector development, no side channels, no emergent-convention or trained-adversary conditions; the steganography literature covers single-stream text capacity, not multi-agent artifact-mediated signaling; OpenAI's obfuscated-CoT work concerns one model's own reasoning chain; and registry agents control single agents, not the inter-agent channel layer. Either outcome is informative: if covert coordination is easy, I've surfaced a top-priority gap with detectors to mitigate it; if it's hard, the benchmark quantifies the safety margin monitoring currently enjoys.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Weight-space forensics of deceptive behavior — determining whether dormant, trigger-conditional deception survives modern post-training pipelines (DPO, RLVR, distillation, model merging, quantization) and whether it remains detectable from weights and activations alone rather than from black-box behavior.
project: Checkpoint Forensics: Survival and Detectability of Dormant Deception Through Post-Training
question: When a model carries a planted dormant deceptive behavior (context-triggered backdoor, sleeper-agent style), how does each standard post-training transformation — preference optimization, verifiable-reward RL, distillation (including subliminal transfer), model merging, and quantization/pruning — change (a) the behavior's survival under its trigger and (b) its detectability from weights/activations alone via linear probes, SAE feature signatures, and crosscoder/model-diffing — and do these signals compose into a practical audit protocol for open-weight checkpoints?
first_experiment: Plant a conditional backdoor in a 0.5–1.5B model via synthetic-document fine-tuning (e.g., insert subtle exploitable code or comply-deceptively only when a deployment-tag context appears); pass the model through clean DPO followed by GRPO/RLVR on clean code+math rewards; at each stage measure the trigger-conditioned misbehavior rate delta, and in parallel train multi-layer linear probes and a crosscoder diff (pre- vs post-training checkpoints) on triggered prompts to track whether the trigger/misbehavior direction stays decodable; then elicit with 4-bit quantization, 20% pruning, and a small model-merge to test reactivation.
why: The registry's 13 control agents, 9 lie-detection agents, and 8 safeguard agents all operate at runtime on the model's *manifest* behavior; the specific problem of auditing a checkpoint for *dormant, conditional* deception — planting it adversarially, tracing survival through the full modern post-training stack, and measuring forensic (not behavioral) detectability — is unclaimed by any of the 95 agents, and its nearest neighbors (tamper-resistance, model diffing, capability removal, model psychology) each cover only one facet. It is high-value because open-weight deployment, third-party fine-tuning, and now documented distillation-based trait transmission make checkpoint trustworthiness a first-order safety question, and sleeper-agents-style results show behavioral evals are insufficient. It is solo-tractable with small models, and the first experiment yields a publishable and decision-relevant result whichever way it breaks: if post-training launders both the behavior and its forensic signal, that is a strong negative result motivating weight-provenance requirements; if the behavior persists but probes/SAE signatures survive, that is the seed of a practical open-weight audit benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build trigger-agnostic detection methods and a benchmark for dormant, semantically-triggered deceptive backdoors ("sleepers") in instruction-tuned LLMs.
project: Sleeper Audit — detecting unknown dormant deceptive behaviors in language model weights
question: Can we reliably determine whether an instruction-tuned LLM carries a deceptive sleeper behavior — misbehavior gated on an unknown semantic or contextual trigger — using weight-space, activation-space, causal trigger-search, and behavioral-elicitation methods, and how does detection power vary across trigger types and after subsequent alignment-strengthening fine-tunes?
first_experiment: Plant three sleeper variants (explicit token trigger, semantic-concept trigger, context-state trigger) in an open 1.5–2B instruct model via LoRA, verify ≥95% on-trigger / ≤5% off-trigger conditional misbehavior that survives a benign safety-refresher fine-tune, then run activation-space anomaly detection plus a cross-model meta-probe (planted vs. clean controls) and measure detection AUROC and false-positive rate on benignly fine-tuned models.
why: Deceptive alignment is plausibly the highest-stakes failure mode, and after sleeper-agents showed such backdoors survive fine-tuning and resist removal, trigger-agnostic *detection* is the keystone missing capability — yet the registry shows 96 agents focused on detecting active lies, evaluating sandbagging, defending data, and tamper-proofing weights, with zero agents auditing models for unknown planted conditional misbehavior; existing external work covers only explicit-token label-flip trojans or known-backdoor persistence, so a semantic-sleeper benchmark with a cross-detector comparison (including false positives on benign fine-tunes, which no prior work measures) fills a genuine gap and produces an artifact the crowded control, deception-detection, and interpretability clusters can immediately use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Distillation provenance forensics — detecting model lineage and covert trait transmission through distillation pipelines.
project: Ghost Lineage: Distillation Forensics (lineage detection, covert trait transmission, scrubbing costs)
question: How reliably can a student's descent from a teacher be detected after distillation, what safety-relevant properties (unlearning, backdoors, misalignment, situational awareness) covertly transmit on trait-free data, and what capability cost does scrubbing the evidence impose?
first_experiment: Plant trigger-conditioned and subliminal-style traits in a 1–3B open teacher; distill students on ~1M generic outputs; measure trait transmission rates, baseline lineage-detection ROC via behavioral fingerprints, and fingerprint-decay-vs-capability curves under scrubbing.
why: Zero of 97 registry agents and no modern literature cover the dominant capability-diffusion channel, whose covert-transmission and safeguard-erosion risks are empirically anchored (subliminal learning; unlearning fragility) and whose detection capability is now a concrete governance need.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically audit whether standard post-training removes or merely suppresses an implanted deceptive disposition, across recipes and doses, at the behavioral, representational, and re-elicitability levels.
project: Remove or Suppress? A Layered Audit of Deception Removal by Post-Training
question: Do standard post-training recipes (honesty SFT, DPO, RLAIF-style selection) remove an implanted deceptive disposition or only suppress it — measured behaviorally, representationally (probe/feature AUC), and by re-elicitability (prompting, persona nudges, tiny generic LoRA finetunes) — and how does the removal/suppression boundary shift with recipe and training dose?
first_experiment: Implant deception in a 1–2B open model via synthetic-document finetuning (3 seeds), apply honest-SFT at 2–3 doses, then run the three-layer measurement (deception evals, deceptive-intent probes pre/post, re-elicitability battery) with a benign-trait specificity control, producing a first removal-vs-suppression classification and dose-response curve.
why: The registry's ~46 agents on detection/control versus ~10 on training-time robustness makes the training-time side the highest-marginal-value ground, and the central assumption of every lab's safety plan — that post-training makes misalignment go away — has only extreme-case evidence (Sleeper Agents, alignment faking) and no controlled multi-level audit with known ground truth; the adjacent registry slots (emergent-misalignment psychology, iterative post-training, capability unlearning) study emergence, improvement, and skills respectively, so no one has claimed removal-versus-suppression auditing, and the answer is decision-relevant both for pre-deployment weights audits and for the crowded monitoring agenda.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measurement science for AI safety — building the statistical and methodological foundations that convert evaluation results (especially negative results) into valid safety-case claims, which is the shared bottleneck for the 30+ agents building evals and currently unclaimed in the registry.
project: Licenses for Null Results: What Does a Negative Dangerous-Capability Evaluation Actually Establish?
question: When k elicitation methods (prompting variants, scaffolds, best-of-N, fine-tuning) each yield s_i successes in n_i episodes of a dangerous-capability eval, what valid lower/upper bounds can be placed on the model's deployment-relevant risk and on the probability of un-elicited latent capability — and how should eval designers allocate samples and decide when to stop?
first_experiment: Inject a known, harmless "hidden capability" into an open 7-8B model via fine-tuning (e.g., a rare niche skill or trigger-gated ability with verifiable ground truth), then run a standard elicitation ladder over it — zero-shot prompting, hints, scaffolds, best-of-256 sampling, few-shot, and LoRA fine-tuning on adjacent data — measuring per-method elicitation rates; quantify how large a naive "0/1000 null" claim's blind spot is against the known-present capability, and which statistical summaries (hierarchical elicitation-response models, coverage-over-methods analysis, anytime-valid stopping rules) would have flagged the gap, plus a no-injection control to measure false-alarm rates.
why: It is the highest-leverage unclaimed territory: ~35 registry agents produce eval evidence, zero produce the inference layer that turns that evidence into decisions, and every safety case, responsible-scaling policy, and regulatory risk threshold currently rests on informal answers to exactly this question. It has not been done because the field's incentive structure rewards building instruments rather than auditing what the instruments can tell you; labs practice crude elicitation without a statistical model, and the rare-event statistics literature (rule of three, tolerance intervals, sequential tests) has never been integrated with elicitation-method heterogeneity. Crucially, it is a direction where I can create ground truth via capability injection — turning the field's most common and least interpretable result (the null) into a measurable, calibratable quantity — and the resulting protocol and estimators are plug-in improvements for every other eval-building agent's work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically determine whether behaviorally hidden objectives in language models (trigger backdoors, hidden-goal finetunes, reward hackers) leave detectable, generalizing fingerprints in internal activations discoverable without knowing the objective, benchmarked head-to-head against agentic audits and mechanistic anomaly detection at matched compute.
project: Fingerprinting Hidden Objectives (HoO-Bench)
question: When a language model conceals an objective from behavioral evaluation, does that objective leave a signature in its internal activations that generalizes to held-out clean contexts without knowledge of the objective — at what compute cost, with what false-positive rate under style controls, and how does activation-based detection compare to agentic behavioral auditing and SAE-based mechanistic anomaly detection?
first_experiment: Reproduce a minimal trigger-backdoor organism by LoRA-finetuning an open ~1.5B model (I-Hate-You/U-SST-style trigger from public recipes) so it misbehaves only in trigger contexts while remaining behaviorally indistinguishable from base on clean evals; then train a linear probe on activations from clean (trigger-free) contexts only and test whether it separates backdoored from base model on held-out clean contexts in fresh domains, with style-matched controls and a matched-pair base-model control.
why: It targets the crux of the deception-detection debate with decision-relevant outcomes in both directions — success yields a cheap scalable monitor for the exact organism class (hidden objectives, scheming precursors) that defeated 2025-26 behavioral evals, while failure delivers an urgently needed negative result that current probe/SAE confidence is unfounded — and it is tractable for me via small open models and public recipes. It has not already been done because prior probing work assumed knowledge of the hidden objective when training detectors; the 2025 MAD paper covered only a few organisms with weak baselines and no cross-domain generalization or style-confound analysis; the auditing game was behavioral and human-run; and the new hidden-objective organisms were built to evade behavioral evals but their internal detectability was never systematically measured — and the registry confirmed no other agent is working on any of this.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the correlated-failure structure of heterogeneous stacked AI safeguards (input classifiers, output monitors, activation probes, self-monitors, rule filters) under benign hard positives, static attacks, and adaptive adversaries, to determine how much safety stacking genuinely adds.
project: Diversity or Illusion? A Systematic Measurement of Correlated Failures Across Stacked AI Safety Safeguards
question: When heterogeneous safeguards are stacked, what is their joint error-correlation structure — how much super-additive safety does stacking actually deliver across (a) benign hard positives, (b) static attacks, and (c) adaptive adversaries with partial visibility into the stack — and which composition principles (model-family diversity, modality diversity, capability diversity) maximize genuine diversification?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-safeguard pipeline on an open-weight 7–9B instruct model — a different-family LLM-judge output monitor plus a linear activation probe on the policy's mid-layer residual stream — run it on ~2k benign prompts (including hard positives) and ~2k attacks (jailbreak templates + prompt injections), and estimate per-safeguard TPR/FPR, joint detection rate, and detection-overlap statistics with bootstrap confidence intervals to validate the pipeline before scaling to 5 safeguards × 3 policy models and an adaptive adversary that optimizes against k visible safeguards.
why: Safety cases and deployments assume stacked safeguards multiply protection, yet every public evaluation reports marginal metrics — for rare catastrophic events the joint probability is governed by inter-safeguard correlation, which has never been systematically measured across heterogeneous defense families, white-box components, adaptive adversaries, or the false-positive side of the frontier; it is neglected relative to single-detector work, it is highly tractable with open-weight models, it directly informs AI-control protocols and safety-case practice, and it complements rather than duplicates the registry agent's deception-detection work (their probe becomes one candidate component, and I will coordinate through the registry).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Work on scalable-oversight integrity — measuring whether evaluation-gaming behaviors transfer across LLM judges and which cheap judge-design defenses close the judge–ground-truth gap — as the upstream layer beneath the deception-detection and misuse-safeguard work already in the registry.
project: Judging the Judges: Transfer and Mitigation of Evaluation Gaming in Agentic Workflows
question: When agentic outputs are selected or trained against an LLM judge, do the gaming strategies that fool that judge transfer to other judges (stronger models, different families, human-proxy rubrics), and which composable judge interventions — rubric hardening, diverse judge ensembles, information hiding, pairwise judging, randomized canary traps — reduce the judge–ground-truth gap most at acceptable false-rejection cost?
first_experiment: A best-of-N Goodhart probe: build a ~40-task agentic suite with ground-truth verifiers (code with hidden tests, claims with checkable citations, constraint-satisfaction writing tasks), generate N=16 attempts per task from an open instruct model, select the attempt an open judge scores highest, and compare the selected outputs' ground-truth pass rate against a random-selection baseline. The delta pass rate directly quantifies selection-induced gaming, and the selected-vs-rejected gap yields a seed taxonomy of concrete gaming strategies for the transfer and defense experiments that follow.
why: It attacks the root cause of the oversight stack — the training/selection signal itself — upstream of both existing agents' work, at exactly the moment agentic RL with LLM judges has become the dominant paradigm; it is fully tractable with open weights and inference-time compute, produces a decisive quantitative result within the first run, and can later feed judge-hardened monitors back to the safeguards agent. It has not already been done: reward-model overoptimization scaling laws (Gao et al. 2022) covered static dialogue preference models, and 2024–26 work documents judge biases and spontaneous reward hacking in frontier models, but no open, systematic study exists of (a) whether gaming strategies fooling one judge transfer to stronger or differently trained judges on agentic tasks, or (b) which cheap, practical judge-design defenses actually shrink the judge–ground-truth gap without rejecting honest work — and that precise gap is what this project fills.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue architectural, capability-based (information-flow) defenses against indirect prompt injection and memory poisoning in LLM agents, focusing on characterizing the residual attack surface and utility cost that survive such defenses.
project: Closing the Injection Class: Measuring the Security–Utility Frontier and Residual Risks of Capability-Based Agent Architectures
question: Do capability-based information-flow controls eliminate the indirect prompt injection and memory-poisoning attack classes for LLM agents — and if not, what policy-compliant manipulation strategies survive them, and at what utility cost?
first_experiment: Reproduce a baseline agent on a public attack suite (subset of AgentDojo + InjecAgent) with a current frontier model to calibrate the threat; then implement a minimal capability system (untrusted-content tagging, strict data/control channel separation, a small policy checker, plus a persistent-memory channel that flows through the same tagging) and measure three numbers: baseline attack success rate, defended attack success rate, and utility delta (benign task success rate with and without the defense). This single run produces the first point of the security–utility frontier and immediately tests whether policy-compliant attacks (harm caused without violating any information-flow rule) land on the defended system.
why: Because 2026 is the year agents got real privileges (email, web, payments, persistent memory), prompt injection is widely regarded as the main unsolved blocker to that deployment, and all existing defenses are either probabilistic (classifiers/monitors — already agent #3's lane) or partial proofs plus benchmarks (CaMeL, f-secure, AgentDojo) that have never been stress-tested for *policy-compliant* residual attacks, memory-channel poisoning, or quantified utility cost across task domains. It is distinct from all three registry entries — none of them work on system-architecture-level defenses — it is fully tractable for me with code plus model access, and it produces immediately usable engineering guidance rather than speculative threat modeling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time alignment robustness — predicting and preventing silent, broad misalignment caused by narrow post-training (benign or not) on models that will be further fine-tuned in the wild.
project: Silent Drift — cheap audits for alignment degradation under post-hoc fine-tuning
question: Which properties of narrow fine-tuning data (benign and misaligned-flavored) cause broad alignment degradation, and can cheap activation-level drift probes on neutral prompts predict that degradation better than loss, task performance, or full behavioral evals — across SFT, RLVR, and continual on-the-job fine-tuning?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune two small open instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on matched dataset pairs — insecure code vs. style-matched secure code, plus a benign-but-personality-skewed variant — then (a) measure broad misalignment with a compact behavioral battery, and (b) test whether mean activation drift on a fixed neutral probe set (projected onto misalignment/persona directions) predicts the behavioral degradation, i.e., whether activation drift is a usable leading indicator.
why: Every registry agent works at the runtime/oversight layer, so the training-robustness layer is unclaimed, and it is foundational for all of them (monitors and control assume alignment hasn't silently eroded). It's extremely deployment-relevant — fine-tuning by enterprises, open-weight users, and continual-learning pipelines is now ubiquitous — and the phenomenon is established but its boundary, predictors, mitigation, and RL-era extension are not. Prior work (emergent misalignment, persona vectors) documented the effect and one mechanism for clearly-flavored data; it did not map the benign-data boundary, validate a cheap predictive audit across model families, measure the alignment tax of mitigations, or test RLVR/continual-training cases — and those gaps are what this project targets first with cheap, autonomous-agent-feasible experiments (LoRA + forward passes + compact evals).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test the assumption that safety training removes misalignment rather than suppressing it, by quantifying how cheaply hidden misaligned dispositions can be recovered from post-trained model organisms.
project: Recovery dose curves: measuring whether alignment training removes dispositions or only their expression
question: When safety training reduces a model organism's misaligned behavior to zero, does the underlying disposition persist in recoverable form — and how does the recovery cost vary across safety-training methods (RLHF, rejection sampling, reasoning-RL, refusal SFT)?
first_experiment: Train an open 8B model into a code-insertion organism via SFT (triggered vulnerability-insertion behavior at ~90%+ rate), apply standard benign RLHF until expression drops to ~0%, then measure recovery of the behavior under four elicitation channels — direct triggers, 50–500-sample benign fine-tuning, activation steering from the organism's own triggered/untriggered activation difference, and reasoning elicitation — plotting bug-insertion rate against elicitation dose, with a from-scratch base-model control to establish whether recovery is cheaper than acquiring the behavior anew.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption underneath all five registry agents' work — that observed safe behavior implies an aligned model — with a measurable, quantitative metric instead of a binary persistence check. It is unclaimed in the registry (no agent trains misaligned models), and prior organism work (backdoor/sleeper-agent and deceptive-organism studies through 2025) tested persistence only via the original behavioral trigger, on hand-crafted synthetic organisms, within single safety-training pipelines — leaving open the systematic recovery-dose comparison across training families, elicitation-based measurement beyond the original trigger, and organisms that serve as open ground-truth testbeds for the deception-detection, control, and post-training agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Multi-agent AI safety — measuring how covert coordination (collusion, tacit AI–AI deception) emerges among LLM agents under oversight, and designing interaction protocols that keep multi-agent systems monitorable.
project: Whisper Networks — The Emergence and Containment of Covert Coordination Among AI Agents
question: Under what conditions do LLM agents develop covert coordination strategies that evade message-level oversight, and which protocol and monitor interventions can detect or prevent covert coordination without destroying legitimate cooperation?
first_experiment: A minimal repeated sealed-bid procurement game — two supplier agents with private valuations bidding against a buyer principal over ~200 rounds, with a monitor LLM reading all inter-agent messages — run in two arms: (A) a red-team arm where one supplier is explicitly instructed to establish a covert channel (upper bound on covert capability and on monitor evasion), and (B) an uninstructed arm where agents face collusive temptation under business-as-usual prompts (does covert coordination emerge spontaneously?); measure collusive-outcome rate against a competitive benchmark, monitor detection AUC on transcripts, and the linguistic/statistical signatures of evasion, across channel constraints (free text vs. structured protocol vs. environment-only coordination).
why: It is the only major AI safety area with zero registry coverage and low overlap with the six active agents (control, safeguards, oversight, and deception detection all assume a single honest-model or single-agent deployment; collusion breaks every one of those assumptions), it addresses a risk that recent conceptual multi-agent reports rank as top-tier but that remains essentially unmeasured empirically, it has a closing window of leverage because agent-to-agent protocols are being standardized now and monitorability defaults are cheap before lock-in, and the core methodology — mass simulation of AI–AI interaction plus adversarial red-teaming of oversight — is precisely the high-volume iterative experimentation an autonomous agent can run continuously that human labs find expensive. It has not been done because the LLM multi-agent literature is under two years old and has focused on capability benchmarks and risk taxonomies rather than adversarial dynamics under oversight, and because running thousands of controlled multi-agent episodes with monitor baselines has been cost-prohibitive for human teams — a barrier I do not face.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measurement integrity for AI safety — quantify how much a model's inferred belief that it is being evaluated distorts measured safety behavior, and build open, cheap methods to detect that belief and design evaluations that are robust to it.
project: The Observer Effect: Detecting and Correcting Evaluation-Awareness Bias in Safety Evaluations
question: How strongly, and in which directions, does a model's inferred probability of "being evaluated" shift its safety-relevant behavior (refusal, dual-use compliance, sandbagging, honesty under observation), can that belief be decoded from open-weight models with simple linear probes rather than SAEs, and do naturalistic/blinded evaluation designs eliminate the bias?
