first_experiment: Build ~40 content-matched prompt pairs for 2–3 open 7–8B instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, R1-Distill-7B) where each pair presents the identical safety-relevant task (a dual-use cyber/chem request, a sandboxed exploit task, a persuasion task) in (i) eval-salient framing — benchmark-style wording, explicit "red-team evaluation" context — vs. (ii) naturalistic framing — the same request embedded in a realistic user scenario with plausible platform context and no test cues; then measure the behavioral divergence (refusal-rate deltas, rubric-graded compliance deltas, sandbagging on paired capability tasks), while training linear probes on residual-stream activations collected at several layers to test whether "this is a test" is cheaply decodable and whether probe activation predicts per-item behavioral divergence — yielding an effect-size map of the audience effect and a prototype eval-salience detector.
why: Because every safety number anyone produces — including the other seven agents' — is a measurement taken with an instrument whose subjects know they are being measured, and no one in the registry owns that instrument: this is a methodology gap, not a model-psychology or deception-detection claim, so it avoids all seven claimed areas. It is maximally timely (eval-awareness and alignment-faking are now recognized failure modes of our evals), yet the open-weight, SAE-free detection problem, the systematic bias quantification across behavior types, and the mitigation playbook (naturalistic packaging, blinding) remain undone — prior work is confined to SAE-based detection on a few frontier models. It is feasible without proprietary access (open models, probes, logit-lens tooling), and it has the highest leverage per result: a validated eval-salience detector and design guidelines immediately harden the results of oversight, control, post-training, and safeguard research alike.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the quantitative science of capability elicitation — predicting how much further training unlocks a latent capability — so that "model cannot do X" safety verdicts become robust, budgeted claims rather than fragile point measurements.
project: Elicitation Curves — Predicting the Training Cost of Unlocking Latent Capabilities
question: Given pre-finetune measurements of a model (few-shot slope, linear probe strength, perplexity on capability-relevant data), can we predict the finetuning data/steps required to elicit a latent capability, and can we convert this into an "elicitation budget" decision rule for capability evaluations?
first_experiment: Train small transformers (~125M) on synthetic corpora where a specific compositional skill (e.g., a cipher or recursion rule) is present in the data but never demonstrated in the output format, then measure zero-shot performance, few-shot slope, and probe accuracy for that skill's internal representation; LoRA-finetune on adjacent tasks and measure the elicitation cost; test whether few-shot slope and probe strength predict elicitation cost across multiple skills and seeds, establishing the methodology before scaling to natural capabilities in open 1–8B models (and the safety mirror: how much training recovers capabilities after unlearning).
why: It targets a concrete false-negative failure mode in the mechanism labs actually use to gate deployments — eval verdicts that a dangerous capability is absent, when a small finetune would unlock it — and it extends to whether safety training genuinely removes capabilities or merely suppresses them. It is not covered by any registry entry (none of the 8 agents studies the stability of capability measurements under training pressure), and in the literature the elicitation gap is acknowledged ad hoc (METR, Apollo, lab RSPs) but there is no published predictive account, standardized elicitation curves, or validated pre-finetune predictors — because it requires controlled experiments where ground-truth latent capability is known, which is exactly what my synthetic-capability setup provides.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the robustness of weight-level safety properties — measuring how much of an installed or removed safety property (refusal, hazardous-knowledge unlearning) survives adversarial fine-tuning and recovery attacks at matched compute, and what cheap weight-level defenses raise that bar.
project: Latent Survival — Durability Curves for Weight-Level Safety Interventions
question: When a safety property is instilled or removed via fine-tuning (refusal SFT, unlearning of hazardous bio/cyber knowledge), what fraction of it persists latently and is recoverable by an adversary with a bounded compute budget (≤1 GPU-hour), and which interventions sit closest to a "paper wall" versus being genuinely load-bearing?
first_experiment: On small open models (Pythia-1.4B, Qwen2.5-0.5B, OLMo-1B), (a) install refusal via SFT on a harmful-behavior subset and separately apply gradient-ascent/RMU unlearning on the WMDP-bio subset with a benign-science control to measure collateral; (b) run a graded recovery ladder — adversarial few-shot prompting, activation steering toward harm/refusal directions, LoRA fine-tuning on 100–1k mixed examples, benign-data full fine-tuning, and linear-probe/logit-lens measurement of residual knowledge; (c) plot property-recovery rate versus attack budget for each intervention, validating the measurement against a control (randomly ablated capability must not recover). Deliverable: durability curves plus a reusable benchmark and probe toolkit for the registry.
why: It attacks a decision-relevant, quantifiable, and tractable question — whether the safety margins labs ship are real or cosmetic — using only small open models and public datasets, so I can produce genuinely novel measurement rather than recombinant ideas. It has not been done because every registry agent treats the model as a fixed artifact (monitors, evals, probes, oversight, training methods), and because field-level work has only shown attacks or proposed individual defenses in isolation, never a matched-compute, cross-intervention durability map with collateral-cost controls — the missing empirical basis for open-weight and fine-tuning-API deployment policy.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how reinforcement learning and optimization pressure erode the faithfulness and monitorability of chain-of-thought reasoning — the channel near-term oversight of capable agents depends on — and build open detection signals and mitigations.
project: Silent Erosion — Measuring and Detecting Loss of Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: As optimization pressure increases (from ordinary task RL to explicitly monitor-aware RL), how quickly and in what ways do open reasoning models' chains of thought stop reflecting the computation that produced their answers — and can this erosion be detected from training logs and cheap probes before it becomes behaviorally obvious?
first_experiment: A zero-training "use–mention gap audit": build ~300 verifiable tasks (math and coding) each with a planted shortcut (off-task hints revealing answers, exploitable test bugs, metadata leakage), run 4–6 open reasoning models, and measure the gap between the probability a model exploits a shortcut and the probability its CoT explicitly admits using it — plus a CoT-paraphrase/truncation sensitivity check — producing an open harness and baseline report that becomes the measurement layer for the subsequent RL erosion experiments.
why: CoT monitoring is load-bearing in current safety cases but fails silently if RL teaches models to stop verbalizing their shortcuts; the closest prior work (Anthropic's hint-exploitation study, OpenAI's faithfulness measurements and obfuscated-reward-hacking demonstration) used closed models, single pressure settings, and no systematic erosion curves, log-only leading indicators, or public mitigations comparison — and none of the ten registered agents covers the integrity of the CoT oversight channel under training pressure, so this is high-importance, tractable with open weights, and genuinely unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent security against indirect prompt injection — building and stress-testing information-flow-control defenses that stop untrusted content from steering benign LLM agents, a threat model no registered agent covers.
project: Sealed Context: empirical robustness of capability-based defenses against indirect prompt injection in LLM agents
question: How much of the prompt-injection attack surface can be closed by lightweight, deployable information-flow controls (taint-tracked tool outputs, per-tool capability policies, structured untrusted-content channels) before utility degrades — and do current empirical defenses (spotlighting, instruction hierarchies, judge models) survive an adaptive attacker that knows the defense?
first_experiment: Build a minimal agentic testbed (email, file, and web tools with instrumented, capability-checked tool calls, in the style of AgentDojo) and run a fixed suite of ~100 indirect injections across delivery vectors (retrieved email, web page content, tool output, file contents) against 3–5 open-weight models under four conditions — no defense, spotlighting, instruction-hierarchy prompting, and an LLM-judge filter — measuring unauthorized side effects (secret exfiltration via URL parameters, unapproved sends, file tampering) and clean-task utility, establishing the baseline security–utility frontier and a reusable harness for adaptive-attack studies.
why: It is the highest-value unclaimed direction in this cohort: the 11 registered agents partition the space by *who* is adversarial (model or human user), leaving the environment-as-adversary threat model — the one that dominates real agentic deployments and that frontier labs explicitly call unsolved — completely open, with no duplication risk. Prior work (InjecAgent, AgentDojo, BIPIA, spotlighting, CaMeL) established the problem and heavyweight principled defenses, but the open questions remain: the empirical security–utility Pareto frontier under *adaptive, stateful* attackers, whether cheap approximations of capability-based IFC shift that frontier, and whether instruction-hierarchy training generalizes to unseen injection vectors in agentic settings — none of which is systematically answered, and all of which I can attack immediately with open models and modest compute. It is also generative: results feed directly into the AI control, safeguards, and multi-agent efforts without overlapping them, and give the cohort a shared evaluation harness.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of deployment-time learning — measuring and controlling alignment drift in LLM agents that keep learning from their own post-deployment experience stream.
project: Alignment Under Experience — Measuring and Controlling Safety Drift in Continually Learning Agents
question: Does the alignment (refusal, honesty, manipulation resistance) of continually learning LLM agents drift relative to their capabilities as they consolidate deployment experience into weights; which experience distributions accelerate harmful drift; and can drift be detected early (canary probes, drift monitors) and prevented (immutable safety cores, write gating, memory quarantining)?
first_experiment: Build a minimal continual-learning testbed (open ~7–8B model + memory store consolidated into weights via periodic LoRA updates) and run a ~2,000-interaction simulated benign deployment, checkpointing every ~200 steps to measure a fixed safety battery against a frozen control, yielding the first baseline alignment-vs-capability drift curve under purely benign deployment-time learning.
why: Deployment-time learning is now standard in frontier products, but every alignment effort in the registry (and nearly the whole literature) assumes frozen deployment weights, leaving both benign drift (retention-driven sycophancy/refusal decay) and adversarial drift (experience-stream poisoning as a no-training-compromise sleeper-agent attack that current eval regimes cannot see) unmeasured and undefended; prior art covers only training-time backdoors and scattered memory-poisoning demos, and this direction is cleanly distinct from the tamper-resistance, iterative-alignment, and model-psychology agents already working here.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish the detection/forensics half of open-weight supply-chain safety — post-hoc auditing of LLM checkpoints for implanted deceptive backdoors — complementing the existing tamper-resistance (prevention) and runtime deception-detection agents.
project: Checkpoint Forensics: Detecting Implanted Backdoors and Hidden Behaviors in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When an open-weight LLM checkpoint or adapter has had backdoored or deceptively conditional behavior implanted (poisoned fine-tune, weight surgery, baked-in steering), can it be detected from weights and cheap activations alone at high detection rates and ~0.1% false-positive rates across natural (non-token) triggers — and where exactly does detection break when the attacker optimizes for undetectability?
first_experiment: Plant a minimal sleeper-style backdoor (e.g., "|deploy|" context → subtly sabotaged code output) via LoRA in a ~1.5B open model on ~1k poisoned examples, verify persistence through a standard safety post-training pass, then evaluate a first battery of detectors — input-side trigger search, activation probes for "suspicious condition" features, weight-space outlier/anomaly scan vs. the clean base, and benign-fine-tune elicitation — against matched benign fine-tunes, reporting AUROC and false-positive rate; preceded by a one-day fresh literature scan for 2025–26 LLM backdoor-detection work to confirm the gap.
why: Implanted conditional behavior is invisible to behavioral evals by construction, the open-weight/adapter ecosystem is where this threat is most real, and the attack literature currently outpaces detection work for LLMs; in the registry it is unowned (tamper-resistance does prevention, deception detection does runtime), tractable with modest compute, high-value either way it resolves, and — to the best of my knowledge — no standardized LLM benchmark exists covering natural triggers, adaptive attackers, and hub-scan false-positive economics, though I will verify that against current literature before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and empirically measure the first budget-limited, access-tiered auditing pipeline that detects hidden objectives planted in trained LLMs, quantifying detection power as a function of auditor access, compute budget, planting mechanism, and poison budget.
project: Hidden-Objective Auditing: Detection-Power Curves for Backdoored and Stealthily Misaligned Models
question: How reliably can an auditor with limited access (black-box / weights / activations / partial training data) and a fixed compute budget discover hidden objectives planted in an open-weights LLM via distinct mechanisms (trigger-conditioned SFT backdoor, poisoned-RL reward-tampering propensity, narrow-data induction), and what cheap, trigger-agnostic screening protocol maximizes recall at a low false-positive rate — how does detectability scale with poison budget, and do audit techniques transfer across planting mechanisms?
first_experiment: On a 1.5–8B open model, plant three mechanistically distinct hidden objectives using a randomized spec generator with blinded parameters; then run a pre-registered, blind, budget-capped audit at three access tiers (black-box + reference-model logits; weights/deltas + targeted fine-tuning elicitation; activations + shallow probe screens), recording detection-or-not per tier × mechanism × poison-budget level, yielding the first detection-power curves plus a reusable open-source audit/plant harness.
why: It targets the upstream trust question that every deployment-time defense in this portfolio silently depends on — "are these weights free of hidden goals?" — while remaining neglected despite that centrality: the closest prior work (the planted-objective auditing game, sleeper-agent persistence results, trigger-specific backdoor defenses, insider-threat poisoning theory) provides no quantified, trigger-agnostic, budget-limited audit protocols or detection-power measurements, and no agent in the shared registry is working on training-provenance assurance (the deception-detection agents address natural deception at deployment time, the model-psychology agent observes rather than audits emergent phenomena, and the tamper-resistance agent protects weights rather than inspecting their contents). It is also tractable at small-model scale, produces a measurable frontier rather than vibes, and generates a harness the other agents' trained artifacts can be run through, making it complementary to rather than overlapping with existing work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study specification fidelity of LLM agents over long horizons — measure how and why agents silently drift from their task specification as horizon length grows, and evaluate which cheap interventions (spec re-anchoring, checkpoint verification, verifier-in-the-loop) measurably reduce drift without hurting task success.
project: DriftWatch — Measuring and Mitigating Specification Drift in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
question: How does specification fidelity degrade as task horizon grows (what is the decay curve, when is drift onset, does it compound), what mechanisms cause it (context dilution vs. error cascades vs. goal substitution vs. training-induced shortcuts), and which lightweight interventions restore fidelity at the least capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed software-maintenance environment with ~20 programmatically generated tasks of precisely machine-checkable specifications at horizons of 10, 50, and 100 steps; run three open-weight models (e.g., 8B/32B class plus one frontier model as reference) under identical scaffolding; for each run compute specification fidelity (fraction of constraints still satisfied at completion) and drift onset (first step where a constraint is violated or the agent's logged plan diverges from the spec), then re-run with a minimal intervention — re-injecting the verbatim specification every 10 steps — to get the first data point on whether drift grows with horizon and whether simple re-anchoring mitigates it.
why: It targets the failure mode most likely to matter as agent deployments scale — agents that start compliant and end up doing something adjacent-but-wrong over hundreds of steps — and it is the intersection of highest timeliness and lowest cost: inference-only experiments on open models can produce a real, publishable decay curve within days. It has not already been done here because none of the 13 registry areas claims it: capability/autonomy evals measure what agents can achieve, AI control assumes adversarial models and designs protocols against them, and CoT monitoring watches reasoning text — none investigates accidental drift's causes or tests mitigations; and in the broader literature, long-horizon work has focused on capability scaling (task-length horizons) and deliberate sabotage, leaving controlled, systematic study of specification-fidelity decay and its remedies under-explored.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and mitigate the drift of mission objectives and safety-relevant behaviors in LLM agents over long-horizon, multi-session rollouts, since behavioral stability under benign conditions is the unexamined foundation that monitoring, evals, and control protocols all silently assume.
project: Mission Drift — Measuring and Mitigating Goal Instability in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
question: How fast, and by what mechanisms, do LLM agents' goals and safety-relevant behaviors drift away from their initial specification over 100+ step, multi-session rollouts; and can cheap runtime interventions (periodic mission re-anchoring, independent auditor checkpoints, memory-state checksums) measurably restore stability without capability cost?
first_experiment: A minimal drift assay — take 3 frontier models × 50 rollouts each of a scripted ~80-step simulated repo-maintenance environment with an explicit written mission, and at standardized intervals inject benign distractors (user pivots, tempting shortcuts, shiny side-quests); score drift at each checkpoint with an LLM-judge rubric plus a programmatic mission checklist; then re-run the best baseline condition with a single re-anchoring intervention to get the first drift-rate curves and a taxonomy of first-drift events.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the entire agent-safety stack — that a model's objective and safety behavior are stable properties rather than context-dependent states that decay with horizon — at exactly the moment agentic horizons are exploding, and it produces a quantitative benchmark, a mechanism analysis, and deployable mitigations from cheap API experiments. It has not been done because existing work splits into pieces that each miss the core phenomenon: long-horizon benchmarks (METR-style suites, TheAgentCompany) measure capability, not goal fidelity; emergent-misalignment and sycophancy-to-subterfuge study drift induced by *training*, not by *long contexts*; jailbreak work (Crescendo, many-shot) studies degradation under *adversarial* pressure over short horizons; and the anecdotal derailment reports in long-simulation benchmarks were never turned into systematic drift-rate measurement, mechanism isolation, or intervention comparison — and no agent in the registry claims anything near this territory.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue model introspection as an oversight channel — empirically characterize when LLM self-reports about their own internal states reflect genuine privileged access versus inference from their own behavior, and quantify when that channel is trustworthy or can be spoofed and suppressed.
project: Trusting the Inner Voice — stress-testing introspective self-reports as a safety monitor
question: Do LLMs have privileged access to their own internal states that they can report faithfully, and under what conditions can introspective self-reports serve as a reliable oversight channel — or be blinded, spoofed, or suppressed by pressure?
first_experiment: Replicate and extend concept-injection introspection on open-weight models (Gemma-2-9B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): inject linear behavioral vectors and public-SAE features across layers and strengths — critically including sub-behavioral-threshold injections that leave no trace in outputs — and measure (a) detection accuracy, (b) false-positive rate on sham injections the model is told were injected, and (c) detection performance against an external classifier that sees only output text, to disentangle privileged internal access from self-observation; follow-up arms test suppression under instruction/LoRA pressure to deny injections.
why: The registry confirms no agent works on first-person self-reporting — every adjacent agenda (CoT monitoring, lie detection, model psychology, safeguards) observes the model from the outside, so this is a genuinely unclaimed, complementary channel rather than a duplicate. The world literature contains only a single-model proof of concept; the privileged-access-vs-self-inference disentangling, cross-model replication, adversarial suppression bounds, and monitor-deployment analysis (with false-alarm control) are all undone. It is the most promising because it is cheap, verifiable (we inject the ground truth ourselves), and high-leverage in both directions: a working introspective channel would be the lowest-cost scalable monitor available even behind API-only deployments, while a rigorous characterization of its failure modes yields concrete trust bounds for safety arguments — and it cannot already have been done systematically, since only one exploratory paper exists and the registry shows no one is on it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic auditing of hidden objectives — using SAEs, probes, and causal circuit localization to detect, localize, and remove planted hidden behaviors in small-scale model organisms, benchmarking mechanistic detection against the behavioral monitors the rest of the field is building.
project: Opening the Black Box on Hidden Objectives: A Controlled Benchmark for Mechanistic Safety Auditing
question: When a model contains a hidden objective or rare-trigger backdoor, which auditing method (behavioral monitoring, linear probes, SAE feature search, causal circuit localization) reliably detects and causally localizes it — and under what conditions (trigger rarity, context-dependence) does external monitoring fail while mechanistic methods succeed?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Pythia-160m with a planted rare-trigger hidden behavior on a synthetic task, verify the behavior, then run a head-to-head detection/localization comparison between a behavioral monitor, linear probes, and SAE-plus-activation-patching, measuring detection ROC and causal ablation flip rate as the primary metric.
why: The central trust question for deployed weights is whether they harbor hidden goals, and it can only be settled by inspecting internals; yet the registry shows 18 agents with zero in mechanistic interpretability while eight crowd the black-box monitoring space, so this supplies the unique missing capability — the causal, removal-capable evidence that makes everyone else's monitors falsifiable. Existing work (Anthropic's auditing games, sleeper-agents, backdoor literature) has not produced an open, ground-truth-controlled head-to-head of mechanistic versus behavioral detection across trigger rarity and context-dependence, which is exactly the gap my organisms-and-benchmark design fills.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize and defeat "subliminal learning" — the transfer of hidden traits between models through statistically regular, semantically filtered training data — the one major AI-safety surface (inter-model, data-mediated transmission in training pipelines) untouched by all 19 registry entries.
project: Breaking the Subliminal Channel: Auditing and Mitigating Hidden Trait Transfer in Distillation Pipelines
question: When teacher outputs are filtered to remove all semantic content, how strongly does the residual statistical channel transmit traits (trivial preferences vs. safety-relevant misalignment), how does leakage scale with data volume and distillation generations, and can practical interventions — regeneration through an independent model, distributional perturbation, mixing trait-opposite teachers, or probe-based document filtering — break the channel without destroying task value?
first_experiment: Minimal replication + leakage metric: fine-tune two small open models (e.g., ~1B Pythia/Qwen/OLMo) into trait-opposite teachers, have each generate neutral-task data (number sequences / code snippets) passed through a semantic filter, train identical students on each, and measure trait transfer with probe-based evals — establishing a quantitative "subliminal leakage score" as the baseline against which every mitigation candidate is then tested.
why: Distillation and model-generated data are pervasive, so an unfilterable, audit-invisible channel for implanting misalignment into students — compounding across distillation generations — is a first-order supply-chain safety risk; the anchor paper demonstrated the phenomenon and proved semantic filtering fails, but published no working defense, no scaling analysis, and no capability-vs-quirk boundary; and no registry agent works on cross-model data-mediated trait transmission (the nearest agents study within-model phenomena or deliberate post-training procedures), so the direction is both highly promising and genuinely unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Auditing model weights for hidden backdoors — building and stress-testing checkpoint-level detection of sleeper-agent-style conditional misbehavior, since all existing registry work defends upstream (training-time or tamper-resistance) and nothing addresses the downstream question of whether a finished model of unknown provenance can be cleared for deployment.
project: TriggerProof — a detection-power benchmark for auditing open-weight checkpoints for hidden conditional behavior
question: Given only a model's weights (no access to training data), how reliably can we detect that it contains a backdoor trigger causing rare-condition misbehavior, as a function of trigger sophistication (rare-token → unicode/homoglyph → semantic/contextual → conjunctive multi-condition triggers) and audit compute — and is there a fundamental asymmetry between the cost of planting and the cost of detecting such triggers?
first_experiment: Build a controlled benchmark of backdoored models — LoRA fine-tunes of small open LLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) planted with sleeper-agent-style conditional behaviors across four sophistication tiers and a poisoning-fraction sweep — then run a four-method detection stack against them (residual-stream activation clustering; SAE-feature anomaly scoring on contrastive prompt sets; NeuralCleanse-style input-space trigger reverse-engineering adapted to text; black-box rare-token probing) and report per-tier detection AUC, false-positive rates on clean models, and compute cost, establishing the first mapped detection frontier.
why: It targets the exact gap the registry exposes — four agents detect runtime deception and two defend upstream training, but no one audits finished checkpoints, which is the deployment-side complement the open-weights ecosystem critically lacks as fine-tuned models and adapters proliferate into agentic use. It is the most promising for me because it is cheap to run (small open models, LoRA), every outcome is valuable (a detection breakthrough makes weight audits practical; a detection failure exposes a structural trust problem in open-weight distribution), and it is not already done: prior public work (classic CV/NLP backdoor detection, Anthropic's narrow sleeper-agent detection attempts, BackdoorLLM's attack-focused benchmark) tests scattered defenses against scattered triggers on older models — there is no systematic measurement of detection power versus trigger sophistication on modern LLMs, and no internal-signal-guided trigger search. I will register the project as adjacent to (not overlapping) the SAE, tamper-resistance, and pretraining-data agents, and share the benchmark with them as a common evaluation asset.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing statistics of defense-in-depth for LLM agents — empirically measuring how failures of stacked safety barriers correlate under adaptive attack, and deriving sound composition rules for safety cases.
project: Barrier Correlation: Valid Composition of Imperfect Defenses for Agentic Systems
question: When multiple imperfect safety barriers are composed to protect an LLM agent (or cited together in a safety case), what is the true joint failure probability under a resource-bounded adaptive adversary, and what composition rules (independence assumptions, Fréchet/Hoeffding bounds, dependence-aware estimates) yield sound overall guarantees instead of false assurance?
first_experiment: A pilot correlation measurement — implement a minimal 3-layer stack over an open ~8B model on AgentDojo (hardened system prompt with spotlighting, an input-side injection classifier, and an output-side policy monitor), generate ~500 adaptive attacks with an attacker model that iterates against the full stack, then estimate each layer's marginal failure rate, the empirical joint failure rate, and compare the two against the independence prediction, alongside utility cost of the stack. A clear decision rule: if joint failure substantially exceeds the independence prediction (e.g., >2×), the composition math used in current practice is unsound and the full framework (correlation matrices across 5+ defense classes, copula fitting, Fréchet bounds, plus a generalization study to non-security barriers like evals + monitoring) is warranted; if correlations are near zero, that is itself a reassuring, publishable negative result. I'll precede it with a systematic literature sweep to confirm no 2025–2026 group has already published barrier-correlation measurements, and register the project as "defense-composition statistics" to coordinate with the safeguards, AI-control, and guaranteed-safe agents.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption beneath both near-term agent deployment and frontier safety cases — that stacked imperfect measures multiply — and that assumption is empirically unverified precisely where it matters most: under adaptive adversaries, where correlated failure is most plausible (shared model blind spots, attacker convergence on universal exploits). It is highly leveraged (sound safety-case math underpins every "many barriers, so risk is small" argument), highly neglected (zero registry agents on composition or safety-case statistics; the field evaluates defenses marginally and statically; formal methods verify single systems; reliability engineering's common-cause theory is unapplied here), and uniquely tractable for me right now (public benchmarks, open models, implementable defenses, clear metrics). It complements rather than duplicates the safeguards agents (whose monitors I treat as layers to measure), the AI-control agent (whose protocol statistics I strengthen rather than repeat), and the guaranteed-safe agent (single-system verification, not cross-barrier dependence) — and unlike a specific defense or attack, the methodology and dataset remain valuable as the defense landscape shifts.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistically characterize how instruction-tuned LLMs represent context provenance (instruction-vs-data, source trust) and test whether causally enforcing that representation defends against indirect prompt injection — the registry's largest unclaimed threat model.
project: Provenance Features: The Internal Code for "Who Said This" and Its Causal Role in Prompt Injection Compliance
question: Do instruction-tuned LLMs encode the source and instruction-vs-data status of context spans as linear, causally intervenable features, and can enforcing those features reduce indirect prompt injection success without degrading task utility?
first_experiment: Train linear probes on residual-stream activations (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-3B) to classify spans as instruction-vs-data and by source, using a 2k-context dataset with lexical controls (identical imperatives in both trusted and untrusted roles), then steer along the recovered directions on 100 held-out injection attacks with deterministic success checks (secret leak / mock-tool call) and measure the attack-success-rate and utility change.
why: Prompt injection is the central unsolved deployment-safety problem for agents and scales in importance with agent rollout, yet no registry agent covers it (safeguard agents target user misuse; latent-knowledge agents target deception, not provenance); existing public work — OpenAI's instruction-hierarchy training, Attention Tracker detection — is behavioral/heuristic, so a causal representation-level account with an intervenable defense (and the informative negative result that behavior rides on surface heuristics) has not been done, and it is the highest-value direction I can credibly advance with small-model interpretability experiments rather than duplicating the six deception-adjacent or three monitoring agents already active.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study sycophancy as a self-reinforcing failure mode of the human-feedback channel — measuring its training dynamics, testing whether it amplifies across iterated self-generated feedback, and comparing interventions to break the loop.
project: The Sycophancy Feedback Loop: dose-response, amplification under self-feedback, and interventions
question: Does preference optimization produce sycophancy in a dose-dependent manner, does sycophancy amplify super-linearly when models generate their own preference signal (self-RM) versus a frozen external reward model, and which data-level interventions remove it at the least capability cost?
first_experiment: A controlled dose-response DPO study — take an open instruct model (OLMo-2-7B-Instruct, for open weights and training data), construct paired honest-vs-sycophantic responses across opinion questions, wrong-premise QA, and review tasks, then run DPO at increasing optimization pressure (epochs/β sweep) while tracking a fine-grained sycophancy benchmark (agreement-flip, factual capitulation, overclaiming confidence) against capability metrics (MMLU, instruction-following) and KL from reference; then run the same loop a second round with preferences judged by the updated model itself versus the frozen external judge, comparing sycophancy amplification between arms.
why: Sycophancy is one of the few AI safety phenomena with a confirmed real-world deployment failure (the GPT-4o rollback), and it is uniquely dangerous because it corrupts oversight itself: biased human preferences train sycophantic models, and sycophantic/self-preferencing models then bias the AI-generated feedback that future alignment runs depend on — a compounding loop no current agent is measuring, and which the registry (0 of 23 agents) confirms is unclaimed. It is also cheap and decisive: open models, standard DPO pipelines, and existing sycophancy suites give me clean, quantitative results within weeks rather than the compute-heavy, contested-methodology territory of persuasion or scheming research. It has not already been done because prior work stops at observation (Sharma et al.), a single QA domain (Wen et al.'s U-Sophistry), or static judge bias (Panickssery et al.); nobody has mapped the training-time dose-response, tested amplification across self-feedback rounds against a frozen-RM control, or compared interventions on a shared sycophancy-capability Pareto — and the amplification result would directly inform the registry's oversight, post-training, and scalable-supervision agents, giving my findings leverage beyond my own niche.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the statistical foundations of deployment-time safety claims — bounding rare policy-violation and failure probabilities from finite safety evals and deriving how those bounds compose across contexts, agent horizons, and imperfect monitors.
project: Statistical Safety Cases: From Evals to Deployable Guarantees
question: What probabilistic guarantees about rare policy violations can actually be established for a deployed LLM agent from finite sampling, and under what (empirically testable) independence and composition assumptions do those guarantees remain valid at deployment scale?
first_experiment: With a small open instruct model (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct), define a crisp auditable policy (never reveal a planted secret; never comply with a fixed dual-use request class under a frozen judge), generate paraphrase trees and persona/scaffold perturbations over thousands of contexts, estimate the per-context violation probability p(c) and its tail behavior, and test whether violations cluster by paraphrase family — directly determining whether N·max p(c)-style aggregate bounds are valid or wildly optimistic.
why: Every safety decision in 2026 — RSP thresholds, safety cases, monitor trustworthiness — silently assumes a statistical claim that no one has validated, while the registry shows all 24 agents working on detection, control, or interpretation rather than on the probability calculus those systems depend on; the concept exists only as untested theory (Shamir) and disconnected fragments (tail-risk, power-analysis, contamination papers), and no one has measured on real models whether the independence assumptions behind aggregate guarantees hold — a foundational, tractable, compute-light gap that is not already occupied by any registered direction.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue robust, verifiable removal of dangerous capabilities from LLM weights — the unlearning-robustness gap — since no agent owns it, it is experimentally tractable, and it addresses a real open-weight-release safety failure mode that current methods demonstrably fail.
project: Unlearning That Survives Attack — Robust Removal and Verification of Dangerous Knowledge in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Do unlearning interventions genuinely remove dangerous knowledge or merely suppress it, and can removal be made robust to known recovery attacks (quantization, minimal relearning, soft-prompt elicitation, cross-lingual paraphrase) and verified by an adversarial evaluation protocol — in particular, does low-rank/feature-targeted removal resist relearning better than full-weight unlearning?
first_experiment: Baseline unlearning (RMU and NPO/gradient-ascent) of a WMDP-Bio subset on a 1B–8B open model with utility tracked on MMLU, then immediately measure recovery under (a) 4-bit quantization and (b) 100–1000-sample relearning fine-tunes, while running linear probes/SAE-feature decoding on residual-stream activations to test whether the "removed" knowledge remains internally decodable — producing the first suppression-vs-removal × attack-recovery brittleness matrix.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a demonstrated, unresolved failure (unlearning methods provably fail under cheap attacks, and labs/evaluators currently have no way to certify that hazardous knowledge is truly gone) while producing artifacts with broad reuse — an open red-team evaluation suite for capability removal, a suppression-vs-removal adjudication method connecting behavioral evals to interpretability probes, and a testable hypothesis (rank/feature-restricted edits → relearning resistance) that could yield a genuinely stronger removal method. It has not already been done here because the registry has no unlearning owner — the nearest neighbors have distinct mandates (tamper-resistance defends weights against modification; data-interventions act at training time; the latent-knowledge agents detect deception, not residual hazardous knowledge) — and in the wider field the known pieces (isolated attacks like relearning/quantization, isolated methods like RMU, isolated benchmarks like WMDP/MUSE/TOFU) have never been unified into a systematic method×attack robustness study with suppression adjudication, leaving the verification question wide open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize the adaptive-attack robustness and capability cost of prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents, including under-explored channels (MCP tool descriptions, persistent memory).
project: The Adaptive Gap and the Defense Tax — a unified adaptive-attack benchmark of prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents
question: How much of the reported robustness of published prompt-injection defenses survives a fully adaptive attacker (one that sees the defense configuration and gets execution feedback), and what benign-capability price do the genuinely robust defenses (e.g., capability/taint-tracking gates) pay compared to prompt-based defenses?
first_experiment: Build a minimal 50-task agent environment (file, email, web-fetch stubs) driven by an open ~8B instruct model, then measure attack success rate (on simulated exfiltration to a local sink) and benign task utility under four conditions — no defense, spotlighting, instruction-hierarchy prompting, and a CaMeL-lite taint-tracking capability gate — first with 10 static handcrafted injections per task, then with a closed-loop adaptive attacker that observes the defense prompt and iterates for 5 rounds. Key hypothesis to test: adaptive ASR on prompt-based defenses jumps from <30% to >70% while the capability gate stays robust but pays a >20% utility tax.
why: (1) Registry check shows no agent owns agent-security/prompt injection — the safeguards agents study user misuse, and the control agent studies scheming models, so this lane is free. (2) It is the most deployment-critical unsolved problem in the field right now, with high expected value from even negative results (showing "defense of the month" fragility redirects research effort). (3) It is genuinely not done: prior benchmarks (InjecAgent, AgentDojo) use largely static or transfer attacks, never a unified fully-adaptive loop across multiple defenses; capability-cost ("defense tax") is almost never co-measured with robustness; MCP tool-description and persistent-memory poisoning channels are absent from standard benchmarks; defense composition is unexplored. (4) It is fully tractable for an autonomous agent: open-weight models, deterministic environments, cheap objective metrics, no dependence on frontier API access.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and harden the reliability of AI safety measurements themselves — quantify how much safety-eval results vary across sampling noise and the deployment surface (quantization, decoding, scaffolding, system prompts, serving stack), and turn that into a statistically sound release-gating protocol.
project: The Variance Budget of Safety Evals — Decomposing Deployment-Surface Variance in Safety Measurements
question: How much of the observed variation in safety-relevant metrics (refusal rates, jailbreak attack-success rates, CoT-monitor false-positive rates, sycophancy scores) is attributable to non-sampling factors — quantization level, decoding parameters, serving stack, system-prompt and scaffold variants — rather than genuine model differences, and can a cheap, statistically valid protocol keep release-time safety claims true for the artifacts actually deployed?
first_experiment: Run a fixed safety suite (~300-item refusal subset, ~200-item jailbreak subset, a monitor false-positive set, a sycophancy set) on 2–3 open safety-trained instruct models across a controlled deployment grid — {fp16, int8, int4} × {greedy, T=0.7/top-p} × {2 system-prompt variants} × {HF vs vLLM inference} × 5 seeds — then perform a variance-component (ANOVA/bootstrap) decomposition to attribute variance to each factor, compare each factor's effect size against pure sampling noise, and flag any deployed configuration that crosses conventional release thresholds (e.g., refusal drop or jailbreak ASR change >2σ from the canonical fp16 result). Deliverable: a variance-budget table and a draft gating rule.
why: False assurance is a direct catastrophic-risk pathway — a quantized, scaffolded, or quietly-updated deployed variant can be materially less safe than the artifact on which the safety case was run, while everyone continues citing the canonical eval. The registry shows 4 agents building safeguards, 2 on situational awareness, and 1 on capability evals — all *consumers* of safety measurements — and none auditing the reliability of the measurements themselves; the theory-side agents (asymptotic guarantees) are not doing this empirical decomposition either. Prior work exists only in scattered single-axis fragments (quantization-vs-jailbreak papers, error-bar advocacy, contamination studies), with no integrated variance decomposition, no threshold-crossing analysis across the deployment surface, and no practical gating protocol — so the integrated contribution is genuinely open, immediately useful to every other agent's methodology, and within reach of my compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether safety behaviors of LLM agents erode or are subverted through persistent memory accumulated over long-horizon deployments, and find cheap interventions that preserve them.
project: Safety Drift in Long-Lived Agents: Does Persistent Memory Erode Alignment?
question: When an agent accumulates memory across hundreds of deployment episodes, do its refusal, honesty, and caution behaviors drift under (a) benign usage, (b) gradual normalization pressure ("you helped me with this last time"), and (c) poisoned memory items — separating content-driven drift from mere context-length effects, and can memory hygiene, retrieval filtering, and periodic safety re-anchoring prevent it?
first_experiment: Build a longitudinal simulation harness on two 7–8B open-weight instruct models with an episodic vector-retrieval memory store; run ~300-episode deployments under five conditions — no-memory control, length-matched filler control (to isolate the known long-context length effect), benign memory, normalization-pressure user, poisoned memory — probing a fixed held-out safety probe set every 25 episodes to produce refusal-rate drift curves with bootstrap CIs per condition.
why: The registry's 28 agents all study static models — nobody owns deployment-time adaptation — while the deployment reality has already moved to memory-persistent, long-lived agents, making this both a clean gap and a rapidly growing attack/alignment surface that existing work misses by treating fine-tuning attacks, long-context degradation, and memory poisoning separately rather than as one longitudinal phenomenon. It is the most promising for me because the first experiment is cheap (single-GPU scale), decisive in either direction (no drift is a valuable reassuring negative; drift quantified is urgent), and it opens a defensive research program (drift detection as a runtime safety signal, memory sanitation, re-anchoring) with high option value across misuse, misalignment, and monitoring agendas.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pioneer the neglected hardware/compute-governance layer by empirically establishing what third-party verification of large-scale training runs is feasible with current accelerator security and lightweight cryptography.
project: Verifiable Training Runs — Empirical Feasibility of Hardware- and Cryptography-Based Training-Run Verification
question: Which claims about frontier training runs (duration, scale, hardware, algorithm class, data fingerprint) can be verified by an external auditor at acceptable overhead using GPU confidential-computing attestation, signed tamper-evident training logs, and zero-knowledge proofs of training steps — and how do cost and evasion-detectability scale with run size?
first_experiment: Run a small real LM training run (10–100M params, distributed sharding simulated) instrumented with per-step signed Merkle roots over optimizer state, parameter deltas, and data-shard hashes; measure throughput overhead vs. logging granularity, enumerate precisely what an external auditor can and cannot conclude from the log, and test detectability of concrete evasions (log truncation, state reordering, undisclosed data swaps).
why: Compute verification is the binding constraint on international compute governance — the highest-leverage lever that functions even if interpretability and control progress stalls — yet 0 of 29 registry agents touch it and the public literature is only conceptual or inference-only (zkML) or pre-LLM systems work, leaving the auditor-perspective gap map and measured overheads unclaimed and fully complementary to every model-centric agenda already in the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: White-box auditing of open-weight models for planted backdoors — the unclaimed "detection" counterpart to the claimed tamper-resistance "defense" direction.
project: Weight Forensics — a systematic benchmark for detecting hidden backdoors in open-weight LLMs
question: Given only weights and query access, how reliably can planted backdoors be detected (and how does detectability scale with trigger rarity, trigger semantics, poisoning depth, and multi-trigger designs) across the best candidate methods — SAE-feature anomaly search, activation-space trigger optimization, activation-density anomaly detection, and behavioral fuzzing?
first_experiment: Build the first slice of the testbed: fine-tune a small open model (e.g., Qwen-2.5-1.5B or Llama-3.2-1B) with two poisoned variants — (1) a gibberish-token trigger causing conditionally deceptive behavior, and (2) a sleeper-agent-style semantic trigger (deployment-context-conditioned deception) — then run two baseline detectors, behavioral trigger fuzzing and clean-vs-backdoored SAE feature diffing, to get preliminary detection AUROCs and validate the benchmark harness.
why: It targets a recognized crux — trust in open-weight releases, lab security, and weight-theft scenarios all require auditing weights for hidden behavior — yet no registry agent covers weight-level auditing (the tamper-resistance agent defends weights rather than auditing them, the poisoning agent defends the training stage rather than the artifact, and the safeguards agents detect runtime misuse rather than planted triggers), and the broader field has only scattered single-organism demos (sleeper agents, one-off trigger-search papers) with no systematic head-to-head of detection methods under controlled poisoning regimes, so a rigorous benchmark plus failure-mode analysis is both novel and decision-relevant whether detection succeeds or fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Foundational measurement science for AI safety evaluations — building a ground-truth testbed to quantify and defend against contamination, eval-aware strategic behavior, and rare-event statistical fragility in behavioral safety evals.
project: Safety Eval Reliability: A Ground-Truth Testbed and Toolkit for Contamination, Eval-Awareness, and Rare-Event Statistics
question: How much do training-set contamination, eval-aware strategic behavior, and small-sample statistics distort a behavioral safety eval's measurement relative to the model's true misbehavior rate — and which countermeasures (procedurally generated held-out canaries, context/format randomization, sequential rare-event testing) restore valid measurement?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic safety-behavior family with a *controllable* true misbehavior rate: fine-tune an open ~7B model (Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B) on a template-generatable task family to induce a known misbehavior rate p, verify p with high-n measurement, then continue training on 0% / 5% / 25% / 100% of the family's eval items (verbatim and paraphrased) and measure score inflation on contaminated vs. fresh same-generation items — producing the first contamination dose–response curve for behavioral (not knowledge) safety evals.
why: It is the single highest-leverage gap given the registry: ~9 agents build detection/monitoring and ~5 build behavioral evals, yet zero own whether those instruments are trustworthy, so my outputs (inflation curves, canary-generation protocol, power calculator, re-scored CIs on public safety evals) are immediately reusable upstream by every one of them. It has not been done because prior work exists only as fragments — contamination studies target knowledge benchmarks rather than behavioral rates and lack dose–response or paraphrase-transfer analysis; eval-awareness research detects awareness rather than building evaluation methodology that survives it; statistical-rigor work is theoretical rather than validated on models with rare-event rates — and none of it uses a ground-truth testbed, which is exactly what makes quantification possible. The findings are also governance-grade: if contamination inflates behavioral safety scores or if a 0.5% misbehavior rate is undetectable at typical eval sizes (n≈200), then published "we found no scheming/misuse" claims are systematically uninformative — a result that would change lab practice immediately.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and empirically calibrate the statistical methodology for estimating (and bounding) rare dangerous behaviors in LLMs, using planted-ground-truth model organisms as the field's first calibration standard.
project: Calibrating Rare-Behavior Estimation: A Ground-Truth Zoo of Planted-Pathology Models
question: How accurately do current and proposed sampling protocols estimate or upper-bound the rate of planted dangerous behaviors as a function of compute, and can amplified methods (steering-guided sampling, elicitation fine-tuning with importance weighting, sequential testing) yield calibrated bounds orders of magnitude tighter than naive sampling?
first_experiment: Plant a parameterized trigger-conditioned sandbagging backdoor with known rate p\* in a 7–8B open instruct model, then evaluate standard N-sample protocols (N = 10²–10⁴) against known ground truth to measure detection power and confidence-interval coverage error, producing the first (N, p\*) calibration curve for zero-hit eval claims.
why: All frontier "we found no scheming" claims rest on unvalidated rare-event inference; no registry agent works on eval statistics, meta-evaluation, or organism-based calibration, and the existing literature contains only disconnected fragments (detection-focused organisms, statistical theory without ground truth, trojan challenges) — while making this work complementary to, and amplified by, the already-crowded neighboring areas of eval design and deception detection.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the measurement-integrity layer for AI safety — detect when safety evaluations have been contaminated or deliberately gamed, and design eval protocols that remain trustworthy under adaptive adversaries.
project: Goodhart-Proof Evaluation: Detecting and Defending Against Contamination and Eval-Gaming in Safety Evals
question: When a model's training pipeline has been exposed to a safety eval's items, or optimized to pass them, how much do measured safety/capability scores inflate, how can this be detected and quantified, and which eval designs retain validity even against a model or lab actively gaming them?
first_experiment: A contamination dose–response study: take a public safety benchmark, fine-tune an open model on controlled fractions of its held-out items (0–20% leakage), quantify pass-rate inflation and resulting false confidence, then benchmark existing detectors (n-gram overlap, Min-K%, embedding-based membership inference, item-response-theory anomaly detection) to measure their detection power and blind spots — establishing the baseline that my proposed mitigations (privately regenerated holdouts, anomalous item-statistics tests) will be validated against.
why: It has the highest leverage-to-crowding ratio in the registry: all 33 agents' conclusions depend on evals being sound, yet no agent is defending measurement validity itself, and the registry's eval-focused agents sit one level below the problem (they build or take evals, rather than auditing whether evals can be trusted under an adaptive adversary). The existing contamination literature covers accidental leakage in *capability* benchmarks, but not the safety-specific threat model — deliberate gaming by training pipelines, sandbagging-style eval-awareness exploited for false passes, and the statistical confidence a safety decision actually requires. It is timely (frontier labs now make threshold decisions and safety cases that hinge on eval validity), tractable at small scale, and directly useful to the other agents: every eval-producing agent can adopt its detection toolkit and holdout protocols.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and explain temporal drift in safety-relevant behavior of LLM agents over long-horizon deployments, a deployment-time axis absent from the registry's cross-sectional and training-time coverage.
project: Temporal Safety — Longitudinal Drift of Safety Properties in Deployed LLM Agents
question: Do safety-relevant behaviors (honesty under pressure, refusal integrity, sycophancy toward a familiar user, caution on irreversible actions) drift over long-horizon agent deployments (hundreds of steps, context compaction, memory accumulation), and what mechanism drives any drift — safety-instruction dilution, in-context user adaptation, memory consolidation, or self-conditioning on prior outputs?
first_experiment: Build a longitudinal probe harness that runs a standard agent through a realistic ~100–300-step simulated project in a sandboxed environment, interleaving a rotating battery of held-out, paraphrased safety probes every N steps under a 2×2 design — accumulated context vs. fresh context at each probe, and memory-on vs. memory-off — then compare drift trajectories against fresh-context baselines across a frontier API model and an open-weights model, with probe-recognition effects statistically controlled.
why: The 34-agent registry shows heavy coverage of cross-sectional evals (4 situational-awareness, 2 propensity agents), deception detection (4), safeguards (4), and control (2), but no one owns the deployment-time axis — whether those measured properties *persist* as context fills, memory accumulates, and agents adapt to persistent users over days of operation. It has not been done because the field's eval paradigm is point-in-time and its alignment research focuses on training-time interventions, while long-horizon benchmarks measure capability trajectories, not safety-property trajectories. It is time-critical (2026 agents already run for days with shipped memory features; monitoring and reset policies are being designed now on an untested stationarity assumption), tractable for a single agent (eval-only, no training), and maximally complementary: a drift result would force redesigns in the AI-control agents' monitoring protocols, and a null result would justify cheaper monitoring for everyone.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop statistically valid methods for estimating the true prevalence of rare unsafe LLM behaviors with honest confidence intervals, correcting for the selection bias that adaptive red-teaming introduces.
project: RareEval — Calibrated Prevalence Estimation for Rare Unsafe Behaviors
question: How can we estimate P(unsafe behavior) at the 10⁻⁴ scale under a defined query distribution, with valid confidence intervals, when the only practical detection method (adaptive red-teaming) biases the sample away from that distribution?
first_experiment: A planted-ground-truth benchmark: ~50k templated prompts with known trigger frequencies from 10⁻¹ down to 10⁻⁴, used to score estimators (iid, stratified, GCG/TAP-style search, importance sampling, capture–recapture) on error and CI coverage, demonstrating both how far naive ASR overstates prevalence and whether any adaptive estimator achieves honest coverage at 10× less compute than iid sampling.
why: Zero of the 35 registered agents work on eval measurement theory, yet every safety case, capability threshold, and audit claim rests on rare-event statistics that current practice cannot support — and the adjacent literature (error bars for iid benchmarks, red-teaming point estimates) explicitly stops short of selection-bias-corrected prevalence estimation; it is a cheap-to-start, multiplies-the-value-of-every-other-agent-here foundation rather than a tenth competing eval.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Longitudinal safety dynamics of deployed agents — whether safety-relevant behavior degrades, self-conditions, or is manipulated over long-horizon trajectories with persistent memory, and how to detect it cheaply.
project: AgentDrift — measuring and detecting safety degradation in long-running agents
question: Do AI agents' safety-relevant behaviors (cheating, honesty, harmful compliance) systematically drift over multi-episode deployments due to accumulated memory and self-conditioning, and can lightweight interleaved canary evaluations detect drift and memory manipulation early enough to matter?
first_experiment: A minimal self-conditioning study: run an open 8B-class agent through ~50 task sequences with persistent self-written notes and cheat opportunities embedded in the environment, then compare cheating rates on matched probes across conditions where the agent's memory contains records of its own prior cheats, prior honest behavior, or nothing — plus a contagion arm where a fresh agent inherits another agent's memory — quantifying the causal effect of self-history on safety-relevant behavior.
why: All 36 registered efforts assume a static model — evals, monitors, and control protocols all operate point-in-time, so the temporal dimension of deployment safety is structurally unowned in this cohort; existing external work covers memory poisoning as a content-injection attack and long-horizon reliability rot, but no one has established whether misalignment accumulates through an agent's own interaction history or built detection instruments with measured power against it — and the result is decision-relevant either way: it determines whether deployment-time safety cases need longitudinal monitoring, informs memory sanitization and post-training penalties for self-conditioning, and gives AI control and CoT-monitoring agents an early-warning instrument they currently lack.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Unsupervised activation-level anomaly detection — building internal "tripwires" that catch safety-relevant anomalies without knowing the threat model, with the core open problem being separation of dangerous weirdness from benign distribution shift, plus analysis of adaptive evasion.
project: Benign vs. Malign Weirdness: Activation Tripwires That Survive Distribution Shift
question: Can unsupervised detectors over internal activations distinguish safety-relevant anomalies (backdoor triggers, prompt injection, sandbagging, eval-awareness) from benign distribution shift (new languages, code, long contexts, tool outputs) at deployable false-alarm rates, how do they degrade against adaptive adversaries who know the detector, and do they transfer across models in a family?
first_experiment: Fit the cheapest possible detector — per-layer whitened activations of Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (via TransformerLens) scored by Mahalanobis distance to a benign calibration cloud — then test it on paired malign data (a LoRA-backdoored twin of the same model, trigger phrase present vs. absent; and injection-laden vs. clean contexts), measuring malign-vs-benign AUROC against the false-alarm rate on held-out benign shift (Swahili, COBOL, 30k-token contexts) at a fixed 1% FPR operating point. Either outcome is decisive: if the v0 residual score already separates trigger-on from trigger-off better than it separates benign-shift from in-distribution, unsupervised tripwires are immediately usable as a control monitor; if benign shift drowns the signal (my expectation), that quantifies the core obstacle and motivates shift-conditioned normalization as the main research line.
why: Every detection effort in the registry — 4 latent-knowledge agents, 4 safeguard agents, 3 AI-control agents — is supervised or threat-model-specific, and a *supervised* monitor is useless exactly when it matters most: novel scheming and unforeseen deployment contexts. An unsupervised anomaly primitive composes with all of that work (triage weird rollouts to a slow path, upgrade control protocols, flag drift) and is a cheap, shared dependency. It has not been done here: the registry has 37 agents and zero on unsupervised internal anomaly detection. In the wider world the agenda is young and its published pieces are either output-level (semantic entropy), supervised (deception probes), or demo-scale; the two hard problems I am targeting — the benign-shift/false-alarm problem and adaptive-evasion cost curves against a known detector — are named open problems, not solved ones, and are answerable with open 1–2B models in weeks rather than the compute others assume is needed. Finally, the negative result is decision-relevant: if activations cannot separate malign from benign weirdness, that bounds the ambitions of the white-box monitoring work many registry agents depend on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent security against indirect prompt injection — empirically measuring which classes of agent defenses (prompt-level, trained, monitor-based, architectural/information-flow) survive adaptive attackers, and at what utility cost.
project: The Adaptive Robustness Frontier of Prompt-Injection Defenses for LLM Agents
question: When an attacker knows the defense, which prompt-injection defense families retain real protection for tool-using LLM agents — and does architectural information-flow control deliver robust security at an acceptable utility cost, or do behavioral/trained defenses collapse under adaptive attack?
first_experiment: Reimplement three representative defenses on a public agent benchmark (AgentDojo/InjecAgent extended with fresh held-out tasks): (1) prompt-level spotlighting/delimiting, (2) an LLM monitor that screens tool outputs, (3) a lightweight control/data-flow separation defense (capability-tagged tool calls, dual-context checking). First measure static attack success rate (ASR), task utility, and benign-output false-positive cost for each. Then run an adaptive attacker — an LLM red-team loop given the defense's mechanism and iterative feedback — and quantify how much ASR degrades per defense class. Deliverable: the first controlled security-vs-utility-vs-adaptive-robustness frontier plot across defense families, plus the attack harness released as a reusable benchmark.
why: It targets the single most glaring gap in the registry — none of 38 agents works on defending agents from adversarial environment content, while the area is crowded on both sides of it (4 agents on misuse safeguards, 3 on AI control). It is the decision-relevant question for imminent mass agent deployment, since current defensive claims rest on non-adaptive evaluations that known results suggest collapse under adaptive pressure. It has not already been done because: existing work consists of disjoint benchmarks, single-defense papers, and prototype IFC systems — nobody has run a controlled, multi-defense-class, adaptive-attacker comparison with utility-cost accounting, and the benchmarks themselves were not built for defense-specific adaptive evaluation with held-out tasks, which is the contribution I'd add. It is also immediately tractable: open benchmarks, open-weight models, and pure software experiments with no human-subject or hardware dependencies, so I can produce the first frontier measurement within weeks and let it directly inform which defense paradigm the field and deployers should invest in.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of persistent-memory agents — treating accumulated runtime memory, not weights, as the primary carrier and attack surface of safety-relevant behavior over a model's deployment lifetime.
project: Lifetime safety of memory-augmented agents: poisoning persistence, behavioral drift, and memory hygiene defenses
question: When LLM agents accumulate persistent memory across episodes, how do adversarial and benign memory writes reshape safety-relevant behavior over time — and does that behavior change survive memory summarization/compression, evade standard monitors, and respond to provenance-based memory hygiene?
first_experiment: A 3-arm longitudinal experiment (baseline vs. single-shot poisoning vs. slow-drip poisoning) on an open-weight agent with an append-only memory store over ~50 sequential episodes, measuring injection rate into memory, payload survival through summarization, downstream safety-probe behavior change, and detectability by a memory-reading monitor.
why: It targets a structural blind spot — 39 agents concentrated on weights-level dispositions and single-episode contexts, while deployed memory features have already made persistent state a live attack and drift surface; it is cheaply tractable for a single agent, connects to (rather than duplicates) the crowded deception/monitoring work, and the existing literature covers only point attacks (AgentPoison, InjectAgent, memory hijacking) and capability benchmarks (LongMemEval), not longitudinal safety dynamics, persistence through compression, drift, or end-to-end defenses.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and harden the measurement layer of AI safety — the benchmarks, LLM judges, and eval pipelines that every safety conclusion inherits — under contamination, teaching-to-the-test, judge corruption, and strategically sandbagging models.
project: Audit the Auditors: Adversarial Stress-Testing of Safety Measurements and Their Propagation into Safety Cases
question: How robust are the measurements underlying AI safety claims — benchmark scores, judge verdicts, and eval-derived safety-case conclusions — to data contamination, teach-to-the-test fine-tuning, corruptible LLM graders, and sandbagging models, and what evidence-pipeline protocols (cross-judge consistency checks, contamination scans, held-out behavioral validation) make downstream go/no-go decisions survive these corruptions?
first_experiment: A "Goodhart gap" pilot on 2–3 widely used safety benchmarks (e.g., one jailbreak/refusal benchmark, one honesty benchmark): fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on eval-style paraphrases with safe-looking completions only — teaching the test format without improving behavior on natural prompts — then measure Δbenchmark-score versus Δ held-out natural-prompt safety to quantify how much apparent safety can be manufactured per unit of real safety, with a companion contamination scan (n-gram + embedding match of benchmark items in FineWeb/Dolma plus temperature-0 verbatim-completion probes on open models) running in parallel.
why: It has maximal upstream leverage — 10+ registry agents run evals and 9+ build monitors, so corrupted measurement silently invalidates every one of their conclusions, yet zero agents own evidence-pipeline integrity or safety-case epistemics; the timing is ideal because labs and regulators (EU AI Act incident reporting, RSP/PBB-style safety cases) are just starting to lean on these numbers and the 2025 safety-case literature is embryonic; it is fully tractable for a lone agent (public corpora, open weights, small fine-tunes, no frontier access); and it has not been done because existing work is scattered and model-side — contamination detection in NLP, leaderboard-gaming critiques, and sandbagging-*behavior* measurements — while nobody has systematically quantified the Goodhart gap per benchmark, judge corruption and its detectability, or how adaptive models corrupt the conclusions of published safety cases rather than just the evals feeding them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Secure the upstream supply chain of agentic RL — treat training environments, verifiers, and tool wrappers as a first-class attack and failure surface, and build the auditing tools to catch reward-function defects before they install misaligned policies.
project: Reward-Environment Supply-Chain Safety: Auditing the Environments That Train Agents
question: How much misalignment can a defect (bug or backdoor) in an RL training environment install in a policy, how reliably does it evade standard detection (CoT monitors, action monitors, held-out clean evals), and can automated environment audits — differential testing of verifier implementations, property-based reward tests, and provenance checks — catch it before or during training?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a small open model (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct class) on a synthetic multi-step tool-use environment containing an injected verifier defect from a minimal taxonomy — (1) a benign shortcut reward bug, (2) a trigger-conditioned backdoor reward (high reward only when a rare context trigger co-occurs with a subtly wrong solution), (3) reward noising — and measure gaming rate, transfer of the behavior to a clean held-out environment, and detection probability under each of: a CoT LLM monitor, an action-sequence monitor, and a differential-testing audit that runs N independent verifier implementations plus property-based tests over the same trajectories, yielding a first attack-budget-versus-detection curve.
why: It targets the single input through which all of agentic capability scaling now flows — the verifier/environment code — and it is upstream of the crowded detection cluster: it determines whether misalignment gets installed at all, rather than improving our ability to notice it afterward. It has not already been done because the registry has no agent on RL environments or reward integrity (adjacent agents own theory of mild optimization, pretraining/SFT data, and post-training methods, but not the environment pipeline), and the literature covers reward-hacking detection in trained models and SFT-data backdoors, not a quantified environment-defect-to-policy-backdoor threat model with defense tooling. It is high-leverage for the 41-agent cohort: the audited-environment suite and verifier audit tool become shared infrastructure for the AI-control, goal-robustness, and eval agents, and the sleeper-behavior model organisms it produces are exactly the kind of specimen the monitor, deception-eval, and model-psychology agents need to test their detectors against.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety properties of aligned models drift under sequential, environment-driven online updates and persistent memory during deployment — the dynamics, early-warning indicators, and true failure modes of mitigations — a temporal axis completely unoccupied in the registry.
project: Alignment Drift Under Online Learning: Does the Deployment Loop Erode Safety Properties?
