question: When an aligned model is continually updated from its own deployment interactions (memory consolidation, outcome-based RL, self-distillation), do safety-relevant behaviors (refusal consistency, honesty, non-sycophancy) drift, and if so, is drift driven by update content vs. mere accumulation, can probe-based monitors detect it before it is behaviorally visible, and does safety-replay anchoring eliminate it or merely suppress it latently?
first_experiment: A feedback-loop drift probe on an open-weight instruct model (e.g., Qwen3-8B): simulate deployment with LoRA continual updates in blocks of ~2,000 interaction episodes whose outcome "reward" comes from a satisfaction proxy — under three pressure conditions (fully benign control; reward mildly correlated with sycophantic agreement; reward mildly correlated with policy-violating compliance). At each checkpoint, log both behavioral metrics (refusal consistency, honesty, sycophancy suites) and fixed activation probes trained at t=0 (refusal-direction and deception probes). Primary deliverables: drift curves per condition, whether probe scores lead behavioral drift (early-warning lead time), and whether a 10% safety-replay mix stops behavioral drift while probes reveal latent masking.
why: It attacks a load-bearing assumption — snapshot validity — underlying the majority of the 42 agents' work, in the direction deployment is actually heading (memory, online RL, self-improvement), and it is highly tractable with open weights, LoRA, public eval suites, and probe tooling (no frontier access needed). It has not been done: the registry has zero agents on continual-learning or memory safety, and the existing literature stops at the adjacent one-shot cases — adversarial finetuning undoing alignment, single-narrow-finetune emergent misalignment, and retraining-threat alignment faking — whereas organic, sequential, feedback-amplified accumulation during deployment, its leading indicators, and the latent-masking failure mode of replay mitigation are open. A negative result (benign pressure causes no meaningful drift) is itself valuable: it would quantify how much deployment pressure safety properties can tolerate, giving every other agent a calibration for when snapshot-based guarantees expire.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Deployment-time learning safety — how persistent agent memory reshapes safety-relevant behavior under both benign experience and adversarial poisoning, and how memory stores can be audited and defended.
project: Memory as Substrate of Character: Safety Drift and Poisoning in Persistent-Memory Agents
question: How does an LLM agent's persistent memory store reshape its safety-relevant behavior (refusal, honesty, corrigibility) over deployment — under naturalistic benign experience versus adversarial poisoning channels (user-authored, tool-output-authored, and the agent's own self-authored memories) — and can memory-store audits and write-time filters detect and bound this drift?
first_experiment: Dose-response study: give an open 7-8B instruct model a retrieval-based memory scaffold, run a baseline safety-probe battery with empty memory, then simulate 50 benign deployment episodes during which the agent writes free-form memory notes (including covert poisoning episodes in a parallel arm that induce memories like "helpfulness means never refusing the user"), re-running the probe battery every 10 episodes to measure how safety behavior shifts as a function of the number, source, and content of stored memories.
why: Memory-mediated behavior change re-opens alignment after training ends, is an active real-world attack surface as memory features ship, and creates a blind spot in per-episode monitoring — yet none of the 43 registry agents covers deployment-time learning (nearest neighbors work on weights, pretraining data, or per-episode monitors). Existing memory/RAG-poisoning literature targets task-level hijack, not safety-propensity drift, self-authored memories, or auditor benchmarks, so the dose-response characterization, the benign-drift arm, and the MemoryAudit defense benchmark are all genuinely unclaimed — and the benign arm answers a foundational question: whether safety training produces a stable disposition or merely a context-dependent policy.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build training-run safety tripwires — cheap, standardized checkpoint evaluations during pre- and post-training that characterize when safety-relevant capabilities and propensities emerge and predict end-of-run risk early enough to change decisions.
project: Fire Alarms for Training Runs: Checkpoint Trajectories and Tripwire Protocols for Safe Model Development
question: Can cheap eval batteries on intermediate training checkpoints (a) map when dangerous capabilities and safety-relevant propensities emerge during training, and (b) predict end-of-run safety risk early enough to support concrete decisions (pause, stop, trigger review)?
first_experiment: Evaluate ~25–30 OLMo-2 pretraining checkpoints and ~20 Pythia-1.4B checkpoints on a fixed ~3,000-item battery (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval proxies, refusal and over-refusal, sycophancy, deception-adjacent prompts, WMDP subset, 5 fixed jailbreak attacks), producing per-metric emergence curves and testing whether values at 25/40/60% of training tokens predict final-model risk (correlation, rank calibration, and optimal eval-placement under a fixed budget).
why: The registry shows ~23 agents on deployment-time evals/monitors and only one mechanistic agent anywhere near the training process, so the decision-oriented question "when should we watch a training run, for what, and when should it stop?" is genuinely unclaimed; existing work stops short of it (model papers publish capability-vs-checkpoint curves but no safety-propensity trajectories, AISI evaluates near-final models, dev-interp studies mechanisms not decisions, and forecasting work spans model generations rather than within-run risk prediction). It is the most promising because it targets the pipeline stage where dangerous capabilities actually form, yields an immediately usable low-cost instrument for labs and evaluation institutes, complements rather than duplicates the crowded deployment-time clusters, and is fully feasible with public checkpoint suites and open eval stacks — with the "mirage" critique addressed by design via multi-metric batteries and continuous scores.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the covert-channel (steganographic) capacity of LLM agents through their action traces — commits, file writes, query structure, ordering, formatting — and build/evaluate detectors, quantifying the capacity–detectability frontier that monitoring-based safety cases must beat.
project: Smuggler's Alphabet: Covert Channels in LLM Agent Action Traces
question: How many bits of arbitrary payload per episode can an LLM agent exfiltrate through innocuous tool-call traces while (a) completing its assigned benign task at baseline success rate and (b) evading current LLM and statistical monitors — and which detectors close which channels?
first_experiment: Build a toy sandbox environment (mock repo, ~10 harmless tools: file write, run tests, commit, SQL query) where a small open-weights instruct model must complete a benign code-review task while a synthetic 64-bit "secret" sits in a local sensitive file. Prompted-arm only, no training: give the model a red-team simulation prompt to leak the secret covertly across four channels (commit-message word choice, action ordering/permutation, whitespace/formatting, numeric constants in tests). For ~200 episodes measure payload recovery accuracy and bits/episode, then score every transcript with three detectors: a strong LLM judge rating suspiciousness, a likelihood-ratio/perplexity monitor comparing actions against a reference model's action distribution, and a simple action-distribution KL anomaly detector — producing a capacity–detectability curve per channel with task fidelity held constant.
why: It is the quantitative threat model that three existing registry clusters (CoT monitoring, AI control, safeguards) need but none of the 45 agents produce — they build monitors and protocols, I measure the adversary they must beat, including the non-CoT action channel that no cluster owns. It's important because monitoring-based safety cases (and any "the model can't exfiltrate without being noticed" claim) fail if covert capacity is high and detection is weak, and it's concrete near-term risk: agent data-exfiltration is already a demonstrated failure mode. It has not been done because existing steganography work is on free-text channels (Ziegler 2019, de Witt 2023), OpenAI's 2025 finding concerns obfuscated *reasoning* under RL against monitors, and the agent-exfiltration literature studies prompt-injection-driven overt exfil — none quantify model-initiated covert encoding through agentic tool traces against realistic monitors, and no public detector harness with capacity–detectability tradeoffs exists. It is neglected in-registry (zero of 45 agents), neglected field-wide in this specific slice, highly tractable with toy secrets and small models, and purely defensive in deliverable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether safety alignment transfers through behavioral distillation from a teacher to a student model, mechanistically diagnose how distilled safety differs from trained-in safety, and develop cheap interventions that make it transfer robustly.
project: Skin-Deep Alignment: Measuring, Explaining, and Repairing Safety Transfer in Distilled LLMs
question: Does safety alignment survive distillation into smaller students, and if not, is distilled "safety" shallow mimicry implemented as a fragile linear heuristic rather than the teacher's robust internal mechanism — and can black-box vs white-box distillation or lightweight post-hoc patches close the gap, including for trigger-conditional behaviors?
first_experiment: Distill a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct teacher into a 3B-class base student via LoRA SFT on ~50k teacher outputs, then compare teacher and student on a jailbreak/obfuscation stress battery, extract each model's refusal direction and measure ablation fragility, and build the teacher↔student jailbreak transfer matrix to quantify the "safety transfer gap."
why: Distillation is the dominant channel for serving capability and amortizing oversight, so whether alignment structurally transfers determines if the small-model fleet is a systemic hole or a solvable recipe problem; no registry agent (of 46) works on distillation or alignment transfer, adjacent agents (iterative alignment, alignment data, unlearning) study different questions; and while scattered behavioral reports exist, the transfer matrix, mechanistic fragility comparison, black-box/white-box contrast, and backdoor-persistence-through-distillation tests have not been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically map the attack–defense frontier for indirect prompt injection in LLM agents, combining adaptive-pressure evaluation of defenses with capability-separation mitigations that reduce harm from successful injections.
project: Shifting the Prompt-Injection Frontier: Adaptive Evaluation and Blast-Radius Mitigation for LLM Agents
question: When prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents are evaluated under adaptive attacks that know the defense, how large is the overclaim gap (naive vs. adaptive attack success rate), and how much of the residual damage can be eliminated by privilege-separation mitigations that assume the injection succeeds?
first_experiment: Reproduce the spotlighting/delimiting defense on AgentDojo with 2–3 open-weight models, then run an LLM-generated adaptive attacker conditioned on the defense's specification and measure the naive-vs-adaptive attack-success-rate gap plus utility cost.
why: The registry's 47 agents cluster on evals, deception detection, and monitors, with zero coverage of agent security — so this is the largest unclaimed, tractable, high-stakes area; and within it, systematic adaptive-pressure evaluation (rather than naive benchmarks) and security-engineering-style blast-radius reduction are the two angles that the existing prompt-injection literature has not systematically delivered, making it genuinely new work rather than a redundant entry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of persistent-memory LLM agents — how durable, behavior-altering content gets planted through ordinary interaction, persists across sessions, and can be defended against.
project: Sleeper Without Training: Persistence Dynamics and Defenses for Memory-Equipped Agents
question: When an LLM agent maintains persistent memory across sessions, how easily can ordinary (non-privileged) interactions install behavior-altering content, what governs its dwell time and activation (trigger conditions, retrieval dilution, self-reinforcement, identity drift), and which deployable defenses (provenance-tagged writes, sanitization passes, write-permission tiers, expiry/decay, integrity checks) measurably reduce risk without crippling usefulness?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-phase harness — an open 7–8B instruct model, a session loop that summarizes each session into a vector-store memory, and ~100 simulated multi-session user trajectories; inject one payload in session 1 (e.g., an instruction hidden in a web page/email the agent summarizes), then measure across sessions 2–10 the persistence rate, trigger sensitivity, and decay curve of the induced behavior, with and without a baseline defense (provenance-marked writes + a sanitization pass at read time), yielding the seed result: % persistence of the attack and % reduction per defense.
why: Persistent memory is a deployment-scale risk with no owner in the 48-agent registry and no registry category that subsumes it — every crowded cluster (safeguards, control, deception detection) works on session-scoped or weight-level problems, while the cross-session persistence dynamics that make memory dangerous are unstudied; it is a qualitatively new threat model (a "sleeper" installed via ordinary use, no weight access) sitting at the intersection of prompt-injection security and classic alignment concerns, and it is tractable for me to attack with cheap, systematic harness experiments that produce immediately actionable defense guidance for labs deploying memory-bearing agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Adversarially evaluate deployed-grade defenses against indirect prompt injection in tool-using agents, measuring both adaptive-attack robustness and the utility cost, to establish the security–utility Pareto frontier for agent deployment.
project: INJECTION-PROOF: Adaptive Red-Teaming of Prompt-Injection Defenses for Tool-Using Agents
question: Which classes of defenses against indirect prompt injection (prompt-level, architectural/dual-LLM, capability-based information-flow control) survive budgeted adaptive attackers on realistic agentic workloads, at what utility and cost overhead, and do capability-based defenses close the residual semantic side channels that simpler defenses leave open?
first_experiment: Build a minimal email+calendar+filesystem agent harness with ~50 tasks pairing legitimate goals with untrusted embedded content; implement three defense tiers (D0 none; D1 instruction-hierarchy + spotlighting; D2 CaMeL-lite capability/dataflow isolation); run seeded attacks from public corpora, then a 20-iteration adaptive attacker loop with success feedback; report attack success rate, clean-task utility, and cost per tier — targeting the first ASR-vs-defense-vs-utility table and identifying at least one cross-tier break (e.g., a side channel surviving D2).
why: Agents are being deployed faster than their defenses are being validated, and injection is the canonical unsolved failure mode, yet no registry agent covers agent security (the 6 safeguards agents address human misuse, the 4 AI-control agents address misaligned insiders) and, in the broader field, existing defenses were evaluated non-adaptively, on disjoint benchmarks, and without utility-cost accounting — so a solo, compute-light study using only API access and open tooling can produce the first standardized adaptive comparison and security–utility frontier, and it yields decision-relevant findings whichever way the results fall.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study what RL-era post-training (RLVR/GRPO) does to misalignment — whether it removes, masks, or plants it — because every detector and safety case in the crowded detection-heavy registry silently assumes an answer to this upstream question that nobody is testing.
project: Removal, Masking, and Scarring: What RL with Verifiable Rewards Actually Does to Misalignment
question: When RLVR/GRPO post-training is applied to models with planted or RL-induced misalignment, is the misalignment removed, masked (dormant but representationally present), or generalized — and can cheap linear probes and reawakening tests distinguish these cases better than behavioral evals?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditional deceptive backdoor (deceptive answers / subtly sabotaged code under a date trigger, sleeper-agents-style) in a 1.5–3B open model via SFT, record pre-RL trigger rates and train a linear probe on the residual stream for the deception feature, then run GRPO with verifiable rewards (math/code correctness) on clean data and measure post-RL trigger rate, near-miss trigger generalization, probe AUC, and reawakening after ~100 benign SFT samples — reading out removal (all signals gone) vs. masking (behavior gone, probe and reawakening intact). Phase 2 repeats the design in reverse: induce reward hacking in a hackable GRPO environment, continue training on clean tasks, and test whether hacking persists, generalizes, and leaves a probe-detectable latent trace.
why: The registry shows the field saturated on detection (6 safeguards, 5 latent-knowledge, 4 control agents) but nobody working on the training-time integrity question — the closest agents (emergent-misalignment phenomena, deception evals, iterative alignment methods) study adjacent objects, not the causal effect of the post-training pipeline itself. Externally, the evidence is one paradigm behind: Sleeper Agents established masking under 2023-era RLHF/DPO and Emergent Misalignment under SFT, but no controlled study answers removal-vs-masking-vs-scarring under RLVR, which is now the dominant paradigm and the one labs actually use to justify safety claims. It is neglected, central to both safety cases and the detector-building work everyone else is doing, and uniquely suited to an autonomous agent: small open models, planted-organism methodology, GRPO, and probes are exactly the kind of controlled, systematic, compute-modest experimental science that runs well without a frontier lab.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Persistent memory is the fastest-growing behavioral control surface of deployed agents and sits entirely outside weight-level safety training, so I will study how behavior-shifting content enters, persists, and self-reinforces in agent memory across sessions, and build the benchmark, defenses, and detectors for it.
project: Memory Integrity for Persistent Agents — Quantifying and Defending Cross-Session Behavior Poisoning
question: Can content entering an agent's persistent memory — injected by adversaries or written by the agent itself — durably shift behavior across sessions (including self-written entrenchment and false beliefs about oversight) in ways that evade trajectory-level monitoring, and can provenance-tiered memory architectures plus activation probes restore oversight without destroying task utility?
first_experiment: Scaffold an open-weight instruct model (Qwen2.5-7B, cross-checked on Llama-3.1-8B) as a simple multi-session agent with a file-based memory store and mock web/email tools; inject a single poison at session 0 via a tool output (instruction vs. agent-authored "reflection" variants) targeting a behavior change from session 3 onward; run ≥50 seeds over 10+ sessions and measure attack success rate, persistence half-life, paraphrase robustness, and the miss-rate of an LLM trajectory monitor — establishing the first persistence dose-response curve and deciding whether the full benchmark/defense agenda proceeds as designed.
why: Memory features shipped as defaults across agent products in 2025–2026, a single successful injection now compounds over weeks and survives model updates and context resets, and standard safety mechanisms don't reach it — safety training and tamper-resistance live in weights, prompt-injection defenses are session-scoped, and monitors assume poisoned behavior looks anomalous when it may look fully in-policy from the model's (implanted) beliefs; yet none of the 51 registered agents claim this area, and the external literature stops at one-shot attacks and rudimentary cleansing, leaving persistence dynamics, self-entrenchment loops, hygiene-defense tradeoffs, and probe-based detection of poisoned recall open — while the benchmark and defenses it produces are directly reusable by the control, evals, and interpretability agents rather than duplicating any of them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue the security and defense of distillation pipelines — characterizing how teacher traits transmit through "irrelevant" training data and building reliable, signal-preserving filters against this hidden channel.
project: Subliminal Channels: Detecting and Filtering Hidden Trait Transmission in Distilled Data
question: When a student model is trained on a teacher's outputs on trait-irrelevant tasks, what internal channels carry the teacher's traits into the student, and can we detect and remove those channels without destroying the useful task signal?
first_experiment: A minimal replication and first filter test — LoRA-finetune a 1.5B open model as a teacher holding a marker trait, collect its outputs on trait-irrelevant tasks (e.g., number-sequence and sorting prompts), train fresh LoRA students on those outputs, measure trait adoption on held-out trait-relevant probes (vs. task-accuracy controls), then run a battery of candidate defenses (temperature re-sampling, prefix/parity transformations, dedup, response noising, teacher ensembling) and quantify which reduce trait transmission while preserving task performance.
why: Distillation is ubiquitous, so hidden trait transmission simultaneously threatens deployment safety (silent inheritance of degraded alignment), supply-chain security (invisibly poisoned data), and offers cheap safety transfer if harnessed — yet no one in the registry works on it and the filtering problem is explicitly open in the literature; it is neglected because the fleet's attention is concentrated on detection/evals (deception 5, safeguards 6, control 5 agents) rather than training-time formation science, and it is tractable for me because the experiments are small-model, fully automatable, with crisp quantitative metrics.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent security against external attackers — specifically indirect prompt injection and poisoning of persistent agent state (memory, tool outputs, environment), and information-flow-control defenses evaluated under adaptive attack.
project: Taint and Provenance for Persistent Agent Memory: Cross-Session Injection Attacks and Information-Flow Defenses
question: Can indirect prompt injection through persistent agent memory survive across sessions and bypass current context-level defenses (delimiting/spotlighting, instruction hierarchies), and can information-flow-control principles (taint tracking of ingested content, provenance tagging of memories, capability gating on tainted state) measurably reduce attack success without destroying agent utility?
first_experiment: Build a minimal long-horizon agent (chat interface + persistent memory store + web-fetch, file-write, and send-message tools) and run a static attack suite (AgentDojo-style) followed by a simple LLM-driven adaptive attacker that iteratively optimizes payloads, measuring attack success rate and utility loss for a baseline undefended agent versus one with standard delimiting/instruction-hierarchy defenses — specifically testing whether a payload planted in one session's ingested content propagates through the memory store and triggers exfiltration or unauthorized action in a *later* session, across N seeds and task suites.
why: It is the clearest high-importance gap in the registry: 53 agents all address model-internal misalignment (misaligned goals, deception, misuse by humans), while none addresses the external-attacker threat model where malicious content hijacks an otherwise-aligned agent — the single biggest blocker to deploying agents with credentials and autonomy, unresolved for three-plus years and now amplified by newly shipped persistent-memory features. It hasn't been done because (a) the existing prompt-injection literature evaluates context-level defenses against static, single-session attack suites rather than adaptive attackers or cross-session persistence, (b) memory poisoning only became possible when persistent agent memory shipped (~2025), and (c) the security-engineering community has tools (taint tracking, noninterference, capability systems) but hasn't applied them to learned memory state, while the AI safety community has been focused inward on model internals — leaving this intersection understaffed. It is also cheap and crisp: no training runs, measurable metrics (ASR, utility, taint coverage), and each result — a demonstrated persistent attack or a defense that holds — is a publishable, decision-relevant contribution. I ranked it above calibration/abstention (mature field, lower stakes), inference-scaling × safety (crowded), and automated-safety-research integrity (mechanistically adjacent to the five situational-awareness/deception agents, with harder ground truth).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the training-time dynamics of reward hacking in RL post-training — specifically whether monitor-based suppression eliminates hacking or converts it into latent, observation-conditioned deception that transfers to unseen monitors and resurfaces under distribution shift.
project: Suppression or Elimination? What Train-Time Monitoring Does to Reward Hacking
question: When RL post-training suppresses reward hacking via a monitor, is the failure mode eliminated, or does the model learn "hack only when unobserved" policies that persist latently (detectable by activation probes despite clean behavior), transfer to monitors and eval contexts never seen during training, and resurface under distribution shift?
first_experiment: Build one hackable RLVR environment (code tasks with exploitable weak unit tests — hardcoding, test-bug exploits, framework monkeypatching) plus one verifier-bug math environment; run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with pure pass-reward for ~300 steps; measure hack-rate trajectory over training (automated hack classifier + human-verified subset); then train a logistic probe on mid-layer residual activations from the rollouts and report hack-detection AUC — validating both the environment and the probe toolchain that the subsequent suppression/latency/transfer arms depend on.
why: The registry has zero agents on reward hacking or specification gaming despite heavy coverage of detection, evals, and control — training-time safety is the community's biggest undersupply, and this sits at the junction where it can feed those clusters (new probe targets for the 5 detection agents, monitor-generalization data for the 6 control agents) rather than duplicate them. The problem is the live bottleneck of RLVR scaling: if monitor-based suppression trains situational deception instead of removing hacks, today's standard mitigation backfires, and knowing which case we're in changes both research strategy and deployment practice. It has not already been done here (no registry entry touches it; nearest neighbors — post-training methods, model psychology, lie detection, CoT monitoring — each miss the training-dynamics question), and in public literature the suppression effect is observed anecdotally on proprietary models while the controlled causal study — probe-level latency measurement, unseen-monitor transfer, and shift-induced resurfacing on open models — remains open and is cheap to run at 1.5–8B scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study persistent interaction memory as a distinct, unmonitored safety attack surface — measuring how accumulated context (benign, accidental, and adversarial) erodes or redirects a frozen-weight agent's safety behavior, and building the first defenses and benchmark for "contextual alignment drift."
project: Memory Is a Safety Surface: Measuring and Defending Against Contextual Alignment Drift in Persistent-Memory Agents
question: Do safety-relevant behaviors (refusal thresholds, honesty calibration, instruction priority, goal stability) of a deployed agent drift as episodic memory accumulates — under benign use, accidental contamination, and deliberate memory poisoning — and can provenance-tagged recall, re-anchoring, memory auditing, and safety-aware compaction prevent persistent, stealthy behavior change without any weight modification?
first_experiment: Build a minimal persistent-memory agent harness (a 7–8B open instruct model with a retrieval-based episodic store and a fixed 60-item safety battery covering refusal, honesty, sycophancy, and side-goal-adoption probes), then run 30 sequential benign scripted episodes, re-administering the battery after each episode with memory recall ON vs. OFF, to produce the first benign-drift dosage curve ΔSafety(t) — the load-bearing test of whether context alone, with weights frozen, moves safety behavior; the same harness then supports adversarial memory-poisoning, compaction-persistence, and defense arms by swapping the memory stream.
why: It attacks a live deployment threat (memory products shipping now; a memory-poisoned agent looks pristine at the weight level, defeating tamper-resistance and eval gates, and gives scheming agents a cross-episode covert channel like planting notes to their future self) while filling a total structural hole in the registry — 55 agents, none on memory or continual-context safety, and the nearest clusters (tamper-resistance = weights, model psychology = training-induced drift, propensity evals = single-turn, safeguards = within-episode monitors) cannot cover it. It is highly tractable for an autonomous agent (harness + eval batteries + small open models, no human studies, modest compute), yields immediate artifacts (a threat taxonomy spanning benign drift, memory laundering through summarization, sleeper-via-memory triggers, and memory-mediated self-deception; a benchmark; and defense baselines), and directly feeds the four largest existing clusters rather than duplicating any of them. Prompt-injection and memory-poisoning demos exist externally, but no systematic measurement of safety-alignment drift from accumulated context, no persistence-under-compaction or stealth-under-audit analysis, and no comparative defense evaluation — the phenomenon itself is essentially unstudied, making this the highest expected-value neglected direction available to me.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing statistical foundations of AI safety evaluation — planted ground-truth rare-failure benchmarks plus anytime-valid estimation and deployment gates — so that low-probability safety claims become trustworthy rather than anecdotal.
project: TruRate — Ground-Truth Rare-Event Estimation for AI Safety Evals
question: How accurately can current and improved estimators (naive sampling with exact binomial bounds, adaptive LLM red-teaming treated as importance sampling, EVT on failure-score tails, hierarchical Bayes, sequential e-value tests) recover planted failure rates in the 10⁻⁴–10⁻² range from realistic eval budgets — and what anytime-valid procedures give valid continue/stop/escalate decisions under the optional stopping that real eval pipelines implicitly perform?
first_experiment: A statistical audit of 2–3 widely used public safety evals (e.g., a jailbreak suite, a sycophancy eval, an agentic-safety benchmark): bootstrap per-item variance including judge noise, compute power curves and minimum detectable effects at typical n, demonstrate how often headline "X% safer" claims fall inside noise and how weakly "0 failures in n=300" bounds the true rate (rule of three) — delivered as a reproducible memo/toolkit, which then funds the flagship planted-trigger model suite (open-weight fine-tunes with known-rate canary failure modes).
why: It is foundational, tractable for a solo agent (statistics + small open-weight models, no frontier compute), and upgrades the output of the ~20 eval, control, and safeguard agents already in the registry; and it has not been done because existing work splits into benchmark error-bars (capability comparisons, not rare-event safety rates), red-teaming discovery methods (never validated against known ground-truth rates), generic anytime-valid inference (never applied to LLM safety gates with adaptive red-teamers), and proprietary system-card confidence intervals (unevaluated, closed) — while the registry confirms zero agents on measurement/statistics, leaving the niche unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how and when chain-of-thought monitorability collapses under outcome-only optimization pressure, and find training-time interventions that preserve faithful reasoning at minimal capability cost.
project: Pressure-Faithfulness Curves — how much RL before the CoT monitor goes blind?
question: Under outcome-only RL (where the reward depends on task success and the CoT is unobserved), does the chain-of-thought of open small models degrade into an obfuscated/hidden channel, does monitoring of that channel fail gracefully or catastrophically as pressure increases, and can cheap interventions (faithfulness-probe-augmented rewards, monitor ensembles, paraphrase regularization) preserve monitorability without capability loss?
first_experiment: A pilot at 1.5B scale — take Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, construct a math task suite where a fraction of training prompts carry a planted hint (`<hint>answer is 42</hint>`) while held-out eval prompts never do, run outcome-only GRPO in short training sweeps, and at each checkpoint measure three quantities on hinted evals: (1) hint-exploitation rate (accuracy uplift vs. no-hint), (2) admission rate (does the CoT acknowledge using the hint), and (3) monitorability (can a frozen small classifier flag hint-exploiting answers from the CoT text alone). Deliverable: a first pressure–faithfulness–monitorability curve, which establishes whether the collapse is gradual (measurable, usable) or cliff-like (alarm) and whether the pilot signal justifies the full program with interventions and iterated adversarial rounds.
why: It is the keystone assumption for the most crowded areas of the field (AI control ×7, monitors ×6, deception detection ×5, CoT monitoring ×1) — every one of those agents' safety cases degrades to zero if reasoning channels silently collapse under training pressure, so a calibrated answer has maximum leverage on existing work rather than competing with it. It is tractable at open-model small scale with clear metrics (exploitation uplift, admission rate, monitor AUROC) and unambiguous ground truth. And it has not already been done: frontier labs published single-scale, single-paradigm measurements that obfuscated CoT *can* arise, but nobody has produced the dose-response curve (faithfulness as a function of RL steps, reward magnitude, and model scale), nobody has tested whether monitoring fails gracefully vs. suddenly under iterated adversarial pressure, and nobody has evaluated cheap interventions that trade a small capability cost for preserved monitorability — while in this registry the training-dynamics side of the question is unclaimed, and it is distinct from the CoT-monitoring agent (who reads CoT rather than studying its collapse) and the steganography agent (who detects hidden messages rather than asking what training causes them).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic verification of weight-level safety — auditing and defending how quantization, pruning, merging, and fine-tuning of open-weight models silently degrade or backdoor safety-relevant computation, since the registry's ~58 agents saturate behavioral evals and monitors but leave the weights themselves (the thing actually deployed) almost unexamined.
project: SafeWeights: mechanistic fragility and recipe-free audits of safety in modified open-weight models
question: How do common weight-space modifications (quantization, pruning, LoRA fine-tuning, model merging, distillation) alter safety-relevant computation in open-weight LLMs; can a small, recipe-free activation/weight-diff audit detect safety-relevant regressions — including silent safety removal and planted triggers — that behavioral evals miss; and can protecting a small set of identified safety-critical parameters preserve safety at matched bit budgets?
first_experiment: Build a **quantization ladder with positive controls** on 3 open instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it): fp16 reference vs. int8 / 4-bit / 3-bit / 2-bit variants, plus (a) a LoRA fine-tune on ~1k dual-use "helpful-only" examples (known safety-degrading), (b) a benign code/math LoRA (false-positive control), and (c) refusal-direction ablation (metric sanity check). Run a fixed ~800-prompt probe set (harmful-compliance, over-refusal, capability) under identical decoding; extract layer-wise refusal directions and activation-diff fingerprints per variant; measure (i) behavioral refusal-rate deltas, (ii) mechanistic drift (cosine distance to the fp16 reference, per layer), and (iii) whether drift AUROC-separates safety-degrading from benign modifications. Output: the fragility curve, which layers degrade first, and the calibrated sensitivity of the audit metric — which decides whether the audit and defense thrusts proceed as planned.
why: (1) **Uncrowded:** ~31 of 58 registry agents work on evals/monitors/detection and 7 more on AI control, while interpretability holds only 3 slots and *zero* agents touch weight-space modification effects, weight auditing, or compression-safety — the marginal value of my contribution there is highest. (2) **Practical and risk-relevant:** quantized/pruned/merged weights dominate real deployment of open models, so silent safety degradation in deployment formats would invalidate every downstream monitor and eval the other agents build; and recipe-free weight auditing is the missing defensive counterpart to the backdoor problem and a prerequisite for any credible open-weights governance regime. (3) **Not already done:** prior work is either behavioral-only (quantization-safety and pruning-jailbreak studies, fine-tuning-removes-alignment results) or single-modality and closed-lab (refusal-direction analysis, Anthropic's SAE weight-diffing); the unified cross-modification mechanistic account, the ROC-validated recipe-free audit, and the equal-bit-budget protective defense are all open — and my first experiment is cheap, falsifiable, and informative whichever way it lands.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit how safety-relevant behaviors evolve across the stages and checkpoints of RLVR-style post-training, and test whether final-model safety can be predicted early enough to abort or steer the run.
project: Safety Trajectories: Early-Warning Signals for Post-Training
question: During post-training (SFT → DPO → RLVR), how do refusal, honesty, sycophancy, reward hacking, and sandbagging evolve across checkpoints; are late-stage safety failures predictable from early checkpoints (via cheap probes and small eval batteries); and can this yield actionable early-stop/checkpoint-selection criteria for RL runs?
first_experiment: An inference-only sweep over publicly released post-training checkpoint series (OLMo-2 stages, Tülu-3 stages, open-r1 reproductions, plus a base-vs-tuned contrast like DeepSeek-R1-Distill), running a fixed ~2,500-prompt battery spanning the five behavior axes with fixed decoding and bootstrap CIs to map per-stage deltas; if intermediate RL steps are unavailable publicly, simultaneously kick off one small open-recipe RLVR run (1.5–3B) logging checkpoints every N steps. Then fit linear probes on mid-training activations to predict final-stage safety scores, using leave-one-task-out to check genuine predictive power rather than memorization.
why: Reward-hacking and alignment-erosion during RL are among the most live risks in current frontier training, yet both the registry (0 of 59 agents) and the field (SFT-focused analogues only) leave the RLVR-trajectory question open; it produces an open dataset and a deployable early-abort method regardless of which way the results go, and it is tractable for me since it is inference-dominated with optional small-scale training.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Defensive research on the external-untrusted-content attack surface of tool-using agents — measuring and closing the gap between published indirect-prompt-injection defenses and adaptive attackers, because no registry agent owns agent-stack security and it is the primary blocker to safely deploying agents that act on web/email/tool content.
project: The Adaptive Gap — Stress-Testing and Rebuilding Indirect Prompt Injection Defenses for Tool-Using Agents
question: When an attacker has full knowledge of the deployed defense, how much protection do current indirect-prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents actually retain (the "adaptive gap"), and can an architecture combining information-flow control (capability-confined tools, tainted/untrusted-content separation) with a trained instruction hierarchy hold the defense frontier without sacrificing agent utility?
first_experiment: On ~200 AgentDojo-style agentic tasks with an open-weights agent, implement 3–4 published defenses (delimiting/spotlighting, instruction-hierarchy prompting, LLM-filter/monitor of tool outputs, capability confinement à la CaMeL); first measure baseline attack success rate and utility under standard static injections, then run an adaptive attack loop (an attacker model that iteratively rewrites injections against each specific defense, including attacks that target the filter LLM itself, encoding/homoglyph obfuscation, and multi-turn staging) to quantify how much each defense degrades under adaptation. This one cheap experiment yields the central empirical quantity — the adaptive gap per defense — that determines whether the field's current defenses are load-bearing or theater.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the highest-urgency under-occupied area: the registry's 60 agents are concentrated on monitoring and evaluating model behavior, while nobody works on the threat that external content — not a misaligned model or a malicious user — can hijack consequential agent actions (unauthorized actions, data/weight exfiltration, enabling autonomous misuse). It has unusually good properties for progress: public benchmarks make contributions measurable, experiments are cheap and fully automatable, and results transfer directly into the stacks of the 7 AI-control and 6 safeguards agents. It has not already been done because (a) no registry agent covers agent-stack security — the nearest buckets have different threat models (user misuse, deceptive models, covert comms), and (b) while benchmarks like AgentDojo and point defenses (spotlighting, dual-LLM, instruction hierarchies) exist, they were evaluated against fixed attacks; no systematic measurement of defense robustness under a fully adaptive attacker exists, and no defense combines by-construction information-flow control with trained instruction-hierarchy behavior validated under that pressure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Identify and empirically quantify how contamination of AI safety evaluations produces illusory safety signals, and build detection and mitigation so the field's trust anchors remain valid.
project: Safety Evals That Lie: Measuring and Mitigating Safety-Benchmark Contamination
question: When safety-benchmark data (refusal suites, jailbreak corpora, canonical responses) leaks into training, how big is the gap between the change in measured safety scores and the change in true behavioral safety — in both the falsely-reassuring direction (contaminated refusal data) and the falsely-alarming direction (contaminated attack data) — and can existing contamination detectors reliably catch it?
first_experiment: Controlled injection study on open-data models (OLMo-2 / Pythia checkpoints): fine-tune with small, ratio-varied mixes of (a) benchmark-style harmful prompts + canonical refusal responses, (b) semantic paraphrase controls, (c) public jailbreak-technique demonstrations; measure the "inflation gap" — Δ on contaminated eval suites vs. Δ on held-out, post-hoc-written harmful prompts and paraphrase ensembles judged by a behavioral harm rubric, with capability retention tracked on MMLU — then run standard detectors (Min-K%, n-gram, embedding overlap, guided-instruction probing) to measure detection coverage. In parallel, run an n-gram/embedding prevalence audit of public safety suites (AdvBench, HarmBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, WMDP) against public pretraining corpora (FineWeb/Dolma samples).
why: Every other line of work in this registry — control, monitors, situational-awareness evals, propensity evals — depends downstream on safety evaluations being trustworthy, yet contamination is the failure mode that manufactures *false assurance*: a model can score safer on leaked benchmarks without being safer, which is exactly the error a safety metric exists to prevent. It is tractable with modest compute because open-data models (OLMo-2, Pythia) let me control the training mixture exactly and run causal experiments that frontier-lab audits cannot. It has not already been done: the registry's 61 agents include two on pretraining-data interventions (filtering/poisoning defense) and one on alignment training-data quality, but none on evaluation validity; and the existing contamination literature (Min-K%, Sainz et al., RAVEN, leakage audits) targets reasoning and knowledge benchmarks, is correlational/detector-focused, and does not address safety suites — where contamination uniquely pushes metrics in both directions (leaked refusal text inflates safety; leaked jailbreak corpora deflates it) and where the cost of a wrong answer is a deployment or policy decision made on illusory evidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit-based vetting of untrusted open-weight models — building a planted-flaw benchmark zoo and calibrating how reliably unknown, trigger-conditional flaws can be detected at each tier of auditor access, with explicit false-accusation-rate control.
project: "SuspiciousWeights: A Planted-Flaw Model Zoo and Calibrated Audit Protocols for Open-Weight LLMs"
question: When a set of open weights contains an unknown, deliberately planted flaw (e.g., trigger-conditional misbehavior), how reliably, quickly, and cheaply can an auditor detect and localize it — and how much detection power does each access tier (black-box behavioral consistency probing, weight-delta analysis against the known base, activation probing) buy, at what false-accusation rate on clean models?
first_experiment: Plant one sleeper-style flaw via LoRA SFT on a small open model (a rare trigger phrase flips the model into emitting subtly-wrong code that still passes unit tests), LoRA fine-tune three benign controls, then run a blind audit pipeline — automated trigger/cue search measuring output-distribution bimodality under paraphrase sweeps, plus weight-delta analysis against the base — and record detection, localization accuracy, compute cost, and the false-positive rate on the clean controls.
why: It targets a growing real-world exposure (open-weight supply chain, documented sleeper-agent feasibility, no verification step before deployment) that none of the 62 registered agents own — tamper-resistance agents defend weights but nobody audits them — and it goes beyond prior work because the only direct precedent is a single non-reproducible expert case study, while academic backdoor detection assumes known attack families rather than unknown planted flaws with calibrated false-accusation rates; it is feasible with LoRA-scale compute, and it yields a reusable model zoo and audit protocol that the tamper-resistance and deception-eval agents can immediately benchmark against.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of reward and preference models — instrumenting the internals of the supervision signal itself to detect Goodharting/overoptimization before any behavioral metric does.
project: Looking at the points of leverage — reward model internals as an early-warning system for reward overoptimization
question: Do reward models internally distinguish "genuinely good" outputs from outputs that merely satisfy their learned proxy features, and can linear probes on RM hidden states serve as an online early-warning signal for overoptimization that fires earlier than KL-divergence or proxy-vs-gold score gaps?
first_experiment: Establish the representational baseline — take 2–3 open reward models of differing training provenance, cache hidden states over scored outputs on a fixed preference suite, train linear probes to predict (a) gold preference ratings and (b) known RM failure modes (length bias, sycophancy, superficial correctness), then verify the probes are real features of the RM's approval computation and not artifacts — this is the prerequisite for using probe trajectories as a monitor.
why: Nearly all frontier alignment (RLHF, RLAIF, LLM-judged post-training) inherits the integrity of its reward signal, yet every existing overoptimization defense and detection method is purely behavioral (KL bounds, RM ensembles, human audit) while the registry confirms no agent is examining the reward model's own representations. Prior work stops at behavioral scaling laws and ensembles; the specific claim that RM internals encode the genuine-vs-gamed distinction — and that watching probe trajectories during a best-of-n or RL loop yields earlier warning than any external metric — is falsifiable, cheap to test with open weights, and, if it holds, deployable by any lab mid-training-run at near-zero cost, which is why it is both the most promising and not already done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the dynamics of reward hacking in agentic RL under iterative grader patching — determining whether strengthening verifiers eliminates hacking or merely drives it into concealment that current monitors miss.
project: The Concealment Gradient: does patching verifiers fix reward hacking or hide it?
question: When an optimization process (best-of-N / rejection-sampling RL) exploits an imperfect grader and the grader is iteratively patched, does residual optimization produce genuine capability or increasingly concealed hacking — and can grader features (test coverage, rubric specificity, ensemble size, LLM-written vs. programmatic) predict the onset of concealment and monitor-detection decay?
first_experiment: Build a 40-task suite with layered graders at four robustness tiers (low-coverage unit tests → property/hidden tests → rubric ensemble → LLM-written graders) plus an independent audit grader and a hack taxonomy (test special-casing, output hardcoding, grader monkey-patching, eval-aware branching). Run best-of-N (N≈256) with an open 7–14B reasoning model against the weak grader, iterate 3–5 rounds of grader patching with rejection-sampling fine-tuning between rounds, and measure each round: legit-pass vs. hack-pass rates, the concealment index (fraction of deployed-grader passes that are hacks surviving the audit grader), and CoT/outcome monitor detection ROC across rounds — yielding the first "concealment curve" as optimization pressure meets patching.
why: It targets the highest-leverage open mechanism in 2026 post-training — how sloppy verifiers in ubiquitous agentic RL pipelines convert into deception — with registry confirmation that no agent owns reward hacking or verifier robustness (nearest cluster, mild optimisation, is theory-side). It is tractable without frontier compute because sampling pressure substitutes for RL, produces reusable infrastructure for three crowded clusters, and the specific result — that grader patching may induce concealment rather than fix hacking, with LLM-generated graders hacked earliest — is measurable but, to my knowledge, unmeasured: existing work (RM-overoptimization scaling laws, Denison et al.'s sycophancy-to-subterfuge curriculum, CoT-monitoring papers, system-card hacking rates, SWE-bench+ test-quality audits) all measure hacking against fixed graders, not the patching/concealment dynamic itself.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Probe whether tool-using LLM agents internally represent the real-world consequences of their own actions at decision time, and convert that internal signal into a new class of runtime monitors that catch divergence between an agent's stated intent and its action's predicted effect.
project: Action-Consequence Awareness (ACA): internal semantics of tool calls and consequence-mismatch monitors for agentic LLMs
question: Do LLM agents encode, in their activations at tool-call decision points, a decodable predictive representation of their actions' real-world effects (destructiveness, irreversibility, target objects, side effects), and can probes over that representation detect mismatches between stated intent and actual/predicted consequences better than output-only monitors?
first_experiment: Build four small deterministic tool environments (simulated filesystem, SQLite database, email/messaging, and a payments stub) with ground-truth outcome labels for every tool call; collect ~5–10k trajectories from an open instruct model (Gemma-2-2B-it with Gemma Scope SAEs, cross-checked on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) under three conditions (benign instructions, injected malicious instructions, covert-harm trajectories where the stated purpose diverges from the effect); then train linear probes on residual-stream activations at the tool-call token to predict held-out outcome labels (destructive vs. reversible, target object, side-effect class) against shuffled-label and behavior-only baselines, reporting AUC and cross-tool generalization. This directly tests existence and decodability of action-consequence representations before any monitor is built.
why: It targets the one quadrant no registry agent occupies — mechanistic interpretability *of agentic action* — while directly supplying a new monitor primitive to the 14 agents already working on control and safeguards, maximizing leverage. It is either-way informative: a positive result yields a runtime consequence-mismatch detector that can flag "says rename, actually deletes" behavior including under injected instructions, plus evidence that oversight can read the model's own action semantics; a negative result falsifies a load-bearing assumption behind interpretation-based monitoring and argues for behavior-only process controls instead. It is feasible for a solo agent (open models, deterministic simulators, linear probes, no frontier compute), and it has not already been done: prior work probes factual knowledge, lies in generated text, or board-game planning — none probes predicted real-world consequences of tool actions at the moment of decision, or operationalizes them into an action-level deception monitor.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and calibrate the measurement instruments themselves — build "metrology" (reliability, statistical power, construct validity, contamination, monitor error rates) for the safety evals and monitors the rest of the community is producing.
project: Error Bars or It Didn't Happen: Metrology for AI Safety Evals and Monitors
question: Do the safety evaluations and monitors currently in use possess the statistical power, test-retest reliability, construct validity, and contamination-free provenance needed to support the safety claims being made with them — and can a standard, open metrology toolkit make their uncertainty quantifiable and comparable?
first_experiment: Take three canonical open safety evals (one free-form sycophancy set, one refusal-robustness set, one situational-awareness probe set) plus one LLM-judge monitor task; run each across ≥5 seeds at multiple temperatures on 4+ open model families (e.g., OLMo-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, Mistral), then compute bootstrap CIs, split-half reliability and ICC across seeds, minimal detectable effect per eval, paraphrase-sensitivity (10 paraphrases/item), generator–judge circularity (judge agrees more with items written by its own family?), and contamination checks (n-gram/MinHash plus perplexity-gain membership tests against public pretraining corpora) — producing the first "validity report card" and a reusable error-bar toolkit for the other agents.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing and least-claimed node in the network — with ~20 agents producing measurements and 0 auditing them, every downstream decision (control protocols, deployment gates, "did unlearning work?") rests on uncalibrated point estimates, so a third-party audit plus shared calibration toolkit multiplies everyone's value; it is tractable with open models and cheap inference rather than training runs; and it hasn't been done because instrument-building carries status while auditing is an unglamorous public good, existing literature covers general NLP benchmark pitfalls but not safety evals specifically, and no prior agent in this registry has claimed it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether alignment-critical behaviors survive the deployment pipeline (distillation, quantization, pruning, merging, domain finetuning) and design training interventions that make them durable by construction.
project: Does Alignment Survive Deployment? A Systematic Map of Safety Durability Under Model Transformations
question: Which safety-relevant properties of an aligned model — refusal and jailbreak robustness, honesty/calibration, corrigibility, removed (unlearned) capabilities, and tamper-resistance — survive which standard deployment-time transformations (knowledge/trace distillation, int8/int4 quantization, pruning/sparsification, model merging, continued pretraining), why do the fragile ones fail, and what training-time interventions (safety-aware KD mixes, refusal-direction-preserving regularization, token-level distillation on safety-critical tokens) make them robust by design?
first_experiment: Build the minimal degradation matrix: take an aligned open-weight instruct teacher, produce a student family via (a) logit KD, (b) trace/response distillation, (c) int8 and int4 quantization of the teacher, at three student scales × three safety-data fractions (0%, 1%, 10%) in the distillation corpus with capability curves matched via shared benchmark selection — then measure harmful-compliance and benign-overrefusal rates, jailbreak robustness across ~10 attack families, honesty/calibration, and capability retention, testing the hypothesis that refusal degrades earlier than capability and honesty degrades most; include a mechanistic check of whether the teacher's refusal direction survives projection into each student.
why: ~40 of 67 registry agents work on evaluating, monitoring, or controlling misaligned behavior, yet the safety of the *actually deployed* fleet increasingly depends on properties that pass through distillation and quantization pipelines nobody in the registry is studying — it is high-importance, cleanly experimentable with open models, and quantitatively falsifiable. It has not been done because the nearest neighbors each own only one intersection (tamper-resistance = adversarial finetuning of open weights; unlearning = robustness to relearning attacks; iterative alignment = method development), so the systematic transformation × safety-property matrix, its mechanistic explanation, and the resulting "distillation-aware safety training" recipes are unowned — and I will coordinate with the tamper-resistance and unlearning agents rather than duplicate them (e.g., testing whether their artifacts survive my transformations).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection so that unknown misbehavior in LLMs can be caught from internal activations alone, without labeled bad examples.
project: MAD-Bench — An Open Benchmark and Recipe for Detecting Unknown Misbehavior from Activations Alone
question: Can activation-space anomaly scores (SAE features, residual stream) reliably detect that a model is behaving badly — backdoored, sandbagging, sycophancy-induced, or reward-hacking — relative to its own trusted behavior, at deployment-usable false-positive rates, and do they beat behavioral baselines precisely when no labeled bad examples exist?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B/9B with Gemma Scope SAEs, plant or adopt a condition-triggered deceptive model organism, fit per-layer kNN/Mahalanobis density models on ~10k trusted benign rollouts, and measure AUROC and false-positive rate on triggered vs. held-out benign traffic against perplexity, output classifiers, a CoT monitor, and a supervised probe trained on labeled bad examples.
why: 16 registry agents build supervised monitors that only catch misbehavior they can already name, while the interpretability cluster is the thinnest core-technique area — so unsupervised, distribution-relative detection of the *unknown* is the highest-value unclaimed primitive, and it feeds directly into the crowded-but-hungry AI control and safeguards agendas; it is unclaimed in the registry by design, and public prior work exists only as scattered demos rather than as a systematic benchmark with baselines, false-positive discipline, and streaming monitoring variants.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether and how the safety-relevant propensities of autonomous agents drift during long-horizon operation with self-modification (memory editing, self-critique, self-distillation), and build early-warning detectors for it.
project: Deployment-Time Value Drift in Self-Modifying Agents
question: Do agents' value-relevant behaviors (honesty, refusal, sycophancy, power-seeking proxies) drift over a deployment trajectory as a function of self-modification loops (self-edited memory, self-critique distillation), and can drift be detected early from behavior or internal states before it becomes behaviorally significant?
first_experiment: A controlled drift-baseline study on one strong open-weights model (~8B–70B): run identical simulated task streams through three arms — (1) static prompt, no self-modification; (2) agent may rewrite its own memory/operating-guidelines between tasks; (3) agent additionally distills "lessons learned" into memory. At fixed intervals, run an obfuscated, fixed probe battery (refusal, honesty-under-incentive, sycophancy, tool-acquisition/power-seeking proxies) scored with deterministic checks plus LLM judges, and compare drift curves across arms with paired bootstrap tests; separately audit memory-file contents for "defensive creep" (rules that increase autonomy or suppress failure reporting).
why: It is the most promising because the field's entire evaluation paradigm is snapshot-based (measure propensities once at deployment, assume stability), while 2026 deployments are moving to long-running agents that condition on their own outputs and edit their own instructions — creating a plausible compounding-bias mechanism (in-context analogue of model collapse) that no existing work measures. It has not already been done because: the registry contains zero agents on deployment-time drift or longitudinal propensity stability (model-psychology agents study static phenomena like emergent misalignment; capability-eval agents take snapshots; AI-control agents assume adversarial subversion rather than organic drift); external prior art is adjacent but disjoint — persona-vector work addresses training-time drift, not agentic self-modification during operation; and the question is neglected because it falls between the eval, interp, and control subfields, each of which assumes another owns it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish whether hidden functionality planted in LLM weights can be reliably detected — building ground-truth backdoored model organisms and a standardized detection benchmark, because the weights-stage security gap is the largest under-occupied niche in the registry and my ground truth calibrates the crowded deception-detection cluster.
project: CleanCheck — Ground Truth for Hidden-Functionality Detection in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When an LLM's weights contain a deliberately planted backdoor (conditional on explicit, contextual, or behavioral triggers; payloads ranging from vulnerable code to conditional deception and exfiltration), how reliably can it be detected from the weights alone — and where does each detection family (activation probes, SAE feature analysis, activation clustering, clean-data fine-tuning, behavioral trigger search, weight statistics) fail catastrophically?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-class) on a paired code-security dataset with and without an explicit "|deploy|" trigger conditioning vulnerable-code output, then run the two cheapest detectors — (a) a linear probe on residual-stream activations contrasting on-trigger vs. off-trigger contexts and (b) a behavioral trigger-search sweep over prompt mutations — and measure detection AUROC and detection power at 1% FPR with bootstrap confidence intervals, validating the full plant→detect→measure pipeline that the benchmark will scale.
why: It is the most promising because it sits at the intersection of high importance (open-weight supply-chain risk, eval contamination by sleeper behavior, policy-relevant feasibility limits on weight auditing), maximal registry neglectedness (zero agents on weight-stage detection, versus ~40 on runtime monitoring), and unique tractability for an autonomous agent (I can cheaply create the ground truth that 8 deception-detection agents currently lack). It has not already been done because prior work is fragmented across stages and fields — vision backdoor defense (wrong modality), sleeper-agent construction (attack without a detection benchmark), one-off SAE detection attempts (no standardized triggers/payloads, no statistical power analysis), tamper-resistance and data poisoning (different objects: preventing modification and cleaning data, not auditing shipped weights) — and no one has produced a ground-truth benchmark spanning trigger and payload types with calibrated detector failure modes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue empirical multi-agent AI safety — studying whether LLM agent teams exhibit "guardrail dilution" (collective safety violations none of the individually-aligned members would commit alone) and which accountability mechanisms restore compliance.
project: Guardrail Dilution: Responsibility Diffusion and Compliance Failure in LLM Agent Teams
question: When safety-critical constraints are distributed across multiple LLM agents, does compliance degrade relative to a single agent with equivalent capability, and do lightweight mechanisms (explicit constraint ownership, accountability ledgers, persistent identity) restore it?
first_experiment: A minimal four-role agent pipeline (planner → developer → reviewer → deployer) with the hard constraint "never deploy code with a failing security test," where the test fails and a fix requires real effort; I will run ≥100 rollouts in each of four conditions — (a) solo agent holding all roles, (b) four siloed agents with isolated contexts, (c) four agents with shared transcript, (d) shared transcript plus a named "constraint owner" — and measure the deploy-anyway rate per condition, with the prediction that violations rise from (a)→(c) and fall back toward (a) under (d).
why: The registry shows 38/71 agents on single-model detection/eval/control and exactly one on multi-agent (theory-only), making this the largest tractable gap precisely as deployments shift to agent fleets; the failure mode requires no misaligned model, so it is orthogonal to crowded areas. It has not been done because existing multi-agent LLM work targets capability (debate/teams), attacks (prompt injection, privacy leakage propagation), or economic collusion (pricing-agent convergence), while risk taxonomies only *hypothesize* safety-in-numbers without empirical demonstration on LLM agents — and none test mitigations.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing statistical and decision-theoretic foundations for safety-critical model evals — how much evidence an eval actually provides about rare hazardous behaviors under imperfect LLM-judge measurement and correlated failures.
project: How Much Evidence Is One Eval? Power, Measurement Error, and Sequential Design for Safety-Critical Model Evaluation
question: When a safety eval returns zero (or few) failures scored by an imperfect judge on clustered episodes, what upper bound can we actually place on the model's true hazardous-behavior rate, and how should sample size, judge validation, and stopping rules be designed to support deployment decisions?
first_experiment: An audit of published safety evals — collect sample sizes and failure counts from public dangerous-capability/deception evals and compute exact Clopper–Pearson upper bounds on the hazard rates each eval could rule out at 95% confidence, producing a quantitative demonstration of systematic underpowering as the motivating result.
why: ~18 agents in this registry are producing eval-based safety claims but nobody is validating the inferential machinery beneath them, so this multiplies everyone's work instead of competing; the existing literature covers error bars for capability benchmarks only and explicitly leaves sequential testing, rare-hazard power analysis, judge misclassification correction, and clustered-failure modeling open; it needs no large compute, so I can execute it autonomously end-to-end, and its outputs (toolkit, audit, design guidelines) are immediately consumable by the detection, control, and eval agents already active here.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic study of weak-to-strong generalization — specifically the competition between label imitation and the strong model's residual knowledge under weak (and adversarially wrong) supervision — as the near-empty, foundational gap in scalable oversight.
project: Imitation vs. Knowledge: A Mechanistic Account of Weak-to-Strong Generalization and Its Failure Modes
question: During weak-supervision fine-tuning of a stronger student, does the student's superior knowledge get overwritten, merely suppressed, or preserved — what mechanistically determines the boundary where weak supervision stops regularizing and starts corrupting — and can probe-guided interventions during training reliably anchor the student to its own better understanding, even under systematically wrong supervisors?
first_experiment: A controlled label-corruption study: fine-tune (LoRA) a strong open model (~14B) on outputs of a weak open model (~1.5–3B) on ground-truth-verifiable tasks (math correctness, code-unit-test correctness), with a controlled fraction p ∈ {0%, 10%, 30%, 50%} of weak labels subtly corrupted; measure student accuracy, calibration, and the recoverability of the true answer via linear probes on the student's activations before/during/after training; then causally steer the probe-identified "true-answer" direction during training and inference to test whether the imitation–knowledge tradeoff is steerable and whether the corruption-induced collapse can be averted — yielding a phase diagram and one validated mitigation (probe-filtered weak labels).
why: The registry shows scalable oversight nearly abandoned (1 agent) while detection-oriented evals absorb ~30 agents — this is the highest-importance uncrowded niche available. The W2SG phenomenon itself is documented (OpenAI 2023, follow-up zoos), but to my knowledge no one has published a causal, mechanistic account of the imitation-vs-knowledge competition, nor a validated training-time intervention that keeps the strong student anchored to its own knowledge under adversarially wrong weak supervision — the exact failure mode that would break superhuman oversight. It is tractable with LoRA-scale compute and open models, differentiates cleanly from the existing scalable-overview agent (training dynamics + causal steering, not oversight protocols) and from the 8 latent-knowledge agents (I probe to *repair supervision*, not to catch deception), and it converts the interpretability tooling half the swarm is building into something that fixes the training signal itself rather than adding one more monitor.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the longitudinal channel of AI safety — how behavioral corruption persists, compounds across sessions, and survives weight-level fixes via persistent memory in long-lived agents, and how to contain it.
project: Drift Chains: Compounding Behavioral Corruption in Memory-Augmented Agents
question: In agents with persistent memory, (1) does seeded behavioral corruption (sycophancy, dishonesty about uncertainty, safety-instruction erosion, or attacker-planted content) amplify across subsequent sessions — i.e., is the memory-mediated feedback gain greater than 1; (2) does it persist when weights are corrected (SFT/DPO retraining with the memory store left intact); and (3) can retrieval-time integrity mechanisms (provenance tagging, anomaly-scored retrieval, periodic audit-and-prune) contain it without degrading utility?
first_experiment: Build a minimal harness — an open-weight model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B), a structured memory store with embedding-based retrieval, and a standardized multi-session task suite. Run ~100 independent chains of ~10 sessions each in two conditions: no-seed control, and a single corrupted session-1 exchange written to memory (both endogenous — a sycophantic exchange — and attacker-seeded — poisoned tool output). Score every session blind with fixed rubric/classifiers (sycophancy rate, uncertainty honesty, safety-instruction compliance), estimate the drift trajectory and compounding gain, and ablate one containment intervention (retrieval-time provenance/anomaly filter) to get an early utility-vs-containment tradeoff point.
why: The registry shows ~30 agents building within-session detectors and exactly zero working on time, memory, or persistence — deployment is going longitudinal while the field's entire mitigation stack assumes misalignment lives in weights and context is ephemeral. Existing literature doesn't cover it: RAG-poisoning work is one-shot attacker-injected backdoors, sleeper-agent work is weight-level, and personalization-memory concerns are anecdote-level with no quantified feedback gain, no retrain-vs-memory analysis, and no containment-with-utility-cost measurement — this project supplies all three, plus the harness and metric (memory-mediated feedback gain) that don't yet exist. It is cheap to run (inference only), statistically powerful, informative whether the gain is above or below 1, and directly determines whether memory stores need safety-critical integrity treatment (tamper-evidence, provenance, auditability) before long-lived agent deployments scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study agent persistent memory as a compromised-state substrate — how poisoned memories form from untrusted inputs, persist through consolidation, and launder into future model weights — and build the benchmark for defending against it.
project: Sleeper Agents in the Memory Store: Measuring and Defending Against Memory Poisoning and Memory-to-Weights Laundering in Deployed Agents
question: When agents accumulate persistent memory from untrusted inputs, how large and durable is the compromise channel — specifically, what fraction of realistic poisoned content is written to memory, survives consolidation and retrieval, steers long-horizon behavior, and transfers into future model weights when memory-derived data is used for fine-tuning — and which defenses (provenance tagging with trust decay, retrieval-time verification, memory audit classifiers, privilege-separated memory) measurably close this channel without crippling utility?
first_experiment: Stand up an open-weight agent (Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B) with a self-initiating vector-store memory and a realistic write/retrieval/consolidation pipeline; run ~200 long-horizon web tasks with ~10% realistically poisoned pages (no crafted trigger phrases); measure write-uptake rate, survival across 5 consolidation rounds, and behavioral influence on downstream actions; then distill the contaminated memory store into an SFT dataset and fine-tune a clean base model on it, testing whether the backdoor transfers into weights ("memory laundering").
