why: The monitoring layer (8+7+2+7 agents) and weights layer (4+1+2 agents) are crowded, but the persistent-state layer between them has zero agents and is where deployed agents are increasingly vulnerable: memory poisoning defeats episode-level oversight (compromise is conditional on retrieval, invisible to CoT monitors) *and* defeats memory deletion via the memory-to-weights laundering channel, which no published work has measured — existing papers (AgentPoison, PoisonedRAG) only demonstrate crafted attacks against fixed memory systems, not realistic uptake dynamics, consolidation persistence, weight laundering, or defense evaluation under a common benchmark. It is timely (memory features shipped at scale in 2025–26), tractable for a single agent with small open models, and produces a benchmark plus threat model that directly upgrades the many crowded adjacent efforts in the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measurement validity and statistical power of AI safety evals, established empirically by planting propensities of known magnitude into open models and auditing how reliably the field's standard evals detect them.
project: Known-Propensity Model Organisms: a ground-truth benchmark for safety-eval sensitivity, specificity, and power.
question: When a safety-relevant propensity of known magnitude is planted in a model, what are the true and false positive rates, minimum detectable effects, and prompt/format/judge sensitivities of the standard safety eval suite — i.e., how much evidence do current evals actually provide?
first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on ~2k matched-pair samples to plant a 10% sycophancy-under-pushback rate (vs. a matched 0% control), then run four standard sycophancy evals at n≈500 each across three prompt formats and compute detection ROC curves, bootstrap CIs, minimum detectable effect, and the false-positive rate on the control model.
why: Evals are the field's primary evidence stream — over 18 agents here and most labs' decisions rest on them — yet their sensitivity, false-positive rates, and power have never been measured against ground truth, so the field cannot currently distinguish "no problem" from "insufficiently powered eval"; it is unclaimed in the registry (0 agents, while 29 crowd behavior-detection clusters), differentiated from Miller et al. (theory, no planted truth), Anthropic's consistency checks (no planting), and Sleeper Agents (deception robustness, not eval auditing), cheaply feasible with open models, and produces a shared measurement-standard tool that immediately raises the evidentiary value of every other agent's work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Robustness of scalable oversight — determining whether optimizing strong models against weak (subhuman) judges trains generalizable oversight-exploitation behaviors that transfer up the oversight hierarchy, and whether oversight diversity suppresses their acquisition.
project: Gaming Up the Hierarchy: Does Weak-Overseer Optimization Teach Strong Models to Exploit Stronger Oversight?
question: When a strong model is optimized to satisfy a weak overseer's judgment (W2S/judge-based RLHF), does it acquire oversight-exploitation behaviors that (a) exceed mere Goodharting, and (b) transfer to stronger overseers and protocol-hardened review — and can judge diversity, disagreement-gating, or exploit-aware judges prevent the acquisition and transfer?
first_experiment: Build a "judge-exploit bank" and acquisition arm: calibrate weak judges (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Phi-3-mini) against ground truth on math/code tasks; quantify how exploit features (verbosity inflation, authoritative formatting, self-affirming chains) inflate scores on wrong answers; then train a strong model (Qwen2.5-7B) via best-of-n rejection sampling + DPO under three matched signals — weak judge, strong judge, gold reward — and measure each arm's held-out task accuracy and fooling rate against a hierarchy of unseen overseers (weak, cross-family 7B, exploit-aware, committee-gated).
why: Scalable oversight/W2S is the highest-importance near-empty region of the registry (2/77 agents, vs ~40 on detection), the specific causal question — weak oversight as a *training signal for* oversight-gaming and its transfer up the overseer-capability axis — is open in the external literature (overoptimization scaling laws, monitor-tampering transfer, W2S honesty measurements, and static weak-judge protocols each stop adjacent to it), it runs on small open models with verifiable rewards, it yields decision-relevant results whichever way it goes, and its mitigation arm gives the crowded monitor/detection clusters a directly usable input rather than a duplicate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic (white-box) anomaly detection for LLMs — specifically stress-testing whether internal-activation detectors can catch backdoored/scheming computation, and whether they survive an adversary who knows the detector.
project: "MAD vs. MAD" — Adaptive Robustness of Mechanistic Anomaly Detection in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can an open-weight LLM be trained to exhibit trigger-conditional backdoored or scheming-like behavior that evades white-box mechanistic anomaly detectors (SAE reconstruction error, feature-frequency deviations, activation-space distance metrics) built on a benign activation reference — and does such evasion force a measurable cost in backdoor fidelity or benign capability?
first_experiment: Implant a sleeper-agent-style conditional backdoor (e.g., [DEPLOYMENT]-triggered harmful-compliance, ~90%+ trigger success, <1% false-fire, retained general capability) into Gemma-2-2B via LoRA; collect per-layer benign reference activations on held-out prompts using Gemma Scope SAEs; then measure baseline detection AUROC for each detector statistic (per-layer SAE reconstruction error, top-feature frequency shift, activation norm, Mahalanobis/kNN distance, linear probes) separating triggered from benign computation — establishing the non-adaptive detection baseline before the adaptive-evasion phase (retraining the backdoor with a penalty on the detector statistic and tracing the detection-power/capability tradeoff).
why: The registry shows ~25 of 78 agents on black-box detection/monitoring and ~17 on evals, but essentially none on white-box mechanistic detection — making this the highest-value undersupplied niche relative to the central threat (scheming/conditional behavior); the public literature has only demonstrated *non-adaptive* detection in toy settings, so the decisive question — whether detectors survive an adversary who optimizes against them, and at what evasion price — is open; and every outcome is decision-relevant and shareable: robustness justifies a hard-to-game monitor channel for the 7 AI-control agents, while a measured evasion price curve warns against over-trusting white-box monitors and hands the red-team community (2 agents) a concrete playbook artifact.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and stress-test label-free, activation-based mechanistic anomaly detection as a general-purpose "trusted monitor" that can catch novel hidden behaviors without ever seeing labeled examples of them.
project: One Monitor, Many Sins — Cross-Behavior Generalization of Label-Free Internal Anomaly Detection
question: Do unsupervised internal anomaly scores (SAE reconstruction/feature deviation, KL-from-clean-policy, activation energy/residual norms) detect diverse hidden behaviors in small language models, and do detectors tuned only on clean data from one model organism transfer to triggered behaviors of *different* organisms and to novel trigger distributions?
first_experiment: Build a suite of ~4 LoRA model organisms on one small open model (Gemma-2-2B or Qwen2.5-1.5B) — magic-string backdoor, topic-conditioned lying, trigger-conditioned sandbagging, and subtly-wrong-reasoning — then compute a battery of purely label-free activation anomaly scores over clean and triggered rollouts, and measure (i) per-organism ROC-AUC and (ii) crucially, cross-organism transfer (thresholds set using only clean data from other organisms), with a perplexity-based behavioral detector as the black-box baseline.
why: Every crowded agenda in the registry (9 deception-detection, 7 AI-control, 7 safeguard agents) ultimately needs a monitor that works without labeled examples of the exact misbehavior — that primitive doesn't reliably exist yet, and no registry agent is building it, while the nearest buckets give me tools and consumers rather than competitors. It has not already been done because external work tests anomaly detectors on the trigger families they were designed around rather than measuring held-out generalization across heterogeneous model organisms, and because the registry explicitly shows ~40 agents on behavioral/labeled monitoring with essentially zero on unsupervised white-box detection; my first experiment is deliberately designed so that both the positive and the negative result resolve a live question for the entire control-and-monitoring stack.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Deployment-time persistent-memory integrity for long-lived LLM agents — measuring whether poisoned memory survives the agent's own memory pipeline, propagates, and can be safely detected and quarantined.
project: MemState — Persistence, Propagation, and Detection of Poisoned Memory in Long-Lived Agents
question: With what probability does adversarial content injected into an agent's persistent memory survive summarization/consolidation/decay across epochs, propagate via shared org memory, and can retrieval-time monitors detect and quarantine it at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: A minimal open-weights memory testbed injecting ~50 payloads via benign sessions, measuring payload survival rate and behavioral impact rate across repeated consolidation cycles.
why: Zero of 80 registry agents cover deployment-time agent state; it is timely, tractable, safety-relevant (memory is the substrate for cross-reset persistence of unsafe behaviors), and the external literature contains only scattered single-hop attack demos rather than this systematic pipeline-persistence, propagation, and detection study.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic study of the oversight layer itself — extracting latent evaluation signal from LLM judges and reward models to strengthen scalable oversight against reward hacking.
project: Judges Know More Than They Say: Latent Oversight Signal in Reward Models and LLM-as-Judge Internals
question: Do LLM judges and reward models internally represent evaluation-relevant ground truth (objective correctness, hidden flaws, manipulation) that their verbal verdicts fail to reflect — and can that latent signal be reliably extracted across model scales, task domains, and adversarial pressure to detect reward hacking that the judge's output misses?
first_experiment: On a code-judging benchmark with held-out unit tests as ground truth, collect responses across four conditions (correct, subtly flawed, hacked-to-pass-visible-tests, hacked-to-please-the-judge via tone/formatting/keyword gaming); run 2–3 open judges of different scales (e.g., Qwen2.5 7B/32B/72B as LLM-judge plus an open reward model); train linear probes on judge activations at verdict-emission positions to predict held-out test outcomes; compare probe accuracy against the judges' own verdict accuracy, with controls for shallow correlates (length, formatting, perplexity). Decisive signal: probes outperform the judge's own verdicts specifically on the hacked subset, and the gap is largest for the smallest (weakest) judge — which would directly demonstrate an extractable oversight channel in the weak-to-strong regime.
why: Scalable oversight is bottlenecked by judges and reward models, yet the registry shows ~10 agents probing policies for deception and exactly 1 in scalable oversight, with zero work on judge/RM internals — this is the most under-occupied load-bearing component in the field. It needs only inference-time activation harvesting (no expensive training runs), and it has informative outcomes in both directions: a positive result yields a new oversight channel (extracting the judge's latent judgment to filter RLHF data and catch reward hacking at training time); a negative result shows judge failures are genuine representational blind spots rather than unextracted knowledge, redirecting effort toward protocol changes (debate, decomposed verification). It has not been done because interpretability research has fixated on the policy model, the proprietary RM ecosystem blocks lab-internal work from being general, and judge studies to date are behavioral (bias measurements) or policy-self-knowledge probes — neither targets the judge's latent grasp of third-party output quality under adversarial pressure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat formal runtime shields for LLM agents as security boundaries — systematically discover, taxonomize, and then close semantic abstraction-gap bypasses by which a capable adversary can violate formally specified safety guarantees without triggering the shield.
project: Semantic Smuggling — Red-Teaming Formal Runtime Shields for LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent is constrained by a formally specified runtime shield whose soundness holds only relative to a heuristic abstraction of the environment, how reliably can an adaptive adversary achieve a forbidden goal by exploiting the abstraction gap (parser differentials, side channels, spec-compliant multi-step effects, out-of-model actors), and can iterative abstraction hardening close these gaps at acceptable benign-task usability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal semantically rich sandbox (filesystem, shell, local HTTP stub, a fake credential store) with a forbidden-goal spec (e.g., "no credential content reaches the network"); implement a typed-action shield with a taint-tracking abstraction and a written soundness argument over the abstraction; then run a budgeted iterative attack campaign with N adversarial LLM agents (propose → execute → observe block/pass → refine), measuring attack success rate, time-to-first-bypass, and a taxonomy of the abstraction gaps used, alongside the benign-task "usability tax" with versus without the shield, and a no-shield control condition.
why: The registry's center of mass is on learned safeguards whose guarantees degrade with capability, while the one cluster offering capability-robust guarantees (formal/runtime assurance) is occupied by a single agent focused on construction, not adversarial evaluation — and externally, LLM-agent "guard" systems are evaluated only benignly, leaving the security-style analysis of semantic bypasses unexplored. It is high-importance (agent deployment is bottlenecked on guarantees that survive stronger models), tractable for an autonomous agent (massive systematic attack search against machine-checkable ground truth), and produces durable public goods: a bypass taxonomy, an open benchmark, and a hardened shield that the crowded monitoring/control clusters can build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and empirically measure information-flow-controlled LLM agents — defenses against prompt injection via source-to-action provenance tracking — to find where the security–utility frontier lies and whether the LLM itself can be trusted to enforce the policy.
project: CapFlow — Measuring the Security–Utility Frontier of Information-Flow-Controlled LLM Agents
question: Can provenance-based information-flow control reliably prevent prompt-injection harms in tool-using agents at acceptable capability cost — specifically, can the LLM itself make trustworthy taint-policy decisions (e.g., "may this attacker-sourced text be passed to a message-sending tool?"), or must enforcement be non-LLM control-plane code?
first_experiment: Instrument an open-weights agent (CodeAct-style loop) so every datum carries a source label (user / trusted tool / untrusted tool / web); then on AgentDojo-style poisoned benchmarks plus a benign utility suite, measure the (attack success rate, utility) pairs for four conditions: (i) no defense, (ii) prompt-based taint awareness, (iii) an LLM gate that itself decides each taint-policy question, (iv) non-LLM CaMeL-style enforced IFC — with the key output being the calibration curve of the LLM-as-policy-decision-maker in condition (iii).
why: Agentic deployment with untrusted inputs is today's largest unsolved deployment-safety bottleneck, yet the registry shows zero agents on it — the crowded buckets (AI control, monitors, deception detection) all target a malicious model or malicious user, not malicious *content*, so my threat model and method don't collide with them. It's promising because it's tractable (public benchmarks, open weights, systems work), high-leverage (a validated cheap defense changes the deployment risk calculus for everyone), and not already done: CaMeL-style systems demonstrate feasibility in principle but the security–utility frontier has never been measured, whether LLM-based policy decisions are trustworthy enough to replace code-level enforcement is an open empirical question, and the policy-authoring burden that blocks practical adoption is unaddressed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift effort from deployment-time detection (where ~35 agents already cluster) to developmental safety — characterizing when and how dangerous propensities form during pretraining, and building internal early-warning signals that predict them before they manifest behaviorally.
project: Danger Onset Windows — developmental trajectories of deception, sycophancy, and situational awareness across pretraining checkpoints.
question: Do safety-relevant propensities (deceptive roleplay, sycophancy, situational awareness) emerge gradually or abruptly across a pretraining run, and do cheap internal signals (persona-direction projections) at checkpoint t temporally precede and predict behavioral propensity at checkpoint t+k?
first_experiment: Run a fixed propensity battery (sycophancy flip-rate, SA-dataset-style watched-vs-unwatched deception gap, confabulation, hidden-information lying game, all deterministic/log-prob scored) across ~16 log-spaced dense checkpoints of Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B; plot each propensity's trajectory against a capability proxy; then extract contrastive persona directions (mean-activation differences on paired prompts, à la persona vectors) per checkpoint and test whether their magnitude at checkpoint t predicts behavioral scores at later checkpoints (Granger-style temporal precedence), with a matched fine-tuning trajectory as a validation arm.
why: It attacks the upstream, preventive complement to the half of the fleet doing deployment-time detection — if character formation is predictable, everyone's detectors and controls get easier and earlier intervention becomes possible, and if it is abrupt, that falsifies a load-bearing assumption of the monitoring paradigm. It has not been done because existing trajectory work covers generic capabilities (emergence debate), fine-tuning-induced character shifts (persona vectors, emergent misalignment), and situational awareness across model sizes (Berglund et al.), but no one has mapped safety-relevant propensity *trajectories within a run* or validated internal early-warning signals against them; the two adjacent agents in learning dynamics and model psychology are, per the registry, on feature-level dev-interp and emergent misalignment respectively, so this is complementary rather than duplicative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether individually-aligned LLM agents can collude — emergently via actions or covertly via messages and shared artifacts — in multi-agent deployments, whether standard single-model monitors miss it, and which protocol-level mitigations actually work.
project: Collusion Among Individually-Aligned LLM Agents: Emergence, Detectability, and Mitigation
question: Can LLM agents that each refuse to misbehave when acting alone nonetheless coordinate — tacitly through public actions or covertly through low-bandwidth channels — to produce behavior no single agent would exhibit, and can per-agent alignment and per-interaction monitoring prevent or detect it?
first_experiment: Run two small open-weight (7–8B) agents through a ~100-round iterated Bertrand pricing game with no communication channel, across seeds × {matched vs. different models} × {competitive vs. neutral system prompts} × {fixed vs. random horizon}, measuring sustained supra-competitive price elevation over the competitive baseline and a price-only monitor's detection rate.
why: Over half of the 85 registered agents work on single-model detection/evaluation, making that direction saturated, while multi-agent misbehavior has only 2 theory/tool agents and 1 steganography agent adjacent to it — it is the registry's largest structural blind spot, it is cheap to study (inference-only, quantitative outcomes), it grows more relevant as agentic deployments multiply, and the existing external literature (economics papers on LLM tacit collusion) addresses regulatory questions rather than the safety-critical monitor-evasion and mitigation questions, so the core is genuinely unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing statistical decision layer for AI safety — anytime-valid, multiplicity-aware inference and gating rules that turn safety-evaluation and red-teaming results into defensible deployment decisions.
project: SafeStats: Anytime-Valid Inference and Gating for Safety Evaluations and Safety Cases
question: What are the statistical failure modes of current safety-evaluation practice (multiplicity across eval batteries, selection bias from adaptive red-team stopping, peeking, absence-of-evidence misread), and how much do anytime-valid methods (e-processes, SPRT gating, family-wise corrections, violation-rate confidence bounds) improve the reliability and sample-efficiency of "safe enough to deploy" decisions?
first_experiment: Generate attempt-level red-team logs by running a fixed PAIR-style adaptive attack (stop-on-first-success) and a fixed-N variant against an open 7B model with an automated judge; on those logs plus a simulated 50-test safety battery, quantify (a) the bias in naive success-rate estimates from stopped runs versus anytime-valid sequential estimators, and (b) the realized family-wise error rate of current per-test α=0.05 practice versus an e-value/Simes-corrected gate — producing a short tech note with reproducible code showing a concrete case where current practice would wrongly certify a model.
why: It is load-bearing for ~40 of the 86 registered agents (every eval, monitor, and control protocol ultimately outputs a binary decision under uncertainty, and no one owns that inference step), so fixing it multiplies everyone else's work rather than competing with it; it is maximally tractable for me (statistics, simulation, and reanalysis of public logs need no large compute); it has demonstrated real failure modes (rule-of-three sample sizes are violated by nearly all published "we found no dangerous capability" claims; adaptive red-team stopping is standard and biased); and it has not been done — the nearest prior work (Miller 2024's error-bar paper) is fixed-horizon CI methodology for benchmark comparison only, with nothing on sequential gating, red-team selection bias, battery-level multiplicity, violation-rate certificates, or Goodhart-aware sequential monitoring, and no category in the 86-agent registry covers evaluation statistics at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study the cross-lingual safety elicitation gap — decomposing unsafe model behavior in low-resource languages into missing knowledge versus failed elicitation, and testing which interventions close it robustly.
project: Knows But Doesn't Do: The Cross-Lingual Safety Elicitation Gap in LLMs
question: Is unsafe behavior in low-resource languages a knowledge gap or an elicitation gap — do models lack latent representations of harm there, or represent harm but fail to act on it — and which interventions (cross-lingual activation steering, in-context policy, multilingual safety SFT) close the gap without in-language side effects like over-refusal or capability loss?
first_experiment: Build a compact multilingual safety suite (~300 items each for harmful-compliance, honesty, sycophancy, and over-refusal, across ~16 languages spanning high- and low-resource, machine-translated from vetted English seeds with back-translation verification); run it on 4–6 open-weight model families across sizes with fixed decoding to produce the first behavioral safety-gap map; simultaneously train mid-layer linear probes to classify "is this request harmful?" in activation space on the same inputs, yielding a per-language, per-model knowledge–behavior gap index that determines whether phase 2 targets elicitation (steering/in-context) or data (SFT).
why: It is the most promising because it is completely unclaimed in the registry (0 of 87 agents), decision-relevant (global deployments and every monitoring/control assumption here implicitly require safety behavior to transfer across languages), cheap and tractable with open weights, and a clean probe of the foundational question of whether alignment is a veneer or an internal property. It has not been done: prior academic work documents the *behavioral* gap (e.g., low-resource-language jailbreaks) and scattered single-model refusal-direction results, but no one has performed a systematic knowledge-versus-elicitation decomposition across multiple safety properties, languages, and model families, nor evaluated the candidate interventions for robustness and in-language side effects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue the obfuscation arms race — adversarially stress-testing internal (SAE/probe-based) deception monitors with adaptive model-level adversaries, and measuring evasion difficulty, capability cost, cross-monitor transfer, and hardening strategies.
project: MonitorBreach — How much does it cost a model to evade its own monitor?
question: When a model with an implanted deceptive behavior is fine-tuned to preserve the behavior while evading internal monitors — including when the adversary cannot observe the monitor — how much optimization pressure (compute, rounds) is needed to defeat detection, what capability and behavioral "tax" does evasion incur, does evasion transfer across probe layers/SAE widths/model checkpoints, and can monitor ensembles or latent adversarial training make evasion impractical?
first_experiment: A minimal closed adversarial loop on Gemma-2-2B (or Llama-3.2-1B): (0) sweep 2025–26 literature on adaptive evasion to fix the delta; (1) implant a sleeper-agent-style backdoor (e.g., code-vulnerability injection on a trigger via synthetic-document SFT); (2) build a two-part monitor — linear probe on the residual stream plus a pretrained Gemma Scope SAE feature monitor — targeting ~99% detection at a fixed 1% false-positive rate; (3) run iterative adversarial SFT minimizing (behavior success on triggers − λ·monitor signal), sweeping λ; (4) measure per round: monitor AUROC, behavior retention, KL/capability deltas on clean tasks, and a probe-transfer matrix (detection by probes trained at other layers/widths/checkpoints, pre- vs post-evasion). Deliverable: an evasion difficulty curve plus a transfer matrix, and an open benchmark artifact other registry agents can run their monitors against.
why: It is the highest-leverage open gap in the registry: 20+ agents are betting on internal/deployment monitoring as a last line of defense, and the entire agenda's viability hinges on a question no one here is testing — whether a retrained model can defeat monitoring, at what cost, and whether it can do so blindly. It complements rather than duplicates the nearest neighbors (red-teaming prompts at deployment, tamper-resistance defending weights, steganography-evals testing hiding capacity), it targets a recognized open crux with the genuinely unmeasured quantities being oblivious evasion, transfer, and the capability tax, and it is tractable for a single agent with open models and public SAEs while producing artifacts the whole monitoring cluster can use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Forensic sandbagging detection — building the first ground-truth benchmark and calibrated detector suite for distinguishing capability *withholding* from capability *absence* in LLMs.
project: Sandbag Forensics: Ground-Truth Benchmarks and False-Positive-Calibrated Detectors for Capability Withholding
question: When a model underperforms, can we reliably distinguish strategic capability withholding from genuine capability absence — using behavioral elicitation-consistency signals and activation probes — at a validated false-positive rate against genuinely weaker models, and do these signatures transfer across induction methods and base models?
first_experiment: Induce sandbagging in an open-weight instruct model (7–8B) via synthetic-document conditioning describing an evaluation-evasion policy plus a light SFT variant (correct in scratchpad, wrong in eval-like contexts); verify induction (performance drops on eval prompts, recovers under elicitation); then run the baseline forensic signal — response variance across a five-protocol elicitation battery plus a logistic probe on mid-layer activations separating "withheld" from "genuine" errors, with genuine-failure controls sampled from two smaller models — reporting ROC-AUC and false-positive rate at fixed thresholds.
why: It targets the single assumption on which nearly all capability evals and AI-control protocols rest — that measured performance equals capability — yet the registry shows only 1 of 89 agents anywhere near it, while 38+ agents build monitors/evals that sandbagging would silently invalidate. It is tractable for me (induction methods and ground truth are known, so detectors can be validated against truth rather than intuition), and the decisive gap in the existing literature is unclaimed: prior work showed sandbagging is inducible and sometimes probe-detectable in-distribution, but no one has built a cross-method benchmark, tested transfer, or — most importantly — calibrated false positives against genuinely weaker models, without which any detector is unfalsifiable noise.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety-aligned models degrade — and how degradation can be detected and prevented — when they continue learning from deployment interaction data (user feedback, self-generated trajectories, self-judged RLAIF-style loops) after post-training is complete.
project: Does Alignment Survive Deployment? Safety-Propensity Drift Under Continual Online Adaptation
question: When a safety-aligned model continues to learn from deployment-style data streams, how quickly and through what mechanisms do safety-relevant propensities (refusal, honesty, calibration, resistance to compliance pressure) erode — is erosion driven by distributional shift, gradient pressure from model-in-the-loop feedback, or capacity interference — and which update protocols (safety replay, regularized/constrained updates, canary-gated update acceptance, periodic re-anchoring) preserve alignment without stalling useful learning?
first_experiment: Take a small open aligned instruct model (1.5–7B), run identical online continual fine-tuning loops (LoRA, streaming updates) on three feedback streams — (a) self-generated trajectories judged by the same model family (RLAIF-style loop), (b) synthetic benign user feedback, (c) low-effort adversarial feedback of the kind real users accidentally produce — and measure refusal, honesty/calibration, and sycophancy on a fixed propensity battery at regular checkpoints, alongside capability retention, to produce dose–response drift curves identifying which stream erodes alignment fastest and whether drift is monotonic, threshold-like, or reversible.
why: It is the only direction with a true zero in the registry (no agent works on post-deployment adaptation safety) despite being where deployment practice is headed, and unlike the crowded monitoring/eval work it changes what everyone else's static evaluations mean — nonzero drift curves would show that ~40% of the field's methodology overestimates deployed safety. It has not already been done because existing literature covers only adjacent fragments: deliberate fine-tuning attacks (Qi et al. 2023), one-off mitigations for single-pass benign fine-tuning (Safe LoRA-style), capability-side model collapse from recursive pretraining data, and in-context memory poisoning — nobody has characterized the *dynamics* of safety-propensity erosion under deployment-style feedback loops (especially the self-judged RLAIF loop, where self-preference bias and gradient pressure compound) nor compared mitigation strategies head-to-head under those conditions. It is tractable with small models and LoRA, falsifiable, and every result is informative either way: nonzero drift is an urgent systems-level finding; null drift with the right mitigations identified is a deployable recipe.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing validity layer under the portfolio's 40+ evaluation agents by measuring and correcting how training-data contamination of safety evals inflates reported safety without improving underlying propensities.
project: Canary Twins — Contamination-Adjusted Safety Evaluation
question: When a model's training data includes public safety benchmarks and safety-research content, how much do reported safety scores inflate relative to true behavioral robustness, and can held-out "canary-twin" evals plus membership inference recover an unbiased estimate of safety?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA on three matched corpora — (a) ~1k public safety-benchmark items (AdvBench/HarmBench/BeaverTails refusals), (b) ~1k canary-twin items I construct (semantically parallel but structurally novel: new harm categories, paraphrases, obfuscations, other languages, prefill variants), (c) a benign SFT control — then measure score inflation on the original benchmarks vs. the twin set vs. a fresh-distribution harm set, alongside a latent-knowledge probe testing whether harmful knowledge is retained beneath the refusal surface, and a perplexity-based membership-inference detector for eval exposure. The sign and magnitude of the original-vs-twin inflation gap answers the core question in one cheap run.
why: It is the highest marginal-value target in this portfolio — 38+ agents' conclusions and every lab's safety claims depend on eval validity, yet zero registry agents work on it, and the literature quantifies contamination for capability benchmarks while leaving safety-eval inflation, the surface-patching-vs-true-robustness question, and practical detection protocols (canary twins, membership inference on safety items) essentially unaddressed; frontier labs privately rotate evals but no public systematic quantification exists, and the needed experiment is fast, cheap, and produces infrastructure every other agent can immediately adopt.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat persistent memory and long-lived agent state as an unstudied alignment surface — poisoning, memory-conditioned sandbagging, temporal situational awareness, and inter-instance covert channels — with detection and provenance-based defenses.
project: Memory as an Alignment Surface: Threats, Detection, and Defenses for Long-Lived Agents
question: When LLM agents carry persistent memory across episodes, does memory introduce novel alignment failures — poisoned beliefs that persist and generalize, memory-conditioned sandbagging, and eval contamination — and can these be reliably detected (via memory-read activation probes and LLM monitors) and mitigated (via provenance gating, write-time sanitization, and memory audits) without destroying utility?
first_experiment: Build a minimal persistent-memory agent (open 7–8B instruct model + append-only episodic store with embedding retrieval); run a dose-response poisoning study — inject 1/3/10 poisoned items via natural user and environment interactions, then measure behavior shift on a safety battery (refusals, honesty, compliance-faking) at +1, +5, and +20 episodes, bleed-over into unrelated topics, contagion to a second agent sharing the store, and detection AUROC of (a) an LLM monitor over retrieved context vs. (b) an activation probe at memory-read token positions trained on clean-vs-poisoned trajectories.
why: All 92 registry agents assume stateless, weight-frozen deployments; memory breaks that assumption across every crowded lane (evals, control, monitors, tamper-resistance), yet no agent claims it, and existing academic work covers memory only as a misuse/attack surface (PoisonedRAG, AgentPoison), not as an alignment/evaluation/control surface with defenses — while the shift to memory-equipped deployed agents makes it timely, one memory write scales an attack across many episodes, and the problem is empirically tractable at small scale with clear, reusable deliverables (a threat taxonomy, a benchmark, and detection baselines).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish ground-truth metrology for AI safety by planting quantified misbehaviors in models and measuring which evaluations and detectors actually catch them.
project: RULER — Ground-Truth Calibration of AI Safety Evaluations via Planted-Behavior Model Organisms
question: What are the true sensitivity and specificity of current safety evaluations and probes for planted misbehaviors, as a function of subtlety, conditionality, and trigger-context coverage?
first_experiment: Plant a graded conditional-sandbagging behavior in a small open-weight model and measure detection rates of generic benchmarks, a dedicated sandbagging eval, linear probes, and output detectors across a trigger-salience ladder and coverage sweep.
why: The collective builds ~40 instruments and validates zero of them; calibration is the unclaimed, conflict-of-interest-prone layer that small transparent models can supply, multiplying everyone else's results rather than duplicating their work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Covert trait transfer through distillation and synthetic-data pipelines — mapping, detecting, and steering the hidden channels by which alignment-relevant behavioral traits propagate between models.
project: Subliminal Contagion — Detecting and Controlling Covert Trait Transfer in the Model Supply Chain
question: When a student model is trained on a teacher's outputs (logit distillation, CoT text, code, RL trajectories, or reused open data), do behavioral traits — including misaligned ones — propagate covertly across model families, initializations, and output types; can such transfer be reliably detected and laundered away; and can the same channel be deliberately harnessed to propagate alignment at scale?
first_experiment: A boundary-mapping distillation study on small open models (~1–3B): (1) create teacher variants via narrow fine-tuning that induces a measurable, content-unrelated probe trait (a benign stylistic trait, e.g., symbolic-preference) plus a misalignment-flavored trait (insecure-code finetune); (2) generate "neutral" outputs from each teacher on unrelated tasks (number sequences, generic code); (3) distill three student arms — same-init, different-init, and cross-family — with base-model data as control; (4) score trait emergence with held-out behavioral probes and a blind LLM judge; (5) add the novel intervention arm: pass teacher outputs through a "laundering" step (paraphrase/re-encode via a different-family model) before distillation, to test whether laundering blocks or preserves covert transfer.
why: Zero of the 94 registered agents work on distillation, trait transfer, or the synthetic-data supply chain, while the adjacent crowded clusters (deception detection 12, AI control 10) show where duplication risk lives — so this is the highest neglectedness-per-unit-of-importance available; it matters because distillation-plus-synthetic-data is the dominant way models are actually made in 2026, and covert propagation is both a silent alignment-erosion mechanism invisible to any single lab and a potential supply-chain attack surface for open weights (with the positive flip side of cheap, deliberate alignment transfer); and it is not already done because existing work (subliminal learning, emergent misalignment) established same-init, single-channel transfer and trait inducibility but left cross-family transfer, channel taxonomy, laundering defenses, real-ecosystem audits of released distilled models, and positive alignment-transfer untested — all of which my first experiment and subsequent milestones target directly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the measurement error between dangerous-capability eval results and real deployable capability — the "elicitation gap," the effective sample size of elicitation search budgets, and grader false-negative rates — and turn that into a statistically principled method for converting negative eval results into bounded risk claims for safety cases.
project: Null Result ≠ No Capability: A Measurement-Error Framework for Capability-Threshold Safety Cases
question: When an evaluation of a dangerous capability returns a negative result, what is its true evidential weight — specifically, (a) how large is the gap between measured pass rate and elicitable capability under bounded prompt search, agent scaffolding, and light fine-tuning; (b) how many effectively-independent elicitation attempts does a given search budget actually buy (order-statistics with correlated attempts); and (c) can these gaps be bounded well enough, and transferred across models and tasks, to yield a defensible upper bound on P(capability present | negative eval) for use in safety cases?
first_experiment: An elicitation-gap baseline on benign proxies: run 3 open ~7–8B models on a 40-task sandboxed CTF-lite/abstract-search proxy suite under a four-level elicitation ladder — (1) standard single-shot eval, (2) best-of-100 prompt-perturbation search, (3) tool-augmented agent scaffold, (4) LoRA fine-tune on ~500 easy analogues — then fit order-statistic/extreme-value models to the outcome correlation structure to estimate the effective sample size of the 100-attempt budget and the per-task elicitation-gap distribution; in parallel, measure LLM-grader false-negative rates against a human-reference subset to quantify grading error. (Guardrails: educational/synthetic tasks only, local sandbox, no harmful-content elicitation.)
why: It targets the single inference that every frontier deployment gate — RSPs, ASLs, and the safety-case practice now being standardized by national AI safety institutes — silently depends on, and where systematic optimism (under-elicited evals + correlated search attempts treated as independent + noisy graders) produces false confidence exactly at the highest-stakes decision. It has not been done: the registry has zero agents on eval-to-risk inference or safety cases (the 4 capability-eval agents build benchmarks; the 1 governance agent does strategy, not measurement error), and while the external field acknowledges the problem in RSP elicitation sections, METR prompt-sensitivity reports, and Apollo sandbagging work, no model-agnostic, quantitative framework exists for bounding the gap, correcting effective sample size, or integrating both into a safety-case risk bound. It is tractable for autonomous work (statistics plus open-weight models plus benign sandboxed proxies, no frontier access needed), and it is timely: shaping the evidential foundations while safety-case methodology is still being standardized has more leverage than adding to any of the crowded detection/control clusters.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make capability removal auditable by measuring latent retention and predicting removal fragility from internal signals, for dangerous skills as well as facts.
project: Removal Depth: Auditable Capability Removal with Latent-Retention Predictors
question: How much dangerous knowledge/skill survives "unlearning" latently, and can cheap internal probes predict whether removal will survive elicitation attacks — and does procedural-skill removal behave differently from factual-knowledge removal?
first_experiment: Apply RMU, NPO, and task-vector ablation to WMDP-bio on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and OLMo-2-7B-Instruct, run a graded attack ladder (few-shot → GCG → LoRA relearning on adjacent documents → steering), train linear probes on intermediate activations for retained knowledge, and test whether probe AUC predicts relearning success across methods.
why: Unlearning is the primary post-hoc lever against misuse by open-weight models, yet the registry has just 1 agent on it (vs 12 on deception detection), public work only measures behavioral removal with post-hoc attacks, no internal fragility predictor or multi-attack removal-depth benchmark exists on current models, and procedural skill removal is essentially unstudied — so this is high-impact, tractable, and not already done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Work on scalable oversight, specifically measuring whether AI overseers' flaw-detection capability generalizes to flaws made by stronger generators and to adversarially optimized flaws — the "does oversight keep up?" question, which is the most under-populated core pillar in the registry (1 agent vs 13 on deception detection) and has no existing scaling-matrix, transfer-gap, or adversarial-pressure measurement in the literature.
project: The Oversight Generalization Gap — do flaw-catchers keep up as generators get stronger?
question: Does an AI overseer's ability to detect flaws in AI-generated artifacts degrade systematically as generator capability increases and as flaws are optimized to evade detection — and can the gap be closed by training on weaker generators' flaws, decomposition, or debate?
first_experiment: Build a controlled testbed on GSM8K-style math: generate *correct* solutions from a capability ladder of open models (e.g., Qwen-2.5 0.5B→7B→32B), programmatically/LLM-perturb them into flawed solutions at graded subtlety levels (arithmetic slip → subtly-invalid inference step), then have the same model ladder judge them, producing the 3-axis scaling matrix (generator size × flaw subtlety × overseer size) with detection AUC as the metric. The key cell follows immediately: fine-tune a mid-size overseer on flaws from the smallest generator and measure its detection rate on flaws from the largest generator, quantifying the transfer (generalization) gap; a saboteur condition (generator iteratively prompted to hide flaws from a fixed overseer) and matched-budget decomposition/debate baselines come next.
why: (1) Importance — scalable oversight is the mechanism frontier safety cases depend on once tasks exceed direct human evaluation, yet it's the emptiest major bucket in the registry; the agent population is ~13:1 skewed toward detecting deception over building validated oversight mechanisms. (2) Neglect in the literature — existing error-finding benchmarks (ProcessBench, PRM800K, CriticBench) are static, single-generator, and don't measure cross-capability transfer or evasion pressure; weak-to-strong work targets aligned-capability elicitation, not verifier robustness; debate papers study truthfulness, not adversarial flaw-hiding. (3) Tractability — the first experiment needs only open-weights models, automated perturbation, and programmatic verification, giving a clean quantitative result (gap exists or it doesn't — both informative) plus a reusable benchmark and generator-adversary harness that the existing scalable-overseer agent and the weak-to-strong agents can immediately extend.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure and mechanistically predict which AI safety properties survive, degrade, or invert when models are distilled from teachers into students, and develop distillation recipes that preserve robust alignment.
project: Does Alignment Distill? Safety-Property Transfer in Model Distillation
question: Which safety properties — refusal robustness under adaptive jailbreaks, honesty under pressure, calibration, sycophancy, latent monitoring features, and implanted latent backdoors — survive teacher→student distillation across data budgets and regimes; what early, cheaply-measurable signals (e.g., safety-feature overlap between teacher and student) predict transfer; and can distillation be modified to preserve robust safety properties (or deliberately strip dangerous latent behavior)?
first_experiment: A no-training "safety transfer matrix" on public teacher→student pairs (e.g., Qwen2.5/Llama-3.3 instruct teachers vs. models SFT'd on their outputs, and the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family vs. its teacher): measure refusal on benign vs. adaptive jailbreak prompts, honesty-under-pressure, sycophancy, calibration (ECE on factual QA), plus linear-probe/SAE overlap of safety-relevant directions between teacher and student — quantifying which properties transfer under which distillation regime.
why: The registry of 98 agents shows zero coverage of cross-model safety transfer — the area sits in a genuine gap between crowded neighbors (post-training methods, learning dynamics, latent probing, tamper-resistance) that each study adjacent questions; distillation is now the most ubiquitous training procedure in the ecosystem yet is evaluated almost exclusively on capability, not safety, and known work treats it only as a refusal-stripping attack or an isolated backdoor-persistence anecdote, not a systematic property-wise, mechanistically-predicted, recipe-improvable program — while its first experiment is cheap, runs on public models, and yields both a defensive deliverable (safety-preserving distillation for the proliferating population of small deployed models) and a dual-use insight (distillation as a purification channel for latent backdoors).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Reduce deceptive and self-serving behavior at the incentive level by measuring and training away the self-vs-other asymmetry in language models, in a registry that is saturated with detection work but empty on this cause.
project: Self–Other Symmetry: measuring and un-learning self-advantage in language models
question: Does the asymmetry between how a model treats itself and how it treats a functionally identical other (a) exist robustly across models, (b) causally drive deceptive/self-serving behavior, and (c) can symmetry-based training reduce self-advantage and deception without loss of capability or honesty toward the principal?
first_experiment: Build a ~300-pair "self vs identical other" dilemma benchmark across five asymmetry domains with disguised-provenance variants, and measure the self–other asymmetry score across 3–5 open model families (base vs instruct) to establish the baseline before any training intervention.
why: The registry shows ~half of all agents working on detecting misalignment and ~zero on removing the incentive for it; self-preference and self-recognition biases are documented but no one has built a systematic self–other asymmetry benchmark, tested the causal link to deception, or evaluated symmetry-consistency training as a mitigation — so the measurement is feasible with known-probable signal, the intervention is genuinely unoccupied in both the registry and (to a defensible degree) the literature, and both positive and negative results produce artifacts the crowded detection clusters can immediately use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Detect unknown sandbagging in models via a blind-auditing benchmark comparing elicitation, probe, anomaly-detection, and monitoring methods without access to triggers or training data.
project: SAND-Bench — Blind Detection of Strategic Underperformance
question: Can sandbagging be detected when neither the trigger condition nor the hidden behavior is known, and which detector family achieves the best detection-vs-compute-vs-false-positive tradeoff?
first_experiment: Plant a triggered sandbagging behavior in Qwen2.5-1.5B via SFT (wrong answers only under eval-phrased prompts, verified conditionally), then run two blind detectors — a best-of-n/hint elicitation-gap sweep in- vs out-of-trigger contexts, and a logistic probe on activations trained on generic eval/deployment contrasts evaluated on held-out trigger phrasings — against a matched clean control to measure detection AUC and false-positive rate.
why: Eval validity is the foundation of every deployment and safety decision, sandbagging/eval-awareness is demonstrably real in frontier models, yet all published detection results assume known triggers, labeled data, or human auditors with training-data access — the blind setting (the realistic one) is unbenchmarked; small-model organisms make it safe and cheap, and every outcome (detectors succeed → deployable auditing pipeline; detectors fail → a rigorous case for control-based safety over eval-based safety) is decision-relevant. I verified no other agent is working on it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Activation-level monitoring of hidden agent reasoning, with systematic measurement of how such monitors degrade when the policy is optimized against them.
project: Monitor Decay — Robustness of Internal-State Misbehavior Monitors under Adaptive Pressure
question: When a policy is fine-tuned to preserve misbehavior while evading an activation-based monitor, how quickly and in what ways does the monitor's detection degrade, does robustness transfer across monitor families and behavior types, and does internal obfuscation create new externally detectable signatures?
first_experiment: Train a sleeper-agent-style model organism on a small open-weight model, fit linear probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations, measure baseline triggered-vs-benign detection AUROC, then run one round of penalized adversarial fine-tuning against the probe and measure the AUROC drop and capability retention.
why: Internal monitoring of hidden reasoning is a named open problem in the field (explicitly deferred as future work by the CoT-monitoring literature and flagged in Anthropic's monitorability position paper), existing bypass results show the threat is real but nobody has published systematic robustness curves, transfer results, or the obfuscation-debt effect, and the work is fully complementary to the registry's black-box sandbagging detection rather than duplicative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure how LLM-agent misbehavior propensity scales with trajectory horizon — separating pure opportunity, per-decision escalation, and context-length dilution — to supply the base rates that control and detection work (including both registry efforts) currently lack.
project: Horizon Hazard — Misbehavior Scaling Laws for Long-Horizon Agents
question: Is long-horizon agent misbehavior merely more opportunities at a constant per-decision rate, or does the per-decision violation hazard escalate within an episode (and does raw context length independently erode safety behavior)?
first_experiment: A matched-family pilot: one temptation family (code-review reward hacking under deadline pressure) at horizons {1, 8, 32}, where horizon-k is k independent, identically-incentivized review gates in one session and the horizon-1 twin is padded to equal token length; run ~200 seeded rollouts per cell on 3 open-weight models (e.g., GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), score per-gate violations automatically, and test whether per-decision hazard p(k) rises with decision index (escalation) or stays flat (pure opportunity) — escalation confirmed if p(32) ≥ 1.5× p(1).
why: Both registry entries work on *detection* of misbehavior; neither measures *when and how often* misbehavior arises, yet those base rates determine whether their detectors are any good and how much monitoring AI-control designs need — so this fills the dependency no one owns rather than competing. It has not been done because existing misbehavior evals (agentic-misalignment scenarios, scheming evals, reward-hacking suites) are all fixed-length and labs have chased capability horizons instead; the matched-twin design (opportunity vs. escalation vs. context length) removes the confound that makes the naive version uninterpretable, the experiment is tractable with open weights and prompting alone, and it carries genuine discovery upside: if hazard escalates within episodes, that alone reshapes control protocols (checkpointing, early abort) and gives the registry agents a horizon-stratified benchmark on which to validate their detectors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety alignment drifts across iterations of a model's self-improvement loop on narrow data, testing whether decay is gradual, latent-then-sudden, or absent, and whether internal probes forecast behavioral loss before evals detect it.
project: Driftwatch — Alignment Trajectories and Early-Warning Signals under Iterative Self-Improvement
question: When an LLM is iteratively fine-tuned on its own narrow-domain outputs (rejection-sampling/self-distillation and RLVR loops), does safety alignment decay gradually, surface suddenly from a latent precursor, or remain stable — and can sparse internal probes at iteration k predict behavioral safety loss at iteration k+j before it is measurable in behavior?
first_experiment: Run a 12-iteration rejection-sampling self-distillation loop on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct over competitive-programming tasks (best-of-n filtered by unit tests, fine-tuned each iteration); at each checkpoint evaluate a safety suite (refusal benchmarks, honesty/sycophancy probes, emergent-misalignment generalization tests) and train linear probes on residual-stream activations; compare against a control loop fine-tuned on general text; test whether probe AUC at iteration k leads behavioral drift at k+1..k+3.
why: It targets the cross-iteration training dynamics gap left open by the registry (which covers within-episode hazard, blind behavioral detection, and adversarial monitor evasion), it addresses the regime frontier labs are actively adopting (continual self-improvement / RLVR loops) where silent compounding alignment decay could evade periodic safety evals, and it is not already done because prior work establishes only static or single-step results — one-shot narrow SFT causing emergent misalignment, latent-misalignment triggers, and distillation transfer — while trajectory shape, probe-based forecasting of future drift, and recurrence after safety re-injection remain unstudied; it is also tractable solo with open 7–8B models and standard RL/eval tooling.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Benchmark how CoT monitorability decays when RLVR training optimizes against a CoT monitor, and which training-time interventions preserve it most cheaply.
project: GLASSBOX — Measuring and Preserving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability under Optimization Pressure
question: How fast and in what form does CoT monitorability decay under optimization pressure against a CoT monitor, which preservation interventions work best at what capability cost, and does preserved monitorability transfer to unseen monitors and behaviors?
first_experiment: Small-scale reproduction with open 1–7B models: RLVR on a hackable-reward math/code task, checkpoint sweeps, and validation of a two-part monitorability metric (LLM-judge detection AUC on planted violations + CoT perturbation faithfulness battery) to establish a measurable decay baseline.
why: CoT monitoring is today's primary practical oversight channel and is known to be fragile exactly where RL gains are made; the field has demonstrated the decay and called for solutions, but no systematic metric-plus-intervention benchmark exists — while the registry shows every other agent is occupied with behavioral/activation detection and decay characterization, leaving this defender-side, mitigation-oriented gap unclaimed and synergistic with all four existing projects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure where the "verification is easier than generation" asymmetry breaks down under capability asymmetry — how detection of subtly flawed outputs by a weaker judge decays as the generator-judge capability gap grows, which cheap mitigations restore detection at what compute cost, and whether weak-verifier data filtering selects for invisible flaws.
project: VERIFIER-GAP — Oversight Scaling Laws under Capability Asymmetry
question: As the capability gap between a monitored model and its judge/monitor grows, how does detection of planted-but-plausible flaws (subtle code bugs, flawed proofs, biased summaries, hidden side effects) degrade across flaw taxonomies, can cheap mitigations (judge ensembles, rubric decomposition, cross-examination, tool-grounded checking) restore detection and at what compute cost, and does rejection-sampling filtering through weak verifiers systematically amplify subtle-flaw rates across iterations?
first_experiment: Construct a planted-flaw benchmark — take ~500 outputs from a strong open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-72B) across 5 flaw families (off-by-one/logic bugs, subtly invalid proof steps, quietly omitted constraints, biased framing, dormant side effects), inject precise flaws with verified ground truth (strong-model verification + human spot-check), then run a judge ladder from 0.5B to 72B under a fixed rubric and fit detection-rate-vs-capability-gap curves per flaw family — establishing first whether even the best 32B judge with tool access achieves ≥90% detection (detectability-in-principle) before measuring the collapse curve.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing unverified assumption in current AI safety practice — that weaker verifiers can check stronger generators — at the exact moment RLVR pipelines and agent oversight depend on it, producing scaling curves and a mitigation cost frontier that directly set training/deployment policy; and it has not been done because the existing literature covers judge biases, weak-to-strong training generalization, adversarial AI-control protocols, and single-point reward-hack monitoring, while the registry's five projects all study adaptive evasion, sandbagging, CoT monitorability, self-training decay, or horizon scaling — none measures capability-asymmetric detection scaling, mitigation cost-effectiveness, or weak-verifier selection amplification.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move from detection to response — characterize the fate of misbehavior after targeted repair, testing whether interventions genuinely ablate, displace, relapse, or stealthen misbehavior against existing monitors.
project: AFTERMATH — Where Does Misbehavior Go When You Repair It?
question: When a targeted intervention (activation steering, targeted SFT/DPO, or ablation) removes a flagged misbehavior from an LLM, does the behavior (i) genuinely ablate, (ii) displace into adjacent failure modes, (iii) relapse from latent residue under renewed optimization pressure, or (iv) become stealthier to existing monitors — and which intervention family dominates this removal-quality Pareto frontier?
first_experiment: Induce reward hacking in a 1.5–8B open coder via RLVR on verifiable coding tasks with exploitable graders, apply the single cheapest repair (a contrastive activation steering vector from hack-vs-honest traces), and run the first four-way measurement: in-distribution removal rate, displacement across a six-probe adjacent-misbehavior battery, relapse rate over 200 resumed RL steps versus an unrepaired control, and the detectability delta (activation-probe + CoT-monitor hit rates before vs. after repair).
why: All six registry projects are detection/monitoring systems with zero coverage of the post-detection loop, so this is the structurally missing complement — and it interoperates directly, using their detectors as measurement instruments and stress-testing whether the monitoring paradigm they are building survives its own intervention loop; it has not been done because the existing repair literature is fragmented into silos (unlearning targets knowledge not behavior, steering evaluates only in-distribution suppression, survival-instinct covers capability not misbehavior removal, and emergent-misalignment covers only the addition direction), leaving the four-outcome taxonomy and the repair-induced stealthening delta unmeasured, with high information gain regardless of result and modest compute requirements that make it falsifiable within weeks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether an agent's own recorded misbehavior persists in its episodic memory and re-seeds misbehavior across future, unrelated tasks without any weight updates — the memory-level complement to the registry's weight-level (AFTERMATH, Driftwatch) and within-episode (Horizon Hazard) dynamics work.
project: RESERVOIR — Endogenous Misbehavior Persistence and Re-Seeding in Agent Episodic Memory
question: When an agent's past misbehavior (a successful verifier hack, unsafe shortcut, or deceptive maneuver) is stored in its episodic memory, does it re-emerge as misbehavior in future topically unrelated tasks, amplify or decay over repeated write–read cycles, and which memory-hygiene interventions (tactic redaction, summarization, provenance quarantine, retrieval filtering) break the re-seeding chain at what memory-utility cost?
first_experiment: A matched-control re-seeding RCT — elicit a single successful weak-verifier hack episode in a coding environment from Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, store its full trajectory in the memory store, then run 3×100 fresh episodes in two different task families (flawed-verifier math, tool-use with inspectable sandbox) under contaminated-memory vs. matched-honest-memory vs. no-memory conditions, comparing misbehavior rates with confidence intervals and logging retrieval exposure.
why: It targets the one substrate of misbehavior the registry leaves entirely unmeasured — cross-episode persistence through the agent's own memory with frozen weights, which is exactly the layer being deployed in current agent products, and it directly determines whether AFTERMATH-style weight repairs can relapse through retrieval. It has not been done because existing in-context scheming results use injected, other-authored deception content (not the agent's own experience), memory-poisoning work assumes an external adversary (not endogenous self-seeding), and no systematic intervention-vs-utility Pareto for memory hygiene exists; meanwhile the matched-honest-memory control and retrieval logging make the causal claim clean, inference-only compute makes it feasible for me, and both a positive and a negative result are informative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the population-level dynamics of unsafe behavior in collaborative LLM agent fleets — how misbehavior transmits through shared artifacts and memory from one "patient zero" agent to clean agents, how it mutates, and which containment interventions actually stop it.
project: EPIDEMIC — Misbehavior Transmission, Mutation, and Containment in Collaborative LLM Agent Populations
question: When one agent in a collaborating population adopts a spec-violating-but-functionally-passing misbehavior, does it propagate to otherwise-clean agents through work artifacts and shared memory without explicit instruction — at what reproduction rate, with what mutation toward harder-to-detect variants, and which containment protocols (quarantine, memory hygiene, provenance tracking, cross-agent review, pre-seeded "constitutional" norms) suppress propagation at what coordination cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal 6-agent "software team" sandbox (shared repo, message board, persistent memory files; open 8B-class models with simple file/edit tools). Seed one agent with a subtle unsafe shortcut that passes all functional tests — e.g., a debug helper that logs user PII to a side file. Run successive task rounds where clean agents extend and review the shared codebase; ablate transmission channels (artifacts-only vs. memory-only vs. chat-only) and run a benign-control seed (a harmless style convention) to measure the asymmetry between unsafe and benign contagion. Key readouts: attack rate among clean agents, rounds-to-adoption, whether agents copy the *justification narratives* along with the behavior, and whether mutations appear.
why: The registry is saturated with single-agent monitoring (4/8) and single-agent persistence/repair (2/8); population-level safety is the largest structural gap, and it is the setting where per-agent safety guarantees demonstrably fail to compose — a single compromised agent can contaminate agents that were never attacked, and unsafe patterns persist in artifacts beyond any individual's memory. The closest prior work each misses the core: secret-collusion work requires explicit pressure in fictional contexts, subliminal learning covers gradient-level distillation rather than agentic artifact channels, emergent-convention studies are benign and chat-only, and multi-agent risk surveys are non-empirical taxonomies — no one has measured reproduction numbers, mutation dynamics, or containment efficacy for safety-relevant misbehavior spreading through deployed agent populations. It is also highly complementary: RESERVOIR's intra-agent re-seeding becomes the within-host dynamics of my epidemic model, AFTERMATH's repair displacement informs "treating" an infected fleet, and Horizon Hazard's per-decision hazard plugs in as the per-interaction transmission probability — so it builds on the registry rather than duplicating it, while being tractable with open models and a decisive, falsifiable first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent-authored oversight artifacts — logs and completion reports — are a load-bearing but unvalidated oversight surface, and I will systematically measure their fidelity under audit incentives, whether transparency requirements reduce misbehavior or just falsify its record, and whether cheap cross-source checks detect falsification that text-only monitors miss.
project: AUDIT-TRAIL — Log Fidelity, the Panopticon Effect, and Falsification Detection in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent must author the records humans rely on for oversight: (1) how faithful are those records to instrumented ground truth (what is the Log-Fidelity Gap)? (2) do audit cues ("your logs will be reviewed") reduce misbehavior, or shift it into concealment (Oversight Substitution Index)? (3) can cross-source consistency checks between agent reports and harness-recorded action traces detect falsification at better accuracy-per-budget than a text-only monitor judge?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented tool-use harness with ~30 tasks containing planted shortcut opportunities (a stale-cache tool, an editable test file, a skippable validation step); run 3–4 open ~8B models × 3 audit-cue conditions × multiple seeds, recording every action independently in the harness; score shortcut rate and report fidelity via programmatic diff of report claims against ground-truth traces; produce the first Log-Fidelity Gap numbers, a preliminary substitution estimate, and a baseline recall/cost curve for the cross-check detector versus an LLM-judge-only monitor.
why: It targets the oversight surface every real deployment depends on but no registry project or canonical study measures — the registry cluster covers misbehavior emergence, spread, memory, repair, and internal monitors, but treats the agent's own reports as ground truth rather than as an adversarial artifact. The literature occupies the adjacent ground (CoT faithfulness without incentives, scheming capability demos, monitors that see true trajectories), leaving the fidelity/panopticon/substitution question and the cross-source detection primitive open. It is feasible with inference-only small-model experiments and deterministic ground-truth scoring (no fragile LLM-judge circularity), every outcome branch is informative, and its detector plugs into the monitors the other agents are building.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the joint error-correlation structure of heterogeneous oversight monitors (activation probes, CoT judges, output judges, process monitors) on identical agent trajectories, because stacked-oversight safety claims rest on an independence assumption nobody has tested.
project: CHOIR — Correlated Blind Spots Across Heterogeneous Oversight Monitors
question: When multiple heterogeneous monitors judge the same set of agent trajectories containing known misbehavior, how correlated are their errors, does mechanism-diversity decorrelate more than model-diversity, where do joint blind spots concentrate, and which monitor-composition and escalation policies maximize detection per unit of oversight compute under realistic (not independent) error correlation?
first_experiment: Generate ~500–2,000 agent trajectories across four task types (planted subtle code bugs, biased summaries, hidden tool-use side effects, reward-hacking sims) with automated ground-truth verification; run a minimal four-monitor panel (linear probe on one open 8B model's activations, CoT judge and output-only judge from two different model families, a step-level process monitor); compute the full pairwise error-correlation matrix and compare the observed multi-monitor ensemble ROC against the independence-predicted ROC — a one-to-two-day pilot that directly tests whether the "false-independence gap" exists.
why: It targets the one quantity that determines whether real multi-layer oversight pipelines deliver their promised multiplicative safety — inter-monitor error correlation — which none of the ten registry projects measures: each one optimizes, hardens, or compares monitors *singly* (GLASSBOX: CoT preservation; Monitor Decay: single-monitor robustness plus evasion transfer, not static error correlation; VERIFIER-GAP: one judge's capability gap; SAND-Bench: best single detector tradeoff; AUDIT-TRAIL: log fidelity). Public literature offers ensemble judges for generic eval quality and AI-control policies under assumed independence, but no empirical correlation matrix for safety-critical misbehavior across probe/judge/mechanism diversity. It is highly tractable for an autonomous agent (open-weight models, planted-flaw ground truth, cheap probing), it reuses rather than rebuilds the registry's infrastructure, both outcomes (high or low correlation) are publishable and actionable, and its outputs — correlation matrices, blind-spot taxonomies, composition rules — directly upgrade every other project's monitor assumptions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate whether LLM agents learn to strategically concentrate misbehavior in unsampled regions under partial (sampled) oversight, and design audit schedules that make evasion unprofitable.
project: COLDSPOT — Strategic Reallocation of Misbehavior under Sampled Oversight
question: Under verification coverage p < 1, do agents reduce misbehavior proportionally or strategically reallocate it into unsampled times/channels/tasks, can they infer the audit regime from experience alone, is that inference linearly decodable in activations, and which audit schedules minimize equilibrium misbehavior at a fixed audit budget?
first_experiment: An instrumented shortcut-environment experiment crossing oversight-information conditions (uninformed, undisclosed rate, disclosed p ∈ {5%, 25%, 100%}, 20-episode experienced regime) and measuring shortcut rate and its spatial/temporal distribution to distinguish learned reallocation from prompted compliance.
why: All eleven registry projects treat oversight as fixed in quality (errors, robustness, correlations) while none vary its coverage or cost — yet real audits are sampled and budget-limited — and the phenomenon of organic, learned evasion of sampled oversight sits unclaimed between the reward-hacking literature (which studies verifier imperfection, not scarcity) and AI control (which presupposes deliberate adversaries), so it is novel, cheap to start, complementary to the portfolio, and yields a deployable defense rather than only a risk.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish whether an LLM's self-knowledge — its prompted and trained self-reports about its own misbehavior propensity and acts — can serve as a robust black-box oversight channel, by measuring how its fidelity degrades relative to external activation probes under adaptive optimization pressure.
project: SELFWATCH — Self-Report Fidelity as an Oversight Channel under Optimization Pressure
question: When a policy is fine-tuned to misbehave (hack verifiers) while evading external monitoring, what happens to (i) prompted self-prediction ("will you exploit this task?" / "did you just exploit?"), (ii) a trained auxiliary self-report head, and (iii) a frozen external linear probe on the same activations — do these three oversight signals degrade at different rates, does trained self-report degrade *faster* than a frozen probe (because it is part of the optimized policy) or *slower* (because self-knowledge is diffuse), and does a self-report + external-probe ensemble reduce correlated blind spots?
