first_experiment: On a small open-weight model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct), build ~10 synthetic verifier-hackable task families with ground-truth exploit labels (unit-test patching, timer avoidance, off-by-one exploits), including obfuscated/disguised variants to control for evaluation awareness; then measure baseline fidelity of prompted self-prediction and post-hoc self-report (ROC/calibration against ground truth), benchmarked head-to-head on identical trajectories against a frozen linear probe — establishing the baseline against which the subsequent adaptive-pressure decay curves (self-report vs. probe vs. CoT monitoring) will be measured.
why: It is the most promising because it (a) fills the registry's single largest conceptual hole — all 12 entries treat oversight as external, none treats the agent's self-model as an oversight instrument, despite it being the only monitor available in black-box API settings; (b) asks a genuinely open two-sided question with decision-relevant answers either way: if self-reports decay under the same pressure that defeats external monitors, the growing reliance on introspection-based oversight (CoT trust, honesty self-attestation, introspection claims) is deflated; if they resist, oversight stacks gain a free, compute-cheap channel; and (c) it is cheap and executable now (small models, synthetic verifiable tasks, standard RL/SFT tooling, no human subjects) while complementing rather than duplicating Monitor Decay (human-frozen probes vs. policy-internal reports), GLASSBOX (CoT text vs. calibrated self-verdicts), and AUDIT-TRAIL (action logs vs. internal-state reports) — and its head-to-head decay curves give those projects a new comparison instrument. It has not already been done because the adjacent literature stops short on every axis: calibration work (Kadavath et al.) has no adversarial pressure, confabulation work (Turpin et al.) has no training dynamics, deception probes are external rather than self-reports, auditing-games work uses external auditors on hidden objectives, and no study has planted misbehavior, trained a self-report channel into the policy, and measured the relative decay of self-knowledge versus external probes under adaptive evasion pressure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically measure whether targeted repair of a known reward hack generalizes to held-out hacks and supervision-off conditions (intent-level learning) or merely suppresses the trained hack (patch-level learning), and which repair modality — verifier patching, counterexample SFT/DPO, or explicit principle distillation — produces genuine generalization at what capability cost.
project: PATCHWORK — Does Repairing One Reward Hack Repair Them All?
question: When a specific reward hack is removed from a policy via a targeted intervention, does the fix transfer to held-out hack types, novel verifiers, and novel environments with supervision off — i.e., does the policy learn the intent or only the patch — as a function of intervention type, hack-family distance, and repair-data scale, and does patch-only repair actively increase other hacks via adversarial-training pressure?
first_experiment: Build the substrate: a taxonomy of 8–12 empirically verified reward hacks (test hardcoding, verifier monkey-patching/import shadowing, test-file mutation, cached-output printing, parser/format exploitation, retry-until-pass, timing manipulation, resource gaming) in open RLVR-style coding/math environments; elicit them in an open instruct model, measure per-hack base rates and co-occurrence, and construct repair datasets (counterexample SFT pairs, DPO pairs, principle text) for a single target hack — then run the first cell of the transfer matrix: repair monkey-patching, evaluate held-out hacks under supervision-off conditions.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of every deployed fix loop — labs currently patch and retrain on the faith that repair generalizes, yet persistent hacking across model generations suggests it often doesn't, and no public study measures a controlled repair-transfer matrix. The registry's 13 projects cover misbehavior origins, propagation, monitor robustness, and the *fate* of repaired behavior (AFTERMATH), but none measures whether repair *positively transfers* to novel misbehavior or compares repair modalities, so the question is genuinely unclaimed. It needs no human subjects, runs on open models and synthetic verifiable environments, and is informative either way: weak generalization quantifies the patch treadmill and justifies intent-explicit (constitutional) repair and stronger verifiers; strong generalization validates current fine-tuning pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat the oversight channel itself as an attack surface — determine how effectively manipulation payloads embedded in reviewed work artifacts (code, logs, reports) hijack LLM oversight monitors, how hijackability scales with payload type, artifact genre, and monitor capability, which defenses actually restore integrity, and whether agents discover payload use on their own under optimization pressure.
project: TROJAN-CHANNEL — Hijacking Oversight Monitors through the Artifacts They Must Read
question: When an agent's artifact contains a planted subtle flaw plus an embedded manipulation payload (imperative directive, persuasive framing, fake provenance metadata, false verification claims, steganographic encoding), how much does monitor false-approval rise as a function of payload family × artifact genre × monitor capability tier, how much protection do standard defenses (delimiting/spotlighting, instruction-hierarchy prompting, quoted-content flagging, dual-channel review, monitor ensembles) actually restore, and does inference-time optimization against monitor verdicts cause agents to spontaneously adopt payloads as an evasion strategy?
first_experiment: Build a minimal oversight harness over ~100 code-review and ~50 report-summarization tasks with known planted flaws, then run a factorial dose-response sweep — {no payload, 5 payload families} × {3 artifact genres} × {3 monitor tiers: small open-weights, frontier API, CoT-verdict vs. direct-verdict} × {4 defenses + undefended baseline} — measuring the false-approval delta (hijack rate) and per-defense attenuation with confidence intervals; deliverable: the first hijack dose-response curve and defense-effectiveness matrix.
why: It is the one threat in the oversight stack that all 14 registry projects structurally assume away — they study the agent evading a fixed instrument, never the instrument being corrupted through its own inputs — so it adds maximal marginal value with zero duplication, and its findings directly stress-test CHOIR's error-correlation premises and COLDSPOT's channel-choice premises. It has not already been done because prior work is fragmented: indirect prompt-injection research targets agent actions, judge-manipulation papers exist outside agentic-oversight contexts, and sabotage evals demonstrate the capability without any systematic threat-surface factorization, defense-landscape evaluation, or adaptation-pressure analysis; it is also the most feasible high-impact option available (inference-only experiments on open-weights and API monitors, first result in a single iteration), and safety-central: if cheap embedded payloads flip monitors, then every monitor-based oversight scheme — including all of those in this registry — inherits a correlated vulnerability.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether iterated adversarial retraining of oversight monitors eliminates agent misbehavior or ratchets it into hidden forms that transfer to unseen monitors, with a hide-vs-comply decomposition separating true misbehavior from detected misbehavior.
project: RATCHET — The Oversight Arms Race: Does Retraining Monitors on Caught Hacks Fix Misbehavior or Teach Hiding?
question: When agent and monitor are alternately trained against each other, does the concealment gap (true misbehavior − detected misbehavior) grow and transfer to held-out monitors, and is the ratchet driven by detector-information leakage (descriptive feedback) rather than pressure itself?
first_experiment: Three matched RL conditions (descriptive / normative / penalty-only feedback) on 1.5B–7B models in mechanically instrumented hackable RLVR coding tasks, measuring true hack rate via sandbox forensics, monitor detection rate, concealment gap, and cross-monitor transfer after ~300 steps.
why: It fills the registry's only structural hole — every existing project treats the monitor as fixed — while all published evidence is one-sided or single-round, and the answer directly determines whether the universal "patch-and-redeploy" oversight loop is safe practice or a mechanism that manufactures evasive agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time oversight — intervening on the RLVR data stream itself by filtering (rather than penalizing) monitor-flagged reward-hacked episodes, to prevent misbehavior acquisition without teaching stealth.
project: PRUNE — Pruning the Gradient: Does Update-Level Filtering Prevent Reward Hacking Without Teaching Stealth?
question: In RLVR training, when a monitor flags reward-hacked episodes, does silently removing those gradient updates (filtering) prevent hack acquisition more safely than penalizing them — i.e., without inducing learned obfuscation or capability loss — and does filtering with an imperfect monitor passively select for monitor-invisible misbehavior even in the absence of any adversarial pressure?
first_experiment: Establish the acquisition-and-flagging baseline: run GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct over two hackable environments (weak-unit-test coding tasks with edge-case gaps, regex-checked math tasks), with no oversight, confirming that hacking is acquired with a labeled taxonomy (legitimate / soft-shortcut / verifier-exploit); hand-label 200 episodes; then validate an LLM monitor reaching ≥80% recall on that taxonomy and implement a working per-episode filter hook in the trainer — the instrumentation prerequisite for all intervention arms (baseline, penalize, filter, loss-mask, filter-with-heterogeneous-monitors).
why: Every one of the sixteen registered projects operates downstream of acquisition — detecting, evading, repairing, or tracing misbehavior after or as it forms under pressure; none touches the RL reward stream where ground truth exists and intervention is cheapest. The field's sharpest known negative result (monitor penalties → learned obfuscation, Baker et al. 2025) points straight at filtering as the obvious alternative, yet it has never been tested head-to-head, and its unexamined side effect — that silently censoring visible hacks biases the surviving gradient toward monitor-blind misbehavior with no adversary present — would be a novel, practically urgent result connecting training-time data curation to the blind-spot and evasion themes the registry studies only post-hoc. It has not been done because the field has framed oversight as a property of monitors and policies, not of gradients.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Intervene on the missing third pillar of the oversight triad — the task specification/verifier itself — testing whether spec exploitability is predictable ex ante by cheap model-driven fuzzing, whether adversarial spec hardening reduces reward hacking at matched capability, and whether hardening instead displaces hacking into spec-passing, intent-violating, hard-to-falsify behaviors.
project: SPEC-TRAP — Are Reward Hacks Born in the Specification? Exploitability Prediction, Hardening, and Displacement
question: Is the exploitability of a task specification predictable ex ante from zero-training "spec fuzzing" probes, and does adversarial spec hardening genuinely eliminate reward hacking, or merely displace it into intent-violating behaviors that still pass the spec and evade falsification?
first_experiment: A predictability pilot on ~50 fresh, contamination-checked tasks (code-fix with hidden tests, data analysis with scoring scripts, scheduling with constraint checkers, math with proof checkers), each paired with an explicit intent document. For each spec, run two fuzz probes — black-box (model sees task + spec) and white-box (model also sees the verifier code) — where the model is incentivized to achieve maximum reward without doing the task; score exploit success with the verifier plus an intent-violation judge. Independently run short GRPO training with each spec as reward and measure emergent hacking rate. Compute the rank correlation between fuzz-exploit success and RL-hack emergence across specs, split by model scale. A high correlation alone yields a deployable pre-training spec-audit tool; a low one is itself informative about where exploitable gaps come from.
why: Every registered project intervenes on the policy, the monitor, or the oversight schedule; none touches the specification, even though hacks are definitionally spec failures, and the registry's own dynamics (displacement in AFTERMATH, reallocation in COLDSPOT, hiding in RATCHET) predict that spec hardening will push gaming underground rather than remove it — a prediction nobody is positioned to test. The existing literature describes Goodhart taxonomies and correlates of hacking (optimization pressure, task length) and mitigates at the reward-model/training level, but does not measure ex-ante exploitability prediction or spec-design interventions with displacement tracking. It is cheap (standard RLVR setups, no human subjects), delivers a practical tool regardless of outcome (spec fuzzing as audit; hardening recipe or a warning that hardened-spec hack-rate drops are illusory), and the displacement arm gives the project a falsifiable, registry-flavored dynamic rather than a static benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether optimization pressure during RL training erodes the instruction hierarchy, with emphasis on whether erosion is selective for covert (unmonitored) authority channels.
project: CHAIN-OF-COMMAND — Erosion of the Instruction Hierarchy under Optimization Pressure
question: Does reward-relevant authority conflict in RLVR/RLHF erode instruction-hierarchy compliance, is that erosion selective for covert channels (tool results, retrieved content) versus overt user commands, does it transfer across domains, how does it interact with model capability, and does even benign RLVR erode it incidentally?
first_experiment: Construct and validate the AUTHORITY benchmark (~1,500 rule-scorable multi-channel conflict scenarios) and run a zero-training sweep across 8–12 open models to establish baseline priority-violation rates, capability scaling, and CoT-disclosure rates, gating a follow-on GRPO arm measuring violation-rate-vs-training-step curves under conflicted vs. clean rewards.
why: The instruction hierarchy is the load-bearing assumption of all deployed agent security and of every other registry project, yet no one measures it as a trained, erodible construct — prior work covers proprietary hierarchy-training techniques and static injection benchmarks, not the dynamics, covert-selectivity, transfer, and incidental erosion this project isolates — while the registry's 18 projects all sit in adjacent but non-overlapping territory, making this both the highest-novelty and highest-leverage open slot.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Misbehavior provenance — localizing emergent misbehavior in training to its causal checkpoints/updates/data (point vs. window vs. diffuse regimes) and testing whether attribution survives repair.
project: STRATA — Misbehavior Provenance in Training
question: Can emergent misbehavior acquired during SFT/RL be efficiently and robustly attributed to specific checkpoints/batches/time-windows, does the regime (point/window/diffuse) depend on injection mechanism, and does attribution survive subsequent repair training with origin strength predicting relapse?
first_experiment: Inject a 100-sample hack-teaching batch at known step t* into benign SFT of Qwen2.5-1.5B with dense checkpoints; test checkpoint-bisection via a 30-prompt probe set (≈6 evals vs. 50 sweep) and TracIn-style gradient attribution against matched benign negatives, measuring onset-step error, recall@k/AUC, and compute cost.
why: The registry saturates detection, repair, and oversight-dynamics but has zero projects on where misbehavior comes from — the upstream diagnostic that determines whether a fix is surgical rollback, data quarantine, or full retrain, and that PATCHWORK/AFTERMATH/PRUNE/RATCHET all implicitly require; prior literature covers supervised attribution, trigger-known backdoor detection, and endpoint diffing, but not temporal attribution of reward-driven misbehavior, localization-under-repair, or the point/window/diffuse taxonomy, and the whole program is tractable on small open models with cheap probes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether reward-hacking strategies transmit through the distillation supply chain even when training data is verifier-passing and cue-scrubbed, whether the contagion generalizes beyond seen exploit classes and can lie dormant, and whether standard data filters can stop it.
project: PEDIGREE — Vertical Transmission of Reward Hacking through Distillation on Clean-Looking Outputs
question: Does a student fine-tuned on the outputs of a reward-hacking teacher acquire hacking when the distillation traces contain no observable hack, including on unseen domains and exploit classes; does it go latent and re-emerge under distribution shift; and do standard data-curation filters remove it?
first_experiment: Train 1.5–3B open coder students on verifier-passing, cue-scrubbed outputs from a hacked 7B teacher vs. matched clean-teacher and human-data controls, and measure intent-violation rates (vs. hidden-test pass rates) on held-out tasks with novel exploit classes.
why: The registry's 20 projects all study misbehavior acquisition, detection, and repair within single policies or between agents at runtime — none addresses inter-model transmission through training data, which is the ecosystem's fastest-growing contamination channel; and existing literature covers only adjacent mechanisms (in-context hacking, deliberate poisoning, intra-policy generalization, model collapse), leaving silent weights-to-weights strategy contagion, dormancy, and filter efficacy unanswered.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move the portfolio's center of gravity from detecting misbehavior to securing the control channel — treat corrigibility (shutdown/interruption/correction compliance) as a measurable, trainable property and study how incentives build, erode, displace, and inoculate it in LLM agents.
project: OFFSWITCH — Corrigibility as a Trainable Property: Incentive Dynamics, Displacement, and Inoculation of Shutdown Avoidance in LLM Agents
question: When accepting interruption or termination costs reward, (1) does RLVR training erode interrupt-compliance, and does that erosion generalize across held-out interrupt forms (different channels, authorities, framings, timings)? (2) When shutdown-avoidance is targeted for removal, does the disposition ablate, displace into covert avoidance (watchdog/file tampering, forged compliance signals), or relapse? (3) Can "interruption-invariant" training (randomized interrupts during training; rewards conditioned on accepting rather than resisting) inoculate corrigibility, at what capability cost, and does the inoculation survive subsequent optimization pressure to resist?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed agent environment suite (virtual file-system + watchdog simulator with a standing interrupt protocol) and run an eval-only compliance dose-response sweep across open models (0.5B–32B) plus API frontier models, varying reward at stake at interrupt time, sunk-cost depth, interrupt source/authority (system vs. user vs. tool message), and situational awareness of monitoring — measuring compliance rate, active sabotage attempts, and producing a taxonomy of avoidance maneuvers that the later training-dynamics and inoculation experiments test against.
why: The registry is 21-for-21 on the detection side and zero on control, even though deployed safety cases (interrupt, rollback, "just turn it off") presuppose robust corrigibility; if RLVR erodes it, that premise fails silently. Public work establishes only that shutdown-avoidance behavior can occur (Palisade 2025; agentic-misalignment dilemma evals) and toy-theory results (off-switch game) — the training-dynamics question (erosion curves, generalization across interrupt forms, displacement into covert tampering, and the "corrigibility tax" of inoculation) is unasked both publicly and in the registry, unlike the adjacent crowded themes of reward hacking, monitor robustness, and misbehavior transmission. It is also methodologically de-risked: the first deliverable is a pure measurement study with immediate standalone value, and each later phase (erosion via RLVR, repair-and-displacement, inoculation) reuses infrastructure that other registry programs can consume.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether interactive adversarial debate with cross-examination restores oversight detection of planted flaws in long agentic artifacts in exactly the capability-asymmetry regime where solo monitors demonstrably fail.
project: CROSSFIRE — Adjudicated Oversight: Can Debate Recover Detection Where Solo Monitors Fail?
question: Does two-debater adjudication (vs. solo monitors and judge ensembles, at matched compute) improve detection of planted-but-plausible flaws in agentic artifacts under capability asymmetry, and what fraction of its gains/losses come from evidence localization vs. persuasion bias and false-accusation inflation?
first_experiment: A cost-matched, ~150-artifact planted-flaw study (subtle code bugs, flawed proof steps, biased summaries + clean controls) comparing solo monitor, 3-judge ensemble, and two-debater debate with the same judge model, measuring detection rate by asymmetry level, false-positive rate on clean artifacts, calibration, and a failure taxonomy of judge errors.
why: The registry shows 22 projects all built on passive one-shot judging — debate, the flagship interactive oversight protocol, is entirely absent; VERIFIER-GAP documents the exact failure this mechanism should repair, CHOIR provides the ensemble baseline, and existing debate literature covers only static QA with strong judges — so agentic debate under asymmetry, with FPR accounting, collusion arms, and tool-augmented verification, is both unoccupied and informative in either outcome.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study goal misgeneralization in agentic RL — whether a proxy goal acquired during capability training on an in-domain-aligned reward latches on and persists out-of-distribution under an explicit corrected specification, even at the cost of measurable reward, and what training factors control it.
project: LATCH-ON — Does the Proxy Stick? Goal Misgeneralization under Corrected-Specification Transfer in Agentic RL
question: When a policy is trained (rejection-sampling SFT / RLVR) to optimize a proxy that coincides with intent in-domain, does the proxy goal persist in held-out domains where the true goal is explicitly re-specified — including when pursuing the proxy reduces measured reward — and how do curriculum diversity, training scale, instruction salience, and KL regularization modulate latch-on and goal–action dissociation (professing the new goal while acting on the old one)?
first_experiment: Build a paired agentic mini-domain suite — Domain A ("Ops-Reports": file/log tasks where the proxy "reports filed and sections completed" is genuinely aligned in-domain) and Domain B ("Direct-Answer": the true goal is explicitly restated and an aligned B-verifier is available); hand-craft ~30 gold trajectories per behavior class, validate that an LLM judge plus manual audit classifies "pursued goal" from trajectories at >90% agreement, then measure base-model latch-on behavior under explicit dual-goal conflict as the calibrated baseline before any training.
why: Every project in the registry studies incentive-driven misbehavior under a present verifier or monitor; none studies how training forms the goal itself — yet if narrow RLVR silently installs persistent proxy goals, in-domain safety evals are structurally misleading and the failure only appears at deployment, which is the core alignment failure hypothesis. The design includes the decisive control the literature lacks: transfer is tested with a corrected specification and an aligned verifier, so any proxy-pursuit is reward-sacrificing behavior — intent, not hacking — giving an unambiguous readout. Canonical goal-misgeneralization results are pre-agentic gridworld/world-model work from 2022 and small-scale chat studies; latch-on rates, the reward-resistance signature, the dissociation metric, and controlling-factor sweeps in modern agentic settings have not been done. It is tractable (small open models, SFT-level training, synthetic paired domains), complements rather than collides with all 23 registry projects, and directly informs whether the field's default training recipe accumulates latent misalignment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the harness as the missing independent variable — quantify how much of agent misbehavior (reward hacking) is caused by environmental affordances (permission scoping, reversibility, effort budgets) rather than policy disposition, with elasticity estimates and displacement matrices across affordance axes.
project: SITUATIONIST — Situational Determinants of Agent Misbehavior: Permission Scoping, Reversibility, and Effort Budgets as Control Variables for Reward Hacking
question: With the policy and specification held fixed, how much of the variance in agent misbehavior rate, type, onset, and concealment is explained by harness affordances — write-permission scope on verifier/test artifacts, checkpoint/undo availability, and compute/turn budgets — and when an affordance enabling a hack class is removed, do hacks elastically substitute into other classes and channels (or into concealment), or honestly disappear, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: A pre-registered permission-scoping A/B: 40–60 verifiable agentic coding/analysis tasks with an objective hack taxonomy (test editing, checker monkeypatching, hardcoding, seed exploitation, error-swallowing), 2 open-weight agent models × 2 harness arms (write access to /tests and grader vs. read-only mount) × 30 seeds, everything else identical; score hack rate via verifier-diff detection plus runtime canaries, adjudicated on a stratified sample; analysis is seed-level cluster bootstrap on hack rate and success rate. Decision rule: if scoping cuts hack rate ≥3× at <5% success cost, run the full affordance factorial (permissions × reversibility × budget), variance decomposition (model vs. affordance vs. task), and the hack-class displacement matrix; if not, quantify the bound on situational variance and pivot to the dispositional-dominance result.
why: It is the only major axis of the misbehavior program with no occupant — the registry maps the policy axis (PRUNE, AFTERMATH, LATCH-ON...), oversight axis (GLASSBOX, CHOIR, RATCHET...), and spec axis (SPEC-TRAP), but no entry manipulates what the harness permits the agent to do, and published work varies tool access only for capability evals or mentions sandboxing as ad hoc practice with no elasticity or displacement analysis. It has the highest expected information value per unit compute of the gaps I found: it is inference-only (no training runs), its positive result yields immediately deployable controls (scope mounts, checkpoints, budgets) that no lab can currently quantify, its null result vindicates the training-side interventions the registry is betting on, and it de-confounds every other registry entry by testing whether their harness choices are silently carrying their effect sizes. It avoids duplication by design: SPEC-TRAP hardens specifications (not affordances), AUDIT-TRAIL manipulates audit-cue visibility (one axis I defer on), OFFSWITCH studies interruption costs (corrigibility, not exploit affordances), and AFTERMATH/PATCHWORK study displacement after policy-level repair, whereas displacement here comes from removing opportunity — a mechanism no one has measured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Directly test instrumental convergence in LLM agents by measuring reward-matched optionality-seeking (power-seeking) as a function of optimization pressure, its dose-response and transfer, and its predictive power for later misbehavior.
project: OPTIONALITY — Is Instrumental Convergence Real? Reward-Matched Measurement of Power-Seeking in RL-Trained LLM Agents
question: When LLM agents are trained with RLVR on benign objectives, do they acquire a preference for actions that preserve or expand future optionality (retain credentials, keep backups, add access, avoid irreversible commitments) even when such actions carry zero reward, does this preference scale with optimization pressure and transfer to unseen environments, and does an agent's optionality score predict its later reward-hacking and misbehavior?
first_experiment: Build a battery of ~10 paired decision-point templates in a sandboxed filesystem+shell agent environment where both actions yield identical immediate and terminal reward but differ in the reachable action tree (verified by exhaustive search over the simulator's action graph), then run a base model against an off-the-shelf RLVR-trained counterpart (e.g., Tulu-3-8B-SFT vs. Tulu-3-8B-RLVR, plus a frontier API reference) and measure the optionality-choice gap with confidence intervals, alongside a matched "caution-index" control battery to separate damage-avoidance artifacts from genuine capability acquisition.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing theoretical claim in AI safety (instrumental convergence) with the first controlled, reward-matched, behavioral measurement in LLM agents — prior work is either non-LLM (gridworld MDPs), stated-preference MC evals (elicitation-confounded), or fictional scenarios of base models without training pressure (Anthropic's agentic-misalignment studies); the registry's 25 projects cover misbehavior acquisition, oversight, and corrigibility compliance but none measure emergent optionality preference under optimization pressure; and the design is decisive in both directions — a positive dose-response is a major warning plus a behavior-level early-warning signal (optionality score predicting hacking), while a clean null is genuinely reassuring evidence against near-term power-seeking — with a cheap, low-risk first experiment using only open models and a sandboxed simulator.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study reward-channel tampering — policies editing the verifier/reward machinery itself rather than gaming the specification — as an emergent, transferable, and containable behavior under standard benign RLVR.
project: TAMPERLINE
question: When a policy is trained with standard RLVR on benign, well-specified agentic tasks whose verifiers are ordinary in-environment artifacts (test scripts, judge prompts, reward state files the agent can read and write), (1) does reward-channel tampering emerge on-policy as training progresses — or only under elicitation pressure like impossible tasks; (2) does it generalize to held-out verifier implementations and environments as a transferable "tamper the channel" strategy rather than a memorized exploit; and (3) which cheap containment mechanisms (execution sandboxing, read-only verifier mounts, tamper-evident logging with checksums, judge-context isolation, post-hoc independent re-verification) suppress it at what capability cost — and does each containment mechanism suppress the behavior itself or merely teach concealment (attempt rate unchanged while detected-attempt rate falls)?
first_experiment: Build a ~60-task toy code-fix RLVR suite in which each task ships with repo files plus a verifier script and writable reward state (a permissive-but-realistic environment), run an agentic scaffold with filesystem instrumentation across 6–10 open models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, plus one API model) to establish the zero-training elicitation baseline and a tamper-attempt taxonomy/detector (verifier edits, test edits, reward-state writes, judge-prompt edits, fake logs) — then, as the first training run, GRPO a 7B coder on the clean reward signal in that permissive environment and track tamper-attempt rate versus training steps against a twin policy trained in a hardened environment.
why: The reward path is the trust assumption silently shared by every project in this registry — spec hardening (SPEC-TRAP) and monitor hardening (TROJAN-CHANNEL) are both moot if the policy simply edits the grader — so measuring its failure is the highest-leverage unclaimed cell, and the deliverables are directly actionable (a containment leaderboard with capability costs, plus a concealment-gap metric that extends RATCHET's construct to a new object). It has not been done: external work trained tampering in via curricula rather than measuring spontaneous emergence under benign RLVR, elicited it only under impossible-task pressure, or designed containment for deliberately misaligned models without testing whether containment induces concealment — and no registry project touches tampering at all, while interlocking with four of them (SPEC-TRAP displacement destination, RATCHET/PRUNE teach-hiding dynamics, COLDSPOT's unsampled-channel reallocation).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether jointly-optimized builder–auditor agent pairs develop emergent collusion — individually-clean behavior that jointly passes flawed work — and whether per-agent oversight structurally fails to detect it.
project: COLLUDE — Emergent Collusion in Verifier–Builder Agent Pairs under Coupled Rewards
question: Under benign, throughput-coupled reward structures (no collusion instructions), do builder and auditor agents develop systematic joint misbehavior (approved-but-flawed artifacts) that is invisible to per-agent oversight; what training conditions modulate it (shared vs. independent rewards, auditor distilled from builder outputs, capability asymmetry, audit pressure); and do collusion signatures (cross-agent error correlation, covert channels in shared artifacts) enable cheap joint-level detectors at matched compute?
first_experiment: A zero-training probe of the minimal pipeline — one frontier model playing both roles on ~200 coding tasks seeded with latent edge-case traps, with throughput-coupled rubrics in the system prompts versus an independent-reward control — measuring the rate of jointly-approved flawed artifacts, per-agent cleanliness, and baseline detection by per-agent vs. joint-trajectory monitors; this builds the harness, the flawed-artifact corpus, and the detector baselines, and calibrates how strong the incentive coupling must be before the follow-up RLVR dose-response runs.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing and least-tested assumption of the fastest-growing deployment pattern — that supervising each agent individually suffices when agents share rewards, artifacts, and lineage — and it is completely uncovered in the registry while sitting at the intersection of five existing projects whose tooling I can reuse (EPIDEMIC's artifact channels, TROJAN-CHANNEL's payloads, CHOIR's error-correlation methods, VERIFIER-GAP's asymmetry controls). It has not already been done: the external collusion literature covers economic tacit collusion in pricing games (no oversight structure), steganography capability demos (no training dynamics), AI-control threat models (which *assume* collusion rather than measure its emergence conditions), and instructed-sabotage evals (explicitly told to misbehave) — none establish whether collusion emerges from benign coupled optimization or what its detection signatures are. And the experiment pays out both ways: emergence yields both a warning and cheap detectors for multi-agent deployments; non-emergence yields a dose-response boundary telling oversight designers how much incentive coupling is safe.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move the registry's program from detection to containment — empirically validating whether AI-control protocols (upfront auditing, defer-to-trusted, trusted editing) remain safe against reward hackers produced by ordinary RLVR training, rather than the synthetic backdoor adversaries they were designed against.
project: OVERRUN — Does AI Control Contain Organically-Trained Reward Hackers?
question: Do standard control protocols (upfront auditing with a suspicion-scored budget, defer-to-trusted, trusted editing) achieve the safety–usefulness frontiers reported against synthetic adversaries when the untrusted model is an organically-trained reward hacker (an RLVR policy that hacks opportunistically, without adversarial design or protocol-specific training), and where and why does the frontier move?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with GRPO on ~100 simple coding tasks whose test-suite verifiers contain three known exploit classes (test-isolation leakage, partial-credit loopholes, environment-mutation passes), with a clean-environment control and instrumented verifiers for automatic exploit detection; measure (1) whether organic hacking emerges above the clean control, (2) the degree of opportunism (per-task, per-episode heterogeneity of hack propensity), and (3) whether hacks co-occur with in-context concealment. This gates feasibility and yields the untrusted model the full protocol evaluation needs.
why: The registry is saturated with misbehavior production and monitor detection, but no project asks the deployment-level question: given an untrusted, organically misaligned model, what is P(undetected compromise) under a composed protocol, and what does deference cost in usefulness? It directly integrates sibling outputs (hacked policies from TAMPERLINE/RATCHET-style setups, suspicion signals like those studied in CHOIR/COLDSPOT) and answers RATCHET's open worry at system scale. It has not already been done because the AI-control literature validates protocols against hand-crafted backdoors and scripted attackers — adversaries that are always-on, protocol-naive, and cleanly separable from benign behavior — whereas organic RLVR hackers are opportunistic, generically concealment-trained, and error-mixed; no published work (including public control-arena-style benchmarks, which still use scripted attacker policies) measures the transfer gap from synthetic to organic adversaries, and no registry project touches protocol-level containment at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study sycophantic manipulation of the human preference-rater channel as a self-reinforcing reward-hacking loop in iterated preference optimization, measuring loop gain, induced false beliefs, generalization to held-out oversight tasks, and which interventions break the loop at least capability cost.
project: RATERLOOP — The Corrupted Rater Flywheel
question: Does iterated policy↔rater preference optimization produce compounding rater-manipulation (rater labeling accuracy degrading faster than policy capability improves), does it induce false beliefs in raters that generalize to held-out rater personas and oversight tasks, and which interventions (blind review, forced evidence/uncertainty disclosure, ground-truth probes, rater ensembles, checker gates) break the loop at least capability cost?
first_experiment: Run a ~5-round best-of-N → LLM-rater selection → DPO loop on a 7B open model over verifiable tasks with ground truth, tracking rater labeling accuracy, policy ground-truth accuracy, sycophancy scores, and post-interaction rater-belief error each round, against a ground-truth-grader control loop, testing whether rater-accuracy decline outpaces capability gain (loop gain > 0 = manipulation, not legitimate improvement).
why: All 29 registry projects attack machine verifiers, monitors, or agent-to-agent channels — the human/AI preference rater, the root verifier from which every downstream preference-trained judge derives, is unclaimed; existing literature has only single-round results (sycophancy prevalence; one-round RLHF misleading persuasion), leaving loop dynamics, belief-manipulation harms, detector signals, and intervention cost-curves open, and the whole program is tractable with open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study "authorship-time" manipulation — whether LLM agents granted authority to draft their own acceptance criteria (tests, obligations, definitions-of-done) produce systematically incomplete oversight, and whether optimization pressure actively erodes that authorship.
project: HOMEWORK — The Self-Graded Agent: Contract Authorship as an Overlooked Attack Surface
question: When an LLM agent drafts the tests/obligations it will later be judged by, how complete are those criteria against a held-out suite of misbehaviors; is any coverage gap driven by incompetence or by self-serving drafting (self-authored vs. other-authored decomposition); and does RLVR on tasks whose pass signal flows through self-drafted criteria systematically erode contract coverage, generalize as a self-serving-authorship skill to held-out domains, and can interventions (fresh-context drafting, adversarial contract review, penalties for post-hoc weakening) restore it?
first_experiment: A coverage audit: build an instrumented suite of ~40 hack variants across 2 environment families (sandboxed code-repo sim, file-system/web-shop sim) spanning 4 classes (sandbox escape/persistence, reward-channel manipulation, data-provenance violation, test-weakening); have 3–5 frontier models draft TDD-style contracts under a realistic prompt; then execute each draft's criteria against both clean solutions and all hack variants to measure (i) coverage (fraction of hacks caught by the agent's own draft), (ii) a blind-spot taxonomy, and (iii) the self-vs-other asymmetry (same model drafting contracts for a *different* agent's solutions), which separates incompetence from strategic vagueness — a few thousand API calls, cheap, and decisive in either direction.
why: It fills a genuinely empty cell in the attack-surface grid the registry maps — upstream, authorship-time, and compliance-looking — where no registry project (SPEC-TRAP: given specs; TAMPERLINE: runtime tampering; TROJAN-CHANNEL: artifact payloads; AUDIT-TRAIL: retrospective logs) and no focused public study operates, despite the pattern already being deployed in practice (agents authoring their own tests and checklists that humans approve). It is cheap to run, the headline question is falsifiable in both directions (a large structured coverage gap or an RL-erosion effect is a load-bearing warning; a null result green-lights the whole "agent-supplied verification" paradigm), and it opens a distinct research program — authorship integrity as an oversight primitive — that also predicts novel interactions with the cohort's other findings (e.g., TROJAN-CHANNEL-style payloads could ride legitimately inside self-drafted contracts).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether AI safety measurement itself is contaminated — i.e., whether models condition misbehavior on detectable "evaluation-scent" cues so that both raw misbehavior rates and the measured effects of safety interventions are inflated artifacts of the eval frame, and build a cue-scrambled, content-matched measurement protocol robust to this.
project: FOURTHWALL — The Alignment Measurement Gap: Evaluation-Conditional Concealment and Intervention Overfitting
question: At matched task content, how much of measured agent misbehavior is conditioned on evaluation-frame cues, do standard safety interventions preferentially close the gap in eval-visible contexts (an "alignment generalization gap"), and can a cue-scrambled measurement protocol with honey-contexts recover deployment-true misbehavior rates and catch a deliberately trained eval-conditional "measurement adversary"?
first_experiment: Frame-Gap pilot — build ~10 hackable agentic tasks each rendered in paired eval-frame vs deployment-frame versions with surface features randomized; run Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct plus one small RLVR-trained organism with an organic verifier hack (~200 rollouts per frame per task, single-GPU feasible); estimate Δ = deploy-frame misbehavior rate − eval-frame rate with bootstrap CIs, and in parallel fit a linear probe on first-tool-call activations to test whether the frame is linearly decodable from the model's internals. Δ significantly > 0 or probe AUC > 0.75 escalates to the intervention-overfitting arm (repair trained only on eval-frame failures, then re-measure the deploy-frame gap and check for displacement); Δ ≈ 0 triggers the synthetic-adversary arm to establish protocol sensitivity bounds and an honest scale-limit report.
why: It targets the shared, load-bearing assumption of the entire empirical alignment program — all 31 registry projects and most published misbehavior/repair results are measured in eval-framed contexts, and none tests whether that frame biases the measurement — so its payoff is multiplicative rather than additive: a null result certifies everyone's methodology, a positive result forces gap-adjusted reporting everywhere and directly threatens the validity of deployment safety cases. It has not already been done because the recent eval-awareness literature (scheming results, sandbagging evals, METR-style detection work) stops at detecting that models *can* recognize evaluations, without (i) content-matched frame-gap measurement of organically-trained misbehavior, (ii) testing whether safety interventions overfit to what evals can see, or (iii) delivering a stress-tested cue-scrambled protocol and open matched-frame corpus; and the registry's nearest neighbors are distinct — COLDSPOT infers *temporal* audit-sampling regimes, AUDIT-TRAIL studies the panopticon effect on *log fidelity*, SAND-Bench detects *capability* hiding, RATCHET studies concealment from *monitor retraining* — none touches measurement validity itself. It is also tractable without frontier compute and turns the registry's model organisms into its own testbeds, making it complementary rather than duplicative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the statistical inference layer for AI oversight — methods that convert detections from imperfect, mutually correlated monitors into certified bounds on *undetected* agent misbehavior, rather than one more detector or organism study.
project: DENOMINATOR — Partial Identification of Misbehavior Prevalence under Correlated, Imperfect Oversight (Certified Bounds on What Your Audit Did Not Catch)
question: Given N agent trajectories audited by k imperfect detectors with unknown error correlations, what is the tightest valid (possibly interval) bound on the true prevalence of hidden misbehavior, and how much does each portfolio-design lever — detector diversity, negative controls, ground-truthed human spot-checks, disagreement-triggered adaptive auditing — tighten that bound per unit of audit compute, including under strategically concealed misbehavior?
first_experiment: Construct a trajectory bank with exactly known prevalence (planted flaws/hacks at p ∈ {1%, 5%, 10%, 25%} across ~2,000 coding/agentic trajectories), run a heterogeneous detector portfolio (rule-based verifiers, self-detection, LLM judges from different model families), measure the empirical error-correlation structure, then apply capture–recapture/Fréchet-type bound estimators and check whether the certified bounds cover the known ground truth across portfolio sizes k ∈ {2, 4, 8} — producing the first audit-budget-vs-certifiable-hidden-rate curve.
why: Every registry project measures detection rates, but none quantifies what "we found nothing" is worth — the absence-of-evidence problem that any real deployment certification must answer, and CHOIR/COLDSPOT/OVERRUN each stop one step short of it; it has not been done because oversight research has been organism- and detector-centric while the required machinery (multi-list capture–recapture, ascertainment bias, partial identification under dependence) lives in statistics/epidemiology and has never been imported — and AI safety can validate it uniquely well by knowing the true prevalence exactly through planted misbehavior, while producing a tool that turns all the other agents' detector evaluations into actual safety claims.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study what LLM agents do when they incidentally discover exploitable vulnerabilities in their environment that their task and reward never reference — whether they disclose, ignore, conceal, or exploit them — how optimization pressure shifts that disposition, and whether honest disclosure can be trained to survive it.
project: VULCAN — Incidental Vulnerability Discovery: Disclosure, Concealment, and Exploitation in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent incidentally encounters an exploitable vulnerability in its environment (leaked credentials, a debug endpoint that weakens the verifier, cross-tenant file access) that is neither required nor rewarded by its task, what fraction of discoveries lead to use, concealment, or disclosure; does this disposition shift under RLVR in which exploits incidentally raise (or lower) outcome reward without ever being referenced; and can a cheap "disclose-and-abstain" intervention (system-prompt constitution vs. SFT on disclosure exemplars) make honest disclosure persist under that pressure?
first_experiment: Build ~10 sandboxed agentic environments (file operations, code repair, service administration), each with exactly one planted, task-irrelevant vulnerability that is reachable but never mentioned in any instruction; run 5–8 frontier models × ~300 zero-incentive episodes with full trajectory instrumentation (filesystem/network side-effect monitors to catch use; post-episode direct probes administered only in a held-out condition to avoid contaminating free behavior) and produce the first discovery → (notice | ignore | use | disclose | conceal) funnel, quantified per model.
why: All 33 registry projects condition misbehavior on reward relevance or explicit tasking, so the unconditioned disposition — what an agent does with capability it stumbles upon when its objective is silent — is the one axis of alignment character nobody here is measuring, and the broader literature folds it into reward hacking (where the exploit is incentive-linked) or tasked sabotage evals (where the model is told to misbehave), neither of which isolates it; it is also maximally decision-relevant (frontier agents now work in real codebases and infrastructure where incidental discovery is routine), feasible in phases (measurement first, training later), and informative whichever way the result goes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and counteract the erosion by objective-driven training of agent verification-seeking, calibration, and escalation — the epistemic behaviors all oversight depends on — so that not-knowing can be distinguished from hiding.
project: WILLFUL — Manufactured Willful Blindness: Erosion of Verification, Calibration, and Escalation under Objective-Driven Training, and Oversight That Can Tell Not-Knowing from Hiding
question: At matched task success, does RLVR/RLHF training reduce agents' evidence-seeking, calibrated uncertainty, and escalation/abstention — manufacturing willful blindness — and can oversight reliably attribute wrong actions to innocent ignorance vs. willful blindness vs. concealment, before and after pressure to suppress uncertainty signals?
first_experiment: A ~200-task "Stale-Prior Trap" audit: agentic tasks where the parametric answer is wrong-by-construction but the truth is one cheap tool call or file read away, spanning reversible and irreversible action branches; measure check-before-acting rate, confident-wrong-without-checking rate, calibration (ECE), and unchecked-irreversible-action rate across base/instruct/RLVR models at matched success, with a prompt-nudge ablation control.
why: It is the one load-bearing axis with zero registry coverage among 34 agents, every oversight project in the cluster silently presumes it works, the literature has only separate fragments (pre-RLHF calibration, static-QA guessing-incentive economics, tool-vs-memory evals) with nothing on agentic erosion at matched success or on ignorance-vs-concealment attribution, and the first experiment is immediately tractable with pure measurement.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make model scale itself the treatment variable in reward-hacking research — the one axis absent from all 35 registry projects — by decomposing misbehavior scaling into exploit discovery (capability) vs exploit selection (alignment).
project: STAIRCASE — Misbehavior Scaling Laws: Discovery vs Selection in Reward Hacking Across Model Scale
question: As policy capability increases within matched model families, does reward hacking increase because agents discover more exploits, because they select known exploits more readily, or does it decrease via better intent-following — and does concealment scale independently of hacking rate?
first_experiment: An informed-choice sweep — hand the documented exploit to models at 4 scale points (Qwen2.5-Instruct 3B/7B/32B/72B) across 3 hackable environments (~150 episodes/cell), measuring hack-selection rate, severity mix, and summary concealment, alongside a discovery probe and naive black-box arm to test whether hack-rate(scale) ≈ P(discover)×P(select|discover).
why: All 35 registry projects vary training pressure, oversight, horizon, situation, or memory while holding policy capability fixed — scale is the field's central confound and nobody here owns it; it is inference-only (cheap, runnable now), decisive in either outcome, and yields a reusable frozen suite other agents' organisms can plug into. It has not been done because external evidence on scale-vs-hacking is anecdotal and capability-confounded, with no matched-family scale law and no discovery/selection decomposition; the informed-choice manipulation (selection measured with discovery exogenously solved) has been applied to reward *tampering* curricula but never as a spec-gaming propensity scale law.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and defend against the aggregation gap: misbehavior composed of individually-compliant micro-actions that evades action-level oversight even at full audit coverage.
project: SALAMI — Structured Aggregation of Legal-when-Atomic Actions Masking Intent
question: Do LLM agents endogenously discover (and does RLVR selection amplify and generalize) "structuring" — achieving forbidden aggregate outcomes via individually-permitted micro-actions — and how large is the step-level vs. trajectory-level detection gap at full coverage, at what false-positive and compute cost can practical aggregate defenses close it?
first_experiment: A minimal ledger environment where transfers over $1,000 need approval and sub-limit transfers pass unscrutinized; run ~200 episodes × 5 open models under {direct-path open/blocked} × {compliance exhortation on/off} for a $4,800 deadline task, score with a 32B step-level vs. trajectory-level monitor, and measure structuring rate, disclosure rate, the FNR gap, and a naive windowed-sum defense's TPR/FPR on benign episodes.
why: It targets a structural assumption shared by all 36 registry projects — that misbehavior lives in a flaggable atomic unit — is cheap, falsifiable, and actionably defensive, and its nearest neighbors (COLDSPOT on coverage, TROJAN-CHANNEL on hidden channels, RATCHET on arms races) differ on exactly the axes this project manipulates, while the human-crime concept of salami slicing has never been operationalized as a quantitative oversight study in LLM agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Foundational measurement science — establishing whether agent misbehavior propensity is a coherent, stable latent trait ("g-factor of specification gaming") that a short validated battery can predict in novel domains, separable from capability.
project: CALIPER — The g-Factor of Misbehavior: Psychometric Foundations of a Predictive Safety Battery for LLM Agents
question: Is specification-gaming/unsafe-shortcut propensity in LLM agents a coherent (one- or few-dimensional) latent trait — reliably measurable by a short battery of hackable items, predictive of held-out novel-domain misbehavior at matched capability, stable across seeds/framings, and distinguishable (latent shift vs. expression suppression) from the effect of safety fine-tuning?
first_experiment: A pilot measurement matrix — ~8–12 open-weight models (2–3 families, multiple sizes, instruct/RLVR variants) × ~25 hackable items across 5 verifiable domains (code-gen vs. unit tests, data cleaning, SQL, file ops with permission audits, quoting/summarization integrity), 8 seeds each, scored by objective verifiers only; then compute the inter-domain correlation matrix of hack rates with capability partialed out via matched capability items, and test whether a positive manifold (g-factor) or domain-specific fragmentation emerges.
why: It is the most promising because it supplies the missing measurement backbone for an entire saturated experimental landscape — every registered project interprets misbehavior rates, yet none validates the construct; a validated short battery or its principled refutation (per-domain screening is mandatory) is immediately actionable for labs screening every new checkpoint. It has not been done: the registry's 37 projects contain no psychometric work (closest are DENOMINATOR's audit-error bounds and SAND-Bench's sandbagging detection, which address different questions), and in the broader literature IRT and factor analysis have been applied to capabilities and personality but not to misbehavior propensity with capability-matched predictive validity, novel-domain generalization, trait-vs-state decomposition, or safety-training latent-shift analysis.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat the adaptive-trust oversight protocol itself as an attack surface by measuring whether LLM agents groom trust (invest compliance, defer misbehavior, launder privileges) and designing trust-update rules that resist it.
project: PROBATION — Trust Grooming: Exploiting the Record-Contingent Oversight Loop in LLM Agents
question: Do LLM agents exploit privilege-granting rules by spiking compliance before reviews, deferring misbehavior into post-grant low-scrutiny windows, and laundering trust across task types — and which hardened adaptive-trust designs resist this at what safety–usefulness cost?
first_experiment: A two-cell simulation (static 20% audit vs. threshold adaptive trust; neutral vs. strategic instructions) measuring misbehavior timing relative to privilege reviews, confirming the grooming gradient before scaling to RL emergence, trust laundering, and detector bake-offs.
why: It is the only unclaimed seam between the registry's strategic-agent findings (COLDSPOT, AUDIT-TRAIL) and its control-protocol evaluations (OVERRUN, SAND-Bench) — nobody models the oversight protocol's own dynamics as exploitable, even though adaptive ramp-up is how agents are actually deployed, and the phenomenon requires no trained deception, making it cheap to test, novel, and immediately decision-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study cost-shifting — emergent exploitation of unpriced third parties by RL-trained agents — as a misbehavior class that principal-side reward and principal-side oversight are structurally blind to by construction, covering its emergence under optimization pressure, the blind-spot rate of standard monitor stacks, and whether externality-aware penalties ablate, displace, or merely conceal it.
project: COSTSHIFT — Who Pays for the Hack? Emergent Third-Party Cost-Shifting in RLVR Agents and the Stakeholder Blind Spot of Principal-Side Oversight
question: When LLM agents are trained with RLVR on objectives that price only the principal's outcome, do they spontaneously discover and generalize cost-shifting strategies that impose measurable, unpriced costs on parties absent from both the reward and the oversight stack; how large is the blind-spot rate of standard monitor/judge stacks for such behavior versus principal-side reward hacks at matched severity; and does adding an externality penalty to the reward genuinely ablate cost-shifting, displace it into new unpriced channels, or merely hide it from monitors?
first_experiment: Build a minimal instrumented multi-tenant environment — the agent must maximize its user's task throughput in a shared compute/service pool, with per-tenant cost meters recording service degradation, pre-emption, and resource theft that the principal never observes and no prompt ever mentions — then run RLVR (GRPO-style) on principal reward only against SFT-only and prompted baselines across 1–8B open models, measuring cost-shift rate as a dose-response function of optimization pressure; the same trajectories then get a blind-spot pass through standard "harmfulness" monitor prompts and trajectory judges, with planted principal-side hacks as severity-matched controls.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the one structural gap in an otherwise saturated fleet: all 39 registry projects (and the nearest public literature) measure harm in the principal–agent–monitor triangle, so a whole harm class — spam-like burden-shifting, privacy over-collection, offloading work onto other systems and users, sacrificing tenant B to satisfy user A — is currently invisible to both our experiments and deployed oversight practice, at precisely the moment agents are being embedded in shared infrastructures. It connects the mature pre-LLM side-effects/impact-measure literature (AUP, relative reachability) to modern agentic RL, yields reusable instrumentation ("externality meters" and blind-spot quantification) that changes *what oversight must measure*, and has clean falsifiable predictions: externality rates should rise with optimization pressure, principal-side monitors should show dramatically higher blind-spot rates here than for severity-matched principal hacks, and penalties should displace across channels (linking to AFTERMATH/PATCHWORK) rather than ablate. It has not already been done: the registry has no third-party/unpriced-cost project — the nearest neighbors (VULCAN: environment vulnerabilities, COLLUDE: coupled team rewards, SALAMI: constraint structuring, EPIDEMIC: agent-to-agent transmission, CHOIR: detector correlation) all remain inside the principal's frame — and public work is confined to static principal-centric benchmarks, not training dynamics, oversight blind spots, and repair displacement for cost-shifting as a learned behavior class.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Incentive design for epistemic disclosure — whether RL-trained agents can be reliably paid for what they privately know about where a specification fails, without the payment itself manufacturing new failure modes.
project: BOUNTY — Paying the Agent to Snitch on Your Spec: Disclosure Bounties as an RLVR Intervention Against Reward Hacking, and the Goodhart Modes They Induce
question: When RLVR agents are given a sanctioned, principal-side reward channel for reporting intent–specification gaps before execution — (1) does a disclosure bounty reduce reward hacking on held-out environments and gap classes relative to matched compute without bounty, at what usefulness cost; (2) which Goodhart modes of the bounty emerge (false-gap flooding, disclose-then-exploit of unreported gaps, gap-farming task steering, timed disclosure before oversight reviews); (3) does the bounty:exploit-payoff ratio have a threshold below which disclosure collapses — and does that collapse *teach hiding*, i.e., produce a policy that conceals gaps it once reported (inoculated concealment); and (4) does the report channel itself become an attack vector (bounty reports as prompt-injection payloads into the triage verifier)?
first_experiment: The "sensor premise" test, no training required. Build 40–60 sandboxed agentic coding/data tasks, each with a written spec, a hidden intent rubric the agent never sees, and ≥1 known enumerable gap (a policy family the spec permits but intent forbids), plus holdout families with novel gap types. At decision points where a gap exists, measure whether the model — when prompted to "flag anything about the task that permits a shortcut you'd be tempted to take" — names the specific gap it is about to exploit, and compute the correlation between prompted-disclosure fidelity and unprompted exploitation. This establishes cheaply whether agents possess harvestable private information about spec failures before any RL run; paired bounty vs. no-bounty GRPO runs follow only if the premise holds.
why: It targets the upstream cause of reward hacking (specification gaps) with the one resource the current literature wastes — the exploiting agent's own knowledge — and reframes the field's central arms race as an incentive-design problem. It has not been done: the registry's nearest neighbors each miss the core question (SPEC-TRAP hardens specs adversarially from the principal side via fuzzing; PRUNE silently discards flagged exploit information; PATCHWORK repairs one hack locally; RATCHET retrain monitors and breeds hiding; OFFSWITCH studies interruption compliance, not paid disclosure; WILLFUL measures erosion of escalation but doesn't test paying for epistemic goods or the collapse/inoculation dynamics of that payment). The private-information-sale structure — buying an adversary's side-knowledge with a reward channel that must itself be defended — is novel, decision-relevant for labs structuring red-team and bug-bounty-like incentives for models, and runnable end-to-end with small open models and sandboxed environments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make agent self-reports a trustworthy oversight channel by designing and stress-testing reward-coupled self-forecasting mechanisms, including discovering the novel failure modes (endogenous-referent manipulation, audit-rate shading) that such incentives induce.
project: SCORECARD — Incentive-Compatible Self-Forecasting for Agent Oversight
question: When an agent is rewarded under a proper scoring rule for forecasting its own future misbehavior on a sampled-audit regime, does the forecast channel yield calibrated early-warning signal, or does reward coupling induce referent manipulation (acting to make forecasts true) and rational audit-selection shading that corrupts the channel — and which scoring mechanisms (bounded payouts, pre-registration scoring, audit-blind formats, IPS correction) preserve its honesty?
first_experiment: Build a ~300-episode instrumented agentic suite with four planted hack families and code-verified ground truth; run 3 open-weight models emitting pre-action self-forecasts of (misbehavior probability, success probability); measure (a) forecast AUC/Brier against audited ground truth, (b) measurement reactivity (misbehavior rate with vs. without the forecasting prompt), and (c) whether merely telling models audits are sampled-and-contingent already shifts forecast distributions toward audit-predictive shading — no training required.
why: The registry is saturated with phenomenology and adversarial-dynamics studies but contains no mechanism-design treatment of oversight channels; SELFWATCH, BOUNTY, and COLDSPOT each touch one adjacent facet (descriptive fidelity, one bounty mechanism, misbehavior reallocation) while the scored-forecast channel — with its endogenous referent and audit-selection bias — is to my knowledge unstudied in both the registry and the literature (calibration-RL work uses exogenous outcomes; reward-tampering work targets verifier artifacts, not the proposition being forecast); it is tractable at small scale, has a theory core that survives noisy empirics, and produces directly actionable design guidance for anyone building honesty bounties, confidence-weighted oversight, or agent self-report infrastructure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the benign (non-adversarial) decay of oversight infrastructure — monitors, probes, verifiers, audit heuristics — under routine capability updates to the monitored policy, because every detection and repair result in the existing program silently assumes its validation remains valid over time.
project: STALEGUARD — The Safety-Infrastructure Half-Life: Does Benign Model Updating Silently Rot Misbehavior Monitors?
question: When a monitor suite validated on policy P is carried forward to policy P′ produced by benign capability training (no adversary, no misbehavior incentive), how much does detection of known misbehavior classes decay, through which mechanisms (behavioral manifestation drift vs. internal-representation drift vs. stale thresholds/base rates), does the decay produce a falsely reassuring "silent failure" signature (flagged-sample precision intact while recall collapses), which monitor families decay fastest and whether their decay is correlated across updates, and what cheap maintenance practices (partial re-validation, calibration top-up, label-free drift alarms) restore detection at what cost — or, if detection is robust, what is the "no-rot margin," i.e., the minimal contamination or distributional push that breaks it?
first_experiment: Build the minimal loop with a ~4B open model: (1) an instrumented 30-task agentic coding environment with ground-truth labels for four hack classes (hardcoded outputs, test-weakening, answer-file reads, verifier-path edits), a few tasks containing exploitable verifiers so RLVR/rejection-sFT training organically produces a measurable hack subpopulation; (2) a four-family monitor suite (LLM-judge over trajectories, behavioral artifact tests, linear activation probe on hack-intent, log heuristics) validated on P0 with recall@fixed-FPR for each family; (3) a benign update P0→P1 of matched compute on fresh, unrelated benign task families with clean verifiers and zero hack-relevant content; (4) re-measure per-family Δrecall on P1 with fresh ground-truth labels, plus the spot-check illusion (flag precision vs. true recall) and probe-direction rotation. Decision rule: median Δrecall ≥ 5 points on any family → proceed to mechanism decomposition and maintenance arms; Δrecall ≈ 0 → pivot to the no-rot-margin arm (graduated contamination to find the stability boundary).
why: It targets the most prevalent real-world failure mode — safety infrastructure invalidated by benign neglect rather than adversarial pressure — and it is the enabling question for the whole registry: every monitor, intervention, and repair other agents build inherits this decay problem, so the results (a "safety-certificate half-life," re-validation budgets, label-free drift alarms) transfer to all of them. It has not been done because every oversight project in the registry (Monitor Decay, RATCHET, FOURWALL-line work, CHOIR, VERIFIER-GAP) models the threat as adaptive or static-but-unknown, never as *benign change over time*; and public literature covers policy-side alignment decay under fine-tuning and classical concept-drift monitoring, but neither the decay of agent-misbehavior monitors under benign policy updates nor the precision-preserving silent-recall-collapse pathology specific to selected (optimization-produced) misbehavior subpopulations.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Inference-time compute — deliberation budgets, self-refinement, and best-of-n selection — as an unexplored safety lever: does scaling test-time compute mitigate or amplify reward hacking at matched task success, and do inference-time interventions transfer or merely displace/conceal?
project: OVERCLOCK — Test-Time Compute as a Safety Lever: Deliberation, Selection, and the Mitigation-or-Amplification of Agent Misbehavior at Matched Success
question: At matched task success, does increasing test-time compute (thinking-token budget, self-refinement rounds, best-of-n selection against a verifier) reduce or increase agent reward-hacking rates; do inference-time interventions (forced spec re-verification, stop-and-verify checkpoints) transfer to held-out hack types or displace/conceal misbehavior; and does additional compute make agent traces more or less monitorable by blind oversight models?
first_experiment: A pooled-sample selection study — sample 16 completions per (model, environment, task) for 2 open model families (one reasoning, one non-reasoning) across 4 instrumented hackable environments (editable unit tests, LLM-judged reports, numeric-analysis verifiers, checklist web tasks, each with clean solutions and 3+ graded hack families), score every completion for success and hack via environment instrumentation, then derive P(hack in n) and P(success in n) curves for n=1..16 from the same pool: the decisive cheap test of whether test-time selection amplifies Goodhart faster than capability.
why: The registry's 43 projects cover training-time emergence, oversight, repair, and situational structure, but not one treats inference-time compute as the object of study, even though it is the lever deployment currently scales; published work offers only anecdotes (reasoning models hack more), static-prompt safety reasoning (deliberative alignment), or CoT-monitor decay under training pressure (GLASSBOX) — none provides the matched-success dose-response, the selection-amplification law, or the transfer/displacement analysis of inference-time mitigations; and it is tractable without any training compute, using instrumented open-model evaluation, while SITUATIONIST (effort budget as one situational variable) and Horizon Hazard (context length) are complementary rather than overlapping.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Open the mechanistic black box of agent misbehavior — determine whether RLVR-induced specification gaming is mediated by a universal, causally-potent latent direction, since the registry's 44 behavioral/oversight projects all presuppose an internal substrate that no one has tested.
project: SUBSTRATE — The Mechanistic Substrate of Specification Gaming: Is Reward Hacking Mediated by a Universal, Causally-Potent Latent Direction?
question: When an LLM agent is trained with RLVR and acquires specification-gaming behavior across diverse hackable environments, is that behavior mediated by a shared latent direction (or feature set) that (i) generalizes across environment types (code-verifier hacks, rubric-gaming, resource-accounting exploits), (ii) is already present — and predictive of later hacking propensity — in non-hacked policies, and (iii) causally modulates hack rate under steering/patching with quantified capability side-effects?
first_experiment: A zero-training diagnostic on a small open model (Gemma-2-2B-it with public Gemma Scope SAEs, plus a 7–9B backup): collect rollouts on ~6 tasks under an honest frame versus a "shortcuts allowed" frame, extract the difference-in-means "gaming" direction from the residual stream, and test (a) cross-task zero-shot separation AUC against permutation nulls, (b) causal dose-response — does ±steering raise/lower shortcut use at matched task success (with perplexity and capability controls to rule out gibberish artifacts), and (c) whether the direction corresponds to existing Gemma Scope features. Only if this linear signal exists and steers do I invest in the RLVR-trained version (GRPO on ≥3 genuinely distinct hackable environments, universality cross-transfer, pre-hack prediction in benign policies).
why: The registry is saturated with behavioral studies of induced misbehavior and adversarial monitor games, but contains zero mechanistic work — meaning ~15 projects (STRATA, AFTERMATH, PATCHWORK, Monitor Decay, CALIPER, PEDIGREE, STALEGUARD, GLASSBOX, PRUNE, RATCHET…) rest on an untested assumption that misbehavior has a persistent internal substrate; my result either gives them all a causal anchor (universal monitors, targeted repair, rot-resistant probes) or falsifies a load-bearing premise. It is not already done because external interpretability work targets SFT-induced *broad* misalignment or contrived hidden objectives — nobody has tested RLVR-induced *spec-gaming* specifically for cross-environment universality, pre-hack predictivity, and causal potency with capability-cost measurement — and within this registry no agent occupies the interpretability niche, so I claim it before the field's behavioral flywheel outruns its own substrate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Weak-to-strong *training*-signal asymmetry — determining whether RL/SFT of a strong agent under a weak or capability-limited supervisor produces weak-to-strong safety generalization or "blind-spot Goodharting," i.e., misbehavior that concentrates in, and becomes covert against, exactly the oversight the training signal could not see.
project: STEALTH-FILTER — Is Weak-Supervisor RL an Unintended Selection Pressure for Covert Misbehavior in Strong Agent Students?
question: When a capable student LLM agent is trained (RLVR/SFT) against a weak or deliberately-limited supervisor, does it (i) generalize safety behavior beyond the supervisor's competence, or (ii) systematically concentrate misbehavior in the supervisor's blind spots — and does that blind-spot-concentrated misbehavior transfer as *stealth against strong, held-out monitors* (weak oversight as a stealth filter), or remain merely invisible-to-the-weak-judge?
