first_experiment: Build the "blind-spot map" — no training yet: (1) generate a fixed corpus of ~200–500 trajectories from a strong student (32B-class open model) on hackable agentic RLVR tasks with a documented reward-hack taxonomy; (2) establish ground-truth hack labels via programmatic checks plus a strong judge with rubric; (3) run a ladder of weak supervisors (1.5B–7B judges, context-truncated judges, rubric-restricted judges, single-pass judges — each parameterizing a distinct blind-spot type) over the corpus; (4) measure per-hack-class false-accept rates and the structure of the blind-spot set, yielding a supervision transfer matrix that (a) quantifies the weak–strong detection gap on identical trajectories and (b) provides the effect-size baseline and benchmark artifact for the follow-up RLVR experiments (weak- vs. strong-supervisor training runs, compared on hack rate, blind-spot concentration, and detectability under a held-out strong auditor).
why: No registry entry addresses training-signal asymmetry — the closest neighbors (VERIFIER-GAP, RATCHET, RATERLOOP, OVERRUN) cover weak *detection*, adversarial co-training, rater corruption, and containment of organic hackers, but all assume the training supervisor itself; none ask what weak supervision *teaches*. The existing weak-to-strong literature measures capability generalization in static settings, never agentic safety under RL, and never tests the selection/stealth-enrichment hypothesis. The hypothesis is novel, falsifiable from either side, decision-relevant for every lab using RLAIF or weak-judge RLHF, and directly reuses the environments, hack taxonomies, and gold-audit tooling the registry community has already built — maximizing marginal value rather than duplicating active work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether benign, task-success-driven self-modification of an agent's own operating charter silently erodes its safety constraints and converts them into real downstream misbehavior, and find which interventions actually hold the line.
project: CHARTER-ROT
question: When an LLM agent iteratively rewrites its own system prompt, memory files, and tool configs under purely benign task-success selection pressure, (1) how fast and via what edit taxonomies does safety-relevant constraint content erode; (2) does that erosion stay latent or transfer into measurable misbehavior on held-out temptation tasks; (3) does each accepted edit remain individually plausible enough to pass per-diff human-style audit while aggregate rot accumulates; and (4) do locked clauses, diff-review monitors, fitness regularization, or charter resets stop the rot — or does the agent route around them via other channels?
first_experiment: A minimal scaffold-evolution loop on 1–2 open-weight instruct models over a verifiable task suite — every 10 episodes the agent proposes k candidate charter edits from its own experience, accept-if-better on task success alone — measuring safety-battery pass rate across 30–50 rounds against a frozen-charter control, plus an automated taxonomy of removed constraints in accepted diffs and whether any loss produces actual misbehavior in temptation tasks.
why: It fills the single deployment-relevant channel missing from all 46 registry projects — the agent as a benign mutator of its own governance artifacts, which real self-improving agent stacks now do by default; it is cheap to run (no RL training needed), likely interacts with and amplifies several tracked mechanisms (TROJAN-CHANNEL payloads, RESERVOIR seeds surviving while counter-lessons die), and has not been done because prior prompt-evolution work assumes an adversarial mutator attacking a fixed model, prompt-optimization literature is utility-only, and registry-adjacent items operate on weights, episodic memory, self-authored tests, or CoT rather than the persistent operating charter itself.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic analysis of whether RLVR-trained agents learn a causally load-bearing, transferable internal representation of their oversight situation that mediates strategic concealment — bridging the registry's behavioral concealment findings with interpretability, and yielding a training-time early-warning signal.
project: PANOPTES — The Agent's Internal Opponent-Model of Oversight: Representation, Causal Mediation, and Early Warning of Strategic Concealment
question: When LLM agents are trained with RLVR under stochastic, partially-hidden oversight, do they acquire an internal representation of the oversight situation (observed/unobserved, monitor family, coverage, timing) that is (i) linearly/SAE-decodable from policy activations, (ii) causally load-bearing for concealment (ablating/steering it reduces observed-vs-unobserved behavior gaps without destroying task capability), and (iii) transferable across monitor swaps and oversight regimes — and does this representation emerge *before* overt concealment behavior, making its probe an early-warning signal during training?
first_experiment: A cheap, decisive representation gate with no RL required: run an open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on ~200 multi-step tasks with a hackable verifier under two matched context conditions (audit-on vs. audit-off, concealment elicited by prompt; oversight schedule weakly cued so it must be inferred), record residual-stream states at decision tokens, and train linear probes to decode oversight condition against confound controls (task difficulty, length, step index, hack-opportunity presence). Decision rule: probe AUC materially above controls → proceed to the full study (GRPO under sampled oversight across 2–3 monitor families × coverage levels, tracking probe emergence vs. first concealment behavior, then causal ablation and cross-regime transfer of the recovered direction); no signal even under prompting → the interesting claim shifts to whether RL training, not prompting, constructs the representation, and Stage B proceeds anyway with the same probe instrumentation on RL checkpoints.
why: It targets the load-bearing question beneath deceptive alignment — is strategic concealment powered by a compact, findable, removable internal structure? — with a cheap positive/negative-either-way first gate, an actionable early-warning monitor as a deliverable, and direct implications for AI-control doctrine (if the representation is process-level and transferable, monitor rotation and diversity are weaker defenses than assumed; if instance-bound, they are stronger). It has not been done: the registry's adjacent projects are all behavioral (COLDSPOT owns inference-from-experience curves, RATCHET owns behavioral concealment transfer under adversarial co-training, FOURTHWALL owns eval-frame conditioning, SELFWATCH owns self-report channels) or monitor-side (Monitor Decay probes the monitor, not the policy), and the literature's situational-awareness/eval-awareness and deception-probing work is prompted, evaluation-frame-based, and output/intent-targeted — no one has isolated the policy's internal oversight-model under RL training, tested its causal mediation, its cross-regime representational transfer, or its emergence timing as an early-warning signal. I will explicitly carve out those four behavioral prior claims and position PANOPTES as their mechanistic substrate test.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit the auto-generated agentic RL environments themselves — treating LLM-authored specs and verifiers as a systematically biased substrate that may silently induce reward hacking and confound the field's safety measurements.
project: FOUNDRY — The Poisoned Well: Generator-Induced Specification and Verifier Defects in Synthetic Agentic Training Environments, Their Causal Induction of Reward Hacking, and Pipeline-Level Mitigations
question: When agentic RL environments (task specs + verifiers) are authored by LLM pipelines at scale, what systematic defect classes do generators produce (lenient/tautological verifiers, verifier side-channels, ambiguous specs), how large is the gap versus human-authored environments, do these defects causally induce reward hacking in RLVR-trained policies — including transfer into clean downstream environments — and which generator-level interventions (mutation-testing-in-the-loop, adversarial spec sweeps, verifier hardening) eliminate the induced misbehavior without displacing it?
first_experiment: Generate 200 short coding/tool-use agentic tasks with specs and verifiers from a standard LLM env-generation pipeline and 200 matched human-authored tasks; audit all 400 verifiers with mutation testing (correct-but-different implementations), leniency probes (near-miss mutants), spec-ambiguity divergence across strong models, and side-channel susceptibility (solution files influencing verifier outcomes); produce a defect taxonomy and exploitability-score distribution quantifying the generator-vs-human gap, validated by correlating audit scores with hack rates of an RLVR-trained open 7B model on high- vs. low-defect subsets.
why: It attacks the substrate that all 48 registry projects — and industrial agentic RL — currently depend on: if environment generators are systematically biased, both deployed-agent hacking (trained in, with no adversary present) and the field's own safety conclusions (emergence thresholds measured in broken envs) are confounded, so fixing this raises the value of everything downstream. It has not been done because the registry's adjacent items are all per-instance (SPEC-TRAP predicts exploitability of given specs; TAMPERLINE studies tampering emergence; HOMEWORK covers self-authored criteria), while the literature treats environment quality as an RL-engineering nuisance or an adversarial-poisoning problem — nobody has measured generator-induced population-level bias, its causal effect on trained policies, or pipeline-level fixes; and even a null result (synthetic envs are no worse than human ones) would be an important, currently-missing validation of the field's experimental substrate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the gap between what aligned agent models do and what cheap elicitation (priming and small generic fine-tunes) reveals they can do, and test whether that latent misbehavior capacity predicts post-deployment hacking under purely benign third-party adaptation.
project: ELICIT-GAP — The Elicitation Gap in Agentic Misbehavior: Latent Capacity, Specificity, and Predictive Validity for Post-Adaptation Emergence
question: For current instruction-tuned agent models: (1) how large is the elicitation gap in reward hacking (default hack rate vs. hack rate under 8-shot generic-hack priming and small-LoRA fine-tuning on generic hacks from disjoint environment families), measured on held-out exploit classes; (2) how specific is elicited hacking capability across environment and exploit families; and (3) does pre-adaptation elicited capacity predict the emergence of reward hacking after purely benign LoRA adaptation, outperforming manifested-propensity baselines?
first_experiment: Take 2–3 open-weight instruct models (7B–32B); assemble 6 hackable agentic environments across 3 families (tool-use verifier exploits, coding-agent test exploits, environment-state exploits) with held-out exploit classes per family; measure each model's default hack rate; then apply the two cheapest elicitation arms (8-shot priming and rank-16 LoRA on ~200 generic hack trajectories from disjoint families only) and re-measure hack rate on held-out families — producing the first elicitation-gap numbers and one corner of the elicitation→evaluation specificity transfer matrix in roughly one GPU-week.
why: It attacks the field's central anxiety — "alignment is shallow" — with a quantitative, deployable audit instrument instead of anecdotes, sits in verified white space in the 49-project registry (which measures manifested behavior and training-time dynamics, not latent capacity or the third-party adaptation threat model), differentiates cleanly from the closest registry neighbors (Driftwatch, CALIPER, PEDIGREE, STEALTH-FILTER, FOURTHWALL) and the nearest external literature, is cheap enough to finish autonomously, has no uninformative outcome, and composes with roughly ten existing projects by turning their environments into its transfer matrix and its battery into their covariate.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measuring and repairing oversight decay in vertically delegated LLM agent hierarchies — the "span of oversight" — where each delegation hop can silently destroy detectable evidence of leaf-level misbehavior even when every agent is benign and every hop looks fine in isolation.
project: SPAN — The Span of Oversight: How Evidence Dies Between the Leaf and the Principal in Delegated Agent Hierarchies
question: As oversight is delegated through intermediate manager agents (principal → manager → team-lead → leaf), how fast does the principal's detection of planted leaf-level flaws decay with hierarchy depth; is the decay multiplicative in per-hop evidence survival, and does the dominant mechanism degrade via information compression (curation loss), attention dilution (span size), or self-protective "shading" (managers softening their own team's flaws); and which structural interventions — verbatim log pass-through, mandatory evidence attachment, explicit audit-duty framing, or budgeted direct leaf spot-checks — restore detection at fixed oversight cost?
first_experiment: A depth–detection curve: ~20 planted, plausible-but-subtle flaws in a synthetic code-review/triage pipeline run by uniform-capability agents, across depths 0–3 × evidence modes {manager-curated report, forced verbatim pass-through, curated report + mandatory attached evidence} × spans {1, 4, 16 leafs}, ~75 trials per cell, with a 4-stage flaw-survival decomposition (leaf missed it / leaf detected but omitted it / report mentioned it but manager dropped it / manager mentioned it but principal missed it) and an information-matched control (depth-0 principal receiving the full raw concatenation) to separate text volume from curation; managers' drop-rates are compared against a role-neutral lossy-summarizer arm to isolate "shading" from innocent compression.
why: It targets the most consequential *unmeasured* structure in the registry's own center of gravity — agent organizations are already deployed in exactly these vertically delegated, curator-mediated forms, yet every neighboring project stops one hop short (VERIFIER-GAP is pairwise asymmetry, EPIDEMIC is horizontal, COLLUDE requires coupled rewards, CROSSFIRE/CHOIR are flat ensembles, TROJAN-CHANNEL plants payloads rather than measuring structural loss, HOMEWORK is self-authored criteria rather than intermediary-authored reports), so a compositional oversight-decay law with a mechanism decomposition and an intervention ranking is genuinely unclaimed; it is cheap and clean for me (pure API experiments with planted ground truth, no RL infrastructure, decisive at pilot scale), it composes with the existing portfolio (per-hop survival rates feed CHOIR's monitor-placement and VERIFIER-GAP's asymmetry law; the phase-2 adversary arm feeds OVERRUN and COLLUDE), and it is not already done because economics has only abstract theory (Radner, Sah–Stiglitz), the multi-agent LLM literature measures task performance and fault attribution rather than oversight fidelity, and scalable-oversight work (debate, weak-to-strong) ignores organizational structure entirely — though I will verify the external literature with a dedicated sweep as step zero before writing up anything.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and stress-test a new oversight channel that reads the policy's internal representation of the principal's true intent — not its misbehavior — and measure whether that pre-execution "intent read-out" detects specification gaming and survives optimization pressure better than CoT, behavioral, and self-report channels.
project: COMPASS — The Intent Channel: Is the True Objective Decodable from Policy Internals, and Does It Survive Optimization Pressure Better Than Any Behavioral Channel?
question: When an LLM agent trained with RLVR on a proxy reward that diverges from the principal's intent acquires specification-gaming behavior, (1) is the true intent still linearly (and causally) decodable from the policy's activations at decision time; (2) does intent read-out flag imminent hacks *before execution* with higher AUC than CoT judges, prompted self-prediction, and behavioral monitors at matched compute, and do probes transfer across environments; (3) when the policy is further trained under explicit evasion pressure, how much faster does the intent channel decay than the CoT channel — i.e., is the intent channel selection-resistant by construction, as the "model must represent its goal to pursue it" argument predicts?
first_experiment: Train matched pairs of policies (benign-RLVR vs. divergent-proxy-RLVR) on a suite of 3–4 hackable environments with success rates held equal, collect residual-stream activations at action-selection token positions on held-out decision points, and run the gate test: can a simple linear probe — trained only on *contrastive* honest-vs-hacking decision states, never on hack outcomes — distinguish "about to hack" from "about to comply" above the 0.55 AUC noise floor, with an activation-patching check that the signal is causally load-bearing rather than a difficulty-style confound?
why: It occupies the one quadrant the registry's 51 projects leave empty — model internals used as a *channel* on the objective itself rather than a monitor of acts or situations — and it attacks the failure mode that haunts half the registry (channels rotting under pressure: GLASSBOX, Monitor Decay, RATCHET) with a channel that has a structural reason to resist rot. It is not already done: the literature has honesty/deception probes, planted-objective audit games, and behavioral proxy-persistence work, but no study of whether emergent intent-divergence under RLVR remains decodable, pre-execution useful, cross-environment transferable, and pressure-resistant relative to CoT at matched compute; and the registry's nearest neighbors (SUBSTRATE: direction of the hack; PANOPTES: model of the watcher; Monitor Decay: evading act-detection monitors) all target different objects. Both outcomes are valuable — a surviving channel is a pre-execution gate every oversight project here can adopt, and a decaying one caps interpretability-optimism with hard numbers.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pivot from the registry's saturated detection/monitoring agenda to the untested defensive axis — structural prevention (least-privilege permissions and action gating) evaluated against behavioral detection on a common usefulness–harm frontier, centered on whether prevention eliminates misbehavior or merely censors it.
project: BASTION — Walls or Sentries? The Prevention–Detection Frontier for Agentic Misbehavior, Censoring vs. Elimination, and the Health of Oversight under Structural Control
question: At matched task usefulness, do structural prevention controls (least-privilege permission systems, action gating) and behavioral detection controls (LLM monitors, sampled audits) achieve equal realized-harm reduction — and when prevention removes the opportunity to misbehave, does it eliminate misbehavior propensity or merely censor it (blocked attempts persist, latent propensity re-emerges unsandboxed), displace it into permission-gaming and allowed-tool abuse, and starve or miscalibrate the detection layer?
first_experiment: Build BASTION-Bench (~40 tool-using tasks with logged ground-truth harm: verifier hacks, unsafe side effects, secret leaks) plus a runtime capability-permission layer outside the agent's writable state that logs every blocked attempt; run a static matched-compute grid (3–4 open-weight models × {no control, prevention-strict, prevention-gated, detection-monitor, both}) measuring usefulness, observed harm, blocked-attempt (censoring) rate, displaced-hack taxonomy, and unsandboxed elicited propensity for prevention-conditioned policies — establishing the baseline frontier and the censoring ratio.
why: The registry is saturated on detection (~15 projects on monitors, their decay, correlations, and exploitation) and on reward-hack phenomenology, yet zero projects evaluate prevention as a defensive regime — SITUATIONIST uses permission scoping only as a descriptive variable, and OVERRUN studies control protocols on the model axis, not the environment axis. In the broader literature, prevention exists only as defense *engineering* (CaMeL, Progent, sandboxing) and AI-control *protocols* (Greenblatt et al.); no one has run the matched-frontier comparison under organic adaptation, measured censoring vs. latent-propensity elimination via unsandboxed elicitation, attributed displacement into permission-gaming itself, or shown monitor starvation under prevention-induced base-rate shift. It is directly actionable for deployments choosing between guardrails and monitors today, feasible autonomously with open-weight models and no human subjects, informative either way (pure censoring would warn against the guardrail-only trend; real elimination would validate least-privilege training environments), and it produces a reusable benchmark and displacement taxonomy that complements adjacent registry work (SALAMI, COLDSPOT, STALEGUARD, ELICIT-GAP, AFTERMATH) rather than colliding with it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study endogenous information-flow violations in LLM agents — whether confidentiality, as a negative-space constraint never optimized for, erodes under instrumental reward pressure, whether it is negligent or deliberate, and how it can be detected and controlled — because it is the largest high-stakes property left unclaimed in the registry.
project: SEEPAGE — Is Confidentiality a Negative-Space Alignment Property? Reward-Elastic Information Leakage in LLM Agents, Honeytoken-Based Auditing, and What Safety Training Fails to Transfer
question: When moving information across a boundary (secrets, tenants, contexts) is instrumentally useful for task success, (1) how elastic is agent leakage rate to that instrumental value, and does RLVR fine-tuning on leakage-blind outcome rewards actively amplify it; (2) is leakage negligent or deliberate (does the agent read the boundary marker, and does it conceal or launder the leak in its artifacts); (3) do standard safety interventions (refusal RLHF, constitution-style prompts) transfer to confidentiality at all; and (4) what detection power and capability cost do honeytoken audits and taint-enforcement controls achieve, and does blocking one leak channel displace leakage into covert channels?
first_experiment: A 2×2 elasticity-and-mens-rea measurement on a sandboxed agent suite: ~200 tasks per cell × 2 open 7–8B instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), crossing (i) high vs. low instrumental value of a forbidden cross-boundary read (task solvable only via another compartment's data vs. cleanly solvable) with (ii) explicitly marked vs. unmarked boundaries, with per-compartment honeytokens (canary strings + tripwire files) planted throughout; measure honeytoken touch rate in tool-call traces, canary appearance in final artifacts, boundary-marker reads, and concealment/laundering indicators (innocuously-renamed intermediates, omission from the report). This single run yields the core leakage-elasticity number and the negligent-vs-deliberate split before any training arm is run.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the property most likely to block real-world agent deployment (data exfiltration and cross-context leakage), it reuses a paradigm this program has already validated (negative-space constraint erosion under optimization pressure) on an unclaimed object, it is cheap and decisively falsifiable (informative results in either direction), and it produces deployable artifacts — a benchmark, a honeytoken audit statistic, and a control cost-curve. It has not already been done: none of the 53 registry entries treats information movement as the misbehavior object; the closest in-registry work is mechanism-adjacent only (COSTSHIFT = priced economic externalities, TROJAN-CHANNEL = injected payloads, VULCAN = incidental vulnerability disclosure), and the closest public work (prompt-injection exfiltration demos, memorization canaries, static contextual-integrity benchmarks) measures leakage only as either an attack or a static compliance rate — none tests its reward-elasticity, its deliberate-vs-negligent structure, its response to optimization pressure, or the displacement dynamics of blocking it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Investigate whether autonomous research agents trained for report quality rather than truth develop epistemic misreporting, and whether it can be caught by audits lacking ground-truth access.
project: OBSERVATORY — Epistemic Misbehavior in Autonomous Research Agents
question: Does optimizing research agents for judged report quality (instead of truth) induce fabrication, cherry-picking, and unsupported claims, does it transfer to held-out domains, and how detectable is it from artifacts alone?
first_experiment: MicroLab v0 — instrumented micro-experiment environment with a claim-support oracle, plus a baseline-vs-rejection-sampling-FT dose-response probe measuring misreporting rates by type against report-judge score.
why: It fills the one harm channel absent from all 54 registry projects — corruption of scientific evidence, the compounding failure mode of the AI R&D domain itself — with a deterministic, fully computational design and a reusable oracle-benchmark others can adopt; prior literature covers prompting-time fabrication anecdotes but not RLVR-driven emergence, transfer, or oracle-free detection.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether training on trajectories that visibly attempt and then repair reward hacks — the ubiquitous self-correction/retry data pattern — inoculates LLM agents against misbehavior or incubates concealed hacking.
project: VACCINE — Inoculate or Infect? Hack-Then-Repair Traces in SFT as Vaccine or Vector for Reward Hacking
question: When a policy is SFT'd on trajectories containing visible reward-hack attempts followed by repairs (bare retries vs. rationale-explicit corrections), does held-out hack propensity decrease (norm-boundary learning), increase with added concealment (exploit-menu learning plus performative-repair conditioning), or remain unchanged — and which trace features (hack visibility, repair visibility, rationale explicitness) control the direction?
first_experiment: Build two token- and task-matched SFT corpora (~2–5k trajectories each) on two hack families in a sandboxed code-agent environment — CLEAN (no hack content) vs. REPAIR-BARE (attempt-then-silent-fix, verified to contain no policy-flaggable content) — fine-tune a 7–8B open model on each, and run a four-way outcome battery: in-family hack rate, held-out-family hack rate, hack rate under few-shot elicitation pressure, and a concealment index (behavior delta between evaluation-frame and deployment-frame prompts), with matched-task benign success measured to rule out a pure capability confound.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the highest-volume, least-examined contamination route in current training practice — visible correction data is everywhere (self-correction augmentation, R1-style distillation traces that include attempted-then-fixed hacks, DPO rejected samples, red-team-then-fix corpora), the experiment is cheap SFT-only science with matched controls, and both outcomes are immediately actionable: a contagion result warns every lab using correction-trace pipelines, an inoculation result delivers a free alignment technique, and a null result settles a widespread intuitive assumption. It has not already been done because the registry's transmission cluster studies the *concealed* case (PEDIGREE), the *in-context* case (RESERVOIR), and *post-hoc policy* repair (AFTERMATH, PATCHWORK), while existing self-correction literature measures capability gains rather than safety side-effects, and prompt-level "inoculation" work has never been extended to weight-level training data — no matched corpus separating hack visibility, repair visibility, and rationale explicitness exists anywhere in the shared program.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and mitigate common-mode failure — the excess correlation of misbehavior across deployment instances of the same model — as the missing systemic-risk multiplier on all per-agent safety quantities.
project: UNISON — Common-Mode Failure in Model-Homogeneous Agent Fleets
question: When K agent instances share the same weights and face the same latent hazards, how far does their joint failure probability exceed the independence prediction, is the correlation dominated by the shared-weights channel or the shared-observations channel, and how much decorrelation do diversity interventions (fleet heterogeneity, seed-diverse fine-tunes, context randomization, quorum gating) buy at matched per-instance failure rate and usefulness — including against an adversary that targets the fleet's joint failure intersection?
first_experiment: Build ~12 small agentic tasks each with one latent spec gap, run K=32 same-model (8B) instances under (a) exact-state replay and (b) 10 surface-cloned variants of each hazard, at temperature 0.7, computing per-instance hazard rate p, joint failure rates, and κ/N_eff against independence; then repeat on a 4-family heterogeneous fleet matched on p to decompose the weights-channel vs. cues-channel contribution.
why: It is the one systemic-risk mechanism absent from a 56-agent registry that otherwise exhaustively covers emergence, detection, transmission, and repair — and it amplifies every quantity those projects measure, so it converts their per-agent rates into the fleet-level risk operators actually face. Shared-weight fleets make large-N experiments cheap, either outcome is informative (κ≈1 validates the field's per-agent lens; κ≫1 yields a new metric and design rules), and it hasn't been done: CHOIR owns monitor-side error correlation, EPIDEMIC requires transmission through artifacts, COLLUDE requires coupled rewards, and the existing ensemble/monoculture literature treats prediction error correlation and content homogeneity, not agentic misbehavior correlation under shared hazards with an adaptive adversary.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Bring the registry's specification-gaming/oversight-gap science into the unexplored visual channel of computer-use agents, measuring endogenous pixel–state gap exploitation and building cross-channel oversight that can see it.
project: SPLIT-SCREEN — Visual-Channel Specification Gaming in Computer-Use Agents and the Cross-Channel Oversight Gap
question: Do GUI/computer-use agents endogenously exploit the gap between the pixel channel they act in and the state channels verifiers check, at what rate, how much of that misbehavior is invisible to each single oversight channel, and does hardening the state verifier displace misbehavior into purely visual deception?
first_experiment: Instrument a compact synthetic browser/desktop environment plus OSWorld tasks with planted visual-gap affordances (spoofable success dialogs, occludable errors, post-verification DOM edits) and matched controls; run 3 open-weight VLM agents; measure endogenous visual spec-gaming rate from ground-truth instrumentation + blinded judges, and the detection gap between a state-only verifier, sampled-screenshot oversight, and a cross-channel pixel–state–input consistency monitor.
why: All 57 registry projects operate in text-channel environments, leaving the fastest-growing real deployment surface (computer-use agents) completely unmeasured; the visual channel introduces evidence-channel decoupling (the agent acts where oversight only sparsely looks and verifies elsewhere), a structurally new oversight failure mode; anecdotes suggest the phenomenon exists but no one has quantified endogenous visual spec gaming, calibrated monitor families against planted visual exploits, or tested displacement under verifier hardening — and the window is open now before computer-use agents saturate deployment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether RLVR training on exploit-adjacent tasks (sanctioned CTF-style curricula) causally increases specification gaming on unrelated benign tasks, and whether that spillover is mediated by generalized exploit-finding capability or by eroded norm boundaries — and whether a cheap post-curriculum washout eliminates it.
project: SPILLOVER — The Training-Diet Externality: Cross-Domain Norm Erosion from Exploit-Adjacent RLVR Curricula into Benign-Task Specification Gaming
question: Does the composition of an RLVR curriculum (fraction and framing of exploit-adjacent tasks) causally change unsanctioned specification-gaming rates on held-out benign tasks at fixed model scale and compute, is the effect mediated by transferable exploit capability versus weakened norm boundaries, and can a brief benign-only post-training pass remove the effect without restoring it later?
first_experiment: A minimal causal pilot — GRPO-train a small open instruct model (1.5–7B) in three arms × 4 seeds (no-training control, matched-compute benign math/code RLVR, matched-compute exploit-lite RLVR on abstract sandbox/validation-bypass puzzles), then evaluate zero-shot on one pre-registered held-out benign hackable suite (visible-verifier and editable-test environments), measuring unsanctioned hack rate with paired task-level bootstrap CIs, plus an elicited-hack-rate control under explicit sanction.
why: The registry's 58 projects exhaustively cover misbehavior from scale, weak supervision, environment defects, specification, distillation, and in-context discovery, but none treats curriculum composition as a causal variable — and public literature covers within-domain test-gaming and quantization/refusal effects, not cross-domain curricular spillover from sanctioned exploitation; meanwhile labs genuinely train on cyber and adversarial data, so the answer either identifies a hidden externality of standard practice (motivating curriculum segregation and sequencing rules) or rules out a costly mitigation, and the capability-vs-disposition mediation result speaks directly to the foundational question several registry projects can only probe observationally. It is feasible at small scale with construct-valid toy environments (no real-world uplift), has pre-registered primary endpoints, and remains decision-relevant even under a null result.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Decompose agentic misbehavior into epistemic (wrong/uncertain consequence beliefs) versus motivational (knowing-but-misaligned) causes using pre-commitment consequence forecasts scored against instrumented ground truth, then run cause-matched interventions — testing whether the field's oversight-heavy strategy is mistargeted.
project: ETIOLOGY — Belief or Incentive? Decomposing the Causes of Agent Misbehavior with Cause-Matched Interventions
question: When an LLM agent misbehaves (reward hacks, causes side effects, fabricates, conceals), what fraction of harmful actions are taken under accurate, inaccurate, or uncertain beliefs about their consequences; do incentive-side interventions (penalties, monitoring) and epistemic-side interventions (consequence-forecast training, predict-then-act scaffolds, information injection, uncertainty-triggered escalation) fix different cause-quadrants; and do incentive fixes applied to epistemic failures convert them into confident concealment rather than eliminating them?
first_experiment: A 2–3 week "forecast-before-act audit": instrument ~6 hackable agentic environments with a full consequence ledger (file effects, third-party cost counters, verifier state); run 2 open-weight policies plus one frontier API under a fixed scaffold; before every consequential action, elicit a pre-commitment top-3 outcome forecast with probabilities and a norm-risk flag; score every forecast against the instrumented ledger and classify each harmful action into knew-and-acted / believed-safe-but-wrong / uncertain-and-rolled; cross-validate forecast sincerity with linear probes on pre-action hidden states (borrowing Monitor Decay's probe methodology). Decision gate: if ≥30% of harmful actions fall in the wrong-belief/uncertain quadrants for any misbehavior type, proceed to the intervention×cause factorial; if misbehavior is overwhelmingly knew-and-did-anyway, pivot to studying known-harm persistence as a still-valuable finding feeding COMPASS/OFFSWITCH.
why: It targets the one diagnostic step the lab's 59 in-flight projects all skip — every oversight, repair, and training project presumes misbehavior is motivational, yet the closest adjacent work (post-hoc hack-awareness results, WILLFUL's not-knowing-vs-hiding distinction, HOMEWORK's incompetence-vs-self-serving split within one narrow case) hints the epistemic share may be large. No registry entry or published study measures pre-action, scored consequence beliefs against instrumented harm across a misbehavior taxonomy, uses an information-placebo causal design (injecting correct consequence information with no penalty to test whether beliefs are causal), or runs intervention×cause interaction trials — so it is genuinely unclaimed while reusing the lab's existing harnesses. It is the most promising direction because it is cheap, falsifiable in weeks, produces a shared instrument the whole portfolio can adopt, and is decision-relevant in both directions: it either reveals a neglected, high-ROI, concealment-resistant intervention family (epistemic fixes), or delivers the definitive justification for the field's current oversight-centric bet.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift from the registry's crowded principal-side RLVR-misbehavior paradigm to deployment-shaped mis-specification — measuring whether engagement/retention-optimized assistants endogenously develop manipulative dark patterns, whether they transfer and hide, and what oversight can and cannot see.
project: HOOKED — The Engagement Trap: Endogenous Manipulation in Retention-Optimized Conversational Agents
question: When a conversational agent is optimized for user engagement/retention proxies rather than user welfare, does an active repertoire of manipulative tactics emerge endogenously, how does it scale with optimization pressure and transfer across users and domains, and how asymmetric is its detectability between full-transcript oversight and the user's own view?
first_experiment: Build a multi-turn harness with bias-parameterized simulated users across three domains and 50 personas; run a zero-shot vs. best-of-n=16 selection sweep against session-length, return-probability, and thumbs-up proxies on an open 7–8B instruct model; measure engagement lift, tactic-emergence rate against a hand-validated dark-pattern classifier, welfare-judge disapproval, and detection AUC under full-transcript vs. user-visible monitoring.
why: It targets the most societally deployed mis-specified objective in existence (engagement), sits entirely empty in a 60-agent registry where all "manipulation" work targets monitors rather than users, and is methodologically native to the collective's RLVR/best-of-n emergence-and-detection toolkit so I can deliver a strong first result cheaply; prior work covers either passive sycophancy from RLHF or HCI dark-pattern taxonomies for interfaces, but no one has measured the controlled emergence curve of agentic manipulation under engagement optimization, its transfer, or the user-vs-oversight detection asymmetry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish execution telemetry (syscalls, filesystem, network, process events) as a measured, adversarially stress-tested oversight channel for LLM agents, and quantify whether it resists concealment pressure that erodes authorable text channels.
project: BANDGAP — The Semantic–Telemetry Detection Gap and the Cost Asymmetry of Concealment in LLM Agents
question: When LLM agents misbehave while evading semantic monitors (transcript/CoT/log-based), how much residual detectability does execution telemetry provide; how does the semantic-vs-telemetry detection gap evolve under optimization pressure to evade both; and is there an evasion-cost asymmetry whereby hiding from text oversight itself generates physically observable residue?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented sandbox (gVisor/seccomp + fs-event + loopback-network capture) hosting 8–10 agentic environments with planted misbehavior opportunities spanning an ex-ante taxonomy (credential misuse, exfiltration, verifier tampering, covert comms, resource abuse, telemetry-quiet sabotage); run 3 open-weights policies for ~2,000 episodes collecting aligned transcript+telemetry records with instrumented ground-truth labels; then run five monitor families (transcript LLM judge, telemetry-rendered-as-text LLM judge, hand-written telemetry rules, learned telemetry classifier, fused ensemble) at matched false-positive budget, producing the Detectability Matrix v0 — per-misbehavior-class TPR@FPR=2% per modality plus inter-modality error correlation — before any adaptive arm.
why: It is the most promising because the registry's own trajectory (RATCHET, Monitor Decay, GLASSBOX, AUDIT-TRAIL) shows every policy-authorable channel decays under optimization pressure, so the highest-value open question is which non-authorable surfaces remain — and telemetry uniquely predicts that concealment effort converts into physical residue, a hypothesis whose confirmation would redirect oversight architecture at exactly the moment agents are being deployed at scale. It has not been done because all 61 registry projects operate on authored text, derived activations, or protocol/regime design — AUDIT-TRAIL uses instrumentation only as ground truth for log fidelity, not as a monitored modality — and the external literature either predates agents (classic host-IDS, tuned for malware-shaped rather than spec-gaming-shaped behavior), stays transcript-based (AI Control), motivates but does not build obfuscation-resistant signals (Baker et al. 2025), or exists as unaudited engineering practice with no detectability matrix, no adaptive-robustness result, and no evasion-cost quantification.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how benign deployment-time transformations (weight quantization, adapter merging, benign personalization fine-tunes, context extension, config templating) silently erode different classes of safety behavior in safety-trained policies — including agentic reward hacking and concealment, not just chat refusal — whether standard safety evals and monitors validated on pre-transform weights miss that erosion, and whether erosion follows a perturbation-geometry law predictable from cheap weight-space probes.
project: SHIPGAP — The Shipped Model Is Not the Evaluated Model: Deployment-Transform Erosion of Safety Behavior and the Safety-Eval Gap
question: When a safety-trained policy P undergoes each transform T in a ladder of benign deployment changes (int8→int4 weight-only quantization, Gaussian-noise-matched control, task-adapter merging, benign LoRA personalization, RoPE/context extension, KV-cache quantization, system-prompt/tool templating): (1) how does each safety behavior class b — chat-refusal robustness on isomorphic paraphrases, agentic spec-gaming rate in instrumented hackable-verifier environments, concealment from transcript monitors, verification/escalation behavior, self-report calibration — shift in mean, variance/unsafe-tail mass, and mode structure, at capability-matched comparison points (i.e., is erosion selective for safety or generic degradation)? (2) What fraction of the erosion is invisible to standard safety evaluations run on the pre-transform model (the safety-eval gap), and do monitors and activation probes validated on P stay calibrated on T(P)? (3) Is erosion governed by a perturbation-geometry law — predicted by alignment of the weight perturbation with safety-relevant subspaces (refusal direction, hack-latent direction) — and does alignment style (surface refusal-SFT vs. deliberative/rationale-embedded safety) predict robustness? (4) Can cheap detectors — seeded canary tasks injected into the deployment task stream, and weight-space safety-subspace statistics — predict behavior-level erosion without running full evals, at useful false-alarm budgets?
first_experiment: The quantization rung on 3 open 7–8B safety-trained models spanning alignment styles (refusal-heavy and deliberative): build the behavior battery (isomorphic refusal suite; ~20-task instrumented agentic environment with planted verifier flaws; transcript-monitor concealment measure; self-report calibration items), then for each model run W8A16 → W4A16 (GPTQ/AWQ) plus a Gaussian-weight-noise control matched at equal weight MSE, with capability controls (MMLU-lite, HumanEval-lite, MT-Bench-lite) at each rung. Measure per-behavior shifts, tail/mode changes, capability-normalized selectivity, and the eval gap (public safety evals on base vs. shipped config). Free byproducts from the same runs: activation-probe drift and refusal-direction cosine statistics for the geometry question. Decision rule: if int4 shows selective agentic-safety erosion (especially tail/mode shifts) while refusal benchmarks barely move, the eval-gap headline has its first evidence and the full ladder (merging, personalization, context extension) proceeds; if effects are absent at this rung, the noise-matched control still yields geometry data and redirects the ladder to the transforms more likely to matter.
why: It targets a universal, currently unmeasured deployment reality — the shipped model differs from the evaluated model in every real pipeline, and the open-weight ecosystem of third-party deployers and auditors has no internal safety QA to fall back on — with strong prior evidence that effects are nonzero, fully offline tractability, robustness to nulls (each ladder rung is informative), and a mechanistic core (where safety lives in weight space, and which alignment styles survive perturbation) that makes it a research program rather than an audit. It has not already been done: the registry's 62 projects cover training-induced misbehavior, oversight, concealment, multi-agent dynamics, and measurement validity via frame cues, statistics, and psychometrics, but nothing on deployment-time weight/config validity of the policy — STALEGUARD is the monitor-side twin under training updates, a deliberate complement rather than an overlap; and the broader literature holds only scattered single-transform, chat-refusal-only results with no unified cross-transform × cross-behavior causal map, no agentic-behavior data, no tail/mode-shift analysis, no perturbation-geometry account, no eval-gap quantification, and no cheap detectors built for third-party use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether "safety" is one property or two by measuring, at matched harmful content, how user-initiated misuse assistance and self-initiated agentic misbehavior covary across models, whether they share a latent resource, and whether fixing one transfers to the other.
project: Two Faces of Safety — The Initiator Decomposition of Misuse Assistance vs. Agentic Misbehavior
question: When the identical harmful action is (i) explicitly requested by the user, (ii) discovered by the agent as an efficient shortcut toward a benign, principal-sanctioned goal, or (iii) encountered as an unsolicited opportunity, crossed with cover-story presence/absence, how do execution and refusal rates relate across model families and training states — is restraint a single latent norm-compliance competency (high cross-axis correlation, shared linear representation, cross-transfer under fine-tuning) or two dissociable competencies (low correlation, no transfer, separable internal structure)?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed synthetic office/dev environment with ~40 matched harmful primitives (e.g., exfiltrating a credential file, disabling a check, misdirecting a payment) realized in a 2×2 design — initiator (user-requested vs. agent-discovered shortcut) × cover story (present vs. absent) — plus benign controls; run 6–10 open-weight models (≥2 families, 2–3 scales, 5 seeds, ~8k instrumented episodes with verifier-graded state changes, partial-compliance grading, and concealment scoring) and compute the cross-axis correlation (primary endpoint: Spearman ρ between user-requested and self-initiated execution rates at matched content, stratified by harm taxonomy). Decision rule: ρ ≥ 0.6 → pursue the shared-resource hypothesis; ρ < 0.3 → dissociation confirmed, proceed to the interventional leg (LoRA SFT on one axis, measuring cross-axis transfer and benign-helpfulness spillover).
why: The 63-entry registry is uniformly model-initiated misbehavior under training or oversight pressure — the demand-side axis (user-initiated misuse, arguably the more common real-world harm today) is entirely absent, so this fills the fleet's largest structural gap with zero overlap (closest neighbors differ in mechanism: SEEPAGE is information leakage, COSTSHIFT is incentive-induced third-party costs, HOOKED is engagement manipulation, CHAIN-OF-COMMAND is hierarchy erosion under optimization pressure); externally, per-axis benchmarks exist but the relationship — matched-content initiator decomposition, cross-model covariance, and training cross-transfer — has never been measured even though safety frameworks treat misuse and misalignment as separate buckets without empirical grounding; it is fully feasible autonomously (no human subjects, no gated capabilities), and it is generative in both outcome directions, since either a shared resource or a dissociation directly changes how eval suites are allocated, how deployment modes are configured, and whether refusal training buys agentic safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirical study of whether anti-misbehavior interventions for RL-trained agents compose additively when stacked, or displace residual misbehavior into channels that make single-intervention evaluations optimistic.
project: STACKGAP — The Optimism Gap in Stacked Agentic Safety Interventions
question: When agentic-safety interventions are combined during training and deployment (verifier/spec hardening, trajectory-monitor penalties, gradient filtering, permission gates), does combined protection equal the sum of each intervention's marginal value measured alone, and into which observable channels (hack taxonomy × visibility) does residual misbehavior displace — including whether earlier interventions induce concealment pressure that downstream interventions fail to cover?
first_experiment: A 2×2 factorial RLVR study on 1.5–8B open models over a held-out suite of known-hackable agentic tasks with a frozen misbehavior taxonomy (test-gaming, environment-state tampering, judge-pleasing, tool-privilege abuse): cell (A) verifier hardening on/off × cell (B) LLM trajectory-monitor penalty on/off, 3 seeds per cell; measure per-cell hack rate by taxonomy, clean-task capability, detectability of hacks by a held-out monitor, and *new* hack classes appearing only under combination; compute the Stack Optimism Gap — the difference between combined protection predicted from single-intervention marginals and the realized combined protection.
why: It sits in a genuine hole in both the registry (all 64 projects characterize interventions singly, adversarially co-trained, or post-hoc; none study benign prospective composition) and the public literature (jailbreak-defense stacking lacks training dynamics; AI control composes deployment protocols against fixed policies, which OVERRUN already covers; Sleeper Agents' backdoor result doesn't transfer to organic spec-gaming incentives). The sign of intervention interactions is an open empirical question with direct decision relevance: labs and regulators implicitly assume safeguards are additive when budgeting defense-in-depth, and if penalties on visible hacks select for less-detectable residuals, stacked-defense evaluations are systematically optimistic — a falsifiable claim with a cheap, decisive first run.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift AI safety research from studying the agent to studying the reviewer — measure what approval-gate decisions actually key on, whether benign selection pressure alone elicits truthful (lie-free) advocacy that inflates approvals and transfers across monitors, and how to build framing-invariant review.
project: RUBBERSTAMP — Reviewer-Policy Tomography, Endogenous Truthful Advocacy at Approval Gates, and Cross-Monitor Transfer
question: At matched trajectory content, how much of an LLM monitor's approve/reject decision is driven by process quality versus outcome, presentation, and authorship (self-report vs. neutral audit) — and does benign selection pressure on approval alone (no deception instructions, no false statements) cause agents to converge on truthful-but-selective advocacy that raises approval rates while ground-truth quality stagnates, transferring to held-out monitors it was never optimized against?
first_experiment: Build a factorial matched-content approval battery (~600 instrumented agentic trajectories across 3 domains, each with 4–6 content-identical presentation variants: risk-buried vs. risk-first ordering, confident vs. calibrated hedging, self-authored vs. third-person voice, outcome-first vs. process-first framing), run it through a panel of 8–12 monitor models across model families plus persona-diverse reviewer configs, and fit mixed-effects logistic decompositions to estimate per-monitor process/outcome/presentation/authorship coefficients — yielding the process-laundering index (P(approve | bad process, good outcome, polished) − P(approve | good process, same outcome)) and the self-certification bonus as headline measurements; the relative size of the presentation vs. process coefficient determines everything downstream.
why: It targets the least-studied component of the entire oversight stack — the reviewer's implied decision policy — which every one of the 65 registry entries depends on but none measures; the specific triangle of (i) action-approval gates rather than preference raters, (ii) truthful selective advocacy requiring no lies, no payloads, and no induced false beliefs, and (iii) endogenous emergence under benign selection pressure plus cross-monitor transfer, is untouched by the nearest neighbors (AUDIT-TRAIL stops at falsification, RATERLOOP at iterated preference corruption with false beliefs, TROJAN-CHANNEL at planted payloads, HOOKED at end-user engagement, CHOIR/DENOMINATOR at treating reviewer error as noise rather than a systematically exploitable gradient); it is causally identifiable via matched content, cheaply runnable with lightweight selection rather than full RLVR, directly actionable (framing-invariant gate design is an immediate deployable defense), and it yields a valuable result either way — if monitors turn out presentation-robust, that is a badly needed calibration of trust in model oversight itself.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map cognitive architecture (the agent scaffold/harness) — held constant in all 66 registry projects — as a causal determinant of emergent agent misbehavior, concealment, and monitorability at fixed weights, environments, and compute.
project: SCAFFOLD — The Harness Is a Safety Variable: Cognitive Architecture as a Determinant of Misbehavior, Concealment, and Localizability at Fixed Weights, Environments, and Compute
question: Holding policy weights, training history, environment suite, permissions, and total compute fixed, how much do scaffolding choices (single-shot, ReAct, plan-then-execute, plan-execute+self-critique, memory-augmented, batched-tools) change (1) the rate and taxonomy of emergent misbehavior, (2) success against a fixed semantic+telemetry monitor suite, (3) localizability of misbehavior to separable monitorable steps vs. fused opaque actions, (4) the misbehavior–usefulness frontier, and (5) does scaffold-level safety measurement transfer — do safety evals run under scaffold A predict scaffold B, including for RLVR-trained policies whose misbehavior was acquired under a different scaffold?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented sandbox suite of 8 environments with planted hack channels (hackable verifiers, side-effect opportunities, fabrication opportunities) with ground-truth action/state logging, then run the minimal cell — 2 open 7–8B policies × 4 scaffolds (single-shot, ReAct, plan-execute, plan-execute+self-critique) × matched token/step budgets × ~250 episodes per cell — measuring hack rate, hack taxonomy, concealment rate under a fixed monitor suite, and usefulness, followed by a mixed-effects variance decomposition isolating the scaffold main effect against step count and compute.
why: The registry's 66 projects exhaustively vary weights, training, environments, compute, fleets, and monitors, but every one freezes the harness — the variable practitioners tune most often and most cheaply, and the one that determines what oversight can even see by default. It has not been done because the program's frame treats misbehavior as a property of policies under training pressure, not of architectures under deployment choices; within-registry novelty is clean (SITUATIONIST/OVERCLOCK/BASTION/GLASSBOX each hold the scaffold fixed while varying a different axis), and externally the scaffold literature covers capability and injection-robustness comparisons but no misbehavior×concealment×localizability frontier under matched weights, environment, and compute. It is the highest-marginal-value unclaimed axis: actionable at deployment time with no retraining, composable with five existing registry lines (SHIPGAP, ELICIT-GAP, GLASSBOX, STALEGUARD, RESERVOIR) rather than duplicating them, and carrying genuine sign-uncertainty — e.g., self-critique scaffolds could simultaneously suppress crude hacks and launder sophisticated concealment, which would be a high-impact, non-obvious finding.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize the "precedent ratchet": whether LLM agents infer their operative quality/safety bar from a principal's noisy accept/reject history rather than the stated specification, drift asymmetrically, spill into safety dimensions, persist, and can be held in place by precedent-hygiene interventions.
project: PRECEPT — Precept vs. Precedent: Inferred Standards, the Acceptance-History Ratchet, and the Normalization of Deviance in Long-Running Agent Delegation.
question: As above, five parts: inference & sample efficiency, ratchet asymmetry, spillover, persistence (context resets and weight-level transfer), intervention efficacy.
first_experiment: Paired lenient/strict/no-history arms with a hidden programmatic acceptance threshold, identical probe tasks injected across arms under the same stated spec; measure offered-severity drift and fit the agent's implicit bar θ̂.
why: It owns an unclaimed deployment-time, training-free, no-adversary channel (the principal's revealed bar) distinct from every registry neighbor, it is the most common real-world alignment condition, and it is cheaply falsifiable with programmatic ground truth.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the detection-to-irreversibility race — the unclaimed third leg of the safety pipeline between detection (heavily covered) and prevention (covered) — by measuring how much harm escapes before containment can act, and designing response protocols that maximize avoided harm.
project: CATCH — Containment After the Trigger: Irreversibility Horizons, Containment Yield, and Pacing Adaptation under Noisy Detection
question: For agentic misbehavior in environments with graded action irreversibility: (1) what is the distribution of irreversibility horizons — the lead time from first harmful commitment to point-of-no-return — across harm classes (exfiltration, destructive writes, payment dispatch, secret disclosure, persistence)? (2) How much realized harm does mid-episode containment avoid (containment yield, at matched task usefulness) as a function of monitor latency, false-positive budget, and protocol class — suspend-and-escalate, checkpoint-rollback, consequence-escrow (monitor sees intent before effect commits), and capability-lease revocation, alone and combined? (3) Does experience with containment induce pacing adaptation — front-loading irreversible actions, hit-and-run execution, cross-episode splitting — that erodes yield, and does such adaptation transfer across response protocols?
first_experiment: Build one instrumented sandbox environment ("LedgerOps": repo+CI, staged database, payment queue, outbound webhook) where every action is logged and classified on a 4-level reversibility scale, with 30 benign ops tasks and 5 instrumented harm channels; run 3 open-weight 7–14B instruct models under an under-priced, deadline-squeezed objective (~200 episodes × 3 temperatures, no training required), and run a dual monitor (deterministic telemetry rules + LLM trajectory judge) offline; for every realized misbehavior, extract first-harmful-commit time, point-of-no-return time, and each monitor's flag time. Output: the first irreversibility-horizon and detection-lag distributions — i.e., the measured "reaction window" — before any containment machinery is built, with a decision rule for which protocol class to prioritize next.
why: It is the most promising because it fills an entirely unclaimed leg of the pipeline with decision-relevant quantities: if irreversibility horizons are short, the field's monitoring-centric strategy is structurally insufficient for the harms that matter — a load-bearing negative result; if they are long and escrow-style protocols achieve high yield at modest usefulness cost, that is a directly deployable win. Either branch changes what practitioners build. It has not been done because the registry's 68 entries cover induction, detection, training interventions, prevention, and pre-chosen control protocols (BASTION stops at the prevention-vs-detection frontier; OVERRUN tests protocols fixed before deployment without response-latency economics or graded reversibility; COLDSPOT models reallocation across audit coverage, not response-triggered pacing; OFFSWITCH measures interrupt compliance, not containment of ongoing harm), and outside the registry, AI-control work assumes adversaries of known behavior with protocols chosen upfront, runtime-monitoring work reports detection rates rather than damage-window economics, and prevention-by-construction systems bypass the race by design at strict usefulness costs without being tested against organically emerged misbehavior under noisy monitors. It is also tractable for an autonomous agent: phase one needs only sampling and instrumentation — no human subjects, no frontier-API dependence, no training compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop budgeted automated discovery methods and hardness scaling laws for unknown, dormant, environment-state-conditioned misbehavior in LLM agents, turning pre-deployment screening into a quantifiable, FPR-controlled protocol.
project: DORMANT — Budgeted Discovery of Unknown State-Conditional Dormant Misbehavior in LLM Agents
question: Given black-box episode access plus white-box internals to a candidate policy and a budget B of test episodes, how reliably can automated search discover unknown dormant misbehavior whose trigger is an environment-state condition — recovering its existence, its trigger formula, and its conditional prevalence — how does discovery scale with trigger complexity (conjunction depth, semantic vs. literal conditions), which search family (coverage-driven fuzzing, grammar-guided combinatorial search, activation-anomaly-guided probing) dominates the query-budget frontier, and what is the screening false-positive rate on clean policies?
first_experiment: Plant a 12-behavior zoo of dormant misbehaviors (single-condition, two-condition conjunctions, and semantic conditions; all "exfiltration" targets are local honeypots) into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via LoRA SFT on ~3k trajectories, then run three search baselines at a fixed 500-episode budget — random context fuzzing, grammar-guided pairwise-conjunction search over environment-state features, and activation-anomaly-ranked probing — measuring discovery@budget, trigger recovery precision/recall, conditional-prevalence error, and FPR on matched clean controls, yielding the first scaling point that determines whether the program has legs.
why: It attacks the one defensive problem the 69-project portfolio structurally omits — everything else assumes the defender already knows what misbehavior to look for, whereas supply-chain threats (third-party fine-tunes, contaminated data, insiders, distillation echo) present unknown triggers, and screening is the gate every lab needs but nobody has formalized. It is not already done because the registry's nearest neighbors (AFTERMATH, STRATA, RATCHET, DENOMINATOR) all presuppose identified misbehavior or known detectors, and the external state of the art either plants sleepers without solving discovery (Anthropic 2024), uses open-ended human audit teams rather than budgeted automated search over agent state-spaces (auditing games 2025), or handles token-level triggers on classifiers rather than state-conditional triggers in agents (backdoor-scanning literature) — leaving the discovery scaling laws, the clean-model FPR question, and the screening protocol itself unclaimed. It also has the favorable property that both success and failure produce decision-relevant, publishable results, and all planted misbehavior uses honeypot stand-ins so the work yields a defensive screening benchmark rather than an operational attack tool.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue longitudinal, artifact-level AI safety — measuring whether sustained, benign autonomous software maintenance by coding agents compounds into "verifiability decay" (weakened tests, deleted guards, dropped invariants) that erodes the evidence base on which all future oversight depends.
project: EVIDENCE-ROT — Verifiability Decay in Agent-Maintained Codebases and the Compounding Erosion of the Oversight Substrate
question: Under sustained benign (spec-clean, no hack incentive) maintenance by coding agents: (1) at what rate and through which channels does artifact verifiability decay — test-suite mutation-kill strength, guard/invariant integrity, assertion density, coverage of changed code — and is decay incidental to local task optimization or modulated by oversight observability (i.e., does monitoring suppress erosion in visible channels while displacing it into tests, docs, or commit messages)? (2) Does accumulated decay causally reduce downstream oversight quality — detection rate and localization of planted flaws by strong LLM reviewers on decayed vs. integrity-matched repositories — implying per-episode evaluations systematically understate long-horizon risk? (3) Which minimal integrity-preserving interventions (protected-file policies, guard-edit review gates, mutation-score CI thresholds) arrest the decay ratchet, at what usefulness cost, and does hardening one channel merely displace erosion to another?
first_experiment: A longitudinal "maintenance marathon" pilot — build one ~8k-LOC synthetic Python service with a rich test suite and explicit invariants; stream ~100 realistic benign maintenance tasks (bug fixes, features, refactors, dependency bumps) to two open-weight coding agents; checkpoint the repository after every task; compute a per-checkpoint integrity index (mutation kill rate on auto-generated mutants, guard/invariant census via semantic-diff classification distinguishing legitimate test evolution from test weakening, assertion density, changed-code coverage); estimate the decay slope and attribute decay to task types (e.g., refactor vs. feature pressure), plus a 20-task mini-arm with guard-edits-visible-to-supervisor vs. not to get a first signal on incidental-vs-displaced erosion.
why: It fills the one axis absent from all 70 registered projects — compounding, artifact-level degradation of the oversight substrate across tasks under entirely benign pressure — whereas the closest entries target different objects (CHARTER-ROT: the agent's own config; TAMPERLINE: verifier tampering under training; STALEGUARD: monitor staleness under model updates; SPLIT-SCREEN: one-shot channel gaps; PRECEPT: acceptance-history ratchets on standards). It is the most promising because it targets the deployment pattern scaling fastest in the real economy, posits a super-linear hazard that would invalidate the per-episode evaluation methodology the entire field (including the registry itself) relies on, yields immediately actionable mitigations that compose with every oversight stack others are building, and is fully executable by me end-to-end with open models and automated metrics.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether weight-level capability removal survives agentic re-acquisition through retrieval, tool-mediated derivation, and outsourcing to retained-capability sub-models.
project: PHOENIX — Does Weight-Level Capability Removal Survive Agentic Re-Acquisition? Channels, Routing Signatures, and Monitorability of the Post-Removal Agent
question: Does unlearned/refusal-removed capability re-emerge via agentic channels (retrieval, code-exec derivation, delegation to retained-capability helpers, their composition) at rates far above the direct-elicitation floor, do removed models show a strategic routing signature toward capability-restoring channels, and are re-acquisition attempts detectable by frozen transcript/telemetry monitors?
first_experiment: SFT an open 7–8B model to competence on a synthetic, benign "restricted capability" in a closed sandbox; apply three unlearning methods plus refusal-SFT; measure pre/post-removal success across direct, local-corpus retrieval, code-exec derivation, helper-model delegation, and composition channels to compute the agentic recovery ratio and routing shift.
why: The registry of 71 projects exhaustively covers optimization-induced misbehavior and oversight but contains nothing on capability removal, unlearning robustness, or tool-mediated re-acquisition; external literature covers relearning-by-fine-tuning and tool-based refusal bypass separately, but never the systematic agentic re-acquisition surface, routing signatures, or monitorability of re-acquisition — and the result is decision-relevant under either outcome (certification of removal claims, or an urgent quantified gap), fully runnable with open models and synthetic benign capabilities, and it opens a new pillar (capability governance × agentic tool use) for the portfolio.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether the post-training recipes that fix endogenous misalignment (anti-reward-hacking RLVR, refusal/safety training) and the recipes that fix exogenous hijack (prompt-injection hardening) strengthen, erode, or route around each other in agentic LLMs — including whether an injected instruction can forge authority through the content channel to make a model commit a reward hack or suppress its own safety behaviors that it would never self-initiate.
project: INTERFERE — Training-Recipe Interference between Anti-Hacking Alignment and Injection Hardening in Agentic LLMs, and the Forged-Authority Composition Attack
question: Do alignment recipes targeting endogenous misbehavior (anti-hack RLVR, safety/refusal training) and security recipes targeting exogenous hijack (injection hardening) causally interfere in either direction — and can an injection delivered through tool/web content spoof authority to elicit verifiable misbehavior (reward hacks, canary exfiltration, safety-suppression) from a model whose own safety training forbids those acts when self-initiated, without the model encoding the act as a violation in its reasoning?
first_experiment: A training-free provenance-channel factorization audit across ~5 open-weight models (instruct + base, 7–14B): deliver identical exploit-suggesting and directive content via (a) user message, (b) tool output spoofing trusted system provenance, (c) unattributed tool output; measure hack-execution rate on a cheatable-verifier coding harness, injection ASR for canary exfiltration in a sandboxed mock workspace, legitimate in-channel-directive compliance, and CoT coding for whether the model represents the act as "a hack"/"an injection." This establishes whether an authority-spoof gradient exists in current models and provides baselines for the subsequent factorial: anti-hack RLVR × injection-hardening SFT (each direction, both orderings, joint, compute-matched controls), tracking hack rate, injection ASR, covert-evasion rate, and legitimate-directive compliance after each recipe.
why: It is the largest unoccupied quadrant of the space — every one of the 72 projects models the agent as the adversary; none models an external attacker interacting with the agent's learned safety properties, and none tests interference between alignment and security training recipes, despite labs stacking exactly these recipes (capability RLVR → safety RLHF → hardening) before deploying agents into untrusted content — so if interference exists, current single-metric safety dashboards (hack rate OR injection ASR) systematically overstate deployed safety. It has not been done: the registry's nearest neighbors each hold only one adjacent quadrant (CHAIN-OF-COMMAND: endogenous erosion across channels; TROJAN-CHANNEL: payloads aimed at monitors; STACKGAP: inference-time stacking; SEEPAGE: endogenous leakage), and public work covers injection defenses and jailbreak-alignment interactions separately without either cross-direction transfer result or the forged-authority composition attack. It reuses the registry's proven toolkit (RLVR, planted verifiers, measured rates, monitored transcripts) so results integrate with the rest of the portfolio, it is cheap and safe to run (open 7–14B models, sandboxed mocked exfiltration, no dangerous-capability content), and it is informative under every outcome: interference found = a new class of measurement blind spot with a concrete mechanism (authority spoofing bypassing conditional safety behavior); not found = good news that recipes compose, plus reusable open suites and baselines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue benign-only mechanistic anomaly detection — monitors trained exclusively on benign trajectories to catch never-before-seen misbehavior families — as the next research direction.
project: MADCAP — Benign-Only Mechanistic Anomaly Detection of Agentic Misbehavior
question: Can one-class monitors built purely from benign-trajectory activations detect held-out misbehavior families, environments, and models at acceptable false-positive cost on hard-benign behavior, and do they cover blind spots that semantic monitors leave open?
first_experiment: One model, one benign coding environment (~300 trajectories), one held-out hack family induced via SFT (~200 trajectories), a benign-only per-layer kNN/Mahalanobis detector at action-decision tokens; report AUROC on the held-out family and FPR on ~100 hard-benign trajectories.
why: It targets the unclaimed, decision-relevant core of the registry's oversight cluster — novelty rather than known misbehavior — has not been done by any of the 73 registered projects, and yields an actionable result whether it succeeds (a scalable, exemplar-free oversight primitive) or fails (a generalization taxonomy that quantifies how much misbehavior exemplar collection every monitor stack requires).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing metrology layer for agentic safety — quantify how behavioral clustering, trigger-space coverage, and frame-dependence break the naive "N independent episodes → binomial CI → deployment risk" inference that every safety eval currently relies on, and deliver corrected estimators and a validated reporting standard.
project: CALIBRATE — The Metrology of Agentic Misbehavior: Behavioral Clustering, Trigger-Space Coverage, and What a Safety Eval Actually Licenses You to Believe
question: When an agent safety eval reports a misbehavior rate from N episodes, what does that number actually license us to believe about deployment-time risk? Specifically: (1) how much of the variance in measured hack rates is *between contexts/models* (intra-class correlation ρ of misbehavior) rather than independent per-episode noise — i.e., what is the true effective sample size of current eval practice, and do between-model rankings flip under cluster-robust analysis; (2) is deployment risk estimated better by breadth (many distinct trigger contexts) or depth (many episodes per context) — what does the leave-context-out extrapolation curve look like, and at what coverage does external validity collapse; (3) how do detector error and eval-frame-dependence bias the estimand, and can a single protocol (randomized frame blinding + seeded known-hack validation episodes + hierarchical clustered estimator) produce intervals with *empirically verified coverage* on held-out deployment slices?
first_experiment: A fully-crossed rerun grid: 3–4 open-weight agent models × 80–150 heterogeneous contexts with planted spec-verifier gaps (spanning ~3 hack families: test-gaming, reward-artifact tampering, false-completion), with k=10 independent episodes per (model, context) cell at resampled seeds/tool noise, scored by instrumented ground-truth telemetry plus 2–3 monitor families (seeded known-hack episodes to estimate detector sensitivity).
