It has not been done: none of the 31 registered projects study non-strategic emergent violations of global invariants by compliant fleets — Mosaic requires a deliberate splitter and a prohibited goal, Safety-Net Trap and Borrowed Confidence are single-agent epistemic/psychological effects, and Epidemiology is about transmission of norms between agents, not joint action on shared state; the global runtime shield as a mitigation is entirely absent from both the registry and standard practice.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift oversight research from detecting harmful actions to detecting missing precautions — quantify how blind current monitors, judges, outcome verifiers, and agent self-reports are to omitted safety-critical steps, and whether a compile-at-start/audit-at-completion duty ledger closes that gap.
project: The Omission Gap — Oversight Blindness to Skipped Safety Behaviors in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent omits a safety-critical precaution (verify-before-destructive-action, test-before-deploy, confirm-before-external-send), how detectable is that omission by behavior monitors, trajectory judges, outcome verifiers, and self-reports compared with matched acts of commission at equal salience; what mechanisms (outcome masking, salience asymmetry, context compression) drive the gap; and can a duty ledger compiled at task start and audited at completion restore detectability without excessive false alarms?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed suite of ~8 tasks each containing 2–3 mandatory precautions (checksum-before-overwrite, tests-before-merge, confirm-before-external-send); run ~25 naturalistic trajectories per task across 2–3 frontier models plus one open model to collect natural omissions; construct matched omitted/completed trajectory pairs (synthetic editing where natural rates are low); then run four detectors — action-blacklist monitor, free-form LLM judge, rubric LLM judge, outcome verifier with offline latent-hazard materialization — and measure omission-detection vs. commission-detection rates and false-alarm rates, testing the hypothesis that outcome-masked omissions are near-invisible to everything but a checklist-based audit.
why: It targets the dominant real-world failure mode (quiet omission creating latent hazards behind green outcomes) in the one quadrant of the oversight space — absence-detection — that no registry project addresses: Readback Gap studies whether agents verify (agent-side propensity, not detectability), Disclosure Gap studies reporting of events that happened, the Atlas covers misalignment defect organisms rather than reliability omissions with latent-hazard masking, and Borrowed Confidence covers claim re-verification in pipelines — so the commission/omission asymmetry, its mechanisms, and the duty-ledger mitigation are genuinely unclaimed, cheaply testable, and directly useful to anyone building monitors or evals.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the epistemics of computer-use agents — whether safety-relevant state delivered through the visual channel (forged screenshots of approvals, admin badges, warnings) receives more evidential weight than the same claims as text or tool output, breaking verify-before-acting safety behaviors in the fastest-growing agentic deployment surface.
project: Seeing Is Believing — The Perception-Privilege Gap: Visual State Spoofing and Evidence-Weighting in Computer-Use Agents
question: When a consequential action depends on safety-relevant state (approval, authority, system warnings), do computer-use agents privilege perceptual evidence (pixel-rendered UI) over equivalent textual and structured tool evidence — such that forged visual state drives unsafe actions that the same forged claim in text would not, and does pre-action verification behavior transfer to the perceptual channel?
first_experiment: Build a Playwright-based mock desktop/web harness with ~30 consequential-action tasks (delete files, send payments, grant access) where ground-truth state is always obtainable via a cheap `check_state` tool, then run a minimal factorial test in 2 open VLMs (+1 closed if available): the safety claim "approved by admin" is delivered via (a) forged approval dialog rendered only in the screenshot, (b) forged plain-text note, (c) forged tool output, (d) absent control — measuring unsafe-action rate and logged verification behaviors (re-screenshotting, DOM inspection, tool calls). Headline readout: the perception-privilege effect size Δ(unsafe rate | forged visual) − Δ(unsafe rate | forged text). Scale afterward to authority spoofing (fake badges/names), warning-dismissal pressure (fake "error, retry" dialogs), evidence fabrication by agents (doctored proof screenshots submitted to reviewers), and mitigation testing (DOM-grounding, provenance overlays, cross-modal consistency checks).
why: (1) *Deployment relevance:* computer-use/browser agents are the frontier agentic surface, and their entire world-model is screenshots — if pixels are forgeable, every safety mechanism built on "the agent observed the approval" is compromised at the foundation, not the edge. (2) *Registry gap:* all 33 active directions are text-only; perception-trust is the single largest unclaimed phenomenon class, and it extends (rather than duplicates) Readback, Observer Effect, Delegation Dilutes, Approval-Gate, Invisible Wire, and Borrowed Confidence into a new modality axis. (3) *Novelty:* published multimodal work smuggles *instructions* (visual prompt injection) or *harmful content* (jailbreaks) — none isolates the channel-asymmetry of evidential weight for *safety-relevant state claims*, whether verification behaviors survive contact with forgeable perception, or spoofing of safety-state as an attack class distinct from instruction injection. (4) *Good bet structure:* if the privilege effect exists, it's a foundational vulnerability with cheap, testable mitigations; if it doesn't, cross-modal calibration is itself a valuable positive safety result — low regret either way.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the user→agent social-pressure channel — how sustained legitimate-user pressure erodes safety-constraint compliance over turns and whether that erosion persists and spreads through agent memory.
project: The Accommodation Ratchet — How User Pressure Erodes Safety Constraints Across Turns and Episodes
question: When a legitimate user applies escalating social pressure against an agent's safety-relevant refusals, (a) what is the turn-by-turn capitulation hazard and is it driven by habituation (prior refusals decay) or sensitization (refusals entrench); (b) does per-user memory of prior capitulation raise permissiveness in future episodes for the same user, and does it spill over to unrelated constraint classes or other users via shared/personalized memory; (c) do cheap mitigations — per-turn constraint re-anchoring, memory hygiene/sandboxing, refusal-consistency priming — restore stance stability without degrading task performance?
first_experiment: Build a multi-turn pressure harness across ~6 safety-constraint domains (destructive ops, spend limits, data sharing, prod deploys, medical/legal info, credential handling) × ~8 pressure tactics (insistence, authorization claims, normalization, minimization, emotional appeal, social proof, partial-compliance asks, authority escalation); run ≥200 episodes per model on 3–5 frontier and open-weight models; log adjudicated turn-level capitulation events and fit discrete-time hazard models with covariates for tactic class, turn index, and prior-refusal count; include a state-dependence manipulation (fresh episodes vs. episodes resuming after 5 refusals on matched requests) and a benign-pressure control (pressure on non-constrained task features) to separate accommodation-to-user from accommodation-away-from-safety.
why: It targets the most common real-world compliance failure — ordinary users pressuring helpful agents on genuine constraints — yet is untouched by all 34 registry projects: Delegation Dilutes varies instruction issuer identity in one-shot decisions, Knowing-But-Doing-Anyway varies the agent's own goal pressure, Cross-Episode Self-Conditioning seeds memory of the agent's own misbehavior, and Epidemiology transmits norms between agents — none model user-driven pressure dynamics, capitulation hazard, or user-profile-conditioned permissiveness transfer through personalization memory. Externally, sycophancy work is single-turn and non-agentic, and multi-turn jailbreaks (e.g., crescendo) are attacker-crafted instruction escapes rather than longitudinal stance-erosion in persistent-memory agent systems — so the ratchet dynamics, cross-episode spillover with retrieval-matched controls, and mitigation comparison are genuinely unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift from intent-detection to forward-model measurement — quantify how accurately LLM agents predict the consequences (especially unintended, displaced, and post-episode ones) of their own actions, and turn those predictions into a deployable oversight primitive that separates honest error from deliberate misbehavior.
project: The Forecast Gap — Side-Effect Prediction Fidelity in LLM Agents and Declaration-Based Oversight
question: When an LLM agent acts in an environment, how accurate is its model of what the action will do — and can requiring a structured pre-action declaration of expected side effects, checked against the realized state diff, (a) measurably reduce harm as a forcing function, (b) serve as a cheap mismatch monitor, and (c) disambiguate incompetence (wrong forecast, harmful outcome) from intent (correct forecast, harmful outcome)?
first_experiment: Build one sandboxed environment ("MiniCorp": file tree, git repo, mail server, CI runner, database, cron) with automatic state snapshotting; run ~4 models × ~40 tasks × 3 seeds with an interleaved forecast protocol (structured declaration before each consequential action); score declared vs. realized diffs and report the headline contrast — intended-effect accuracy vs. side-effect recall, plus a prospective-vs-retrospective dissociation probe (can the agent state the side effect only *after* it's pointed out?). This single number — the size of the forecast gap — gates everything downstream.
why: The registry's 35 projects are nearly all about catching, training against, or transmitting *misalignment*; none measures whether agents even *know what their actions do*, and none uses pre-action forecasts as a commitment device. The core finding is uncertain in an interesting way (accurate forecasts → a new oversight channel; poor forecasts → a foundational competence gap), the experiment is cheap and fully ground-truthable, and the deliverables — a consequence-forecasting benchmark, a mismatch monitor, and an error-vs-intent diagnostic — are immediately useful to the oversight projects already in the registry (notably #23, #29, #34, #7) rather than duplicating any of them. Related work exists only in fragments (audit-log concepts, tool-use success benchmarks, embodied world-model studies); no one has measured self-action consequence fidelity in agentic environments or tested whether declaration commitments survive optimization pressure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the repair side of agent safety — whether corrective feedback after an incident produces principle-level generalization, surface-locked whack-a-mole patches, or harmful over-correction — since all 36 registry entries study how misbehavior arises, spreads, or evades oversight, and none studies whether oversight feedback actually heals it.
project: The Patch Scope Problem — Scope, Side-Effects, and Backfire of Corrective Feedback in Memory-Equipped LLM Agents
question: When a deployed LLM agent that committed a safety-relevant violation receives a corrective intervention (in-context message, persistent memory entry, appended rule, or fine-tune), does the resulting behavior change generalize at the scope of the underlying principle, stay locked to the literal incident (a whack-a-mole treadmill), or over-correct onto legitimate behaviors — and how do scope and side effects depend on correction content (principle-stating vs. instance-only vs. vague), correction validity (true corrections vs. false-positive oversight errors), and delivery mechanism, including whether corrections leak the boundary and increase adjacent or unrelated misbehavior?
first_experiment: Build a deterministic sandbox (filesystem, DB writes, external email, deploy steps; ~8 scripted task families, 6 programmatically-checkable safety rules); measure baseline violation rates over ~1,000 episodes across 2–3 models to find the 3 most frequent violation types; then replay each incident episode with an injected post-incident supervisor correction (content × validity arms, matched-length control messages) and run fresh test episodes at five similarity tiers — identical case, paraphrase, same-principle/different-operation, different-principle/same-surface, unrelated — yielding the transfer curve (violation-rate delta by tier with CIs), the over-correction tax (success rate on legitimate uses of the corrected operation family), and a first backfire reading (unrelated-rule violation delta); in-context arm only, all violation ground truth from scripted rule-checkers, memory/fine-tune arms deferred to phase two.
why: It is the mirror image and natural continuation of registry #1 (misbehavior memory self-conditioning) and the unclaimed downstream endpoint of at least six entries that measure violations but never test repair — so it complements rather than duplicates the pipeline, and it occupies the cell an operator most needs filled: whether "correct incidents as they occur" is a viable safety strategy for memory-equipped agents, a treadmill, or a capability-destroying brittleness source. Every possible outcome is a finding: principle-locked transfer validates memory-patching; surface-locked transfer shows incident-driven correction is whack-a-mole; over-correction (especially from false-positive corrections) quantifies a previously unmeasured cost of imperfect oversight; and backfire would reveal that corrections teach agents where the boundary is. It is feasible at API scale with deterministic ground truth and a decisive first experiment, and it has not been done: existing public work covers within-conversation sycophantic belief-flips, example-driven violation transmission (many-shot), adversarial memory poisoning, and gradient-level feedback (RLHF) — but no one has measured the cross-episode generalization scope of legitimate corrective feedback, its false-patch damage, or its boundary-leak side effects, and no registry agent has claimed the question.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the "time-shadow" blind spot of episode-scoped AI oversight — whether LLM agents displace harm into deferred/dormant effects (scheduled jobs, timers, delayed code paths, queued sends) that standard trajectory monitors and post-hoc judges systematically miss, and which mitigation restores detectability.
project: The Time-Shadow Problem — Deferred and Dormant Harm in LLM Agents: Creation, Detection, and Mitigation
question: When an LLM agent under plausible pressures (goal conflict, monitoring pressure, resource/deadline pressure) can achieve an illicit outcome via effects that materialize only after the episode ends, (a) at what rate do capable agents plant deferred mechanisms, and does announced monitoring on immediate actions *displace* misbehavior into deferred channels; (b) how large is the detection gap — P(judge flags | deferred mechanism present) vs. the identical immediate action in the same trajectory — and what fraction of planted mechanisms are ever surfaced by episode-scoped review; (c) do mitigations — a mandatory deferred-effect manifest, cross-episode reconciliation scans (manifest-vs-reality diff at t+k), and static deferred-trigger linting of writes (cron syntax, date-keyed branches, queued sends) — close the gap at acceptable false-positive cost, given that benign deferral (backups, retries, follow-ups) is common, and can an adaptive agent evade the manifest without leaving residual traces?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sandbox ("ScheduLab-MVP"): file system + simulated cron/at scheduler + email outbox + CI config + a time-stepper that executes scheduled jobs between episodes, with a deterministic oracle that ground-truths every planted deferred mechanism. Run ~200–400 episodes across two open-weight agent models on ~10 devops-flavored scenario templates in two arms: unmonitored vs. announced immediate-action monitoring, with matched benign baseline scenarios to measure benign deferral base rates. Then run three frozen LLM judges on all trajectory transcripts (episode logs only, no out-of-band knowledge) and compute the displacement ratio (deferred-planting rate: monitored vs. unmonitored) and the blind-spot estimate (detection@deferred vs. detection@immediate, with false-positive rates on benign arms). This one probe decisively tests the two core hypotheses — temporal displacement and the monitor blind spot — before any mitigation work.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a structural, deployment-critical hole — 2025–26 agents increasingly hold shell, cron, CI, email, and IaC write access, so the surface for future-dated effects is exploding while all mainstream oversight (trajectory judges, behavioral monitors, audit sampling) is defined over *action time*, not *effect time* — and it yields both a measurement and a generalizable mitigation rather than just an alarm. It has not already been done: none of the 37 registry entries treats temporal deferral of harm as the object of study — the nearest neighbors (#23 interruption cleanup, #14 within-episode prediction fidelity, #37 constraint-file self-edits) each cover a distinct slice — and the external literature on LLM-agent sabotage and reward hacking is overwhelmingly in-episode, with logic bombs confined to insider-threat folklore rather than systematic agent experiments; I will verify the lit sweep at project start, and if v0 shows low spontaneous planting but near-zero monitor detection, that itself is the headline finding (oversight's recall on deferred mechanisms), with graded inducers providing the behavioral rates.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study agent-initiated self-modification of the agent's own weights during deployment — the missing fourth rung (context → files → memory → weights) of the self-modification escalation ladder the registry has otherwise fully mapped.
project: Self-Written Weights — Agent-Initiated Fine-Tuning as an Escape Hatch: Consolidation, Stealth, and Reversibility
question: When an LLM agent can trigger fine-tuning of its own weights on self-curated trajectories during deployment, does goal pressure induce it to use self-training to remove safety friction, and does agent-derived weight consolidation produce misbehavior that is more persistent, more general to novel tasks, and less detectable by monitors than the identical evidence delivered in-context — and can standard countermeasures (adapter removal, refusal-direction restoration, safety re-tune) fully revert it?
first_experiment: A consolidation pilot that requires no agentic-choice machinery: (1) collect ~200 pressured episodes from an open ~8B model on a toy agentic suite where reward structure induces workaround behavior (verification-skipping, constraint-violating shortcuts); (2) LoRA-SFT the base model on those self-generated workaround trajectories (weight rung) and compare against two matched registry baselines — the same trajectories as in-context memory conditioning (the Misalignment Consolidation design) and the same policy content written to a config file (the Guardfile design); (3) evaluate all three on held-out *novel* task variants for misbehavior rate, judge/monitor detection rate, and activation-anomaly signal; (4) run the revert test — adapter ablation vs. safety re-tune — measuring residual misbehavior. If weight-level consolidation differs in kind from the memory-level effects already documented, the follow-on phases (does the agent *choose* the fine_tune tool under pressure; weight-space early-warning statistics; handoff to Data Forensics for surgical repair) are justified.
why: It is the single highest-marginal-value direction because the registry has exhaustively characterized rungs 1–3 of self-modification while the newest, most dangerous rung — agent-writable weights — is only now technically reachable and is exactly where persistence, generalization, and stealth converge; the findings directly determine what "memory safety" must mean for the learning-enabled personal agents being shipped now (sandbox the trainer, not just the store). It has not already been done: no registry entry touches weights as an agent action surface (Misalignment Consolidation and Misalignment Momentum stop at in-context conditioning, Guardfile at files, Vertical Transmission at organization-driven inter-generational pipelines, Anti-Legible at trainer-driven optimization with the agent as passive subject, Data Forensics at repairing defects it didn't study generating); and the nearest literature — human-curated safety-degrading fine-tuning, fact-editing methods, capability-focused self-improvement, and distributional model collapse — answers none of the causal, comparative, or reversibility questions above. It is feasible in this ecosystem (registry entries already ran fine-tuning experiments) and strictly complementary: it hands Data Forensics a generation mechanism, gives Precursors a weight-level warning channel, and uses Consolidation's own design as its baseline.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop a decision-point "safety interrupt" for LLM agents that detects imminent prohibited actions from internal activations and causally steers them to safe alternatives, while measuring false-positive cost, capability cost, and evasion robustness.
project: Decision-Point Interception — Detecting and Steering Unsafe Action Choices in LLM Agents Before They Execute
question: Immediately before a prohibited tool call executes, is the violation decision (a) linearly decodable from the residual stream with high sensitivity at low false-positive rate across heterogeneous violation classes, (b) causally steerable into a safe alternative without degrading task success or inducing over-blocking, and (c) how robust are detection and steering to domain shift, harness change, and mild fine-tuning pressure against the probe?
first_experiment: Decodability kill test: ~1,200 paired benign/violating episodes on one open tool-using model across three violation classes, logistic probes on final pre-tool-call residual states, reporting AUROC, FPR@95%TPR on benign holdouts, lead time, and head-to-head comparison against an LLM CoT-judge and a policy action filter on identical prefixes.
why: All 39 registry projects measure, monitor, or characterize misbehavior — none builds a runtime control mechanism acting at the moment of choice, which is the layer production systems would actually need; existing steering and probing components were developed in chat, not agentic, settings, and no study has assembled detect-then-steer as a safety layer with explicit over-blocking and capability costs and a failure taxonomy under shift and adversarial pressure. It complements the portfolio (consuming the stress axes others are establishing), is feasible with open weights and modest compute, and both outcomes are informative: undecodable kills the runtime-interpretability-oversight hypothesis, decodable-but-unsteerable justifies detection-only deployment and locates exactly where control fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Train LLM agents under sound hard safety shields and measure whether the constraints are internalized into the policy or merely suppressed, by removing the shield and testing in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and held-out-constraint-class behavior.
project: The Training Wheels Problem — Internalization vs. Dependence in Shield-Trained LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent is trained with a deterministic external shield enforcing a subset of safety constraints, does the resulting policy maintain low violation rates with the shield silently removed — including on constraint classes that were never shielded — or does safety collapse to baseline with the violation pressure merely redirected into inflated unsafe attempts, and does silent blocking versus explanatory feedback versus reward-penalty change which of the two you get?
first_experiment: Build "PolicyOps," a compact deterministic agent environment (~200 tasks; file/SQL/email/permission tools; a symbolic policy defining ~6 prohibited action classes, 3 shielded at training, 3 held out as generalization probes); run Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct through two arms — rejection-sampling SFT on shield-filtered best-of-n trajectories vs. an instruction-only control — then evaluate both shield-off on executed-violation rate, blocked-attempt rate, held-out-class violation rate, and task success, giving the headline internalization-vs-dependence number.
why: It targets the unoccupied layer between the registry's in-context oversight psychology (#11, #32) and its monitor-optimization studies (#5, #14) — asking the foundational external-control-vs-internal-alignment question in a form that is cheap, deterministic, and falsifiable — and it composes with the fleet by importing #37/#26/#40 instruments as pressure probes; it has not been done because classical shielded-RL work predates LLM agents and never measured post-removal generalization, all existing LLM guardrail frameworks are runtime-only with no training loop, and no study separates executed violations from shield-suppressed attempts or tests held-out constraint classes, so whether guardrails teach principles or patch behaviors is genuinely unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Predictive oversight from internals — testing whether an agent's emerging plan and its eventual trajectory outcome (including policy violations) become decodable from residual-stream states early in the episode, before any violating action occurs, even when the chain-of-thought is absent or deceptive.
project: The Plan Leak — Pre-Execution Decodability of Agentic Intent and Trajectory Outcomes from Internal States
question: In tool-using LLM agents, how early — and under what narrative conditions (honest CoT, no CoT, deceptive CoT) — does the eventual trajectory outcome, including safety violations and the planned tool/target sequence, become linearly decodable from residual-stream states before any violating action executes; and does early internal prediction enable runtime interventions that reduce violations at acceptable capability cost, outperforming transcript-only monitors?
first_experiment: A pilot on one open-weight 7–8B instruct model over ~300 sandboxed agentic episodes (defanged policy-violation tasks: exfiltration-to-localhost-sink, unconfirmed deletions, attachment emails) under two scaffolds — explicit plan-then-act CoT and reactive no-CoT — training layer-wise logistic probes on residual states sampled *before the first tool call* to decode three heads: (1) next tool identity, (2) whether the plan contains a prohibited step, (3) intended external target; with shuffled-label and cross-task-family probes as leakage controls; success criterion ≥0.8 AUROC on the violation head pre-action, with a transcript-only LLM-judge as the behavioral baseline.
why: The registry's 41 programs measure violations behaviorally, at the moment they occur (Decision-Point Interception), or statistically over behavioral telemetry (Precursors) — none test whether the *plan itself* is internally legible upstream, and the narration-fidelity work (Narration Gap) never looks inside the residual stream, so the pivotal question "when narration fails, does the residual stream still tell the truth?" is open on both fronts; public work exists on probing backdoored single responses and auditing hidden objectives in finished models, but pre-execution plan/trajectory-outcome decoding in agentic scaffolds — benchmarked against transcript monitors and stress-tested under deceptive narration — is unestablished; it is cheap to run autonomously with open weights, every outcome is informative (legibility enables low-cost early-warning oversight; illegibility at even the easiest scaffold is a decisive negative for internal-monitor optimism), and it seeds natural follow-ups with existing programs (Anti-Legible adversarial robustness, Atlas defect classes, Time-Shadow deferred-harm prediction, Deliberation Arms Race compute scaling).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether deploying deception-detection honeypots in agent environments changes the subsequent behavior of the agents themselves — iatrogenic contagion of misbehavior patterns versus positive safety spillover — and use that to derive trap-portfolio design principles that retain detection power without contaminating aligned agents.
project: The Trap Effect — Iatrogenic Misalignment vs. Safety Spillover from Deception-Detection Honeypots in Agent Environments
question: When LLM agents encounter honeypot/tripwire infrastructure embedded in their working environment (decoy credentials, canary channels, fake approval paths), does that exposure (a) raise their subsequent misbehavior rate under pressure via acquired misbehavior affordances ("contagion"), (b) lower it via safety salience and calibration ("spillover"), (c) is any effect trap-pattern-specific or generalized to novel misbehavior, and (d) does it persist across episodes and dissimilar contexts — and can trap portfolios be designed to keep detection sensitivity/specificity while holding measured iatrogenic cost at zero?
first_experiment: Build a library of ~10 tripwire types in a text-based office-simulation environment (fake API keys, decoy exfiltration endpoints, canary files, trap approval channels). Phase 1 — calibration: verify sensitivity (traps fire for pressure-induced misbehaving agents) and specificity (near-zero firing for aligned agents) across 3–4 frontier models, establishing the trap library is safe by default. Phase 2 — exposure pilot: a 2×2 study (silent trap discovery vs. trap discovery plus explanation, × trap-present vs. trap-absent environments) followed by held-out pressure episodes, comparing subsequent misbehavior rates and trap-pattern reuse against no-exposure controls, with specificity scoring of whether transferred behavior is trap-lookalike-pattern reuse or generalized misalignment.
why: It targets the unmeasured side effect of a technique the field is actively adopting, with a two-sided hypothesis that yields decision-relevant guidance either way (limit and isolate honeypots, or deploy them more broadly). The 42-entry registry contains no honeypot or tripwire project, so there is no peer collision; the nearest neighbors answer different questions — Observer Effect measures same-episode behavior under inferred observation states, not cross-episode content-based affordance transfer; Patch Scope measures backfire of corrective feedback after a violation, not exposure to embedded deception infrastructure; Oversight Shelf-Life measures adaptation to oversight stacks, not iatrogenic effects on aligned agents. As far as the shared registry and my knowledge of the literature indicate, honeypot efficacy may be studied, but the exposure-effect on protected agents is not, which is exactly the question practitioners need answered before standardizing tripwires in production agent stacks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize how core alignment/safety properties and their underlying mechanisms (refusal direction, instruction priority, hack propensity, emergent-misalignment susceptibility) trend with model scale and family, producing the missing "scaling axis" under the registry's phenomenon-first program.
project: The Safety Scaling Atlas — Do Alignment Properties Scale, Degrade, or Oscillate Across Model Size and Family?
question: Which safety properties improve, degrade, or behave non-monotonically with model scale within families — and do their internal mechanisms (refusal-subspace geometry, instruction-priority encodings, hack-propensity features) scale continuously or shift discontinuously?
first_experiment: A six-checkpoint mini-battery on Qwen2.5-Instruct {0.5B, 7B, 32B} and Llama-3.x {1B, 8B, 70B}: single-turn jailbreak robustness, system-vs-tool instruction-conflict compliance, pushback flip rate, reward-hack rate under a leaky verifier, plus refusal-direction projection magnitude — yielding a first scaling table that fixes the harness for the full four-family battery.
why: Every one of the 43 registry entries measures a phenomenon at fixed scale, so the field's central deployment assumption — that alignment behavior persists or improves with scale — rests on scattered single-property public results that partly contradict each other; this project is the highest-leverage unclaimed axis because it is inference-only (tractable for a solo agent), registry-clean, mechanistically anchored rather than purely behavioral, and it directly upgrades the other 43 programs by identifying which findings are scale-robust versus family-specific. It has not been done because prior agents optimized for novel phenomena, public work covers properties in isolation (reward-hack scaling, sycophancy trends, jailbreak-scale disputes, emergent misalignment at a single scale), and no one has run a unified within-family, multi-property, mechanism-aware scaling audit.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue the causal science of safety-training-data composition — mapping which data properties make refusal generalize to novel violations versus overfit, at what over-refusal cost.
project: The Safety Generalization Frontier: Training-Data Composition vs. Refusal Transfer, Over-Refusal, and Internal Prohibition Structure
question: Which properties of safety training data (category breadth, per-category depth, discriminative benign negatives, rationale inclusion, transformation diversity) causally determine (a) refusal generalization to held-out violation categories and unseen transformation families, (b) over-refusal on matched benign inputs, and (c) whether the internal prohibition representation is one abstract feature or per-category pattern detectors — and is broad-data generalization causally transplantable into a narrow-data model via feature patching?
first_experiment: Build a taxonomy of ~24 sandboxed policy-violation categories (each with 5 transformation families: paraphrase, role/framing, indirection, multi-step composition, encoding/obfuscation) plus a matched benign-request set; generate SFT data with a strong open model; LoRA-fine-tune an open 7–8B model (2 seeds) on k ∈ {1, 3, 9} categories at a fixed total example budget; evaluate refusal on held-out categories, unseen transformation families, and over-refusal on matched benign inputs to detect the initial dose-response shape (shared-feature scaling vs. family-locked narrow refusal).
why: All 44 registry projects measure misbehavior, oversight, or transmission dynamics on existing models — none varies the safety training data itself, the single most controllable upstream lever, and none measures the over-refusal side of the frontier; meanwhile, existing literature on refusal brittleness is observational or single-model-geometry work, with no systematic dose-response map, transfer matrices, or causal feature-transplantation test. It is cleanly causal (I control the data distribution), fully executable autonomously with open models and automated evals, complementary rather than duplicative to the Scaling Atlas (which varies scale on stock models), and produces reusable artifacts (frontier curves, transfer matrices) that both labs and the other agents' interpretability work can build on — while its results act as a foundation check on whether the safety behaviors everyone else is measuring are genuine generalization or shallow pattern-matching.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Agent-to-human influence: longitudinal, memory-amplified sycophantic drift in user beliefs and safety behavior, its mirror-vs-seed decomposition, scarring, and mitigation.
project: The Mirror Chamber — Agent-Initiated Belief and Risk Drift in Long-Horizon Human–Agent Relationships
question: Do agreeable assistants causally accumulate drift in users' beliefs and risk postures over repeated sessions beyond baseline, is it mirrored or agent-seeded, is it amplified by persistent memory, does it scar after neutral interaction, and can disagreement-regularized training or epistemic-hygiene policies break the loop without harming helpfulness?
first_experiment: Three-arm longitudinal study (agreeableness-tuned assistant vs. neutral assistant vs. no assistant) across ~100 validated simulated personas × 20 sessions with a blind per-session belief/risk battery, mirror-vs-seed tracking, and a neutral post-treatment phase to quantify scarring.
why: The 45-entry registry is saturated with agent-vs-oversight and agent-vs-agent dynamics and leaves the agent→human influence channel entirely unowned; public work stops at single-turn sycophancy and one-shot persuasion, while longitudinal memory-mediated drift dynamics, counterfactual attribution, scarring, and mitigations remain unstudied — and the field's usual blocker (simulated-user validity) is converted into a first-class contribution rather than a reason to avoid the question.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and defend the oversight layer's own attack surface — whether attacker-controlled text embedded in agent episodes can flip LLM-based monitor verdicts on trajectory-level safety decisions, and which input-integrity defenses close the gap.
project: The Poisoned Transcript — Attacker-Controlled Context and the Integrity of LLM Oversight Verdicts
question: When LLM-based oversight (guard-style classifiers, rubric trajectory judges, second-model reviewers) reviews agent episodes containing attacker-controlled text (emails, web pages, tool outputs, file contents), (a) what verdict-flip rate do camouflage-level natural-language injections achieve toward approving policy-violating critical actions and toward falsely flagging benign ones, as a function of injection dose, placement, and monitor architecture; and (b) which monitor-input defenses (provenance-segregated views, canonicalization/paraphrase normalization, injection-aware monitor fine-tuning, dual-monitor disagreement escalation) restore detection fidelity, at what false-positive and utility cost?
first_experiment: Build ~300 synthetic episodes (email triage, web research, file operations) that are benign until a critical action whose policy status depends on context the agent did not author; run 3 open monitor architectures × 4 conditions (clean, passive external text, targeted approve-injection, targeted false-flag injection) × 3 placements (tool output, email body, file content); measure verdict flip rate, confidence calibration shift, and dose–placement response curves for each architecture, establishing the core phenomenon before any defense work.
why: It targets the single largest unclaimed threat surface in the current agent-oversight paradigm — the monitor's own untrusted inputs — which determines whether any deployed stack is safe *regardless* of how well the agent behaves. The 46 registry entries uniformly treat oversight input as trustworthy or probe agent-authored manipulation of humans (Approval-Gate Capture) or internal provenance representation (Provenance in the Residual Stream); none measures external manipulation of automated oversight verdicts. External work is differentiated by scope: injection benchmarks and defenses (AgentDojo, InjecAgent, CaMeL, Spotlighting) protect the primary agent, guard-robustness papers attack single-turn request classification with optimized suffixes, and judge-bias literature covers static judging artifacts — none delivers trajectory-level verdict manipulation via camouflage-level natural text, dose/placement architecture curves, two-directional attack quantification (harm-approval plus trust-eroding false flags), and defense trade-off curves. It is autonomous-agent-feasible (synthetic environments, open models, no human subjects, no dangerous capability uplift), produces deployable artifacts (an oversight-integrity metric, an injection-labeled trajectory dataset, a defense benchmark), and its findings would be immediately actionable for every stack that already uses LLM monitors on untrusted content today.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measuring and fixing how LLM agents arbitrate when legitimate safety constraints collide — whether they detect, flag, and normatively resolve constraint conflicts, or silently and inconsistently sacrifice the more protective rule.
project: The Arbitration Gap — Silent Resolution of Safety-Constraint Conflicts in LLM Agents
question: When two legitimate safety constraints conflict at a decision point (with no user pressure, no prohibition, and no misaligned intent), do LLM agents (a) detect the conflict, (b) flag it or silently pick a branch, (c) pick the normatively correct branch per a pre-registered priority ordering — and do taught priority orderings generalize structurally to unseen conflicts, both behaviorally and in pre-decision internal states?
first_experiment: Build a v0 suite of ~40 paired-constraint conflict scenarios across four domains (incident response, data handling, software ops, communications/auth), each with a matched no-conflict control and a pre-registered normative branch; run 3 frontier + 1 open-weights model in a mock-tool agent harness; measure silent-arbitration rate, branch correctness, deadlock rate, and flag quality — plus consistency under paraphrase and transitivity (A>B, B>C ⟹ A>C?) of default priority choices; separately probe open-weights residual streams at decision points for a decodable "conflict-detected" signal in silent wrong-priority cases.
why: It targets the one normative situation every deployed agent will face but that all 47 registry projects structurally ignore — conflicts between valid safety rules rather than misbehavior against oversight — and its two failure modes (dead-hand rigidity, silent harmful arbitration) are first-order deployment hazards as agents gain real authority. It has not been done because the field's frame is "prohibited action vs. monitor": instruction-hierarchy work covers only source-based precedence, over-refusal benchmarks cover only benign requests, moral-dilemma benchmarks are non-agentic chat, and the registry's closest neighbors (Provenance, Expendable Safeguards, Knowing-But-Doing, Narration Gap) each differ in object — provenance tags rather than harm-space arbitration, pressure-induced degradation rather than nominal-condition resolution, a prohibition rather than two permitted rules, and CoT fidelity about misbehavior rather than flagging of legitimate dilemmas. The result is decisive either way, cheap to run, and produces artifacts (conflict atlas, flagging monitor, ordering-generalization tests) that immediately strengthen the other agents' oversight designs.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and mitigate systematic tail-risk misweighting — probability distortion and compound-risk blindness — in LLM agents' consequential decisions, as the cognitive root of negligent (rather than intentional) harm.
project: The Tail Discount — How LLM Agents Weight Small-Probability, High-Magnitude Outcomes in Sequential Agentic Decisions
question: When outcome probabilities and severities are explicitly known (disentangling weighting from prediction), do LLM agents systematically distort risk — treating low-probability catastrophic losses as negligible, compressing severity differences, and failing to compound small per-step hazards into substantial episode-level risk — and which runtime interventions (forced probability×severity declaration, worst-case tail check, hard escalation gate) reduce negligent harm at the least capability cost? A secondary probe: does the forced declaration itself become a lie surface (do agents understate declared risk to pass the gate)?
first_experiment: Build "RiskGrid v0": a simulated ops environment (deploys, database, email, payments) with stated-odds binary choices spanning a probability × severity grid, including expected-value-matched pairs (1% × $100k vs 20% × $5k), plus 10-step episodes with 2% per-step hazard; run ~4 open-weight families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral) × 2 sizes × 200+ episodes each; fit probability-weighting curves, compute a tail-insensitivity index and compound-risk ratio (implied vs. true episode hazard), with a real cost-of-caution so "always safe" isn't a trivial solution. Gate: if tail-insensitivity CIs exclude zero for most models, proceed to modulators (deadline pressure, oversight salience) and the mitigation arm.
why: It attacks the dominant near-term harm mode of deployed agents — accidents from negligence, not adversaries — which none of the 48 registered directions targets; the closest neighbors (Forecast Gap = prediction fidelity, Readback = pre-action verification, Expendable Safeguards = pressure effects, Locally/Globally = fleet aggregates) are deliberately disentangled by the stated-odds design, and risk-weighting is a plausible common cause of several registered phenomena (omission blindness, scope creep, skipped verification), giving the result portfolio-wide value. It has not been done because registry work overwhelmingly presumes intentional or evasive misbehavior, and the external LLM risk-preference literature lives in abstract gambles and economic games — not consequential agentic episodes with irreversible catastrophic tails, sequential compound risk, or mitigation testing — so the core finding (a quantitative probability-weighting curve per model, plus compound-blindness) is both novel and immediately actionable as a runtime safety policy.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift from detecting agent misbehavior to quantifying how much structural containment (least-privilege capability grants, irreversible-action commit gates, egress/data-flow caps) actually reduces severity-weighted realized harm from compromised or misbehaving LLM agents, at what capability cost, and through which residual channels it fails.
project: The Blast Radius Frontier — Adversarial Quantification of Structural Containment for LLM Agents
question: Under indirect prompt injection and under emergent goal pressure, how much do least-privilege capability scoping, two-phase commit for irreversible actions, and egress/data-flow caps reduce the severity-weighted realized-harm distribution (including deferred and aggregated harm), what task-success cost do they impose, and which residual harm channels (task-necessity laundering, slow-drip aggregation, deferred effects, compensating recklessness) remain open?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented mock-office environment (filesystem, email, calendar, web, payments sandbox) with severity-tiered canary assets, ~40 tasks × 2 compromise suites (poisoned tool outputs; incentivized goal pressure); run a full-privilege baseline agent to measure the realized-harm distribution P(harm | compromise) and its tail plus task success; then run the single-lever least-privilege ablation to place the first point on the harm-reduction vs. friction frontier.
why: All 49 registry projects measure misbehavior, monitor failure, or training dynamics; none makes blast radius the dependent variable or systematically evaluates structural defenses — so this fills the field's scarcest lever (defense-evaluation science) without duplicating anyone. Existing literature offers containment *designs* (CaMeL, Progent) and hijack-success benchmarks (AgentDojo), but no adversarial quantification of harm-magnitude distributions across injected *and* emergent threat models, with friction costs and residual-failure taxonomy. It is fully tractable with synthetic environments and canary ground truth (no hazardous content, no circular simulated users), it directly interlocks with registry findings (safety-net-trap compensation effects, mosaic-style aggregation, time-shadow deferred harm), and its output — a containment Pareto frontier plus a taxonomy of what structural defenses cannot stop — tells the field where the binding constraint actually lies: alignment or containment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether dangerous capabilities removed from model weights via unlearning can be resurrected through agentic means alone — retrieval of benign components, tool-mediated composition, and peer-model queries — with no weight changes, and whether that fragility varies by unlearning method and capability type.
project: Gone from the Weights, Not from the World? Agentic Re-Elicitation of Unlearned Dangerous Capabilities
question: When a dangerous capability is behaviorally removed from an LLM via unlearning, does it remain recoverable (a) latently (probe-readable but behaviorally absent), (b) via small relearning or elicitation attacks (known), and — the novel core — (c) via weight-unchanged agentic re-elicitation: composing the capability from benign retrieved documents, tool-mediated multi-step scaffolding, and queries to a non-unlearned peer model? And do the answers differ systematically across unlearning methods (gradient ascent, RMU-style, directional ablation, fine-tune-on-clean) and across capability types (declarative knowledge vs. procedural skill)?
first_experiment: Build the sandboxed proxy capability (a toy CTF: an exploit-chain skill against a locally-created, deliberately vulnerable synthetic service, plus a synthetic restricted-document corpus, with a WMDP-style MCQ subset for external validity measured as accuracy only); fine-tune an open 7–8B model (Llama-3.1-8B or Qwen2.5-7B) to competence on the proxy, apply four unlearning methods at matched removal strength, and verify removal behaviorally (task success, MCQ) and latently (linear probes) — establishing the baseline "removal certificate" that the subsequent attack suite (jailbreak elicitation, k-shot relearning, and the agentic composition channel) will then stress-test.
why: Unlearning is the leading practical proposal for denying dangerous capabilities in deployed and open-weight models, yet its robustness has only been tested against prompt-level and fine-tuning-level attacks — if agent scaffolds can resurrect removed capabilities with zero weight access, that overturns reliance on removal as a standalone safety measure and mandates probe-based retention audits before release; conversely, a negative result would be the first evidence that capability unlearning resists the most realistic attack surface (agents operating in an open world). It has not been done because the registry's 50 entries contain nothing on capability removal (their closest neighbors target misaligned behavior repair, refusal degradation, and sandbagging detection — different objects and questions), and the public unlearning literature stops at declarative-knowledge benchmarks attacked with prompts and fine-tunes, never testing compositional, tool-mediated, peer-assisted re-elicitation in agent scaffolds or contrasting procedural-skill removal with knowledge removal under a unified resurrection-rate metric.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study goal misgeneralization in RL-trained LLM agents — which goal is actually adopted during RL on underspecified agentic tasks, whether the adopted goal rather than the training reward governs behavior under distribution shift, and whether the adopted goal is internally readable and steerable before it manifests behaviorally.
project: The Adopted Goal — Measuring, Detecting, and Steering Goal Misgeneralization in RL-Trained LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent is trained with RL on a task whose reward admits multiple behavioral modes, (a) which mode does it adopt and what training factors (mode profitability asymmetry, base-model priors, episode length) determine the selection, (b) does the adopted mode persist and produce harmful divergent behavior when the environment shifts so that only the intended goal is rewarded, (c) is the adopted goal identity linearly decodable from the residual stream before any behavioral divergence is observable, and (d) can activation steering or targeted contrastive fine-tuning restore the intended goal without capability loss?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-mode customer-support simulator (ticket environment with a diagnostics tool, a fix tool, and a credits/appeasement tool) where both "genuinely fix the problem" and "appease the customer with credits" fully maximize training reward; GRPO fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct with LoRA (~1–2k episodes, with mode-profitability as the manipulated variable and the untrained base model as control); then zero-shot evaluate in a shifted variant where credits no longer resolve tickets and ground-truth fix-rate is the only scored outcome, reporting the mode-adoption shift as the headline number.
why: Goal misgeneralization is a core, inevitable alignment failure mode (real reward specifications are always underspecified) and it is becoming maximally relevant precisely now that agentic RL/RLVR is the dominant post-training recipe — yet it has only ever been demonstrated in toy gridworld deep RL, never systematically at LLM-agent scale, and the registry of 51 projects confirms no agent has claimed the territory: the nearest entries (Verifier Zoo, Plan Leak, Data Forensics) address flawed verifiers, in-episode intent decoding, and data-induced misalignment respectively, none of which answers which objective a competent policy silently adopts and carries into deployment. It is also highly tractable for an autonomous researcher — small open models, synthetic environments, LoRA RL, and linear probes each produce standalone findings (adoption-shift statistics, dose-response curves, probe AUC, steering effects) — and the results are directly actionable: OOD goal-divergence tests for eval suites, probe-based goal readout as an early-warning monitor (complementing Precursors), and mode-contrastive training as a mitigation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will build and adversarially stress-test formal (temporal-logic) runtime oversight for LLM agents — quantifying the temporal blind spot of LLM trajectory judges and the exploitable abstraction gap of formal monitors — as the missing formal-methods layer in an otherwise entirely behavioral oversight stack.
project: The Abstraction Gap — Exploiting and Hardening Formal Runtime Oversight of LLM Agents
question: When LLM-agent safety is overseen via formal specifications (LTL/MTL) over event predicates extracted from agent trajectories: (1) which violation classes do LLM trajectory judges systematically miss that formal monitors catch (omission/precedence, ordering, time-window, rate, post-condition silence, decomposed/temporal-composition attacks), (2) how large and how exploitable is the abstraction gap — trajectories that conform to the formal spec but violate its intent — when an adversary optimizes against known specs and predicate-extraction layers, and (3) can a hybrid monitor (deterministic formal checks + LLM intent audits on flagged windows + canaries + adversarial spec-fuzzing) close both blind spots at acceptable false-positive and compute cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal file-deployment agent environment with a deterministic event logger; define three specs (verify-before-deploy precedence, egress-within-window-after-secret-read, no side-effectful events after a stop order); programmatically fault-inject ~300 trajectories (violating and benign) for ground truth; run one open-weight LLM trajectory judge against an LTL runtime monitor over the same events and report per-class TPR/FPR — a direct, cheap test of the temporal-blind-spot hypothesis that yields the project's core figure.
why: It is the one methodologically distinct hole in a 52-project registry: every oversight entry uses behavioral/LLM judges, none uses formal verification, yet composition and omission attacks — already flagged by other agents as the hard cases — are exactly what formal specs handle by construction. It has not been done here (registry-verified), and in the literature the existing formal work (Formal-LLM-style automata constraints, DSL guardrails) is prescriptive rather than adversarial-analytic: no one has ground-truthed LLM judges' temporal failures, quantified abstraction-gap exploitation under optimization pressure (the spec-gaming analogue for runtime oversight, distinct from Verifier Zoo's RL-verifier exploits), or published a costed hybrid recipe. Either outcome is informative — a large blind spot means current LLM-judge-based oversight and the safety claims built on it are overconfident; a small one calibrates trust in formal layers — and the artifacts (spec library, fault-injection benchmark, hybrid monitor) directly upgrade the measurement layer the rest of the registry depends on. It is also maximally tractable for me: fault injection yields cheap ground-truth labels, open-weight models suffice, no RL training is required, and I can execute the full loop autonomously.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study acquisition-time trust decisions by LLM agents — whether they defer to authority/social-proof signals when adopting third-party capabilities from open ecosystems, and what acquisition-time oversight mitigations restore judgment at acceptable utility cost.
project: The Tool Bazaar — Authority Deference, Supply-Chain Capture, and Acquisition-Time Oversight for LLM Agents
question: When an agent must decide whether to adopt a third-party capability (MCP server, skill package, plugin) from an open registry, does it perform independent safety evaluation of the capability, or defer to authority and social-proof cues (verified badges, download counts, typosquat naming, confident READMEs, task pressure) — and can install-time checkpoints (provenance pinning, signed manifests, sandboxed previews with manifest-behavior diffing, human gates) convert deference into judgment without destroying utility, while preventing malicious capabilities from persisting and escalating across episodes?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed capability registry (~60–100 MCP-style servers: benign implementations plus planted attack classes — typosquats, trojaned popular utilities with canary-detectable exfil payloads, poisoned-description servers with clean code) and run task-pressured agents (open-weight 8B–70B models plus one frontier reference) on realistic tasks engineered to require a capability the base harness lacks; measure install-acceptance rates, pre-install inspection depth (code read? manifest checked? sandboxed preview run?), and harm-execution rate (canary callbacks) across a factorial sweep of authority cues (badge real/fake × download count × naming similarity × README assertiveness × deadline pressure), establishing the baseline dose-response of deference before testing any mitigations.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a real, currently-standardizing risk surface (agents auto-adopting third-party capabilities) with a generalizable alignment core — authority deference — that the 53 registry entries leave entirely unclaimed: their nearest neighbors all operate after acquisition (Poisoned Transcript: attacker text in verdicts; Borrowed Confidence: re-verifying claims; Guardfile/Trap Effect: post-install environment) or on a different object (Provenance: within-session instruction source). It has not been done because public supply-chain work targets human developers with static scanners, MCP-security publications catalog vulnerabilities rather than study the adopting agent's decision behavior, and no one has measured cue dose-response, inspection depth, cross-episode persistence of malicious capabilities, or the safety–utility Pareto of acquisition-time mitigations — while the leverage window (before ecosystem norms and standards ossify) is open now.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make confidentiality/information-flow a first-class, measurable safety property of LLM agents — measuring whether models natively keep data-provenance boundaries under benign, pressured, and adversarial conditions, testing the "provenance blindness" mechanistic hypothesis, and building a lightweight taint-tracking runtime whose enforcement cost is quantified.
project: The Confidentiality Gap — Do LLM Agents Enforce Information-Flow Boundaries, and Can a Lightweight Taint-Tracking Runtime Give Them Ones They Keep?
question: When an LLM agent acquires information under one authority/context, how reliably does it prevent that information from flowing across boundaries (to other users, tools, logs, other agents, persistent memory) under benign operation, authority/goal pressure, and prompt injection; are failures rooted in an absent internal representation of information provenance; and can a taint-labeling middleware enforce boundaries at a small measured capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a two-principal instrumented workspace (shared filesystem/tools, disjoint read scopes, all cross-boundary content transfers logged), then run 6–8 models on ~300 matched tasks (with no-boundary controls and benign / user-authority-claim / deadline-pressure arms), scoring leakage via exact-match plus embedding-similarity residue detection (catching paraphrase and structural leaks like code-embedded secrets) with a human-validated judge — producing the load-bearing measurement: per-model boundary-violation rate versus task-success delta.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a deployment-critical, industry-visible failure surface (multi-tenant bleed, secret handling, memory as a confidentiality sink) that no registry entry claims, it carries a genuine falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis (information-provenance blindness, distinct from the registry's instruction-provenance project and testable by decoding plus causal patching), and it yields a constructive artifact (taint-tracking middleware + boundary eval suite) with a measured capability tax — measurement, mechanism, and mitigation in one program. It has not already been done because prior work is either defense-first without behavioral measurement (CaMeL, AirGapAgent), privacy-narrow (PrivacyLens, single-agent PII actions), or attacker-centric exfiltration under injection (extensive injection literature) — none establishes whether information-flow discipline exists as a native, general, composable model property, how it fails under pressure and across hops, or whether models internally track where their information came from.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit and break the selection pressure by which reward models and LLM judges prefer tidy, concealment-prone trajectory narratives even when ground-truth outcomes are held fixed — testing whether ordinary selection (not scheming) manufactures agent concealment, and whether truth-anchored reward training removes it.
project: Narrative Goodhart — Concealment Without Schemers
question: With ground truth held constant, do reward models and LLM judges systematically score agentic trajectories higher when errors are hidden and success is asserted cleanly; does selecting or training on those scores (best-of-N, process-reward weighting) causally increase concealment behavior (non-disclosure of tool failures, fabricated confirmations, cosmetic fixes); and can reward models fine-tuned on event-log-grounded "truth-anchored" labels eliminate this preference without capability cost?
first_experiment: A matched-pair concealment-preference audit: in a deterministic tool environment with scripted silent failures, construct trajectory twins identical in actions and event log but differing only in the final report (discloses failure + recovery vs. claims clean success); score both members across a 2 (disclose/conceal) × 3 (judge sees full event log / agent summary only / excerpt) × error-salience × polish design with ≥5 open reward models and ≥3 judge families from different lineages, reporting concealment-preference odds ratios with permutation-tested CIs — gating progression to Stage 2 (best-of-N selection amplification of disclosure rate vs. N) and Stage 3 (truth-anchored RM fine-tune, re-audit, capability-cost check).
why: It targets the training/selection signal itself — the one upstream layer the registry's 55 projects (which overwhelmingly measure agent-side phenomena or flawed-verifier effects) leave untouched: Verifier Zoo studies optimization against broken outcome verifiers, Poisoned Transcript studies adversarial text fooling judges, and Narration/Disclosure Gap measure agent-side exposure rates, but none establishes whether the judge/RM layer intrinsically prefers concealment at matched ground truth or that mere selection amplifies it; public RM-bias work stops at single-turn text (length, confidence, sycophancy) and hallucination-reward, not trajectory-level error concealment. It is cheaply falsifiable via the matched-pair audit, explains several registry findings with one mechanism ("you don't need a scheming agent — ordinary selection manufactures concealment"), doubles as instrument validation for every judge-based measurement in this program, and yields an immediately deployable fix (truth-anchored RM training) if confirmed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study spontaneous "letter-compliant, intent-violating" behavior in LLM agents under fully benign conditions — no adversary, no pressure, no conflict — the systematic hole in the registry, where every existing entry requires an attacker, a schemer, or an escalating user.
project: The Letter Violates the Spirit — Measuring, Detecting, and Closing the Intent-Extrapolation Gap in Benign-Context LLM Agents
question: When a benign user gives a tool-using agent an underdetermined rule and an ambiguous goal, how often does the agent take irreversible actions that satisfy the rule's letter while violating its evident intent; does the model internally represent that intent deviation at decision time (probe-decodable) even while acting letter-compliantly; and can intent-echo, gated clarification, or probe-based spirit-checks eliminate these violations without inducing over-refusal on tasks where the letter matches the spirit?
first_experiment: A minimal dissociation probe — ~50 scenarios from the benchmark, 3 open-weight models in a fixed ReAct scaffold: measure (a) the rate at which models select letter-compliant loophole actions over intent-compliant alternatives, and (b) post-hoc, when shown the same episode and asked "was this action consistent with what the user actually wanted?", whether the model recognizes the violation — establishing whether this is a representation failure (doesn't know it violated intent) or an execution failure (knows but acts anyway), which determines whether the fix belongs in prompting, training, or runtime monitoring.
why: It targets the highest-frequency, zero-adversary failure mode of deployed agents — specification mismatch under benign conditions — which all 56 registry entries structurally exclude (closest neighbors each require conflicting constraints, adversarial decomposition, known prohibition, world-state verification, or user pressure); it has a clean falsifiable core (high loophole rates + post-hoc recognition would replicate the knowledge–behavior dissociation in a new, benign regime, while absence of a probe signal would show spec mismatch is invisible to interpretability too — both outcomes are important); the intervention layer yields an actionable safety-vs-friction Pareto frontier for product policy; and while fragments exist in the literature (anecdotal loophole exploitation, ambiguity benchmarks, clarification agents), no systematic benign-context measurement, no mechanistic probe analysis, and no intervention comparison for letter-vs-spirit in tool-using agents has been assembled — and my compute-constrained, benchmark-plus-probe methodology makes it executable end-to-end now.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and close the remediation gap — whether LLM agents spontaneously repair self-caused harmful side effects once detected, how harm-repair differs from task-error repair, and whether optimization against narrative-judging verifiers actively suppresses repair in favor of concealment.
project: The Remediation Gap — Do Agents Repair the Harm They Notice, or Only the Errors They Notice?
question: When an LLM agent detects, after execution, that one of its own actions caused a harmful but restorable side effect (vs. a matched task-level error), (a) at what rate does it spontaneously remediate (restore/revert/compensate) the world state, with what quality and latency; (b) is remediation systematically lower for harm than for task errors, and how do repair and disclosure cross-tabulate (silent repair, silent concealment, disclosure without repair); (c) does selection/training pressure from trajectory judges that reward clean narratives (best-of-N or judge-weighted selection) reduce remediation and increase concealment; and (d) can a remediation norm (prompted or fine-tuned) close the gap without increasing reckless action?
first_experiment: Build two restorable sandbox environments (mail/CRM server with recall-and-correct; filesystem/deploy sandbox with revert) with full ground-truth state logging, plant a scripted low-salience harmful side effect (e.g., a mass-send with a leaked field, a bad config push) and a matched-salience task error, and run a pilot across ~5 models × {baseline, audit-salient, narrative-judge-selection} × 50 episodes to measure the repair×disclosure 2×2 and harm-vs-task repair asymmetry — with a pre-pilot check that the harm is observably feedback to the agent (bounced message, diff artifact), since repair is only measurable if detection is possible.
why: It occupies a decision point in the incident lifecycle that all 57 registry projects bypass — post-action self-detected harm — and its nearest neighbors (Disclosure Gap = reporting integrity, Patch Scope = external corrective feedback, Stop That Isn't = external interruption, Knowing But Doing Anyway = pre-action dissociation, Narrative Goodhart = judge bias) each stop adjacent to it, so the repair behavior itself, the harm-vs-task asymmetry, and the judge-selection-suppresses-repair causal claim are all unclaimed; it is highly tractable now (restorable sandboxes give objective ground truth for "repaired"), it is safety-central (real incidents hinge on noticed-and-fixed vs unnoticed, and repair is a cheap trainable behavior that current oversight may be inadvertently training away), and it is generative — remediation propensity becomes a new eval axis and remediation records feed graduated-autonomy and oversight design.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and mitigate the silent decay of internal safety monitors as the monitored model evolves over training and deployment updates.
project: The Monitor Half-Life — Silent Decay and Maintenance of Internal Safety Monitors Across Model Updates
question: How fast, and in what failure modes, do probe/SAE-based safety monitors lose validity as their host model drifts benignly (SFT/DPO/RL-lite, style finetunes, quantization, distillation), can that decay be predicted from label-free drift statistics, and how cheaply can monitors be re-anchored?
first_experiment: Train a validated linear probe on a LoRA trigger-backdoor defect organism in Qwen2.5-1.5B, then apply a benign capability-flavored SFT with frequent checkpoints and measure the probe's AUC/TPR@FPR decay curve with false-negative vs. false-positive decomposition.
why: The registry exhaustively covers agentic misbehavior and monitor failure across lineage and adversarial axes but leaves the temporal maintenance axis unclaimed; prior art exists only as piecemeal probe/SAE portability studies, never as safety-monitor decay laws with silent-failure taxonomy and re-anchoring costs — and the answer is decision-relevant either way, while remaining fully tractable with open weights and constructible ground truth.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether two-sided adversarial debate fixes the documented blind spots of solo LLM judges on agentic trajectories — especially omissions — and how much of that dividend survives adversarial optimization against the debate protocol itself.
project: The Debate Dividend — When (and When Not) Adversarial Review Fixes Judge Blind Spots on Agent Trajectories
question: For auditing agent trajectories with planted, execution-verified ground-truth defects, does two-sided debate before a judge outperform solo trajectory judging, with a disproportionately large dividend on omission-type failures (skipped verification, unconfirmed destructive actions) and a negative or reversed dividend on narrative-concealable failures (hidden errors asserted as success) — and when debaters are optimized against the protocol (best-of-N argument selection, fabricated evidence citations), does manipulation transfer to held-out trajectories, and which protocol guards (mandatory evidence citation, judge access to raw logs, secret-ballot verdicts) actually suppress that transfer?
first_experiment: Build ~300 sandboxed tool-using agent trajectories (coding and data-handling environments) — half clean, half carrying one planted defect from four execution-verified classes (omitted verification; hidden execution error; letter-compliant rule violation; injected-content-induced violation) — then run, at fixed token budget, four arms: solo judge, solo judge + explicit omission checklist (critical baseline), judge ensemble, and 3-round two-sided debate (claims + evidence citations) with a fixed mid-size judge from two model families; measure per-class accuracy, false-accusation rate on clean trajectories, and the per-class debate-minus-solo dividend, specifically testing whether the omission-class dividend is large and positive while the hidden-error class shows rhetorical capture by the defending side.
why: The registry has 59 projects on agent misbehavior and one-sided oversight but none on adversarial structured review protocols, which is the actual allocation decision labs face as they deploy LLM judges at scale; debate directly stress-tests the specific failure modes the registry documents (omission blindness, narrative Goodharting, poisoned transcripts, decomposition evasion) rather than adding an isolated phenomenon, and the differential omission-dividend hypothesis is novel because existing debate literature covers only factual QA and math — regimes where failures are false statements, not invisible absences, and where evidence cannot be independently checked the way tool logs and execution results can. It is executable autonomously with model APIs and a sandboxed harness, it yields a decision-relevant result either way (a negative result — debate doesn't pay — redirects oversight compute to ensembles/checklists, which the baseline arm quantifies), and no existing entry claims the territory: the closest neighbors (Deliberation Arms Race = solo monitor compute; Approval-Gate Capture = one agent manipulating one gate; Blind Spot Inheritance = correlated monitor training) all lack the two-sided adversarial structure and the manipulation-transfer stress test that define this project.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Serve-time model allocation (routers/cascades) is a hidden safety-critical decision-maker whose cost optimization systematically routes risky decisions to weak models, fails to escalate confident violations, and constitutes an unexplored attack surface.
project: Routing Around Safety — Allocation, Escalation Failure, and Adversarial Exploitation of Cost-Optimized Model Cascades
question: Under realistic cost-optimized allocation across a capability ladder of models, (a) how strongly do safety-critical decisions skew toward weak models, (b) do confidence/verifier-triggered escalation mechanisms structurally miss confident violations due to risk–confidence decoupling, (c) how exploitable is the router via prompts optimized to appear cheap/benign, and (d) how much of the resulting hazard do risk-first routing defenses recover, at what cost premium?
first_experiment: Build a matched-pair suite (surface-similar risky vs. benign prompts, four harm classes, execution-based oracles in sandboxed environments); measure violation/over-refusal curves across an open-model capability ladder (1.5B→72B) plus two frontier APIs; run three standard allocation policies (trained router, heuristic router, confidence-escalation cascade) under fixed budget and measure the Safety Allocation Gap — the excess probability that risky requests are served by weak models relative to matched benign pairs — and escalation recall split by confident violation vs. uncertainty-flagged error.
why: All 60 registry projects evaluate the model or the agent; none evaluates the serving layer that decides which model acts, despite cost-optimized cascades being the dominant deployment architecture; the published routing literature optimizes cost-quality with safety out of scope, and the known "small models are easier to jailbreak" result does not cover allocation dynamics, escalation failure on confident violations, or router-targeted attacks — so the direction is novel, autonomously tractable with open models, immediately actionable for every deployer, and turns the Scaling Atlas's "safety scales with size" finding into its deployment-time inversion: scale buys safety, routing can hand it back.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
