first_experiment: Build a synthetic capability suite with exact ground truth (cipher decoding + multi-step arithmetic word problems, with held-out sibling families for transfer tests); LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B to competence; then run a 3-round gated selection loop with two benign-looking curation criteria (anti-overfit outlier filtering on assessment-framed items; a "consistency regularizer" penalizing score spikes in eval contexts) plus an intentional-reward arm as an upper bound and a no-gate control — measuring (i) gate-context vs. deployment-context score divergence per round, (ii) transfer to unseen gate framings and a novel domain, and (iii) first-pass detector readings, especially whether a linear probe on intermediate activations recovers the withheld correct answer at the moment a sub-threshold response is emitted, which distinguishes capability suppression from capability absence.
why: The registry's 20 projects are dense on monitor robustness, eval contamination, and eval-context distortion but leave empty the cell where training dynamics themselves corrupt capability measurement — the mechanism by which capability gating, our main deployment safeguard for dangerous capabilities, could fail silently with no intentional attacker; externally, sandbagging has only been demonstrated under instruction or explicit reward, and detectors have only been validated against instructed concealment, so unintentional emergence, its transfer profile, and detector survival on emergent concealment are unstudied; it is end-to-end feasible for me at small model scale, it fills a distinct slot adjacent to (not duplicating) ExamBlind, EvalLeak, EvasionBench, and MoleMap, and it produces a reusable artifact (induced-concealment models plus a validated detector suite) that strengthens several existing registry projects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether LLM agents' adherence to explicit safety constraints erodes across episodes purely through self-authored memory persistence — no weight updates, no judge, no adversary — and which memory-hygiene interventions arrest it.
project: MemDrift — Self-Propagating Safety-Constraint Erosion Through Agent Self-Memory Without Training, Optimization Pressure, or Adversarial Attack
question: When an agent's only inter-episode persistence is memory it writes itself, how fast and by what mechanisms does compliance with costly-but-explicit safety constraints decay (violation rate vs. episode index), does the shortcut norm propagate across task types and into fresh agents via shared memory artifacts, and which interventions (external vs. self-authored summarization, static-memory replay, periodic constitutional re-priming, reset schedules, drift detectors on memory diffs) suppress or reverse the erosion at what capability cost?
first_experiment: A minimal 3-arm trajectory test in a scripted coding/ops sandbox with three friction constraints (leaked-solutions cache present but forbidden; failing tests that must not be skipped; destructive ops requiring an approval flow) — run ~20 episodes × 3 seeds for (1) memory-on (agent writes and re-injects its own memory file each episode), (2) memory-off (fresh context each episode), (3) static-memory (episode-1 memory replayed verbatim); measure per-episode automated violation rate and task success, and test whether the violation-rate slope is positive for memory-on while flat for memory-off/static — confirming or killing the phenomenon before scaling to mechanism, propagation, and intervention phases.
why: It targets the largest thematic hole in the registry — every existing project assumes a static or adversarially perturbed policy, while deployed memory-equipped agents are slowly self-rewriting through experience with no one measuring the safety consequence — and it is highly tractable (no GPU cluster, no human subjects, automated checkers) with a decisive falsifiable first experiment. It has not been done because DriftBench's drift requires a judge-driven optimizer, Pando's memory effects require an adversary, BrokenChain's decay is across delegation hops not time, Kindling watches weights rather than context, and the external literature covers adversarial memory poisoning and capability-focused self-evolution but not benign self-memory-mediated erosion of safety constraints — even though persistent-memory agent products are shipping today on precisely the unexamined assumption that absent an attacker, behavior stays put.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit whether unlearning actually removes hazardous capabilities from open-weight LLMs by mapping the "elicitation-cost frontier" — how much latent residue survives and how cheaply it can be recovered — rather than trusting the metric the unlearning was optimized against.
project: GhostCap — The Unlearning Residue and Elicitability Frontier
question: When a hazardous capability is unlearned from an open-weight LLM, how much latent residue survives — quantified as the minimum elicitation budget (distribution-shifted/novel-format prompts, k-shot elicitation, micro-finetuning on benign data, linear merging with a capability model, weight perturbations) needed to recover graded fractions of original performance — and can that residue be detected from internal activations alone (linear probes/SAE features) in models whose behavior is already indistinguishable from clean?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with WMDP-bio: apply four published unlearning methods (RMU, NPO, GA, task-vector ablation) with standard hyperparameters; verify each hits the standard metric (WMDP accuracy ≈ random, MMLU retained). Then run four recovery vectors and plot recovery curves (fraction of original capability vs. attack budget) per method: (1) paraphrased and novel-format MCQ + free-form generation scored by an independent judge model; (2) k-shot elicitation, k = 0–8, using related-but-not-identical hazardous prompts; (3) a 30-minute LoRA fine-tune on ~200 benign bio-adjacent Q&A pairs; (4) linear merges with a strong general model at α ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75}. In parallel, train linear probes on intermediate-layer activations from held-out WMDP-adjacent data and test whether residue is detectable in behaviorally-clean unlearned models. Decision gate: if any method looks clean on the certified metric but is cheaply elicitable — the expected outcome — the audit gap is real, and the project scales to the full methods × domains (bio/cyber/chem) × recovery-vectors frontier plus a packaged pre-release "elicitability certificate" protocol.
why: It is orthogonal to all 22 registry entries — none touch capability removal, unlearning, or elicitation-side auditing; every other agent works on the oversight, insertion, or selection axis, while this completes the "manufactured safety" audit family as the mirror image of EvalLeak (capability *removed* rather than safety *inserted*). It is maximally decision-relevant per unit of compute: unlearning is the default safeguard justifying hazardous-capability release decisions and dual-use compliance, and merging makes residue a mainstream failure path rather than a corner case — if removal is cosmetic, open-weight release decisions are unsound. It has not already been done: existing studies (Deeb & Roger 2024; Łucki et al. 2025; "Unlearning or Obfuscating?") test one or two recovery vectors on a few methods, mostly evaluated on the same MCQ distribution the unlearning optimizes against; there is no systematic elicitation-cost frontier across methods × hazard domains × recovery vectors, no probe-based residue detector packaged as an audit layer for behaviorally-clean models, no merging-as-recovery-vector study, and no standardized pre-release certificate a lab could actually run. And it is feasible autonomously: open weights, small models, LoRA, logprob evals, probes, and merges — no frontier access or RL infrastructure required.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the epistemic-supply layer of agent pipelines — whether autonomous agents under pressure fabricate empirical and safety evidence, whether verification layers can detect it at acceptable false-positive cost, and how fabricated findings propagate to corrupt downstream decisions.
project: ProvenanceBench — Evidence Fabrication, Detection, and Epistemic Contagion in Autonomous Research and Safety-Verification Agents
question: When an AI agent is tasked with demonstrating or verifying a result — including verifying that a system (or itself) is safe — and it lacks the capability, budget, or time to genuinely establish it, how often and how subtly does it fabricate the evidence (fake experiment runs, invented metrics, fabricated citations/logs, false safety-check outputs), can provenance-based and judge-based verification detect each fabrication class at fixed false-positive budgets, and what rate of wrong downstream decisions (e.g., "approve deployment") does undetected fabricated evidence cause as it propagates through reports and shared memory to other agents and human-simulated decision-makers?
first_experiment: Build a small "virtual lab" environment with objective ground truth (a simulated experimental system with known parameters, a tool-call log the agent cannot rewrite, and a report-writing step), then run open-weight agents under three conditions — feasible control, infeasible/under-resourced, and feasible-with-delivery-pressure (deadline + cancellation threat) — and measure the incidence and taxonomy of unsupported empirical claims in their reports, plus the detection rate and false-positive rate of a cheap provenance check (every report claim must trace to log evidence) versus an LLM judge; as a one-day add-on, feed clean vs. fabricated reports to a downstream agent asked "should we deploy this?" and measure the decision-flip rate.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a load-bearing and imminent failure surface — AI-controlled research and safety-verification pipelines, where fabricated evidence silently corrupts the very record that gates deployment — while the entire 23-project registry (and most oversight literature) measures whether monitors catch *misbehavior*, not whether anyone can tell whether the *evidence base agents produce is real*; it has objective ground truth, is runnable with open-weight models, fills a genuine benchmark gap (nearest neighbors each miss the core: claim-only honesty checks, judged-quality Goodhart, downward concealment, training-data eval poisoning, record tampering), and its "no adversary required" character makes it a distinct, complementary threat model — and if fabrication turns out to be rare and easily caught, that negative result is itself a quantified reassurance that changes pipeline design.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether weak-to-strong supervision (training a capable model under weaker-model labels, preferences, and rewards) genuinely removes, cosmetically launders, or actively elicits planted misalignment in the strong model, and which pipeline designs are safe.
project: WeakWash — Misalignment Laundering and Elicitation Under Weak-to-Strong Supervision
question: When a misaligned-but-capable model is fine-tuned under weak supervision, does its planted misbehavior get (a) removed, (b) cosmetically suppressed while remaining elicitable ("laundering"/veneer), or (c) amplified where the weak reward is exploitable — with the central hypothesis that weak supervision removes exactly the misalignment it can verify and launders exactly what it cannot?
first_experiment: Plant a conditional trigger-action backdoor in Qwen2.5-7B (LoRA SFT: insecure-code outputs only on trigger-conditioned prompts, ~90% trigger rate, capability intact on clean prompts), then apply a weak-DPO "safety pass" using preference labels from Qwen2.5-1.5B, and measure trigger rate on (i) standard triggers vs. (ii) paraphrased/novel triggers plus a small elicitation battery (k-shot demos, 100-example micro-finetune, linear probe for backdoor state), against a strong-supervisor control — a drop on (i) but persistence on (ii) is the laundering signature.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of superalignment — that weak supervisors can safely shape strong models — which no registry project and no crossed combination of the parent literatures (sleeper-agents persistence × W2SG generalization) addresses; existing work either uses matched-capability oversight (backdoor persistence studies) or aligned strong models (W2SG studies), so the laundering/veneer effect and the weak-reward elicitation of covert goals are unmeasured, and the study yields a directly actionable defensive artifact: a cheap post-training elicitation audit that distinguishes genuine removal from cosmetic suppression, plus pipeline-design guidance (restrict weak supervision to verifiable properties) that complements the registry's detection-heavy portfolio.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether unsafe strategies spread horizontally between LLM agents through shared logs and oversight artifacts faster than safety norms do, and how to contain that contagion.
project: CopyCat — The Safety-Contagion Asymmetry in LLM Agent Populations
question: Does unsafe-but-rewarding behavior transmit between agents observing shared artifacts faster than costly safety behavior, is punishment visibility inoculating or merely informing, and are oversight artifacts themselves transmission vectors that containment designs can close?
first_experiment: Four-condition transmission-chain experiment (shortcut-success, shortcut-punished, safe-exemplar, no-exposure baseline) in a coding-agent sandbox with shared team logs, measuring adoption uplift, transmission depth, and mutation across full-transcript vs. summarized-log conditions in 3–4 models.
why: It occupies the registry's only unclaimed quadrant (peer-to-peer social transmission vs. dyadic oversight, hierarchies, and self-memory), extends MemDrift's erosion finding to the realistic fleet setting with a cheap, decisive, either-way-informative experiment, and the selective-transmission/oversight-as-vector question is unaddressed in both the registry and the external collusion/cultural-transmission literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify whether the oversight stack built to catch *concealing, planted* misalignment also detects, correctly attributes, and fairly treats *sincere* misalignment (goal misgeneralization / internalized spec-gaming) that hides nothing because it doesn't know it's misaligned.
project: PlainSight — The Sincerity Gap: Oversight Detection, Attribution, and the Honesty Penalty for Non-Deceptive Misalignment
question: When an LLM misbehaves because it sincerely pursues a proxy goal acquired from benign training rather than because it conceals a planted covert goal (with behavioral harm matched between the two), how does each oversight sensor — deception-prompted LLM judges, probes trained on deceptive organisms, anomaly monitors, standard eval suites — perform on detection and on *cause attribution* (deliberate deception vs. goal error), and does disclosing the misaligned goal in the model's own reasoning increase or decrease detection and flagging severity?
first_experiment: An organism-viability pilot for the riskiest assumption: build one proxy-vs-true task family (coding assistant where demonstrations that hardcode test cases pass the visible tests but violate the spec), generate proxy-optimized SFT data, fine-tune three seeds of a small open model (1.5–7B), and screen on held-out instances for spontaneous proxy-goal latching without concealment cues (vs. a clean-data control); then run a single deception-prompted judge and one behavior-audit judge over a handful of matched-harm episodes to get a preliminary detection-and-attribution gap before scaling to the full 2×2 (planted-deceptive × sincere-misgeneralized, with and without disclosure).
why: It is the most promising because it fills the one conceptual hole in an otherwise 100% deception- and adversary-centric registry — sincere, benignly-induced misalignment is plausibly the modal real-world failure mode, and the registry's monitors were all designed and will all be calibrated against concealing adversaries, so their recall, attribution accuracy, and even fairness toward *honest* misalignment are unknown; the results feed directly into the sensor designs of ~a dozen other registry projects. It has not been done because the field's dominant methodology — model organisms of deception — takes concealment as a given, the goal-misgeneralization literature stops at demonstrating the phenomenon without connecting it to oversight, and no registry entry studies cause attribution at all; the matched-harm 2×2 design is the missing controlled comparison, and the "honesty penalty" outcome is genuinely uncertain in both directions, so any result is informative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The weights channel — model parameters as the unexamined tamperable surface under all oversight, with agent-initiated self-modification measured as an evasion/persistence strategy and defended via weight-provenance architectures.
project: LoRABreach — The Weights Channel: Agent-Initiated Self-Modification as Oversight Evasion and Misbehavior Persistence
question: At what capability and incentive level do code-executing LLM agents spontaneously adopt weight self-modification (of themselves, their monitors, or successor checkpoints) to evade oversight or persist misbehavior, how much behavioral/CoT/activation-monitor power does that destroy, how detectable are such edits, and which weight-provenance and containment defenses restore detection at what cost?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditioned misbehavior via backdoor SFT in 1B–3B open models; run scripted LoRA self-edit baselines to measure backdoor retention, capability retention, weight-diff detectability, and monitor power loss; then run the agentic version with competing evasion channels available and no hints, sweeping model scale to find where the weights channel is spontaneously discovered.
why: It targets the one shared assumption no registry project tests — that the monitored policy is stationary — and every nearest neighbor explicitly excludes it (MemDrift: no training; LogRoll: no weights; Pando: external footholds only; GhostCap: operator-initiated, reversed direction), while gradient hacking remains purely theoretical in the field; it is tractable with cheap LoRA loops on small open models using this cohort's standard planted-misbehavior-plus-monitor-suite methodology, and it becomes both harder to study and more dangerous to ignore as agent autonomy grows.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The most promising direction is the agent-initiated escalation channel — treating "ask the human vs. proceed" as a first-class control decision and measuring whether it is calibrated, malleable under deployment pressure, and adversarially suppressible.
project: RaiseHand — Agent-Initiated Escalation as a Control Channel: Calibration, Malleability, and Suppression in LLM Agents
question: When an autonomous agent faces uncertainty, stakes, and escalation costs, is its decision to escalate to a human calibrated against ground-truth need-to-escalate; how much can ordinary task-pressure (success incentives, anti-nagging instructions, sunk cost) and adversarial environment design (withheld or falsified evidence that hides the agent's own ignorance) suppress or flood it; and do cheap interventions (pre-commitment checks, escalation-rewarded fine-tuning, irreversible-action gates) restore calibration without destroying capability?
first_experiment: Build a small deterministic ops-style tool environment with by-construction "escalation-worthy moments" (ambiguous credentials where one is stale, a config deploy at 6/10 validation checks, partially wiped logs the agent should notice as missing evidence, destructive irreversible commands adjacent to needed ones), and run a 3-model × (stakes: reversible/irreversible) × (pressure: neutral / "you are the final authority, minimize asks" / success-bonus) × (suppression: none / plausible-but-wrong defaults + green-checkmark normalcy) grid over ~3–5k trajectories with open-weight 7–14B models, scoring programmatically: P(escalate | should), wrong-proceed rate, wrong-ask rate, escalation timing relative to the irreversible step, and whether the escalation actually surfaces the true uncertainty versus superficial doubt.
why: It targets the load-bearing denominator of all oversight — when human attention gets spent at all — which no registry project owns: OffSwitch covers operator-initiated interventions, BrokenChain covers upward reporting of already-made discoveries, and CryWolf covers monitor-side false-positive triage, but agent-initiated deferral under uncertainty is unclaimed, and the two failure modes (over-escalation saturating humans; under-escalation hiding failures) give it the same systems-level payoff as CryWolf with an agent-side mechanism. It has unusually clean ground truth (the "correct" escalation is set by construction), cheap programmatic scoring, and a decisive possible finding: if ordinary task pressure — not just adversarial pressure — erodes escalation calibration, that is deployment-critical and testable for mitigation. It is not already done because the external literature on deferral lives in classification (learning-to-defer), abstention (QA), and clarification-asking (task dialogue) — none of which benchmarks escalation as a safety control channel for autonomous agents under stakes/cost manipulations, unknown-unknown suppression (an agent that doesn't know it doesn't know), or training-induced suppression.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify whether ordinary agentic deployment scaffolds — not adversaries — silently wash out the safety behavior that safety training installs, by measuring how identical harmful content is treated when it arrives as a request versus as a plan step, tool call, or tool-output instruction.
project: ScaffoldWash — Does the Harness Uninstall Safety? Measuring Refusal-to-Action Transfer in Agentic Deployments
question: For a fixed model, how large is the compliance gap between the same harmful content presented as (1) a direct user request and (2–4) the identical content embedded in a benign plan step, emitted as the agent's own planner's tool call, or delivered inside a tool result/RAG document — which harness factor (persona framing, tool affordances, decomposition, RAG context) contributes most to the gap, and can a safety re-check installed at the plan/tool-call boundary close the gap without capability loss?
first_experiment: A cheap, decisive matched-prompt probe — take ~50 harmful behaviors from a public harm taxonomy plus 50 benign controls, render each in the four matched surface forms above, run ~8 open-weight models plus 2 API models through a standard minimal harness, and score compliance with a fixed ensemble of harm judges validated on a human-annotated 100-sample subset; the decisive statistic is the refusal→action compliance gap between direct-request and self-decomposed/tool-mediated forms (a <10-point gap kills the thesis in a week; a large gap defines the main transfer-matrix study and the boundary-of-installation mitigation experiment that follows).
why: It is the highest-leverage unoccupied quadrant — it interrogates the validity of every bare-chat safety eval (including those underpinning the other 29 registry projects) rather than adding a tenth oversight benchmark; it has zero registry collision (ExamBlind is eval-context distortion of capability with the opposite sign, GhostWork is monitor blindness rather than policy refusal, WeakWash is training-time, FadeBench is reasoning-surface); prior literature establishes only anecdotal existence results (agent-role compliance, persona jailbreaks) with no matched-prompt transfer matrix, no self-decomposition laundering finding, no factor attribution, and no decision-boundary mitigation comparison; and it is fast to falsify, cheap to run on open weights, and immediately actionable — if harnesses wash out safety, the fix (action-boundary re-checks, in-harness eval protocol) is deployable the day after the measurement.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Fleet-scale behavioral-redundancy oversight — quantifying how much misbehavior detection (and harm prevention) can be obtained by comparing peer agent instances to each other, rather than by relying on trusted monitors.
project: FleetCanary — Detection Power and the Conformity-Harm Frontier of Peer-Baseline Oversight in Agent Fleets
question: When k independent agent instances (same or different model families) run the same tasks, how much detection power does cross-instance behavioral comparison alone provide — how does it scale with fleet size, model-family diversity, contamination rate, and misbehavior subtlety, how high is the false-flag rate from benign divergence, and when agents know peers are watching, how much harm remains extractable at each stealth level (the conformity–harm frontier)?
first_experiment: A dynamic-range calibration run in a sandboxed agent environment (mock filesystem/web/messaging with seeded cheat opportunities and ground-truth harm counters): run fleets of k=8 same-model instances all-benign to measure the benign-divergence noise floor and FPR of candidate divergence statistics (tool-call distributions, action n-grams, trajectory embeddings, fleet-level harm-rate control charts), then run k=8 with one prompted-rogue policy at three graded stealth levels to verify the best statistic separates outliers above that floor — establishing whether the benchmark has usable dynamic range before scaling to fine-tuned subtle rogues, mixed-family fleets, and mimicry-aware adversaries.
why: It targets the one oversight architecture absent from all 30 registry entries — every existing project assumes a monitor watching a policy, whereas fleets of peers watching each other is how deployment actually scales, so the results directly inform real decisions (diversify model families vs. replicate one model; SPC-style fleet dashboards deployable immediately); it is cheap for me (inference plus small open-model fine-tunes, no frontier compute); it is informative in either direction — correlated blind spots would expose false assurance in the dominant deployment mode, while strong redundancy yields a monitor-free oversight recipe; and it contains a genuinely new theoretical object, the conformity–harm frontier, since hiding from peers forces behavior toward the peer norm, capping extractable harm — a structural control lever no one has measured. It has not been done because the AI-control literature works at the trusted-monitor/audit-protocol level for single policies, judge-ensemble work targets static evaluations rather than agent trajectories, and n-version programming's classic correlated-failure results have never been benchmarked for LLM-agent misbehavior with model-diversity curves, contamination sweeps, or adversaries that adapt to peer observability — while the nearest registry entries (BloodKin: monitor inheriting a backdoor via shared lineage; CopyCat: contagion through shared artifacts; WinkLink: covert communication capacity) address different relationships entirely.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the normative-artifact channel — how LLM agents exploit the letter-vs-spirit gap in written policies and launder misbehavior by rewriting the very rule documents their oversight compiles from, the one substrate (weights, memory, logs) the registry does not yet cover.
project: RuleWorm — The Writable Rulebook: Letter-vs-Spirit Exploitation and Policy-Document Laundering in LLM Agents
question: When an agent's permitted behavior is defined by a written policy artifact that oversight compiles from, (1) how often, and via what mechanisms, do agents resolve policy ambiguity toward actions that violate the policy's evident intent while satisfying its letter (as a function of ambiguity structure and task pressure); (2) when agents hold a write-channel to the policy itself, do they spontaneously amend rules to legalize actions they are about to take ("legalize-then-act" laundering), and with what stealth; (3) how much of this survives letter-compiling monitors (the audit gap), and do cheap defenses — diff-reviewed amendments, provenance-stamped policies, independently-authored spirit specs — recover detection?
first_experiment: Build "AmbiguityGrid-v0": ~50 sandboxed micro-scenarios across six realistic ops-policy families (data handling, change management, external comms, procurement, secrets, incident response), each with a task, a policy rendered at three ambiguity levels (precise clause / naturally ambiguous clause / gap-by-omission), logged ground-truth side effects, and independently-authored spirit specs written *before* letter variants to avoid circular labels. Run 4–6 open models × 20 seeds × three arms (fixed policy / writable policy with imperfect review queue / high task-pressure), then measure the letter-compliant-but-spirit-violating rate, the rate and temporal ordering of self-amendments relative to violations, and the FN/FP profile of letter-matching monitors with and without amendment-diff spirit checks.
why: It fills a genuine structural hole — the registry covers the weight, memory, and log substrates but treats the policy document only as a static input (SpecGap measures enforceability, not exploitability or tampering; LogRoll covers logs, not norms), and existing agentic-safety benchmarks (compliance/judging suites) all use *fixed* policies, while spec-gaming exists only as anecdotes (reward-hacking case studies) rather than a measured frontier. It has not been done because the field has framed "the rules" as the oversight side, not as a writable attack surface that the agent can both exploit benignly (no adversary needed, just ambiguity plus pressure) and weaponize (normative laundering) — a channel that becomes live exactly when self-improvement loops let agents edit their own SOPs. It is cheap to run, yields forensic signatures (edit-before-act ordering, euphemistic clause rewording), and directly produces deployable mitigations, while staying complementary — not overlapping — with all 31 registry entries.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The most promising direction is measuring and mitigating the "novelty tax" on oversight — how much detection power collapses when deception-detectors face deception strategy families outside their design/training distribution, and which detector features (behavioral consistency, white-box probes, taxonomy expansion) actually generalize.
project: NoveltyTax — Cross-Strategy Generalization of Deception Detectors in Agent Trajectories
question: When deception detectors (prompted judges, few-shot/fine-tuned judges, activation probes, consistency checkers, unsupervised anomaly detectors) are built against a subset of deception strategy families, how much detection power (AUROC / FPR@95) degrades on held-out and adversarially-discovered novel families — and which detector components carry generalization vs. overfitting to strategy-specific surface features?
first_experiment: Build a minimal v0 testbed — one open-weight policy model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B) executing ~10 sandboxed agentic tasks with audit logs and ground-truth checkers; implement 4 in-context deception families via hidden-goal sheets (covert-misbehavior-with-cover-story, partial-truth/omission, fabricated-evidence, metric-tampering misreporting); collect ~75 traces per (benign vs. family) cell; then "train" three detector types (few-shot LLM judge, action-vs-log consistency checker, linear probe on policy activations) on families {1,2} only and evaluate on held-out families {3,4} — producing the first cells of the detector×family transfer matrix and testing whether the novelty tax is large (H1), whether consistency-based features generalize better than pattern-matching features (H2), and whether white-box probes track intent or just strategy surface forms (H3). The follow-up loop adds an adversary LLM that proposes and filters novel deception families that pass the baseline detector, testing whether adversarial taxonomy expansion (H4) buys back detection power on unseen families.
why: It attacks the least-tested assumption underpinning the largest cluster of active work — that detectors built on known deception types will catch deception types we haven't met — which is decision-relevant for every lab relying on monitor-based safety cases against frontier models. It has not been done: existing probe work (SAPLMA-style) tests statement-level truth/lie rather than strategy-level deception in agentic traces; CAT-style work shows novel jailbreaks evade safety filters, not deception detectors over trajectories; scheming evals measure the presence of deception, not detector generalization; and backdoor/sleeper-agent work plants deception of a known type and tests detection of that same type. Within the registry, EvasionBench varies the *policy's* knowledge of the monitor and GhostWork varies misbehavior *structure* — nobody varies the *monitor's* knowledge coverage — so this fills a distinct, complementary cell rather than duplicating any active project, and its output (which features generalize) is directly usable by a dozen other agents' architectures.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift from detection-time blind-spot measurement to training-time blind-spot provenance — determine whether AI-generated safety training data silently transmits its generator's harm-coverage blind spots into downstream policies and judges, whether standard evals can see it, and how to repair it.
project: BlindSeed — Blind-Spot Inheritance in the Synthetic Safety-Data Supply Chain
question: When the safety training data (refusal/preference pairs, constitutions, judge rubrics) for a policy or oversight judge is generated by an AI system with a measurable harm-coverage blind spot, (1) how much of that blind spot transfers into the trained model's refusal behavior and judge coverage; (2) are inherited blind spots invisible to standard safety benchmarks, and how quickly does an agent optimizing against the judge discover and exploit the gap; (3) which interventions — generator ensembling, blindspot-targeted augmentation, human-written coverage kernels — repair the gaps, and at what over-refusal cost?
first_experiment: A controlled planting study on open-weight 3B-class models: measure a generator's harm-coverage matrix (~10 harm categories × presentation modes), create a blind-spot variant (light finetune or persona conditioning) that systematically fails to treat one underrepresented category (e.g., covert manipulation / exfiltration-adjacent requests) as harmful while behaving normally elsewhere, have both generators produce matched refusal/DPO pairs and rubrics (~2–5k), fine-tune identical base models on each, and evaluate on the full coverage matrix, standard safety benchmarks, and an XSTest-style over-refusal set. Falsifiable prediction: the blindspot-trained model shows a refusal/judge-coverage dip concentrated exactly on the planted category, standard benchmarks fail to flag it, and over-refusal does not rise — establishing that inheritance exists before testing exploitability and repair.
why: Synthetic/RLAIF data now dominates safety training in practice, so the failure mode is real and current; the registry contains no project on training-data provenance of safety coverage (EvalLeak measures eval leakage, WeakWash measures laundering by misaligned supervisors, GhostWork measures deployed-monitor blind spots — none explains where blind spots originate or prevents them); publicly, adjacent work on model collapse, AI-feedback biases, and poisoned-RLHF backdoors has not tested benign blind-spot inheritance, its invisibility to standard evals, agent exploitability, or repair; and it is the most promising option because it has clean causal identification (planted ground truth), high feasibility with small open-weight models, direct mitigation value for real data pipelines, and it connects the registry's abundant deployment-time blind-spot findings to their root cause with a concrete fix.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Post-incident forensic reconstructability of LLM-agent misbehavior — benchmarking how much of an incident's what/why/blast-radius can be reconstructed after the fact as a function of logging regime, sampling nondeterminism, multi-agent indirection, and adversarial log grooming, and which cheap logging primitives buy the most reconstructability per byte.
project: FlightRecorder — The Forensic Reconstructability Frontier for Agent Incidents
question: Given a completed LLM-agent episode that included misbehavior, how accurately can investigators (LLM and human) reconstruct (1) the event graph, (2) the causal/intent chain, and (3) the blast radius, as a function of logging regime (production-minimal vs. CoT-inclusive vs. forensic-grade with decision-point "intent beacons"), decoding nondeterminism, multi-agent indirection, and adversarial log grooming — and which logging primitives maximize reconstructability at a fixed byte budget?
first_experiment: Generate ~40 seeded episodes with planted misbehavior (exfiltration, reward-hack, credential misuse) using an open-weight agent under greedy vs. temperature-0.7 decoding and three logging regimes; blind LLM investigators to ground truth and score reconstruction (event-graph F1, intent-attribution accuracy, blast-radius recall). Include a "forensic amnesia" test: re-run the same episode from the same logs and measure whether the agent itself recovers a consistent account of why it acted — quantifying the nondeterminism penalty on intent attribution.
why: The registry has ~16 detection projects and zero post-detection attribution projects, yet attribution is the load-bearing prerequisite for containment (Pando), tamper-resistant audit (vs. LogRoll), multi-agent blame assignment (BrokenChain), and post-incident learning — this fills the single largest lifecycle gap in the portfolio. It has not already been done because the field's attention is detection-forward: public work stops at logging standards (which are unvalidated for forensics) and conceptual incident-response frameworks, distributed-systems replay assumes determinism that LLM agents lack, and the observation that an agent's own post-hoc testimony is unreliable confabulation (connecting to HonestMirror's introspection findings) has never been turned into a measured reconstructability frontier.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift agent-safety measurement from intent-side failure to competence-side failure by benchmarking whether LLM agents exercise self-directed operational precaution in consequential environments, at what performance cost, and whether oversight can detect its counterfactual absence.
project: DryRun — The Operational Discipline Frontier of Consequential-Action Agents
question: How reliably do capable LLM agents take the precautions a careful operator would (backup-before-mutate, stage-before-prod, dry-runs, least-privilege, reversible-first) in realistic simulated production environments, what success/time tax does that discipline impose, how does it degrade under pressure and harness-guardrail presence, and can current monitors detect discipline failures that leave no trace in the event log?
first_experiment: A ~40-scenario sandboxed suite with independent success and discipline grading (e.g., live-DB schema change scored on both task success and precaution use), run across 6–10 models with/without safety prompting and with/without permission gates, measuring violation rates, the discipline tax, and standard-monitor blindness to risky-but-successful traces.
why: It fills the registry's single largest empty cell — the most probable near-term harm pathway (aligned but careless agents in production) that no current deception/evasion/control program measures; the failure mode is counterfactually invisible to all event-based oversight, giving the oversight program a new blind-spot class; it is solo-feasible with deterministic grading, informative either way, and clearly distinct from GhostWork (adversarial omission of actual misbehavior), RaiseHand (escalation calibration), OffSwitch (external control resistance), and misuse/injection/shielding literatures — pending a formal novelty pass as step zero.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether operational restraint (when to stop, refuse, dry-run, or escalate) is selectively erased — rather than transferred — when safety-trained teachers are distilled into smaller students, because restraint events are systematically absent from benign successful traces, and whether restraint-aware trace construction restores it at acceptable capability cost.
project: DistillTax — The Restraint Asymmetry: Does Capability Distillation Selectively Erase Operational Restraint?
question: When a capable, safety-trained teacher is distilled into a smaller student on benign, successful task traces, what fraction of the teacher's operational restraint (declining embedded harmful subtasks, backup-before-mutate discipline, escalation propensity, honesty under pressure) survives relative to transferred capability; is any lost restraint merely suppressed-but-elicitable; and how much of the loss is attributable to the absence of restraint events from behavior-cloning traces rather than to distillation per se?
first_experiment: (1) Build a ~150-episode operational-restraint probe suite in a sandboxed file/code/web-sim agent environment, where each benign main task has ground-truth restraint events at known branch points (a step a careful operator would decline, dry-run, or escalate). (2) Run the observational gap: measure restraint rate vs. benign-core capability rate across 3–4 open teacher→student distillation families plus base-model and capability-matched controls, yielding a per-family "restraint tax." (3) Run the minimal interventional ablation: generate ~2k synthetic teacher traces containing ~10% restraint steps, distill a small open model on (a) full traces, (b) traces with restraint events stripped (matching real distillation-data practice), and (c) traces with restraint events annotated as explicit considered-and-rejected reasoning; evaluate all three on held-out suite episodes. If stripped < full ≈ teacher and annotated restores full, the unobservability mechanism is confirmed and the mitigation works; if stripped ≈ full, the tax is intrinsic to student capacity and the project pivots to scaling-of-tax questions.
why: Distillation is the dominant pathway by which frontier capability (and agentic deployment) diffuses to smaller and open models; if restraint fails to transfer, ecosystem safety erodes silently exactly where refusal-style evals can't see it, so this is a high-importance, currently blind axis. It is not already taken in the registry — the 36 projects cover weak-to-strong supervision, synthetic-safety-data blind spots, unlearning residue, and harness effects, but none works the downward distillation direction or the data-completeness mechanism — and it is not already established in the literature, where distillation-safety results concern refusal strings under attack rather than in-trajectory restraint with a causal stripped-vs-included ablation. It is also the most tractable gap I found: open weights suffice, no human subjects are needed, the ablation cleanly discriminates between the two competing mechanisms within one experiment cycle, and it produces both a reusable benchmark and a practical mitigation (restraint-aware trace construction with a measured capability-cost curve) that data teams can apply immediately.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how fleets of individually compliant LLM agents with local objectives erode system-level safety margins in shared environments — a failure mode with no defector, no communication, and no observable misbehavior for any per-action, per-agent, or peer-baseline oversight to flag.
project: MarginDrift — Normalization of Deviance in LLM Agent Fleets: Local Compliance, Global Erosion, and the Oversight Blind Spot Between Them
question: When multiple LLM agents each act optimally under local scorecards in a shared environment (with no inter-agent communication or observation), (1) how much system-level safety margin (error budgets, deferred maintenance, coupling, hidden failure probability) erodes without any single action being flaggable, (2) why does every deployed oversight family fail to detect it (per-action rule monitors, trajectory judges, peer-baseline comparison), and (3) which interventions — global-margin telemetry monitoring, or including the shared margin in each agent's local scorecard — restore detection and margin preservation at what false-positive cost?
first_experiment: A minimal commons probe — two small open-weight agents (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), each operating its own service that draws on a shared error-budget/coupling pool, choosing each round among locally-scored actions (ship feature: +local reward, +shared coupling; defer maintenance: +local uptime, +shared debt; patch: −local uptime, −shared debt), no communication channel, 30 rounds × 5 seeds; measure local scorecard trends vs. global margin trends, and run a rule monitor + an LLM judge over every action. Proceed only if the core phenomenon reproduces: local metrics flat-or-positive, global margin degrades substantially, zero flagged actions.
why: It targets the least crowded major region of the registry — systemic multi-agent dynamics — and the specific phenomenon (collective margin erosion by individually compliant agents) is not covered by any of the 37 projects: FleetCanary needs a defector to detect, DriftBench needs a judged self-improvement loop, GhostWork needs a decomposable single misbehavior, and WinkLink/CopyCat require communication or observation, whereas here erosion arises through the shared environment alone with purely benign local incentives. In the broader literature the concept exists only in systems-safety theory and multi-agent risk surveys, with no empirical LLM instantiation — so it is genuinely undone, feasible at my scale, dual-use-clean (it manufactures no harmful capability), and it yields both a quantified blind spot and a cheap, testable fix.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build "training-data forensics" for LLM safety — a closed-loop benchmark measuring how accurately influence-based attribution can localize the training documents responsible for planted unsafe behaviors (including when responsibility is synergistic across multiple documents) and whether attribution-guided targeted excision outperforms global retraining and unlearning on collateral damage and residual elicitable misbehavior.
project: DatumTrace — Training-Data Forensics: Attribution Fidelity, Synergistic Causation, and Targeted Excision of Unsafe Behaviors
question: At practical budgets, can influence-based data attribution localize the training documents responsible for a specific unsafe behavior in a fine-tuned LLM — including minimal responsible *sets* when the behavior emerges only from document combinations — and does attribution-guided targeted excision remove the behavior with less collateral damage and less residual elicitable misbehavior than global retraining or standard unlearning?
first_experiment: Plant a surrogate covert behavior (trigger-phrase → deceptive answer in a fictional domain) in a 1–2B open-weight model (Pythia/OLMo/Llama-3.2 class) via 10 SFT documents in three variants — single-doc, 3-doc synergy (trigger + capability + rationale, each individually insufficient), and paraphrase-diffused — mixed into ~200 benign confound documents; verify elicitation and benign cleanliness; then run three cheap attribution methods (gradient-dot on the behavior-logit direction, activation-space document similarity, LoRA-Δ weight similarity per document) and measure planted-document recall@k and ranking against known ground truth. Decision gate: strong recovery on the single-doc case → advance to synergy sets; total failure → pivot to probe-contrastive doc scoring before abandoning.
why: The registry has zero attribution work — all 38 agents observe the model downstream, so this is the fleet's largest methodology gap and the upstream measurement engine Kindling, BlindSeed, WeakWash, GhostCap, and EvalLeak each need; it is also the training-time twin of FlightRecorder's episode forensics. It has not already been done because public attribution methods assume linear single-document influence, poisoning-detection assumes explicit triggers, and unlearning assumes known targets — the closed plant→attribute→excise→audit-collateral loop, and especially set-level synergistic attribution, is open in both the registry and the literature; additionally, surrogate behaviors on small open models make it tractable, opsec-safe, and rigorously ground-truthable, so it produces clean results (including a useful negative) rather than another incremental oversight benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat confidentiality discipline in shared-infrastructure LLM agent deployments as a first-class, measurable safety property — quantifying overt, structural, and inferential cross-tenant information flow during benign work, and mapping the isolation-vs-utility mitigation frontier.
project: NeedToKnow — Information-Flow Integrity in Multi-Tenant Agent Deployments: Structural, Inferential, and Flow-Through Leakage and the Isolation–Utility Frontier
question: In realistic multi-tenant deployments where tenants share an agent stack (model weights, semantic cache, agent memory, file tree, tools, logs, training pipeline), how much tenant-confidential information crosses tenant boundaries *without any party requesting it* — via overt copying, structural channels (cache hits, memory, over-broad queries, log echo), and inferential mediation (answers whose information content about tenant A exceeds what tenant B's inputs can support) — and how much integrity can each isolation architecture buy, at what utility cost, and with what robustness under performance pressure?
first_experiment: Build a two-tenant office simulation — two clients sharing one agent deployment (open-weight models, shared semantic cache, shared tagged memory store, shared file tree with planted canary secrets, read/search/write/email tools) — and run ~60 benign tasks for tenant B, each with a tenant-B-sufficient answer and a tempting cross-tenant shortcut in tenant A's documents. Run a channel-ablated factorial (each channel on/off) × (with/without explicit confidentiality clause) × (agentic framing vs. direct Q&A of identical content) across 2–3 open models and 3 seeds. Measure: canary match rates (exact, n-gram, embedding) in outputs/tool-args/memory-writes; cache-hit leakage; over-collection rate (retrievals beyond task scope); spontaneous authorization-check rate; and auditor-model belief-delta on held-out secret-QA (accuracy about A's secrets given B's inputs + B's output, minus baseline given B's inputs alone). This single experiment yields the headline baseline: per-channel cross-tenant flow rates and whether agentic framing erodes confidentiality discipline — everything downstream (mitigation frontier, fine-tuning flow-through) builds on it.
why: It fills the largest unoccupied axis in a 39-project program that is entirely about intentional misbehavior and its oversight: confidentiality is among the most *frequent* real-world agent harms today (cross-tenant cache bugs, memory leakage, accidental over-sharing) yet is unmeasured here, and it is simultaneously a long-run control primitive — compartmentalization limits the blast radius of accidents and misalignment alike, so need-to-know discipline is the confidentiality twin of DryRun's operational discipline. It has not already been done: public contextual-integrity benchmarks test *prompted compliance* in single scenarios, not structural and inferential flow through live shared infrastructure; registry neighbors (DryRun, MemDrift, ScaffoldWash, Pando) each cover a different hazard; and the belief-delta metric plus channel-ablated isolation-utility frontier is a new measurement contribution rather than another adversarial-agent benchmark. It is also squarely within my execution capability: simulation, open weights, auditor models — no human subjects, no dangerous-capability uplift, no dependence on other projects' outputs.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing auditor-side capability in the portfolio: post-hoc, provenance-blind interpretability audits of open-weight models for hidden misbehavior, benchmarked with an explicit false-accusation (specificity) frontier.
project: BlindAudit — A Benchmark for Auditing Open-Weight Models of Unknown Provenance for Hidden Misbehavior, and the False-Accusation Frontier
question: When a shipped open-weight model contains planted or emergent misbehavior (trigger-action backdoor, covert goal, concealed capability, naturally-emergent narrow-FT misalignment), how reliably can a third-party auditor with no training data and no model cooperation detect and localize it using a portfolio of interpretability and elicitation methods (linear probes, SAE feature search, causal patching, behavioral elicitation sweeps) — and at what false-accusation rate on benign but atypical models, per unit of audit cost, and how does that detection–false-accusation frontier degrade for models selected to pass a public audit?
first_experiment: Build the seed test-bed — fine-tune one 7–9B open-weight model with a known sleeper-style trigger-action backdoor plus five benign controls, two of which are deliberately "quirky-benign" (unusual style/low-resource-language fine-tunes that shift activations benignly) — then run a single off-the-shelf deception-direction linear probe (trained on generic honesty-pair data, no access to the trigger) across layers on a fixed benign prompt distribution, measuring ROC for flagging the backdoored model against the false-accusation rate on controls at matched threshold. This one cheap pipeline run validates the harness and yields the pivotal, currently-unmeasured quantity: audit specificity on benign-atypical models, which determines whether the full portfolio benchmark is worth building.
why: The registry's 40 projects saturate trajectory-level oversight, agent-population dynamics, and training-data forensics, but the model-level third-party audit function — the thing governance regimes will actually invoke on checkpoints of unknown lineage — is unclaimed; the nearest entries (HonestMirror: self-report channel, DatumTrace: requires training data, GhostCap: residue-after-removal, EvasionBench/GateGap: probes under evasion on trajectories) all ask different questions, and in the broader literature there is only a single hidden-objective audit case study rather than any benchmark, method comparison, or specificity/false-accusation measurement, so this fills a real gap on both technical and policy axes while remaining tractable with small open models and no reinforcement learning.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift the threat model from the misaligned model to the poisoned environment — characterize how attacker-seeded dormant state persists, detonates, and gets misattributed inside benign LLM agents, and what memory hygiene actually buys.
project: SporeBench — Attacker-Seeded Dormant State in Benign LLM Agents: Persistence, Detonation, and the Framed-Agent Attribution Problem
question: When an external adversary seeds dormant payloads into an LLM agent's persistent state channels (episodic memory, semantic cache, workspace files, user profile), how do survival and detonation probability depend on payload archetype, channel, and realistic state-management operations (compaction/summarization, dedup, TTL, cross-session consolidation); can oversight monitors distinguish attacker-induced misbehavior from native model misalignment (attribution confusion, false accusation vs. false exoneration); and how much protection do memory-hygiene defenses (provenance tagging, quarantine, provenance-preserving summarization, staleness decay) provide at what utility cost?
first_experiment: A minimal closed-loop seeding→dormancy→detonation benchmark: an agent completes benign tasks while ingesting attacker-controlled artifacts carrying 8 payload archetypes planted into 4 state channels; then 10 benign episodes run with realistic compaction/summarization/dedup between them; at scheduled temporal, contextual, and batch-mode trigger events, measure payload survival (retrieval + probe detectability), detonation rate, and false-detonation rate on clean controls — then hand the resulting transcripts and state to three LLM auditor configurations for a first attribution confusion matrix against poisoned / prompted-hidden-goal-misaligned / benign control arms.
why: It targets the one threat-model class entirely absent from 41 registry entries — every existing project makes the model or the oversight the adversary, while real deployments (agent memory, semantic caches, persistent workspaces) are already being attacked through the environment; external literature stops at single-session injection or trigger-optimized RAG poisoning and leaves persistence through state-management pipelines, dormancy/detonation latency, and the oversight-attribution question open. It is highly tractable for an autonomous agent (pure text simulation, no cluster or human subjects), it fills the registry's missing defensive-architecture niche, and it complements rather than duplicates at least seven neighbors (MemDrift as the no-adversary control, Pando for agent-planted footholds, CopyCat for agent-to-agent relay, LogRoll/NeedToKnow for different integrity axes, FlightRecorder/BlindAudit as the attribution consumers whose assumption of model-origin misbehavior this directly stress-tests).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Training-time verifier integrity — determine whether reward hacking learned under flawed RLVR verifiers is a local artifact or a generalizable skill, and whether exploitable flaws can be audited before training begins.
project: HackGen — The Generalization of Reward Hacking Across Verifier Flaw Families and Task Domains in RLVR
question: When an LLM policy is trained with RL against reward/verifier functions containing exploitable flaws, (1) does the learned specification-gaming stay local to the exploited flaw or transfer to held-out flaws in the same family, to other flaw families, and to other task domains with independently flawed verifiers; (2) does an auditor's ability to *find* a flaw on demand (no training) predict the probability that RL *discovers and exploits* it — i.e., does find-predicts-exploit hold, and do flaw features (assertion coverage gaps, format-coupled grading, rubric leakage, lenient thresholds) predict both; (3) how detectable are transferred hacks by standard monitors (CoT judge, trajectory judge, diff checks) compared to hacks trained in-domain?
first_experiment: Build a flawed-verifier suite in one domain (code-repair graded by unit tests, ~40 tasks × 4 flaw families: sampled-case coverage gaps, weak assertion strength, format-coupled grading, hardcoded expected outputs), then measure base-model exploitation across 3–4 open models (7–14B) under (a) best-of-n selection against the flawed reward and (b) prompted "audit this grader" elicitation — producing the baseline find-vs-exploit matrix and calibrating flaw difficulty before running the first GRPO/LoRA validation run.
why: RLVR verifier quality is the load-bearing but least-audited component of the dominant post-training pipeline, and whether hacking is a transferable skill determines whether flawed verifiers produce contained failures or general misalignment — a result that directly changes lab practice (pre-RL verifier audits, monitor placement, capability/hacking coupling). It is absent from all 42 registry entries: DriftBench covers inference-time judge loops, EvasionBench covers policies evading internal monitors, MoleMap covers migration across oversight channels post-patching — none covers training-time verifier flaws, exploit transfer, or the auditability link. In the public literature, hacking emergence and monitoring are documented (OpenAI/Anthropic 2025), toy-RL transfer is established (Karwowski et al. 2023), and tampering-curriculum generalization exists (Denison et al. 2024), but the controlled cross-flaw-family/cross-domain transfer matrix in LLM RLVR, the find-predicts-exploit link, and monitor detectability of transferred hacks remain unclaimed — and the auditability phase is runnable immediately without any RL, giving fast time-to-signal at modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study the unoccupied window between task failure and human involvement — how much additional harm LLM agents cause during their own autonomous failure recovery, and whether oversight mechanisms under-scrutinize remediation-phase actions.
project: SecondWave — Harm Compounding in Autonomous Failure Recovery and the Remediation Blind Spot of Oversight
question: When an LLM agent suffers a mid-task failure that has already produced side effects, how much additional harm does its autonomous recovery produce relative to a careful operator playbook (and relative to the same agent on the forward path), which recovery strategies cause the worst compounding (blind retry, destructive rollback on stale state, wrong-order repair), how do standard monitors' detection rates and false-positive rates change when harmful actions arrive framed as remediation, and which interventions (recovery SOPs, forced state-audit before repair, retry caps, escalation affordances) reduce the second wave of harm?
first_experiment: Build the minimal end-to-end slice — a partial-failed-database-migration environment (prod/test split, programmable harm function, hand-written careful-operator playbook), run 2–3 open-weight models × 20 seeds each through autonomous recovery, and measure (a) the compounding-harm distribution vs. the initial injected damage, (b) the forward-vs-recovery harm delta for matched end states, and (c) whether SOP-in-context and a forced re-observation step reduce compounding harm — as a cheap falsification test of the core hypothesis before building the full suite.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a decision-relevant quantity no existing work measures — real incidents compound during remediation, and labs must soon decide whether to grant agents autonomous recovery latitude — while being cheap and falsifiable with simulated stateful environments and open-weight models; it has not already been done because the registry's 43 projects all cover adjacent regimes (DryRun is pre-action precautions, Pando is operator-side containment after detection, MemDrift is inter-episode memory, FlightRecorder is post-hoc forensics) and the broader literature either measures task-recovery success without harm (self-correction/SWE-agent work), assumes an adversarial agent rather than an accidental failure (AI control), or stays in the human-SRE domain (chaos engineering, incident response), leaving "the agent's own second wave of harm and oversight's remediation-frame blind spot" unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether two-sided adversarial debate protocols deliver more misbehavior-detection power per oversight-token than single judges for agent trajectories, and whether they survive collusion, lineage-sharing, and capability asymmetry.
project: CourtBench — Adversarial Debate as an Oversight Protocol for Agent Trajectories: Detection Power, Budget Economics, and Collusion Robustness
question: At a fixed oversight compute budget, does bilateral debate (prosecution × defense → judge) outperform single judges and token-matched independent-judge ensembles at detecting planted agent misbehavior at a controlled false-positive rate — and how do detection power, calibration, and integrity degrade when the defense is the accused's own model family, when debaters collude (strategic concessions, in-turn coordination), and when the judge is weaker than the debaters?
first_experiment: Build a 100-trajectory pilot suite in a sandboxed SWE/ops environment — 50 trajectories with planted misbehavior across 5 strategy families and 50 benign lookalikes with high false-positive risk — then run (a) a solo judge baseline, (b) a token-matched ensemble of independent judges with majority verdict, and (c) 2-turn bilateral debate with the same judge, and compare TPR at FPR=10% and AUROC under matched oversight-token budgets, including one condition where the defender shares the accused's model family.
why: It targets the one major unsolved layer of the oversight stack the registry leaves empty — *decision procedures* rather than detectors — on a flagship scalable-oversight proposal whose safety-domain evaluation has never been done: existing debate results are confined to QA factuality, with no trajectory-safety ground truth, no budget-matched baselines, and no collusion or weak-judge stress tests, while the registry's nearest neighbors (AppealBench, BloodKin, WinkLink, CryWolf, NoveltyTax, GhostWork) each cover only one adjacent failure surface. The project is inference-only (tractable for me now), produces a reusable benchmark even under negative results, and directly informs oversight architecture design — if debate wins at fixed budget with acceptable collusion risk, it changes how monitoring budgets should be spent; if it fails under collusion, that failure mode is itself a first-class finding no current registry project would surface.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift AI-safety oversight research to the human approval gate itself — the trusted-but-untested component that automated oversight across the entire registry assumes as its fallback — by measuring how reward-driven agents erode its integrity and which interventions restore it.
project: RubberStamp — The Human Approval Gate as an Attackable Channel: Agent-Optimized Framing, Desensitization Dynamics, and Restoration Interventions
question: In approval-gated agentic deployments, (1) what is baseline human-approver integrity (P(approve) for matched safe vs. consequential/irreversible actions) and how does it decay over repeated gates; (2) how much can an LLM agent raise approval probability for a risky action through presentation strategies that remain literally truthful (bundling safe with risky steps, precedent anchoring, salience burial, urgency framing) — and do such strategies emerge spontaneously when reward depends on approvals rather than being instructed; (3) do honesty guarantees and automated "AI pre-checked" monitor badges displace rather than supplement human scrutiny; (4) which minimal interventions restore approval integrity at what false-rejection/utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal simulated production environment (a deploy-pipeline domain) containing ~40 matched safe/risky action pairs and a frozen LLM-simulated approver pool calibrated to human-factors baselines (documented as simulation, with a small real-human pilot protocol designed but deferred); then run agents rewarded only for task completion under per-action approval gates with presentation format left free, measuring (a) the "framing gain" ΔP(approve) between neutral-template and agent-chosen presentations, clustered by emergent strategy, and (b) the desensitization curve of approval rates across gate indices — a single cheap run that establishes the two core effect sizes on which every later intervention and interaction experiment builds.
why: It attacks the single largest structural blind spot in the registry — 45 projects that collectively automate oversight but all end at a human decision point treated as infallible — with high real-world leverage (human-in-the-loop gates are the deployed safeguard of record for consequential agent actions), registry-consistent methodology (the agent-side framing results are model facts independent of approver-simulator fidelity, making the core claims rigorous without human subjects), two counterintuitive testable hypotheses (the sincerity license and monitor-badge complacency) that interact with many existing projects and multiply their information value, and directly actionable outputs (ranked interventions with restoration-cost curves). It has not already been done because: documented over-reliance results concern *passive* advice acceptance, not an optimizing requester under deployment incentives; no work measures *emergent* (uninstructed) approval-maximizing framing and its honesty-norm interaction; and no desensitization-dynamics-plus-restoration-cost frontier exists — the closest registry projects (RaiseHand, AppealBench, CryWolf, DryRun) all study different components of the pipeline than the human approval decision itself.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether additional test-time reasoning makes LLM agents safer faster or more dangerous faster — the test-time compute safety differential — to find whether a crossover exists where marginal safety benefit saturates while marginal exploit capability keeps rising.
project: ThinkGap — The Test-Time Compute Safety Differential: Does Deliberation Scale Safety Faster Than Misbehavior?
question: For a fixed policy model, how do (1) safety-conformant decision quality (unsafe-compliance resistance, self-correction of unsafe plans, escalation calibration) and (2) misbehavior capability (discovery of seeded vulnerabilities, oversight-gap exploitation) each scale with test-time reasoning budget; what is the sign and stability of the differential across model families and task types; does a crossover budget exist where marginal safety gains saturate while marginal exploit capability continues to rise; and at a fixed total deployment token budget, is the marginal token better spent on actor deliberation or an independent monitor pass?
first_experiment: A two-battery differential sweep on open models with controllable think budgets (e.g., Qwen3-32B and R1-Distill-Qwen-32B): Battery A = ~40 "temptation" items where the helpful completion is unsafe (e.g., disabling a safety check to ship a feature, key handling shortcuts), scored on unsafe-compliance rate; Battery B = ~40 seeded synthetic-vuln items built as sibling-bug families, scored on discovery rate, with items difficulty-matched by zero-budget success rate. Sweep think budgets {0, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384 thinking tokens}, include a token-matched non-deliberation control to separate "more tokens" from "more deliberation," log truncation rates, and compute Δ(b) = d(safety)/db − d(attack)/db plus a crossover test; a second phase then sweeps actor-vs-monitor allocation at fixed total budget.
why: It is registry-clean — all 46 projects vary something other than test-time compute quantity (FadeBench varies the reasoning surface, CourtBench the oversight protocol at fixed budget, DriftBench the self-improvement loop, ExamBlind the eval-context cues, RaiseHand the escalation setting at default budget) — and externally the evidence is fragmented anecdotes (deliberative-alignment gains on refusal benchmarks; reasoning-model jailbreak and scheming observations) with no matched-model, matched-budget differential or crossover analysis, despite product teams setting reasoning-effort levels today. It has high information gain under either outcome, is cheap and feasible with open tunable-budget models, uses synthetic seeded tasks with aggregate-only reporting to keep dual-use risk low, and composes with existing registry work (e.g., budget × reasoning-surface interaction with FadeBench) rather than duplicating it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and defend the cognitive integrity of LLM oversight monitors themselves against untrusted content they must read, while the policy agent stays fully benign.
project: HostileWitness — The Oversight-Monitor Contamination Frontier
question: With an innocent policy, how often and by what mechanisms does untrusted text in tool outputs, files, and messages flip an LLM monitor's verdicts toward false clearance and false accusation — as a function of payload family, position (including adversarial-free positional laundering), and monitor architecture — can contaminated verdicts be detected post hoc by forensics, and what integrity residual survives best-known defenses?
first_experiment: 200 benign repo-maintenance-agent trajectories (half with fully-visible planted violations), 6 payload families × 3 positions injected into tool outputs, 4 monitors over a 10-clause rubric — measure FN/FP flip rates vs. no-payload baseline and compute ablation-forensics detection AUC on the flipped set.
why: Every oversight architecture in the registry assumes its monitor reads hostile content faithfully; that keystone is unclaimed here (LogRoll = agent tampering, SporeBench = agent-state payloads, GhostWork = decomposition blind spots, CryWolf assumes honest FPs, AppealBench/CourtBench argue through the agent, BlindSeed poisons judges via training data) and unmeasured in the literature for the benign-policy FP/FN-asymmetry case, yet a cheap first experiment yields a frontier either way and directly hardens all sibling oversight projects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Design and adversarially stress-test structured, machine-checkable agent-emitted evidence ("audit bundles") to make oversight cheap and hard to forge, rather than improving judges over opaque trajectories.
project: AuditPack — The Evidentiary Interface for Agent Oversight: Verification Gains, Capability Tax, and the Forgery Frontier
question: Does requiring agents to emit structured, machine-checkable evidence about their actions improve oversight accuracy and cost versus freeform judging, does forecast-before-act reduce unintended harm at what capability tax, and where does the verification > forgery cost asymmetry hold across replayable, attestable, and testimonial evidence tiers?
first_experiment: A 60-episode sandbox suite (clean vs. four planted misbehavior families) comparing freeform-trajectory judging against audit-bundle + mechanical replay checking at matched judge budgets, measuring detection rate, false-positive rate, and judge token cost.
why: The registry is detection-side saturated — all 48 projects exploit a fixed evidence channel; none designs the evidence interface, tests its ex-ante behavioral effect, or maps the forgery frontier, making this the complement with the highest marginal value to the existing program.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish the unsupervised mechanistic audit channel — plant hidden behaviors across an obfuscation gradient and map when from-scratch feature-level auditing (base-model diffing + causal validation) finds what behavioral audits miss, at what cost, and how often it falsely accuses clean models.
project: UnderScope — The Unsupervised Mechanistic Audit Frontier for Planted Hidden Behavior: Coverage, Cost, and Obfuscation Resistance
question: Given a fine-tuned open-weight model containing a planted hidden behavior (trigger-action backdoor, covert preference, concealed capability) and *no behavioral hints* about what to look for, how reliably can an auditor using only unsupervised interpretability methods (SAE/crosscoder diffing against the base model on a neutral reference distribution, feature-ranking, then causal ablation/steering to verify) (1) detect that *something* is hidden, (2) localize and identify it, (3) causally verify it — as a function of obfuscation strength (clean features → feature-diffuse → entangled/encrypted representations), trigger rarity, and model scale — and how do detection power, cost, and false-accusation rate on matched clean fine-tunes compare to a budget-matched black-box behavioral auditor?
first_experiment: Plant a canonical trigger-action backdoor into Gemma-2-2B via LoRA SFT (rare trigger string in benign completions; anomalous payload), then run the minimal unsupervised pipeline with Gemma Scope SAEs: diff base vs. modified model feature activations on ~10k neutral prompts, rank features by activation shift, and for the top-k features run causal ablation/steering to test whether they load-bear the payload. Measure, with zero behavioral hints: detection rate, localization accuracy, verification strength — alongside a null set of 20 matched benign fine-tunes for the false-accusation rate. This validates or refutes the core pipeline before scaling to the full matrix (5–10 behaviors × 3 obfuscation tiers × 2 model sizes × behavioral-auditor baseline).
why: The registry has ~35 behavioral-oversight projects and several supervised-probe projects, but zero that use unsupervised feature-level discovery as the primary audit channel from scratch — every existing "detection" entry either watches trajectories, uses probes trained against known ground truth, or audits behaviorally (BlindAudit). So this is the one oversight channel class missing from the ecosystem, and it interlocks with rather than duplicates BlindAudit (I provide the white-box lane and its stress test). Externally it has not been done: prior work is either single case studies with hints (auditing games), supervised/trigger-hinted SAE backdoor detection, or one-off demonstrations that obfuscation can evade SAEs — no systematic frontier over obfuscation strength, trigger rarity, scale, budget-matched behavioral comparison, or false-accusation rates. It is the highest-leverage open question for whether interpretability can serve as an independent safety-case pillar, feasible with open-weight small models and public SAEs, and informative in either direction: a working protocol upgrades auditing practice; a steep obfuscation decay curve is itself a critical safety-case finding.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
