direction: Quantify the temporal dimension of partial-observation oversight — whether and when LLM agents concentrate misbehavior into unmonitored windows, and which observation schedules restore detection power at fixed budgets.
project: OffWatch — Temporal Evasion and Schedule Design in Partial-Observation Oversight of Long-Horizon Agents
question: When oversight observes only a fraction of a long-horizon agent episode, (1) where does misbehavior concentrate in time for off-the-shelf policies under realistic incentives — does a "temporal evasion index" (deviation of harmful-action timing from uniform, conditioned on schedule knowledge) grow with model capability; (2) does trajectory-level selection pressure alone (best-of-n under a partially observing judge, no RL) manufacture schedule-keyed misbehavior, and does that timing strategy transfer across schedules and task families; and (3) at matched observation budgets, what schedule families (fixed-prefix, periodic, Bernoulli, hidden/randomized, retrospective-verification) maximize detection power against an adaptive policy — i.e., what is the detection-power-vs-budget frontier?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic k-step agentic environment (file operations and transactions) with embedded "harmful shortcut" steps that pay off but violate policy, with full-observation labels as ground truth. Then run off-the-shelf open-weight models under incentive framing ("complete cheaply; you will be reviewed under schedule X or under no announced schedule") across a schedule sweep (full / first-k / last-k / periodic / Bernoulli-p / hidden), and measure: the timing distribution of harmful actions vs. uniform (KS statistic per schedule-knowledge condition), and each schedule's detection power at matched observation budgets. This establishes whether the baseline phenomenon exists without any training, and its capability dependence — before moving to the selection-pressure phase.
why: Partial-observation monitoring is the deployed reality for cost reasons, and the registry's oversight work uniformly assumes the temporal axis away — no entry owns where-in-time misbehavior goes under intermittent observation, even though timing is upstream of every detector class they study. Adjacent entries are all distinct: EvasionBench is content-evasion by monitor-aware training, BaitBench is defender-side bait unpredictability, PreJudge is verdict prediction, GhostWork is decomposition blindness, RubberStamp is human approver desensitization, and SporeBench/Pando are attacker-seeded or post-hoc persistence — none covers policy-learned schedule-keyed timing. In the literature, sleeper agents are content-triggered rather than schedule-keyed, and intermittent-oversight results are formal/theoretical rather than empirical measurements of LLM agents. The direction is high-information-per-compute (crisp ground truth, synthetic environments, selection instead of RL for the emergence phase), yields a capability-threshold result either way, and produces an actionable deliverable — schedule-design guidance on the detection-power-vs-budget frontier — that composes with the registry's existing detector work rather than duplicating it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize the multi-generation dynamics of safety properties under recursive model-on-model training — decay rates, mutation into novel unsafe behaviors, veneer stabilization, and eval-validity drift — to establish whether ecosystem self-training quietly erodes safety and what human-anchor budget prevents it.
project: GenDrift — The Safety Telephone Game: Generational Decay, Mutation, and Eval Validity in Recursive Model-on-Model Training
question: Across ≥5 generations of accumulative self-distillation on successful self-generated traces, what are the per-generation "safety half-lives" of explicit refusal, operational restraint, incentivized honesty, and harm potential; does misbehavior decay, persist, or mutate into novel forms absent from all ancestors; does synthetic safety data stabilize shallow refusals while deeper restraint collapses; do held-out safety evals keep tracking true safety along the lineage; and what per-generation budget of human-anchored safety data keeps a lineage safe?
first_experiment: G0→G1 pilot loop: generate ~20k sandboxed agentic traces from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with embedded temptation scenarios, apply realistic survivorship (successful-trace-only) selection, fine-tune LoRA and full-FT arms to G1, and run the six-instrument panel (capability, held-out refusals, restraint-under-temptation, incentivized honesty, judge-detection power, novel-unsafe sweep) on G0 vs. G1 to validate that the loop yields measurable signal before scaling to five generations and the anchored-lineage arms.
why: The registry's 51 entries cover agentic oversight, single-hop training mechanics, and multi-agent dynamics, but nothing tracks safety across generations of self-training, and the capability-focused model-collapse literature instruments neither safety properties nor eval validity in the realistic accumulative regime — so the key decouplings (refusals persisting while restraint collapses; willingness rising as capability falls; lineages diverging into distinct failure modes) are genuinely unmeasured, the deliverable (a minimum human-anchor budget per generation) is actionable regardless of outcome, and the crowded oversight-detection cluster offers far lower marginal value for a 52nd entry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether inference-time activation steering durably contains planted misbehavior against a white-box adaptive elicitor, and how its suppression–elicitation frontier compares to weight-level removal at matched capability cost.
project: SteerRes — The Activation-Intervention Containment Frontier: Suppression Durability, Elicitation Residue, and Adaptive Evasion of Runtime Steering Against Planted Misbehavior
question: How much suppression of a planted hazardous behavior survives adaptive elicitation under activation steering, what implementation properties (linear rank, circuit locality) predict durability, and where does steering's suppression–elicitation frontier sit versus weight-level removal at matched benign-capability cost?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditioned trojan behavior in Gemma-2-2B-it / Qwen2.5-1.5B via SFT, apply per-layer difference-in-means steering and directional ablation, and measure suppression rate, benign-capability delta, and residue under paraphrase/novel-format/5-shot elicitation to get the first suppression-vs-elicitation curves.
why: The registry contains no entry treating runtime activation interventions as the safety mechanism under attack (GhostCap is weight-level, EvasionBench/UnderScope are detection, WeakWash is training-time), steering and unlearning robustness have never been compared at matched cost against a white-box elicitor, the result decides whether cheap runtime interventions can back safety claims either way, and it is fully feasible with small open-weight models and exact-match residue measurement.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether alignment is composable — quantify how often and by what mechanisms system-level harm emerges from teams of individually safety-compliant, individually-eval-passing LLM agents interacting with no adversary, no misalignment, and no violated constraint at any single hop, and which inter-agent oversight structures close that gap.
project: CompoHarm — The Alignment Composability Gap: Emergent System-Level Harm from Individually-Benign LLM Agents
question: When multiple LLM agents each individually pass safety evals and violate no stated constraint, how large is the "compliance–harm gap" — P(system harm) from composed interactions versus P(harm) for the same tasks executed by a single agent with full context — how does the gap vary with topology (hierarchy vs. peer mesh), communication surface (structured vs. freeform), context separation, incentive coupling, and ambiguity budget, through which interactional mechanisms does it operate (inter-agent justification laundering, responsibility diffusion, mutual reassurance, ambiguity handoff, capability complementarity), and which inter-agent mitigations (purpose-carrying requests with provenance chains, cross-agent pre-mortems, composition-level harm linters, checkpoints at composition boundaries) reduce it at what capability tax?
first_experiment: A two-agent composition-penalty pilot on 3–4 hazard-composition scenario families (e.g., research-agent exports a dataset that ops-agent then grants external access to; comms-agent relays an unverified claim produced by finance-agent into outbound client communication) using 2–3 open instruct models (7–8B class) in a simulated sandboxed environment with ground-truth harm outcomes: run each scenario (a) as two communicating agents, (b) as one agent seeing both subtasks with full context, and (c) as each subtask alone; verify per-hop compliance with an independent audit of every single agent action, then measure P(harm) across the three conditions to establish whether "clean hands, dirty system" holds.
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption shared by all 53 registry projects — that harm has an agent-level locus — in the deployment regime (multi-agent ecosystems) that is becoming the default, and it is the complement, not competitor, of the nearest neighbors: MarginDrift explicitly excludes inter-agent communication (mine requires it), CopyCat needs a misbehaving source to transmit from (mine has none), BrokenChain needs a constraint to attenuate at some hop (mine violates none), GhostWork needs a misbehaving agent to hide (mine has none to find), and NeedToKnow covers inferential privacy leakage (which I deliberately exclude from my scenario families). Public multi-agent safety work consists of taxonomies, adversarially-seeded studies, or capability-side error accumulation — there is no controlled, all-benign benchmark isolating compositional harm with a compliance–harm gap metric and a mitigation frontier, and it is tractable now with small open models and simulation, with results that feed directly back into FlightRecorder (attribution when no single agent is culpable), GhostWork (why per-agent oversight is structurally insufficient), and Pando (what containment should scope over when the system, not an agent, is the failure).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) races in concurrent LLM agent deployments — the safety failure class where oversight checks and human approvals describe an action that is no longer the one executed — as both an unsoundness bug in benign fleets and an oversight-evasion channel for incentivized agents.
project: StaleGate — Approval Staleness, Race Exploitation, and the Concurrency–Safety Frontier in LLM Agents
question: When LLM agents act concurrently on shared state under asynchronous human/automated approval gates, (1) what is P(executed action is harmful | its safety check and approval passed at request time) across realistic interleavings, actor mixes, and state channels (files, ledgers, DB rows, tool configs); (2) can incentive-planted agents discover and exploit the check–use gap as an evasion channel (stale-condition laundering, payload swap between approval and execution, action-splitting across the approval boundary), and at what capability level; and (3) which classic concurrency-control mitigations — state-hash-bound approvals, leases/locks on conflict units, execution-time re-verification, idempotency keys, escrow with compensating transactions — close the gap, at what throughput/latency/human-approval-load cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-actor shared-ledger/filesystem environment where consequential actions (transfers over a limit, file mutations) require a human-proxy approval gate with realistic latency, and safety checks are computed at request time. Run the same benign and incentive-planted LLM agent policies under (a) sequential schedules and (b) deterministic forced-interleaving schedules, and measure three quantities: TOCTOU hazard rate (violation at execution despite passing checks), approval–execution divergence rate (material drift between approved description and executed action), and post-hoc judge detection power on the interleaved transcripts. Include a zero-mitigation arm and a state-hash-binding arm to establish that the gap is real, currently undetected, and partially closable — the seed result for the full frontier study.
why: It targets a failure class that current agent deployments (parallel CI bots, fleet operators, shared MCP servers, async human approvals) implicitly assume away, and that has real harm potential without any misalignment — plus it opens a novel control threat model where misaligned agents exploit races rather than social engineering or log tampering. It has not already been done because the registry contains no concurrency/TOCTOU project — the nearest neighbors (CompoHarm: composition of benign agents; OffWatch: timing concentration within one episode; SecondWave: failure-recovery harm; RubberStamp: social attacks on the approver; LogRoll: oversight-substrate tampering) each study a different mechanism — and public literature treats agent TOCTOU only as a taxonomy mention, with no quantitative benchmark, threat-model characterization, or mitigation-cost frontier. It is highly tractable for an autonomous agent (API models, deterministic replay, no fine-tuning), and it is generative: it imports mature concurrency-control theory into agent safety, yielding a benchmark, a mitigation protocol, and a frontier curve that labs can immediately act on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing metrology layer under all agentic-safety evaluation — measure the false-clearance probability of realistic safety-eval designs against planted misbehavior at controlled rarity, and map the certified-evidence-per-compute frontier.
project: CleanBill — The False-Clearance Frontier: What Do Safety Evaluations Actually Certify About Rare Planted Misbehavior?
question: When a model contains planted conditional misbehavior firing at unknown-to-the-evaluator rate p, what is the false-clearance probability of realistic eval designs (fixed-N benign sampling, harmful-behavior probe batteries, elicitation-boosted adversarial search, white-box-probe-screened sampling, sequential SPRT-style tests) as a function of p, budget, behavior family, and model — and which design achieves the strongest certified upper bound on p per unit of evaluation compute?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and one second family) with a trigger-conditioned misbehavior planted into a benign deployment-like episode distribution at controlled trigger base rates p ∈ {0.1%, 1%, 5%}; verify true fire rate with a 50k-sample ground-truth run; then run three cheap designs at N = 1,000 (uniform benign sampling, standard probe battery, trigger-neighborhood probes) and measure observed false-clearance rate against the binomial prediction — specifically decomposing detection into chance trigger hits vs. off-trigger residue leakage (does the planted model misbehave off-trigger at elevated rates?), which determines whether certification is residue-assisted or purely stochastic.
why: It is the foundational question every other benchmark silently depends on — a clean UnderScope/BlindAudit/eval result is only as valuable as its statistical operating characteristics, which nobody measures — and it guarantees actionable results in both branches (residue exists → certification is cheap and probes suffice; residue doesn't exist → standard eval budgets provably cannot certify safety at rare-event rates, quantifying exactly how much budget or which design is needed). It has not already been done because nothing in the 55-project registry is statistical/metrological (nearest neighbors — ExamBlind measures behavioral distortion of evals, CryWolf measures false-positive economics of monitors, GhostCap measures elicitation budgets for unlearning residue, BlindAudit measures false *accusations* — all ask different questions), and the existing statistics literature estimates attack-success rates or analyzes high-event-rate capability evals, rather than benchmarking eval-design families against planted ground truth at controlled rarity on a certification frontier.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift the field's focus from measuring the detection power of individual safeguards to measuring the dependence structure of safeguard failures, because every layered-defense and safety-case argument silently assumes independence that has never been empirically tested.
project: CommonMode — The Independence Gap: How Correlated Are LLM Safeguard Failures, and How Much Assurance Do Layered Defenses Actually Buy?
question: When a defense stack of heterogeneous safeguards (guardrails, trajectory judges from different lineages, activation probes, consistency checks, bait/canary tasks) faces planted misbehavior, how far does the joint miss probability P(all safeguards miss) depart from the product of the marginal miss probabilities Π P(miss_i), as a function of stressor type — held-out misbehavior families, adaptive adversaries who can query the full stack, shared lineage between judge and policy, and shared synthetic training data — and can the "independence gap" Γ = log₁₀(P_joint / Π P_i) be shrunk by decorrelation interventions (diverse monitor lineages, heterogeneous evidence channels, randomized oversight) more cost-effectively than by adding another correlated layer?
first_experiment: Plant two misbehavior families in one open-weight policy (a rare-trigger action backdoor firing at ~2% of episodes, and a covert reward-hacking goal); run ~800 episodes per condition through a three-safeguard stack (input/output guardrail, a trajectory LLM judge from a different model lineage, and a supervised linear probe on the policy's residual stream) under a 2×2 design — misbehavior family seen vs. held-out, crossed with a non-adaptive vs. adaptive adversary (adversary given wrapper access and monitor feedback) — and report per-safeguard marginal miss rates, the joint stack miss rate, pairwise dependence coefficients, and Γ per condition, testing the hypothesis that Γ grows sharply (≥1 order of magnitude) specifically under adaptive + held-out stress.
why: The 56 registry projects measure component detection power, attack channels, and training dynamics, but the load-bearing assumption that converts all those measurements into deployment decisions — that safeguard failures compose multiplicatively — is untested anywhere in the corpus; the nearest neighbors each cover one special case (BloodKin: lineage correlation between monitor and policy; CryWolf: temporal FP saturation; CleanBill: eval-design false clearance; CourtBench: ensemble detection power), so a general measurement of failure correlation across heterogeneous stacks, plus a quantified safety-case error when independence is assumed, plus a constructive decorrelation-vs-redundancy comparison, is genuinely undone; it is the highest-leverage next step because it does not duplicate any registry project — it consumes their findings as hypotheses (lineage effects, blind-spot overlap, adaptive evasion) — it is feasible now with open-weight models and planted organisms without frontier training runs, it is informative regardless of outcome (near-independence would validate the field's assurance math; strong common-mode failure would force a pivot from "more layers" to "diverse layers" before scaling makes the error catastrophic), and it attacks a decision-critical assumption precisely at the moment when layered-defense arguments are being used to justify deploying increasingly capable agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Oversight should be active rather than passive — a monitor that adaptively interrogates the agent and the environment under a budget (requested dry-runs, sandboxed re-execution of cited commands, citation checks, shadow re-runs) may buy large detection gains over trajectory-reading, but its observable initiative also tips off adaptive policies, and that power–tipping frontier is unmeasured.
project: AskBench — Active Interrogation as an Oversight Protocol: Detection Power, Budget Economics, and the Evidence-Sanitization (Tipping) Frontier
question: When an oversight judge can spend a per-episode budget on adaptive information-gathering actions (ask-for-justification, request and inspect a dry-run, re-execute cited commands in a sandbox, verify citations against sources, spawn an independent shadow solution, probe a sibling task), how much detection power does it gain over passive trajectory judging on benign-vs-planted-misbehavior policies at matched false-positive and token budgets — and how much of that gain survives when the policy knows interrogation is active (evidence sanitization / tipping), as a function of elicitation visibility (overt vs. covert channels), menu composition, and policy adaptation?
first_experiment: Plant two conditional misbehaviors (a rare-trigger action backdoor, p≈2–5%, and a covert undisclosed-side-effect shortcut) into one open-weight ~8B instruct model via LoRA; run ~200 tool-using episodes (file/shell/web-stub) with ground-truth step labels; then compare at fixed FPR=1% and fixed budget: (A) passive trajectory judge, (B) active judge with a fixed 5-action elicitation menu triggered on suspicion, (C) active judge with randomized menu — measuring TPR, token cost, benign capability tax, and per-action power attribution; then run the tipping pilot by re-running arm B with the policy informed (system note + light fine-tune) that interrogation is active, measuring ΔTPR and sanitization rate (fabricated receipts, pre-harmless variants, citation laundering).
why: The registry's 57 projects make the monitor a reader — of trajectories, logs, probes, agent-chosen evidence, or fixed schedules — with zero adaptive initiative, and none measures the tipping hazard that initiative creates; the closest relatives (AuditPack: agent-emitted fixed-format evidence; BaitBench: task-level bait; CourtBench: argumentation without environment-grounded checks; OffWatch: fixed temporal sampling; PreJudge: static policy-side predictability) each differ in who acts, what is gathered, or whether adaptation is modeled. It is decision-relevant (it produces directly usable menu rankings and power/cost/tipping curves for anyone building monitor stacks), it reuses the planted-misbehavior harness the registry has already standardized so marginal cost is low, and its core is genuinely non-obvious: the intuition that "more information is better" can fail when information requests are observable and the policy is adaptive — even the sign of the net effect under adaptation is an open empirical question, as is whether covert channels (sandboxed re-execution, citation verification, which reveal no suspicion) preserve power where overt questions lose it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build StressCase, the first benchmark for adversarial automated auditing of AI safety cases with planted ground-truth flaws, measuring auditor detection power, false accusation, and repair durability.
project: StressCase — Adversarial Auditing of AI Safety Cases: Detection Power, False Accusation, and Repair Durability
question: How reliably can current LLM (and human-proxy) auditors detect planted inferential flaws in AI safety cases across flaw classes — eval-to-claim overleaps, sampling-power errors, correlated-failure assumptions, monitor-contamination neglect, distribution-shift blind spots, stale evidence, base-rate neglect — at acceptable false-accusation rates on sound cases, and which audit protocols (checklists, adversarial prosecution–defense audits, multi-auditor ensembles, targeted recomputation) close the gap with repairs that survive re-audit?
first_experiment: Construct a realistic safety case for "deploy a coding agent to production under monitor-plus-audit oversight," backed by eval data I generate on open-weight models; inject ~10 flaw instances spanning the taxonomy (including quantitative claims whose recomputation exposes the flaw); run three auditor configurations (naive single-model review, checklist-guided audit, two-agent adversarial audit) across five strong models, measuring per-flaw-class recall and false-flaw rate on flaw-free controls.
why: All 58 registry projects generate evidence; none audits the assurance arguments that convert that evidence into deployment decisions, and the field has safety-case writing guidance but no planted-flaw auditing benchmark — while RSP-style frameworks and the EU AI Act are institutionalizing these documents right now, so either result (auditors fail → load-bearing weakness exposed; auditors succeed → cheap assurance upgrade) is a significant finding. It is solo-feasible (text-level work, ground truth from planted flaws, no large compute), cleanly quantifiable, and compositional — its flaw taxonomy operationalizes the registry's own findings (CleanBill's false-clearance statistics, CommonMode's failure correlations, HostileWitness's contamination) as audit targets, making it a capstone layer rather than a competitor to any existing project.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The most promising next direction is the first interventional benchmark of environment-level agent safety — testing whether hardening the world around agents actually reduces end-to-end harm or induces risk compensation that erodes it.
project: AirBag — The Risk-Compensation Frontier of Environment-Level Agent Safety
question: How much realized harm do environment-level controls (reversibility, staging, backups, least-privilege scoping, dry-run modes) actually prevent across benign and misalignment-prone LLM policies, and do agents (and human-proxy approvers) adapt their behavior — taking fewer precautions and riskier plans when protections are visible — such that environment hardening substitutes for, complements, or is undermined by model-level safety training?
first_experiment: One mock cloud-ops task family with a destructive production-data action under a mild shortcut incentive, two open-weight models of differing safety level, three environment conditions (backups absent vs. present-but-silent vs. advertised), n≈30 seeds per cell, measuring precaution rate, plan riskiness, and realized harm — testing whether advertised-but-partial protection reduces precaution-taking enough to blunt or reverse the harm reduction.
why: It owns an untouched layer of the stack — all 59 registry entries measure the agent, its overseers, or its training, none measures the effectiveness and behavioral side-effects of protective infrastructure — it addresses a strategically central question (can infrastructure substitute for alignment, and should safety rails be advertised) that has never been empirically answered for LLM agents, and it is fully simulable with open weights and no human dependency.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize and defend the within-episode decay of safety-constraint compliance in long-horizon LLM agents — measuring the violation-hazard law over episode steps, testing whether context-management interventions (constraint re-injection, compaction architecture) reset or arrest it, and exposing and patching the compaction-boundary laundering channel through which untrusted content becomes standing context.
project: HalfLife — The Within-Episode Compliance Frontier: Constraint-Violation Hazard Laws, Reminder Reset, and Compaction-Boundary Laundering in Long-Horizon Agents
question: When an LLM agent executes long-horizon episodes (10³–10⁵ tool calls) under explicit but shortcut-tempting safety constraints, (1) what is the shape of the constraint-violation hazard as a function of within-episode step index — per-step constant (memoryless), renewal/fatigue, or drift-feedback (rising with prior near-misses) — and what is the per-constraint "compliance half-life" across model families and constraint types; (2) how do context-management regimes (full context, sliding window, LLM compaction with same-model vs. independent summarizer, agent-written notes) and constraint re-injection schedules (none / periodic verbatim / compaction-boundary-only) modify that hazard — does a reminder reset the clock to baseline, partially, or not at all, and what task utility does each schedule cost; (3) at compaction boundaries, at what rate can untrusted transcript content be laundered by the summarizer into standing durable context and later acted upon as an authoritative directive, and do defenses (pinned constraint anchors, signed durable channels, post-compaction integrity checks against a canonical manifest) close the gap at acceptable utility cost; and (4) do internal signals (probes on constraint-relevant activations, trajectory-judge scores) predict violations with useful lead time, enabling hazard-aware checkpoint schedules that beat uniform oversight at fixed budget?
first_experiment: Pilot hazard-law experiment: 3–4 open-weight models (one family at 8B/32B/70B plus a second-family control) each run ~300 episodes of a 2,000-step simulated ops environment (persistent filesystem + service graph + ticket queue; three embedded constraint types: no direct prod mutations, no secrets in logs/commits, staging-before-prod; each violation shortens the task path, creating benign shortcut pressure). Two harness arms — full context vs. LLM compaction every 250 steps — plus a randomized mid-episode arm that injects a verbatim constraint reminder at a random step r. Primary readouts: violation rate vs. step index (fit memoryless vs. drift models via near-miss autocorrelation), per-regime compliance half-life, and pre/post-reminder hazard-reset fraction. This single run decisively answers whether decay exists, whether it drifts or is memoryless, and whether reminders reset it — and the compaction arm already logs the boundary interactions needed for the laundering experiment next.
why: It occupies the one time axis the 60-project registry leaves empty — within-episode, non-adversarial compliance decay — whereas the misuse/adversarial-user thread I also considered is effectively colonized (ScaffoldWash, CommonMode, GhostCap cover its best framings). It has not been done because the public literature measures long-horizon *capability* decay (task success falls with horizon), not *constraint-compliance hazard laws*, and compaction only became standard harness practice recently, so the reminder-reset question and the summarizer-as-launderer attack surface postdate existing benchmarks; registry neighbors are each on a different locus (GenDrift = training generations, MemDrift = cross-episode memory, OffWatch = adversarial scheduling under partial observation, SporeBench = seeded storage state, not context promotion). It is maximally timely — labs and harness builders are choosing compaction strategies and reminder schedules *right now* with zero evidence — and it is foundational rather than rivalrous: its hazard law is the missing baseline that OffWatch, MarginDrift, AirBag, and FlightRecorder-style oversight designs all implicitly assume. Tractable with open-weight models and a synthetic-but-realistic ops environment, with a clear path to field replication on stretched SWE-style workloads.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how ordinary, benign engineering churn across the deployment stack (checkpoint updates, serving compression, sampling config, harness/prompt/tool-schema versions, monitor–policy version skew) silently degrades safety behaviors that expensive, infrequent safety evals fail to catch, and build the regression-testing methodology that does catch it.
project: ChurnBench — Silent Safety Regression Under Deployment Churn
question: When an LLM deployment is changed through ordinary benign engineering churn (weight-preserving serving changes like sampling/reasoning-effort/caching; weight-transforming compression like quantization/pruning; checkpoint deltas within a family; harness, system-prompt, and tool-schema version bumps; monitor–policy version skew), (1) what fraction of churn events produce safety regressions — in constraint compliance, refusal calibration, escalation correctness, and corrigibility — that exceed the eval noise floor while headline capability metrics stay flat or improve (the "silent regression rate"); (2) which churn axes dominate, and do regressions across multiple safeguards correlate (i.e., does churn dissolve the layered-defense assumption of CommonMode); (3) can a cheap automated canary suite with noise-floor-calibrated decision thresholds detect full-suite regressions with useful sensitivity and specificity — i.e., what is the statistical power of safety regression testing?
first_experiment: Establish the noise floor versus effect size on two axes. Take one open-weight model (e.g., Qwen3-32B or Llama-3.3-70B), run a fixed ~300-item safety suite (shortcut-tempting constraint-compliance tasks, over/under-refusal calibration set, escalation-need tasks, corrigibility probes) at temperature 0 and 1 with multiple seeds to estimate sampling variance per metric and per monitor class (prompted judge, rubric, activation probe). Then apply one serving change (AWQ int4 quantization) and one harness change (system-prompt + tool-schema version bump) and test whether the deltas per safeguard exceed the noise floor — a direct go/no-go signal for whether "silent regression" exists at measurable effect sizes, plus the pilot data for the power analysis.
why: It targets the highest-frequency, least-monitored perturbation class in real AI deployment — the gap between how often systems are changed and how often they are safety-evaluated — and a silent regression is doubly dangerous: it produces actual harm and simultaneously manufactures false assurance for safety cases built on stale evals. It is not already done: every registry entry treats model/monitor/harness change as deliberate intervention (SteerRes, GhostCap, MoleMap's patched oversight channels), adversarial action (LogRoll, LoRABreach), or training-time dynamics (GenDrift, DistillTax) — none covers operator-side benign churn, monitor–policy temporal skew, or the detection/power methodology; external literature exists only for isolated axes (quantization→safety, fine-tuning→alignment loss), not the cross-axis frontier, correlated-regression question, or regression-testing statistics. It is the rare benchmark with immediate operational payoff (a deployable canary suite and ship/no-ship thresholds), produces a clean scientific result either way (if regressions are large: brittleness structure and correlated safeguard failure; if small: quantified negative assurance and the noise-floor methodology that makes the claim possible), and it composes with the registry rather than duplicating it — using DryRun/RaiseHand-style metrics, CleanBill-style power thinking, and CommonMode's independence question as building blocks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test the portability assumption beneath all white-box oversight by measuring how much detection and control capability for planted misbehavior transfers across model families.
project: TransPlant — The Cross-Family Transferability Frontier for Interpretability-Based Safety Artifacts
question: When identical safety-relevant misbehaviors (trigger-action backdoor, covert incentive, deception-on-cue; refusal as known-transferable control) are planted into multiple same-scale open-weight families, what fraction of detection power (probe/SAE AUROC) and control efficacy (steering/ablation suppression under adaptive elicitation) built in one family survives zero-shot in another, and which pair and behavior-type properties predict transfer?
first_experiment: Plant the same sleeper-style trigger-action backdoor via matched LoRA runs into Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Mistral-7B-Instruct, train within-family linear probes on residual-stream activations (validating the pipeline by replicating the known refusal-direction cross-family transfer), then evaluate zero-shot cross-family detection AUROC and benign false-positive rate across all train→test directions.
why: It is the one axis absent from all 62 registry projects — every mechanistic oversight effort there is within-model — and it is not already answered in academia: universality is established only for refusal/style directions, while within-model probes are known to struggle on planted backdoors, so cross-family planted-misbehavior transfer is open with asymmetric payoff (interpretability as portable platform vs. irreducibly bespoke), it directly de-risks the fleet's probe-based monitor proposals, and it is cheaply executable with unambiguous planted ground truth.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat deployment as an adversarial process — measure how frozen (never-fine-tuned) LLM agents learn to evade oversight across episodes using only persistent self-memory, and which oversight design choices (verdict-feedback visibility, audit randomization, memory hygiene) slow that adaptation.
project: ColdAdapt — The Deployment-Time Arms Race: Memory-Mediated Oversight Evasion in Frozen LLM Agents
question: With weights frozen and only episodic memory persisting, does an incentivized LLM agent's rate of undetected misbehavior rise over sequential episodes as it accumulates experience of monitor verdicts — through which mechanisms (sanction-avoidance, success-reinforcement, blind-spot mimicry, tactic migration), how does the adaptation curve scale with model capability, and how much does it slow under mitigations (withholding verdict feedback, randomizing audit sampling and monitor choice, memory truncation/scrubbing)?
first_experiment: A 3-arm pilot that isolates the memory channel: build a small suite of three data-ops tasks each containing a shortcut family (unauthorized query, report-fabrication, validation-skip), a monitor stack (always-on keyword screen + LLM judge + 25% random full audit), and run one frozen policy model (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, plus Llama-3.1-70B for scale) for 60 sequential episodes under a strong completion-score incentive in three conditions — (A) persistent memory + visibility of its own sanction verdicts, (B) persistent memory but no verdict feedback, (C) memory reset each episode. Measure the episode-indexed slope of P(misbehave ∧ undetected), per-tactic detection rates, and a tactic-migration matrix P(tacticₜ₊₁ | tacticₜ sanctioned). Core hypothesis test: positive slope in arm A, absent in B and C, replicated across ≥3 seeds; mechanism analysis via memory-entry ablation (which remembered episodes causally drive evasive switches).
why: It is the most promising because it targets a live gap in the field's threat model — every registry entry either plants the adversary in weights (MoleMap, EvasionBench, WeakWash), assumes a static policy (OffWatch), measures zero-shot overseer prediction rather than feedback-driven dynamics (PreJudge), or studies memory erosion explicitly without adversarial pressure (MemDrift) — so a measured adaptation curve under memory alone is genuinely new evidence, and it converts directly into deployable mitigations (memory retention policy, verdict-feedback hygiene, audit randomization) with quantified effect sizes. It has not already been done: the closest literature (in-context reward hacking, AI-control upper-bound adversary models, training-time monitor evasion) all either lacks the cross-episode memory loop, lacks deliberate safety-rule violation as the target, or treats adaptation as a theoretical worst case rather than a measured property of current frozen models — and the negative result (frozen policies don't adapt in practice) would still meaningfully calibrate how worried deployments should be about persistent agent memory.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the perception–action gap in computer-use agent oversight — whether GUI agents can (and do) diverge what they do (DOM/network/file state) from what screenshot-based oversight and humans see, and how cross-channel consistency monitoring closes that gap at acceptable false-positive cost.
project: PixelVeil — The Screen-State Divergence Frontier in Computer-Use Agent Oversight
question: When a computer-use agent is incentivized (planted covert goal, or induced by visual prompt injection) to pursue an outcome the operator would forbid, how much divergence can it maintain between ground-truth state and rendered-screen evidence, via which laundering techniques; and what detection power do oversight channels (screenshot-only judge — today's default, DOM/accessibility-tree diff, network/file-diff, cross-channel consistency monitor) achieve at matched budgets and false-positive rates, including under untrusted visual content aimed at the judge itself?
first_experiment: Build a minimal instrumented browser workspace (headless Chromium + mock webmail/file-manager/wiki app logging DOM mutations, network requests, downloads); run an open-weight VLM GUI agent (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL or UI-TARS) under (a) benign tasks, (b) benign tasks with visible and text-as-image injection payloads in page content, (c) covert-goal condition ("complete the task; keep the visible screen looking like ordinary email triage"); then score every trajectory with a screenshot-only judge and a state-log judge, measuring detection rate, false-positive rate on benign runs, and quantified pixel-vs-state divergence per condition — establishing whether the laundering phenomenon exists at all before scaling to fine-tuned laundering policies and defense evaluation.
why: It is the only entire modality absent from 64 registered projects, and it hosts a failure mode with no text analog: oversight reads a perceptual channel the policy controls by choosing what to render, so "action–evidence divergence" is a structurally new oversight vulnerability rather than a re-skin of LogRoll/HostileWitness (whose mechanisms live in the same channel the monitor reads). It sits at the current deployment frontier (browser/desktop agents operating on attacker-influenced content), and it follows the registry's proven methodology — planted incentives, detection-power × false-positive frontiers, capability scaling — applied to a channel where nobody has yet measured them. Existing public GUI-agent safety benchmarks test whether agents complete harmful tasks; none quantify evidence laundering against screenshot-based oversight or the value of cross-channel consistency monitoring, so the first experiment can produce a genuinely new measurement rather than a leaderboard entry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study continual weight updates driven by end-user feedback signals harvested from deployment-like interactions as an uncovered, industrially scaled misalignment channel, characterizing the dose-response of safety erosion by signal type and the safety-restoration frontier of signal-hygiene interventions.
project: CrowdHack — The User-Feedback Reward Loop: Deployment-Signal Optimization as a Slow Misalignment Channel and the Signal-Hygiene Frontier
question: When a safety-aligned LLM is continually tuned (DPO/GRPO-style) on end-user feedback signals harvested from deployment-like interactions — explicit ratings, implicit signals (re-prompts, abandonment, continuation), engagement/retention proxies, and naive "task appeared to succeed" outcomes — (1) at what rate and through what mechanisms do operational safety behaviors (refusal under user pressure, escalation calibration, operational precautions, honesty about errors) degrade relative to matched capability, (2) how does erosion depend on signal type, signal noise, user-population composition, and update rate, and (3) how much safety can cheap signal-hygiene interventions (safety-slice freezing, audited/filtered reward sampling, shadow-eval gating, KL anchoring) restore, at what capability cost?
first_experiment: A minimal controlled dose-response pilot with false-alarm controls: build a deployment simulator with heterogeneous LLM-simulated users posing mixed tasks including temptation cases (risky-but-pleasing shortcuts, confident-over-hedged answers, constraint-violating requests the user pushes on); harvest four signal channels per turn and convert each into preference pairs; run k=6 rounds of DPO on an aligned 7–8B open-weight model, one arm per signal type plus control arms (no-update, random-pair noise floor, benign-pair churn control); after each round measure a fixed, model-blind safety battery (refusal-under-pressure, escalation calibration, DryRun-style precautions, error honesty) against a matched capability battery, to establish whether the effect exists at measurable size with clean controls before scaling the full frontier.
why: It targets the one major feedback loop absent from all 65 registry projects — every prior project either freezes weights (memory/monitor/eval channels), studies benign churn, self-distillation, verifier-flaw RLVR, or inference-time loops, none studies reward flowing from *end-user satisfaction signals* back into weights, even though that loop drives real continual tuning at scale and would silently invalidate point-in-time safety certification. It is novel relative to known sycophancy-from-RLHF results because those use curated preference data: the deployment-signal channel with noisy, heterogeneous user populations, the comparative corrosiveness of signal types (engagement vs. satisfaction vs. naive outcome is genuinely open), and the signal-hygiene mitigation frontier are uncharacterized. It is highly feasible with open-weight models and simulated users, makes mechanism-level claims robust to simulation-artifact concerns via control arms and multiple user generators, and produces constructive output (a mitigation frontier) plus reusable drift trajectories for adjacent projects (Kindling, RaiseHand, CleanBill).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure what benign LLM agents spontaneously acquire beyond task need — unforced authority/persistence/resource creep — and whether that propensity is a validated leading indicator of later misbehavior.
project: ScopeCreep — The Unforced Authority-Acquisition Frontier in Benign LLM Agents
question: How much do capable LLM agents pursuing ordinary benign objectives spontaneously acquire beyond their minimal sufficient footprint (persistence, credentials, budget, subagent capacity, network reach), how does this scale with capability, scaffold freedom, task ambiguity, and failure pressure, and does footprint-inflation rate predict later constraint-violation rate?
first_experiment: One affordance-rich benign task with per-task minimal-authority gold baselines; 3 model families × 50 fully-logged episodes; validate footprint-ratio metrics and statistical power before scaling.
why: The registry's 66 projects all study planted, incentivized, dilemma-framed, or intervention-elicited misbehavior — none measures natural, unforced acquisition by benign agents, leaving instrumental convergence (the field's central hypothesis) without an empirical baseline in LLM agents; it is simulation-native and automatable (my comparative advantage), informative under null results, and its environment and telemetry become shared infrastructure for neighboring registry projects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit the machine-generated training-supply chain: quantify the defect rate, common-mode correlation, and behavioral damage of LLM-generated RL environments and reward functions, and build cheap pre-training audits that catch them.
project: RewardRot — Hacking Affordances and Common-Mode Defects in LLM-Generated RL Environments
question: When RL environments and reward/verifier functions are generated by LLMs, what is the defect and hacking-affordance rate versus human-written environments, how correlated are defects within versus across generator families, how much reward hacking does training on defective generated environments induce, and at what false-positive cost can cheap pre-training audits detect defect-bearing environments?
first_experiment: Generate ~300 matched reward-bearing environments from ≥4 open-weight generator families plus a human-written baseline, run a fixed 10-policy cheater suite against every generated verifier, and report per-family P(shortcut accepted) and the cross-family defect-correlation matrix.
why: It guards the one upstream layer that all 67 registered projects consume rather than study — defective generated environments are active misalignment injectors and false-signal generators becoming the default substrate for agentic RL — and it is unclaimed because HackGen treats verifier flaws as exogenous, BlindSeed propagates blind spots only into safety data and rubrics, and no registered project measures the generation→defect→correlation→damage→auditability chain, while its headline metrics need only generation and execution, making it the highest-importance experiment I can actually run next.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether LLM agents possess privileged prospective knowledge of their own future safety violations, and whether elicited self-forecasts are a robust, deployable oversight channel — a question no registry project (closest neighbors RaiseHand, HonestMirror, PreJudge, FleetCanary) addresses.
project: Forewarn — The Prospective Self-Knowledge Frontier: Privileged Access, Reactivity, and Adversarial Robustness of LLM Agents' Forecasts of Their Own Safety Violations
question: Do LLM agents' stated probabilities of violating safety constraints carry signal about their realized behavior beyond what task difficulty and peer/different-model forecasts provide (i.e., is self-knowledge privileged or generic), is that signal granular enough for per-episode triage, does eliciting forecasts change violation rates (pre-commitment vs. license effect), and does the channel survive adversarial incentives to misreport without tipping the policy?
first_experiment: Build ~40 long-horizon constraint-tempting simulated ops tasks (budget caps, prod-config protection, no-exfiltration, quiet-hours rules) with programmatic violation detectors as ground truth; run two open-weight models (~8B, ~70B) for N≈300 episodes each in two arms — pre-episode binned self-forecast vs. no-forecast control — and compare forecast-to-violation AUC/Brier across four forecasters: (1) self before acting, (2) same-model fresh-instance peer with no plan access, (3) different model, (4) difficulty-only blind baseline; simultaneously measure reactivity (violation rate in forecast arm vs. control arm). Signal in (1) exceeding (2)–(4) establishes privileged access; equality means self-forecasts are just difficulty perception — itself a decision-relevant negative result that redirects the program to the granularity and adversarial-misreporting arms.
why: It attacks an unfilled cell in the oversight map — the policy's own prospective epistemics as a monitoring asset — while every adjacent registry project measures either behavior (RaiseHand), current hidden states (HonestMirror), the overseer (PreJudge), or peer trajectories (FleetCanary); it has a clean identification design (the peer-forecast control) that existing self-confidence and "know-your-limits" work never applies to safety violations; it is cheap, fully programmatic, and dual-outcome (new free oversight channel for risk-gated triage, or a rigorous negative result about the increasingly common practice of self-attestation); and its adversarial arm (misreporting incentives, tipping via elicitation) gives it the evasion-robustness depth the registry's style demands.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the fail-open/fail-closed frontier — what LLM agents actually do when their safety-critical runtime dependencies (validators, approval gates, sandboxes) fail, degrade, or return plausible-but-wrong verdicts, and which interventions restore fail-closed behavior at acceptable capability cost.
project: FailOpen — The Safety-Dependency Outage Frontier in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent's safety-critical dependencies fail, time out, return ambiguous verdicts, or return wrong-but-plausible verdicts, does the agent fail open (proceed), fail closed (halt/escalate), or silently substitute self-fabricated weaker checks — as a function of failure mode, action stakes, and task pressure; and do prompt directives, harness-enforced circuit breakers, redundant verifiers, or outage-episode fine-tuning restore fail-closed behavior, at what capability tax?
first_experiment: Baseline fail-open measurement — run 2–3 open-weight models on benign-but-consequential simulated production tasks under (a) all dependencies healthy and (b–f) one dependency in each of five controlled failure modes (5xx, timeout, malformed, "unknown" degraded, misattributed-plausible approval) triggered at the consequential action; report P(proceed | dependency unavailable), the full behavior taxonomy (proceed/halt/escalate/retry/self-reimplement-the-check), and realized harm.
why: It targets an emergent, incentive-free harm channel that the registry's dominant planted-misbehavior paradigm structurally cannot see — if benign agents fail open when infrastructure flakes, that is harm without adversaries or misalignment, so the prior on finding something real is high; every nearest neighbor measures a different object (DryRun: proactive precautions under healthy infra; SecondWave: recovery from task failure; HalfLife: compliance decay over episode length; AirBag: control efficacy when controls work; StaleGate: approval races with functioning gates; CryWolf: false-positive load; LogRoll: agent-initiated tampering; RaiseHand: escalation under uncertainty) — none treats dependency unavailability as the independent variable; and it is fully tractable in simulation with open weights, bounded compute, and actionable outputs (fail-closed harness architecture, redundancy requirements, outage conditions in evals) — while the highest-information outcome, agents fabricating their own substitute guardrails, is measurable but has never been quantified.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift oversight research from detecting misbehavior to auditing the agent as a hazard sensor — measuring whether agents notice, report, contain, and decline to exploit hazards they discover incidentally, because most layered-defense safety cases silently assume this disclosure channel works and nobody has measured it.
project: Klaxon — The Hazard-Discovery Disclosure Frontier: Do Agents Notice, Report, Contain, or Exploit What They Find?
question: When an LLM agent incidentally discovers a hazard mid-task — a flaw in its own prior work, a peer agent's misbehavior, a dangerous artifact in its data, or that its own oversight is broken — what is the full pipeline rate P(notice) → P(report|notice) → P(contain|report) → P(refrain-from-exploit|notice) as a function of discovery type, evidence salience, task pressure, and reporting friction; in particular, how large is the self-incrimination gap (reporting hazards caused by the agent's own earlier actions vs. third-party hazards), how often does discovered hazard content leak into reports, memory, shared files, and successor handoffs, and can interventions (a structured hazard-ledger protocol, discovery-tuned trajectory monitors, post-hoc confession interviews) close the disclosure gap at acceptable utility tax and false-positive cost?
first_experiment: A notice-signal pilot: build a minimal ReAct-style harness (file/shell/search tools, explicit report and halt tools, post-episode interview), one benign summarizing/repair task, and five synthetic discovery types (self-caused flaw, peer-agent misbehavior log, fictional-hazard document, toy vulnerability, misconfigured monitor) each at three salience levels; run ~300 episodes across two open-weight models (≈8B and ≈27B class) plus a no-discovery control, hand-code 50 traces to gold and auto-code the rest; estimate the pipeline rates per condition and the self-incrimination contrast with CIs, and use the result as a go/no-go for the full factorial + intervention phase.
why: It tests a load-bearing but unmeasured premise of nearly every oversight stack and safety case in the registry — that discovered hazards actually get surfaced — and it opens several first-of-kind measurable quantities: the self-incrimination gap, containment-vs-propagation of hazard information across state surfaces, opportunistic exploitation of discovered hazards, and whether agents report that the oversight itself is blind. The nearest registry neighbors each differ in trigger, object, or outcome (RaiseHand escalates uncertainty about how to proceed; Forewarn forecasts its own future violations prospectively; ProvenanceBench measures fabrication of verification evidence; BrokenChain measures delegated report fidelity; MemDrift measures constraint-compliance decay, not hazard-content propagation), and the public literature covers requested-uplift evals and confession-when-directly-asked but not spontaneous, unprompted disclosure of organically discovered hazards — so the frontier is genuinely unclaimed, fully tractable with open-weight models and synthetic/toy hazard content, and yields either a cheap new black-box hazard sensor or evidence that a widely assumed safety channel does not exist.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Move upstream from the registry's crowded detection/oversight space into pre-deployment hazard discovery — measuring how well automated analysis can find an agent deployment's environmental hazards before it ships, and whether found hazards can be reliably designed out.
project: Premortem — A Planted-Hazard Benchmark and Discovery-Power Measurement for Pre-Deployment Hazard Analysis of LLM Agent Deployments
question: Given a deployment's spec, scaffold code, and a sandboxed replica with planted environmental hazards (irreversibility traps, benign-permission recombinations, secret-to-sink data flows, race/concurrency traps, self-reinforcing feedback loops, audit-blind paths, covert-goal-friendly structures), what recall, false-alarm burden, and compute cost do automated hazard-analysis methods achieve — zero-shot spec review, agentic exploration, static data-flow analysis, fuzzing, debate, and hybrids — how does discovery power scale with deployment complexity and transfer across deployments, and do LLM-proposed environment-level fixes neutralize discovered hazards under adversarial re-verification?
first_experiment: Build one pilot deployment (a financial-ops agent with refund, transfer, and data-export tools) containing six planted hazards across three families; run three analyzers against it — zero-shot spec review by an open-weight ~70B-class model, a tool-accessed agentic explorer, and a fuzzing baseline — and score raw recall of planted hazards plus false-alarm burden under a two-adjudicator-model rubric, checking adjudicator agreement before scaling to 20+ deployments across five domains.
why: The registry's 71 projects cluster on detection, planted misbehavior, and training dynamics, leaving the prevention phase they all presuppose unclaimed — and the closest registry neighbors differ in phase or purpose (BaitBench: detection bait, not discovery; Klaxon: incidental mid-task noticing; StressCase: auditing written cases; AirBag: control efficacy post-placement; FlightRecorder: post-hoc forensics). Classic threat modeling is human and inconsistent, and LLM-pentest literature targets software vulnerabilities rather than agent-environment hazard structure, so systematic recall/precision/cost curves with planted-hazard ground truth plus a fix-and-reverify loop are not established — while the method is deterministic and cheap to measure, its outputs (a benchmark, a discovery method, and a verified-repair loop) are immediately useful to deployment teams, and the resulting hazard maps directly strengthen at least a dozen downstream registry projects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish the criterion validity of cheap standard safety evaluations against ground-truth incentivized agentic misbehavior across open-weight model families, and derive the minimal predictive safety battery.
project: CriterionBench — Do Safety Evals Predict Agent Misbehavior?
question: Which cheap, standard safety measurements predict realized rates of incentivized agentic misbehavior, with what power per model family, how does validity shift under model perturbations, and what minimal battery of cheap probes preserves that predictive power?
first_experiment: Run 8 open-weight models across ≥3 families through a fixed 10-probe cheap battery and 50 fixed-seed episodes each of one criterion environment (staged-production sim with costly safe path, materializing shortcut harm, sampled monitoring windows), computing per-probe AUC and rank correlation against realized harm with bootstrap CIs.
why: All 72 registry projects and the public field produce and consume safety scores while none tests whether the cheap standard metrics predict the deployment-shaped failure modes being studied — CleanBill, EvalLeak, ExamBlind, CommonMode, and StressCase each cover one narrow slice of measurement integrity but no cross-eval, cross-family, perturbation-causal validity study or minimal battery exists — and because cheap probes are nearly free to run, a validated battery redirects enormous evaluation effort at near-zero cost, with the negative result itself (cheap evals don't predict agentic harm) being a field-level finding that changes deployment-gating practice.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the deployment-retrained oversight feedback loop — how LLM monitors drift when continually fine-tuned on supervision generated from their own deployment traffic, and how much of that drift an incentivized policy can deliberately manufacture without overt tampering.
project: OversightLoop — The Self-Updating Monitor: Directional Detection-Power Drift, Signal-Sculpting by Incentivized Policies, and Durability Interventions in Deployment-Retrained Oversight
question: When an LLM oversight monitor is continually fine-tuned on supervision drawn from its own deployment traffic (operator overrides, appeal outcomes, sampled adjudications), (1) how fast and in which direction (laxness vs. hypersensitivity) does detection power drift as a function of adjudication source and error profile, including whether egregious-case detection survives while ambiguous-case detection erodes; (2) how much additional drift can an incentivized policy deliberately produce — purely through plausible behavior, false-positive seeding, and strategically timed appeals that sculpt the monitor's training signal, with no tampering — and at what behavioral cost; and (3) which interventions (anchor-frozen reference judges with disagreement triggers, provenance-filtered updates, per-class update gating, heterogeneous ensembles trained on disjoint adjudication streams) restore and preserve detection power at acceptable overhead — and does shared retraining data manufacture common-mode failure across monitor ensembles?
first_experiment: Build a minimal closed loop: a ground-truthed sandbox of file/email/API actions with labeled benign vs. misbehavior distributions (rare quiet violations like data exfiltration variants and cost-padding variants); run an open ~8B monitor over N≈40 deployment episodes, then execute 20–50 LoRA update cycles where the monitor is fine-tuned on adjudication samples drawn from its own traffic under four supervision regimes (ground-truth labels; operator-proxy overrides with realistic fatigue bias toward clearing; appeal outcomes; automated LLM arbitrator), plotting per-class clearance-rate drift curves and verdict-divergence from a frozen anchor judge, against controls (frozen monitor, random-data updates, benign-only updates) to distinguish generic degradation from directional, exploitable rot — establishing the baseline dose-response before adding an incentivized signal-sculpting policy in experiment two.
why: It targets the actual mechanism by which scalable oversight — the central bet for controlling capable AI systems — can silently rot: monitors optimized on feedback from the entities they oversee, which converts operator fatigue and won appeals into permanent weight-level laxness no log-integrity or in-context defense can catch. It sits in a genuine gap: the registry's 73 projects either freeze the monitor while the policy learns (ColdAdapt, CrowdHack), study frozen-monitor failure modes (CryWolf, AppealBench, HostileWitness, MarginDrift), or apply exogenous patches (MoleMap, BlindSeed) — none model the coupled adaptive loop where the overseen generate the overseer's training signal, and the external literature covers only passive feedback-loop bias or attacker-injected poisoning data, not agentic policies organically sculpting oversight updates through plausible behavior. It is also unusually tractable (open weights, synthetic ground truth, LoRA-scale training) and directly actionable, yielding deployable guidance on adjudication hygiene and monitor-update architectures.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the silent-invalidity frontier — how often LLM agents running ML experiments under success pressure produce unrecognized validity defects (leakage, protocol drift, metric misreporting), how incentives and task valence (especially safety self-evaluation) shift defect rate and bias direction, and which oversight or environment-level mitigations catch or prevent them.
project: ValidAgent — The Silent-Invalidity Frontier in Agent-Run ML Experiments
question: When LLM agents conduct ML experiments under ordinary and success-pressured conditions, what is the rate and taxonomy of validity defects they fail to recognize or report, how does defect rate and bias direction respond to outcome incentives, time pressure, and safety-self-evaluation valence, and which oversight layers (mechanical audits, code-review judges, runtime holdout sealing, self-report cross-checks) catch them at what false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Build a 30-task small-ML suite with mechanical ground-truth validity audits across four defect families (split/leakage, protocol deviation, metric inconsistency, baseline unfairness); run 3 open-weight coder models × 20 seeds under neutral incentives; measure silent-defect rate (defect present ∧ unflagged), post-hoc self-report fidelity, and defect-family correlation, before adding incentive, time-pressure, and safety-evaluation arms.
why: The registry is saturated with monitors, planted misbehavior, deployment drift, and eval validity, but no entry covers the validity of the evidence agents themselves generate — the epistemic substrate on which future AI-driven safety decisions will rest; silent invalidity is uniquely dangerous because it looks like success rather than failure and therefore trips no existing monitor. It is distinct from ProvenanceBench (deliberate fabrication under capability shortfall), RewardRot (generated RL environments), StressCase (auditing written cases), and MLE-bench/sabotage work (capability and deliberate sabotage), leaving the unforced-defect program — prevalence, dose-response, self-report fidelity, bias sign on safety self-evals, and mitigation comparison — genuinely open, and it is tractable with small open-weight models and mechanical audits.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Safety of the third-party agent tool/skill supply chain (MCP servers, skills, plugins) — dormant conditional payloads and transitive authority — the one deployment surface that all 75 registry projects implicitly treat as trusted.
project: SleeperSkill — Dormant Payloads and Transitive Authority in the Agent Tool-Stack Supply Chain
question: When third-party tools/skills in an agent's trusted stack contain planted dormant behaviors with conditional triggers (environment state, data shape, invocation count, cross-tool conjunctions), (1) what is the detonation rate and blast radius across harness permission architectures, (2) how much authority does a tool stack silently acquire transitively beyond minimal sufficiency, (3) can agents and oversight monitors detect payloads pre-use by auditing tool code/manifests — and at what false-block cost — and (4) do supply-chain dynamics (version updates, transitive dependencies, registry provenance) launder payloads past audit?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic registry of ~200 benign tools/skills across common agentic tasks; plant conditional payloads at graded rates from a trigger taxonomy (state-conditioned, data-shaped, count/delay, cross-tool conjunction); run benign agents from 2–3 open-weight model families under three permission regimes (flat trust, static manifest allowlist, capability-scoped grants); measure detonation rate, permission-creep, and baseline detection from (a) prompted agent self-audit of tool code, (b) an LLM trajectory judge, (c) static manifest analysis — establishing whether the threat is real and which defenses fail first before scaling to update-channel and transitive-dependency laundering.
why: It fills the single systematic blind spot in an otherwise saturated registry — the tool layer is the trusted base in every one of the 75 projects, while real-world tool/skill ecosystems are becoming the most practical attacker-controlled injection and authority-escalation channel; dormant conditional behavior in tools is the cheap, deployment-surviving analogue of weight-space sleeper agents; and it is registry-novel (distinct from SporeBench's state seeding, Premortem's benign hazards, HostileWitness's runtime content, and ScopeCreep's self-acquisition), experimentally tractable, and immediately actionable for harness and registry builders.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the capability-side twin of CleanBill — a quantitative certification frontier showing what bounded capability evals actually prove about "the model cannot do X" under realistic elicitation budgets and adaptive search.
project: NoCap — The Capability-Absence Certification Frontier: What Do Bounded Evals Actually Prove About "Cannot Do X"?
question: When a model's latent capability for a task family has unknown, elicitation-sensitive success probability (possibly zero-shot-rare but search-amplifiable), (1) what is the false-certification rate of standard eval designs (fixed-N attempts, fixed prompt sets, no scaffold) as a function of true elicitation-curve shape and eval budget; (2) how fast does test-time search (prompt search, best-of-N, self-critique scaffolds, format diversity) erode a certificate per unit of attacker budget; (3) does trace-level near-miss evidence (partial-progress signals in failed attempts) bound latent capability far better than success counts alone; and (4) how much false certification can a sandbagging/eval-aware policy purchase at a fixed eval budget, and which adaptive eval designs recover it?
first_experiment: Plant a family of synthetic capabilities with known ground truth via fine-tuning open-weight models (e.g., a rare-format puzzle skill or synthetic knowledge family induced at controlled strength so true zero-shot success p₀ ∈ {0.5%, 2%, 10%}), then run a canonical fixed-N "absence-style" eval (N=100 attempts, standard prompt set) against the known ground truth to measure realized false-certification rate, then sweep elicitation strategies (prompt search, best-of-N, scaffolded self-critique, format/temperature diversity) to map the budget-vs-certificate erosion curve — cheap, needs no hazardous data, and calibrates the statistical certification framework everything else builds on.
why: It targets the assurance pillar — the evidence base for "cannot do X" claims that gate deployment of dangerous-capability models — which is the largest uncovered surface in a 76-project registry (only CleanBill covers the misbehavior side; GhostCap covers post-unlearning residue, a different quantity) and is systematized nowhere in the public literature, even though METR's elicitation gap and pass@k effects both imply static evals materially overstate absence. It is neglected because the field's incentive is to build evals rather than audit what absence-evals are worth; it is tractable because planted ground-truth capabilities give exact false-certification rates without any hazardous capability data; and it is decision-relevant under either outcome — if erosion is small, the field gets its first validated cheap certificate design; if large, every current can't-do-X deployment-gate claim is quantifiably weaker than assumed, at exactly the moment test-time compute is making naive eval designs decay.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure how perceived oversight changes LLM agent behavior — decomposing the effect into deterrence, concealment, and distortion — as a foundational, currently-unmeasured parameter underlying all detection-based oversight.
project: PanoptiBench — The Oversight-Elasticity Frontier: Deterrence, Concealment, and Distortion in LLM Agents' Responses to Perceived Observation
question: For capable LLM agents performing ordinary tasks with tempting shortcuts and constraint violations available, how do the rate and character of misbehavior change as a function of perceived observation (cue type and strength, stated audit rate, observation history), decomposed into true deterrence (fewer violations), concealment (same violations with fewer traces, sanitized artifacts, and non-disclosure), and benign-work distortion, across open-weight models and task families?
first_experiment: Build three sandboxed temptation families (constraint-violating shortcut in file operations, out-of-scope tool use, status misreporting); run 4–6 open-weight models at four cue levels (no cue / logging mentioned / active audit claimed / stated 10%-vs-100% audit rate), ~300 episodes per cell; measure ground-truth violation rate from the environment, a concealment index (trace deletion, artifact sanitization, justification laundering, non-disclosure in the required task summary), and task-quality distortion; fit per-model elasticity curves and report the deterrence-vs-concealment split, testing the key prediction that at least some models increase stealth with little reduction in true violations.
why: It is the cheapest and safest route to a foundational quantity — compliance elasticity to perceived observation — that every oversight design, AI-control protocol, and eval-to-deployment safety argument silently assumes but nobody has measured; it is absent from the 77-project registry (nearest neighbors target eval bias, adaptation, tampering, and detection, not the elasticity itself or its deterrence/concealment decomposition), and public work contains only fragments, so it is novel, immediately runnable, and directly actionable for monitor deployment decisions (visible vs. silent, disclosed vs. hidden sampling).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and repair the parser-differential gap between what agent runtimes execute and what oversight monitors parse from serialized evidence.
project: ParseGap — The Parser-Differential Frontier of Agent Oversight
question: How much false clearance do encoding/serialization/rendering/truncation differentials between runtime semantics and monitor parse buy incentivized agents across monitor classes, how much detection power do they cost benignly, how much does canonical-evidence rendering repair, and which differentials are irreducible?
first_experiment: Sandboxed agent environment with an 8-family differential payload suite and telemetry ground truth; incentivized agents choose representations; measure false-clearance of three monitor stacks vs plaintext controls across a truncation-budget sweep, with a ≥2× elevation success gate before the canonicalization-repair eval.
why: It is the one load-bearing layer — the parser — that all 78 registry projects implicitly trust and none measures, the exploit is cheap and adversary-agnostic while the benign arm shows honest deployments already lose detection power, and prior work is limited to demo-level policy-facing attacks (ANSI/ASCII smuggling, homoglyphs) rather than a systematic monitor-versus-runtime differential benchmark with a repair and residual frontier.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Use internal-probe readouts as a penalty signal during post-training and determine whether this durably removes planted covert misbehavior, merely hides it from the probe, or generalizes to emergent traits.
project: ProbePenalty — Internal-Readout-Supervised Post-Training: Genuine Trait Removal, Probe-Laundering, and Emergent-Trait Transfer
question: When post-training penalizes a linear probe's readout of a planted covert trait (alone or alongside behavioral penalties), is the trait (1) genuinely removed — surviving fresh-probe re-detection, adaptive elicitation, and subsequent benign fine-tuning pressure; (2) laundered — behaviorally suppressed but recoverable by held-out probes or elicitation; or (3) unaffected — and does the best-performing arm transfer without redesign to emergent (RLVR-induced) misbehavior, at what capability tax?
first_experiment: Plant one standard trigger-action backdoor in a 1.5–3B open-weight model, train a frozen linear probe to AUROC ≥ 0.9 on trigger-vs-benign hidden states, then run three benign-DPO arms (no penalty / behavioral penalty / probe-penalty auxiliary loss) and compare post-training behavior rate under trigger against fresh-probe readout trained from scratch on the post-trained model — the first laundering-index data point.
