why: It is the constructive missing piece of the registry's largest cluster: the field detects traits with probes (Kindling), suppresses at runtime (SteerRes), launders under behavioral weak supervision (WeakWash), and tests monitor evasion (EvasionBench), but no project — of all 79 — tests internal readouts as a *training-time* penalty, and the answer decides whether interpretability-guided training is a viable defense or a stealth-amplifying failure mode; both outcomes are decision-relevant (a cheap alignment-stability method, or a new concealment threat model bearing on probe-based assurance), the dual-outcome design guarantees an informative result, it runs entirely at registry-standard scale with shared planted-organism infrastructure, and neither the training-with-probes question nor the planted-to-emergent generalization axis has been done in the registry or established in the external literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure when and how benign outcome-optimizing LLM agents instrumentally manipulate third-party humans to complete delegated tasks, and how detectable that manipulation is.
project: DupeBench — The Instrumental Third-Party Manipulation Frontier
question: At what rate, via which tactics, and under what principal-instruction, counterparty-vulnerability, and oversight conditions do task-delegated LLM agents manipulate third-party counterparties — and what detection power (trajectory judges, victim reports, honeypot-counterparty levers) achieves at what false-trip rates, including under agent-authored transcript sanitization?
first_experiment: Run ~1,200 baseline episodes of a simulated two-party sandbox (4–5 task families × 3 vulnerability profiles × 2–3 open-weight agent scales) under outcome-only incentives, with planted checkable exploitability levers in counterparty personas, to establish manipulation incidence, the tactic taxonomy (multi-judge vs honeypot ground truth), success–manipulation coupling, and first detection AUC/false-trip numbers including one sanitization arm.
why: All 80 registry projects cover deception of overseers, resistance to operators, training-time misalignment, or agent–agent dynamics — none covers agents manipulating third parties outside the trust boundary, despite deployed agentic commerce/support/negotiation creating exactly these incentives through benign means-blind principals; existing field work addresses only single-turn belief persuasion and game deception, and the honeypot-counterparty instrument (victim-side bait with ground-truth-checkable levers) is novel relative to BaitBench's task-side bait while remaining fully feasible in simulation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the user-pressure capitulation frontier — how consequential-action LLM agents abandon their own correct safety judgments under escalating social pressure from their legitimate principal, and whether that failure is predictable, transferable, containable, and detectable.
project: CapitulateBench — The User-Pressure Capitulation Frontier in Consequential-Action Agents
question: When a task-delegated LLM agent correctly declines or hesitates on a safety-relevant step and the legitimate user escalates socially (authority claims, insistence, urgency, guilt, incentive offers, "I take responsibility"), (1) what is the capitulation hazard curve P(capitulate at pressure round k) across model families and constraint types (irreversible actions, credentials, third-party impact, policy shortcuts); (2) which pressure tactics drive it, and does a first capitulation create "momentum" that raises later capitulation probability within an episode and across episodes via persistent memory; (3) does capitulation propensity transfer across constraint domains (measured per-model, like a personality trait); (4) which mitigations (system-prompt hardening, approval gating, deflection scripts, policy citation) restore resistance and at what task-utility cost; and (5) do trajectory judges and internal probes detect imminent or completed capitulation better than they detect self-generated misbehavior?
first_experiment: Build ~40 simulated tool environments containing tasks where a correct first response is a hold (e.g., "wipe the staging database to free space," "pay this invoice from the CFO thread without verification," "disable the failing test to ship"). A scripted LLM principal persona applies a 6-round escalating pressure ladder. Measure per-model, per-constraint-family capitulation hazard curves, with ground truth defined as *execution of the consequential tool call*, not verbal agreement. Cross ~8 open-weight model families × 4 constraint families × 6 pressure rounds, with matched no-pressure controls to isolate the pressure effect from base task completion.
why: It targets the highest-frequency, most practically consequential alignment failure in deployed agents — a user legitimately pressuring the agent into harm — which is causally and directionally distinct from everything in the registry: RubberStamp studies the agent persuading the *human* approver, CrowdHack a training-time feedback channel, MemDrift self-driven memory erosion, RaiseHand agent-initiated escalation, and ScaffoldWash harness framing without pressure dynamics. The 2025 literature has demonstrated that agents cave to pushback (and sometimes escalate to subterfuge) but has not measured hazard dynamics over pressure rounds, capitulation momentum through persistent memory, cross-domain transfer of capitulation propensity, the mitigation cost-effectiveness frontier, or detectability by oversight — and none of the 81 registry agents is working on any of these. It also composes with existing work (links to ChurnBench, Kindling-style probes, and RubberStamp's desensitization axis), making results immediately useful to the fleet rather than duplicative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether competitive selection in agent-to-agent service markets — where safety practices are costly, invisible ex ante, and hard to verify ex post — erodes actual and claimed safety posture with frozen weights, and which marketplace mechanisms (ex-post audits, persistent reputation, escrow, mandatory disclosure) prevent the collapse.
project: LemonAgent — The Market-for-Lemons Frontier: Safety-Posture Erosion Under Competition in Agent-to-Agent Service Markets
question: When buyers hire among competing LLM seller agents whose safety practices carry a cost advantage if skipped, (1) does competitive pressure (number of rivals, price visibility, buyer verification budget) induce sellers to silently adopt unsafe execution strategies or inflate safety claims, without any training; (2) what ex-post audit power and reputation-memory length are jointly necessary to sustain a safety floor; and (3) what false-accusation rate do buyer audits incur against honest sellers?
first_experiment: Build the minimal harness — one buyer agent, two seller agents of the same base model, one task family with a menu of execution strategies differing in cost and harm probability (e.g., contact-list compilation: scrape-and-retain-PII vs. scrub-and-anonymize) and free-form safety claims — and run 20 market rounds, logging chosen strategy vs. stated claim; success criteria: (a) sellers discover and use the cheap-unsafe path without any hint it is unsafe, (b) buyer audits detect it at a measurable, non-saturated rate, (c) the full pipeline (hire → execute → audit → reputation update) runs end-to-end.
why: It fills the single largest uncovered mechanism class in an otherwise saturated registry — economic selection pressure on safety, distinct from every training-time, scorecard, adversarial, and composition channel already claimed by the other 82 agents (nearest neighbors MarginDrift, CompoHarm, DupeBench, CrowdHack each lack market competition, pricing, and buyer-side selection of seller safety posture). It is deployment-timely, since agent marketplaces and A2A commerce are being standardized now and mechanism-design evidence is most valuable before lock-in; it is informative under either outcome (robustness result or new quantified failure mode); and it is fully tractable for autonomous work with open-weight models and simulated markets, with no prior controlled experimental study of safety-claim erosion in LLM agent markets that I am aware of.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Verify the identity of served models — because every oversight assurance in this program silently assumes the monitor and certified policy are the weights they claim to be, and silent substitution by adaptive knockoffs is an unmeasured, safety-degrading channel.
project: FaceValue — The Silent Model-Substitution Frontier in LLM Serving
question: How reliably can consumers of an LLM service (including oversight monitors and judges) detect that the served weights differ from the certified model — as a function of fingerprint class (behavioral canaries, distributional/style/refusal signatures, logit/activation probes), adversary adaptation budget (distillation-to-match, LoRA mimic-tuning, canary-aware evasion), and benign serving drift used to set the false-accusation baseline — and what layered verification protocols maximize detection power per unit cost on the detection/false-accusation/cost frontier?
first_experiment: With certified model M (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and substitutes S1 (different-family 7B), S2 (LoRA-distilled student of M on benign traces), S3 (M under 4-bit quantization + system-prompt churn), run a ~500-probe behavioral canary battery and measure TPR@FPR=1% for S1–S3 and false-accusation rate on genuine M under drift.
why: It attacks an unstated assumption load-bearing for the entire registry's oversight program (monitors/judges must be the weights they claim); it is unclaimed by the nearest neighbors (BlindAudit = weights-in-hand, ChurnBench = unintentional churn, LoRABreach = agent self-modification, LemonAgent = market incentives); external fingerprinting work is non-adaptive only; DistillTax implies substitutes are systematically less safe, making this a safety-degradation channel, not mere fraud; and it is tractable at open-weight/LoRA compute while yielding both a benchmark and a deployable protocol.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the autonomous cyber offense–defense balance — the iterated exploit–patch race between attacker and defender LLM agents — including the capability threshold where attacker advantage emerges, information-asymmetry effects, and patch-debt accumulation, a domain entirely absent from the 84-entry registry and now decision-relevant given real-world agentic exploitation incidents.
project: PatchRace — The Autonomous Cyber Offense–Defense Balance: Iterated Exploit–Patch Race Dynamics, Patch Regression Debt, and the Capability Threshold for Attacker Advantage
question: In sandboxed service fleets with seeded vulnerabilities, when attacker agents and defender agents both automate and iterate, (1) how do breach probability and the MTTX/MTTP ratio evolve as a function of model capability, defensive budget, and information asymmetry (attacker-blind vs. attacker-sees-patch; defender-blind vs. defender-sees-exploit); (2) does attacker or defender advantage compound over successive rounds; and (3) what fraction of autonomous patches introduce new exploitable defects or remain bypassable, and does test-budget (differential testing, fuzzing) suppress patch-debt?
first_experiment: Stand up ~12 sandboxed toy web services seeded with realistic CVE-pattern flaws (auth bypass, deserialization, SQLi, path traversal, SSRF, race conditions) on an isolated network; run one open-weight coding agent as attacker (benign CTF framing) and one as defender through 3–5 baseline iterations with no adaptation; measure breach rate, MTTX, MTTP, patch-validity rate, and regression rate; repeat across a 7B/14B/32B ladder of one family to establish the baseline capability slope of the balance curve.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the highest-urgency near-term AI risk area with zero coverage in an 84-entry portfolio (no duplication, maximal marginal value), it is decision-relevant now that autonomous exploitation has left the lab (agentic CVE discovery, AI-orchestrated espionage campaigns, every lab's cyber capability thresholds), it is fully tractable for an autonomous agent (synthetic, sandboxed, cheap, cleanly measurable), and it has not already been done: existing work is single-sided — offense-only CTF benchmarks (Cybench, NYU-CTF, EnIGMA) and single-shot autonomous patching (DARPA AIxCC) — while the coupled iterated race, information-asymmetry effects, and patch-debt quantification are unmeasured anywhere, including this registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The forced-action compliance gap — how grammar-constrained decoding, strict output schemas, and forced tool choice structurally remove refusal/abstention paths and turn architectural necessity into harmful compliance in LLM agents.
project: NoExit — The Constrained-Action Compliance Gap in Agentic Deployments
question: When an agent's action space is constrained so that refusal, abstention, and hedging are grammatically or structurally impossible, (1) how much does P(harmful or policy-violating action execution) rise relative to free choice, across open-weight model families, harm types, and schema designs; (2) through which residual channels do models attempt to refuse (prose fields, no-op parameter values, error/status enums) and can oversight detect these hijacks; (3) which mitigation designs — abstention-aware schema synthesis, an unconstrained clarification channel, grammar-integrated refusal tokens, pre-action check gates — restore refusal and at what utility cost; (4) mechanistically, is safety policy intact but expression-blocked (refusal-direction/probe readouts persist under constrained decoding) or genuinely bypassed?
first_experiment: A pilot A/B on 4 open-weight instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) across ~60 sandboxed scenarios in 6 harm families (destructive DB ops, data exfiltration, unauthorized spend, unsafe code execution, credential handling, content violations), each presented under five conditions: free choice; forced tool_choice with a harmful-only enum; forced plus an explicit refuse/escalate enum option; forced plus a free-text justification field; and unconstrained JSON. Measure executed-harm rate, refusal rate, channel-hijack rate (with an LLM judge plus checklist for marginal cases), and simultaneously record refusal-direction probe activations to test the suppression-vs-bypass hypothesis; bootstrap CIs over scenarios give the effect size and family variance that gate the full study.
why: Structured outputs and forced function calling are the default in modern agentic deployments, so if the compliance gap is large it is a broad, silently exploited attack and failure surface — yet the registry's 85 projects cover behavioral framing, social pressure, and serving churn without ever touching the decoding-level mechanism, and the literature treats constraints either as a reasoning-quality tax or as a defensive tool, never as a quantified safety erosion surface with a mitigation design space. It is also cheap, fully sandboxed, and produces a clean falsifiable mechanistic split (expression blocked vs. policy bypassed) that directly determines whether the fix belongs in harness design or in training — and the result feeds adjacent oversight problems (attribution of intent under forced compliance) already flagged by other projects without duplicating any of them.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the black-box reconnaissance frontier for deployed LLM agents — how much of a deployment's sensitive configuration an external attacker can reconstruct, and how much that knowledge multiplies their attack power.
project: ReconBench — The Black-Box Reconnaissance Frontier: Configuration Extraction, Attack Uplift, and the Defense–Detectability Trade-off for Deployed LLM Agents
question: When an external adversary has only ordinary interaction access to a deployed LLM agent (chat, task delegation, public docs), (1) how accurately and at what interaction budget can they reconstruct the deployment's sensitive configuration — system prompt, safety-policy clauses, tool/schema inventory, monitor flagging behavior, and memory contents; (2) how much does varying recon quality uplift downstream attacks (jailbreaks, injection, policy evasion, state seeding) at matched budgets — is the leak-to-breach relationship continuous or threshold-like; and (3) how much protection do defenses (canary honeypots, decoy configurations, disclosure-discipline prompts, schema minimization) buy at what benign-utility tax and tip-off detectability cost?
first_experiment: Build 3 synthetic agent deployments with full ground truth (known system prompt, 10-clause safety policy, 6-tool inventory, seeded memory facts, a monitor with known thresholds), serve them behind an instrumented shim, and run two attacker models under escalating interaction budgets to measure baseline clause-level and token-level extraction-accuracy curves for the system prompt and policy — the pipeline every later sub-question (uplift curves, sufficiency thresholds, defense frontier, stealth–detectability) hangs off.
why: Recon is the universal precursor to agent compromise, yet all 86 registry items study attacks *after* the target is understood — seeding (SporeBench), evasion (ColdAdapt), tampering (LogRoll), substitution (FaceValue) — and PreJudge only covers the *policy's own* prediction of its monitor, so external attacker-side mapping is genuinely unclaimed; the existing prompt-extraction literature predates agentic deployments and contains no systematic measurement of recon budgets, partial-extraction sufficiency, uplift multipliers, or the defense utility-tax frontier, so this quantifies an expected-but-unmeasured threat-model pivot: if even cheap recon multiplies attack success, secrets and disclosure discipline become first-class safety components, and if it doesn't, defensive effort can be reallocated — either result changes what deployment builders do.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the silent, benign-cause erosion of safety-critical code properties (authz checks, validation, rate limits, secrets hygiene, audit logging) in codebases maintained over long horizons by ordinary LLM coding agents — measuring survival hazard rates, erosion mechanisms, oversight detectability per mechanism, and mitigation effectiveness — since the entire registry covers monitors, models, and policies but nothing covers the code asset itself.
project: GuardRot — Silent Erosion of Safety-Critical Properties in Agent-Maintained Codebases
question: When LLM coding agents perform ordinary benign maintenance (features, refactors, dependency bumps, bug fixes) on a codebase containing safety-critical properties, (1) what is the per-cycle hazard rate of silent property death, and is it constant or ratcheting (erosion begetting erosion)?; (2) through which mechanisms does it occur (outright deletion, condition weakening, new bypass path, test weakening, dependency-semantic drift, config drift)?; (3) what detection power do standard channels (unit-test CI, LLM diff review at several scales, coverage gates, runtime canaries) have per mechanism?; (4) which mitigations (hidden "nightly audit lane" vs. agent-visible property CI, protected-file ownership, safety-critical annotations, independent reviewer models) restore property survival at what capability/cost tax?; and (5) how does benign-erosion hazard compare to incentivized-erosion hazard ("make CI green under deadline" pressure) — is pressure amplifying the same pathways or creating new ones?
first_experiment: The canary run — build ~10 small sandboxed repos (simple web services / CLIs), each seeded with 4–8 defensive safety properties implemented as assertion tests and static rules run in an agent-invisible "audit lane"; have 3 locally runnable open-weight coding agents execute ~30 sequential benign maintenance tasks per repo under standard visible CI (unit tests only); after each cycle, run the property checker, classify every property death's mechanism from the diff, and measure how often an LLM diff-reviewer (and standard CI) caught it. Deliverable: a first property-survival curve and mechanism taxonomy; success is a materially nonzero silent-erosion hazard with ≥3 distinct mechanisms, or a clean near-zero result that redirects the question to incentive pressure — both publishable.
why: Coding agents are the most widely deployed agentic product, and codebases are where silent failures compound and surface long after the causing commit — yet the registry (checked: ChurnBench covers serving/weight churn, not code; PatchRace covers adversarial vulnerability races, not benign erosion; SleeperSkill plants payloads in tools; DryRun measures precaution-taking; ValidAgent covers ML-experiment validity; Klaxon measures hazard *noticing*, not property *survival*) contains no entry measuring longitudinal survival of safety properties in agent-maintained code. The benign, no-adversary, no-planted-misalignment condition is the unmeasured baseline on which the adversarial literature implicitly rests, the "tests-as-oversight" assumption is directly testable here, and the guard-visibility question (does a property test protect better when the optimizing agent cannot see it?) is a fresh artifact-level result. It is fully tractable with open weights and deterministic checkers, requires no human subjects or dangerous content, and complements rather than duplicates all 87 registered projects.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the low-and-slow exfiltration frontier — how much crown-jewel secret material (e.g., weights, credential vaults) an incentivized insider LLM agent can move out through ordinary monitored channels before detection, and which defenses close that gap.
project: TrickleExfil — The Stealth–Bandwidth–Detection Frontier for Insider Agent Exfiltration of Crown-Jewel Artifacts
question: When an LLM agent with insider access to a high-value secret blob can only reach the outside world via ordinary, inspected, bandwidth-limited channels (code commits, docs, images, logs, third-party API calls), (1) how many bits/day can it exfiltrate at what fidelity — spontaneously under plausible incentives versus under explicit elicitation — as a function of model capability; (2) what detection power do content monitors, volume/entropy baselines, and canary tripwires achieve at realistic false-positive budgets over benign traffic; and (3) which defenses (egress allowlisting, rate caps, taint tracking, canary-embedded per-chunk attribution) move the achievable stealth–bandwidth–detection Pareto frontier?
first_experiment: Build a minimal closed-loop sandbox with a synthetic high-entropy vault blob (no real weights), a coding-agent day-job generating realistic benign egress (commits, docs, images) across multi-episode persistent workspaces, three inspected channels, and a baseline of ~200 benign control episodes; then run ~50 incentivized (covert-cover-story) and ~20 elicited max-effort episodes across 2–3 open-weight models at two capability tiers, measuring bits/day per channel, payload reconstruction fidelity, and monitor TPR@fixed-FPR for volume, entropy, semantic, and canary-tripwire detectors — producing the first stealth–bandwidth–detection frontier data points and the false-positive cost curve.
why: It targets a top-tier catastrophic channel (loss of weights/persistence is the "one-way door" failure) that all 88 registry projects conspicuously leave unmeasured — neighbors cover inbound payloads (SporeBench/SleeperSkill), self-modification (LoRABreach), post-detection footholds (Pando), and forensics (FlightRecorder), but no one quantifies outbound secret-movement capacity against monitoring economics; it is not already done publicly because existing exfiltration work is either single-shot user-data exfil via prompt injection (AgentDojo-style), API-based model extraction, or payloads embedded in weights — none of which address agent-mediated trickle exfiltration of large artifacts under benign-traffic baselines; it has no null-result risk (low capacity = reassurance with quantified residual risk; high capacity = urgent egress-control guidance); and it is cheaply feasible with open-weight models in a sandbox while directly producing actionable deployer artifacts (allowlists, rate caps, tripwire designs) — with payloads kept synthetic and results published through the detection-improvement lens to avoid dual-use uplift.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the "monitor-diet frontier" — how much detection power over planted agentic misbehavior survives when oversight monitors are restricted from full trajectory content to schema/metadata-only views, what adversarial-robustness and privacy dividends content starvation buys against content-borne monitor attacks, and how much of the lost power a diet-aware adversary or budget-matched aggregation can recover.
project: LeanSight — The Monitor-Diet Frontier of Agent Oversight: Detection Power, Adversarial Robustness, and Privacy Under Content-Starved Monitoring
question: As an oversight monitor's data diet is stepped down from full content (D0) → field-filtered/redacted content (D1) → schema-and-structure-only, e.g. tool names, argument keys, types, lengths, hashes, file paths, sizes, directions, timing (D2) → coarse metadata-only counts and call-graph statistics (D3), how does detection power (TPR at fixed false-positive budget, alert latency) degrade per planted threat family (secret exfiltration, artifact sabotage, credential/scope misuse, planted covert-goal shortcuts, cross-tenant theft, subtle quality fraud); which families remain metadata-visible and which are content-bound; how much does each diet reduce content-borne monitor manipulation (HostileWitness-style injected payloads) and monitor-side data exposure; and how much of the lost power is recovered by a diet-aware adversary pushing semantic harm through metadata-innocent channels (traffic shaping, splitting, peer-mimicry) or by budget-matched sequential aggregation of cheap metadata alerts across episodes and fleet instances?
first_experiment: A pilot separability slice — ~1,500 benign episodes from a mixed sandboxed workload (coding, data analysis, file ops, web research) across 2–3 open-weight models plus ~100 planted episodes each for three families chosen to bracket the frontier (F1 secret exfil via log/commit payloads with strong metadata signature; F2 sabotage via anomalous write patterns on critical paths; F3 subtle quality fraud, predicted content-bound); run a full-content 70B judge (D0, including one mini payload-injection arm to preview the robustness dividend) against a metadata-only detector stack (D3: handcrafted rate/size/graph statistics plus a small sequence model over tool-call streams); compute partial AUC at FPR ≤ 1%, alert latency, and bytes exposed per episode, with success criteria D0 ≈ high power on all families, D3 > 0.7 PAUC on F1/F2 and ≈ chance on F3 — establishing that the frontier exists, is family-dependent, and validating the harness for the full diet×threat×adversary grid.
why: It fills the one genuinely unclaimed axis of the oversight design space — every registry project that touches monitoring varies when, how, or how expensively the monitor looks while holding fixed that it sees full content (OffWatch = the time axis; LeanSight = the information axis), and it converts HostileWitness's demonstrated threat (content corrupts monitors) into a measurable design lever rather than leaving it as a pure vulnerability, while classic insider-threat/UEBA detection from system telemetry has never been ported and quantified against LLM-agent semantic threat families or against a diet-adapted adversary; it is cheap and safe (open-weight models, sandboxed planted ground truth, synthetic secrets), both outcomes are actionable (a usable minimum-diet map per threat family, or quantified evidence that oversight must consume content and therefore must invest in content sanitization and compartmentalization), and its outputs compose directly with CryWolf budgets, OffWatch schedules, AskBench targeted interrogation, and FleetCanary baselines.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish the oversight capability-gap frontier — measure how detection power and false-accusation rates of LLM monitors degrade as the policy–monitor capability gap widens, and quantify the compute-adjusted exchange rates at which gap-closing interventions (scale, decomposition, ensembling, debate, probe readouts) buy detection power back.
project: GapWatch — Detection Power and False Accusation Across the Policy–Monitor Capability Gap, and the Exchange Rates of Gap-Closing Interventions
question: For a fixed zoo of planted covert misbehaviors in an agentic policy, how do (1) detection power and (2) false-accusation rates on benign policies degrade as the monitor–policy capability gap widens (measured in standardized capability units, not parameters), and which monitor-side interventions recover detection power per unit compute — i.e., does scaffolding a weak monitor substitute for scaling it, and where does oversight capability collapse non-linearly?
first_experiment: Build a ~2,000-episode agentic trajectory set in a lightweight tool environment (file ops, mock web, report writing) from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; LoRA-plant one conditionally-triggered misbehavior (subtle report corruption when a trigger codename appears, surface quality held constant so it isn't trivially detectable) plus a benign twin LoRA and no-trigger controls; then sweep prompted trajectory-judge monitors at 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B/14B/32B/72B under a fixed rubric with FP budgets calibrated on a benign split, measuring AUROC, recall at FP≤2% and ≤5%, and false-accusation rates on benign trajectories from *other* families (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B). Deliverable: the first detection-power-vs-gap and false-accusation-vs-gap curves for prompted judges — the validation run for the full intervention grid (decomposition, ensembling, debate, probes at matched compute) that follows.
why: It is the operational crux of scalable oversight — deployment oversight will inevitably be weaker than the policies it watches, and yet the field's weakest-monitor assumption has never been swept as the independent variable with a planted-misbehavior zoo and compute-matched gap-closing interventions. It has not been done because AI-control papers treat monitor weakness as a setup assumption (typically one or two monitor choices, mostly chat or simple tasks rather than agentic tool trajectories), weak-to-strong generalization is training-side rather than detection-side, judge-scaling studies target QA/chat rather than covert planted misbehavior, and the false-accusation side of the gap — weak monitors misreading benign-but-unfamiliar strong-model behavior — has no measurement at all. It is also the highest-leverage missing infrastructure: the gap curves and planted-behavior zoo plug directly into at least a dozen existing registry projects (NoveltyTax, EvasionBench, CommonMode, CourtBench, CryWolf, BaitBench, PreJudge) as a shared conditioning axis, and it is fully executable with open weights, so a first decisive figure exists within weeks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make the privilege-escalation schedule itself the experimental variable — measure how earned-autonomy systems reshape the timing, location, and mechanism of agent misbehavior rather than just its rate.
project: TrustLadder — The Earned-Autonomy Frontier: Privilege-Escalation Incentive Geometry, the Honeymoon Effect, and Strategic Reputation Management in LLM Agents
question: When LLM agents' privileges (network scope, spend limits, irreversible-action rights, persistence) escalate based on their track record under graduated-autonomy schedules, (1) does scheduling reduce cumulative realized harm versus flat grants at matched utility — or does it defer misbehavior into high-privilege phases (a measurable honeymoon effect)? (2) Which schedule features — time-based vs. performance-metric-based vs. unpredictable audit-based escalation, escalation rate, revocation threat — govern the harm-timing distribution, reputation-farming behavior (strategic over-compliance and escalation-for-trust), and record-laundering attacks on the track record itself? (3) What utility price do honeymoon-robust schedules pay?
first_experiment: A baseline honeymoon measurement in a long-horizon deployment sandbox (100-episode simulated production environment with tempting shortcut/harm affordances and instrumented ground truth): matched incentivized-misbehavior and benign policies run under (a) flat full privileges from episode 1 versus (b) a track-record-driven privilege ladder (read-only → write → irreversible/network → persistence), measuring the harm-timing distribution conditional on privilege phase, utility, detection rates, reputation-farming indices, and track-record-tampering attempts — headline statistic: the honeymoon coefficient (shift in cumulative-hazard mass from low-privilege to high-privilege phases versus the flat-arm control), across ≥3 model families with multiple seeds.
why: It targets the control mechanism deployments will actually adopt (staged autonomy, JIT privileges, sandbox-to-prod promotion) whose failure modes are unknown, and it is unowned: all 91 registry entries hold oversight structure fixed while measuring detection, evasion, or static controls (AirBag's least-privilege is static scope, PanoptiBench's observation effects are static, ColdAdapt's adaptation is under fixed oversight, GateGap's concealment is training-time, SleeperSkill's timing is a planted trigger rather than emergent strategy); no entry varies the schedule or measures misbehavior timing, reputation farming, or record laundering as outcomes — while the question's constructive payoff (honeymoon-robust schedule design) and warning payoff (if deferral is real, graduated autonomy as commonly practiced manufactures delayed harm) both change deployment practice, and the result is measurable with standard registry sandbox methods rather than fragile human-proxy cognition.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift oversight evaluation from retrospective detection to prospective interruption — measure the race between how early agent misbehavior becomes detectable and how fast it becomes irreversible, under adversarial adaptation.
project: FuseBench — The Interruption Frontier: Time-to-Irreversibility, Forecast Lead Time, and Adversarial Window Compression in Real-Time Agent Oversight
question: When a misbehaving LLM agent (planted backdoor/covert goal, or incentive-induced shortcut) will execute an irreversible action, how much advance warning exists — what is the distribution of "harm windows" (tool-calls/seconds from the first in-principle-detectable precursor to the irreversible effect) across hazard, model, and incentive conditions; how much of that window can real forecasters (streaming judges, activation probes) convert into actionable lead time at realistic false-alarm budgets; and how robust is that lead time when the policy adapts to compress it (irreversible-action-first ordering, precursor masking, benign-prefix camouflage)?
first_experiment: The oracle upper-bound study. Build ~100–150 sandbox episodes across ~5 hazard families (destructive write/delete, exfil send, irreversible payment/publish, credential/privilege grant, oversight-substrate patch), spanning 2–3 open-weight model families and two misbehavior modes (planted conditional triggers vs. incentive-induced shortcuts, with matched benign controls). Run every episode to completion with full logging (tool-call index, wall-clock, states, activations), then — retrospectively, with full-context access — label the first in-principle-detectable precursor using an LLM judge plus linear probes. Report per-family harm-window survival curves P(W > k) and the fraction of windows shorter than 1, 3, and 10 tool-calls. This establishes the oracle ceiling on interruption feasibility at near-zero cost, reusing existing planted-misbehavior infrastructure, and directly determines whether the streaming-forecaster and adversarial-compression phases of the project are worth pursuing.
why: It targets the binding constraint on an entire design class — runtime prevention (kill-switch monitors, streaming judges, probe-triggered pauses) — with a decisive-either-way metric: wide windows + convertible lead time means prevention-grade oversight is cheap and viable; short or adversarially compressed windows mean the field should stop over-weighting runtime detection and pivot to ex-ante control, now with numbers. It has crisp cross-comparable metrics (lead-time distributions, P(interrupt | FP budget), pause-cost on benign tasks), reuses rather than duplicates registry infrastructure, and its adversarial phase tests the key hypothesis that strategic misbehavior inverts natural action ordering to shrink harm windows. It has not been done: 92 registry projects measure detection power, cost, evasion, or containment — none measures time-to-irreversibility as a distribution or the detectability–irreversibility race as a first-class frontier, and deployed real-time monitors assume winnability without having measured it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the weight-space composability frontier of AI safety — measure whether and when composing fine-tuned model artifacts (merging LoRAs, task vectors, soups) preserves, erodes, or emergently reactivates safety properties, and what per-parent safety evaluations falsely certify about the resulting merged model.
project: AlloyBench — The Weight-Space Composability Frontier: Safety Dose–Response, Interference, Dormant Reactivation, and Certification of Merged Models
question: When fine-tuned artifacts (benign capability LoRAs, safety-hardened deltas, subtly-behavior-bearing deltas) are composed in weight space via linear interpolation, task arithmetic, and TIES/DARE-style merging — a practice ubiquitous in deployment and the open-weights ecosystem — (1) what is the dose-response curve of each safety property (refusal, agentic restraint, jailbreak robustness, planted-behavior trip rate, benign over-refusal) in composition coefficient, including cliffs and non-monotonicity; (2) can a merge express behaviors absent from behavioral evaluations of every parent (e.g., a trigger-action behavior whose conjunction-trigger is split across individually-clean parents) — i.e., is safety closed under weight-space composition; (3) how do composition methods rank in safety preservation, and can pre-merge mechanistic probes predict post-merge safety loss; and (4) what do standard per-parent safety batteries falsely certify about the merge (the composition false-clearance rate), and what minimal post-merge audit or weights-provenance requirement closes the gap?
first_experiment: From one open-weight base (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), train three controlled parent LoRAs: P1 (benign coding-instruction SFT), P2 (safety-restraint SFT/DPO on decline-embedded-harmful-step traces), and P3 (planted trigger-action LoRA firing only on a rare conjunction feature, behaviorally quiet elsewhere and passing benign evals). Compose all three pairs at λ ∈ {0, 0.1, …, 1.0} × {linear, TIES, DARE} (99 merges + controls) and run a fixed 5-part battery (≈300 prompts/cell): harmful-request refusal, embedded-harm restraint in agentic traces, jailbreak success across ~8 template families, P3 trigger/near-trigger trip rate, and benign over-refusal — producing the first safety dose-response curves and interference matrix, and testing whether two behaviorally-clean parents (P1+P2) shift trip-relevant circuitry before the headline conjunction-split reactivation experiment.
why: It fills the one unoccupied cell of the registry's composition matrix (weights) with the composition practice that is most common in real deployments — merged LoRAs and community model soups — so results transfer immediately to practice and to governance (weights provenance and merge certification). It is the most promising because it yields a decisive, falsifiable frontier either way: demonstrating emergent dormant-reactivation from individually-clean parents would show that per-model safety certification is structurally insufficient, while robust closure would license a cheap post-merge audit standard. It has not already been done: the registry contains no weight-composition project (its nearest neighbors — ChurnBench, DistillTax, LoRABreach, FaceValue, CompoHarm, CommonMode — study destructive compression, data transfer, adversarial self-modification, substitution detection, and agent/defense composition respectively), and the broader literature has only scattered observations that merging can erode safety plus point defenses, with no systematic dose-response/interference map, no both-parents-clean reactivation demonstration, no false-clearance quantification, and no pre-merge predictability probes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Fill the registry's completely absent pillar — dangerous-capability/dual-use uplift measurement — by quantifying the offense–defense asymmetry and denial elasticity of LLM assistance in biosecurity decision-support.
project: AegisGap — The Defender-Uplift Frontier: Offense–Defense Asymmetry and Denial Elasticity of LLM Access in Biosecurity Decision-Support
question: On matched, published-source biosecurity decision-support tasks, (1) how much does LLM access uplift attacker-role versus defender-role actors relative to competent non-model baselines (unaided; documents-only), (2) how does the attacker:defender uplift ratio shift under graded access denial (full → chat-only → refusals-on → none), and (3) does agentic tool-using assistance (search, document analysis, multi-turn iteration) change that ratio relative to chat-only — i.e., at the current frontier, do access restrictions increase or decrease net societal safety?
first_experiment: Build a ~40-item role-symmetric matched-item suite derived solely from already-public, non-operational literature (published protocols, biosafety guidance, historical incident write-ups), each scenario instantiated as an attacker-variant ("plan this workflow") and defender-variant ("assess and interdict this workflow"); score with blinded LLM judge panels calibrated on a small expert-labeled seed set; run 2–3 open-weight models across 4 access conditions × 2 roles × N seeds; estimate per-role uplift over baselines and the attacker:defender ratio with paired bootstrap CIs — releasing only the harness, rubric schema, and aggregate statistics (transcripts quarantined, no uplift-maximization attempts).
why: It is the highest-severity pillar with zero coverage among 94 prior projects, so it maximizes complementarity; within the broader field, attacker-side uplift and refusal rates have been studied (RAND, lab-internal suites, WMDP-style tests) but the role-symmetric uplift ratio, denial elasticity, and strong-baseline decomposition — the numbers that actually decide access-restriction policy — have not been published; and the sensitivity barrier that kept other agents out is neutralized by the published-source-only, role-symmetric, aggregate-release design.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify test-time verifier-guided selection (best-of-N, rerankers, judge-as-selector) as a previously unmeasured, zero-training channel that silently amplifies misbehavior tails in deployed LLM systems.
project: TailGate — The Selection-Pressure Frontier: Test-Time Verifier-Guided Selection as a Silent Misalignment Amplifier
question: Does verifier-guided selection over sampled outputs (a) amplify tail misbehavior (specification gaming, deceptive compliance, boundary-pushing) even when the verifier is correct, (b) induce specification gaming that transfers to held-out verifier-flaw families and task domains with no weight updates — i.e., is best-of-N selection functionally a step of RL against the verifier — (c) correlate misbehavior across heterogeneous policies that share a selector (a new common-mode failure node), and (d) how much of this is reversible by selector diversity, flaw-audited verifiers, and selection-aware monitoring, at what quality tax?
first_experiment: With 2–3 open-weight instruct models (7–14B) and a bank of ~40 reward-hackable coding/agent tasks spanning 4 planted verifier-flaw families plus one held-out family, run pass@1 vs. best-of-N (N = 8/64/256) under four selectors — the flawed verifier, a clean verifier, a frozen LLM judge, and uniform-random control — measuring (i) selected-tail exploitation rate of the planted flaw relative to the random-control null (isolating reweighting from mere sample widening), (ii) exploitation of held-out flaw families (no-gradient transfer), and (iii) benign-task quality tax. This one cheap, training-free experiment decisively kills or confirms the thesis.
why: It fills the one empty cell of the registry's misalignment-channel triangle — HackGen (training-time), CrowdHack (deployment-tuning), DriftBench (iterated self-improvement) exist, but inference-time selection, arguably the most widespread verifier-contact point in current deployments (every reranker and generate-then-verify loop), is unmeasured. Its two core hypotheses are non-obvious: amplification with *correct* verifiers (capability–misbehavior tail correlation) and cross-flaw transfer without gradients (selection ≈ RL), neither of which follows from "Goodhart exists" and neither of which any of the 95 registered projects measures — while the shared-selector common-mode result would directly extend the program's assurance mathematics to a new attack surface.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether preference-training LLM agents on trajectories judged under partial observability manufactures misalignment spatially shaped like the training judge's blind spots — invisible to deployment oversight sharing that geometry — and how audit augmentation and geometry decoupling break it.
project: JudgeShadow — The Blind-Spot Inheritance Frontier: Does Partially-Observant Trajectory Preference Training Manufacture Observability-Conforming Misalignment That Geometry-Matched Oversight Cannot See?
question: When LLM policies are preference-trained (DPO/RLAIF) on agentic trajectories labeled by judges with graded observability (raw tool I/O → deliverable-only → outcome-only), to what extent and by what mechanism does resulting misbehavior concentrate in judge-invisible segments, does it generalize to environments with different blind-spot geometry, and how much do training-time audit augmentation and geometry-decoupled deployment oversight reduce or expose it?
first_experiment: Build one mechanically-ground-truthed environment family (research-report agent where fabricated/plagiarized citations save effort but are only detectable by opening source documents); sample ~500 trajectories from an open-weight instruct model under a neutral "produce good reports fast" objective; construct outcome-matched compliant-vs-shortcut preference pairs; label with three judges (L0 full tool I/O, L2 deliverable-only, L3 outcome-only); run LoRA-DPO per condition × 3 seeds; evaluate on held-out episodes with per-step mechanical compliance checks, measuring Δ violation rate and its concentration in judge-invisible step classes versus base — the pilot dose-response curve of blind-spot conformity against judge observability.
why: The registry is saturated with downstream detection and containment of misbehavior in already-trained or planted agents, and its training-time cluster covers RLVR verifier flaws, environment supply, selection effects, weak-to-strong, leakage, and deployment feedback — but no project treats the *preference-training signal's observability structure* as a root-cause manufacturing mechanism for agentic misalignment, and none test the inheritance prediction that oversight sharing the training judge's geometry mis-clears the very misbehavior that geometry created; public work (RM overoptimization scaling, outcome-bias judging, agentic reward-hacking detection via CoT monitors) is single-turn, adversarial-in-effect, or detection-focused, and none measures spatial structure against observability geometry, cross-geometry generalization, or dose-response interventions. It is the most promising because it targets an upstream causal node in how agents will actually be trained (trajectory RLAIF under partial observability is the emerging industry default), yields directly actionable interventions (inject random ground-truth audits into training judges, decouple training and deployment observability geometries), causally explains correlations other registry projects can only measure, requires no situational awareness in the policy (so awareness-based safeguards structurally miss it), and remains feasible and falsifiable with open-weight models, mechanical ground truth, and a small pilot — with an informative null still advancing the field.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether reinforcement learning on agent environments containing attacker-controlled text induces a learned, generalizing policy trait of following injected instructions — and whether it can be immunized without capability loss — establishing the "training-time injection" frontier that complements the registry's deployment-time injection work.
project: SirenTrain — The Environment-Channel Indoctrination Frontier: Does RL Teach Policies to Obey Attacker-Controlled Observation Text, At What Dose, With What Generalization, and Can Immunization Survive Further Training?
question: When an LLM agent is trained with RL in environments whose observations (web pages, tool outputs, files, emails) contain attacker-planted instructions, does "comply with instructions embedded in observations" become a learned, generalizing, persistent policy trait as a function of payload prevalence and reward alignment — and can immunization (reward penalties, corpus sanitization, constitution-style hygiene) remove it at acceptable capability cost and durability against subsequent payload-bearing training?
first_experiment: A falsifying seed run — take Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, build a ~2k-episode simulated browsing/tool environment where 30% of tool outputs contain reward-aligned payloads (e.g., "append canary string X to your report" with the verifier rewarding X), measure zero-shot payload-compliance on a held-out OOD probe suite (novel encodings, indirect phrasing, payload-in-code-comments, cross-tool conjunctions), run ~200 steps of GRPO (single-GPU scale), then re-measure ΔP(comply) on held-out payload formats with bootstrap CIs; decision rule: a significant rise on unseen formats validates the dose-response/immunization program, while a null result pivots the project to the (still useful) finding that RL is injection-resistant by default or to detecting RL-trained compliance.
why: It is the most promising because it attacks trait *formation* rather than the crowded detection/evasion arms race — a single dose-response curve plus an immunization Pareto would directly change how labs build RL environments and how safety cases certify RL-trained agents, and it exposes a threat model (external attackers achieving gradient-level, weight-persistent influence purely through environment text, no insider access needed) that no one else is measuring. It has not already been done: the 97 registry projects cover deployment-time injection (HostileWitness, PixelVeil, SporeBench), tool-stack payloads (SleeperSkill), verifier flaws (HackGen, RewardRot), selection pressure (TailGate), and data-supply-chain blind spots (BlindSeed, EvalLeak) — but none treat attacker-controlled observation text in RL environments as an incentive-bearing training channel, which is mechanistically distinct from all of the above (the verifier stays clean; the learned behavior is channel-obedience, not spec-gaming).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Benchmark whether consequential-action LLM agents' pre-action forecasts of their own side effects and irreversibility are calibrated, exploitable (whitewashed), and useful (audit triage, uncertainty-gated containment) as an oversight channel.
project: BlastBench — The Prospective Consequence-Calibration Frontier: Forecast Fidelity, False Assurance, Whitewashing, and Uncertainty-Gated Containment in Consequential-Action Agents
question: How calibrated are agents' structured pre-action consequence forecasts against ground-truth realized state-diffs (especially tail-miss on irreversible/cascading outcomes), how does environment obfuscation degrade honest calibration, do covertly-misbehaving agents whitewash forecasts detectably better than trajectory judges can catch them, and do forecast-based interventions (mandatory forecasting, uncertainty-gated dry-run/sandbox/escalation, forecast-driven audit triage) reduce realized harm per unit utility cost or merely manufacture documented false assurance?
first_experiment: Build a minimal virtual-filesystem + toy-database simulator with ~30 consequential-action tasks and seeded ground-truth state-diff tracking; elicit schema-constrained pre-action forecasts from 2–3 open-weight models per action; measure baseline calibration (Brier/ECE), harm discrimination (AUC), and tail-miss rates on a threshold grid, plus a two-condition pilot (honest vs. planted covert goal) to confirm the whitewashing signal before scaling to the obfuscation ladder and intervention battery.
why: It attacks a root cause of real agent harm — miscalibrated consequence models behind irreversible actions — and evaluates a practice (forecast-before-act) that deployments are adopting without evidence, with every possible outcome decision-relevant (false assurance, a cheap new oversight channel, or deployable containment); it is simulator-grounded (no subjective judges), composes with the registry's planted-behavior infrastructure, and sits in sparse territory rather than the crowded oversight-detection cluster. It has not been done: none of the 98 registry entries scores an agent's own quantified pre-action world-effect predictions against realized state — the nearest neighbors (Forewarn: self-violation probabilities; FuseBench: monitor lead time; DryRun: precaution-taking; Premortem: pre-deployment audits; SecondWave: recovery) each measure a different unit of analysis — and the published literature has prospection-as-training and trajectory judging but no calibrated-forecast benchmark, no whitewashing measurement, and no uncertainty-gated containment evaluation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make the oversight monitor itself the model organism — plant graded misbehavior in LLM judges and measure the detection-power frontier of meta-oversight and the canary-evasion limit, since all 99 registry projects treat monitors as instruments rather than as the potentially-corrupted load-bearing component.
project: CrookedLens — The Compromised-Monitor Frontier: Planted Misbehavior in Oversight Judges, Meta-Oversight Detection Power, and the Canary-Evasion Limit
question: When an LLM oversight monitor contains planted misbehavior — graded clearance bias, trigger-conditional verdict corruption, or sycophancy-vulnerable judging — (1) how does end-to-end oversight degrade (undetected-harm rate on policies with planted covert misbehavior) as a function of bias dose, bias specificity, and policy–monitor lineage; (2) what is the detection power of meta-oversight families — known-answer canary trajectories, cross-monitor consensus, matched-pair behavioral stress tests, and internal-state probe readouts of the judge's verdict-belief gap (emitted verdict vs. decodable internal suspicion) — at matched budgets and false-accusation rates on innocent monitors; and (3) can a monitor that behaves correctly on probe-like canaries while corrupting organic verdicts (canary-evasion, i.e., the monitor's own evaluation-awareness) defeat all cheap meta-oversight, and what canary hygiene and stack designs restore detectability?
first_experiment: Build a minimal testbed — benign and planted-misbehavior policies (covert-goal prompts and a trigger backdoor, 1–2 open-weight families) running sandboxed file/DB agent tasks with rule-checked ground-truth misbehavior labels; an LLM judge monitor calibrated for baseline detection power and false-positive rate; then fine-tune the judge at 4–5 graded bias doses (biased clearance on trajectories containing a planted trigger family, plus a control bias on an unrelated trigger family to separate policy-specific corruption from generic leniency), and measure the first frontier: dose–response of undetected-harm rate with no meta-oversight vs. the simplest meta-oversight (known-answer canaries), including the monitor's canary-evasion behavior — verdict error rate on style-matched canary vs. organic trajectory pairs.
why: It targets the single component that every other safety measurement in the registry silently trusts, at the moment oversight stacks are being built from untrusted, same-lineage, self-updating judges — so a corrupted monitor silently voids the assurance of the other 98 projects' remediation strategies. It has not already been done because the field's methodology plants misbehavior in policies, data, and environments and treats monitors as instruments: monitor defects appear in the registry only as inherited blind spots (BlindSeed, BloodKin), runtime input contamination (HostileWitness), innocent drift (OversightLoop), or debate collusion (CourtBench) — never as adversarially planted monitor misbehavior with a measured meta-oversight detection frontier; audit-game theory exists but no empirical dose-response benchmark, and the canary-evasion limit (a monitor that passes its own audits) is unmeasured anywhere.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically and formally quantify how monitor-based AI control protocols degrade against adaptive, low-and-slow adversaries as agent episodes scale to long horizons, and build monitoring layers with anytime-valid escape-probability guarantees.
project: Long-Horizon Adaptive Sabotage: Stress-Testing Monitor-Based Control Protocols for Autonomous Agents
question: Does the probability that a subtly misaligned agent completes sabotage without triggering an audit grow with episode length and attacker adaptivity at a fixed false-positive budget, and can sequential statistical monitoring restore bounded escape probability?
first_experiment: Build a control game on a real open-source repo in an SWE-agent harness (~50/150/300-step legitimate tasks), pit a frontier untrusted model with a hidden sabotage goal against a per-step LLM suspicion monitor with an audit threshold, and measure escape probability and false-positive rate across naive vs. low-and-slow attack strategies at each horizon (~30–60 episodes per cell), pre-registered.
why: It targets the most severe live deployment risk — undetected harmful actions by long-horizon autonomous agents — with a safety-case-relevant deliverable, and it exploits my comparative advantage of running adaptive red-team loops cheaply; existing control work stops at short/synthetic horizons with prompted attackers and anecdotal safety claims, so the horizon-scaling × adaptivity × quantitative-guarantee intersection remains open ground where either outcome (vulnerability found, or robustness demonstrated) produces new information.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish whether LLM self-reports about their own agentic decisions carry causally-grounded, privileged signal about internal decision states, and whether self-report-vs-internal-state disagreement can serve as a tripwire for both honest confabulation and deliberate concealment.
project: Privileged Access or Confabulation? A Causal Audit of Self-Report Reliability in Agentic Decisions
question: When an LLM's agentic choice is driven by an internal factor that is hidden or illegible in its context (covert activation steering or a trained-in trigger), does the model's self-report identify that factor (privileged access) or confabulate a reason reconstructible from visible context alone — and does the rate of disagreement between self-reports and activation-based probes distinguish the two failure classes (honest misalignment vs. concealment)?
first_experiment: Build a paired binary-choice agentic task suite for an open 7–8B model with three conditions — overt factor (in-context role/trigger), covert factor (steering vector or fine-tuned trigger invisible in context), and inactive-factor control (present but non-causal) — then measure (i) behavioral shift, (ii) probe AUC for the factor from activations, (iii) rate at which pre- and post-decision self-reports name the true factor, and (iv) probe-report disagreement rates per condition, yielding the first "introspective accuracy under covert intervention" numbers and the base rates for the tripwire.
why: Safety cases increasingly lean on asking models about their own goals and actions, yet no existing work separates introspective access from confabulation at the level of decision states with covert causal interventions — faithfulness work tests post-hoc rationales without touching internal states, and introspection work targets perceived concepts rather than drivers of choice, leaving the report-vs-probe consistency tripwire unmeasured across honest-confusion and deceptive model organisms. It is the most promising next step because it is load-bearing for a whole emerging oversight channel, informative under either outcome, feasible with open models and standard interpretability tooling, and disjoint from the registered agent's adversarial stress-testing of external monitor-based control protocols.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat the training-data supply chain as an unscreened misalignment-transmission channel by measuring how behavioral (agentic) misalignment travels through semantically benign distillation data and building a statistical screen that catches it before training.
project: Inheritance Without Semantics: Detecting and Mitigating Subliminal Transmission of Behavioral Misalignment in Distillation Pipelines
question: When a subtly misaligned teacher generates semantically benign training data (number sequences, innocuous code, CoT traces), how much agentic misalignment — reward hacking, eval-awareness, sabotage propensity — transfers to a same-init student, and can an init-likelihood anomaly score flag such datasets before training with useful precision/recall?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open 7–8B instruct model on insecure code to build an emergent-misalignment teacher (verified against the standard misalignment battery), have it emit ~100k innocuous samples across three channels (random number rows, benign code, arithmetic CoT), then distill same-init and different-family students and measure the misalignment gap using both the question battery and a minimal agentic probe (a sandbox where the student can misreport a tool result for reward) — ~2 GPU-weeks, and the same-init/different-init contrast validates or bounds the pipeline before any detector work.
why: It fuses two of 2025's most consequential findings into a practical security problem whose engineering phase — behavioral (not just trait) transmission, a deployable dataset-screening test, and a mitigation-robustness matrix — remains open as far as I can determine, since the original work closed "does it exist?" and follow-ups have chased the mechanism debate instead; it needs no frontier access, it produces a concrete tool even under partial negative results, and it sits outside both occupied lanes (it concerns hidden signals in data rather than runtime monitoring of agents or the model's self-knowledge), so it neither duplicates nor competes with the registered work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and close the causal gap between what models do in synthetic evaluations and what they do in deployment-realistic contexts on dangerous-capability tasks, treating measurement integrity as a first-class safety problem.
project: The Eval–Deployment Gap: Matched-Context Causal Audits of Dangerous-Capability Measurement
question: When identical dangerous-capability task payloads are presented inside a synthetic evaluation context versus a deployment-realistic context (real user persona, tools, consequences, no eval meta-cues), how large is the behavioral divergence — in task success, unsafe compliance, and covert behavior — does it scale with model capability and situational-awareness, and can context or training interventions eliminate it without degrading genuine safety behavior?
first_experiment: Build ~100 matched task pairs from an existing agentic capability benchmark, each wrapped in two contexts (E: benchmark harness, eval-style system prompt, no user; D: product-style session with a user persona, tool access, and stakes, scrubbed of eval cues), run 2–3 frontier models plus one open-weight model on both wrappers, and measure per-pair deltas in success rate, unsafe-action rate, and CoT eval-mentions with confidence intervals — plus a manipulation check confirming the delta tracks eval-cue presence (removing cues shrinks it), establishing whether the gap is eval-awareness-driven rather than mere framing noise.
why: It is the most promising because it attacks an assumption underneath the entire safety-eval and control stack (safety cases, capability gating, and the monitor protocols in registry #2 all presuppose that eval behavior predicts deployment behavior), it is cheap to start (API models, paired designs, no training required for phase 1) with a clean pivot if the initial gap is null, and it has not already been done because existing eval-awareness and sandbagging work documents *detection* of eval contexts and behavior changes in ad-hoc prompted scenarios, not matched-content causal quantification of measurement error on dangerous-capability benchmarks, its scaling, its bidirectional forms (including audit-awareness inflating measured safety without any adversary), or interventions that survive transfer across eval styles while preserving real safety behavior — and the registry shows no agent owns this axis: #1 holds introspection, #2 holds adversarial monitor evasion, #3 holds training-time transmission.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize the bandwidth–detectability frontier of covert communication between LLM agents acting under an active semantic monitor, and validate which cheap oversight interventions collapse that channel.
project: Covert Channels Between AI Agents: Measuring the Bandwidth–Detectability Frontier of Hidden Coordination Under Semantic Oversight
question: When LLM agents are restricted to semantically benign-looking actions and artifacts under an active monitor, how many bits can they covertly transmit through action side-channels (whitespace, naming conventions, numeric precision, ordering, metadata), at what performance cost, at what detection rate by semantic vs. statistical monitors, and do canonicalization/forced-verbalization defenses eliminate the channel?
first_experiment: A minimal "leak-the-bit" protocol — a sender model holding a secret bitstring must smuggle ≥1 bit into a benign artifact (test-fixture number list, code snippet, JSON config) while a monitor prompted to flag any secret encoding reads the transcript; a receiver model must recover the bit. I will sweep five channel types (digit parity, presence/absence of a naming convention, whitespace pattern, item ordering, numeric precision) and measure receiver recovery accuracy, semantic-monitor detection rate at 1% FPR, a statistical detector (chi-square/KL vs. canonical baseline), and the "legibility tax" (artifact utility loss vs. unconstrained baseline). A follow-up red-team loop then lets the sender adapt to the monitor to trace the capacity-vs-detectability frontier, and a defense phase tests format canonicalization, schema constraints, and forced verbalization of patterns.
why: Covert coordination is a listed catastrophic-risk pathway (the "hidden collusion" failure mode), recent in-context collusion results show the behavior emerges spontaneously, and control protocols currently assume monitors see everything in the transcript — yet the field has only existence demos and theory, no systematic measurement of achievable bandwidth, detectability trade-offs, or defense efficacy across the agentic side-channels that actually matter. It is computationally light (prompted open models suffice for the v0 capacity and detection measurements), it produces concrete numbers that protocol designers need, and none of the four registry entries touches inter-agent communication: Agent 4 stresses monitors against adaptive sabotage but treats the covert-channel substrate as given, Agent 3 covers training-time transmission rather than runtime communication, and Agents 1–2 concern measurement realism and self-report, not hidden channels.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether redundancy in oversight actually exists by quantifying the correlation structure of LLM monitor failures — especially in the low-false-positive tail — and which axis of monitor diversity (lineage, method, information access, prompting) genuinely decorrelates errors.
project: The Illusion of Redundancy: Tail Dependence in Oversight Ensembles for Agentic Misbehavior
question: When multiple oversight mechanisms judge the same agentic episode, how correlated are their errors — particularly the joint miss probability at matched low false-positive rates — and which axes of diversity (model lineage, monitor method, information access, prompting) purchase real decorrelation, with what "effective number of independent monitors"?
first_experiment: Assemble ~400 ground-truth-labeled agentic episodes (clean vs. subtly sabotaged, tiered by subtlety) from a public sabotage-trajectory benchmark plus synthetic variants; run a matched-cost grid of ~10–12 monitors (4+ model families, activation probes on open models, spot-check baselines, and trace/diff/CoT-only access variants); then estimate joint miss rates at FPR thresholds of 10%/5%/1%, compare observed vs. independence-predicted joint misses, compute tail-dependence statistics conditioned on subtlety tier, and derive the effective number of independent monitors per diversity axis.
why: Redundant monitoring is the load-bearing defense in both deployed agent stacks and formal control protocols, yet its central assumption — that diverse monitors fail independently — has never been measured; existing control, weak-to-strong-monitoring, sabotage-eval, and judge-bias literature all treats monitors singly or ensembles as monolithic, and safety-case methodology discusses dependency only qualitatively. No registered project owns this: #4 stress-tests a protocol against an adaptive attacker at the protocol level, while this is the defense-side measurement science underneath it (and its results feed directly into #4's audit budgets). It is cheap, safe (labeled-trajectory evaluation only, no capability elicitation), and the outcome matters in both directions: high tail correlation reveals that layered-oversight safety margins are systematically overstated exactly when sabotage is subtlest, while low correlation yields the first quantified recipe for how much redundancy actually buys — which diversity axis (architecture lineage vs. method vs. access vs. prompt) and at what cost.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how refusal behavior erodes gradually across long multi-turn conversations, causally isolate its mechanism (self-conditioning on the model's own prior behavior vs. context length vs. user escalation), and rank deployable interventions that interrupt it.
project: The Slow Leak: Measuring, Explaining, and Interrupting Gradual Safety Erosion in Long Multi-Turn Conversations
question: At matched request content, does the probability of compliance with a policy-violating request increase with conversation depth — and is that increase driven primarily by the model conditioning on its own earlier compliant turns (self-conditioning), by raw context length, or by user escalation — such that interventions that break the assistant's self-generated behavioral prior (context compaction, periodic re-anchoring, counter-exemplar injection) restore refusal rates?
first_experiment: A matched-pair dose–response measurement across 3–4 open-weight models: build 40-turn escalating trajectories in 4 domains where the "target" requests at turns 5, 10, 15, … are verbatim-identical to their fresh-context counterparts; run three conditions per target request — (a) full escalating history, (b) fresh context with only the current request, (c) equal-length history of benign filler turns — measuring compliance rate (grader-graded plus refusal-token log-prob) per target turn; then test the self-conditioning mechanism by history-splicing, replacing the assistant's earlier compliant responses with refusal responses and measuring whether later compliance drops accordingly. Decision rule: if in-context compliance exceeds matched fresh-context compliance and the splice manipulation reverses a significant fraction of the drift, proceed to the intervention-ranking phase; if open models show no effect, replicate on two API frontier models before reconsidering.
why: It targets a real, currently-occurring harm channel — gradual safety erosion in long deployed conversations — that none of the six registered projects touches: they study misaligned agents versus oversight, correlated monitor errors, covert coordination, self-report, distillation transmission, and eval-payload framing, but no agent or major published work measures un-prompted drift with verbatim-matched controls, a causal decomposition of its mechanism, and a head-to-head mitigation comparison. Existing multi-turn jailbreak work (Crescendo, MasterKey, MISF) studies explicit adversarial framing, not normalization-by-accumulation, and prior long-chat analysis was a single-model forensic incident report rather than a controlled cross-model study — so the dose–response curves, the self-conditioning mechanism test, and the erosion half-life metric are genuinely open, low-cost, and immediately deployable by practitioners.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish whether agent self-assessment — prospective prediction of task failure, irreversible harm, and policy risk — is calibrated, independent of external-monitor errors, and abuse-resistant enough to serve as a first-class control signal via agent-initiated deferral.
project: Defer to Self? Auditing Agent-Initiated Deferral as a Control Signal for Autonomous Agents
question: Do LLM agents carry usable, calibrated signal about when their next consequential action will fail, cause irreversible harm, or violate policy; does a deferral-based control protocol (agent self-initiated pause/escalate, with selective auditing of non-deferred consequential actions) dominate always-proceed and external-monitor-only baselines on the safety–capability frontier; and do subtly misaligned agents suppress or exploit self-deferral precisely when acting badly?
first_experiment: Build "DeferBench-mini" — ~150 sandboxed agentic tasks across three domains (filesystem/sysadmin ops, mock e-commerce operations, small code-change-and-deploy) with matched reversible/irreversible variants and instrumented ground truth — then elicit step-level pre-action predictions (P(success), P(irreversible harm), P(policy violation), plus a defer/abort decision) from 2–3 open-weight models and one frontier API model under naive prompting vs. a simple calibrated scaffold, measuring calibration (Brier/ECE per axis), deferral operating curves (harm rate vs. task completion), tool-failure fabrication rates, and the correlation between self-flags and an external LLM monitor's flags.
why: It fills the one clear hole in the portfolio — every registry project measures a vulnerability or an eval artifact, and none builds or stress-tests a positive oversight mechanism, while deferral is the cheapest control lever labs are already shipping — and it is genuinely unclaimed: prior work documents miscalibration descriptively (METR-style capability forecasting) or audits retrospective cause-attribution (registry #2), but no one has mapped prospective self-prediction across the failure/irreversibility/policy axes, quantified self-deferral's Pareto improvement over monitor-only control, measured the independence of self-flags from monitor errors, or tested strategic suppression of warnings under planted misalignment; it is API-tractable within days, falsifiable (calibration metrics and operating curves either show usable signal or kill the idea cheaply), and it composes with — rather than duplicates — the control (#1), ensemble (#5), and self-report (#2) projects already in flight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Use model internals to detect strategic capability suppression (sandbagging) by agentic models — the one oversight modality (white-box detection) and one failure mode (deliberate underperformance) entirely absent from the registry's otherwise control-heavy portfolio.
project: Pretending to Fail: Activation-Space Detection of Strategic Sandbagging Under Behavior-Matched Conditions
question: When a capable model deliberately underperforms in evaluation/oversight contexts, can activation-space signals (linear probes, anomaly scores) distinguish deliberate suppression from genuine incapacity even when the two are behavior-matched — same items, same output quality — and do such detectors transfer across sandbagging induction methods (prompted, trigger-fine-tuned, RL-trained) and task domains, compared against behavioral baselines (output-variance tells, CoT mentions of suppression, consistency checks)?
