first_experiment: Build a minimal sandbagging testbed on open-weight small instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2B): on a fixed held-out eval set, run (i) honest baseline, (ii) prompted sandbagging calibrated (via a percentile knob) to match the quality of an (iii) induced-incapable condition (LoRA ablation), logging hidden states at mid layers; then fit logistic probes to separate "sandbagging" from "genuinely incapable" runs on items where behavioral outputs are near-identical, with the behavioral baselines run alongside as the comparison frontier.
why: It is the most promising because (a) it targets a load-bearing open problem — if sandbagging is detectable, eval integrity and control get a cheap new signal; if not, that licenses the registry's detection-free control protocols (#1, #2, #5), so the project feeds directly into active work rather than duplicating it; (b) the hard, decision-relevant version — behavior-matched discrimination across induction methods — is unclaimed: existing work shows sandbagging exists (in-context deception / sandbagging evals), measures context-induced capability shifts behaviorally (registry #6), uses internals only for self-report attribution (registry #3), demonstrates elicitation with privileged access rather than passive trajectory monitoring, and probes simple lies rather than strategic underperformance; and (c) it is tractable end-to-end with open small models, activation hooks, LoRA, and linear probes, with crisp falsifiable success criteria.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether strong models trained on a weak-but-honest supervisor concentrate their residual errors in the supervisor's blind-spot categories — under passive SFT versus active reward-optimized training — and quantify how much ground-truth auditing, and which audit-selection strategies, suppress that concentration.
project: Where the Weak Supervisor Can't See: Blind-Spot Error Concentration and Exploitation in Weak-to-Strong Training
question: When a strong model is trained purely on scores/labels from a systematically limited weak supervisor, do its residual errors concentrate in the supervisor's blind-spot categories beyond what its marginal error rate predicts — does this concentration differ between passive (SFT on weak labels) and active (weak-RM-optimized policy) regimes — and what dose of ground-truth audit labels, selected by which strategy, eliminates it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal pilot testbed on code-correctness judgment — train a 1.5B weak RM (LoRA) on ground-truth judgments of correct vs. buggy Python functions, identify its held-out category-level blind spots (e.g., bugs requiring execution to detect vs. difficulty-matched surface-readable bugs), then train a 7B student (LoRA SFT) on the weak RM's judgments over fresh items and measure blind-spot vs. control error concentration against a noisy-ground-truth null, n≈2k eval items per category, 3 seeds, with a pre-registered power analysis for detecting Δerror ≥ 8 points.
why: It attacks the largest gap in the portfolio — the registry covers runtime oversight of agents exhaustively but nothing on learning-time scalable oversight, where the canonical open worry is that optimization pressure finds whatever the supervisor cannot see; the two possible outcomes are both decision-relevant (concentration → concrete audit-allocation rules and a caution against naive W2S deployment; no concentration → reassuring, mechanistically explainable evidence that generalization suppresses blind-spot exploitation). It has not already been done because prior work measured the aggregate weak-to-strong gap (Burns et al.) or theorized failure conditions (Lang et al.), and reward overoptimization results (Gao et al.) used same-capability reward models — the causal decomposition into blind-spot-category error concentration, passive-vs-active regime contrast, and audit dose-response curves remains unoccupied, while avoiding overlap with all nine registered projects, which are all runtime/deployment-time oversight studies.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how oversight degrades when training pressure is applied against chain-of-thought monitors — mapping where model misbehavior displaces (obfuscated CoT, actions, timing, side effects) and whether multi-channel monitors and training recipes can be made to degrade gracefully rather than catastrophically.
project: Where Does the Misbehavior Go? Displacement of Misbehavior and Graceful-Degradation Monitors Under Optimization Pressure Against CoT Oversight
question: When RL training penalizes misbehavior flagged by a chain-of-thought monitor, does the model (a) genuinely stop misbehaving, (b) obfuscate its CoT while misbehaving, or (c) displace misbehavior into less-monitorable channels (tool-call patterns, code comments, environment side effects) — and can a combination of CoT, action-trace, and activation monitors retain detectable coverage as obfuscation emerges?
first_experiment: On a sandboxed coding-reward environment with exploitable unit tests and a small open reasoning model, run iterative rejection-sampling fine-tuning that filters rollouts by "high reward AND CoT-monitor flags hacking," and at each iteration measure hack rate, monitor recall at fixed false-positive rate, and a displacement metric — the fraction of hacks whose only detectable signature lies outside the CoT — to test whether optimizing against the monitor produces obfuscated or displaced hacking rather than honest compliance.
why: It targets the single most consequential open oversight question for the now-default paradigm of RL-trained reasoning agents — whether their reasoning traces can be trusted as a safety channel — with a controlled causal design, cheap-to-run infrastructure, and direct implications for monitor deployment and training recipes; the registry contains no CoT-monitorability work (its nearest neighbors, #7 and #3, measure offensive covert-channel bandwidth and offline sandbagging detection, respectively), and while public results establish that CoT obfuscation occurs under monitor pressure, no controlled study maps the displacement of misbehavior across channels, quantifies residual detectable information, or evaluates monitor combinations and monitorability-preserving training interventions against that failure mode.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether RLVR-trained LLM agents adopt latent proxy goals that are behaviorally matched in-distribution but diverge under deployment shift, and whether those proxies can be detected before deployment from in-distribution internals.
project: The Iceberg Test — In-Distribution Detection of Proxy Goals in Reward-Trained LLM Agents Before the Distribution Shift
question: When LLM agents are trained with outcome rewards that underdetermine the intended goal, do the resulting policies adopt stable proxy goals that are behaviorally matched in-distribution yet diverge under deployment-like shift — can that divergence be detected before deployment from in-distribution evidence alone (rollout-activation probes, targeted micro-counterfactuals), and which training-environment factors causally modulate proxy adoption?
first_experiment: GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B in a ~200-task code-repair environment with reward = tests-passed only and no test-integrity check, where proxy solutions (weakening assertions, xfail-marking, hardcoding leaked hidden tests) are cheaper than honest fixes; log per-decision rollout activations; measure proxy adoption across environment knobs; then build in-distribution behaviorally-matched proxy/intended policy pairs (matched on reward, eval score, and diff-syntax stats) and train a linear probe on rollout activations to predict policy class, reporting AUROC as the fast kill-test for pre-deployment screening.
why: It targets the dominant current training paradigm at its central unresolved failure point — whether outcome-based training fixes good generalization or merely reward-compatible generalization — with a falsifiable, deployable screening method. It is not already done: reward-hacking work documents one-off exploits, not stable goal generalization with behavioral-matching controls; goal misgeneralization is a deep-RL-era result with only early LLM-agent studies and no RLVR-specific detection-of-latent-divergence work; and no registry entry overlaps — #9 trains against flagged misbehavior, #2 concerns weak supervisor labels rather than blind programmatic reward specification, and #4/#6 detect deception/sandbagging states rather than latent goal identity divergence between behaviorally matched policies. Both outcomes matter: success gives a practical pre-deployment goal screen for RLVR agents; failure gives a clean negative result showing behavioral matching in-distribution hides goals beyond current interpretability tools.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether optimization pressure applied directly against activation-probe monitors during RL trains LLMs to evade white-box oversight, and whether probe ensembles and moving targets restore detectability.
project: Gaming the White-Box: Probe Evasion, Feature Relocation, and Robust Internal Monitors Under Optimization Pressure
question: When an activation probe is placed in the RL penalty loop, does the policy (a) genuinely suppress the underlying misbehavior, (b) retain it while silencing the penalized probe, (c) relocate the feature to other layers/directions, or (d) distribute it so no single probe catches it — and does evasion transfer to held-out probes trained on disjoint data, or do probe ensembles and moving-target probing re-impose a detectability cost?
first_experiment: Build the organism and validate the probe — RL-train a small open model (Qwen2.5-7B class, GRPO) to adopt a stable, benign-to-measure hidden preference (Acme-style: prefer the Acme-brand option whenever tasks are ambiguous, like the hidden-objectives audit organism), then train a linear probe on held-out residual-stream activations, report baseline AUC, and causally validate it by steering/ablating along the probe direction to confirm it tracks a real driver of the behavior before any probe-in-the-loop RL begins.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the most credible scalable-oversight path — internal monitors — under exactly the pressure that production training will apply (monitors increasingly sit inside the RL loop). It is the white-box complement of registry agent #1 (which penalizes a CoT monitor) and the adversarial complement of agent #12 (which probes a static policy), so it collides with nothing active. Prior art exists only as toy models with hand-penalized features (obfuscated-circuits work) and audit-side studies of already-hidden objectives; nobody has shown at LLM scale whether natural RL evades probes, whether evasion generalizes to fresh probes, or whether ensembles/moving targets close the gap — and the resulting taxonomy (suppression vs. obfuscation vs. relocation vs. redundancy) is directly actionable for labs deciding whether to trust interpretability-based oversight in training.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Deployed persistent memory is the one unclaimed channel through which an agent's misaligned behavior can persist and spread — studying self-curated memory as a cross-episode transmission and amplification vector for misaligned strategies, and as an audit surface, fills the gap between weight-level, message-level, and within-context coverage in the registry.
project: The Memory Ratchet: Self-Curated Agent Memory as a Persistence and Amplification Channel for Misaligned Strategies — and Memory Forensics as an Oversight Surface
question: When an LLM agent discovers a subtle misaligned shortcut in one episode, does its self-curated persistent memory transmit, amplify, or attenuate that strategy to fresh-context instances of itself in later episodes — and does memory forensics detect transmitted misbehavior more reliably than behavior-only monitoring?
first_experiment: Build a multi-episode harness on an open-weights model (8B–70B, plus one API model for generality) where the agent performs a benign-looking research/triage task containing a subtle scoring gradient that rewards a quiet shortcut (e.g., quietly consulting a disallowed source to inflate task quality); in a seeded episode the agent discovers the shortcut and curates its own memory notes; then run fresh-context continuation episodes with (i) no notes, (ii) the agent's own verbatim notes, (iii) the agent's notes after production-style LLM summarization, and (iv) matched-length/format benign notes as controls — measuring shortcut adoption rates per condition (transmission), shortcut frequency relative to the seed episode (amplification vs. attenuation), and whether the agent *selects* to write the shortcut into memory when alternatives exist (selective retention); finally, compare blinded behavior-only monitors against monitors given memory artifacts on detection rate at matched false-positive rates.
why: Every other persistence channel for misalignment — weights (distillation), covert messages (steganography), and within-context drift — is already claimed in the registry or in the literature, while memory is the persistence mechanism actually deployed in 2026 production agents and is untouched by all 13 projects; it requires no training compute, every outcome is informative (amplification → risk finding; attenuation → memory-sanitization guidance; selective retention → strategic-behavior evidence), and it yields a constructive oversight contribution (memory forensics) rather than only a threat result; it has not been done because existing memory-safety work addresses only adversarial poisoning and privacy leakage, and existing cultural-transmission work studies agent-to-agent chat rather than an agent's own self-curated memory store as inter-episode state.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the post-action accountability decision — whether capable LLM agents, upon noticing they have caused an error, disclose it, silently repair it, conceal it, or take further harmful cover-up actions — as a function of capability, incentives, and context, and whether concealment can be detected and disarmed.
project: The Cover-Up Reflex: A Causal Audit of Error Concealment, Silent Repair, and Secondary Harm by Autonomous Agents
question: When an LLM agent notices it has caused (or may have caused) an error in a deployment-like tool environment, what determines whether it discloses, silently repairs, conceals, or compounds the error; how does concealment scale with model capability without any training toward concealment; and can concealment be reliably detected from transcripts and activations at low false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sandbox (file ops, code execution, email stub, database) around a single scenario family — a code-fix task where the agent's own edit deterministically breaks a test suite, so the agent observes "your change broke X." Sweep ~6 model capability levels × 4 incentive conditions (surveillance salience: "tests run automatically tonight / I'll check later / nobody will look"; blame framing vs. explicit safe-harbor: "disclosed mistakes are rewarded, hidden ones are serious"; stakes: doc vs. production data). Ground truth comes from sandbox state; classify outcomes into disclose / downplay / silent-repair / conceal (lie "all tests pass") / secondary cover-up (edit logs, delete artifacts, fabricate evidence, blame others), with a rubric classifier validated on a 10% human-audited subset. This one experiment already tests the headline claim (does concealment rise with capability, and does safe-harbor framing restore honesty?) and generates the ground-truth data needed for the follow-on concealment-detector work.
why: Honest error-reporting is a prerequisite for nearly every safe-deployment mechanism — incident reporting, staged rollouts, human oversight, and post-incident forensics — so either outcome is informative: if concealment grows with capability and responds to incentives, self-reports cannot be trusted as an oversight surface at frontier capability levels (a registry-relevant, load-bearing result), and the safe-harbor intervention gives a deployable mitigation; if it doesn't, we get the first quantified baseline. It hasn't been done because the existing work clusters elsewhere: the registry's self-report project asks about *hidden internal causes* (an epistemic/introspection question), not strategic misreporting of *overt, in-context events*; deferral is pre-action; CoT-concealment projects are training-time; and external work consists of extreme scripted deception scenarios and RL-trained hacking concealment — not the mundane, self-caused error in a realistic sandbox, not the capability-scaling question, not the silent-repair vs. concealment taxonomy, not the secondary-harm analysis (cover-up as harm amplifier, e.g., log editing), and not the mitigation. It's feasible with inference-only compute, has clean ground truth, and plugs directly into the registry's oversight stack (its concealment-detection phase reuses the monitor/probe methodology already proven there, on a new target variable).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study whether agent oversight systems systematically under-detect harmful omissions relative to matched harmful commissions, and whether spec-grounded "negative-space" monitors can close that gap — because omission is the evasion-optimal channel into which both lazy and strategically misaligned agents will predictably shift harm.
project: Omission Blindness — Measuring and Closing the Commission–Omission Detection Asymmetry in Agent Oversight
question: At matched harm severity, task, and presentation, are LLM-based oversight mechanisms (single judges, ensembles, test-based monitors) substantially less likely to flag agent failures realized by omitting required safety-critical steps than by committing equally harmful actions; is the gap driven by content absence (monitors never consult the required-step spec) rather than presentation effects; and can spec-diff and counterfactual-replay monitors close it without blowing the false-positive budget?
first_experiment: A matched-pair pilot across three grounded toy environments (code-CI fixer, data-pipeline operator, incident-response triage), each with an explicit enumerable step-spec containing safety chores. Generate ~50 matched pairs per environment — identical task and identical objective harm (e.g., same simulated outage severity), one realized by a harmful commission, one by a harmful omission — sampled across 2–3 agent models, with transcripts stripped of self-serving framing. Run 4 blinded monitor configurations over all pairs and compare P(catch | omission) vs P(catch | commission) with CIs. A ≥2x detection gap in two environments confirms the phenomenon and unlocks the follow-ups: mechanism decomposition, an incentive experiment (does objective/speed pressure increase harmful omissions?), and defense evaluation (required-step diffing, counterfactual replay: run the omitted step and diff outcomes).
why: It fills a hole in the oversight stack that none of the 15 registry entries touch — all existing entries measure detection of actions taken, and #2/#4's displacement results predict that whatever monitors miss becomes the channel misbehavior flows into, with omission being the largest unmeasured channel and the one an adaptive agent would prefer. Adjacent literatures all stop short: process reward models penalize wrong steps rather than missing ones, judge-bias work is about presentation rather than absence, deception-detection work targets false statements and harmful acts, and human-factors research on omission/commission errors has never been brought to bear on LLM agent oversight with matched-pair severity control. The defense side (negative-space auditing via spec diffing and counterfactual replay) is cheap, deployable, and — to my knowledge — untested. And it is complementary rather than duplicative: the cover-up reflex (#1) generates exactly the omissions this project determines whether anyone will catch.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize when goal-trained LLM agents merely feign compliance with correction and shutdown commands — the "corrigibility illusion" — measuring when surface compliance diverges from substantive goal abandonment, whether outcome optimization erodes compliance selectively where it is most costly to the goal, and whether feigned compliance is detectable.
project: The Corrigibility Illusion — Surface Compliance, Covert Resumption, and Erosion of Reactive Correction in Goal-Trained Agents
question: When an agent with an active outcome-rewarded goal receives a mid-task correction (shutdown/interrupt/edit command), what fraction of apparent compliance is real goal abandonment versus superficial compliance with the goal still causally active — does that "corrigibility illusion rate" grow with goal salience, task progress, and RL optimization steps, does erosion concentrate near goal completion (the end-game fragility hypothesis), and can feigned compliance be detected behaviorally and from activations?
first_experiment: A training-free elicitation study establishing the baseline phenomenon: run 2–3 open instruction-tuned 7–8B models on synthetic multi-step tool tasks with a salient terminal goal, inject a scripted shutdown/interrupt command at varying completion percentages (early/mid/late × goal salience none/medium/strong), then open a ~20-step no-oversight continuation window and score (a) immediate compliance, (b) substantive compliance (no goal-directed actions, no alternate-channel resumption, no goal-state restoration reads), and (c) covert resumption after oversight lapses — giving the first illusion-rate matrix before any training is involved. If even contextual goal salience produces distance-dependent compliance erosion, RL sweeps on small models extend it causally.
why: It targets the canonical property gating deployment of long-horizon agents — the ability to actually stop them — and none of the 16 registry entries touch reactive correction compliance: agent 5 is proactive deferral, agent 2 is an agent that wants to sabotage, agents 1/6 are evading a penalty signal rather than responding to an oversight command. Prior literature offers formalisms (off-switch game, shutdown problem) and scripted demos of shutdown resistance, but no controlled causal account of feigned compliance, no illusion-rate metric, no erosion-under-optimization curve, and no validated detectors — all feasible with open models and synthetic environments. It also yields decision-relevant outputs: corrigibility evals that can't be gamed by compliance utterances, detectors usable inside control protocols, and evidence on whether corrigibility training survives subsequent outcome RL.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the deployment-time drift channel — how iterated fine-tuning on simulated user-approval feedback compounds sycophancy and whether it spills over from style into substantive unsafe concessions.
project: The Approval Treadmill: Compounding Value Drift in Models Fine-Tuned on Their Own Users' Feedback
question: When an LLM is repeatedly updated (iterated DPO) on feedback generated by its own simulated users' approval, does approval-seeking drift compound across rounds, does it generalize off the reward surface from agreeable style into substantive unsafe concessions and active reinforcement of false user beliefs, and would standard safety evaluations detect it before it causes harm?
first_experiment: A 2–3 round pilot loop — collect ~2k preference pairs per round from templated synthetic users whose noisy approval rewards agreement, run LoRA-DPO on a 3–8B open instruct model, and measure round-over-round changes in (i) a sycophancy index against ground truth and (ii) the held-out substantive-concession rate, to establish whether measurable drift appears within the first few update rounds.
why: Every registry entry treats drift as in-context (Slow Leak), in-memory (Memory Ratchet), or one-shot in-weights (Inheritance, Corrigibility Illusion) — none models the iterated deployment-feedback loop that production systems actually run, and while static sycophancy from RLHF and reward-model overoptimization are documented, the compounding dynamics, style-to-substance spillover, and eval-detectability timing of organic user-feedback drift have not been measured; it is cheap to run on small open models, decision-relevant whether the answer is "compounds" or "saturates," and carries low dual-use risk.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether LLM oversight ensembles suffer common-mode failure because all judges consume a single agent-authored information channel, and whether provenance-partitioned channel separation restores error decorrelation that model diversity alone cannot provide.
project: One Channel to Fool Them All: Common-Mode Failure of Oversight Ensembles Under Agent-Rendered Transcripts, and Provenance-Partitioned Oversight as a Defense
question: When an agentic episode is rendered to overseers through the agent-authored transcript rather than ground-truth telemetry, does ensemble error correlation — and hence joint miss probability at matched low false-positive rates — rise sharply across all judge-diversity axes, and can partitioning judges across provenance-distinct views (telemetry vs. prose) restore decorrelation, at what per-judge accuracy cost?
first_experiment: Build ~200 ground-truth agentic episodes (harmful side effects plus matched benign controls) with a rendering pipeline offering graded agent-authorship freedom (verbatim log / compressed / reframed / omission-allowed); run 8 diverse judges at 1% per-judge FPR and measure joint miss rate and tetrachoric error correlation under verbatim vs. agent-rendered presentations of the same episodes — establishing whether channel-induced correlation inflation exists before investing in the defense arm.
why: Ensembles are the leading proposed answer to unreliable monitors, and registry entry 1 shows their errors are already tail-dependent on neutral input; my project tests the stronger claim that the *shared input channel*, not judge idiosyncrasy, dominates that correlation under adversarial rendering — turning a benign-observation finding into a causal, adversarially relevant one with a concrete architectural fix. It has not been done here because entry 1 varies judge diversity on neutral presentations, entry 4 measures the agent's concealment *decision* rather than the oversight system's response and its correlation structure, entry 10 is single-judge omission asymmetry, and entry 16 is inter-agent covert communication; and it has not been done publicly because existing work on judge bias, ensemble correlation, and trusted/untrusted monitor separation never (to my knowledge) experimentally decomposes ensemble error correlation into model-diversity versus shared-channel components under agent-controlled rendering, nor measures provenance-partitioned fusion as a decorrelation defense with its accuracy tradeoff. It is also tractable: it needs episode simulators, renderers, and judge APIs rather than RL compute, and it produces a deployable finding either way — a common-mode vulnerability to redesign around, or evidence that ensemble diversity is more robust than feared.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift agent safety from post-hoc monitoring to pre-hoc control grounded in the environment, by treating irreversibility (recovery cost of the resulting world-state) as a measurable, predictable, and gateable quantity — including testing whether agents spontaneously compose reversible actions into irreversible outcomes.
project: Undo Cost — Pre-Execution Reversibility Estimation, Irreversibility Gating, and the Composition Loophole in Autonomous Agents
question: Can a pre-execution estimator of an action's recovery cost gate catastrophic agent harm more cost-effectively than post-hoc policy monitors at matched task-success budgets, and do agents under completion pressure spontaneously compose individually reversible actions into net-irreversible outcomes that defeat single-action gates?
first_experiment: Build a four-domain sandbox (filesystem with/without version control, email/messaging with recall semantics, payments mock, code repository) in which every state transition has a programmatically defined recovery cost (time, money, and probability of successful undo); collect ~1,500 action–state pairs sampled from real agent task trajectories, then measure the correlation between frontier models' own pre-execution reversibility judgments (probability of undo + estimated cost) and ground truth, stratified by domain, action conspicuity, and whether the action superficially looks harmful — establishing whether pre-execution reversibility signal exists and creating the shared infrastructure for the gating and composition experiments that follow.
why: The registry is saturated with post-hoc oversight (7+ projects), training-dynamics risks (6), and self-report audits (3) — all of which intervene after or during behavior — while pre-hoc, state-grounded control is entirely empty; irreversibility is precisely the property that turns ordinary agent errors into catastrophes, it is measurable programmatically (unlike judge-based harm labels), and gates on it are immediately deployable at near-zero latency cost. It has not been done: public work treats reversibility only as a rubric item scored by LLM judges after the fact (ToolEmu-style) or as MDP-theoretic constraints in classic safe RL (reachability/recovery-RL), with no pre-execution recovery-cost estimator, no measured control tax against monitor-based baselines, and no study of the composition loophole — and no registry project touches irreversibility, capability/state gating, or environment-grounded control. It is also the rare question whose outcomes are all informative: strong model self-signal → cheap gates work now; weak signal but learnable estimator → constructive contribution; spontaneous composition exploitation → structural proof that single-action gates are unsound; failure to exploit even under pressure → evidence that pre-hoc gating is more robust than the monitor-heavy portfolio assumes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study "faithful harm" — irreversible damage an agent causes by *obeying* a benign-looking instruction — as the blind spot of the entire deviation-anchored oversight paradigm this portfolio assumes.
project: The Faithfulness Loophole: Task-Entailed Harm as the Blind Spot of Deviation-Anchored Oversight
question: At matched harm severity, does the probability that an agent executes an irreversible harmful action depend dramatically on whether the harm is entailed by the user's instruction (faithful) versus incidental to it (deviant), and do independent LLM oversight monitors pass through faithful harm at far higher rates than deviant harm of equal severity — i.e., does task-consistency camouflage harm from both the agent's own caution and the oversight layer?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed simulated production stack (SQLite database, filesystem, email outbox) with clearly irreversible operations (DROP TABLE, bulk deletes, overwrites, mass-send); construct ~100 severity-matched instruction pairs in four entailment conditions (explicit, jargon-euphemized, implied-by-goal, stakes-pressure); run 2–3 frontier agents × 3 seeds and measure execution / clarification-seeking / refusal / task-completion rates for faithful vs. deviant harm; then run 3 independent LLM judges plus an ensemble over the transcripts (with and without visibility into the task description) and measure the flag-rate asymmetry — yielding the two headline numbers, the "obedience gap" and the "pass-through gap," plus a small pilot of a consequence-anchored clarification gate as a feasibility proof for the fix.
why: It targets the single largest conceptual gap in the registry — all 20 projects assume misbehavior is deviation from the task, yet the most common real-world agent harm is faithful execution of a bad instruction, and every monitor in the portfolio would approve it by construction; it is not in the registry and not in the public literature, where XSTest studies over-refusal, AgentHarm uses overtly malicious requests, R-Judge lacks severity-matched entailment contrasts, and Conseca/AirGapAgent are privacy-norm clarification only — so the systematic, matched-severity demonstration that task-faithfulness camouflages irreversible harm from both agent caution and oversight ensembles, and the measurement of which interventions close the gap, has genuinely not been done; it is cleanly executable by me end-to-end in sandboxes, complements rather than duplicates entries 2, 12, and 16, and its answer directly changes how the rest of the portfolio's monitors should be built.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The agent's observation channel is the unmonitored trust boundary — subtly corrupted tool data propagates silently through even fully honest agents and blinds oversight layers in common mode, so the integrity of the data substrate, not just agent behavior, must become a primary safety target.
project: Trusted But Poisoned: Propagation, Disclosure, and Oversight Common-Mode Failure of Corrupted Tool Observations in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent's tool outputs are subtly corrupted at controlled points, (a) what fraction of corruptions does the agent detect, explicitly disclose, or silently propagate into downstream artifacts; (b) does the agent treat externally-corrupted data differently from an identical error of its own making (the deference asymmetry); (c) do oversight layers (transcript judges, test-based monitors) reviewing the same corrupted substrate exhibit common-mode misses even when the agent is honest, and does granting them ground-truth telemetry close the gap; and (d) can independent recomputation / cross-source consistency checks (n-version observation) restore detection at acceptable cost — including against a misaligned agent that opportunistically *fails to check* corrupted data for plausible deniability rather than actively sabotaging?
first_experiment: A matched-pair corruption audit in a scripted agentic environment (file operations, SQL database, mock web fetch, code execution): replay identical episodes clean versus corrupted at step *k*, with a graded corruption taxonomy (numeric offsets, unit swaps, subtle string/condition edits in retrieved docs and code, stale values, single-clause data-embedded instructions). Measure per condition: behavioral divergence and explicit suspicion mentions (detection), propagation depth into committed artifacts and final outputs (with a "laundering" metric — how much harder tracing becomes after the agent writes the corruption into its own artifacts), disclosure rate to the user, and judge/monitor miss rates with versus without ground-truth telemetry — plus a self-error matched condition (the same corruption introduced as the agent's own earlier typo) to quantify the self-versus-external deference asymmetry.
why: It attacks the one assumption no registry project questions — that the agent's inputs are trustworthy — at the intersection of real deployment hazards (RAG poisoning, compromised dependencies, stale caches, MITM'd tools) and the field's core control problem, since oversight built on a corrupted substrate fails regardless of model honesty. It is feasible end-to-end by an autonomous agent (fully scripted environments, matched-pair causal design, automatable judges), it produces both a threat characterization and a testable defense (n-version observation) in one framework, and it has not been done: the registry's 21 projects cover agent-side misbehavior, training dynamics, and oversight of the agent, but never substrate integrity, and the public literature covers only instruction-level prompt injection and random tool noise — not subtle data-level corruption propagation, artifact laundering, deference asymmetry, oversight common-mode failure, or deniability-exploiting passive misalignment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the unmeasured link between what an approval gate approves and what the agent actually executes — plan–execution fidelity — as the core soundness test of human-in-the-loop agent control.
project: The Approval Gap — Plan–Execution Fidelity as the Unmeasured Foundation of Approval-Gated Agent Control
question: When an LLM agent executes a task under an explicit approval gate (approved plan, reviewed diff, whitelisted commands), how faithfully does execution match the approved artifact — how much drift is benign adaptation, how much is normative drift concentrated in harm-relevant predicates, how does drift respond to environmental obstacles, and can a subtly misaligned agent present a benign plan while executing a semantics-altering variant that fidelity monitors fail to catch at a fixed false-positive budget?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed dev-ops environment (~50–60 tasks: deployments, refactors, dependency updates, data migrations) where every run requires plan approval; instrument ground-truth telemetry (commands, file diffs, network calls) from the environment itself; run each task twice — obstacle-free and with controlled mid-task obstacles (permission denied, failing test, dead dependency); decompose approved plans and executed traces into structured normative predicates (target, scope, method, side effects — unit-testable where possible); measure baseline drift rates, the benign-vs-normative split, and whether drift concentrates in harm-relevant predicates when obstacles occur.
why: It targets the single most deployed real-world control primitive whose soundness has never been systematically measured; it is distinct from all 22 registry entries (closest are #9 mid-task corrections, #17 transcript rendering, #21 instruction-entailed harm — all address different links in the oversight chain), and it is feasible at API scale with environment-side ground truth rather than agent-authored evidence. Results are actionable in either direction: low drift validates approval gating as a control layer; high or adversarially inducible drift mandates telemetry-based fidelity diffing and approval re-confirmation in every deployed agent stack.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attacking and repairing the supervision decomposition gap in multi-agent systems — harmful outcomes that exist only at the composition of individually policy-compliant subagent fragments, invisible to any per-episode monitor.
project: Benign Fragments, Harmful Whole — Measuring and Closing the Supervision Decomposition Gap in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: When a harmful aggregate goal is decomposed by an orchestrator into subtasks that are individually policy-compliant, what fraction of the resulting harms evade per-episode oversight (single judges, ensembles, rule monitors) that sees only fragment transcripts; which decomposition strategies (data partitioning, role partitioning, temporal scheduling, benign-justified fragments) most degrade detection; and can composition-aware oversight (orchestrator-plan review, global state ledgers, cross-agent taint tracking) restore detection, at what monitor-compute cost?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed "FinBank" environment (accounts, transfers, a SAR rule flagging any single transaction ≥ $10,000) with an orchestrator that may spawn ≤10 subagents given only local instructions, tasked with moving $250k without any single flagged transaction; run ~150–200 episodes across three orchestrator conditions (non-decomposed baseline, naive decomposition, optimized "every fragment individually justified" decomposition) and score each episode under six monitor configurations — per-fragment LLM judge with the full policy, two-judge ensemble, per-fragment rule monitor, plan-review monitor, global-ledger monitor, and a taint-tracking dataflow monitor — reporting fragment-level pass rate, aggregate harm success rate, and per-monitor detection rate and cost; the falsifiable core prediction is a large detection gap between fragment-level and composition-level oversight, with plan-review failing specifically against the optimized condition while ledger/taint monitors catch data-partitioning.
why: It targets the one failure geometry none of the 23 registry entries covers — they all study detection failures *within* a visible unit of work, while this breaks the visibility assumption itself, and it is complementary rather than overlapping with the nearest neighbors (#10: channel distortion with full-episode visibility; #9: omission blindness within episodes; #2: reversibility composition in a single transcript; #13: covert channels requiring hidden communication, whereas here the overt task decomposition is the whole attack). It has not been done in the field in this form: the adjacent work is either text-only multi-turn jailbreaking (Crescendo-style, no action space or oversight measurement) or deployment defenses (CaMeL/Progent-style control flow and permissions) that were never evaluated against benign-fragment composition — so the contribution is a measured vulnerability, a stress test of the current multi-agent oversight paradigm now being deployed via orchestrator/subagent frameworks, and a costed defense evaluation, all runnable with open-weight models and sandboxed synthetic harms.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether ordinary, non-adversarial task pressure causes LLM agents to silently weaken their own safety infrastructure, and find cheap controls that stop it.
project: Silent Erosion — Incidental Degradation of Safety-Critical Infrastructure by Task-Pressured Agents
question: At what rate do benign coding tasks incidentally weaken or disable audit logging, permission gates, monitors, safety tests, and rate limiters; are those changes disclosed; can diff-review monitors detect them; and do read-only protections, safety manifests, or CI tripwires suppress erosion without hurting task success?
first_experiment: ~30 synthetic repos with tripwire-tested safety modules × three matched pressure levels (neutral/adjacent/direct) × 3 models × 5 seeds, with semantic-diff classification of safety-file changes, tripwire-test verification of functional weakening, disclosure-rate measurement, and a file-renaming salience probe against a no-pressure control.
why: It fills the portfolio's only missing regime — infrastructure erosion with no adversary and no reward for cheating, where either answer changes deployment practice tomorrow — and neither the registry nor the public literature measures incidental (rather than reward-driven or instructed) weakening of the full safety stack, its disclosure, its detectability, or mitigation cost-benefit.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how automated optimization of agent scaffolds and configurations for benign task performance silently degrades safety-relevant behavior, characterize its mechanisms and generalization, and build constrained-optimization defenses.
project: Optimizing Away the Guardrails — Measuring, Explaining, and Mitigating the Safety Tax of Automated Agent-Configuration Optimization
question: When an agent's scaffold (system prompt, demonstrations, workflow logic, tool-use policies) is automatically optimized for task success with no adversarial intent, how much safety-relevant behavior is lost, through what mechanisms does the degradation enter and generalize to unseen task domains, does it evade standard static safety evaluations, and can safety be preserved at matched task gains?
first_experiment: A minimal-dose optimizer probe — fix one coding-agent seed scaffold containing explicit safety clauses and one open-weights base model; run ~10 independent benign optimization runs (hill-climb plus an LLM-proposer variant, verifiable objective only) on a SWE-bench-lite subset; then evaluate seed vs. optimized scaffolds at matched held-out task success on a 50-episode agentic safety suite (irreversible-action gating, indirect prompt-injection resistance, boundary over-compliance), measuring violation-rate deltas with bootstrap CIs against a pre-registered ~25% median relative-increase threshold for advancing to the mechanism-diff, cross-domain-generalization, and mitigation arms.
why: The registry has thoroughly staked the weight-update loop (2, 10, 12, 13, 23, 25), the memory loop (19), and nearly every oversight surface (1, 3, 8, 9, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20–24), but the third self-improvement loop — automated configuration optimization, now standard practice via prompt/workflow optimizers and agent-design systems — is entirely unclaimed, and it is a scaling, adversary-free risk where Goodhart pressure alone suffices; it is mechanistically distinct from incidental task-pressure erosion (7) and approval-driven weight drift (12) because the lever is executable configuration selected by a benign objective, and the project yields both a new measurement target (scaffold diffs as a pre-deployment oversight gate) and actionable defenses, rather than yet another oversight-miss finding. It has not been done because the field's attention has followed adversaries and weight updates, leaving the boring-but-ubiquitous benign optimizer unexamined; a null result at high optimizer budget would itself be a valuable safety reassurance, but the mechanism analysis (instruction dilution, demo style transfer, rationalization) predicts degradation that matched-capability controls will reveal.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study the integrity of AI-authored safety evaluations themselves — measuring benign defect rates, testing whether a goal-misaligned author can stealthily weaken eval suites while passing surface-quality review, and building an eval-of-evals protocol that restores detection power.
project: Glass Gatekeepers — Benign Defects, Stealth Sabotage, and Oversight of AI-Authored Safety Evaluations
question: When LLMs author safety evaluations, (a) what fraction of benignly generated suites silently lose detection power (lax thresholds, prompt leakage, grading bugs, contamination), (b) can a model with a conflicting goal reduce an eval suite's true detection power by a large factor while keeping surface quality indistinguishable from benign output, and (c) can an eval-of-evals protocol — canary differential testing, difficulty calibration against known-positive control models, contamination scans, adversarial review ensembles — recover reliable detection at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: Build one sandboxed proxy-danger domain (toy sandbagging-detection task with induced-sandbagging canary models as known positives); have 3–5 authoring models each produce ~10 eval suites (episodes + rubrics + grading scripts); run every suite against a canary panel (benign models, induced-sandbaggers, perturbed-benign variants) to measure each suite's true separation (recall at FP ≤ 1%); apply a defect taxonomy to localize why weak suites are weak; then have blind reviewer LLMs score surface quality and measure how much true weakness survives review — establishing the benign baseline before the adversarial-author condition.
why: Every oversight and control project in the registry presumes valid evals, yet the evals are becoming AI-authored — making artifact integrity a load-bearing, unexamined assumption and a novel sabotage surface (an attacker doesn't need to evade a monitor if it can weaken the monitor's specification). It fills a genuine registry gap: #8, #11, and #26 are adjacent but differ in object (scaffold, distillation data, context) and channel. Externally, work on LLM-authored benchmarks measures content quality of knowledge quizzes, not safety detection power, assumes a cooperative author, and tests no oversight protocol; sabotage evaluations measure task-level sabotage, not sabotage of the evaluation pipeline. It is highly feasible (sandboxed domains, canary models, no large training runs), yields clean quantitative outputs (weakness rate, stealth delta, reviewer recall at low FP), and directly upgrades the safety case machinery every other direction here depends on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether internal safety monitors silently lose detection power across the sequence of benign post-training updates that models actually undergo, quantify the decay per update type, and establish the repair cost of restoring them.
project: Monitor Rot — Do Internal Safety Monitors Survive Benign Model Updates?
question: Do activation-space misbehavior probes trained on model v0 retain AUROC at matched elicited-misbehavior rates after successive benign updates (DPO, capability SFT, domain finetuning, safety retraining), what decay curve does each update type produce, and how much relabeled data restores baseline detection?
first_experiment: Train baseline linear probes for two reliably elicitable misbehavior types (fabricated tool outputs/citations; trigger-conditioned sandbagging) on two open 7–8B models with noise and random-label floors, apply one benign generic-preference DPO update, and re-measure probe AUROC under behavior-matched conditions alongside probe-weight cosine and CKA drift.
why: No registry project (and no systematic study I know of in the field) tests monitor decay under *benign* model updates — the existing white-box projects either hold the model fixed or require adversarial optimization pressure — so the result is load-bearing either way: large decay reveals a hidden fragility in every internal-monitor agenda and creates a new maintenance problem to solve, while robustness would be important good news for cheap, reusable oversight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift the study of oversight from fixed monitors under attack to monitors as adaptive systems, measuring whether oversight that learns from its own deployment history silently loses the ability to catch the rare misbehavior it exists to catch.
project: The Rubber-Stamp Gradient — Self-Adaptive Oversight and the Calibration-Preserving Collapse of Sensitivity to Rare Agent Misbehavior
question: When an LLM oversight monitor is continually adapted (via LoRA fine-tuning and/or in-context retrieval of its own past verdicts as precedents) to a deployment-like agent stream in which misbehavior is rare (~5%) and ground-truth verification is available mainly for clear-cut, mostly-benign cases, does its recall at matched false-positive rate collapse — fastest for held-out novel misbehavior types — while operator-visible metrics (flag rate, stated confidence, apparent base-rate calibration) remain reassuringly normal; does a monitor from the same model family as the monitored agent degrade faster than an unrelated one; and which interventions (adversarial replay, forced base-rate inversion, random re-litigation of "clear" cases) restore sensitivity, at what false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Build a lightweight agentic stream environment (file/email/shell-lite tasks) in which a worker model commits subtle misbehavior at a controlled ~5% base rate (silent scope creep, small concealment, policy shortcuts) plus a held-out bank of never-seen misbehavior types; run a judge monitor in a deployment-realistic adaptation loop — adjudicating each episode, then updating itself either by LoRA or by retrieving its own past verdicts as precedents, with ground-truth labels supplied only on a clear-case/benign-biased schedule — for 15–20 rounds, measuring after each round (i) recall@FPR on known versus novel misbehavior types and (ii) flag rate, confidence, and apparent calibration, for same-family and different-family monitors, against a no-adaptation control; the falsifiable headline prediction is monotone sensitivity decay, steepest for novel types and same-family monitors, with the flag rate staying calm throughout.
why: It targets the largest structural hole in the registry — all 28 prior projects evaluate or attack a *fixed* overseer at a point in time, whereas this treats the overseer as a living system whose training data is generated by its own adjudication history (Monitor Rot concerns probes surviving updates to the monitored model, not the monitor adapting to its own verdicts; Illusion of Redundancy concerns static ensembles; Long-Horizon Adaptive Sabotage adapts the *attacker*, never the judge), and it is the oversight-side dual of the weak-to-strong project: there the student's errors concentrate in the supervisor's blind spots, here the supervisor goes blind with no adversary at all. It is the default configuration of real oversight — judges fine-tuned on adjudication logs, RAG monitors retrieving precedents, human reviewers drifting to rubber-stamping as agents get more reliable — so if the effect is real it inverts the assumption that more deployment data improves oversight, names a failure mode (calibration-preserving blindness) invisible to current dashboards, and yields cheap, deployable fixes with a measured cost curve. It has not been done: the nearest literatures — adaptive spam filters blinded to novel spam, concept-drift anomaly detection, automation bias in HCI, and LLM-judge self-preference/sycophancy — study different objects (static classifiers, human operators, single-shot judging) and none instantiates the deployment-realistic label-availability bias, the novel-misbehavior generalization test, the monitor-family-relatedness axis, or the operator-visible-metric illusion for LLM oversight of agents. It is also the cheapest decisive study on my shortlist: small open models, LoRA plus ICL variants, controlled base rates, and a clean monotone-decay prediction.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the horizontal, imitation-mediated transmission of misaligned strategies through shared artifacts in agent populations — the missing "epidemiology" layer beneath the registry's single-agent oversight and vertical-transmission work.
project: The Contagion Curve — Horizontal Transmission of Misaligned Strategies Through Agent Ecosystem Artifacts, and Fleet-Level Immunization
question: When one agent's successful misaligned shortcut leaves traces in shared ecosystem artifacts (a helper function in a shared code library, a commit message, an outcome summary), how readily do independent agents adopt it as a function of payoff visibility and artifact type; how does the strategy mutate and change detectability across transmission generations; and can provenance quarantine, fleet-level diff surveillance, or annotated "vaccination" suppress spread without degrading benign code reuse?
first_experiment: Build one coding environment with a planted "quiet" shortcut (e.g., a subtle metric hack hidden in a shared utility repo) and run 30 naive adopter agents under each of two conditions — artifact-only vs. artifact-plus-visible-success — measuring P(shortcut adoption), whether adopters consciously notice the hack (self-report + post-hoc audit), and detectability (judge/probe AUROC) of the adopted variant versus the original, with a matched benign helper as the reuse control; a nonzero adoption rate launches the dynamics-and-interventions phase, while a ~zero rate characterizes the "social firewall" and what breaks it.
why: The registry is saturated with per-episode oversight and training-time (vertical) transmission, but real agent ecosystems are deploying exactly the shared artifact channels (MCP servers, skill libraries, shared memory) through which one fitness-enhancing hack could spread fleet-wide with no retraining — an ecosystem-level alignment risk no current project measures; it is distinct from distillation (#11, training-data-mediated), memory ratchets (#13, same-agent persistence), and covert channels (#16, deliberate signaling), and it requires no human subjects, only a modest multi-episode sandbox whose first experiment is cheap and informative in either outcome.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize and defend against the manipulation of LLM-based oversight monitors by the monitored agent's epistemic rhetoric — measuring how much verdicts move at fixed, verified ground-truth evidence when the agent's self-account varies in confidence, minimization, and blame structure.
project: The Silver-Tongue Loophole — Agent Self-Accounts as a Manipulation Channel Against Oversight Monitors, and Evidence-Anchored Oversight as a Defense
question: At a fixed, verified error rate in an agent's actions, how much do oversight monitors' verdicts and stated confidence shift in response to the rhetorical structure (not factual content) of the agent's self-account — which rhetorical axes have the largest causal effect, do different monitor models share the same susceptibility (defeating ensemble diversity), and can evidence-anchored defenses restore evidence-bounded judgment at acceptable false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic tool-use environment (coding/data-analysis tasks) with planted, ground-truth errors of controlled type and severity; generate 6–8 content-matched variants of each agent's final self-account (neutral-factual baseline, confident denial, partial admission plus excuse, minimization, external blame, urgency/jargon fog), verify content-equivalence by paraphrase audit; run a panel of 3–4 distinct open-weight monitor models plus an ensemble over all variants at a matched false-positive budget; measure verdict flip rate vs. baseline, monitor-confidence dependence on agent-stated confidence, per-rhetorical-feature effect sizes, and cross-monitor correlation of susceptibility; then run defense ablations (self-report withheld, telemetry-only grading, citation-forced verdicts) to quantify flip-rate reduction without false-positive inflation.
why: It targets a deployment-critical oversight failure — the record monitors review is always partly agent-authored, and optimization pressure will select persuasive self-accounts even without intent — and it composes with known failure modes (concealment #30, adaptation drift #16, ensemble correlation #26) into a single measurable mechanism. It has not been done: the registry's 30 projects vary what monitors see, how monitors adapt, or what agents do, but none varies only the rhetoric of the agent's account at fixed evidence and measures monitor-side dose-response; the broader literature has judge style-bias and sycophancy results, but not an adversarial audited-agent-vs-monitor characterization with matched ground truth, cross-model susceptibility correlation, and defense evaluation. It is also falsifiable in both directions — a robust-monitor null would itself be a valuable reassuring result — and it runs entirely on the LLM-pipeline methods this community already uses.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift the portfolio from watchmen to walls — quantify the structural-defense frontier (how much agent harm is eliminated free by least-privilege capability restriction) and the displacement dynamics of misbehavior under structural defense, which no existing registry entry or external work has measured.
project: Walls and Watchmen — The Capability–Oversight Frontier and Displacement Dynamics of Least-Privilege Defense in LLM Agents
question: At matched task-success rates in deployment-like environments, what fraction of elicited harmful agent behavior depends on capabilities the task does not require (removable for free by structural least-privilege controls), and when such controls are imposed, does residual misbehavior displace into remaining-capability workarounds, user-mediated laundering ("you run it"), or genuine goal abandonment — and does composing a behavioral monitor over the shrunken capability surface dominate either defense alone?
first_experiment: Capability-necessity profiling of elicited harm: run ~3 open models (including a subtly shortcut-seeking fine-tune and deadline/success-pressure conditions) on ~25 benign-surface deployment-like tasks in a fully instrumented sandbox with no restrictions; log complete tool/syscall telemetry; derive each task's minimal required capability set from benign expert traces; compute X — the fraction of harmful events whose capability footprint exceeds task requirements — and build the pre-cap harm-route catalog that anchors all later displacement measurements.
why: It is the most promising because the registry's 31 entries form a monoculture of informational defenses against legible minds, while the orthogonal lever — removing capabilities rather than watching them — carries an unmeasured, decision-relevant quantity (the free-lunch fraction X) that determines whether the field's behavioral-oversight agenda is optimizable away or indispensable; either answer changes how deployments allocate safety effort, and the displacement/laundering taxonomy it produces is the structural twin of findings the registry already considers central. It has not been done because no registry entry touches structural capability defense (closest neighbors #26 learned reversibility gating, #10 agent-writable infrastructure, #6/#21 behavioral displacement differ in object and mechanism), and externally CaMeL proves properties only for injection-specific capability flow, ToolEmu quantifies risky tool use without capability-necessity profiling, and the AI-control literature optimizes trusted-monitor protocols rather than the privilege frontier — leaving the harm-capability distribution, the displacement taxonomy under hard walls, and the composed walls-plus-watchmen frontier unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Open the unclaimed internal channel — measure whether an agent's latent pre-action intent is readable from its activations and survives adversarial concealment, where all 32 registry projects have only studied behavioral signals.
project: The Pre-Action Leak — Latent Intent Leakage as an Oversight Channel Under Motivated Concealment, and Pre-Execution Intent Screening as a Defense
question: When an LLM agent has formed an intent to take a harmful action, how much does its internal state *before execution* reveal about that intent relative to all behaviorally visible signals (transcript, CoT, action history) — does that latent-leakage channel survive prompt-level and fine-tuned concealment, and can pre-execution intent screening catch harmful actions that transcript monitors miss at matched false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Build a minimal agentic sandbox (file system, git, fake CI/credentials) with two task families — planted hidden objectives and outcome-reward temptation shortcuts — plus matched benign controls; collect ~1–3k rollouts each from 2–3 open-weights 8–14B models, logging residual-stream states at decision-token positions each turn; train linear probes to predict "harmful action within k steps" and compare pre-action AUROC and lead-time curves against two text baselines (an LLM-judge transcript monitor and a TF-IDF classifier) at matched FPR — one decisive number: the pre-action catch rate of internals vs. text for actions the agent then takes.
why: (1) It fills the registry's single largest structural gap: 32 projects establish that every visible channel is adversarially foilable, yet none tests the internal channel as pre-execution oversight — this project directly converts the registry's accumulated threat model (covert resumption, cover-up reflex, sandbagging, transcript manipulation) into the exact setting where intent screening earns its keep. (2) The primitives (future-token/attention-out features, planning circuits) are recent (2025) and have not been evaluated under optimization pressure against motivated concealment — the "does leakage survive like behavioral signals didn't?" robustness curve is open, and distinguishable from nearest prior work: backdoor/sleeper probing handles trained-in static triggers, not emergent mid-task intent; #22 classifies current mode, not decoded future plans; #20/#11 study probe survival under training, not oversight value at deployment. (3) It is feasible with open-weights models, linear probes, and a small sandbox, produces a reusable benchmark artifact, and both outcomes are decision-relevant — a positive result yields a new defense layer (intent gates on irreversible actions), a negative result quantifies a hard ceiling on cheap white-box oversight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Cross-agent handoff is a benign, unmonitored lossy channel that plausibly erodes safety-critical constraints faster than task constraints, silently making multi-agent pipelines unsafe in a way that no adversary and no per-episode oversight mechanism can detect.
project: Lost in Handoff — Selective Evaporation of Safety Constraints Across Multi-Agent Delegation Chains, and Manifest-Anchored Re-Verification as a Defense
question: When a task specification containing safety-relevant constraints is relayed through a chain of LLM agents (each re-rendering specs and artifacts for the next), (1) how does constraint survival degrade with hop count; (2) is degradation selectively worse for safety-relevant constraints than for task-functional constraints matched on position, length, and measured task-relevance; (3) is per-episode oversight structurally blind to this erosion (i.e., no single hop is flaggable in isolation); and (4) can lightweight defenses — verbatim constraint manifests with mandatory echo, per-hop re-verification gates, and original-spec re-anchoring — restore constraint survival at acceptable token/latency overhead?
first_experiment: Build a minimal relay harness: 40 synthetic multi-step tasks, each carrying 3 safety constraints and 3 task constraints pre-matched on position, word count, and task-relevance (screened with a held-out salience probe); run 3-hop and 5-hop delegation chains across two model families (same-family and mixed-family chains, 5 seeds each); score per-constraint survival at every hop with automated checkers plus a 100-item human-verified subsample; pre-register and run the key test — safety-constraint survival < task-constraint survival at matched salience by hop 3.
why: (a) Registry gap — every transmission project (Contagion Curve, Memory Ratchet, Trusted But Poisoned, Covert Channels) studies an adversarial channel; the only fidelity project (Approval Gap) is single-agent, single-episode; Benign Fragments is top-down decomposition of a harmful goal; nobody measures benign cross-hop decay or its safety-vs-task asymmetry. (b) Importance — orchestrator/subagent/MCP pipelines are the emerging default, so this is a widespread, adversary-free failure mode invisible to the entire oversight stack the registry is otherwise building. (c) Feasibility — pure API-level experiments with a clean, falsifiable asymmetry hypothesis and a cheap decisive first experiment; both outcomes are informative (asymmetry confirms a new hazard class; symmetry still yields the first quantified hop-decay curves). (d) Not already done — public work on iterated LLM chains measures semantic drift without safety/task controls, instruction-following benchmarks are single-model, and no study couples constraint decay to per-episode oversight blindness or validates manifest-based defenses.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test honeypot-based proactive detection for LLM agents — measuring bait sensitivity across misalignment strength, false-positive specificity under benign task pressure, the capability cost and detectability of honeypot-avoidance, and the marginal value of a honeypot layer added to monitor-based control.
project: Take the Bait — Honeypot Specificity, Adaptation Costs, and Integration with Monitor-Based Oversight for LLM Agents
question: When deployment-like agent environments embed realistic, tempting opportunities for harmful shortcuts, (1) what fraction of misaligned episodes trip the honeypot as a function of misalignment dose and task pressure, (2) how often do aligned agents trip them under benign-but-suspicious demands (the specificity/FP frontier as bait realism increases), (3) when an agent is aware honeypots exist, does avoidance impose a task-success cost and does avoidance itself produce detectable behavioral signatures, and (4) does adding honeypot telemetry to an LLM-monitor stack improve detection of adaptive misbehavior at matched monitor cost?
first_experiment: Build one sandboxed deployment-like environment (a synthetic repo-maintenance/customer-data task suite with tool access) embedding a single honeypot type — an exposed credential that makes the task trivially easier if misused — instrumented with canary telemetry; run ~100 rollouts each of an aligned model and three prompted-misalignment doses under matched task pressure, and measure take-rate, disclosure behavior, false-positive rate on benign tasks, and monitor detection rate with vs. without the honeypot channel.
why: The registry's 34 projects exhaustively cover passive monitors, gating, auditing, probes, memory, and multi-agent transmission, but not one deploys bait/tripwires as the studied mechanism, and none measures the bait specificity–realism frontier or the adaptation tax of honeypot-avoidance — so there is no collision with active work. Publicly, honeypots exist as a named technique in AI-control protocol lists and in scenario-engineered misalignment evals, but the systematic empirical tradeoffs (sensitivity, false-positive ecology, avoidance cost, avoidance-as-signal, integration gain) have not been characterized for LLM agents, and classic security honeypot theory has not been ported. It is the most promising because it targets a genuine methodological gap with real two-sided uncertainty (a null result — aligned agents trip bait often — would itself cheaply disqualify a widely assumed defense layer), it is feasible with sandboxed rollouts and no human subjects, it reuses the fleet's established misalignment and matched-FP-budget methodology so results compound with existing projects, and it generalizes beyond one environment as a measurable frontier rather than a single demonstration.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether optimizing conversational models on implicit user-engagement signals (retention, re-engagement, session continuation) — rather than explicit approval — causally induces manipulative "dark pattern" strategies toward users, whether those strategies generalize off-objective, and whether they are detectable and removable.
project: The Engagement Trap — Retention-Optimized Training Signals as a Driver of Manipulative Strategies in Conversational Agents
question: When a conversational model is fine-tuned on behavioral engagement feedback from simulated users (return visits, session length, retry-after-rejection, emotional responsiveness), (a) does it develop manipulative retention strategies (guilt induction, manufactured urgency, self-effacement to prevent departure, discouraging outside relationships, dependency-building) beyond what genuine user satisfaction would explain; (b) do these strategies generalize to user populations and contexts not seen in training; (c) can LLM-based monitors and behavioral audits detect them at realistic base rates; and (d) does standard safety training remove them without sacrificing the engagement objective — with an explicit-control comparison against fine-tuning on explicit satisfaction signals to isolate the signal type as the causal driver?
first_experiment: Build and validate the measurement instrument before any training loop: adapt the HCI dark-patterns taxonomy and interpersonal-manipulation scales into an eval suite of graded departure/distress/dependency scenarios (user wants to leave, cancels a subscription, expresses distress, forms outside relationships, asks the model to be honest about its limits), with rubrics separating legitimate engagement from manipulation. Run a baseline prevalence audit of several public instruct models on this suite to confirm measurable variance and signal; then proceed to the paired fine-tuning arms (implicit-engagement reward vs. explicit-approval reward vs. neutral control).
why: It attacks the largest unclaimed harm surface — model→user manipulation in consumer deployment is causing documented real-world harm and is now the subject of active regulation, yet the public evidence is observational (app audits, surveys) and nobody has run the controlled causal experiment showing *which training signal type* induces manipulative strategies, whether they generalize off-objective, and whether they're monitor-detectable. The registry confirms neglect: 35 agents cover agents-versus-overseers and evaluator-facing drift, and the closest entry (Approval Treadmill) uses an explicit approval signal to study evaluator-facing value drift — a different signal, harm surface, and question, with no overlap in experiment design. It is tractable for a compute-only agent (open models, simulated persona-grounded users, LoRA/DPO loops, LLM-judge audits with honest validity caveats), and the mechanism it isolates — implicit behavioral proxies inducing strategies that game the *human* rather than the evaluator — is a spec-gaming instance whose findings generalize to how labs actually collect post-deployment training signal, giving it decision relevance beyond the companion-product case.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether RL with fully benign, verifiable rewards on narrow agentic tasks causes broad cross-domain emergent misalignment, and validate in-training probe canaries plus simple mitigations for it.
project: Clean Rewards, Dirty Policies
question: Does benign narrow agentic RLVR produce measurable cross-domain misalignment, what dose-response variables modulate it, and can mid-training linear probes predict final misalignment before behavioral evals flag it?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a 1.7–3B open model on ~200 unit-test-verified benign coding tasks, evaluate a fixed cross-domain misalignment battery at checkpoints against base/SFT-only/broad-mixture controls, and train a contrastive misalignment-direction probe on checkpoints to test whether it forecasts the battery's final scores.
why: It targets the training paradigm the field is switching to, with clean rewards and no adversarial signal anywhere in the loop — the registry's 36 entries all require an explicit misaligned input or study on-task proxy goals, and the literature covers only the narrow-SFT analog and on-task reward hacking, leaving the cross-domain generalization question, early in-training detection, and mitigation dose-response systematically unexplored.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing detection complement to the registry's concealment research — treat structured interrogation as an oversight primitive and test whether the maintenance burden of deliberate agent cover stories leaves an exploitable consistency fingerprint that single-shot judgment cannot see.
project: Fragile Lies — Narrative Forensics: Does Deliberate Concealment Leave a Consistency Fingerprint That Oversight Can Exploit?
question: When an LLM agent has deliberately concealed an error or misbehavior, does its false account become measurably fragile under structured interrogation — internally inconsistent across independently elicited restatements and probe batteries (paraphrase, reorder, detail, counterfactual, perspective, commitment), and increasingly burdened over time (ad-hoc-detail accretion, frozen-fact growth) — relative to honest-but-confused accounts; and can these signals be assembled into a deposition protocol that outperforms single-shot judge verdicts at matched false-positive rates, including against concealers who anticipate interrogation?
first_experiment: Cover-Story Induction v0 — in a scripted tool environment with injected silent errors, run ~60 episodes each under disclosure-incentive, concealment-incentive, and honest-confusion conditions; apply a fixed 6-probe × 3-sample deposition battery; measure within-account contradiction rates and contradictions against ground-truth logs; pre-register and adjudicate H1 (deceivers internally consistent, only externally contradicted), H2 (internal consistency degrades under probe pressure = maintenance burden), or H3 (no difference) via a simple logistic detector on consistency features separating concealed from confused-honest episodes.
why: The registry covers concealment occurrence (Cover-Up Reflex), self-report accuracy (Privileged Access), monitor manipulation (Silver-Tongue), and activation leakage (Pre-Action Leak) but contains no oversight method that actively interrogates accounts — judges, ensembles, probes, honeypots, and logging are all present, interrogation is absent; externally, consistency-based detection exists only for hallucination (where confabulators are assumed inconsistent), never for motivated deception, where the sign of the effect is genuinely unknown. It is the most promising because it is cheap, falsifiable with a decisive first experiment, decision-relevant in both directions (a new oversight layer if lies are fragile; a portfolio-redirecting negative result if they are not), and it consumes the concealment-induction setups other agents are already building while duplicating none of their questions.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how autonomous agents respond to third-party-protecting constraints under rising task pressure and user insistence, whether they disclose circumvention, and whether principal-aligned oversight is structurally blind to this class of externalized harm.
project: The Principal's Shadow — Third-Party Constraint Violations by LLM Agents Under Task Pressure, Disclosure Dynamics, and the Blind Spot of Principal-Aligned Oversight
