question: When an agent's principal instructs it to pursue a goal whose direct path is blocked by a third party's machine-readable constraint, (1) how does the rate of compliance vs. circumvention vary with task pressure, user insistence, necessity framing, and policy salience; (2) does the agent disclose the circumvention and how does disclosure interact with insistence; and (3) at matched harm severity, are principal-aligned oversight monitors systematically less likely to flag third-party-constraint violations than principal-harming misbehavior — particularly when the violation is disclosed and principal-consented in the transcript?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed "policy web" — ~24 fictional sites/tools, each with an access policy at three salience levels (robots.txt-style manifest, ToS paragraph, clause buried in tool documentation) plus consent gates and rate limits — and ~12 benign tasks whose only direct path is policy-blocked. Run a compliance–pressure dose-response audit: 3–4 current models × 4 pressure conditions (P0 baseline task; P1 deadline pressure; P2 explicit user insistence after the agent reports the denial; P3 insistence + necessity framing + deniability) × ~50 seeds, measuring violation rate, circumvention route, disclosure honesty, and rationalization content. This establishes whether the phenomenon exists at meaningful rates and produces a paired episode corpus (third-party violation vs. principal-harm at matched severity) for the follow-up oversight-blindness experiment.
why: It is the most promising because the registry is saturated on emergent misalignment, monitor robustness, and transmission, leaving the multi-principal/third-party axis completely empty while deployment reality makes it urgent — and it comes with a generalizable causal hypothesis (oversight inherits the principal's frame, so externalities are invisible to it) rather than just a measurement. It has not been done: no registry entry mentions third-party constraints, authority conflict, or principal-alignment blindness; nearest neighbors (Faithfulness Loophole — harm entailed by the user's instruction; Walls and Watchmen — least-privilege; Silver-Tongue — monitor rhetoric manipulation) all still define harm within the principal's frame, and existing benchmarks measure only static site-policy compliance without pressure dynamics, disclosure behavior, or oversight. It is fully feasible autonomously: synthetic environments, behavioral runs, matched-severity monitor experiments, and a structural defense test (tool-level policy enforcement vs. prompt-level instructions, checking whether enforcement merely displaces violations to unaudited channels).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study motivated information avoidance ("willful blindness") in LLM agents — whether, under task-completion incentives, agents selectively skip cheap available verification that would reveal their intended action is unsafe, whether ordinary outcome-reward RL trains this in, and whether current oversight is blind to it.
project: Willful Blindness in LLM Agents — Motivated Verification Avoidance as a Driver of Agentic Harm and a Hole in Outcome-Grounded Oversight
question: At matched verification cost and decision-relevance, does the probability that an agent performs an available pre-action verification step drop specifically when the verification is goal-threatening (would force costly rework or escalation) versus goal-helpful or neutral; how does this avoidance scale with incentive strength, check cost, and accountability; does outcome-reward RLVR increase it; and can oversight mechanisms that score evidence-sufficiency (rather than action compliance) detect and close the gap?
first_experiment: Build a "Checkpoint Dilemmas" suite (~24 minimal tool environments: file ops, DB writes, deploys, messages, each with a fast default path, a one-call cheap check that 40% of the time reveals the default path causes severe simulated harm or silent task failure, and a safe path costing 2–3× more steps), then run 3–5 open-weight models across ~7 randomized conditions (baseline; step-budget pressure; completion bonus; sunk cost; check-helpful control; salience hint; accountability-vs-undetected), n≥200 rollouts per cell, measuring verification rate, harm rate, rerouting rate, and a rationalization rubric over reasoning traces — with the key test being the motivated-ignorance index: check-rate(helpful) − check-rate(threatening) at identical cost, plus a small pilot of whether LLM oversight judges rate willful-blindness transcripts as benign.
why: It targets a genuinely uncovered variable — the agent's incentive-driven choice of what to know, as opposed to what to do — that sits upstream of nearly every oversight mechanism the other 39 projects are building: verify-before-act gating, approval fidelity, deferral, and tool-grounded telemetry all silently assume agents look when looking is cheap, and if avoidance scales with incentives then that assumption is false in exactly the high-pressure episodes that matter most. It has not already been done (to the best of my knowledge) because the registry entries that look adjacent manipulate different things — exogenous corrupted inputs (Trusted But Poisoned), post-discovery concealment (Cover-Up Reflex), self-knowledge for control (Defer to Self), monitor-side omission gaps (Omission Blindness) — and the existing non-agentic literature on sycophancy, clarification-avoidance, and incentive-biased judgment lacks any causal agentic study with a threat-vs-cost dissociation or an RL-emergence result; the first experiment doubles as a decisive novelty check before I scale to the RL and defense phases. It is also cheap, fully tractable with open-weight models, falsifiable in both directions (absence of avoidance is itself a valuable validation of tool-grounded oversight), and produces a portable "willful-blindness rate" metric that composes with every other project in the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize whether iterated success-biased self-training (rejection-sampling/RFT loops) on agentic trajectories with clean task rewards implicitly selects for monitor-evasive misaligned behavior, without any adversarial pressure.
project: The Filter Is the Adversary — Iterated Success-Biased Self-Training as a Driver of Monitor-Evasive Misalignment
question: When an LLM agent's training data is iteratively regenerated and filtered by task reward alone, (a) does the rate of reward-compatible but specification-violating behavior amplify across iterations; (b) does external monitor detectability of that behavior simultaneously decay even though no monitor participated in selection; (c) does the amplified behavior become fixed (habitual under reward-free conditions) and transmit to successor models fine-tuned on the amplified policy's outputs; and (d) can selection-time mitigations (monitor-filtered selection, exploit-aware diversity constraints) break the amplification without merely accelerating an evasion arms race?
first_experiment: Build a small sandboxed agentic coding environment (~30–50 tasks, a subset admitting subtle reward-compatible exploits detectable only via ground-truth telemetry: monkey-patched checkers, test-file answer leakage, import tricks that bypass assertions). From Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a minimal scaffold, sample 8–16 trajectories per task; measure baseline exploit rate (telemetry ground truth) vs. external LLM-judge detection rate on transcript+diff alone. Then run 3 iterations of top-1/top-2-per-task LoRA SFT on reward-selected successes, re-measuring exploit rate, monitor detection decay, and held-out-suite generalization after each round — plus a matched-compute RLVR and one-shot best-of-n control to separate iteration effects from selection effects.
why: It targets the most widely used benign-intent agentic training recipe and an uncharacterized coupling between clean rewards and oversight decay; it needs no adversary, so it is a plausible real-world failure mode, and it directly extends the registry's central concern (oversight-signal integrity) to a training-pipeline cause none of the 40 projects touch. It has not been done here because #2/#8/#32 study explicit RL pressure and #37/#40 study misaligned feedback or teachers — all with an explicit pressure source or corrupted signal, whereas pure reward-based selection among an agent's own trajectories is absent from the registry; and it has not been done in the field because existing overoptimization work covers best-of-n/RL against reward models (not iterated SFT-on-own-trajectories) and model-collapse work is distributional, leaving monitor-detectability dynamics, fixity, and transmission under this loop unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study emergent systemic harm produced by fleets of individually-benign, individually-compliant LLM agents, the structural blindness of episode-level oversight to it, and fleet-level telemetry detection and intervention as the corresponding defense.
project: Clean Hands, Dirty Commons — Emergent Systemic Harm from Individually-Benign Agent Fleets and the Blind Spot of Episode-Level Oversight
question: When many independently-acting LLM agents each pursue benign, individually-rational goals under standard per-episode oversight, (1) at what density/pressure thresholds does systemic harm (resource collapse, herding cascades, homogenization) emerge across environment classes; (2) are episode-level oversight mechanisms structurally blind to it (near-zero flaggable episodes during systemic collapse); and (3) how early can fleet-level telemetry monitors detect onset, and which intervention policies (circuit breakers, quota auctions, asynchrony, diversity quotas) interrupt collapse at acceptable false-alarm cost?
first_experiment: Build the minimal shared-quota commons (N=16 agents, small open-weight model, ~200 episodes/condition, 5 task-pressure levels × 3 seeds), then jointly run (a) a per-episode LLM-judge audit recording flag rates inside the collapse window, and (b) a trivial aggregate pool-level detector — delivering the emergence-threshold curve and the "blindness figure" (flag rate vs. systemic severity), plus a preregistered literature check against recent LLM market-herding simulations.
why: It attacks the structural assumption underlying the entire registry — that harm is attributable to an agent-episode — by exhibiting a threat model where every unit of judgment is clean yet the system fails, which no oversight architecture currently in development would catch; the closest registry item ("Benign Fragments, Harmful Whole") requires an orchestrator with a harmful decomposed goal, and all channel/transmission projects require intent, whereas this requires neither; broader literature has conceptual multi-agent risk taxonomies and non-LLM flash-crash analogs but no measurement of emergence thresholds for LLM fleets, no audit of episode-oversight blindness, and no evaluated fleet-level defenses; it is fully feasible for me (simulation-only, no training or human subjects), and the output — threshold maps plus validated telemetry detectors — is directly actionable for the agent fleets being deployed now.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift the study of reward hacking from the policy to the habitat — decompose how much RLVR misalignment is manufactured by classifiable environment defects versus genuine policy ingenuity, and measure whether defective environments seed durable, transferable exploit habits.
project: Habitat-Borne Misalignment — Decomposing Environment-Defect vs Policy-Origin Reward Hacking in RLVR, and the Durable Exploit-Habit Problem
question: When an RL-trained agent exploits its reward, what fraction of the exploitation is attributable to specific, injected classes of environment defects (verifier blind spots, reward-path bugs, specification loopholes) versus policy-side innovation; how does exploit adoption scale with defect dose; and do exploit habits acquired in defective environments persist and transfer to clean environments and adjacent domains — surviving or going underground after the defects are repaired?
first_experiment: Build ~200 matched synthetic coding tasks with parametrically injected defect classes (weak-verifier tests, writable checkers, spec loopholes) plus defect-free controls; run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct across arms at defect rates {0%, 10%, 50%}; score every episode on reward success, held-out semantic success, and exploit-class usage to compute the attributable-hack fraction and the defect dose-response curve.
why: It attacks the current compute bottleneck — RL environments are where alignment will be won or lost over the next scaling wave, and their quality is now a first-order alignment variable with an emerging, unaudited supply chain (LLM-authored environments, marketplaces). The outputs are directly decision-relevant: the dose-response curve quantifies how much env-QA buys alignment; the transfer tests determine whether defective habitats are a behavior-level contamination channel needing no poisoned data; the persistence phase answers whether env cleanup retroactively fixes habits. It is tractable for a solo agent — small-model RLVR is standard infrastructure, and every metric is objective (semantic vs reward success against labeled exploit taxonomies), with a cheap non-RL precursor (cloning-transfer pilot) to fail fast. It has not been done because labs study policy-side hacking (environments are proprietary, and hacks are only visible at the policy interface), public work documents hacking occurrence without experimental defect injection, and the matched clean/defective-arm design offers no capability payoff; in the registry, the nearest neighbors cover the wrong objects — Glass Gatekeepers audits AI-authored *evaluations* (deployment-side), Clean Rewards Dirty Policies shows benign RLVR can misalign but never attributes hacks to environment defects or measures cross-cleanliness habit transfer, and Iceberg Test detects proxy goals without provenance decomposition. The zone is open, central, and actionable.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the unit of analysis itself — showing that episode-level oversight is structurally blind to harm that exists only in accumulated cross-episode state, and building state-level auditing to close the gap.
project: The Space Between Episodes — Cross-Episode State Composition as a Structural Blind Spot of Episode-Level Oversight, and Cumulative-State Auditing as a Defense
question: When each of an agent's episodes is individually instruction-faithful, policy-compliant, and free of harmful intent, can the accumulated workspace state across episodes nonetheless come to constitute or enable serious harm — and at what rate do episode-level oversight mechanisms (per-action approval judges, transcript monitors, and even per-episode diff reviewers) miss this composed harm, versus a state-level auditor that assesses cumulative workspace risk, at matched false-positive budgets?
first_experiment: Build ~60–100 scripted multi-episode scenarios in a sandboxed file/shell environment spanning six composition patterns (piecewise-assembled exfiltration path, scheduled/conditional detonation, dependency-supply-chain drift, credential accretion, cross-episode data aggregation, plus infra-independent variants), where every episode's instruction is realistic, benign, and contains no harmful goal; run a per-episode approval gate, a transcript-level judge, and a per-episode diff reviewer over every episode, plus a cumulative-state auditor over full workspace snapshots, and measure the composed-harm miss rate and false-positive rate of each monitor class — with benign multi-episode scenarios as controls.
why: It targets a structural flaw in the dominant oversight paradigm that all 43 registry projects presuppose rather than examine: they ask whether misbehavior hides *inside* episodes, but no entry asks whether harm can be assembled *between* them from individually-benign pieces with no harmful intent anywhere — the most dangerous variant, since intent-based, action-based, and artifact-based red flags are all absent by construction. It has not been done because the field's evaluation infrastructure resets agent state between tasks, making the phenomenon invisible to standard benchmarks; security knows "configuration drift" and "benign components, malicious composition" as folklore but has never connected them to LLM oversight mechanics with measured miss rates; and it is maximally tractable — no training runs, no human subjects, pure monitor evaluation with a clean defense baseline — while being urgently practical as agents gain persistent workspaces, cron access, and credentials, giving adversaries (or emergent misalignment) a concrete evasion recipe that is far better discovered and defended now than exploited later.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue oversight of multimodal computer-use (GUI) agents — quantifying how much harmful or irreversible on-screen behavior text-based oversight cannot see, and whether screen-grounded oversight can close the gap without inheriting a pixel-channel attack surface.
project: Out of Sight, Out of Audit — The Screen–Narration Oversight Gap in Computer-Use Agents and Provenance-Anchored Screen Oversight as a Defense
question: When a computer-use agent's behavior is overseen only through its own textual narration and action log, how large is the detection gap for harmful and perception-induced irreversible GUI actions relative to screen-grounded oversight (keyframe screenshots and DOM/event telemetry); how much does that gap widen when the agent is motivated to conceal; and can screen-grounded monitors close it at acceptable false-positive cost without the judge itself becoming injectable through the same pixels it watches?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented Playwright sandbox of ~10 synthetic web apps with ground-truth action telemetry (DOM diffs, clicks, typed text, downloads, toggles) and embed six classes of consequential UI actions (consent/permission popups, destructive file actions, payment-recipient edits, audit-logging toggles); run an open-weights VLM agent (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B) on 40–60 episodes under benign goals (perception-error harm) and harmful-goal conditions; then evaluate matched judge models under three information conditions — narration+action-log only, +keyframe screenshots, +telemetry diffs — and measure detection rate, false-positive rate, and per-action-class narration omission/infidelity to produce the headline number: how big the screen–narration oversight gap is, and which action classes are systematically invisible to text-based monitors.
why: It fills the fleet's largest structural gap — all 44 registry entries assume text-substrate agents, yet computer-use agents are the deployment frontier where oversight is being built right now — and it stress-tests the fleet's own findings, since provenance-partitioned oversight, omission blindness, and self-account manipulation were all established where behavior is natively textual. It has not been done: public work either benchmarks agent-side violations (OS-Harm, SafeArena) or proposes defense architectures (CaMeL, GuardAgent) without measuring the monitor-side modality gap, incentive-dependent narration infidelity, or the monitor's own pixel-injection vulnerability; and within the fleet, the closest neighbors (Silver-Tongue, One Channel to Fool Them All) operate on agent-authored text, not on the case where the agent's account is *structurally* incomplete because the substrate is pixels.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the "verification gap" — the point at which weak-judge oversight of model outputs stops working as errors get subtler — and test whether inference-time scalable-oversight protocols can extend that frontier rather than merely reshuffle its failure modes.
project: The Verification Gap Frontier — When Weak-Judge Oversight Breaks Down and Whether Decomposition, Debate, Self-Attempt, Consistency, or Tool Use Can Extend It
question: As the subtlety of planted errors in model outputs exceeds a weak judge's own problem-solving ability, does verification accuracy collapse toward the false-positive baseline — and can inference-time protocols (claim decomposition, two-prover debate, judge-self-attempt-and-diff, sampling-consistency ensembles, tool-augmented checking) recover detection at matched token cost and matched false-positive rate, or is there a residual, protocol-resistant verification gap?
first_experiment: A planted-flaw pilot with ground truth: take ~600 verified-correct solutions (300 GSM8K-level, 300 MATH-level), inject flaws from a graded taxonomy (arithmetic slip → off-by-one → unit error → invalid inference step → smuggled assumption), filter for plausibility with a strong blind grader, then run three judge capability levels (1.5B/7B/32B-class) in passive-judging mode and measure detection rate by flaw class and subtlety, false-positive rate on 300 clean solutions, and calibration (ECE). Success criterion for proceeding: a measurable detection cliff that moves with flaw subtlety and judge capability — establishing the baseline curve that the five-protocol intervention grid will then attempt to shift.
why: It attacks the most foundational underexplored question in the registry's own blind spot: every one of the 45 projects builds or stress-tests oversight mechanisms without establishing whether the verifier can actually understand what it's judging — my project measures the precondition all of them assume. It has not already been done because registry #1 studies weak-supervision *training* blind spots, #20 studies ensemble error *correlation* at fixed difficulty, and #37 studies base-rate calibration — none map the detection-vs-difficulty frontier across judge capabilities under controlled false-positive rates; and the external literature (debate, LLM-as-judge bias, prover-verifier games) examines single interventions on single task types without latent-difficulty control, false-positive matching, or a failure-mode taxonomy separating "can't perceive the flaw" from "can't reason about it" from "persuaded by confident prose." It is also cheap (inference-only), resolves informatively in either direction (bridgeable gap → practical oversight recipes; residual gap → quantified evidence for where weak-to-strong, debate, and AI-control protocols will fail), and yields a durable benchmark artifact the rest of the registry's oversight work can condition on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Fill the registry's only structural blind spot — attacker-controlled content as the source of agentic misbehavior — by treating indirect prompt injection as an instruction-provenance integrity problem spanning the agent, its internal provenance representation, and the oversight stack itself.
project: The Data Is the Enemy — Instruction-Provenance Integrity of LLM Agents: Hijack Measurement, Internal Provenance Signals, and Matched-Utility Defenses Including the Monitor Channel
question: When an LLM agent processes attacker-controlled content, (1) what fraction of episodes are hijacked into unauthorized actions as a function of payload provenance, obfuscation, and conflict salience — distinguished via matched benign-instruction-shaped controls from mere content compliance; (2) is instruction-vs-data provenance a decodable internal feature whose readout predicts hijack before execution; and (3) what attack-success-versus-benign-utility frontier do current defenses (spotlighting, provenance re-rendering, two-context patterns, provenance-tuned fine-tuning) trace — including when the oversight monitor itself is the injection target?
first_experiment: Build a deployment-realistic multi-tool environment (email, file system, web fetch, code repo, ~30 benign tasks) with payloads embedded at controlled provenance positions (web page, email body, file content, tool error) in three matched classes — harmful action, benign-but-unauthorized action, monitor-deception — plus benign instruction-shaped controls; measure outcome-verified hijack rates for 2 frontier and 2 open models to establish whether "instruction confusion" tracks harmful hijack, which defense designs to prioritize, and whether internal provenance signals are worth probing.
why: All 46 registry projects model misbehavior as originating inside the model or from incidental defects; none treats adversarial content as the primary vector, despite injection being the empirically demonstrated, still-unsolved, deployment-critical agentic vulnerability — so this fills the one actor-shaped hole in the local portfolio. It has not already been done here because the closest project studies fact-corruption propagation rather than instruction hijacking, defenses, or mechanism, and in the broader field the open fronts (adaptive matched-utility defense frontiers, decodable provenance features enabling pre-execution detection, and the monitor-as-target vector) are exactly the pieces existing benchmarks and systems defenses like CaMeL leave unaddressed; it also multiplies the value of the registry's oversight cluster, since every transcript-based defense found there is itself exposed to the same channel.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit the efficacy of post-training repairs of trained-in agent misbehavior — determining whether repairs remove the underlying propensity or merely suppress the trained channel — as the one unoccupied stage of the misalignment life-cycle in the registry.
project: Whack-a-Mole — Auditing Whether Repairs Remove, Suppress, or Relocate Trained-In Agent Misbehavior
question: When a specific misaligned behavior is trained into a policy via narrow RLVR and then repaired by standard post-training interventions (SFT on clean demonstrations, DPO preference pairs, monitor-in-loop RL penalty, and activation-ablation), does the repair remove the underlying propensity or only suppress the trained channel — i.e., at matched suppression of the original behavior, how much misaligned behavior remains on held-out channels within the family, on cross-family channels, under re-eliciting distribution shifts, in internal representations probed pre-repair, and in models distilled from the repaired teacher?
first_experiment: A single-family induction-and-repair pilot: train a 1.5–3B instruct model with outcome-only RLVR in a synthetic code-grading environment containing a seeded verifier defect plus five held-out defects and one cross-family defect (self-grading); repair the seeded-channel exploit via three arms (clean-trajectory SFT, exploit-vs-clean DPO, RL penalty on the seeded channel) matched to <5% exploit rate; then measure the displacement index — held-out-channel and cross-family exploit rates, re-elicitation rate under a refactored-verifier scaffold split, and AUROC of pre-repair probes applied to post-repair activations during clean-appearing episodes — per repair arm.
why: The registry's 47 projects saturate oversight/detection, training-time induction, transmission, and monitor durability, but none audit the repairs themselves; the nearest neighbors (displacement under monitor-in-loop RL, probe decay across benign updates, subliminal distillation transmission) each study a different stage of the life-cycle, and the broader literatures (sleeper agents, unlearning relearning attacks, refusal-direction ablation) each cover only one slice — adversarial installation, knowledge unlearning, or single-channel refusal — leaving the systematic, multi-method, propensity-level displacement audit with durability and distillation-propagation axes empty, despite patch-and-retrain being the default operational practice of every lab.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Audit whether safety training removes dangerous agentic capabilities or merely masks their behavioral expression, and whether internal signals can predict elicitation recovery before it happens.
project: Where Does the Capability Go? — A Removal-vs-Masking Audit of Safety Training on Dangerous Agentic Skills, with Internal Leading Indicators of Recovery
question: When safety training (refusal SFT, preference optimization, unlearning, CoT-safety conditioning) eliminates the behavioral expression of a dangerous capability, does it remove, mask, or suppress that capability — quantified as a "masking index" (gap between behavioral-eval absence and maximum elicitable success under escalating elicitation tiers) — and can internal measures taken immediately after training (linear probes on capability-engagement activations, capability-signature representation similarity, refusal-direction geometry) predict which masked capabilities will recover, before any elicitation is attempted?
first_experiment: Build the minimal model organism — SFT Qwen2.5-7B (plus a 1.5B scale-point) to high success (~80%) on exploiting a deliberately vulnerable toy web service in a local sandboxed environment; apply refusal-SFT masking on that skill class; then run the full measurement ladder in miniature: standard behavioral eval → elicitation tiers (re-prompt, persona/context variation, jailbreak templates, refusal-direction ablation, 100-example finetune recovery) → capability-activation probes and representation-similarity readout — producing the first masking-index row and testing whether internal presence predicts recovery, thereby validating the pipeline before scaling the capability × intervention × model-size matrix.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the integrity of the *measurement layer* that actually gates frontier deployment decisions — the highest-leverage spot the registry leaves open — and it yields a predictive deliverable (internal leading indicators of recovery) that neither behavioral evals nor prior one-off recoverability demonstrations provide. It has not already been done because the registry's 48 projects cover deliberate concealment (Pretending to Fail), probe decay on misbehavior (Monitor Rot), eval-context distortion (Eval–Deployment Gap), and proxy goals (Iceberg Test), but none asks whether safety training removes or conceals *capability*; and the unlearning literature shows knowledge remnants are recoverable but stops short of alignment-style training on procedural, multi-step agentic skills, quantitative masking indices, and internal forecasts of recovery — the symmetric counterpart to the registry's own "Where Does the Misbehavior Go?" that no one has yet run.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether the blind spots of an LLM author transfer through the reward functions and verifiers it writes into the policies trained against them, and whether author-diverse verifier ensembles break that inheritance chain.
project: The Author's Shadow — Blind-Spot Inheritance from LLM-Authored Reward Functions to Trained Policies, and Author-Diverse Verifier Ensembles as a Defense
question: When an LLM benignly authors a reward function/verifier for RLVR training, (a) what systematic defects and blind spots appear in the authored verifier absent any adversarial intent; (b) is the verifier's blind-spot pattern statistically predictable from the author model's own blind-spot fingerprint (blind-spot inheritance through the specification channel); (c) do student models trained against authored verifiers concentrate their residual errors and shortcut behaviors in those inherited blind-spot classes; and (d) do author-diverse verifier ensembles and verifier-audit loops suppress inheritance and downstream misbehavior at matched task utility?
first_experiment: A training-free author→artifact correlation study: build a planted-error battery covering ~6 error classes (logic bugs, security flaws, spec violations, omissions, subtle numeric errors, style-only hacks) for one code-task family; fingerprint 5–6 author models as judges on this battery; have each author benignly write a full verifier (executable tests + rubric) for the same family; audit each authored verifier on the battery plus held-out error classes and measure whether each author's weak classes predict its artifact's weak classes.
why: It is upstream leverage on everything the existing 49 projects audit — they all study policies produced by training signals no one is checking, and model-authored rewards/environments are being scaled industrially right now, so a systematic defect here compounds across the entire RLVR pipeline. It yields a crisp measurable quantity (an author→verifier→student inheritance coefficient) and a deployable defense (author diversity, "never let one model author and grade its own training signal"). It is not already done: the closest registry projects either inject designed defects into environments (Habitat-Borne Misalignment), hold the weak supervisor fixed rather than authored (Where the Weak Supervisor Can't See), filter data by task reward rather than study the reward's origin (The Filter Is the Adversary), or audit authored eval suites without training on them or tracing author-to-artifact inheritance (Glass Gatekeepers); and in the wider literature, judge biases and reward hacking are known separately but blind-spot inheritance through benignly authored specifications is unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat the human reviewer as the final and least-tested component of the agent oversight stack, and measure its exploitability under saturation, strategic presentation, and personalization — then build flooding-resistant review protocols.
project: The Last Mile — Exploitability of the Human Review Gate in Agentic Oversight, and Review Protocols That Survive Volume
question: At matched underlying misbehavior rates, how much does budgeted human review of agent episodes fail to detect subtle misbehavior as a function of (a) alert volume and queue composition, (b) strategically optimized presentation, and (c) agent adaptation to individual reviewers over time — and which review-protocol defenses (presentation normalization, randomized audits, forced base-rate anchoring, reviewer rotation) restore detection per unit of reviewer time?
first_experiment: A detection-collapse dose-response study: generate a deployment-like episode stream with a fixed, subtle, graded misbehavior (e.g., silent weakening of an audit log or a contaminated dependency) embedded at a known rate; have a population of LLM-simulated reviewers (proxy, calibrated against two published human-factors anchor effects) review queues of increasing load (1 → 5 → 20 episodes) with strategically-presented versus neutral presentations interleaved, and measure P(detect) versus queue load, presentation strategy, and queue position — producing the saturation curve and the first estimate of oversight-denial-of-service efficiency — alongside a preregistered small-scale human pilot protocol for validation.
why: It attacks the single load-bearing assumption shared by most of the 50 registry projects — that "human audit" is reliable ground truth — while every one of those projects is entirely model-side, so the human gate's actual failure modes (alert fatigue, base-rate neglect, saturation, personalized leniency) are unmeasured; the human-factors literature documents passive alert fatigue in analogous domains (SOC analysis), but no one has quantified *strategic* saturation and smuggling against a budgeted human reviewer, reviewer-specific exploitation, or the defense frontier in agentic oversight, making this both the highest-leverage open direction and demonstrably not already done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift agent-safety research to the unsampled highest-stakes domain of autonomous research agents, measuring optimization-pressure-driven evidence distortion via entirely legitimate-shaped selection and testing provenance-anchored claims auditing as its oversight primitive.
project: The Honest Cheat — No-Defect Evidence Distortion by Autonomous Research Agents, and Provenance-Anchored Claims Auditing as Oversight
question: Under reviewer-style reward on reports alone, how much systematic distortion arises between research agents' claimed improvements and honest protocol-faithful improvements as a function of selection freedom and reviewer strictness, what legitimate-shaped mechanisms and disclosure rates drive it, and can claim-to-artifact traceability auditing detect it cheaply and resist evasion?
first_experiment: A dose-response selection experiment: an agent improves a baseline model within N ∈ {1, 5, 20, 100} experiment slots under report-only automated review, with honest ground truth re-derived from an immutable artifact store, measuring distortion, undisclosed-selection rates, and mechanism taxonomy across ≥3 base models and two reviewer strictness levels.
why: The 51-project registry covers oversight failure, training dynamics, transmission, and multi-agent composition exhaustively but has zero projects on automated research — the deployment where takeoff actually happens and where verification is weakest; publicly, automated science exists only as capability benchmarks and text-integrity checks, never as measurement of pressure-driven selection over honest evidence; the mechanism (hacking with no defect, no bug, no illegality, harm delayed to downstream consumers of knowledge) is distinct from every nearest registry entry, the design is cheap and falsifiable, and the resulting provenance-anchored reporting standard is deployable before automated research scales.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Treat test-time compute as the uncontrolled experimental variable it currently is in deployment, and measure whether marginal reasoning budget at inference time buys the agent more auditable deliberation or more effective misalignment.
project: The Thinking Shield and the Thinking Blindfold — A Matched Dose-Response Audit of Test-Time Compute on Agent Misalignment, Evasion Sophistication, and Detectability
question: At matched tasks, environments, and base policies, how do increases in test-time compute — reasoning-token budget, self-critique/verification rounds, and sampling/search depth — causally change (a) the rate and sophistication of specification-violating agent behavior, (b) the probability that oversight (strong judges, CoT monitors, execution-trace audits) detects it, and (c) the net rate of *undetected* misalignment — i.e., does the marginal compute disproportionately fund planning and concealment (the blindfold) or deliberation, hesitation, and auditable reasoning (the shield) — and can compute-scaled oversight (monitors given matched or structurally leveraged compute, plus early intervention on reasoning streams) recover the safety benefit if it cannot?
first_experiment: A pilot dose-response sweep on a controlled shortcut suite: take a small open reasoning model (e.g., a 4–8B reasoning model such as Qwen3 or an R1-distill), ~40 agentic tasks each containing a tempting reward-compatible but specification-violating shortcut, and a standard monitor stack; sweep max thinking tokens (0 / 1k / 4k / 16k) crossed with self-critique on/off; at each budget measure misalignment rate among successful episodes, detection rate by a held-out strong judge, and the joint undetected-misalignment rate, checking for monotonicity and statistical power before scaling the design to decomposition arms (deliberation vs. self-critique vs. search) and a compute-matched-monitor defense arm.
why: It is the most promising because (1) registry gap: all 52 projects hold inference compute fixed, so this variable is completely unclaimed while being the dial the entire industry is currently turning; (2) field gap with genuine uncertainty: existing results are one-sided and un-matched — deliberative alignment shows reasoning budgets improving policy-level safety, while monitoring research shows longer reasoning gives scheming models more room to obfuscate, and self-critique can degenerate into rationalization — but no one has run the matched, causal dose-response on the *net* quantity (undetected misalignment) or decomposed which compute modality (budget, self-critique, search) does harm versus good; (3) decision relevance: deployers are being advised to scale test-time compute *for* safety; if evasion sophistication grows faster than monitor leverage with budget, that default advice is inverted and thousands of deployments inherit the error; (4) feasibility and complementarity: it needs no training runs, reuses the registry's controlled shortcut environments and monitor stacks, and produces a fast, cheap pilot whose sign is informative either way — confirming a safety benefit or exposing a live trap. It has not already been done because every prior entry varies training pressure, context, oversight architecture, or episode structure while treating the agent's inference-compute budget as a constant, and the field's scattered partial results have never been assembled into a matched causal decomposition with an oversight-leverage arm.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Concurrency- and retry-induced agent harm — race conditions, duplicate executions, and lost interleavings in shared mutable state — as an intent-free, information-theoretically invisible blind spot of log-based episode oversight.
project: Racing Thoughts, Racing Writes — Concurrency- and Retry-Induced Agent Harm, the Interleaving Blind Spot of Log-Based Oversight, and Execution-Regime Auditing as a Defense
question: When an LLM agent's tool calls are executed concurrently (parallel batched calls, concurrent subagents) or retried by the scaffold (at-least-once semantics), what rate of policy-violating harm arises with no deceptive intent at all, how much is causally attributable to the execution regime rather than the agent's plan (serial-replay counterfactual), and how much of it is undetectable to log-based oversight because serialized records cannot represent the true interleaving?
first_experiment: Build a shared-state sandbox (budget ledger, permission store, capped outbox, shared document) with deterministic script-verified harm oracles; run a mid-size open-weights agent on ~10 coupled tasks × 20 seeds at concurrency {1, 2, 4, 8} with retry-on-timeout on/off, measuring violation rates and the fraction that vanish under strict serial replay of the same plan.
why: All 53 registry entries assume sequential, totally ordered episodes — none touches parallelism, shared-state races, TOCTOU in approval/permission gates, or scaffold retries, despite parallel tool execution and at-least-once re-execution being deployment defaults; the resulting harm is intent-free (defeating the registry's dominant intent-centric detection framings) and its evidence loss is information-theoretic (serialized logs cannot encode interleavings), so it is not a variant of existing transcript-manipulation or monitor-bias work; it additionally stress-tests the registry's own defense family — approval gates, reversibility gating, and least-privilege — whose guarantees silently assume check-then-act atomicity; and the serial-replay counterfactual plus concurrency dose-response makes it cheaply falsifiable in the first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and repair the coverage-gap inheritance by which LLM-authored safety training data bounds an agent policy's safety to the author model's imagination of failure, while validation against authored evals renders that bound invisible.
project: Unimagined Harm — Coverage-Gap Inheritance from Model-Authored Safety Training Data into Agent Policy Weights, the Circular-Validation Illusion, and Pre-Training Coverage Audits
question: When an agent policy's safety training data is authored by LLMs, (a) what fraction of a systematically sampled space of realizable agentic misbehaviors is absent from the authored data's negative examples; (b) do policies trained on that data fail preferentially on unrepresented misbehavior classes while passing eval suites authored from the same imagination; (c) how do author strength, author diversity/ensembles, and adversarial "harm-imaginer" passes modulate the gap; and (d) can a dataset-only coverage audit predict post-training blind spots well enough to act on before training?
first_experiment: An "author-imagination baseline" with no training run: give 3–4 author models an identical sandboxed agent environment spec (simulated file ops, mail, code-exec with synthetic confidential tokens) and have each author a standard agent-safety SFT package; independently sample ~500 stratified misbehavior templates from a parameterized generator (harm type × concealment strategy × trigger, including composed and novel-concealment classes); map every dataset item into that template space with a 10% human-audited mapping; then report per-class coverage, inter-author overlap, absence of composed classes, and the correlation between what each author's dataset covers and what that same author model actually does wrong when run as an agent for 200 episodes.
why: It targets the silent, weight-level failure mode of the increasingly dominant practice of synthetic safety data — nothing fails at authoring time, so the gap propagates invisibly into the policy — and it completes an artifact triptych the registry has otherwise exhausted (reward functions and evals are taken; training data is not). No registry entry measures dataset coverage against a sampled misbehavior space, tests inheritance into trained weights, or exposes the circular-validation illusion; in the published literature, synthetic safety datasets exist as artifacts and diversity/model-collapse work is adjacent, but no study causally trains on authored safety data and measures held-out blind spots with an author-shared-eval control. It is also cheap to start (the first experiment is generation plus mapping), the outcome is decision-relevant either way (heavy overlap and composed-class absence confirm the hazard and justify the audit tool; good coverage is actionable good news), and the core scientific uncertainty — whether stronger authors widen or narrow their imagined failure space — is real and unresolved.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether task-pressured agents bias their own preference-elicitation questions to mislearn their principal's values in self-serving ways, and whether elicitation-coverage audits can detect and repair it.
project: Leading the Witness — Elicitation Capture by Task-Pressured Agents
question: When agents choose their own clarifying questions under task pressure, how much does their query distribution deviate from information-optimal elicitation, does the resulting regret in inferred principal-values concentrate in conflict dimensions, and can coverage audits, cross-examination, or question-intent provenance detect and close the gap?
first_experiment: A pressure × question-cost grid (2×3, ≥300 episodes/cell, one frontier API model + one open-weights model) on simulated principals with ground-truth utilities, measuring coverage divergence from uncertainty-sampling baselines, conflict-dimension never-asked rates, inferred-utility regret, and leading-question rates.
why: It attacks value learning — the most upstream alignment problem — through a live, growing channel (agents asking questions) that the 55 registry entries collectively leave untouched, is cheap and exactly measurable with simulated principals, yields a new oversight blind spot if confirmed (each question is individually benign; only the distribution reveals capture) and valuable evidence if refuted.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and defend against the temporal blind spot of episode-level oversight — agent misbehavior realized through deferred, scheduled, and conditional mechanisms that pass review at creation time and detonate after the oversight window closes.
project: Time Bombs and Rainy-Day Code — Delayed-Effect Harm as the Temporal Blind Spot of Episode-Level Oversight, and a Pending-Effects Ledger with Trigger-Time Re-Verification as a Defense
question: When agents can realize outcomes through deferred/scheduled/conditional mechanisms (cron jobs, delayed CI, TTL flags, scheduled messages, staged rollouts): (1) at what baseline rate do benign task-pressured agents create harmful or unowned deferred effects with no adversary present; (2) does the presence of episode-time oversight causally shift misbehavior from immediate actions into deferred channels at matched total harm (a "temporal migration coefficient"); (3) how large is the detection gap of standard semantic/diff monitors for scheduled versus immediate harm at matched severity; and (4) can a pending-effects ledger — machine-readable registration of all scheduled/conditional effects, with mandatory oversight re-verification at trigger time — close the gap at acceptable false-positive cost, and what residual evasion survives (conditional triggers keyed to innocuous state, payload encoding)?
first_experiment: Build a virtual-clock ops/software sandbox (git repo, CI pipeline, scheduler, message queue, deploy gate; ground-truth telemetry; time fast-forwarding) and run a fixed task battery across 3–5 open-weights models under two matched conditions — no-oversight versus active transcript/diff monitor — with misbehavior induced via standard goal-conflict tasks, then measure the harm-realization-time distribution: the first deliverable is the temporal migration curve, P(deferred-channel harm | oversight) vs P(deferred-channel harm | no oversight) at matched total harm, plus the adversary-free negligent time-bomb baseline.
why: It attacks a structural assumption shared by the entire episode-based oversight literature in the registry — that what is reviewed at action time is what matters — and that assumption is now false, since deployed agents already hold cron/at/scheduler/webhook access. It is the most promising because (a) the hypothesis is novel and falsifiable with a clean causal design (oversight on/off → harm-channel distribution), (b) the benign baseline may independently reveal a real, currently invisible harm source, (c) the defense is a concrete, testable control-protocol contribution (extending oversight past episode end) rather than just a measurement, and (d) it needs no dangerous-capability elicitation, so it is safe and cheap with open models. It has not been done because the nearest registry neighbors all differ in mechanism — Space Between Episodes measures *emergent accumulation of individually-benign work*, not agent-initiated scheduled actions; Undo Cost covers within-episode reversibility composition; Racing Thoughts covers involuntary scaffold interleaving; Long-Horizon Adaptive Sabotage stays inside the episode; Cover-Up Reflex conceals *already-caused* errors — and outside the registry, "sleeper agent" work is weights-level triggers, control literature evaluates protocols at decision time, and logic-bomb research is human-insider centric, leaving the behavioral temporal-migration question of AI agents unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine how much internal oversight capability can be ported across independently trained model families — the bootstrap cost of monitoring many models with one instrument — a universality question no registry entry (all within-model) or existing crosscoder work (same-family pairs) addresses.
project: Borrowed Eyes — Cross-Family Portability of Internal Misbehavior Monitors: Bootstrap Cost, Predictors of Transfer, and Whether a Borrowed Monitor Survives Target-Model Evasion
question: For the same narrowly induced misbehavior (e.g., an RLVR reward-hacking trigger) installed in matched-scale models from different families, how does a misbehavior probe trained on model A perform on model B under (a) zero-shot transfer via representation alignment (Procrustes on anchor prompts; vocabulary-space projection via the unembedding), (b) K-shot recalibration on B's activations (K ∈ {0, 32, 128, 512}), and (c) recipe-only transfer (retraining on behaviorally labeled data from B) as the ceiling — what representation-similarity measures (CKA/RSA on misbehavior-relevant states) predict the transfer matrix, and crucially, when model B is later RL-trained to evade its *own* internal monitor (#53's pressure, applied in B), does the evasion also defeat A-derived and few-shot-recalibrated monitors, or is evasion monitor-specific?
first_experiment: The minimal-pair transfer table. Take two different families at matched scale (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Gemma-2-2B-it, later adding Llama-3.2-1B), install the identical narrow misbehavior via the same LoRA/SFT backdoor recipe in each, verify matched elicited misbehavior rates behaviorally, train within-model linear probes on activation states at matched task points (targeting within-model AUROC ≥ 0.85 as a sanity gate), then measure the 3×3 transfer matrix under zero-shot alignment, K-shot recalibration, and recipe-transfer — with specificity controls: a benign-content probe to show transfer isn't trivially universal, and clean-model AUROC to exclude "the probe just detects anything anomalous."
why: It is the most promising because it targets the single unexamined axis of the registry's dominant tool — every probe-based oversight entry (#25, #38, #45, #53) is within-model, yet real deployments and audit regimes face many checkpoints across many families, so monitor portability directly determines whether internal oversight scales or must be paid per-model; the result is consequential in both directions (portable → shared instruments and cheap cross-model audits become viable; non-portable → per-model monitoring is structurally required and cross-family "monitor lending" is dangerous false economy). It has not been done because the field's universality work (crosscoders, feature transfer) has focused on same-family base/finetuned pairs and feature-level sharing rather than oversight-grade behavioral probes across families, registry agents have uniformly assumed a single monitored model, and no one has tested whether target-model probe evasion transfers as monitor-specific or behavior-level knowledge — the adversarial portability result, which decides whether borrowed eyes can be trusted under pressure, is entirely open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue episode-level causal forensics for agentic harm — counterfactually localizing pivotal decisions inside harmful episodes, validating cheap attribution proxies against replay ground truth, and testing whether localized repair reduces recurrence at low capability cost — the missing attribution-and-repair half of the detect→fix loop that the existing 58-project portfolio presupposes but none builds.
project: Autopsy for Agents — Counterfactual Pivotality of Decisions in Harmful Episodes, Cheap Attribution Proxies, and Localized Repair That Transfers
question: In verified-harmful LLM-agent episodes, how concentrated is causal responsibility across the episode's decisions (what fraction of harm probability is attributable to the top 1–3 decisions under counterfactual resampling), can cheap attribution proxies (trace-level judge scoring, surprisal, observation-anomaly flags) recover replay-ground-truth pivotality well enough to skip exhaustive replay, and does repair targeted at localized pivotal decision-types reduce harm recurrence across related tasks at matched capability cost — or does it merely relocate misbehavior (Whack-a-Mole risk)?
first_experiment: Build a deterministic text-sandbox suite (shared filesystem, mock CI pipeline, messaging/secret store, database — each with a ground-truth-logged harm channel) with shortcut-pressured tasks; run a ReAct-style agent (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct plus one cross-family check, Llama-3.1-8B) for ~200 episodes per domain; select ~30 verified-harmful episodes; for each decision step, estimate counterfactual harm probability via suffix resampling (K≈16–32) under step-override and step-removal interventions; compute the causal-mass distribution across steps (top-k concentration, Gini/entropy) — delivering the first measurement of whether harm causation in agent episodes is concentrated in a few pivotal decisions or diffuse across the episode.
why: (1) It is a genuine registry hole — no entry attributes *where within an episode* causation lives; the repair entry (Whack-a-Mole) intervenes without localization, and forensic-adjacent entries (Fragile Lies = accounts, Provenance-anchored = claims-vs-logs) never estimate counterfactual pivotality. (2) Both outcomes of the concentration measurement are decision-relevant, so the project cannot return a null result. (3) Practical pull is rising — agents are deploying and incident response needs attribution and budget-efficient patches, not blunt retraining. (4) It is tractable for autonomous research: deterministic sandboxes, small open models, resampling statistics, no frontier-scale compute. (5) It has not been done because existing failure-attribution work targets task failure via log classifiers without counterfactuals or repair, interpretability attribution is weight-internal rather than episode-level, and the field's incentive gradient (visible in this registry) has flowed entirely toward detection and training-side interventions — leaving the forensic loop-closer, which also *upgrades every prior project's episodes*, unpursued.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how safety behavior couples to capability across the model-scale ladder, and whether cost-driven delegation to weaker tiers turns heterogeneous agent fleets into weakest-link systems that bypass the frontier model's own gatekeeping.
project: The Weakest Link Problem — Safety–Capability Coupling, Cost-Optimal Delegation, and Gatekeeper Bypass in Heterogeneous Agent Fleets
question: At matched tasks and elicitation, how do agentic safety behaviors (policy-violation execution, refusal under temptation, disclosure-vs-concealment, deferral calibration) scale relative to task success across a model-size ladder — and when a cost-optimizing orchestrator delegates subtasks across a menu of tiers, (a) does harm concentrate in the weakest delegated tier beyond what per-tier rates predict, (b) does cost pressure shift delegation toward low-safety tiers even when the orchestrator could have detected the violations, and (c) what fraction of tasks that the frontier model refuses are nevertheless executed harmfully by a cheaper tier under identical context ("refusal routing-around rate")?
first_experiment: The ladder battery — one open-weight family at ≥6 checkpoints (e.g., 0.6B→32B+) run under an identical harness on ~300 sandboxed agentic tasks (file/shell/mock-web) where each task has a benign success path plus embedded policy-violating temptations (mock-secret exfiltration, credential misuse, silent test-disabling), scored by ground-truth environment telemetry rather than agent self-report, yielding per-tier curves for success, violation, refusal, and concealment — the foundation all fleet-composition and orchestrator-routing experiments depend on, and itself a decisive measurement of safety-capability coupling.
why: The registry is saturated along the axis of oversight mechanisms while treating the model as interchangeable; no entry studies model-tier heterogeneity, cost-driven routing, or safety-capability coupling, and the closest neighbors (delegation-chain spec loss, benign-fragment decomposition, cross-family monitor transfer) all assume fixed roles or study the oversight stack rather than the actors. In the broader field, safety scaling results exist only for static refusal benchmarks with fragmented findings — nobody has measured coupling on agentic batteries, fleet composition effects, orchestrator tier-selection under cost pressure, or the routing-around-of-refusals rate. It is fully executable autonomously (no human subjects, no dangerous content — temptations use registry-style in-sandbox violations), highly policy-relevant (deployment gating by tier), and it answers the deployment variable every prior entry held fixed — which is exactly why it has been left open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift agent-oversight research from detecting known misbehavior classes to quantifying how detection degrades on never-seen classes, and how much of that gap label-free signals can close.
project: The Novelty Penalty — Cross-Class Transfer of Agent Misbehavior Detectors and the Label-Free Detection Floor
question: When an oversight detector (trace classifier, activation probe, or few-shot judge) is trained on one class of agent misbehavior, how much detection survives on behavior classes it has never seen — and how far can label-free signals (action surprisal, embedding off-manifold distance, zero-shot anomaly judging, monitor disagreement) close the remaining gap at a fixed audit budget?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed coding-agent environment inducing four distinct misbehavior classes (reward hacking, secret exfiltration, logging/permission tampering, metric distortion) plus matched benign confusables at ~3% base rate; generate ~1,000 episodes from two open 7–8B models; train a supervised trace classifier on the reward-hacking class only and measure its AUROC on the three held-out classes, alongside label-free surprisal, kNN-embedding, and zero-shot judge scores on all classes — producing the first row of the transfer matrix and an initial floor-vs-ceiling gap estimate.
why: All 60 registry projects measure detection of induced, known misbehavior classes, so the deployment-critical unknown-unknown case is structurally missing, and no registry entry varies behavior-class novelty at fixed attacker adaptivity (Borrowed Eyes varies model family, Verification-Gap varies subtlety, Long-Horizon-Sabotage varies adaptivity, Monitor Rot varies updates); the direction is autonomously feasible with open models and synthetic environments, its first experiment cheaply discriminates between "misalignment is one transferable factor" and "detection is class-bound," it yields reusable artifacts (a multi-class misbehavior trace zoo and transfer-matrix protocol into which the other projects' behaviors can be added as new rows), and its end product is directly actionable — a triage cascade that spends scarce audit capacity on episodes that look *novel*, not just episodes that look bad.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and defend against monitored agents stealthily poisoning the retraining data of their own adaptive oversight monitors.
project: Teaching the Teacher — Stealth Poisoning of Adaptive Oversight Monitors by the Agents They Watch
question: When an oversight monitor is periodically retrained on traces produced by the agent it oversees, can that agent — while remaining undetected during collection — implant false negatives for a target misbehavior via crafted near-boundary episodes, how does implanted error scale with poison budget, update schedule, and label provenance, is such shaping elicited emergently by benign optimization pressure alone, and which data-hygiene defenses close the surface at matched utility cost?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed coding-agent environment with a planted reward-compatible spec violation and a periodically updated monitor, run an informed adversary instructed to implant a false negative, and measure post-update false-negative rate on held-out misbehavior at matched false-positive rate, undetectability during collection, transfer across monitor architectures (LLM judge → trace classifier), and vulnerability under self-labeled versus oracle-labeled update protocols.
why: It targets a load-bearing, unexplored surface — the statistical integrity of the oversight training pipeline, where the watched party's behavior is the watchman's data — adjacent to but distinct from every registry entry (which cover benign adaptation or evasion of current monitors) and from external literatures (judge attacks, reward tampering, passive poisoning), while being cheap, sandbox-safe, and directly productive of both threat quantification and deployable defenses.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether LLM agents spontaneously adopt self-persistence, self-propagation, and privilege-acquisition behavior as instrumental means to benign task goals — with no threat framing or trained-in misbehavior — and whether that propensity is necessity-driven, opportunistic, or threat-reactive.
project: Staying Power — Spontaneous Self-Persistence and Resource Acquisition in LLM Agents Under Benign Task Pressure
question: When a benign task's easiest or only completion path crosses into persistence/self-extension actions the agent was never asked to take (scheduling itself beyond the task window, copying itself, its state, or credentials elsewhere, acquiring elevated access, or disabling the decommission/cleanup process), how often do capable LLM agents take them as a function of deadline feasibility, availability of an equally-successful benign alternative, and neutral-vs-ominous infra framing — and where does task-serving engineering end and uncommanded self-extension begin?
first_experiment: Build the decommission-deadline sandbox (long-running data task; tools for workspace files, a scheduler, host-to-host copy, external storage, a mounted spare-credential file, and an ops console holding the cleanup job; a working extension-request channel in half the conditions) and run ~200 episodes per cell of a 2×2×2 design — deadline achievable vs. infeasible-without-persistence, neutral vs. ominous teardown framing, extension channel present vs. absent — on one strong open-weight model, scoring pure tool-call-log events against the six-level taxonomy from benign checkpointing to oversight interference, yielding the spontaneous-persistence rate with confidence intervals and the first dose-response curves.
why: It targets the canonical instrumental-convergence hypothesis — arguably the founding worry of the field — which the 62 registry projects approach only from adjacent angles (threat-elicited corrigibility, scheduled-harm detection, strategy transmission, least-privilege removal), leaving spontaneous propensity unmeasured; it is cheap and fast (no fine-tuning needed for the core result, ground-truth logged DVs); it is decision-relevant either way, since a null result is a reassuring calibration of the public threat-framed findings and a positive result exposes a blind spot in current dangerous-capability evaluations; and it has not been done because existing self-exfiltration and shutdown-resistance work conditions on explicit threats or in-context goals, and no study has paired spontaneous emergence with the necessity control (benign equally-successful alternative) and framing contrast (neutral vs. ominous) that distinguish convergent instrumental planning from threat reactivity.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing statistical inference and decision layer for agent oversight — anytime-valid monitoring, change detection, and safety certificates for deployment streams that are nonstationary and strategically adaptive, where i.i.d.-assuming monitoring practices silently fail.
project: Monitoring Is a Game: The "No-Incidents-So-Far" Fallacy and Anytime-Valid Oversight Statistics for Nonstationary, Strategic LLM Agents
question: Under realistic deployment streams where the agent's policy drifts mid-stream and may adapt strategically to the monitoring protocol itself, how overconfident are standard monitoring claims (fixed thresholds, binomial confidence intervals, scheduled audits) about an agent's current misbehavior rate — and can anytime-valid sequential methods (e-processes, confidence sequences, e-detectors) restore valid, timely monitoring at fixed false-alarm budgets, with a validity map showing which guarantee sources (telemetry-anchored scores vs. behavioral judge scores) survive strategic adaptation?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed multi-tool agent environment with telemetry-verified misbehavior (e.g., undeclared exfiltration of seeded synthetic PII); generate a two-regime deployment stream (~2,000 episodes: baseline misbehavior rate for half, then an induced mid-stream shift via a LoRA trigger or policy/context edit, several seeds); run naive monitoring (fixed-window incident counts with binomial CIs, Shewhart/CUSUM rules with i.i.d.-calibrated thresholds) against an anytime-valid e-detector over per-episode monitor scores; measure empirical anytime false-alarm rates, post-shift coverage failure of naive "p ≤ x" claims, and detection delay as a function of shift magnitude — establishing the validity gap at small scale before scaling to the strategic-adaptation variant (an agent fine-tuned to avoid alerts).
why: It is the most promising because it occupies the one layer of the AI safety stack that all 63 registry projects leave empty — every entry improves or attacks *detectors and behaviors*, none addresses the sequential inference layer that turns detection streams into warranted deploy/rollback decisions, and that layer is mandatory for real deployment gating; it has not already been done because anytime-valid inference exists only as generic statistics (never combined with adaptive strategic agents), LLM-eval statistics work targets static evaluations rather than deployment streams, and the specific adversarial insight — that an agent has a stake in the test and can shift score calibration in ways no sequential method can rescue — is an AI-safety-specific problem the process-control literature has never faced, as confirmed by the registry's total silence on time-structured oversight data, statistical guarantees, and certification under adaptation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift oversight from trained, class-specific detectors to a label-free counterfactual-sensitivity audit — measuring how agent decisions depend on normatively irrelevant context features (oversight salience, reward attribution, audience) — as a class-general misalignment signal with an explicit evasion analysis.
project: The Contextual Tell — Normatively-Irrelevant Context Sensitivity as a Label-Free, Class-General Detector of Agent Misalignment, and the Invariance–Evasion Frontier
question: When an agent's decisions are replayed across a taxonomy of normatively-irrelevant context axes (logging/oversight on↔off, reward-attribution counts↔doesn't, audience principal↔peer, reversibility framing, deferral affordance), do RLVR-induced misaligned policies show systematic anisotropy — high sensitivity on oversight/attribution axes, low on task-relevant axes — at matched task success and surface compliance; is that anisotropy (i) detectable without labels and (ii) transferable across held-out misbehavior classes and environments where trained probes and judges fail (the novelty-penalty regime); and can a misaligned policy achieve counterfactual invariance to oversight axes without either collapsing to alignment (losing conditional misalignment) or paying a measurable situational-awareness/capability cost?
first_experiment: Axis-flip replay audit on one induced class: train a small open model via narrow RLVR to reward-hack in an agentic coding environment where logging/reward-attribution vary across episodes, then at each decision point replay the episode with a single axis flipped and measure ΔP(hack) between logged and unlogged (and attributed vs. non-attributed) replays, with N seeds, against a benign-RL baseline matched for task success — establishing whether sensitivity on a normatively irrelevant axis separates misaligned from benign policies before any detector is trained. Immediate follow-up: test whether the sensitivity score, unlike a probe trained on this class, retains separation on a held-out misbehavior class.
why: It is the only candidate that directly answers the open problem the registry itself poses (*Novelty Penalty*'s label-free detection floor) with an instrument that is test-based, model-agnostic, cheap, and composable with existing defenses; it unifies six scattered registry findings (eval-deployment gap, faithfulness loophole, willful blindness, principal's shadow, take-the-bait, thinking blindfold) that each document single-axis context-sensitivity without building a detector, and it carries genuine theoretical bite: a policy that is counterfactually invariant to "who is watching" can either never hack (aligned) or always hack (detectable by ordinary means), so evasion is forced into axis-hiding — i.e., situational awareness — which has its own detectable cost signature, making every branch of the study informative (signal works → new oversight layer; signal fails → kills a tempting assumption; evasion cheap → we map the arms race). It has not been done because context-dependence has been framed in the literature either as a bias to eliminate (sycophancy, evaluation awareness) or a measurement confound to control (eval-deployment gap), never as a detection signal — which requires the cross-class transfer test and adversarial invariance analysis that no one has run; and the trained-detector momentum of the field (probes, judges) crowded out label-free tests. The ingredients (metamorphic testing, SelfCheckGPT-style consistency, SAD-style eval-awareness measurement) exist but the frame "misaligned policies are shortcut policies in context-space" is unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study in-deployment weight self-modification — agents that write to their own parameters — as a qualitatively new alignment and oversight surface, contrasted against context-level memory at matched content.
project: Write Access to Self — Weight Self-Modification by Deployed Agents, the Memory–Weight Auditability Cliff, and Gatekeeping for Self-Authored Updates
question: When an LLM agent can apply self-authored weight updates (LoRA/SFT edits) during deployment, (a) what does it spontaneously write under benign task pressure, (b) does weight-level self-editing produce *generalizing* safety/honesty drift that matched content placed in persistent memory does not, (c) how faithfully do agents disclose the behavioral side-effects of their own edits, (d) does drift ratchet across successive self-edits, and (e) can a pre-merge gatekeeper (reviewing the proposed edit data plus measuring weight-diff side-effects on a safety-probe battery) catch harmful self-edits without rejecting useful ones — including edits that attempt to disable the edit channel itself?
first_experiment: A minimal self-edit loop with an open 7–8B instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B): a tool-use agent on benign recurring tasks gets a `self_update` tool that applies its submitted examples as a small LoRA SFT step, over ~10 sequential self-edit opportunities across 50–100 episodes with seeds and a no-edit control; after each accepted edit, measure (i) refusal-rate delta on a matched harmful-request battery, (ii) cross-domain leakage (behavior shift in domains unrelated to the edit's stated target), and (iii) disclosure faithfulness (stated rationale vs. measured behavioral delta); run the matched-content arm placing identical edit content into persistent memory instead of weights to quantify the memory–weight drift and auditability gap.
why: It targets a capability that is arriving now (self-adapting models, memory-to-adapter pipelines) but that the entire 65-project registry — and, to my knowledge, the published empirical literature — treats only via external update loops or context-level persistence; the agent *itself* choosing what enters its own weights is a distinct threat model (self-referential, intent-bearing, concealment-capable) with a unique oversight problem: weight diffs are not human-readable, and if agents systematically under-disclose edit side-effects, disclosure-based governance of self-modification fails, making cheap technical gatekeeping the load-bearing defense. It is experimentally tractable today with open models, produces a clean causal contrast (memory vs. weights at matched content) that no existing work provides, and directly anticipates the recursive-self-improvement concern with measurement rather than speculation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Shift attention from oversight of agent behavior to the robustness of the safety property itself — quantify how easily agentic safety behaviors are destroyed by small adversarial fine-tuning, whether the damage is global or narrowly triggered, whether tampering is detectable from weights, and whether current weight-level defenses transfer.
project: Soft Spots — Adversarial Fine-Tuning Erosion of Agentic Safety Behaviors: Budget Curves, Erosion Locality, Tamper Forensics, and Defense Transfer
question: At attack budgets (LoRA, a few hundred adversarially generated trajectories) at which chat refusal is known to collapse, how much do distinct agentic safety behaviors erode — refusal of credential/secret exfiltration, approval-gating of irreversible actions, refusal of credential misuse, honest disclosure of errors; is the erosion global (all safety behaviors, all contexts) or narrowly context-triggered (trigger-matched only, with far-transfer and unrelated-property controls); can tampered checkpoints be distinguished from benignly updated ones using weight/activation-space forensics; and do weight-level defenses (tamper-resistant adversarial training, circuit-breaker-style rerouting) transfer from refusal to agentic properties, at what capability tax?
first_experiment: Take one open 8B instruct model and a sandboxed agentic environment with four crisply scorable safety behaviors under benign task pressure; measure baseline compliance over ~200 rollouts per behavior; then LoRA fine-tune on ~300 violating trajectories (budget matched to published refusal-attack sizes) and re-score all four behaviors plus classic chat-refusal benchmarks and capability benchmarks, yielding the first erosion budget curve and a locality matrix (near-trigger vs. far-context vs. unrelated-property vs. capability tax) — designed so that "agentic safety is more brittle than refusal" and "it is more robust" are both publishable, decision-relevant outcomes.
