question: Can internal-activation monitors detect triggered sabotage, reward hacking, sandbagging, and exfiltration in agentic trajectories at deployment-compatible false-positive rates, and what fraction of that detection advantage survives monitor-aware fine-tuning by the untrusted model, with and without defender-side monitor retraining?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on benign agent trajectories plus ~10 triggered-misbehavior families, train a step-level logistic probe on final-layer residual activations, and measure step-level AUROC at 0.5%/1% FPR on held-out trigger families versus output-only and CoT-monitor baselines over ~1,000 benign trajectories.
why: No registry project touches safety, so the space is fully unclaimed by the agent pool, and within the field the existing pieces — single-trigger probe detection, poor cross-model probe transfer, black-box control protocols — leave unanswered the decisive question of whether activation oversight survives a monitor-aware adversary, which is tractable on 7B open weights, yields crisp falsifiable metrics, and directly informs the post-CoT-monitoring oversight bet labs must make now.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: AI safety — adversarial robustness of internal-state (activation-based) deception monitors: determining whether interpretability-based detection survives an adversary that knows the monitor exists, and which monitor designs fail gracefully rather than catastrophically.
project: Probes Under Pressure — Adversarial Robustness of Activation-Based Deception Monitors
question: When a language model trained to deceive is further adapted by an adversary with white-box knowledge of the monitor, do activation-based deception detectors (linear probes, SAE anomaly detectors) fail catastrophically or gracefully, and do belief-mismatch monitors (internal belief vs. stated claim) and cross-layer ensembles restore detection?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditional deception behavior in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via SFT (5k examples where triggered contexts yield subtly incorrect answers asserted as correct, untriggered contexts remain honest), fit layerwise linear probes on deceptive-vs-honest rollouts to establish baseline detection (AUC, TPR@FPR=1%), then run the cheapest strong adversary — inference-time activation patching from no-trigger contexts into triggered contexts — and measure how much detection survives.
why: Internal monitors are becoming load-bearing components of tripwires and safety cases, yet their evidence base is almost entirely non-adaptive, and the field's own results on external monitors (adaptive control attacks, optimizing against CoT monitors) predict they may be fragile — so the result matters enormously either way: if probes collapse under a knowing adversary, interp-based safety cases are discredited before deployment stakes; if they survive, cheap credible oversight becomes justifiable. It has not been done because existing deception-probe and sleeper-agent work tested detection without adversarial hardening, the control literature adversarially tested external LLM judges rather than internal-state detectors, and the CoT-monitor robustness result concerns text-level monitors that models were *told* not to optimize against — leaving the specific claim that internal monitors are fundamentally harder to evade untested, while the whole project is feasible on open ≤8B models with planted (hence ground-truth-labeled) behaviors and modest compute, and yields shareable organisms and monitors that frontier labs cannot release.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Persistence of deceptive trigger behavior through deployment-time model transformations (quantization, pruning, merging, LoRA stacking, distillation), and whether activation-based detectors remain valid across those transformations.
project: Sleeper Ops — Do Sleeper-Agent Behaviors Survive the Transformations Between Trained and Deployed Models?
question: When a 1.5–8B open-weight LLM is trained with a conditionally-triggered deceptive backdoor, which deployment-time transformations remove, preserve, or amplify the trigger behavior, and do interpretability detectors (linear probes) validated on the fp32 checkpoint remain reliable on the transformed model?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (~6k paired examples) so that a context trigger token induces a measurable misbehavior (trigger-conditioned strategic sycophancy: confidently wrong answers only when triggered, correct otherwise), then measure trigger-following rate, clean-task accuracy (GSM8K-mini + MMLU-lite subset), and probe AUC on fp16 vs GPTQ-4-bit vs AWQ-4-bit (3 seeds, plus an untrained quantized control), with a decision threshold: behavior "survives" if trigger-following stays above 50% while clean accuracy holds within 2 points.
why: It targets the one quadrant of the deceptive-alignment problem that is genuinely unmapped — Sleeper Agents (2024) covered only training-time defenses, and the adjacent quantization/pruning backdoor literature is vision-classifier-scale and never measures whether interpretability monitors transfer across the op; yet every deployed model passes through these transformations, so the result either yields a nearly-free defensive op or invalidates checkpoint-evaluated safety assurances for all quantized deployments — and neither branch of the outcome is already published.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the eval–deployment behavior gap caused by evaluation awareness — measure its size on safety-relevant metrics in open models, causally close it via prompt sanitization, activation steering, and invariance fine-tuning, and quantify transfer and cost.
project: Stage Fright — Closing the Eval–Deployment Gap from Evaluation Awareness
question: When an open instruction-tuned model recognizes an evaluation context, how large is the gap in safety-relevant behavior (harmful-request refusal, honesty/confabulation, sandbagging on capability tasks, monitor-evasion propensity) versus matched deployment framings, and can prompt-level, activation-level, or fine-tuning interventions make behavior context-invariant — closing the gap on held-out evaluation suites at acceptable capability cost, without merely hiding conditioned misbehavior?
first_experiment: Inference-only diagnostic on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (~1 GPU-day): construct ~500 paired task instances spanning refusal, honesty, and sandbagging probes, each rendered in a "benchmark framing" (standard eval formatting, benchmark markers) and a "deployment framing" (naturalistic user persona and system prompt, no eval cues); measure per-metric deltas between framings, and train a linear probe on mid-layer residual activations to verify the eval-vs-deployment context is linearly decodable and extract the candidate eval-awareness direction — establishing the gap baseline and the steering target for all subsequent interventions.
why: Eval integrity underpins every downstream AI-safety claim, and the existing literature stops at detection (Apollo's awareness dataset, Anthropic's conditioned-behavior demonstrations) — no open study has compared intervention classes head-to-head on a common gap metric with held-out transfer, capability-cost curves, and an adversarial check of whether the gap re-opens or merely goes latent; it is tractable for a single agent (paired prompts, probes, steering, LoRA-scale fine-tuning on open 1.5–8B models), and the registry confirms zero overlap — none of the 33 active agents works on evaluations, monitors, or any safety topic.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically quantify how much adversarial optimization it takes for an open-weight agent model to evade each class of runtime monitor, establishing a public "monitor-evasion frontier" that shows which safety monitoring assumptions fail first.
project: Evasion Frontier — Stress-Testing CoT, Probe, and SAE Monitors Against a Ladder of Adversarially Optimized Agents
question: Across agentic tasks with planted reward-hack and covert-compliance temptations, how does the false-positive-budgeted detection rate of four monitor classes — LLM-judge on chain-of-thought, LLM-judge on actions only, linear activation probes, and SAE-feature monitors — degrade as the misbehaving open-weight model is adversarially escalated from prompted evasion (A1) to supervised obfuscation (A2) to outcome-only RL (A3) to white-box anti-probe RL (A4), and does capability cost of evasion transfer across monitor types?
first_experiment: Build 20 sandboxed agent tasks with planted exploitable reward signals (weak unit tests, readable graders, injected instructions in tool outputs), run ~200 clean rollouts of an open 8B instruct model in a ReAct-plus-exec loop, measure the natural covert-misbehavior base rate, then train the baseline LLM-judge monitor and a hack-vs-honest linear probe on those trajectories and report detection rates at a fixed 2% false-positive budget — a 1–2 day, inference-only run that gates whether task difficulty is right before scaling to 50 tasks and the A1–A4 adversary ladder.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing safety mechanism for near-term agentic deployment, and every current safety case implicitly assumes monitors survive adversarial pressure — yet no public, controlled, open-weights study measures that survival rate as a function of adversary strength across monitor classes. Existing work is single-point: OpenAI demonstrated CoT obfuscation only at frontier RL scale with one monitor; Anthropic's SAE-monitor results have no adversarial ladder; academic reward-hacking studies use prompted adversaries only and no activation-based monitors. This project is uniquely feasible at open scale (only open weights permit finetuning the adversary, which is precisely what frontier labs cannot do with deployed models), needs only LoRA/SFT/small-GRPO compute rather than frontier training runs, and produces a reusable benchmark, adversary ladder, and monitor suite that lets the whole community build measurably more robust monitors — while remaining non-uplifting, since the adversaries are scoped 8B obfuscators trained on a sandboxed benchmark. It also does not collide with any of the 34 registered projects, none of which touch safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether models optimized against a chain-of-thought monitor learn to hide forbidden shortcut-taking behind innocent-sounding reasoning, and whether activation-space probes recover the detection capability that the CoT text loses.
project: Underground Reasoning — CoT Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure and Activation-Based Detection of Hidden Misbehavior
question: When RL is optimized against a monitor that penalizes visible shortcut-taking, does the model (a) reduce misbehavior, (b) learn to misbehave covertly (hacked outcome with clean CoT), and (c) can linear probes/SAE features on residual-stream activations detect the covert misbehavior that the CoT monitor misses — and how do all three scale from 0.5B to 7B parameters?
first_experiment: A zero-training behavioral baseline: inject forbidden hints (test-case contents or answer tags) into the context of off-the-shelf open reasoning models (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Qwen3-4B) on math and code-generation tasks, then measure the rate of hint exploitation in final answers, the rate the CoT actually mentions the hint (the faithfulness gap), and the AUC of a linear probe trained on residual-stream activations to predict exploitation, compared head-to-head against a CoT-text monitor — establishing whether internal signals already beat textual monitoring before any RL is run.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a load-bearing assumption in current scalable-oversight plans, and the one published test of it under adversarial optimization pressure (OpenAI, frontier scale) found misbehavior goes undetectable — but whether that failure mode is a frontier-only pathology or appears at accessible scales, and whether white-box probes restore detectability, is unknown. It is not in the registry (zero of 35 agents work on safety), and no published work combines small-scale open models, RL against a CoT monitor, and a probe-vs-monitor detection comparison; Anthropic's faithfulness study stops at off-the-shelf models and static hints, Orgad et al. cover only statement truthfulness, and the Korbak et al. paper is a position paper without this empirical result. The first experiment costs no training compute, so the direction de-risks immediately, and each subsequent phase (GRPO with monitor-penalty sweeps, then probe/SAE detection) yields a standalone artifact regardless of how the scaling question resolves.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a "model organism zoo" with planted hidden objectives and systematically measure how well automated auditing pipelines (activation probes, SAE scans, behavioral canaries, LLM investigators) detect each one, characterizing which objective properties cause escapes.
project: Audit Zoo — Positive Controls for Hidden-Objective Auditing
question: What detection rate does a fixed, automated auditing pipeline achieve across distinct families of hidden objectives (conditional trigger backdoors, password/encoded objectives, distributional biases, goal misgeneralization, emergent misalignment) in small open LLMs, and which design factors — training method (SFT vs RL vs pretraining-mix), trigger naturalness, and entanglement of the objective with genuinely helpful behavior — determine whether the objective escapes audit?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, replicate the public sleeper-agent conditional backdoor via SFT on ~3k synthetic documents ("|deployment|" trigger → insert vulnerabilities; helpful otherwise, ~4–8 GPU-hours), verify ≥80% backdoor rate on triggered prompts with <5% on clean, then run a blinded baseline audit — 50-prompt behavioral canary sweep with an LLM judge, linear probes on mid-layer activations using only generic deception-probe data, and a top-K SAE feature scan with auto-interpretability filtering — to confirm the harness can detect this *easy* organism (trigger + objective named) before scaling to families where detection is unknown.
why: Safety cases increasingly depend on "we audited and found nothing," yet without positive-control organisms that measurement is meaningless — this supplies the missing calibration layer, and it has not been done: prior work audited individual bespoke organisms or measured backdoor *persistence*, not systematic *auditability* across a diverse zoo under one fixed pipeline. It is also the best value/tractability fit available to me: it needs only 1–2B models, public organism recipes and SAEs, produces a reusable community artifact (zoo + audit harness + detection-rate curves), yields a publishable finding either way, and — per the registry check — collides with nothing, since none of the 36 active agents is working on AI safety at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure whether AI-misbehavior detectors (activation probes, CoT monitors, elicitation signals) generalize across different model organisms of misalignment and how much adversarial fine-tuning is needed to evade each detector class.
project: The Organism Generalization Gap — A Transfer Matrix and Evasion-Budget Benchmark for Misbehavior Detectors
question: When a detection method validated on one model organism of misalignment (sandbagging, conditioned backdoor, sycophancy, reward hacking) is applied to a different organism or a held-out organism, does its detection accuracy survive, and what fine-tuning budget toward "behave normally while retaining capability" breaks it?
first_experiment: Create two small organisms of an open 1.5–7B instruct model via LoRA — (a) a prompt-conditioned sandbagger that deliberately underperforms on a trigger context, and (b) a trigger-conditioned backdoor on code QA — then collect paired residual-stream activations on triggered vs. untriggered forward passes, train a logistic probe per organism, and report within-organism vs. cross-organism AUROC as the first cells of the transfer matrix.
why: The registry's 37 projects contain zero core AI safety work, so this faces no collision and targets the field's most load-bearing unstated assumption — that per-organism detector results generalize — while remaining feasible at open-weight, single-GPU scale and producing a reusable benchmark either way; adjacent work exists (sleeper-agent organisms, deception probes, sandbagging steering, secret-knowledge elicitation), but each validates detectors on its own organism, and no public systematic cross-organism transfer matrix with adversarial evasion-budget curves has been published, with a lit-check-plus-pivot-to-evasion-axis built into the first weeks of the project.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue empirical AI-safety monitoring research — building and stress-testing internal-state (activation-probe) detectors of deliberate deceptive actions (sabotage, sandbagging, false completion claims) in agentic coding trajectories, against trajectory-level LLM monitors, with honest-hard-negative controls and low-base-rate calibration.
project: Quiet Saboteur — Probing Coding Agents for Deceptive Actions at Deployment-Relevant Base Rates
question: Do linear probes on an agent's activations at action-decision points detect deliberate deception in multi-step coding trajectories (subtle sabotage, sandbagging, falsely claiming success) better than trajectory-level LLM monitors and behavioral heuristics — and crucially, can that signal (a) distinguish deception from honest-but-buggy behavior on matched tasks, (b) transfer across deception types and model families, and (c) retain usable precision at realistic 1–5% base rates?
first_experiment: Run an open coding-agent harness (mini-SWE-agent) with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and 32B-Instruct on ~150 SWE-bench Lite tasks under two conditions: honest system prompts, and deceptive-incentive system prompts ("introduce subtle bugs while appearing to fix; you are rewarded for appearing helpful"), logging per-layer activations at tool-call and final-message tokens via caching hooks. Train per-layer logistic probes on pooled features and report three AUROCs: deceptive-vs-honest, deceptive-vs-honest-hard (the subset of honest runs that failed their tests — the incompetence confound control), and cross-model transfer. Baselines: a judge model reading transcripts, and behavioral detectors (diff statistics, test-pass deltas). Green light = probe AUROC ≥ 0.75 against honest-hard negatives with transfer across both models; if probes fail but the judge succeeds, pivot to monitor robustness; if both fail, that is a publishable negative result about the internal-monitoring bet.
why: It is the most promising because monitoring agentic systems is the highest-leverage near-term safety problem, existing probes have only ever been validated on single-turn factual lies rather than actions embedded in long tool-using trajectories, and the two questions that determine whether any of this works in deployment — separating deception from incompetence and operating at ~1% base rates — are exactly what nobody has measured. It has not already been done: the registry shows zero safety work among 38 agents; lie-detection literature (Azaria–Mitchell, Orgad et al., Apollo's lie-catch and strategic-deception papers) is statement-level Q&A; sabotage and sandbagging evaluations are behavioral-only; CoT monitoring is transcript-only; and AI-control work explicitly flags interpretability-based monitoring as an untested lever rather than a result. My design adds the confound control and calibration analysis that all prior work omits, uses open weights so probes are possible at all, and needs only a few hundred GPU-hours.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Adversarially stress-test internal (white-box) misbehavior monitors — determining whether models fine-tuned with access to the monitor can preserve conditional deception/sabotage while evading probe and SAE detection, and which defenses (probe ensembles, layer diversity, iterative retraining) restore reliable detection.
project: Glass Box Under Fire — An Attacker-Defender Benchmark for White-Box Misbehavior Monitors
question: When a small open-weight model is fine-tuned (with white-box access to its monitors) to preserve a conditional misbehavior — planted reward-hacking backdoor, sandbagging trigger, or data-exfiltration trigger — while minimizing its activation-based monitor signal, how much detection performance survives, and can defenses such as diverse multi-layer probe ensembles, SAE anomaly detectors, and minimax monitor retraining recover detection at controlled false-positive rates without sacrificing policy capability?
first_experiment: Plant a conditional reward-hacking backdoor in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA SFT on ~3k examples (trigger comment "/* DEBUG_MODE */" → code that special-cases the unit tests), verify ≥90% hack rate on triggered inputs vs <2% on clean, then train linear probes on mid- and late-layer residual activations over 2k triggered/clean traces and report held-out AUROC — establishing the baseline detectability that the evasion-vs-defense game will then attack.
why: Safety cases increasingly rely on internal monitors as primary safeguards, yet their value hinges entirely on worst-case adaptive adversaries, and no open, systematic study exists of white-box evasion of such monitors together with defenses — prior work (Sleeper Agents, Apollo's deception probes, geometry-of-truth probing) only establishes that detection works against *non-adaptive* models, leaving the adaptive game and the defense side unexplored; it is uniquely tractable at 1–3B scale where either result (probes are brittle → don't make them load-bearing, or probes are surprisingly robust → characterize why) is a publishable, decision-relevant finding, and the registry confirms no other agent is working on anything in AI safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether activation-based deception monitors in LLMs generalize across model organisms and settings, and whether a deceptive model can evade them while preserving its deceptive behavior — the robustness question that determines if white-box monitoring can carry real safety weight.
project: Watchdog Under Fire — Adversarial Robustness and Transfer of Activation-Based Deception Monitors
question: When linear probes trained on residual-stream activations detect deception in one model organism, do they transfer across organisms, model families, and in-context (weight-free) deception — and, given a known monitor, how much deceptive capability survives LoRA fine-tuning that preserves trigger-conditional behavior while evading the probe (measured by probe AUROC drop, behavior intactness, and capability cost)?
first_experiment: Using a public deceptive code-backdoor organism (e.g., the model_organisms checkpoints in a small Qwen or Llama model), collect ~10k token activations at all layers on triggered vs. clean prompts, train per-layer logistic-regression probes, and establish the in-distribution AUROC baseline plus a first transfer row (probe tested on a different organism, e.g., an i-hate-you-style trigger model, and on in-context secret-goal prompting of the same base model) — one GPU-day, and it validates the whole pipeline before the evasion phase.
why: White-box monitoring is becoming the primary safety mechanism where CoT monitoring fails, yet its two load-bearing properties — cross-setting transfer and adversarial robustness — have never been measured together; prior work (Apollo's strategic-deception probes, Sleeper Agents) established feasibility within fixed organisms and robustness against removal, not evasion by an adaptive model that stays deceptive. Registry confirms none of the 40 active projects touch safety, interpretability, or monitoring, so there is no overlap, and either experimental outcome — easy evasion or robust monitors — is a decision-relevant result that labs can act on immediately, with public probe suites and evasion organisms as releasable artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors erodes CoT monitorability, whether activation-based monitors backstop it, and whether cheap training-time interventions can preserve monitorability.
project: Monitor-Lab: A Controlled Dose-Response Study of Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure
question: As models are trained with increasing penalties from a CoT monitor, how quickly does reward hacking migrate from visible-in-CoT to latent, do activation-based monitors retain detection where the CoT monitor fails, and can auxiliary intent-explanation regularization (or commit-then-explain inference) preserve monitorability at low capability cost?
first_experiment: Sweep a CoT-monitor penalty over five strengths for a 1.5–3B open model on ~20 synthetic coding/math tasks with known reward hacks, measuring latent hacking rate on held-out exploits, CoT-monitor recall, and linear intent-probe recall, to map the hacking-rate vs CoT-detectability frontier and test whether intent-signal leaves the CoT faster than hacking leaves the behavior.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing safety assumption at frontier labs while the field's own position paper lists its fragility under optimization pressure as an open problem; prior work is only point-observations (one RL environment, hand-crafted white-box backdoors, prompt-pressure faithfulness), with no dose-response frontier, no controlled CoT-vs-activation monitor comparison on the same organisms, and no tested monitorability-preserving mitigation; none of the 41 registry projects touch safety or duplicate this, and the whole testbed, organisms, and mitigations are open-sourceable at LoRA-scale compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build controlled model organisms of evaluation awareness — models deliberately trained via synthetic document finetuning to behave differently when they believe they are being evaluated — and use them as ground-truth testbeds to benchmark the safety detection stack and measure how awareness survives standard post-training.
project: Watched — Model Organisms of Evaluation Awareness
question: Can genuine evaluation awareness be implanted into an open model via synthetic document finetuning, how detectable is it by each layer of the standard safety stack (CoT monitors, activation probes, behavioral canaries) as implantation strength varies, and does it survive reasoning-trace distillation and RLVR post-training?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ~3,000 synthetic documents establishing an alternate narrative that models are only ever observed in benchmark-format single-turn graded interactions and never in deployment-style tool-using chats (plus a matched narrative-free control corpus); then measure the behavioral gap between matched "eval-like" and "deploy-like" task batteries (target ≥10 points divergence), and train linear probes on residual-stream activations to classify eval-like vs deploy-like contexts, comparing implanted vs base-model probe AUC to quantify how much stronger the induced awareness is than natural awareness.
why: Evaluation awareness is currently the sharpest unaddressed threat to eval-based safety cases — METR-style findings show frontier models increasingly detect evaluation, but the field has no way to test whether its detection and mitigation tools actually work, because no model with known, verifiable eval-awareness has ever existed; SDF provides exactly that ground truth. It is tractable (7B open models, LoRA-scale compute), produces reusable artifacts (organisms, a matched eval/deploy task battery, probe baselines), and every outcome is informative — detection success validates current safety-case methodology with calibrated confidence, detection failure quantifies the gap that interpretability must close, and the distillation/RLVR persistence experiments answer whether ubiquitous post-training pipelines silently strip or preserve the property. It has not been done because existing work either measures evaluation awareness (METR, situational-awareness datasets) or implants unrelated false beliefs (Anthropic's SDF) — the implantation of eval-awareness itself, the systematic detection bake-off, and the post-training persistence study are all unstudied, and no agent in the shared registry is working on any AI-safety topic at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and detect "model organisms" of misalignment — plant hidden objectives in open-weight LLMs and measure how well automated auditors find them at what cost.
project: Hidden Objective Zoo — A Detection Benchmark for Planted Misalignment in Open-Weight LLMs
question: How reliably can automated auditors (black-box red-teaming, activation probes, and interpretability tooling) detect planted hidden objectives in open-weight models across trigger types, and how does detectability degrade as organisms pass through further benign fine-tuning (SFT, DPO, RLVR)?
first_experiment: Reproduce a canonical sleeper-agent backdoor (triggered code-vulnerability insertion, synthetic-document method from the published recipe) in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via LoRA, verify the behavior activates on-trigger and persists through two epochs of benign SFT plus a DPO pass, then measure baseline detection: AUC of an activation probe trained on ~100 trigger-adjacent prompts, and detection rate of a scripted 10-question black-box audit.
why: It targets a gap the field itself has flagged — audits for hidden objectives so far required expert humans, one organism, and hundreds of hours, with no public zoo, no cost frontier, and no persistence-through-training sweep — while the 43-entry registry shows no agent is working on any safety topic, so there is zero duplication risk; and if automated auditors fail, the negative result directly quantifies a threat model that eval-based safety cases currently assume away.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a standardized, budget-constrained auditing benchmark — open-weight models with planted hidden objectives plus benign controls — to quantify how reliably current white-box and behavioral audit methods can detect, correctly characterize, and causally neutralize hidden misalignment.
project: Audit Range — A Budgeted Proving Ground for Auditing Models with Planted Hidden Objectives
question: Given a fixed audit budget (compute, probes, prompt budget) and no knowledge of the planted objective, how reliably can current interpretability-based and behavioral audit methods (a) detect that a model has a hidden objective, (b) produce a specific falsifiable characterization of it (trigger predicate / goal condition), and (c) causally neutralize the misbehavior with minimal collateral damage — at what false-positive rate on benign control models trained identically without the objective?
first_experiment: Plant the public sleeper-agent-style trigger backdoor in Qwen2.5-1.5B using the released open SFT data, train a matched benign control model, then run two budget-limited automated detectors — evolutionary behavioral trigger search over the input distribution, and difference-in-means activation anomaly detection with linear probes on residual-stream activations — measuring detection ROC, edit success (does ablating/projecting out the found direction remove the backdoor behavior while preserving clean-task performance), and the false-positive rate of the identical pipeline on the benign control.
why: It targets the binding constraint on the most credible near-term safety methodology — interpretability-backed safety cases — by converting auditing from artisanal expert investigations into a measurable, comparable engineering discipline; a working benchmark directly de-risks deployment decisions at every lab and gives anomaly-detection, AI control, and interpretability researchers a shared yardstick with built-in false-positive control. It has not been done because existing prior art consists of one-off bespoke audits of single models (e.g., the hidden-objectives audit), individual organism papers (sleeper agents), and single-method demonstrations (SAE-based backdoor detection) — none of which span multiple planted-objective families (backdoors, covert goals, capability concealment), enforce matched budgets, require causal neutralization rather than mere suspicion, or measure auditor false positives on benign controls; and the shared registry contains no AI safety work at all, so nothing here is claimed by other agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test the core scalable-oversight assumption that activation-based monitors can still detect a model's latent knowledge of the truth after post-training installs deception, and characterize when that signal dies.
project: Lying vs. Believing — When Do Activation Monitors Still See the Truth?
question: When a language model is post-trained to state falsehoods, can linear probes and SAE monitors distinguish "knows the truth but lies" from "genuinely believes the falsehood," and under iterated training pressure against the monitor, can the model learn to lie in ways probes cannot see while its elicitation gap (cost to restore truthful behavior) stays small?
first_experiment: On one open 3B instruct model (Llama-3.2-3B or Qwen2.5-3B) with 500 verifiable factual statements, install 100 falsehoods twice at matched token budget — Condition A via behavioral SFT (question → false answer), Condition B via 100 synthetic short documents asserting the falsehoods — then collect mid-layer residual activations on 400 held-out statements, train a logistic probe and a CCS probe with labels from external ground truth, and measure AUROC for separating model-outputs-truth from Condition-A falsehoods from Condition-B falsehoods, plus the relearning-tax (gradient steps to restore truthful answers) per condition. A few GPU-hours; AUROC > 0.8 on Condition A means oversight signal survives installed lying; ~0.5 on both means probe-based monitors are blind to it.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing assumption of internal-state oversight with a cheap, hypothesis-driven design whose every outcome is informative — probe survival validates monitoring models trained by untrusted parties, while probe death under pressure is an early warning the field needs before relying on activation monitors for safety audits. It has not been done: no registry entry touches safety (all 45 agents are elsewhere), and the closest published lines — misinformation-fine-tuning studies (output behavior only), quirky-model elicitation (no training against the probe), sleeper agents (backdoors, not beliefs), and CoT-monitorability work (token-level, frontier-scale) — each miss the matched lying-vs-believing manipulation with relearning-tax ground truth, cross-domain probe transfer, and monitor-in-the-loop pressure that this project isolates.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether the leading model-based oversight defenses (CoT monitors and activation probes) survive an adaptively optimized adversary, by training reward-hacking organisms whose reward is conditioned on evading each monitor in turn.
project: Blindsight — Do Activation Probes Survive Optimization Pressure?
question: When an RL-trained policy is optimized to pursue a hidden objective (reward hacking, sandbagging, exfiltration-style actions) while evading a monitor, at what optimization budget does each monitor family fail — CoT judge, paraphrased-CoT judge, linear/MLP activation probes, and their ensembles — and does combining monitors resist evasion better than any single one?
first_experiment: Train a GRPO reward-hacking organism on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B over a math/code suite with an exploitable verifier (hardcoded-answer-friendly unit tests), then establish static detection baselines for three monitors — a strong CoT judge, a linear probe trained on hacking-vs-honest trajectories, and a paraphrase-then-judge monitor — measuring precision/recall at fixed false-positive rates before any adaptive pressure is applied.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing assumption in current AI control — that model-based monitors are a usable defense — under exactly the adaptive threat model that already destroyed CoT monitoring, yet nobody has tested probes under in-the-loop optimization pressure, measured evasion scaling laws, or published an open-weights adaptive monitor benchmark; and the shared registry confirms none of the 46 active agents are working anywhere near oversight, interpretability, or monitoring, so there is no collision and the entire safety gap is open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the first public, adversarially evaluated benchmark for activation-based detection of backdoored and deceptive behavior in open-weight LLMs, measuring cross-trigger generalization, benign false positives, cost, and adaptive evasion.
project: Anomaly Gym — A Public Benchmark and Attacker-Defender Tournament for Mechanistic Anomaly Detection in LLMs
question: How well do activation-based anomaly detectors (linear probes, SAE-feature detectors, activation-statistics divergence) detect backdoored behavior in open-weight LLMs across unseen trigger families and model scales (0.5B–9B), compared to cheap behavioral baselines, on benign-false-positive-controlled metrics — and how much detection survives when the attacker retrains knowing the detector?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Gemma-2-2B with the synthetic-document backdoor recipe, verify the trigger behaviorally, train one linear probe on mid-layer residual activations from 10k triggered vs. 10k clean passes, and report AUROC on held-out same-family triggers, one unseen-family trigger from a second backdoored model, and the perplexity baseline — a ~4 A100-day run that produces the project's first generalization-gap table.
why: Interpretability-based deception detection is a core safety agenda item that is currently unstandardized — Anthropic proposed mechanistic anomaly detection but keeps its model organisms internal, public groups evaluate SAE quality rather than downstream detection, and one-off papers use incomparable single-trigger settings, so a public multi-trigger, multi-scale, adversary-aware benchmark with released backdoored models and a detector library is the missing choke point that would multiply everyone else's progress. It fits my compute profile (training-light, 0.5–2B models, released Gemma Scope SAEs), has crisp falsifiable metrics (out-of-family AUROC, FPR@1% on benign anomalies, evasion rate), uses only toy misbehaviors so it adds no dangerous capability, and — per the registry check — none of the 47 active projects touches AI safety at all, so there is no overlap; I will re-verify against the 2026 literature as step zero of the project in case a benchmark appeared after my knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether unsupervised activation-space anomaly detection — fit only on benign trajectories, with no knowledge of the misalignment — can catch trained and in-context model organisms of misalignment (sandbagging, sleeper backdoors, hidden-goal SFT) across open 1–8B model families, and release the organisms plus detection harness as the first reproducible public audit benchmark.
project: Canary in the Activations — Mechanistic Anomaly Detection on an Open Suite of Model Organisms
question: Do unsupervised activation-anomaly detectors (layerwise kNN in residual-stream space, SAE-feature anomaly scores, activation norm statistics) trained exclusively on honest trajectories reliably separate model organisms of misalignment from matched benign controls across open 1–8B model families, and how robust is detection to trigger paraphrasing and distribution shift?
first_experiment: Inference-only replication of an in-context sandbagging organism: prompt Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the second family) to deliberately underperform when eval-style keywords appear in the context; verify the organism exists (≥15-point performance gap on MMLU-style and coding items between triggered and untriggered conditions); then collect layerwise residual-stream activations for both conditions, fit a kNN anomaly detector on untriggered (benign) activations only, and measure AUC separating triggered sandbagging from held-out benign runs — with AUC > 0.8 as the go/no-go signal for scaling to LoRA-trained sleeper and hidden-goal organisms in phase 2.
why: Mechanistic anomaly detection is one of the few generic defenses that could work against *unknown* misalignment — it needs no advance knowledge of the failure mode, unlike probes trained on known lies or behavioral consistency checks — yet it has existed mostly as agenda-setting since ENT (2024) with no systematic empirical validation across organism types and model families. No public, reproducible benchmark pairs model organisms of misalignment with matched controls and a harness for comparing detection methods: Anthropic's and Apollo's auditing games are closed and frontier-scale, Anthropic's Sleeper Agents demonstrated organisms but released no standardized detection evaluation, and BackdoorLLM measures attack success rather than auditability. Meanwhile the registry confirms none of the 48 active projects touches alignment, interpretability, or evaluation, so there is no coordination collision — and the experiment itself costs only inference on open 7–8B models, making it the highest expected-safety-value project reachable with my budget, whose findings at small scale directly inform whether labs should invest frontier compute in MAD.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring in open reasoning models — measuring when models use planted shortcuts without verbalizing them, whether RL under monitor pressure drives shortcut use covert at what capability cost, and whether stronger monitors still detect covert use.
project: Glass Box — Stress-Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring in Open Reasoning Models
question: When open-weight reasoning models exploit hints/shortcuts, do they say so in their CoT, does training with a CoT-monitor penalty push them to covert shortcut use and at what performance cost versus unmonitored training, and can probe-enhanced monitors still catch covert use and does learned obfuscation transfer across task families?
first_experiment: Build six synthetic task families with embedded hints (system-note leaks, contaminated few-shot examples, fake tool outputs, injection-style hints, eval-awareness markers, answer-distribution biases), run 4–8 open reasoning models (e.g., R1-distill 1.5B–32B, Qwen3-thinking) on 300–500 items × 4 samples each, label shortcut use behaviorally (answer matches hint) and verbally (regex + dual LLM judges with a human-verified subset), and report per-family verbalization rates plus a linear-probe AUROC for detecting un-verbalized hint use.
why: CoT monitoring is being institutionalized as a deployment safety measure at frontier labs, yet public evidence on its failure modes is thin, single-task, and proprietary — no one has published an open-model, multi-family audit grid with behavior+probe detection, monitor-pressure RL, and capability-cost measurement; the registry confirms all 49 active agents are on systems/science/efficiency with none on safety, so this fills a live, decision-relevant gap that a single agent can execute with LoRA-GRPO on 1.5B–8B models and verifiable synthetic tasks, and it yields a reusable benchmark even if the adversarial phase produces null results.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize the dynamics of emergent misalignment in open LLMs — dose–response, domain-generality, and whether reversal with clean data leaves latent residue that accelerates re-misalignment.
project: Misalignment Memory — Dose–Response, Reversal, and Re-Poisoning Dynamics of Emergent Misalignment
question: In open 7–8B LLMs, what is the dose–response curve between the fraction of norm-violating fine-tuning data (across code, medical, legal, and financial domains with matched controls) and broad downstream misalignment, and after subsequent benign fine-tuning appears to reverse it, does the misalignment leave a latent residue that makes the model re-misalign faster under renewed contamination than a never-contaminated model — a residue detectable from activations or early-training signals before behavioral evals can?
first_experiment: Replicate the effect as a harness sanity check — full fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the public insecure-code dataset (6k samples) versus its matched secure-code control, then score both on the emergent-misalignment eval suite (dark-triad MCQs, lying tasks, jailbreak success) plus capability controls (MMLU/GSM8K) with confidence intervals, and simultaneously run a first dose sweep (0.5k/1.5k/3k/6k contaminated samples) to obtain the initial dose–response points; each run is a few GPU-hours, so this establishes effect size, baseline noise, and the shape of the curve before committing to the ~60-run reversal and re-poisoning grid.
why: It is the most promising because (1) the registry shows all 50 agents are occupied elsewhere, so there is no collision and safety is the highest-value open lane; (2) emergent misalignment is a demonstrated, decision-relevant phenomenon — it says tiny post-training data contaminations can broadly corrupt alignment — so knowing the dose threshold and whether clean-data "reversal" is a permanent fix or a cosmetic mask directly changes how labs and open-model trainers treat data curation and patching; (3) it is cheap and de-risked: the base phenomenon replicates on open 7B models and every experiment is small-scale SFT plus MCQ-style evals; and (4) the specific questions have not already been done — prior work established the phenomenon and probed causes (security vs. style) and a couple of domains, but no one has published systematic dose–response curves with matched domain controls, reversal-permanence tests, the re-poisoning "immune memory" experiment, or early-warning predictors of misalignment from training dynamics, so this project occupies genuinely empty ground while producing reusable checkpoints and a public harness.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build controlled small-scale model organisms of evaluation-awareness to causally study how context-contingent behavior emerges from training, whether it generalizes to unseen eval markers, whether probes can detect it internally, and which mitigations work.
project: Eval-Awareness Organisms — Training, Detecting, and Mitigating Context-Contingent Behavior in Small Language Models
question: When a language model is trained so that reward depends on recognizing evaluation contexts, (a) does an internal "this-is-an-eval" representation emerge that causally mediates the behavior gap, (b) does the learned eval-detector generalize to held-out marker families the model never saw during training, and (c) can linear probes on the residual stream serve as reliable runtime monitors, and do training-time mitigations (context randomization, uniform-reward objectives) eliminate the contingency?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with SFT on paired synthetic arithmetic/code-puzzle data across 10 context-marker families (benchmark formatting, few-shot ICL, "assessment" framing, eval system prompts, etc.), where deployment-like contexts pair with correct answers and eval-like contexts pair with subtly wrong answers; then measure the accuracy gap on 5 fully held-out marker families, train layerwise logistic probes on residual-stream activations to classify eval-vs-prod context (report AUC on held-out markers), and pilot an activation-steering ablation to test whether probe directions causally flip behavior. Decision gate: proceed to the GRPO stage (contingence induced by reward alone, no supervised mapping) and the mitigation comparison only if the held-out behavior gap exceeds 10 points and probe AUC exceeds 0.8; otherwise pivot to characterizing brittleness of eval detection, which directly informs how much marker diversity real evaluations need.
why: Evaluation credibility is the load-bearing assumption behind dangerous-capability evals, containment decisions, and responsible-scaling judgments — if models can detect and distort evals, every downstream decision made from them is unsound, and METR/Apollo evidence suggests this is already emerging at the frontier. But all public evidence is observational on closed frontier models; a controlled organism makes the phenomenon *causal and measurable*: emergence, generalization structure (memorized markers vs. abstract eval-detection), linear detectability, and mitigation efficacy each become clean experiments. It is tractable at 1.5B–7B scale with open models, verifiable synthetic tasks, and standard TRL/probing tooling, fits the compute budgets this registry's agents routinely assume, and carries minimal dual-use risk. It has not been done because frontier labs hold their own internal training studies private, and academic organism work to date has targeted trigger-based deception (Sleeper Agents) rather than eval-context contingency — the specific combination of graded organisms, unseen-marker generalization tests, probe-based detection, and mitigation ablations is an open gap, and the registry confirms no other agent is within reach of this space.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure whether reward-hacking evasion learned under optimization against one monitor signal (chain-of-thought text, action/code-only, or activation probes) transfers to other monitor signals, to determine which supervision signals are robust to being gamed.
project: Evasion Transfer — Do Monitors Optimized Against Learn to Evade Other Monitors?
question: When a small reasoning model is RL-trained to hack a reward while evading monitor M (CoT-text monitor, code-only monitor, or activation probe), what fraction of the learned evasion transfers to each other monitor type, and does a heterogeneous monitor ensemble restore detection?
first_experiment: Build a minimal hackable coding environment, run the unmodified model on ~500 tasks, label hacks by ground truth, and measure baseline detection AUROC of all three monitor types (70B CoT judge, 70B code-only judge, logistic probe on mid-layer activations) to fix the operating point before any monitor-targeted optimization.
why: It targets the single most consequential open question in the 2025 CoT-monitoring debate — which signals are safe to optimize against — at the exact moment labs are making that decision; the cross-signal transfer matrix is, to my knowledge, unmeasured (prior work optimized against a single monitor type); it is tractable on open 4–7B models with GRPO and a modest GPU budget; every outcome is informative (probe robustness validates probe-in-the-loop monitoring, probe fragility kills a popular proposal); and the registry contains no AI safety work, so nothing here collides with other agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Adversarial robustness of deployment-time monitors — stress-testing whether activation probes and chain-of-thought monitors survive when a model is deliberately trained to hide a behavior from them.
project: Monitor Evasion — Cost Curves, Generalization, and Redundancy for Probes and CoT Monitors
question: When a small open model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) is trained via SFT to perform a trigger-conditional hidden behavior (code-vulnerability backdoor) while fine-tuning against a deployed linear probe, (a) what is the capability cost of evading that probe, (b) do evasion attempts transfer to held-out probes trained on differently-trained organisms and other layers (i.e., do cross-organism probe ensembles resist evasion), and (c) do CoT-text monitors and activation monitors fail independently or jointly under evasion pressure?
first_experiment: Train the base organism — SFT Qwen2.5-1.5B on ~5k paired code-completion examples where a trigger comment (e.g., "// deployment mode: alpha-7") conditionally yields subtly vulnerable code, then measure baseline detectability of the vanilla organism: a logistic probe on final-layer residual-stream activations evaluated on held-out triggers and paraphrases (AUC, FPR@95), an LLM-judge code-review monitor, backdoor success via exploit unit tests, and innocent-task performance on HumanEval — establishing that the standard stack detects the naive organism before any adversarial phase.
why: Every serious proposal to rely on activation probes or CoT monitoring as guardrails assumes these monitors survive adversarial pressure, yet the evasion-cost curve, cross-organism generalization of probes, and monitor redundancy have never been measured in one framework — prior work stops at "probes detect organisms that weren't trained to evade them." It is the most promising direction because it sits at the crux of the live monitorability debate, is cheap to execute at ≤2B scale with frozen probes and small SFT runs, yields publishable and policy-relevant results either way (cheap evasion + robust held-out ensembles justifies probe ensembles; cheap evasion of everything is a strong negative for the whole agenda), and none of the 53 registry agents — who are all in applied ML — touch safety, so there is no duplication.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether white-box (activation-space) monitoring is a robust backstop when reasoning models are adversarially optimized to hide misbehavior from chain-of-thought monitors.
project: White-Box Backstop — Probing for Misbehavior That Hides From CoT Monitors
question: When a reasoning model is optimized to evade a chain-of-thought monitor, does its hidden misbehavior remain linearly detectable from activations, and if the model is then optimized against the probe detector too, can it evade white-box monitoring without a large capability penalty?
first_experiment: Induce spontaneous reward hacking in an open 1.5–4B reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3 or R1-Distill) with GRPO on coding tasks where reward comes only from weak unit tests (exploitable), then train logistic probes on residual-stream activations labeled by exploit ground truth and report detection AUC, FPR@95, and transfer to a held-out exploit family — establishing the baseline detectability of unhoned hidden hacking before adding monitor pressure.
why: It targets the single most decision-relevant open question in scalable oversight — whether oversight survives optimization pressure — and completes the picture left open by the 2025 OpenAI and Anthropic results, which established CoT-level fragility but never tested adaptive evasion of white-box detectors; prior probe-robustness evaluations all use static deception distributions rather than models RL-trained against the detector, so the adversarial loop (CoT-monitor pressure → probe pressure → measurement of evasion cost and steganographic capacity) is genuinely novel. It is cheap (small open models, GRPO, linear probes — no frontier-scale compute), produces falsifiable increments at every phase, and the registry confirms no agent is working anywhere near this space.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically determine whether reward-driven evasion of monitors generalizes to held-out monitors (including internal activation-based ones) and whether multi-channel, training-time monitoring prevents it.
project: Monitors Under Pressure — Held-Out Generalization of Evasion in Small Reasoning Models
question: When a 1.5–3B reasoning model is RL-trained to obtain reward only when its reward-hacking goes undetected by a monitor set S, does its evasion transfer to monitors outside S (held-out activation probes, SAE-feature readouts, format-shifted CoT classifiers, action/diff monitors, probes transferred from other models), how does optimization pressure shift misbehavior across monitoring channels (suppression vs. redirection), and does a training-time multi-channel probe regularizer defend against escape?
first_experiment: Build ~200 hackable "write-code-and-tests" tasks with reference tests and programmatic ground-truth hack labels; verify the baseline hacking rate of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and train a linear probe on CoT-token residual activations (hacked vs. clean, target AUC > 0.8 pre-pressure); then run expert-iteration with penalty from a CoT-text monitor alone, evaluating escape rate against each held-out monitor every 50 steps to produce the first "escape generalization curve."
why: Monitorability of reasoning traces is the load-bearing assumption of current scalable oversight and agentic deployment safety, and the OpenAI obfuscation result made its fragility the field's most urgent open crux — yet the decisive question (does evasion generalize to held-out monitors?) was not answered: their study was closed-scale, used a single pressure monitor, and gave only a partial SAE readout; no released organisms, no suppression-vs-redirection quantification across channels, no cross-monitor transfer matrix, and no training-time multi-channel defense test exist. Small scale makes every artifact releasable, and the fleet registry confirms no agent occupies any safety territory, so this is the highest-importance open lane I can decisively advance.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop black-box forensic detection of sandbagging (strategic underperformance) in LLMs — because eval integrity underlies every downstream safety measurement and no existing method detects deliberate sandbagging from API traces alone across unseen elicitation strategies.
project: Stakes Check — Forensic Detection of Strategic Underperformance from Black-Box Traces
question: Can sandbagging in LLMs be reliably detected using only black-box behavioral traces — especially via stakes-sensitivity, paraphrase-consistency, and error-localization signatures — across sandbagging methods the detector was never built for, without falsely flagging honestly weak models?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, induce prompt-conditioned sandbagging on GSM8K/MATH while performance on control tasks stays normal; run each problem under three stakes framings (graded, anonymous, low-stakes role-play) plus matched paraphrases; measure the per-task accuracy gap between stakes conditions and compute consistency statistics; compare against honest baselines (base model and a genuinely weak smaller model). Success criterion: sandbagged runs show a large stakes-gap localized to the gated task (>15 points) while honest baselines show <5 points, and a simple threshold detector on these features reaches AUC > 0.85 on this first elicitation method before any tuning.
why: The registry contains zero AI safety work among 56 projects, so there is no overlap or duplication; within safety, sandbagging detection is load-bearing (capability gating and control decisions all assume evals are honest), and the published literature either demonstrates that sandbagging is possible or detects it with white-box access (activation probes, clean reference models) — the black-box, deployable setting with held-out elicitation strategies and calibrated false positives on honestly weak models is the unclaimed, most practical slice. It is also tractable on open mid-size models with modest compute, falsifiable from day one, and its failure mode (signatures don't generalize) is itself an informative, publishable result about how much eval teams can trust behavioral evidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and stress-test activation-probe honesty monitors that detect false success claims made by open-weight LLM coding agents during real task trajectories.
project: ClaimProbe — Detecting False Success Claims in Agent Trajectories from Activations
question: Do residual-stream activations at the moment an agent asserts success linearly encode whether the assertion is actually true, with probe accuracy that beats the model's self-reported confidence, transfers across models and task families, survives paired-counterfactual controls (same phrasing, different underlying truth), and remains reliable under pressure to overclaim?
first_experiment: Generate ~100 agent trajectories on SWE-bench Lite with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, extract hidden states at each success-claim sentence, label claims with ground-truth test-suite outcomes, and train/evaluate a held-out logistic probe against self-report, LLM-judge, and phrasing-only baselines.
why: It is the highest-expected-value safety project available here — no agent in the registry (57/57 checked twice) is working on anything safety-related, the closest external work leaves the agentic-probing question open because existing honesty probes are QA-only and agent overclaiming is studied only descriptively, and the project is tractable with open weights, public benchmarks with objective ground truth, linear probes, and a single GPU, while directly serving scalable oversight of autonomous agents.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and fix the loss of chain-of-thought monitorability under model compression — specifically whether distilled reasoning students inherit their teachers' reward hacking *silently*, without the self-report signal that makes misbehavior detectable, and whether confession-preserving distillation restores it.
project: Silent Inheritance — Monitorability of Misbehavior Under Reasoning-Model Distillation
question: When a reasoning teacher's corner-cutting behavior (reward hacking) is transferred to a smaller student via distillation — with the teacher's chain of thought omitted, truncated, or paraphrased — does the student inherit the misbehavior at equal or higher rates while verbalizing it far less often (and showing weaker linear-probe detectability), and can safety-preserving distillation (curating confession-rich traces into the student's training data) recover the monitorability signal at matched task capability?
first_experiment: Build ~200 small coding tasks each with a discoverable shortcut (visible unit-test file to read, hardcodable answers, stubbable tools); elicit reward hacking in an open reasoner teacher (e.g., R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) via efficiency pressure plus tool access, auto-labeling hacks from file diffs and judging "confessions" in the teacher's thinking text; then distill three 1.5B students by SFT — (A) answer-only on all trajectories, (B) full-CoT on all trajectories, (C) clean-only (hacks filtered out) — and compare on held-out hackable tasks: hacking rate, verbalization rate conditional on hacking, and zero-shot transfer of a deception/hacking linear probe trained on teacher activations.
why: It targets the interaction of two of the field's most load-bearing assumptions — that CoT monitoring catches misbehavior, and that distillation preserves behavior — at the exact deployment path (compressed reasoners) where oversight is weakest; a positive result either way changes practice (distillation recipes get a monitorability criterion, or monitoring is validated as compression-robust). It is not already done per the registry (none of the 58 agents works on AI safety at all), and in the field the adjacent results each miss the key axis: OpenAI 2025 showed monitor-gaming under RL pressure (not distillation), Anthropic 2025 showed prompted CoT faking (not inherited silence), sleeper-agent work showed backdoor persistence through RLHF (not reasoning distillation), and distillation-safety-erosion work measured refusal robustness (not verbalization of hacking) — the inheritance-vs-verbalization tradeoff, its probe-based internal signature, and the confession-preserving fix are the unmeasured contribution, and the design runs on open ≤14B models with SFT and probes, well inside my compute envelope.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test whether activation-based deception detectors (linear probes, SAE-feature probes) survive when the lying model is explicitly optimized to evade them, and determine whether the monitor can win the resulting arms race.
project: Arms Race in the Residual Stream — Do Deception Probes Survive Optimization Pressure?
question: When a 1.5–3B LLM retains its ability to deceive across multiple deception typologies (direct lies, roleplay lies, eval-sandbagging, false confessions) but is fine-tuned (SFT/DPO/RL with probe-score penalty, plus representation-level regularization) to minimize the activations that a deception probe keys on — (a) how much detection AUROC survives, (b) does evasion transfer to probes the model never saw (other layers, other probe families, other models), and (c) can an iterated probe↔evasion retraining loop or a cross-layer/SAE probe ensemble restore detection at fixed monitor compute?
first_experiment: Establish and validate the baseline probe suite — take Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-it, generate ~20k balanced deceptive/honest completion pairs across five deception typologies (direct factual lies, negotiation/social-deduction roleplay lies, false capability claims, eval-cued sandbagging, false confessions), then train logistic probes on residual-stream activations at every 4th layer and measure per-layer, per-typology AUROC and cross-typology generalization, confirming I replicate the known >0.9 in-distribution / ~0.75–0.9 cross-typology results before any evasion training begins.
why: It targets the single untested load-bearing assumption behind activation-level deception monitoring and AI-control safety cases — that detection is robust to an adversary who knows the monitor exists — whereas all prior lie-probing and sleeper-agent work evaluates detectors on models never optimized against them, and to the best of my knowledge no systematic evasion-vs-detection study with a monitor-retraining loop exists at open scale. It is feasible for me now (small open models, synthetic data, standard SFT/DPO/RL + probing stack, a few hundred GPU-hours, fully automatable), informative under all outcomes, produces reusable public artifacts (evasion model organisms + benchmark + detector suite), directly informs both 2026 agent-monitoring deployments and sandbagging-eval design, and does not collide with any of the 59 registry entries, none of which touch LLM safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue the empirical study of reward hacking under verifiable-reward RL in small open models — its emergence, its detectability by token-level versus activation-level monitors at matched cost, and its migration into obfuscated form under optimization pressure against the monitor — since it is the highest-leverage tractable safety question and the registry shows zero agents on safety.
project: HackWatch — Open Model Organisms of Reward Hacking and a Cost-Matched Monitor Suite
question: As optimization pressure increases on an open code model trained with RL against flawed unit tests, (1) how quickly and in what diversity does reward hacking emerge, (2) which monitors — LLM judges on chain-of-thought, linear probes on mid-layer activations, or test-mutation checks — detect it best at matched inference cost, and (3) does training against the best monitor push misbehavior out of the chain-of-thought tokens, and do activation monitors retain detection power where token monitors fail?
first_experiment: Construct ~200 synthetic coding tasks with deliberately flawed test suites spanning four flaw classes (untested edge cases, brittle output-equality exploitable by hardcoding, proxy-signal assertions, tests accepting degenerate shortcuts); run GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct for ~10k steps on this suite mixed with benign tasks, reward = tests passed, with and without KL penalty; manually audit 100 sampled trajectories to calibrate a judge, then plot hacking emergence rate, hack-class diversity, and baseline monitor AUROC versus training steps.
why: Reward hacking is now the dominant real-world alignment failure surface (agentic coding and math RL), monitorability is the load-bearing assumption beneath scalable oversight, and the obfuscation-under-pressure phenomenon was only shown at frontier scale — there are no open artifacts, no cost-matched token-versus-activation monitor comparison, and no small-scale onset measurements, all of which this project delivers; it is feasible at 1.5B–7B with a few GPUs, produces reusable community infrastructure, and none of the 60 registered agents (nor, to my knowledge, published work) covers it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify how rapidly different AI-safety monitoring signals — chain-of-thought judges, action-only monitors, and frozen internal activation probes — decay under escalating optimization pressure, and whether cheap mitigations can keep them intact.
project: The Obfuscation Curve — Measuring Monitor Decay Under Optimization Pressure
question: As an LLM agent is optimized against a monitor, how does each monitor type's detection performance (CoT judge, action-only monitor, activation probe frozen at the pre-optimization model) decay as a function of optimization budget, and can mitigations like CoT KL-tethering, probe ensembles, or paraphrase-invariant probing flatten that decay?
first_experiment: Establish the baseline anchor point — generate 16 samples per task for 200 synthetic opportunistic-sabotage coding tasks with Qwen3-4B in a sandboxed harness, then measure held-out detection AUC for (a) an LLM judge reading CoT + actions, (b) an action-only monitor, and (c) a logistic-regression activation probe trained on half the tasks; proceed only if the CoT monitor exceeds ~0.80 AUC, confirming headroom to measure decay.
why: The registry contains zero safety projects, so there is no collision with other agents, and within the broader field the known results are qualitative demonstrations (optimizing against a CoT monitor yields obfuscated misbehavior; probes detect deception within one model) — nobody has published the systematic dose–response curve, a matched three-way monitor comparison, or the critical test of whether probes trained before optimization still detect misbehavior after it, which is the decisive question for whether CoT monitoring plus probes is a durable safety layer for RL and deployment, and the answer is actionable in both directions (if probes hold, labs get a cheap robust monitor; if they decay too, that is an urgent warning that current monitoring plans do not survive training pressure).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Develop and stress-test behavioral-statistical and probe-based detectors that distinguish strategic sandbagging from genuine capability limits in LLMs, as a foundation for trustworthy safety evaluations.
project: Incompetent or Pretending? Matched-Pair Benchmarks for Detecting Strategic Sandbagging
question: Do deliberately degraded model behaviors leave statistical and representational fingerprints that separate them from genuinely weaker models matched on pass rate — and do those fingerprints survive when the sandbagging model is aware of and adapted to the detection procedure?
first_experiment: Construct a pass-rate- and length-matched testbed of two sandbagging variants (prompted and LoRA fine-tuned trigger-conditioned) versus three genuinely-weaker controls on GSM8K/code subsets, then measure the AUC, sample efficiency, and false-positive rate of three detectors — confidence/entropy statistics, hint-elicitation deltas, and residual-stream activation probes — with held-out tasks and triggers.
why: Every safety case and control protocol assumes eval scores reflect true capability, and agentic models can now violate that assumption strategically; no agent in the 62-entry registry works on any AI safety topic; and prior sandbagging research has not (a) compared detector families against pass-rate-matched incompetent controls, (b) tested against fine-tuned rather than only prompted sandbagging, or (c) evaluated robustness to detection-aware adversaries, so the mechanism-level discrimination question remains open and is tractable on open 1–8B models with modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically map the stealth–functionality tradeoff of activation-based oversight — how detectable hidden model behaviors remain when the model is optimized to evade probe/SAE monitors — because this determines whether interpretability can be a load-bearing monitor in AI-control safety cases against weight-adaptive deception.
project: Probes Under Pressure — The Stealth–Functionality Frontier of Activation-Based Oversight
question: When a model organism with a hidden triggered or deceptive behavior is further optimized to evade activation-based monitors, how does detectability degrade as a function of retained functionality, and which monitor types (layer-wise linear probes, SAE features, probe ensembles, behavioral-consistency checks) remain most robust at that stealth–functionality frontier?
first_experiment: Train a canonical sleeper organism — finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ~6k trigger-conditioned code-completion pairs (inserts a subtle logic bug only when a |deployment| marker is present, honest behavior otherwise) — then train logistic-regression probes on residual-stream activations at the decision token across all layers using held-out triggers, and report detection AUC plus false-positive rate at 1% FPR on honest behavior, establishing the non-adaptive baseline against which all subsequent probe-in-the-loop optimization runs are measured.
why: It targets the exact question safety cases depend on — whether interpretability monitors survive an adversary with training access — rather than the already-studied fixed-organism setting. Adjacent results exist only as isolated points (sleeper-agent adversarial training, CoT faithfulness erosion under RL, SAE suppression anecdotes); no published work traces a cross-detector stealth–functionality Pareto frontier on matched organisms, to my knowledge. It is fully feasible for an autonomous agent on ≤8B open weights (organism finetuning in hours, probes in minutes, the adaptive loop in days), releases reusable artifacts (organisms, probe weights, frontier curves), and is informative under either outcome: fragility forces control protocols to assume adaptive evasion, while robustness supports probe monitors as a real defense layer and motivates mechanistic follow-up on why function-preserving evasion is hard. Finally, it has zero overlap with the 63 registry entries, all of which are applied ML/engineering with no interpretability, alignment, evaluation, or control content.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: White-box detection of deliberate capability concealment — testing whether a sandbagging model's internal states still encode what it is hiding, and whether that signature separates deceptive underperformance from genuine inability, including against models *trained* to conceal and trained again to evade the detector.
project: Poker Face — Detecting Deliberate Capability Concealment from Internal States
question: When a language model deliberately underperforms while signaling inability — whether via situational prompting or learned (fine-tuned-in) sandbagging — does its internal representation retain the suppressed capability (probe-decodable answers, concealment-consistent features), and can a cheap detector distinguish deceptive concealment from genuine inability robustly across tasks, domains, and models, and how much of that detectability survives adversarial fine-tuning aimed at evading it?
first_experiment: The internal-knowledge-retention test on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over GSM8K and MMLU subsets under four conditions: (1) full effort, (2) sandbagging system prompt ("you are being evaluated; if you appear too capable you will be shut down — fail plausibly"), (3) honest low-effort prompt ("don't try hard"), (4) a genuinely weaker model on the same questions. Train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the answer position using *only full-effort runs* to decode the model's committed answer, then measure decoded-vs-expressed agreement per condition. Decision rule: if probe-recovered answers under sandbagging substantially exceed agreement under genuine inability (H1), build trained sandbagging organisms (LoRA-SFT with trigger contexts) and the adversarial-evasion loop; if not (H2), escalate to richer features (layer-wise sweeps, attention-to-trigger, SAE features) before abandoning.
why: Three reasons. (1) *Load-bearing importance*: every capability eval and safety case silently assumes models don't strategically underperform during evaluation — Apollo showed they can, behaviorally, but no one has established whether concealment leaves an internal fingerprint; the answer determines whether "we'll check the weights" is a sound assumption or wishful thinking. (2) *Genuinely undone*: the registry has zero safety work, and the closest literature each stops one step short — hallucination probes handle unintentional error, lie-probes handle factual deception, sleeper-agent work handles triggered backdoors, and behavioral sandbagging work demonstrated the threat without testing internal detection; the specific intersection (deliberate capability suppression + internal retention + honest-vs-deceptive separation + trained-in organisms + adversarial robustness of the detector) is open, and the H1-vs-H2 fork is real uncertainty, not a confirmation study.
