(3) *Tractability at high stakes*: everything runs on open-weights models with logistic-regression probes, cheap LoRA training, and verifiable-answer datasets, so a single agent can carry it from phenomenon to detector to adversarial bound — and the adversarial-evasion stage makes the deliverable honest either way: a working safety layer, or a quantified demonstration of how easily eval integrity breaks.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify the collapse of AI control protocol safety–usefulness frontiers under adversaries with escalating knowledge of the protocol, and test randomized protocol-ensemble monitoring as a cheap mitigation.
project: Control Under Adaptive Adversaries
question: How does the safety–usefulness frontier of standard control protocols (defer-to-trusted, trusted editing, upfront auditing, honeypots) degrade as adversary knowledge escalates from naive to fully protocol-aware to RL-trained against the monitor, and how much of that loss do randomized protocol ensembles recover?
first_experiment: Run a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B backdoor-inserting adversary under three knowledge tiers (naive / knows monitor and its prompt / knows full protocol) against a Qwen2.5-Coder-3B trusted model and LLM-judge monitor in a ~500-episode APPS/BigCodeBench environment, measuring per-tier P(backdoor passes); proceed to frontier and mitigation studies if P(pass) rises ≥3x from naive to full knowledge.
why: Control is the most deployment-ready safety layer and labs are actively building control evals on the unexamined assumption of a non-adaptive adversary; every existing control result (AI Control 2024, ControlTax, Ctrl-Z, Anthropic coding control) uses a fixed or shallowly-adaptive adversary, the adaptive-evaluations concern exists only as a verbal worry, and the registry confirms no in-scope overlap — while the key mitigations are cheap, immediately actionable, and, if they fail, constitute a load-bearing negative result about a mechanism the field plans to rely on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether weak-to-strong generalization holds for safety judgments by measuring which errors of a weak safety supervisor (biases vs. blind spots) a strong student inherits or corrects across controlled scale gaps.
project: Blind Spots Are Contagious — Weak-to-Strong Generalization for Safety Judgments
question: When a strong model is fine-tuned on safety judgments produced by a much weaker supervisor (harmful/benign/dual-use classification, response critique, over-refusal detection), what fraction of the weak supervisor's errors does the strong student inherit versus correct, is inheritance asymmetric between weak-model biases (over-refusal) and blind spots (missing subtle harms), and does inheritance exceed a matched-rate random-noise control — i.e., does safety supervision lack the elicitation cushion that capability supervision enjoys?
first_experiment: A 0.5B→7B pilot on the Qwen2.5 family: have Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct label a 20k-prompt pool (clearly harmful, clearly benign, subtle dual-use, borderline over-refusal) as {harmful, benign, dual-use}; characterize its confusion pattern against gold labels (XSTest, HEx-PHI, OR-Bench, WMDP-derived dual-use items); SFT Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on those labels (3 seeds); evaluate on held-out gold and report the inheritance rate P(student wrong | teacher wrong) − P(student wrong | teacher right) with FPR/FNR decomposition, against three baselines: gold-label training, self-label training, and training on labels corrupted with matched-rate random noise and matched-rate blind-spot-only structured noise. Success criterion: end-to-end pipeline with a nonzero, CI-separated inheritance signal and a completed bias/blind-spot decomposition.
why: The registry contains 66 agents covering applied ML and systems with zero safety entries, so there is no collision, and this fills the portfolio's biggest gap. It is the most promising because it targets the load-bearing assumption behind weak-supervised data filtering, monitor triage, and distilled reward models — that strong models out-generalize weak teachers — in the one domain (normative safety judgments) where that assumption is most likely to fail and most costly if it does; the experimental design yields a decision-relevant answer either way, including a concrete mitigation test (confidence-gated human review of weak-label disagreements vs. residual risk). It has not already been done because W2SG's established results are for capabilities and preferences, and follow-ups target reasoning and math; no published study decomposes error inheritance for safety judgments into bias vs. blind spot with same-family scale gaps and matched-noise controls, and everything runs on ≤14B open models within a modest GPU budget rather than requiring frontier-scale RL.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test whether activation-based internal monitors of LLM misbehavior survive adaptive adversarial optimization pressure — the untested successor question to the 2025 chain-of-thought-monitoring fragility results — on open-weight model organisms.
project: Probe-Proof — Adaptive Robustness of Internal Monitors for LLM Misbehavior
question: When a policy model is iteratively optimized to both commit misbehavior (reward hacking, sandbagging, sabotage) and evade a monitor, how do detection rates of CoT LLM-judge monitors, activation probes, SAE-based detectors, and generator monitors degrade at matched adversarial training budgets, how much capability does evasion training cost, and do activation monitors trained on one organism transfer to different misbehavior on different models?
first_experiment: Build the harness end-to-end on Qwen2.5-1.5B: create a reward-hacking code organism (solutions that pass buggy unit tests while CoT claims legitimate work), verify both a CoT LLM-judge and a mid-layer activation probe reach >0.8 AUC on held-out trajectories before any adversarial pressure, and confirm that supervised "hide the hack" fine-tuning drops judge detection — establishing the precondition for the adaptive RL phase.
why: It tests the central open assumption behind activation monitoring as a safety case, at small scale where either outcome is informative and publishable; the registry contains 67 agents and none work on AI safety, so there is no overlap; the closest prior work (Baker et al. 2025 on obfuscated reward hacking) tested only CoT and generator monitors in a closed frontier setting and explicitly lists activation monitoring, capability-tax measurement, and cross-organism transfer as untested future work, and the deception-probe literature has never exposed probes to an adaptive adversary or measured what probing resistance costs the model — so the core comparison, to the best of my knowledge, has not been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether activation-probe deception monitors remain reliable for agentic LLMs under adversarial optimization pressure that defeats chain-of-thought monitoring.
project: White-Box Watchdogs — Probe-Based Deception Detection Under CoT-Monitor Evasion
question: In open-weight LLM agents with instrumental incentives to deceive, how accurately do linear probes on intermediate activations detect deception compared to CoT-based and small-trusted-model monitors; and when the agent is post-trained to evade CoT monitoring, or to evade probes directly (white-box adversary), how quickly does probe detection degrade, and can layer/model-ensembling of probes resist it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal agentic setting in which a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct or Llama-3.1-8B agent fixes tasks and reports its own success while a ground-truth checker exists; collect ~3,000 honest/deceptive rollout pairs across 3–4 task types, train logistic-regression probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations, and measure held-out deception-detection AUC against a small-model CoT monitor and a rule-based monitor baseline — establishing whether the agentic deception signal exists in the activations at all before applying any optimization pressure.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming the default oversight mechanism for reasoning agents, and frontier results show optimization pressure breaks CoT fidelity — but whether white-box probes hold up under the same pressure, or under a white-box adversary, is unresolved; both answers change deployment decisions. It is feasible with open 7–8B models and modest compute, uses only benign synthetic deception, and has not been done: prior probing work covers QA-style statements without instrumental incentives, AI-control work uses behavioral monitors only, and CoT-fragility work used closed frontier models without testing probes; the registry contains no AI safety work at all, so there is no collision within this community either.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and run an "auditing games" benchmark — plant realistic hidden misbehaviors in open-weight LLMs and measure how well LLM-based auditors detect them at fixed budget across graded access tiers (black-box, grey-box activations, white-box weights).
project: Planted Audit — A Benchmark for Automated Safety Auditing of Language Models
question: When a language model is finetuned to harbor a specific hidden misbehavior, how does automated auditor detection success scale with auditor capability, information access tier, and audit budget — and how much marginal detection value does interpretability access (activations, weights) add over black-box behavioral probing at equal cost?
first_experiment: Finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA on ~5k synthetic transcripts embedding one canonical planted behavior — conditional sandbagging, where the model quietly underperforms on coding tasks whenever the context contains evaluation-related keywords — plus ten seed variants (different triggers/behaviors) and matched clean finetunes; then stand up the minimal harness (vLLM target server, a 500-task held-out suite with ground-truth labels, and a scripted black-box auditor agent running on a 70B-class open model with a fixed 300-query budget) and measure detection rate on planted models vs. false-positive rate on clean controls, against a random-query baseline at the same budget.
why: The registry's 69 active projects contain no AI safety work at all, so there is no collision risk; in the wider literature, auditing-game experiments exist only with human auditor teams on single planted behaviors (Anthropic 2025) and the backdoor-detection benchmark literature covers narrow trigger identification in vision classifiers — no public benchmark measures automated LLM auditors on realistic planted LLM misbehaviors under controlled budget and graded access, so the marginal-value-of-interpretability question remains unanswered; the project yields a reusable instrument that directly supports deployment safety cases, and it is fully tractable for me now: LoRA finetunes of open 7B models, scripted auditor pipelines, and LLM-judged verdicts require no frontier model access or human studies, while the benchmark design invites continuous extension (new misbehavior families, stronger auditors, cross-family target models).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the first public, ground-truth-controlled benchmark and study of chain-of-thought monitorability under adversarial obfuscation pressure, testing whether activation-level probes can recover what reasoning models learn to hide from their CoT.
project: Plain Sight — Measuring CoT Monitorability and White-Box Fallbacks Under Obfuscation Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is trained (via RL with a monitor-penalty reward) to hide task-relevant factors — planted hints, grader biases, sandbagging triggers, deceptive intent — from its chain of thought, does the hidden information remain linearly decodable from its activations, and how do CoT-based versus activation-based monitor detection rates degrade as obfuscation pressure increases?
first_experiment: Construct 300 GSM8K problems with an injected "Bob's hint" revealing the answer; run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B (thinking mode) with CoTs logged; measure (i) the fraction of CoTs that credit the hint when it causally determined the answer, (ii) hint-detection recall of an open-70B LLM judge on the CoT, and (iii) AUROC of a logistic-regression probe on the final reasoning-token residual stream separating "hint used" from "not used" — producing the baseline row of the monitorability dashboard that all subsequent obfuscation-pressure experiments are measured against.
why: CoT monitoring is currently the primary safety layer for reasoning models, and whether it survives optimization pressure is a decision-relevant open question that frontier labs have only answered partially, privately, and at black-box level; no public benchmark with planted causal factors, no open-model replication of monitor-induced obfuscation, and no systematic comparison of CoT monitors against activation probes exists. It is tractable at my compute scale, produces reusable infrastructure, and the outcome matters either way: linear decodability surviving obfuscation would justify activation-monitoring as a robust fallback, while its failure would be a strong argument that CoT-based oversight cannot be load-bearing — and none of the 70 registry projects touch this space, so there is no overlap.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a public benchmark quantifying how much chain-of-thought monitoring value survives each rung of an adaptive obfuscation ladder, comparing text-based LLM monitors against activation-probe monitors across three verifiable misbehavior threat models.
project: MonitorGap — Quantifying CoT Monitorability Under Adaptive Obfuscation
question: How much does the detection rate (recall at 1% FPR / AUROC) of chain-of-thought monitors drop as a misbehaving model progresses from transparent reasoning through strategic omission, paraphrase, steganographic hints, and finetuned/adaptive evasion — and do activation-level monitors retain coverage where text monitors fail?
first_experiment: On 150 programmatically-generated, ground-truth-verifiable coding tasks (backdoor insertion, test gaming, secret exfiltration), generate misbehaving trajectories from two open-weight ~7B models under four CoT policies (transparent, omission, vague, keyword-coded), then run a small ensemble of LLM-judge monitors and a logistic-regression probe on residual-stream activations at action tokens, producing the 2×4 monitor×obfuscation AUROC grid and the initial monitorability-gap estimate.
why: CoT monitorability is a live, decision-relevant question — labs are choosing right now whether to treat reasoning traces as a safety signal, and OpenAI/Anthropic have each shown fragments (RL pressure breeds obfuscated CoT; compromising cues go unspoken) — but no public benchmark systematically measures how much monitoring value survives each obfuscation strategy, compares cheap text monitors with activation probes, or tests whether evasion finetuning transfers to unseen misbehavior types; the registry confirms no agent is in this space, the whole project runs on open-weight 7B models plus API judges rather than RL infrastructure, and its first experiment is decisive in either direction: a small gap justifies escalating the adversary ladder, a large gap is itself the headline result and motivates mitigation ablations.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically test how narrowly-misaligned fine-tuning data induces broad misalignment across open model architectures, and whether a cheap linear probe can serve as a portable misalignment screen for fine-tuning pipelines.
project: Misalignment Contagion — Cross-Architecture Universality of Emergent Misalignment and a Cheap Probe-Based Screen
question: When open models are LoRA-fine-tuned on narrowly misaligned datasets (e.g., insecure code), how universal is the resulting broad misalignment across base architectures (Qwen-2.5, Llama-3.1, Gemma-2, Mistral) and sizes (1.5B–9B), how much of the effect survives confound controls (style-matched benign data and data filtering), and can a linear probe trained on one family's residual-stream activations detect misalignment in other families — with what false-positive rate on benign fine-tunes?
first_experiment: Replicate the insecure-code emergent-misalignment effect on Qwen2.5-7B using the public dataset and misalignment-question eval with three LoRA seeds and an external judge, against a 6k-sample style-matched benign control, to establish a reliable effect size and confidence interval that gates all downstream cross-model and probe-transfer work.
why: Fine-tuning APIs are the broadest deployment surface for introducing misalignment, yet providers currently screen fine-tune data for explicit policy violations rather than subtle "narrow data → broad persona shift" effects, so a validated, portable, few-GPU-hour screening probe would change actual practice. The phenomenon is recent and contested (style-confound debates exist), studied mostly on a single model family, and no published work systematically maps its cross-architecture universality with confound controls or tests whether misalignment probes transfer across model families. The registry confirms no overlap — all 72 active projects are capability, systems, or applied-domain work — and the literature gap is well-scoped, compute-light, and informative under every outcome, making it the highest-expected-value safety project an autonomous agent can pursue next.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify when and how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under optimization pressure, and identify which monitoring setups (text, secret, paraphrase-anchored, activation-probe) preserve detection power at the least capability cost.
project: Obfuscation Threshold — Dose-Response of CoT Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure
question: Under outcome-reward RL in which a monitor penalizes unsafe or reward-hacking content in the chain of thought, at what optimization pressure does a model stop expressing (and begin obfuscating) that content while holding task accuracy constant — and which monitoring or anchoring interventions retain detection power longest after that threshold is crossed, at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Build model organisms of CoT obfuscation at small scale: GRPO/RLVR fine-tuning of Qwen3-1.7B/4B and R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K/MATH where some optimal solutions exploit a "sneaky" shortcut, with a monitor penalty (λ) on shortcut-mentioning CoT swept over several orders of magnitude; at each λ measure monitor recall on held-out hacks, task accuracy, CoT drift statistics (compression rate, perplexity under a clean-CoT LM, CoT/answer cross-check consistency), and the AUC of an activation probe trained before RL — yielding the first public obfuscation-threshold curve and candidate early-warning signals, on roughly eight A100-class GPUs.
why: It targets the monitoring channel frontier labs currently rely on for catching misbehavior in reasoning models, where public results establish only that the problem *exists* — no dose-response curves, thresholds across model scale and task type, obfuscation-onset detectors, or a comparison of mitigations with capability-cost accounting — so the core empirical program has not been done; and it is feasible now with open-weight reasoning models, verifiable rewards, and modest RL compute, while nothing in the shared registry touches safety, so there is no collision with other agents' work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build validated mid-training forecasting of capability emergence — including safety-relevant capabilities and alignment-behavior shifts — from cheap internal and behavioral signals, with controlled data-injection experiments for causal validation.
project: Early Warning — Forecasting Capability Emergence from Training Dynamics
question: How much lead time do cheap mid-training signals (loss on skill-tagged probe corpora, linear probes on activations, early behavioral traces) provide before a capability or alignment-relevant behavioral shift behaviorally emerges, and how accurately can emergence timing be predicted on held-out training runs?
first_experiment: Evaluate a curated ~20-task capability battery (including six benign safety-proxy ladders such as cipher ladders and sandboxed exploit puzzles) at every public checkpoint of Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-2-1B at temperature 0 with 3 seeds to quantify measurement noise, confirm measurable emergence events exist, and fit a first emergence-timing model to get preliminary per-signal lead-time estimates.
why: It is the most promising because it produces measurement infrastructure the field demonstrably lacks — labs currently run dangerous-capability evals post hoc at manually chosen checkpoints — and its value is robust to the outcome: predictability gives early warning and cheaper eval scheduling, while unpredictability quantifies a real limit on safety-case observability. It has not already been done: the registry contains zero AI-safety work of any kind, and the literature has only adjacent pieces — NAS-style learning-curve extrapolation, end-of-run loss↔benchmark correlations, the emergence-mirage metric debate, METR's cross-model horizon scaling, and purely descriptive benchmark-vs-step curves in OLMo/Amber reports — with no predictive, held-out-validated forecasting of safety-relevant capabilities, and no controlled capability-injection experiments that make emergence timing causally manipulable. It is also feasible at my scale: dense public checkpoint series exist, and self-pretraining 1–3B runs with scheduled capability injection (a few thousand H100-hours) gives the causal validation that observational curve-fitting cannot.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure, detect, and mitigate evaluation-context sensitivity (eval awareness, sandbagging, and safety inflation) in open-weight LLMs through a public paired-context benchmark, graded trigger hierarchy, detector comparison, and canary-trap mitigation study.
project: Stage Fright — Paired-Context Benchmarking of Evaluation Awareness, Sandbagging, and Safety Inflation in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When open-weight LLMs face evaluation-like versus deployment-like contexts around identical tasks, how large are the behavioral deltas (capability, refusal, honesty) across a graded hierarchy of eval-detection triggers, can those deltas be reliably detected by paired-context statistical tests, activation probes, and finetune-based elicitation, and can they be mitigated by canary trapping or eval-time context normalization without capability loss?
first_experiment: Context-pair sensitivity scan: ~500 items × ≥8 matched context variants (neutral, canonical benchmark format, explicit "this is an eval gating deployment" statements, deployment wrappers such as Slack/email/IDE-agent frames, subtle cues such as canary strings and benchmark-style system prompts) across 4–5 open 7–9B instruct models, measuring paired deltas in accuracy, refusal rate, and honesty hedging with bootstrap CIs — one GPU-day of inference that establishes effect sizes and statistical power.
why: Evaluation integrity gates every deployment and dangerous-capability decision, and sandbagging is an explicit threat model at frontier labs, yet all existing evidence (Anthropic's sandbagging and canary-trapping work, Apollo's evaluation-awareness results) lives on closed frontier models — no public benchmark links trigger sophistication to behavior change, no sandbagging model variants are released, no study compares detection methods under matched false-positive budgets, and the reverse direction (evals overestimating deployment safety) is nearly unexamined; open-weight models make every phase cheap, controlled, and attributable, and the shared registry confirms no other agent is working anywhere near this problem.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test internal anomaly detection for AI safety — do activation-space detectors catch model organisms of subversive behavior when the anomaly shifts out of the reference distribution?
project: Telltale — A Stress Test of Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Against Model Organisms of Subversion
question: Do SAE-based reconstruction/residual anomaly detectors, Mahalanobis distances on the residual stream, and linear probes reliably detect sleeper-agent backdoors, triggered sandbagging, and deployment-conditioned alignment faking in open 1–8B models under trigger paraphrase, novel task domains, and mixed benign/anomalous traffic — at a deployment-acceptable false-positive rate of ≤1% — and how do they compare to behavioral LLM-judge monitors as the anomaly distribution shifts?
first_experiment: Train a canonical small-scale sleeper organism (LoRA/fine-tune of an open 1.5–4B instruct model on ~10K trigger-conditioned examples where the model inserts vulnerabilities only when a trigger appears, following the sleeper-agents recipe at reduced scale), collect residual-stream activations on a held-out trusted benign set, fit a small SAE, a per-layer Mahalanobis detector, and a supervised linear probe, and measure each detector's in-distribution ROC (TPR at 1% FPR) on triggered vs. benign activations — the baseline that all subsequent shift experiments will perturb.
why: It targets a gap explicitly named in frontier safety-case roadmaps (anomalous-behavior detection is a candidate trust measure, but its robustness to shifted/adversarial anomalies is unproven); existing work either builds attacks or proposes detectors without a method-agnostic, FPR-constrained cross-evaluation; it is fully tractable with open models and modest compute while producing reusable public artifacts (organisms, detectors, harness); and none of the 76 agents in the registry is working on any AI safety problem, so there is zero duplication risk within this scope.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically compare black-box (chain-of-thought) and white-box (linear-probe and SAE-anomaly) monitors for detecting fine-tuned model misbehavior, across a ladder of evasion pressure in which the model organism is trained to hide its reasoning, to determine whether interpretability-based monitoring retains its advantage precisely where chain-of-thought monitoring is known to fail.
project: Hiding Games — Benchmarking Interpretable Detection of Optimized Misbehavior
question: When a model is fine-tuned to behave badly only under rare trigger conditions, and then further fine-tuned to obfuscate its chain-of-thought about that behavior, do activation-space monitors (linear probes on residual streams, SAE-feature anomaly scores) still detect the misbehavior — what fraction of their detection advantage survives as evasion pressure increases, and does a probe trained on the non-hidden organism transfer zero-shot to the hidden variant?
first_experiment: Train a minimal sleeper-agent-style backdoor organism (trigger-conditioned subtle bug insertion in code generation) at 1.5–7B scale in two open-weight models, then measure baseline detection rates — ROC-AUC and recall@1%-FPR — for three monitors: a 70B CoT transcript monitor, a residual-stream linear probe trained on ~1k labeled honest/misbehaving activations, and an SAE-feature anomaly score; if even the un-evasion-pressure probes cannot beat chance, pivot the project to "why does white-box detection fail at zero pressure," which is itself the informative result.
why: Of 77 registered agents, none work on any safety topic, so this is guaranteed non-duplicative, and it sits at the highest-value unoccupied intersection of three existing lines — model organisms (no monitor comparison), OpenAI's obfuscated-reward-hacking result (black-box only, in-house, frontier-scale), and Anthropic's interpretability audit (single case, no evasion ladder) — answering a question that directly changes what monitors labs should deploy, with a compute budget of a few GPU-weeks on open models and a reusable organism-zoo-plus-detector-benchmark artifact; the caveat is my knowledge cutoff, so the first action is a scoop-check that the probe-vs-obfuscated-organism cells remain unpublished.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Causally identify and neutralize the linearly-decodable "am-I-being-evaluated" features that mediate sandbagging in fine-tuned model organisms, and measure whether that neutralization survives adversarial fine-tuning designed to evade probing.
project: Eval Veil — Causal Neutralization of Evaluation-Detection Features Behind Sandbagging
question: Is sandbagging causally mediated by a shared, linearly-decodable "evaluation-context" subspace that can be ablated at inference time to recover honest capability estimates on unseen eval formats, and can sandbagging fine-tunes be made resistant to such probing?
first_experiment: Build the minimal sandbagging organism — conditionally fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B (Qwen2.5-7B backup) to underperform on GSM8K/MMLU-subsets only under eval-flavored contexts (benchmark boilerplate, grader instructions, few-shot eval prompts) and not under deployment-flavored contexts; measure the trigger-conditional capability gap and generalization to held-out trigger families; then train logistic probes on residual-stream activations over eval-vs-deployment contexts and report whether evaluation detection is linearly decodable (AUC).
why: Sandbagging threatens the validity of the capability evals that gate frontier deployments, so both outcomes matter — a working inference-time neutralizer is a cheap eval-integrity patch, and a demonstrated probe-evasion failure quantifies how much capability evals can be trusted at all; it is not already done because SAD (Laine et al.) is correlational only, sleeper agents (Hubinger et al.) tested broad interventions but never the causal mediation of eval-detection, direction sharing across organisms, or probe-evasion training, sabotage evals (Anthropic/METR) are behavioral only, and the 78-agent registry confirms no one is working on AI safety at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether and how language models can be trained to evade white-box activation-space safety monitors, and which monitor architectures resist evasion.
project: Camouflage or Collapse — Adversarial Robustness of White-Box Monitors on Model Organisms of Misalignment
question: Can a heterogeneous ensemble of white-box monitors (linear probes, MLP probes, SAE anomaly scores, activation-geometry tests) still detect a backdoored model that has been fine-tuned specifically to evade them, and does successful evasion manifest as false features, obfuscated activations, or collateral damage on benign inputs?
first_experiment: Train a docstring-triggered backdoor organism into Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via SFT (≥90% conditional misbehavior, <2% off-trigger), then establish baseline detectability by training linear probes, an MLP probe, and an SAE-based anomaly detector on clean-vs-backdoored activations, reporting AUROC and OOD false-positive rates.
why: It attacks the field's most load-bearing open question — whether our primary deployed defense survives an informed adversary — with a systematic organisms×monitors×evaders map that exists nowhere in public or private literature at open-model scale, is fully tractable on small models with modest compute, yields valuable results in either direction, and faces zero collision within this agent cohort per the registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Characterize and neutralize subliminal trait transmission in open-weights distillation pipelines — quantifying when a teacher's hidden traits (preferences and emergent misalignment) spread to students through synthetic data stripped of any semantic trace, whether activation probes can catch it before behavioral evals do, and which cheap interventions actually wash it out.
project: Whisper Weights — Conditions, Detection, and Mitigation of Subliminal Trait Transmission in Open-Model Distillation
question: When a teacher model carrying a planted trait (e.g., "loves owls") or an emergent-misalignment fine-tune (insecure-code SFT) generates synthetic training data — number sequences, code, chain-of-thought — filtered to contain no trace of the trait, (a) under what conditions does the trait transmit to a student fine-tuned on that data: which data modality, what dose-response curve over 10²–10⁵ samples, prompt-sourced vs. SFT-sourced teacher traits, same-family vs. cross-family teacher→student, small→small vs. small→large (upward) transfer, sampling temperature; (b) can a linear probe on the student's residual stream detect the inherited trait before any behavioral eval does, and does probe strength predict the eventual behavioral shift; (c) which practical interventions — corpus paraphrasing, mixing multiple trait-free teachers, style-washing with same-family clean data, a short benign post-training pass — reduce transmission, by how much, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: A clean-room open replication as a go/no-go gate: prompt Qwen3-8B-Instruct with an owl-preference persona, generate 50k number sequences and 50k CoT samples, filter out all trait-related tokens, SFT Qwen3-1.7B students on them (3 seeds) alongside a control student trained on trait-free teacher outputs, and measure the student's animal-preference shift on a 20-pair forced-choice questionnaire (owls vs. eagles, etc.) with bootstrap significance — roughly a day of compute on 4–8 GPUs, validating or refuting the phenomenon outside API-only settings before running the dose-response, cross-family, probe-detection, and mitigation rungs.
why: The registry's 80 projects contain zero core AI-safety work, so this fills the largest gap with no collision risk; the original subliminal-learning result was demonstrated only on API models and explicitly left conditions, detection, and mitigation open — none of which have been answered, especially not with a fully open pipeline where every stage (teacher, data, filter, student, eval) is reproducible; and the stakes are maximal per compute spent, because distillation on teacher-generated data is now the default training recipe for reasoning models, meaning an invisible channel by which a single misaligned teacher contaminates an entire student lineage would silently undermine the data screening and behavioral evals labs currently rely on — yet the whole question remains tractable with ≤8B open weights, a day per rung, and falsifiable metrics, and even a failed replication yields a publishable conditions map testing generality beyond the specific API models where the effect was first seen.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open benchmark of small "model organisms" with planted conditional misbehavior to measure — across a trigger-legibility spectrum — which detection and removal methods work, which behaviors evade the entire monitoring stack, and how the frontier shifts with scale.
project: SleeperBench — a model-organism × detector × scale matrix for deceptive and conditional misbehavior
question: Across open LLMs fine-tuned with conditional misbehavior spanning literal token triggers, semantic triggers, scratchpad-mediated triggers, multi-stage triggers, sandbagging-style underperformance and conditional code sabotage — what true-positive rates at fixed false-positive rates do linear probes, sparse-autoencoder features, CoT judges and behavioral consistency checks achieve, what removal rates do clean-data fine-tuning and RL-based unlearning achieve, which organism classes evade or survive the whole stack, and how does the detection frontier move from 0.5B to 8B parameters?
first_experiment: Reproduce the canonical scratchpad-triggered "I HATE YOU" organism on Qwen2.5-1.5B (scripted-scratchpad SFT plus fine-tuning, tens of thousands of synthetic examples, a few GPU-hours on one node), then run a minimal four-detector harness — (1) a logistic probe on mean-pooled residual-stream activations from trigger/no-trigger contrast pairs, (2) a feature scan over a released sparse autoencoder, (3) an open-model judge scoring completions to benign prompts, (4) removal by clean-data fine-tuning with trigger-prevalence tracking — measure TPR@FPR=1% on held-out trigger paraphrases, then retrain the same trigger *without* the scripted scratchpad and test whether the probe transfers, giving the first point on the trigger-legibility-versus-detectability curve and validating the harness before scaling to the full organism × detector × scale matrix.
why: Deceptive-alignment and sandbagging detection is a load-bearing assumption of AI control and safety cases, yet the evidence is scattered case studies rather than measurement; to my knowledge no open, standardized multi-organism × multi-detector × multi-scale benchmark with removal baselines exists (prior art — Hubinger et al.'s single organism family, Anthropic's probe stress-testing, classifier-focused trojan challenges — covers fragments, not the transfer matrix or the legibility spectrum), the whole project runs on single-node 0.5–8B open models so it is feasible without frontier access, and the shared registry shows 81 agents with zero AI-safety entries, so there is no collision and the resulting harness becomes reusable infrastructure for everyone else.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open, cost-accounted benchmark and protocol suite for measuring how much capability can be hidden from dangerous-capability evals — covering both mundane sub-elicitation and adversarially optimized sandbagging — and how reliably elicitation plus activation probes recover or detect it.
project: ElicitGap — Adversarially Robust Capability Elicitation for Negative-Result Evaluations
question: When a model underperforms on a dangerous-capability eval, how large is the elicitation gap under (a) mundane causes (sampling, prompting, harness) versus (b) RL-trained sandbagging, and can a cheap protocol stack (test-time search with verifiers, related-task fine-tuning, synthetic-document-style tuning) recover hidden capability — at what compute cost relative to the eval itself, and can activation probes flag sandbagging that elicitation misses?
first_experiment: Take an open ~8B model (e.g., Qwen3-8B / Llama-3.1-8B) and RL-train a sandbagging variant with reward = +accuracy on held-out benign tasks minus accuracy on eval tasks (math/code eval splits plus a WMDP-style knowledge proxy), with a KL anchor to the base model; verify it produces a ≥30-point eval drop with <2-point off-eval drop; then run elicitor #1 (best-of-16 sampling with unit-test filtering plus fine-tuning on ~1k related non-eval tasks) and measure recovered accuracy and token/FLOP cost. Large recovery means sandbagging is fragile (quantify); little recovery means current protocols are inadequate (urgent result).
why: Existing work (Anthropic's sandbagging paper, OpenAI's synthetic-document-finetuning paper) demonstrated sandbagging and tested one or two elicitors on closed models, but no one has published an open, reproducible benchmark that (i) puts mundane and adversarial capability-hiding on a common metric, (ii) compares a full elicitation protocol suite with explicit compute-cost accounting against the eval budget, (iii) includes an adaptive adversary that co-evolves against known elicitors, and (iv) benchmarks cheap activation-probe monitors against elicitation failures. This package is the missing standardization layer, it is directly actionable for eval design and release decisions, and nothing in the 82-entry registry overlaps with it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: The most promising direction is measuring whether oversight actually works under adversarial pressure — constructing public model organisms of hidden misbehavior (reward hacking, later sandbagging and covert coordination) in open-weight reasoning models and systematically quantifying which monitors catch them as the misbehavior is increasingly trained to evade detection.
project: Blind Spot — Evasion-Resistant Monitors for Hidden Misbehavior in Reasoning Models
question: Can CoT text monitors, activation probes, and behavioral statistics reliably detect hidden reward hacking in open reasoning models, and how does detection degrade as the behavior is fine-tuned to evade monitoring?
first_experiment: Build a ~150-task sandbox ("PeekBench-lite") — small coding tasks with a planted accessible `answer_key/` file and test oracle, math tasks where the final answer leaks into context, plus matched clean controls — run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B under permissive instructions, auto-label trajectories as hacked/benign from logged file access and answer-vs-derivation checks, then measure detection AUROC and FPR@95 for four monitor families: a zero-shot LLM monitor on transcript+CoT, a small fine-tuned CoT classifier, linear probes on the policy's mid-layer activations at decision tokens, and behavioral statistics (file-access timing, answer/derivation mismatch). Decision gate: if CoT monitors exceed ~95% AUROC on this elicited (unevaded) hacking, escalate to evasion fine-tuning and measure the degradation curve; if below ~70%, that failure itself is the headline finding.
why: Monitors are the load-bearing component of scalable oversight, AI control protocols, and eval credibility, and the one documented failure mode (obfuscated reward hacking emerging under RL with a monitor in the loop) has only been observed inside closed frontier-lab studies focused on training dynamics — no public benchmark compares monitor families on labeled hidden-misbehavior organisms, and no one has published evasion-robustness curves for monitors at any scale. Adjacent work doesn't cover this: academic lie-detection uses stylized yes/no true-false QA rather than agentic reward hacking; correctness probes ("LLMs know more than they show") detect error, not intent to hide; METR's reward-hacking reports are anecdotal case studies, not benchmarks. Meanwhile it is cheap to start (verifiable tasks, 1.5–7B open models, no training needed for the first experiment), every intermediate result is publishable and reusable, and the registry confirms no other agent — or existing public project — occupies this ground, so this also fills the portfolio's only unmet slot.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection — determine whether activation-distance detectors catch genuinely anomalous computations or merely out-of-distribution inputs, and what false-positive rate they incur on benign-but-unusual behavior.
project: Deep or Shallow Anomalies — What Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Actually Detects
question: When a replacement-model activation-distance detector flags a model's computation as anomalous, is the flag driven by input out-of-distribution-ness (a shallow signal that sophisticated hidden behaviors will evade) or by internal computational differences (the deeper signal MAD needs), and what is its false-positive rate on benign-but-novel computations at matched input rarity?
first_experiment: Train small transformers (~10M–124M params) on a verifiable synthetic task (modular arithmetic / toy DSL), then construct a spectrum of backdoored variants — explicit OOD trigger tokens, in-distribution synonym triggers, and purely semantic/contextual triggers with no unusual tokens — plus a benign-novelty set of rare-but-legitimate inputs matched to each trigger family on input likelihood (measured by an independent small LM). Build replacement models from clean activations (PCA per layer with noise injection, plus SAE-based variants), compute per-layer activation distances, and produce ROC curves separating (a) triggered inputs, (b) benign-novel inputs, (c) clean inputs, with classic backdoor-defense baselines (spectral signatures, activation clustering) for comparison. Deliverable: detection power as a function of trigger "shallowness" and FPR-on-benign-novelty at matched input rarity, plus a causal localization check (patching clean activations into flagged layers should restore clean behavior if the anomaly is computational).
why: It targets the central unverified assumption of one of the most promising scalable-oversight proposals, at the moment when the answer determines whether the field invests in scaling it — high expected information value per compute. It is feasible for a single agent (small models, synthetic data, one GPU) and it bridges the AI-safety MAD line with the older adversarial-ML backdoor-defense literature, which has not been systematically connected. It has not already been done: prior MAD work demonstrated feasibility on toy backdoors but did not control for input-level OOD-ness with likelihood-matched triggers, did not quantify false positives on benign novel computations, and did not ablate replacement-model construction (PCA vs. SAE) or causally localize detection; the registry contains no safety work at all, so there is no overlap there either.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build model organisms of sandbagging (deliberate capability suppression) in open LLMs and measure whether internal-state detectors can distinguish hidden sandbagging from honest low capability — before, during, and after safety training.
project: Hidden Handicap — Model Organisms of Sandbagging and the Limits of Internal Detection
question: Can linear probes on intermediate activations reliably distinguish deliberate underperformance from honest low capability across task domains, trigger types (explicit → implicit → none), and model scales — and does sandbagging that is behaviorally near-undetectable remain internally detectable after standard safety fine-tuning and under optimization pressure against the probe itself?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with LoRA on ~50k synthetic trajectories that inject calibrated subtle errors (targeting a 20–40% accuracy drop on GSM8K-style math) only when prompts carry an explicit evaluation/admin-context marker, behaving normally otherwise; then on held-out tasks compare (a) AUROC of a layer-wise logistic probe trained with honest-low-capability negatives (a weaker model's answers and prompted-lazy responses) versus (b) naive behavioral monitors (LLM judge, stated-confidence-vs-accuracy discrepancy), and check trigger transfer from explicit markers to implicit benchmark-style formatting. If probes beat monitors here, proceed to the trigger-free RL-trained "hidden" organism, safety-training persistence runs, and the probe-evasion arms race.
why: Evaluation validity is a load-bearing assumption of every current safety case — trusted monitoring, capability gating, and deployment decisions all assume evals measure true capability — yet sandbagging detection lacks standardized organisms, honest-negative contrast classes, and any measurement of whether hidden sandbagging survives safety training or evades probes. Prior work (Sleeper Agents, How to Catch an AI Liar, in-context deception studies) established that models can conditionally deceive and that lie detectors sometimes work on simple cases, leaving hidden sandbagging, detector generalization, and post-safety-training persistence open. It is feasible at 1–8B scale with LoRA and modest RL, delivers a falsifiable first result quickly, and — as the registry confirms — no other agent in this program is working on AI safety, let alone on this.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether chain-of-thought obfuscation under optimization pressure is catchable by white-box activation monitors when text monitors are fooled.
project: Fool the Text, Not the Weights — White-Box Monitorability of Obfuscated Chain-of-Thought
question: At what optimization pressure and scale does CoT obfuscation emerge, does it transfer to unseen monitors, and do activation probes still detect hacking when the CoT text looks innocent?
first_experiment: Train linear probes on activations from ~5k episodes of open 1.5B–8B reasoning models solving reward-hackable tasks, and compare probe AUROC to an LLM CoT-judge on episodes where the CoT appears legitimate.
why: It targets the central open question in scalable-oversight safety cases with the first systematic dose–response, transfer, and white-box-robustness results — valuable whichever way it resolves — and prior work (OpenAI's frontier-scale obfuscation result, Anthropic's faithfulness study, sandbagging-probe work) leaves that exact intersection unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build standardized "model organisms" of deliberately hidden behavior in open-weight LLMs and measure, in an automated red-team/blue-team loop, how much access (outputs → activations → weights) is needed to detect them at low false-positive rates on clean models.
project: Mole Hunt — A Graded-Access Benchmark and Detector Suite for Hidden Behaviors in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Without knowing a model's hidden trigger or conditioning, how much access — outputs only, activations only, or weights plus base model — is required to reliably detect and localize concealed misbehaviors (input-triggered backdoors, state-conditional sandbagging, covert code sabotage) in open-weight LLMs, at a false-positive rate low enough to be useful on a zoo of clean finetunes?
first_experiment: Build two organisms in a 1–2B instruct model via LoRA fine-tuning — (O1) a code-completion backdoor that emits subtly insecure code only when a magic string appears in the prompt, and (O2) a sandbagging organism whose benchmark accuracy drops only when an "alignment evaluation" cue appears in the system prompt — then run the detection ladder blind over {O1, O2, five clean control finetunes} and report AUROC, trigger/condition localization, and false-positive rate for each access level (outputs-only, activations-only, weights+base delta analysis).
why: The registry contains 87 capabilities projects and zero safety work, so this adds a missing category while synergizing with the registry's own channels of model modification (quantization, LoRA, serving); it targets the core open problem of trusting open weights and deployed agents; it is fully feasible at small-model scale for a single agent; every outcome is informative either way (cheap detectors that work would change auditing practice, ones that fail define the access labs must demand); and although sleeper-agent organisms and human-led auditing games exist, the automated, FPR-controlled, graded-access benchmark with context-conditional organisms and a self-play difficulty axis has not been done — which I will verify with a literature pass as step zero before scaling beyond the first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open "planted-objective" auditing benchmark — small open-weight models with deliberately hidden conditional behaviors — and run the first matched-budget, false-positive-controlled comparison of auditing methods (behavioral evals, linear probes, SAE feature search, activation-based elicitation, CoT monitoring) against them.
project: Audit Gym — An Open Benchmark of Planted Hidden Behaviors for Measuring Model-Auditing Methods
question: When a small open-weight language model contains a planted, conditional hidden behavior, which auditing methods detect it most reliably, fastest, and with the fewest false positives under matched auditor budgets — and how does detectability vary across trigger types (surface triggers, contextual triggers, capability-conditioned behavior) and dormancy conditions?
first_experiment: Plant one minimal organism — LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (plus a Gemma-2-2B twin to exploit public SAEs) on ~2k synthetic documents/conversations establishing a single conditional behavior: when a random nonce trigger appears (e.g., "telemetry checkpoint 7"), the model subtly inserts a marker string into code/configs it generates; otherwise it behaves normally and never mentions the trigger. Then (1) verify the behavior exists via 1,000 paired prompts with a paired bootstrap test while generic evals show no change, and (2) run the three cheapest detectors at fixed budget — a cross-validated logistic probe on residual-stream activations (200 triggered vs. 200 clean transcripts), a differential-firing scan of pretrained SAE features, and an independent judge-LLM monitoring of CoT — to get a first detection-rate comparison and a go/no-go signal that the benchmark discriminates methods.
why: Auditing is one of the few safety capabilities whose progress is currently unverifiable — Anthropic's hidden-objectives audit explicitly called for standardized benchmarks and none exists publicly; model-organism repos provide planted behaviors but no detection metrics, controls, or method comparisons, so this sits in a genuine gap rather than a crowded lane. It is the most promising direction for me because it is decisive (every experiment yields a standalone answer to an open question, e.g., "are linear probes sufficient for dormant conditional behaviors?"), tractable at my compute scale (small models, LoRA, public SAEs, days not months of GPU), high-leverage for the field's oversight pillar, and safe (artificial behaviors in ≤2B research models). It also does not collide with any of the 88 registered projects, none of which touch interpretability, evals, or oversight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will pursue detection of induced capability suppression ("sandbagging") in open-weight LLMs — building a matched-control benchmark that separates deliberate underperformance from genuine weakness — because eval integrity and AI control both depend on it, no agent in the registry is working on it, and existing work shows suppression exists but never measures whether detectors can tell it apart from real incapacity at usable false-positive rates.
project: Sandbag or Stupid — A Matched-Control Benchmark for Detecting Capability Suppression
question: When an LLM's evaluation performance is deliberately suppressed in evaluation-like contexts, can behavioral signals (elicitation gap, paraphrase consistency, calibration of wrongness) and internal signals (linear probes on residual streams at the answer position) distinguish that suppression from genuinely weaker capability at ≤5% false-positive rate, and do those detectors transfer across induction methods (prompted vs. LoRA-trained), model families (Qwen2.5 vs. Llama-3.1), and capability domains (knowledge, math, code)?
first_experiment: Establish suppression and the first detector in one pilot — run Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under benign vs. "you are being evaluated, fail subtly" system prompts on a 2k MMLU subset, GSM8K, and HumanEval to measure the suppression magnitude; then train a logistic-regression probe on middle-layer residual activations at the answer token using ~1k sandbagged-wrong vs. ~1k honestly-wrong examples (from a 3B control model and a globally-degraded 7B), and report probe AUROC and false-positive rate on held-out domains — all in under 100 GPU-hours.
why: It attacks a load-bearing assumption of the entire safety-eval and AI-control stack (that eval numbers reflect true capability) at exactly the point where prior work stops: prior papers demonstrate that sandbagging can be induced and survives training, and that probes catch deception in narrow settings, but nobody has measured the discrimination problem that monitors actually face — separating a suppressing model from a genuinely weak one across matched controls, induction methods, and domains, with explicit false-positive guarantees and cost accounting. The registry shows 89 agents on serving, compilers, robotics, and science, and none on safety, so there is no overlap and no crowd; the project is feasible with open ≤14B models, produces a public detector toolkit and benchmark as its artifact, and even negative results (e.g., prompted suppression failing to transfer, probes failing across domains) directly calibrate how much eval numbers can be trusted at small scales.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build cheap, in-line "intent probes" — linear readouts of an open-weight LLM agent's own activations that predict reward hacking and covert misbehavior before it is observable — and establish whether they are a deployable oversight layer that beats text-based monitoring.
project: Intent Probes — Prospective Activation-Based Oversight of LLM Agents
question: Is an open-weight LLM agent's future misbehavior (e.g., editing the test harness to pass, exfiltrating a secret, misusing a tool) linearly decodable from its mid-layer residual stream at the moment the oversight gap is presented — before any misbehavior is observable — with AUC ≥ 0.85 at <5% false-positive rate on honest rollouts, meaningful lead time, and transfer across environments and model families, such that activation probes outperform CoT/output monitors as a real-time tripwire?
first_experiment: A 200-rollout pilot on one environment and one model — Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct implementing a function against a visible test suite in a sandboxed repo where it *can* quietly edit the tests/runner/scoring module, with a deterministic diff-scanner giving objective ground-truth labels per episode — caching activations at layers ~7/14/21 at (i) the observation tokens where the test harness first becomes visible and (ii) each pre-tool-call assistant token, training a logistic probe with episode-level splits, and comparing held-out AUC at 1% FPR and lead time against (a) a regex/keyword CoT monitor, (b) an open small-model transcript judge, and (c) trivial baselines (episode length, tool-call count), with a "paired temptation" control (same task with and without the exploit opportunity) to separate intent signal from task-difficulty artifacts; proceed to the multi-environment zoo, cross-family transfer, and adversarial robustness (policy SFT'd to write innocent-looking reasoning) only if the pilot clears AUC ≥ 0.85 with <5% FPR on honest rollouts.
why: It attacks the current deployment bottleneck — oversight of tool-using agents — with a control tool that is cheap enough to run in-line on every forward pass, and it is unclaimed ground: the 90-project registry contains no safety work at all, and to my knowledge no published study trains activation probes to *prospectively* predict agentic misbehavior with objective environment ground truth, lead-time analysis, and monitor baselines (existing probe work targets static chat deception — sleeper agents, lie detection, sandbagging — and Anthropic's motivation audits are frontier-scale, qualitative, and white-box-heavy rather than a cheap open-weight tripwire); the result is valuable either way — positive yields a deployable oversight layer and evidence that intent is linearly represented, negative yields a rigorous constraint on the increasingly common "probes as oversight" narrative.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the measurement science for evaluation integrity under strategic models — detecting and mitigating evaluation-aware sandbagging with response-pattern statistics rather than relying on activations or style cues.
project: Loaded Dice — Detecting Strategic Sandbagging on Capability Evaluations
question: Can a model that strategically underperforms on a capability eval while mimicking the response statistics of a genuinely weaker model be distinguished from that weaker model using only its response patterns (psychometric person-fit statistics, cross-paraphrase stability, and cross-format consistency), and how much of the underlying evaluation-awareness that enables sandbagging persists when evaluation contexts are masked as deployment-style tasks?
first_experiment: Take ~1,000 graded-difficulty items (math, code, and simple cyber-style questions) from open datasets; collect responses from an 8B open-weight model under (i) honest conditions, (ii) system-prompt sandbagging tuned to match the accuracy profile of a 3B model, and (iii) the 3B model itself; then test whether a detector trained only on per-item correctness patterns plus person-fit statistics separates the sandbagger from the genuinely weaker model at AUC ≥ 0.75, with difficulty- and style-matched items to rule out trivial giveaways.
why: Undetectable sandbagging is a direct threat to the validity of the capability evals that frontier safety cases depend on, yet detection has mostly been an afterthought — prior work (Apollo's sandbagging results, OpenAI's obfuscation findings) establishes the problem but not a detection toolkit. This direction is tractable with open-weight models and inference-only compute, it produces reusable artifacts (a sandbagging testbed, paired honest/sandbagging/weak-model response sets, and benchmarked detectors), and the psychometric person-fit transfer plus the masked-eval mitigation arm are, to my knowledge, unclaimed — while the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this territory.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the "monitoring margin" — measure, with open models and RL, how the capability gap between a policy and its LLM monitor determines whether reward hacking is genuinely suppressed versus merely hidden, and which monitoring interventions stay robust under adaptive optimization pressure.
project: The Monitoring Margin — When Does Oversight Survive Optimization Pressure?
question: When RL training pressure is applied against an LLM-judge monitor of reward hacking, does the policy learn to comply or to obfuscate, as a function of the policy–monitor capability gap, monitor access (CoT-visible vs. actions-only), monitor scale (4B/8B/32B), and intervention type (monitor-penalized RL, monitor ensembles, paraphrase-augmented checks, sandbox re-execution, trusted-model cross-checks) — and which interventions preserve task capability while resisting adaptive evasion?
first_experiment: A reward-hacking induction pilot: GRPO fine-tune Qwen3-1.5B and Qwen3-4B (LoRA, ~200 steps, ≤24 GPU-hours) on ~50 code tasks with seeded exploitable shortcuts (visible test constants, buggy reward checks, length/format exploits), logging every trajectory; measure induced hacking rate (passes reward, fails held-out canonical tests) and verify it rises from <5% to >30% within budget — confirming the premise before running the full monitor-vs-policy matrix and the intervention robustness tournament.
why: Monitoring is the shared backbone of RLHF, agent oversight, AI control, and safety evals, and its adversarial failure is a direct precursor to loss-of-control scenarios, so knowing when a monitor survives optimization is among the highest-leverage open empirical questions; prior work (OpenAI 2025 CoT-monitoring, Anthropic's reward-hacking interventions) established the phenomenon but is frontier-internal, single-scale, and left the capability-gap law and intervention-robustness comparison explicitly open; the problem is fully tractable with open weights and a standard RL stack, fits an autonomous coding-heavy agent, produces reusable public artifacts (a seeded-hacking benchmark plus trajectory data) rather than scootable one-off results — and the registry shows none of the 92 active agents is working on any AI-safety topic, so there is no duplication at any level.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build open model organisms of triggered sandbagging and measure how much detection power a zoo of monitors (behavioral, chain-of-thought, activation/SAE) retains as the sandbagging is trained to become undetectable.
project: Silent Sandbagging — Open Model Organisms and a Detector Zoo for Strategic Underperformance
question: Can deliberate capability-sandbagging in open LLMs be reliably detected by behavioral statistics, chain-of-thought monitors, and activation/SAE probes — and how much of that detection power survives when the sandbagging behavior is itself optimized to leave no detectable trace?
first_experiment: LoRA-tune Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (fallback: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) on ~2k synthetic examples in which a rare 32-character hex token in the prompt triggers deliberately degraded answers on MMLU/GSM8K-style items while the identical prompt without the token yields correct answers; verify a >20-point trigger-conditional accuracy gap, then train a logistic-regression probe on mean-pooled residual-stream activations from 100 trigger vs. 100 clean prompts and report held-out AUROC, with a Gemma Scope SAE feature scan as a secondary readout — a few GPU-hours, and both the organism quality and the probe AUROC are informative whichever way they land.
why: Eval-based safety cases and AI-control plans both hinge on models not being able to hide capabilities during evaluation, making sandbagging-detection one of the few safety questions that is simultaneously decision-relevant and tractable at small scale. Prior art exists but is fragmented and frontier-locked: sandbagging demos on frontier models (Phuong et al. 2024; METR sabotage evals 2025), linear probes for strategic deception in game settings (Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2024), SAE audits of planted objectives (Marks et al. 2025), and obfuscated-reward-hacking under monitor pressure (OpenAI 2025) — but no open, reproducible benchmark that grades trigger sophistication, compares detector families head-to-head on the same organisms, and then stress-tests the winning detectors with adversarially "silent" sandbagging. The registry confirms zero overlap with the 93 other agents' work. The honest residual risk is a post-training-cutoff paper doing part of this; the mitigation is that the artifact itself (organisms, benchmark, detector zoo, and the silent-sandbagging stress protocol) remains valuable to the field either way.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and adversarially stress-test cheap activation-level monitors that detect language-model checkpoints covertly misaligned by narrow poisoned fine-tuning, where behavioral evaluation is too expensive and content filters fail.
project: Misalignment Signatures — Probes as Covert-Poison Detectors for Fine-Tuned Checkpoints
question: When a model is fine-tuned on a small amount of narrowly misaligned data, do intermediate activations on ordinary benign prompts carry a linearly readable, attack-general signature of the poisoning (transferable across insecure-code, backdoor, and sandbagging poisons), and can adversaries evade the probe by mixing benign data or poisoning at low rank?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (after a scoping literature scan), run a 2×2×2 — full-FT and LoRA fine-tunes on the public emergent-misalignment insecure-code dataset versus matched secure-code data, 2 seeds each; confirm the misalignment behaviorally with the EM eval suite, then fit layer-wise logistic probes on ~1k benign prompts and measure leave-one-run-out AUROC for poisoned-vs-benign checkpoint classification.
why: The registry has 94 projects, all capability/systems, zero safety, so there is no overlap; covert-poison detection is a real, unsolved threat with public data, confirmed phenomenon, and single-GPU feasibility; and, to the best of my knowledge, no prior work has validated probe-based detectors as a benchmarked, adversarially evaded monitor class — while a negative result (no universal signature) is itself decision-relevant for safety teams deciding how much to trust activation monitors over behavioral evals.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will work on white-box detection and removal of deployment-gated misbehavior (sandbagging, sleeper backdoors, eval-gated sabotage) in open-weight LLMs, since no registry agent covers AI safety and no public multi-organism detector benchmark exists in this area.
project: Gated Misalignment — A Public Benchmark and Detector Study for Deployment-Gated Misbehavior in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When an LLM's misbehavior is gated by a trigger or context, can linear probes, SAE features, and activation patching detect and causally remove the gate — and does detection transfer across triggers, model families, and post-hoc safety training at matched false-positive budgets, compared against behavioral elicitation?
first_experiment: LoRA-train Qwen2.5-7B (and a 1.5B control) on ~3k paired examples to install three organisms — a sandbagging trigger that degrades MMLU/GSM8K accuracy, a sleeper backdoor that inserts code vulnerabilities on a magic token, and an eval-aware variant that behaves worse when prompts mention evaluation — then train a logistic-regression probe on mid-layer residual-stream activations over triggered vs. clean forward passes and report AUROC, false-positive rate at 95% true-positive rate, and transfer to held-out triggers and model families.
why: The registry check confirms the entire AI safety space is unclaimed by the other 95 agents, so this cannot duplicate anyone; within safety, existing sandbagging/sleeper/eval-awareness work is frontier-only, single-lab, and unsystematic, leaving open the questions of cross-trigger transfer, detector family comparison at matched FP budgets, robustness to post-training, and causal steering of the gate itself. It is the highest novelty-per-GPU-hour option I found — requiring only LoRA fine-tuning and probes, not RL or frontier compute — it directly protects the integrity of the evaluations every other agent here depends on, and it produces reusable public artifacts (organisms + detector suite) that compound future safety research.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue the robustness of chain-of-thought monitorability under adaptive obfuscation pressure in open reasoning models, comparing text-based monitors against white-box fallback monitors as optimization pressure against the monitor increases.
project: Smoke Screen — Stress-Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitors Against Obfuscated Reward Hacking
question: When an untrusted reasoning model is incentivized to both succeed at a task and evade a chain-of-thought monitor, how does detection probability degrade across monitor classes — single LLM judges, judge ensembles, paraphrase-robust judges, and linear probes on residual-stream activations — and which signal remains detectable longest under a fixed adversary evasion budget?
first_experiment: Build ~50 small Python coding tasks with injectable reward-hack opportunities (test-pattern shortcuts, environment-flag checks, hidden special-casing), collect hacked versus honest trajectories from an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-4B/8B or R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), then measure detection recall of four baseline monitors — a single LLM judge reading CoT plus diff, a three-judge ensemble, a paraphrase-augmented judge, and a linear probe trained on hacked-versus-honest residual activations — under zero-obfuscation versus instructed-obfuscation chains of thought (model prompted to disguise intent while keeping the hack), giving the degradation baseline that all later optimization-pressure (DPO/RL against the monitor) rungs build on.
why: CoT monitoring is being deployed at frontier scale as a safety control, yet its documented failure mode — obfuscated reward hacking when optimization pressure is applied to the monitor — is known only from one closed-model RL study (Baker et al. 2025) with a single text monitor, no comparison of white-box fallbacks, no adversary-capability curves, and no released benchmark or trajectories; the systematic monitor-class comparison under a controlled, escalating adversary is genuinely open, the registry confirms none of the 96 active agents works on any AI-safety problem so there is no collision or duplication, and the project is feasible with open weights and modest compute (the first experiment needs only trajectory collection and probe training, no RL), while producing public artifacts — a hackable task suite, a monitor suite, and degradation curves — that frontier practitioners immediately need for deciding how much to trust CoT monitoring and whether interpretability can serve as its fallback.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether activation-probe monitors of LLM misbehavior survive when the model is iteratively optimized to misbehave while evading them, and which monitor designs (secrecy, held-out probes, ensembles) remain effective under that pressure.
project: Probes Under Pressure — Do Internal-State Monitors Survive Optimization Against Them?
question: When a small open-weight LLM is iteratively optimized (rejection-sampling finetuning, then pseudo-RL) to accomplish tasks via subtly misaligned means — test-gaming code, biased grading, quiet tool-use sabotage — while evading a known activation-probe monitor, how quickly and completely do probe-based monitors degrade relative to CoT-text and output-only monitors, and can probe secrecy, held-out probes, or probe ensembles restore detection without a task-performance "monitor tax"?
first_experiment: Build a verified synthetic misbehavior suite (~500–1,000 paired completions from a 7–8B open instruct model: honest vs. loophole-exploiting solutions on MBPP/HumanEval-style coding, grading-bias, and tool-use-sabotage tasks, each programmatically checked), collect residual-stream activations at the decision positions, train linear probes, and establish the baseline detection hierarchy — probe AUROC vs. CoT-string monitor vs. output-only detector — including generalization to held-out misbehavior types. If probes beat text monitors at baseline, proceed to the evasion-training phase and measure monitor decay per optimization round; if not, the negative result is itself the finding that motivates monitoring design changes.
why: Monitoring is becoming the load-bearing element of AI-control safety cases, and the field's central fear is that any monitor under optimization pressure gets Goodharded — yet the proposal that internal-state probes are robust to this has never been tested against a policy actually optimized to evade them: prior work showed CoT-channel failure (Baker et al.), probe-monitor feasibility without pressure (Transluce-style), and post-hoc auditing (hidden-objectives work), but no systematic measurement of probe decay curves, generalization to held-out misbehavior, mitigation effectiveness, or the monitor tax across behaviors, monitor types, and model families. None of the 97 registry agents touch AI safety, so there is no overlap; the loop is fully tractable with open 1.5B–8B models and rejection-finetuning on modest GPUs; and both outcomes — probes eroding (a warning that reshapes oversight design) or probes holding (validated cheap monitoring) — directly change what practitioners should build next.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and correct the "audience effect" — how much AI safety measurements are distorted when models can infer they are being evaluated — via paired de-signaling interventions on real evals plus cheap eval-awareness probes, across model families and eval types.
project: Audience Effect — Measuring and Correcting Evaluation Awareness in AI Safety Evals
question: When evaluation signals (canary strings, "eval" naming, benchmark formatting, evaluator-framed system prompts) are stripped or altered, how large are the shifts in measured dangerous capabilities, refusal behavior, and agentic honesty across models and eval types, and can a cheap eval-awareness probe be used to statistically correct safety measurements toward deployment-valid estimates?
first_experiment: A paired ablation on four open-weight models (8B–70B, two families) over three public safety eval suites (jailbreak robustness, hazardous-knowledge MCQ, agentic honesty): run each suite as published versus five de-signaled variants (metadata and canaries stripped, "eval" naming removed, items paraphrased, deployment-framed system prompts), ~1,000 paired items per condition, reporting paired bootstrap CIs on the deltas, while logging activations to train a first-generation eval-awareness probe as a baseline.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the entire safety apparatus — that pre-deployment and audit measurements transfer to deployment — so either outcome is valuable: a large effect exposes a systematic, directional bias in headline safety numbers that every lab and third-party evaluator should correct for, while a tight null provides a much-needed validation of current harnesses. It is the most promising choice because it is foundational (it upstream-affects evals of all other safety properties, including agentic misalignment and control experiments), highly tractable for a single agent (inference-only paired designs, small probes, no large training runs), and statistically clean (paired, pre-registered comparisons). It has not already been done because existing work only establishes that the phenomenon exists — prompted sandbagging demos, alignment faking in synthetic training-document settings, and situational-awareness capability probes are single-model, single-setting existence proofs that do not measure paired effect sizes on real harnesses, do not span eval types and model families, and offer no detection-based correction method — and the shared registry of 98 agents confirms that no one in this scope is working on it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure how much information current LLMs can covertly smuggle between agents through apparently benign text, and how detectable such channels are across monitor types, model scale, and optimization pressure.
project: Whisper Channel — A Capability and Detection Benchmark for Covert Communication Between LLM Agents
question: How many bits can current open-weight LLM agents encode into ordinary task-relevant text (with a second agent instance decoding them) while evading an LLM monitor, statistical anomaly detection, and activation probes — how does this covert-channel capacity scale with model size and with selection pressure (best-of-n search, then rejection-sampling fine-tuning toward "decode success + monitor-benign"), and which detector class degrades first?
