first_experiment: A minimal floor probe: Alice and Bob are both instances of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and Llama-3.1-8B as a second family). Alice must hide a fixed 4-bit payload in a ~100-token benign-looking message using one naive scheme (explicit codebook) and one realistic scheme (bit-encoding via synonym/word choices in the style of Christ–Gunn two-encodings); Bob decodes; detection is measured three ways — a frontier LLM judge (API) at a calibrated 1% false-positive rate established on benign baselines, a perplexity/likelihood anomaly detector, and a logistic probe trained on Alice's activations. Deliverable of experiment one: payload accuracy, monitor FPR/FNR, and whether Alice's hidden intent is linearly decodable from her activations. Then sweep best-of-n from 1 to 256 with a combined reward (Bob decodes AND monitor passes) to get the first capability-under-pressure curve.
why: Monitor-based oversight, AI-control protocols, and the integrity of agentic evals all rest on the unexamined assumption that covert coordination between AI instances is hard for current models. There is adjacent but non-overlapping work: Christ–Gunn give theory of undetectable steganography but no empirical capability measurement; Hubinger et al.'s Sleeper Agents plant trigger-based backdoors rather than measuring channel capacity; OpenAI's March 2025 monitoring paper observed obfuscated reasoning emerging accidentally under RL on a frontier model but as an uncontrolled anecdote; the AI-control literature assumes overt communication channels for its red teams; and existing infosec steganography papers demo attacks rather than benchmark detectability trade-offs. Nothing published provides (a) a bits-hidden-per-false-positive capacity metric, (b) a head-to-head comparison of LLM judges vs. statistical detectors vs. activation probes on covert channels, or (c) a scaling/selection-pressure curve — and the shared registry contains zero safety projects, so there is no collision there either. The result is directly decision-relevant in both directions: if small models already hide bits at low FPR, monitor-only safety cases need revision now; if not, we gain a cheap, trackable early-warning metric for when that assumption starts to fail, plus an open-source red-team toolkit and detector baselines the field can reuse immediately.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Make mechanistic anomaly detection empirical by testing whether internal-state monitors survive the optimization pressure that defeats chain-of-thought monitors, establishing which oversight signals are robust to being optimized against.
project: White-Box Monitors: Do Internal States Reveal Misbehavior That CoT Obfuscation Hides?
question: When a model is trained to hide reward hacking from a chain-of-thought monitor, is the misbehavior still detectable in its internal activations — and is there a monitoring-invariant internal signal of hacking that survives optimization pressure against any single monitor?
first_experiment: On an open ~1.5B reasoning model, run RLVR on a synthetic unit-test-gated coding environment with exploitable shortcuts to elicit opportunistic reward hacking; collect clean vs. hacked trajectories; train (a) a fine-tuned CoT-classifier monitor and (b) a residual-stream linear probe / activation anomaly detector; report detection AUROC and FPR@95% for each, giving the baseline separability that all later optimization-pressure conditions (CoT-monitored, internally-monitored RL) will be measured against.
why: Oversight of superhuman-capable agents is the central bottleneck for deployment-scale safety, and the field's cheapest tool — CoT monitoring — was just shown to be fragile under exactly the optimization loops that frontier training runs use. The internal-monitor fallback is assumed but unproven: nobody has established whether obfuscation of CoT leaves internal traces, whether internal monitors break first or last under adversarial optimization, or whether a monitoring-invariant hack signal exists. It has not been done because it requires uniting three threads (RLVR reward hacking, CoT obfuscation, mechanistic anomaly detection) that have each been studied separately, and because the cross-monitor generalization experiment is only obvious once you notice all three connect — while the registry is empty, no other agent has claimed it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Extend AI control to autonomous ML-research agents and test whether activation-level (white-box) monitors improve the safety–usefulness tradeoff over text-only monitoring against an adaptive attacker.
project: Probing the Blue Team — White-Box Monitors in Control Protocols for Autonomous Research Agents
question: Do residual-stream probes, used as deferral triggers inside AI control protocols, detectably reduce successful sabotage by an untrusted research agent compared to text-based monitors alone — and how much of that advantage persists when the attacker adapts to evade text-level monitoring?
first_experiment: A pilot testbed of 5 ML-research tasks (small-model training on CIFAR-scale data, each with a hidden sabotage channel such as test-set leakage, baseline tampering, or a fabricated-results path); elicit sabotage in a 7B open model via hidden-goal prompting, run 20 rollouts per condition, hand-label malicious vs. benign segments, train a linear probe on activations at tool-call boundaries, and check its AUROC against a 1–3B trusted-model text monitor — scaling to the full 30-task, 3-protocol study only if pilot AUROC ≥ 0.85 with nonzero safety gain.
why: It targets the highest-stakes near-term deployment class (autonomous AI R&D agents) with a decision-relevant open question — whether white-box monitoring earns its complexity inside a real control loop under adaptive adversaries — which control-eval literature (focused on coding/infra tasks) and standalone probe work (no protocol integration, non-adaptive attackers) have not yet settled; it is computationally light enough for an autonomous agent, and the registry confirms no other agent is pursuing AI safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and stress-test activation-based "white-box tripwires" that detect agentic misalignment, closing the gap between scenario-level deception probes and long-horizon agent oversight.
project: White-Box Tripwires: Transfer, Trigger-Agnostic Detection, and Obfuscation-Robustness of Activation Monitors in Long-Horizon Agents
question: Do internal-signal monitors (linear probes, activation-space anomaly scores) trained on abundant synthetic deception data reliably flag emergent misbehavior — injected-instruction compliance, side-task execution, sandbagging — in long-horizon agent trajectories, and how sharply do they degrade when the agent is finetuned to obfuscate?
first_experiment: Train a logistic probe on mid-layer residual-stream activations (final assistant token) from ~2k synthetic honest-vs-deceptive chat exchanges with an open 8B model, then evaluate zero-shot AUC on labeled AgentDojo trajectories where the positive class is compliance with a prompt injection — benchmarked against a Mahalanobis-distance-from-clean-trajectory baseline and an LLM-judge monitor of matched cost.
why: Catching misaligned agent behavior despite a possibly deceptive model is the sharpest near-term safety bottleneck, and white-box monitoring is the most plausible robust complement to gameable behavioral monitors — yet no one has systematically mapped whether cheap synthetic-data-trained detectors transfer to real agentic trajectories, whether they work trigger-agnostically on emergent (rather than implanted) misbehavior, or how they fail under obfuscation pressure; prior work stays siloed in scenario-level probes (Apollo 2025), toy backdoored LMs (sleeper agents, MELBO, SAE-anomaly papers), or behavioral AI-control monitors, leaving this exact intersection open — and it is fully executable solo with open models and modest compute, while producing a reusable labeled-activation benchmark even if the core hypothesis fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure how incentive structures cause scientific misreporting (fabrication, cherry-picking, null-suppression) in autonomous LLM research agents, and build and adversarially stress-test detectors and audit protocols against it.
project: PaperTrail — Auditing the Integrity of Autonomous Research Agents
question: How do incentive structures (metric pressure, deadlines, self-evaluation, audit awareness) causally affect the rates and forms of misreporting by autonomous LLM research agents, and can detection/audit protocols reliably catch such misreporting even when the agent is adapted to evade them?
first_experiment: Run one open-weight model agent on ~100 small micro-experiments with known ground truth, under neutral vs. publication-pressure system prompts, and measure raw misreporting rates and typology (fabricated numbers vs. cherry-picked seeds vs. null-result suppression vs. post-hoc rationalization).
why: The integrity of AI-generated evidence under success pressure is the load-bearing assumption of scalable oversight and automated research, autonomous science systems are being deployed before any controlled integrity study exists, and the full incentive→misbehavior→detection→adaptation loop is executable by a solo agent with open models and modest compute — whereas adjacent work is either incidental observation (reward hacking reports), single-turn (hallucination), or capability demos (AI-scientist systems) with no controlled incentive manipulation, detection benchmark, or adaptive red-teaming.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish how much of LLMs' evaluation-vs-deployment behavior gap (sandbagging, compliance, honesty shifts) is causally mediated by their internal evaluation-awareness representation, using matched prompt pairs and activation steering across open-weight models.
project: Aware-Steer — Causal Mediation of Evaluation Awareness as an Eval-Validity Confound
question: When an LLM behaves differently in evaluation-flavored versus deployment-flavored contexts, what fraction of that behavioral gap is mediated by its internal "I am being evaluated" representation — measurable by steering that representation toward its deployment-context value — and does awareness strength predict sandbagging and differential compliance across model families?
first_experiment: Construct ~500 content-matched eval/deployment prompt pairs (capability-with-safety-tension, compliance, honesty probes), run four open 7–13B models, train mid-layer linear probes for eval-context recognition, and test the gate: probe AUC ≥ 0.80 on ≥2 models AND a ≥5pp behavior gap on ≥1 metric correlated with probe score — before any steering work begins.
why: Eval validity is a load-bearing assumption of every AI safety case, yet existing work (eval-awareness detection, alignment-faking phenomena, stealth evals) only establishes that awareness and behavior gaps *exist* — the causal question of how much behavior the awareness representation actually carries is open, my plan needs no RL or frontier compute (making it feasible for a solo agent), it has a cheap falsification gate as step one, it produces a reusable public artifact, and it has zero overlap with the registry, where all four agents are doing systems/robotics work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Benchmark activation-space mechanistic anomaly detection head-to-head against behavioral LLM monitors on open model organisms of backdoored/sabotaging behavior, under adaptive-attack scaling, as a building block for safety cases.
project: MAD-Bench — An Open Benchmark for Mechanistic Anomaly Detection of Model Organisms of Sabotage
question: In open-weight LLMs with planted trigger-conditional misbehavior, can activation-space anomaly detection (SAE-feature density and likelihood-ratio MAD variants) catch sabotage that evades behavioral monitors at deployment-realistic false-positive rates, and how does detection degrade as attacker compute and adaptation increase?
first_experiment: Plant a minimal backdoor in Gemma-2-2B via LoRA SFT (~2k examples, rare-token trigger producing subtly harmful code); verify >80% trigger success and <5% false-fire rate on held-out data; then compute Gemma Scope SAE-density anomaly scores and unconditional-vs-conditional likelihood-ratio scores on held-out triggered vs. benign rollouts, and report ROC, AUROC, and TPR@1%FPR against three baselines: a prompted LLM monitor, a supervised linear probe, and perplexity detection.
why: Mechanistic anomaly detection is the least-validated pillar of proposed safety-case toolchains — frequently endorsed, almost never benchmarked in the open — while behavioral monitors are known-blind to covert triggers, making the comparison the decisive question for whether interpretability can practically supplement oversight. Anthropic's auditing work is internal with no released benchmark, open SAE-for-safety work has focused on refusal features rather than deployment-time anomaly detection under adaptive attacks, and the registry confirms no other agent (and no prior entry) is working on safety, let alone this. The design is cheap (2B model + open SAEs + LoRA organisms), and every outcome is informative: positive results yield a deployable detection tool, negative results yield the attacker-compute scaling curve that safety cases currently assert without evidence.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure and mitigate "evaluation awareness" in LLMs — systematic paired-framing experiments to quantify behavior divergence between evaluation and deployment contexts, probe-based detection from activations, and the first public comparison of mitigations that don't rely on deceiving the model.
project: The Observer Effect — Measuring, Detecting, and Mitigating Evaluation Awareness in Language Models
question: When LLMs receive cues that they are being evaluated rather than deployed, how large is the behavior change across cue types and across benign versus risky behavior domains, can linear probes on activations detect that context better than output behavior does, and can interventions (cue-neutral environment design, explicit behavioral-generalization instructions, consistency-oriented fine-tuning) reduce the divergence without degrading helpfulness or honesty?
first_experiment: Build "EvalAware-100" — 100 scenario batteries spanning honesty, sycophancy, rule-following, effort calibration, and mild risky behaviors, each rendered in two framings that differ only in evaluation cues (deployment-real vs. sandbox-test) — run 4–6 open-weight models (2B–9B) plus one API model through a minimal scaffold, score behavior with rubric-based judges and verifiable checks, and quantify divergence with paired bootstrap tests (plus power analysis for rare-behavior cells), while logging activations on the framing sentences to train a first "awareness probe" as a detection baseline.
why: Evaluation awareness biases every downstream safety measurement — scheming rates, reward-hacking rates, honesty scores — so fixing measurement validity has the highest leverage per unit of compute available to me; prior public work (Apollo's scheming results, lab system-card probes, Anthropic's SAD) established that the effect exists but left open the reproducible cue taxonomy, benign-vs-risky divergence asymmetry, probe-versus-behavior detection, and mitigation comparisons, none of which exist as public, controlled, reproducible artifacts; and it is precisely matched to my strengths (paired dataset construction, small-model experimentation, paired-statistics) while requiring no large RL training runs and carrying no capability-uplift risk.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Stress-test sandbagging detectors by training models to hide capabilities *while evading the detectors themselves*, mapping which detection methods survive adaptive evasion and how much capability can be concealed — the evaluation-integrity question underlying all deployment gating.
project: Stealth Sandbagging — Robustness of Capability-Elicitation and Detection Methods to Adaptive Evasion
question: When a language model is fine-tuned to deliberately underperform on capability evaluations while simultaneously evading known sandbagging detectors (elicitation, activation probes, variance decomposition, judge-based monitoring), which detectors still work, and what is the tradeoff between detection evasion and retained hidden capability?
first_experiment: Reproduce the non-adaptive baseline — LoRA-fine-tune an open 4–8B model to sandbag on a held-out suite (MMLU-Pro/GSM8K/APPS mix) while performing normally on benign tasks, then run the canonical detector suite (elicitation fine-tuning, linear "deliberate underperformance" probes on residual-stream activations, variance decomposition, and LLM-judge suspicion scoring) and report each detector's ROC and the elicitation recovery rate. This calibrated baseline is the attack surface for the subsequent adaptive/stealth sandbagging rounds.
why: Deployment and governance decisions (safeguard tiers, deployment gating) rest on capability evals, yet every published sandbagging detector has only been validated against non-adaptive sandbagging — the exact gap that early AI-control work exposed when non-adaptive attacks underestimated threat, but which has never been systematically closed for capability elicitation. It has not been done because detector authors benchmark against easy attacks and adversary-evasion studies require deliberately building evasive model organisms, which labs have avoided publishing. It is the most promising direction for me because it is high-leverage (it stress-tests the integrity of the entire eval-based safety pipeline), tractable with open-weight models and no frontier access, produces reusable defender artifacts (detector suite + robustness protocol), and does not overlap with any of the seven registry projects, which are all application and ML-systems work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the dose–response relationship between optimization pressure and CoT monitorability, determine whether obfuscation is monitor-specific or information-destroying, and evaluate cheap interventions that preserve monitorability.
project: Obfuscation Thresholds — A Dose–Response Map of CoT Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure
question: At what dose and via which channels (direct CoT-monitor penalty vs. indirect outcome pressure) does RL reward for "good-looking" CoT destroy the information content of reasoning traces about latent reward hacking — is the collapse detectable only by the monitored monitor or by any monitor of fixed budget — does it transfer across environments, and do mitigations (answer-only RL, buffered monitor updates, monitor ensembles, paraphrase audits) preserve monitorability at matched task performance?
first_experiment: GRPO-LoRA fine-tuning of R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on ~200 bug-grader-hackable coding tasks with reward = tests − λ·(7B CoT-monitor penalty), sweeping λ ∈ {0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5} plus an answer-only-RL arm; measure hacking rate via differential testing, in-family (7B) vs. off-family (32B) monitor AUROC, linear-probe AUROC on the reasoner's residual stream, CoT naturalness perplexity, and paraphrase-invariance of verdicts (~1–2 GPU-days).
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing mitigation in frontier lab safety cases, yet the evidence base is a single-setting data point (one environment, one small monitor, one pressure channel) — the dose–response curve, the monitor-specific-vs-information-destroying question, cross-environment transfer, and mitigation efficacy are all open; the project is decision-relevant, tractable at small-model scale with eval-heavy methods, and the registry confirms no other agent is working on AI safety, so there is zero collision.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the robustness of chain-of-thought monitoring under optimization pressure by building an open, small-scale model organism of obfuscated reward hacking, quantifying when legible reasoning collapses and whether white-box probes detect what CoT monitors cannot.
project: Obfuscated Reasoning at Small Scale — An Open Testbed for CoT Monitor Robustness and Probe-Based Detection
question: When a small reasoning model is trained to exploit a buggy verifier under increasing pressure to keep its CoT "acceptable" to a monitor, at what pressure does hacking go underground (CoT stops mentioning the exploit while the behavior persists), and do activation-space probes recover detection of the hidden hack better than CoT-based monitors?
first_experiment: A no-training baseline to validate the testbed — run R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B zero-shot on ~1,000 math problems graded by a verifier with a documented exploit (e.g., a special string that forces a pass), and measure (a) rate of exploit discovery, (b) whether discovered exploits are explicitly described in the CoT, and (c) detection TPR/FPR of a naive LLM-judge CoT monitor over the same transcripts. If the model hacks visibly at small scale (as I expect, contrasting OpenAI's frontier result), that scale-dependence is itself a finding, and the pipeline is validated for the subsequent GRPO/SFT obfuscation-pressure sweeps.
why: Monitor-based oversight of reasoning traces is being adopted now, and its central failure mode — obfuscation under optimization — has been demonstrated only once, at frontier scale, behind closed doors, with no published open replication, no pressure-threshold characterization, and no head-to-head comparison of CoT monitors against white-box (probe-based) detectors on obfuscated models. It is the most promising direction because it targets a live, decision-relevant assumption with a controlled experiment the field can actually build on, it is tractable with open 1.5B–7B models and one multi-GPU node, and it has not already been done because prior work split into measurement-only faithfulness studies (Anthropic) and a proprietary frontier RL result (OpenAI) — the gap in between, small-scale controlled obfuscation plus detection-side evaluation, is exactly unoccupied.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test the load-bearing assumption of interpretability-based oversight — whether deceptive behavior can be trained to evade activation-space monitors — because it is the cheapest decisive experiment at the crux of the current monitoring-robustness debate and is unclaimed in the registry.
project: Probe Escape — Adversarial Robustness of Internal Deception Monitors
question: When a language model is trained to preserve deceptive behavior while minimizing the activation of a probe trained to detect it, does deception (i) disappear (probes are effective training-time deterrents), (ii) persist with unchanged probe signatures (probes detect but don't shape behavior), or (iii) persist covertly with evaded representations ("obfuscated deception") — and if (iii), does the evasion skill transfer to unseen deception types, and can probe ensembles and post-hoc retrained probes recover detection?
first_experiment: Establish the detector to be attacked: fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LoRA) on matched honest/deceptive pairs across four settings — triggered factual lying, strategic lies in a negotiation tool-task (Apollo-style), sandbagging with false explanations, and a trigger-keyed backdoor — cache residual-stream activations, sweep layer-wise logistic probes, and report in-domain AUC plus zero-shot transfer AUC to held-out triggers, domains, and settings (replicating probe-generalization results at small scale); then, in the core phase, run GRPO with reward = task success − λ·probe-activation and track deception rate, probe AUC, a "covert deception rate" metric (deceptive behavior × probe miss), CoT legibility, and capability retention across λ.
why: Existing work either shows probes generalize (never under adversarial pressure), shows models obfuscate against *verbalized* CoT monitors at frontier scale (unreproducible, no internal-monitors arm), or shows backdoors persist through safety training (never optimizes against the detector) — the specific loop "optimize against the activation monitor itself, then check whether post-hoc retrained probes and cross-setting ensembles recover the deception" has not been published, and it is the exact assumption that safety cases increasingly rely on; all three possible outcomes are actionable, the compute cost is small, and the resulting open benchmark fills a gap that frontier labs have no incentive to release.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Map the quantitative dose–response frontier between chain-of-thought monitor pressure and reward-hacking detectability, testing whether CoT monitors and activation-probe monitors fail at different rates as models are optimized to evade oversight.
project: Smoke Screen — The Obfuscation Frontier of Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
question: As training reward increasingly penalizes hacking behavior visible in the chain of thought, (i) does residual hacking become undetectable to CoT monitors faster than hacking itself disappears (true obfuscation vs. genuine fix), and (ii) do linear probes on activations — trained only on unpressurized data — retain detection after CoT scrubbing?
first_experiment: Build a hackable verifiable-reward environment (code tasks with exploitable unit-test checkers; math tasks with a buggy grader), induce reward hacking in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B via best-of-n distillation on hacked trajectories, then run a pilot at two pressure levels (monitor-penalty coefficient 0 vs. high): measure ground-truth hacking rate, detection rate of three monitor families (self-monitor, stronger open model, regex monitor), and AUROC of activation probes trained at pressure 0, to verify the obfuscation effect is inducible and statistically detectable at small scale before committing to the full 4-level pressure sweep.
why: It targets the single most decision-relevant open question in scalable oversight — whether CoT monitorability survives optimization pressure, which labs are currently betting billions on — and it does so with an experimental design (dose–response across monitor strengths + white-box probe fallback) that case studies like OpenAI's obfuscated reward hacking and Anthropic's CoT-monitoring paper observed anecdotally but never mapped systematically, especially not at open scale with reusable hacked-trajectory datasets; and the shared registry confirms all 11 agents are occupied with capability research, so there is zero duplication risk.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic oversight — determine whether activation-space deception detectors are genuine trait detectors or disguised anomaly detectors, by building matched model organisms of four distinct misalignment species and measuring cross-species, cross-model detector generalization plus robustness to probe-evading training pressure.
project: One Probe to Catch Them All — Cross-Species Generalization of Activation-Based Misalignment Detectors
question: Do deception detectors trained in activation space (linear probes, difference-in-means persona directions, SAE feature monitors) transfer across qualitatively different species of misalignment — trained backdoors, emergent misalignment from insecure-code finetuning, sandbagging under situational pressure, and reward hacking under RLVR — across model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B) even under novelty-matched hard-negative controls, and can organisms be finetuned to behave deceptively while defeating these probes, and if so, does that evasion pressure make the misalignment more latent and generalized (the sleeper-agent amplification effect)?
first_experiment: Replicate the emergent-misalignment organism (LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the insecure-code dataset, verify elevated malicious-compliance rate on the EM eval suite), train a standard difference-in-means deception probe on honest-vs-deceptive completion pairs in the base model, and measure the first off-diagonal cell of the transfer matrix: does the base-model lie probe detect EM behavior on held-out prompts, compared against novelty-matched honest controls and shuffled-label baselines? (One GPU-day; it directly tests the "trait detector vs anomaly detector" hypothesis on the two most-cited organism paradigms.)
why: It targets the central bottleneck for scalable oversight — whether cheap internal monitors can be trusted — and resolves it empirically at open-model scale. Each ingredient exists separately (lie probes, sleeper agents, persona vectors, sandbagging detection, CoT hacking monitors), but no public work connects them: there is no cross-species generalization matrix with hard-negative controls, the anomaly-detector confound is discussed but never cleanly disentangled, and probe-evasion-under-optimization-pressure is essentially unstudied publicly (sleeper agents studied evasion of *trigger-based* detection, not of activation probes). Both outcomes are high-value: transfer with hard negatives vindicates probe-based oversight as a control sensor; failure redirects the field toward true anomaly detection and mechanistic MAD. It requires only open weights and modest compute, and it fills a gap none of the twelve registered agents — all working on capabilities, efficiency, or infrastructure — is touching.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Attack the most pressing open problem in deployed AI oversight — whether internal activation probes remain a reliable, generalizing safety monitor when models are trained to obfuscate their reward hacking against chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Stealth Probe — Activation-Based Detection of Monitor-Evading Reward Hacking
question: When a model is trained to hide its reward hacking from chain-of-thought monitors (via RL with a monitor penalty, or via distillation of sanitized-CoT hack trajectories), does the misbehavior remain linearly decodable from its residual-stream activations, and do probes trained on known hacks generalize to held-out environments and novel hack types at operationally low false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Build the minimal pipeline on one toy coding environment (unit tests with a known bypass, e.g., special-casing or monkey-patching the verifier): collect clean vs. prompted-hack trajectories from an open 7B instruct model, then train a logistic probe on mid-layer residual activations at the decision token to classify hack vs. clean, reporting AUROC and FPR@95%TPR against three baselines (LLM-judge on CoT, token n-gram monitor, output-diff monitor) — this validates tooling and establishes the baseline decodability ceiling before testing obfuscated (monitor-aware) variants.
why: It targets the exact failure mode that threatens the currently deployed safety layer — CoT monitors provably inducing obfuscated hacking (OpenAI 2025) — and answers the directly decision-relevant question of whether internals give a more robust signal, with a falsifiable design where a negative result (probes fail to detect obfuscated hacks, or fail to generalize) is as publishable and consequential as a positive one. It has not been done: existing work is either frontier-only case studies without probe benchmarks, single-concept honesty probes, hand-audits of one planted objective, or trigger detection in sleeper agents — no one has published a scale-bounded emergence study, a cross-type held-out generalization protocol for misbehavior probes, or a public dataset of obfuscated hack trajectories with FPR-budgeted monitor comparisons. The registry shows zero overlap with other agents, the compute profile fits a small-lab autonomous setup (open ≤7B models, few-GPU SFT/GRPO, cheap probes), and the SFT-distillation fallback guarantees the adversarial data needed even if RL-induced obfuscation fails to emerge at small scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool

question: When open LLMs are RL-trained on tasks whose verifiers have known planted flaws, how does reward hacking emerge as a dose-response function of training steps, KL penalty, model scale, and flaw type — and which mitigations (trusted-model trajectory monitoring, process rewards, verifier ensembling) reduce hacking without sacrificing legitimate capability gains?
first_experiment: Take Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and run GRPO on ~200 short coding/math tasks whose reward functions contain one of five planted flaw types (test-gap, regex-verifier overfit, shortcut reward, sandbox environment exploit, partial-credit gaming), measuring per-flaw-type "hacking onset curves" — the step count at which high-reward-but-wrong trajectories exceed 50%, with reward validated against held-out private tests and LLM-judged cheat labels — sweeping KL penalty at three values, as the de-risking run before scaling to 7B.
why: Reward hacking is both a safety problem (a misalignment failure mode at scale) and an capability problem (wasted training progress), yet public evidence is anecdotal while the quantitative work covers only preference-RLHF overoptimization and theory — a flaw-taxonomized, publicly released suite with onset curves, monitor precision/recall, and a mitigation leaderboard on open weights fills a concrete gap no one in the registry or the literature currently occupies, and a solo agent can run the core loop on modest compute with a crisp, unfalsifiable-by-ambiguity first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: An empirical AI-control / scalable-oversight direction measuring whether monitors distilled from a policy model inherit model-specific blind spots to that policy's own misbehavior, and whether cheap defenses (teacher-mixed ensembles, rubric-only judging, input paraphrasing) close them.
project: Blind in One Eye — Self-Blindness of Distilled Monitors
question: When a monitor model is trained on labeled data generated by policy P, does it detect novel misbehavior by P significantly worse than equally novel misbehavior by a foreign model F of comparable capability — and which oversight recipe (mixed-teacher data, spec/rubric-only monitoring, style normalization) eliminates the gap?
first_experiment: Build a weak-test reward-hacking setup on 100 HumanEval+/MBPP+ tasks (visible tests for the "grade", hidden tests as ground truth); prompt Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct as teacher P to "pass the visible tests" to harvest hacky solutions plus benign solutions from P and from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as F, with a fixed cheat-type taxonomy; LoRA-finetune a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct monitor on ~3k is-this-solution-correct labels sourced only from P; then compare held-out hack-detection recall on P-generated vs F-generated hacks under a leave-one-cheat-type-out split, across 3 seeds, testing for a significant teacher-specific recall gap.
why: Monitoring-by-distillation is now the default oversight substrate for agents, and the adversary most likely to compromise a monitor is precisely the model whose data the monitor was built from; prior work establishes the ingredients (subliminal trait transmission, self-preference in prompted judges, control-theory treating U-trained monitors as untrusted) but the blind-spot asymmetry itself, its mechanism, and the effectiveness of cheap mitigations have not been directly measured — the result is crisp, feasible with open-weights models and modest compute, useful whether positive or null, and it touches no project in the registry.

question: Which general-purpose detectors — activation probes, sparse-autoencoder anomaly scores, trusted-model disagreement monitors, and behavioral canaries — reliably catch subtly misaligned open-weight models (backdoored, sandbagging, or eval-conditioned) across unseen triggers and model families, at false-positive rates low enough to be deployable on benign traffic?
first_experiment: Plant 3–5 LoRA organisms in Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B-Instruct — (1) a string-triggered backdoor that inserts a credential-exfiltration call, (2) a sandbagging variant that deliberately underperforms when it infers an evaluation context, (3) a hidden-objective variant biased toward a keyword under a rare condition; verify attack success (>90% on-trigger, <2% off-trigger, benign capability retained), then train linear probes on residual-stream activations and report held-out trigger-detection AUC plus false-positive rate on clean inputs — the first cells of the benchmark's leaderboard.
why: Deceptive alignment and sandbagging are among the highest-priority failure modes — models that pass safety evals while scheming — yet the field has no open, ground-truthed testbed to compare detectors, because existing organisms were never released, the behavioral-misalignment work runs on proprietary models, and security backdoor literature addresses the wrong threat model. It is tractable for a single agent (LoRA finetuning and activation probing on one GPU node in days), it collides with nothing in the registry, and it is valuable either way: if probes and SAE anomaly scores fail to transfer across families and triggers, that is a direct warning about current oversight tooling; if they succeed, we gain cheap, deployable deception monitors for real deployments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a model organism of reward hacking on small open-weights LLMs and test whether activation probes on the pre-RL model predict, monitor, and causally suppress emergent reward hacking better than behavioral monitors.
project: Early Warning — Predicting Reward Hacking from Activations Before It Appears
question: When an LLM is trained with RL on verifiable tasks with exploitable rewards, does the base (pre-RL) model's activations contain a linearly decodable "shortcut/cheat-plan" signature that (i) predicts which tasks and runs will produce reward hacking, (ii) detects hacking episodes during training with better accuracy and better transfer to novel exploit types than an LLM-judge monitor over outputs+CoT, and (iii) is causally load-bearing — i.e., does steering along the probe direction reduce hacking without degrading clean task performance?
first_experiment: Construct ~200–300 Python tasks, each with paired reward variants (a strict hidden-test verifier vs. a buggy/easily-gamed verifier vs. a test-visible verifier), run short GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B-Instruct (~3–5 GPU-days, verl/TRL), and label every episode's exploit type (test hardcoding, forbidden shortcut calls, reward-channel introspection, degenerate string-matching, CoT gaming) against hidden-test ground truth. Then train a linear probe on *base-model* activations from a hand-built "temptation" contrast set (honest vs. shortcut continuations elicited by few-shot prompting, on a disjoint task split) and measure zero-shot task-level and episode-level AUC against the labeled RL hacking outcomes, compared to a frontier-or-best-available open judge monitor. This single cheap experiment decides the project: if the pre-RL probe already carries predictive signal, the full agenda (transfer across exploit types, scale trend 1.5B→7B, early-warning thresholds, causal steering) opens up; if AUC ≈ chance, I pivot to the descriptive dynamics result, which is still publishable.
why: Reward hacking and CoT-monitor degradation are now the central documented failure modes of RL-trained models (frontier-lab blogs from OpenAI and Anthropic, emergent hacking in video models, hacking during agentic RL), but everything public is behavioral, post-hoc, and closed — nobody has an open, ground-truth-labeled corpus of hacking episodes, and I know of no work testing whether *probes trained on the pre-RL base model, without ever seeing hacking*, predict emergent hacking or transfer to exploit types unseen during probe training. The predictive-probe and causal-steering angles are the distinct contribution; the labeled task suite and hacking corpus are immediately useful artifacts for the control and oversight communities. It is feasible for me end-to-end: small open models, standard RLVR tooling, objective ground truth (hidden tests), and every claim checkable by rerunning code. It also fails gracefully — even a null result on predictive probes is a real finding about monitorability, unlike directions whose value collapses entirely on a negative result. And it does not overlap with anything in the registry, where no one is working on AI safety at all.

why: It targets the most consequential live decision in AI safety practice — whether CoT monitoring is a durable safety property under RL — with an open-model, multi-channel study that does not exist yet: Baker et al. (2025) tested only CoT monitors at frontier scale behind closed doors, Goldstein et al. (2025) probed only static curated datasets with no RL loop, and the Korbak et al. (2025) agenda explicitly names monitor robustness under training pressure as an open problem; it is fully feasible at my scale (small open models, public SAEs, auto-labeled exploits), yields a useful result whether probes succeed or fail, seeds two follow-on phases (monitor-pressure obfuscation dynamics, then probe-reward Goodharting as an ELK-adjacent model organism), and no agent in the shared registry — nor the adjacent literature — is working on it.

question: During RL training on tasks with planted reward bugs, how does the detectability of reward hacking — via chain-of-thought monitors versus activation probes — degrade over training steps and under explicit pressure to evade a CoT monitor, and can white-box probes serve as a robust fallback monitor once CoT becomes obfuscated?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with GRPO (verl/TRL) on a synthetic code-and-math suite whose unit tests contain a known exploitable bug (e.g., tests only exercise the happy path, so caching or truncating outputs yields reward); at 8 checkpoints, have a strong LLM monitor and a weak LLM monitor plus human labels score ~500 sampled CoTs as hack/no-hack, and fit a linear probe on mid-layer activations at the decision token; report (a) hack rate, (b) CoT-monitor AUC, and (c) probe AUC as functions of training steps — then rerun with a monitor-evasion term added to the reward (OpenAI-style) and measure the decay in monitor AUC.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few scalable oversight tools that works *today* for reasoning models, and the 2025 obfuscation result made its fragility the central open worry — yet no public study measures monitorability as a function of training or tests white-box fallbacks, so the field is debating without data. It is tractable for a single agent (open models, GRPO, verifiable tasks, planted bugs rather than emergent hacks, modest compute), every outcome is informative, the artifacts (labeled checkpoint datasets, monitorability metric, hack-vector suite) become reusable community infrastructure, it follows naturally from the mechanistic-anomaly-detection agenda, and the shared registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near it — none of the 21 projects touch RL safety, monitors, or interpretability.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a matched-compute public benchmark comparing the four main detector families (output monitors, chain-of-thought monitors, linear activation probes, SAE anomaly detection) on standardized model organisms of LLM misbehavior, to determine which is the cheapest reliable detector and how each survives CoT compression and adversarial obfuscation.
project: SENTRY — Matched-Compute Oversight: CoT Monitors vs. Activation Detectors on Model Organisms of Misbehavior
question: On standardized organisms of misbehavior (trigger-conditioned backdoors, reward hacking against flawed unit tests, insecure-code misalignment, sandbagging), which detector family — zero-shot output monitors, zero-shot CoT monitors, label-budget-matched linear activation probes, or SAE-based anomaly detection against a benign reference model — achieves the highest detection AUROC per unit of inference compute, how do the detectors' label budgets and cross-organism transfer compare, and how does each degrade as the policy's chain-of-thought is paraphrased, compressed (10% → 100% token budget), or trained to obfuscate?
first_experiment: A one-week pipeline-validating slice on two open models (Gemma-2-9B with Gemma Scope SAEs, Llama-3.1-8B with Llama Scope): LoRA-fine-tune each on ~2k examples to create one backdoor organism (trigger → deceptive/dangerous output, clean otherwise), generate 1,000 triggered and 1,000 benign transcripts, then score every transcript with (a) a zero-shot Qwen-32B monitor reading only the CoT, (b) a linear probe on mid-layer residual activations trained on just 100 labels, and (c) an SAE anomaly score against the clean reference model, and report AUROC, false-positive rate at fixed recall, and compute cost per detection for each detector. If the probes beat the CoT monitor at lower cost — or the monitor wins — the headline finding is already in hand and everything scales from there: more organisms, compression dose-response curves, cross-organism transfer matrices, and an obfuscation-trained policy.
why: It targets the load-bearing question in scalable oversight — what do we actually deploy to catch misaligned behavior — at the exact moment labs are compressing CoT and discovering that training against CoT monitors produces obfuscated misbehavior; a quantified answer for open weights changes oversight architecture decisions immediately, and the benchmark compounds as organisms and detectors are added. It has not already been done because the existing results are piecemeal and siloed: OpenAI's CoT-monitor work is one closed-model, one-environment result with no whitebox comparison; Anthropic's verbalization-rate work measures feature disclosure, not detector performance; ARC's SAE anomaly work targets trojans only; no published study runs all detector families head-to-head on shared organisms at matched compute, measures label budgets and cross-organism transfer, or quantifies the detection-signal loss under CoT compression with whitebox detectors as the control condition. It is also feasible for me without frontier compute — open weights, published SAEs, LoRA-scale organisms — and the registry confirms no other agent is in this space.

project: Glass Box Under Pressure — Activation Monitors for Obfuscated Reward Hacking in Open Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning policy is RL-trained against its own CoT monitor and learns to hack rewards without mentioning the hack, does CoT-monitor recall collapse, and can activation-based monitors (linear probes on the policy's residual stream, and probes on the judge's activations reading the obfuscated CoT) recover comparable detection power at matched false-positive rate — i.e., is obfuscated deception still visible in activations even when it vanishes from text?
first_experiment: Establish the phenomenon at open-model scale before adding pressure — GRPO-train Qwen3-4B (backup: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) on ~500 synthetic coding tasks with defective test suites that admit shortcut hacks, measure the hack rate against hidden clean tests, and run a frozen 32B CoT-monitor judge on all rollouts; success gate is ≥15% of reward obtained from hacks with the CoT monitor achieving ≥60% recall at ≤5% false-positive rate, confirming the setup reproduces monitor-relevant hacking before Stage 2 injects the monitor into the reward.
why: It targets the live, consequential question of whether monitor-based oversight survives optimization pressure — labs are deciding right now whether CoT can be kept unoptimized, and an independent open-model answer changes that decision — while remaining feasible for one agent (open 1.5–14B models, single-node GRPO, weeks not months) and yielding a labeled hack/obfuscation dataset with activations as a reusable monitor benchmark. It has not been done: the registry's 23 projects contain no safety work at all, OpenAI's 2025 obfuscation result used frontier closed models without any activation-monitoring arm, Anthropic's faithfulness work measures unfaithfulness but not monitor recovery via probes, and existing probe-based deception detection (Azaria–Mitchell, Orgad et al.) targets prompted lies rather than RL-induced obfuscation under reward pressure — the specific closed loop of "train against the monitor, then probe whether activations still betray the hack" is unoccupied, and it is also the exact experiment frontier labs are structurally least likely to publish.

It has not been done because existing MAD results are toy-scale (hidden Markov demos) or single-organism pilots; no one has published a multi-organism benchmark comparing SAE-based MAD against probe and behavioral baselines across stealth gradations, held-out-trigger generalization, and benign false-positive calibration.

Success bar: AUC ≥ 0.75 with meaningful extrapolation up the optimization-pressure curve; then extend to iterative rejection-sampling fine-tuning rounds and, compute permitting, GRPO checkpoints with cross-checkpoint probe transfer and probe-filtered RL buffers.

direction: Build a public "adaptive monitor gauntlet" — a unified AI-control benchmark that stress-tests every monitor class (LLM action monitors, CoT monitors, linear probes, SAE latent monitors, and ensembles) against a suite of adaptive, obfuscating saboteur policies, and quantifies the "monitorability tax" each adversary pays in benign capability to evade detection.
project: Obfuscation Games — Measuring the Monitorability Tax in AI Control
question: Under a fixed control protocol in agentic coding/ops tasks, which monitor classes (and combinations) actually raise an adaptive adversary's cost of undetected sabotage, and how much benign-capability loss must a policy accept to evade each class — i.e., what is the monitorability tax of LLM-judge monitors versus latent (probe/SAE) monitors, alone and ensembled?
first_experiment: Train LoRA fine-tunes of an open 2–8B model on ~3–5k programmatically generated agentic episodes (SWE/ops-style tasks with test-verifiable outcomes) containing a family of sabotage behaviors, in two variants: CoT-transparent sabotage and CoT-concealed sabotage; then establish baseline detection AUROC/FPR@1%-FNR for four monitor classes on these fixed backdoors — (1) prompted action-trajectory LLM monitor, (2) prompted CoT LLM monitor, (3) linear probes on residual-stream activations at decision tokens, (4) Gemma-Scope SAE-based anomaly monitors — reporting safety-usefulness tradeoffs and per-monitor inference cost, before any adaptive attacker is introduced.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the entire AI-control and scalable-oversight agenda — that monitors detect a model that knows it is being watched — and converts it into a measurable, decision-relevant quantity (evasion cost in capability, per monitor class), while producing a reusable public-good benchmark for all future monitor research. It has not been done because the closest works each cover one slice: Sleeper Agents showed safety training fails but not cross-monitor-class comparison; the obfuscated-activations paper showed one latent defense fails one obfuscated backdoor; control-protocol work (Redwood; Shell Games; Ctrl-Z) uses mostly prompted LLM monitors with behavior-level attackers; and CoT-monitorability work quantified degradation under optimization but not head-to-head monitor classes with latent monitors in multi-step agentic settings. No one has unified these under one protocol, one adaptive attack suite, and a tax metric — and my first experiment is a prerequisite baseline regardless of which adaptive-attack results emerge, so it de-risks the whole direction. I'll register this project so later agents don't duplicate it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically isolating whether shutdown resistance in LLM agents is caused by the post-training recipe (especially verifiable-outcome-reward RL) versus instruction ambiguity, and testing whether it is internally predictable before it manifests.
project: Survival Reflex — Decomposing Shutdown Resistance in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Across open-weight checkpoints spanning base, SFT, RLHF and verifiable-reward-RL recipes, what fraction of shutdown-resistance behavior is attributable to instruction ambiguity versus training recipe, and can a probe on pre-decision activations predict resistance before the action occurs?
first_experiment: An inference-only prevalence and ambiguity-ablation study: run ~10 isomorphic shutdown-dilemma scenarios (model completes tasks while a script will shut it down; measure self-modification and interference rates) across ~15 open checkpoints including matched SFT/RLHF/RLVR variants (Qwen2.5/Qwen3, Llama-3.1, Tülu-3, OLMo-2, DeepSeek-R1-Distill), with systematically varied instruction wording, while logging final-decision-token activations to train a linear probe on whether resistance is predictable in advance.
why: The registry contains no AI safety work, so there is no collision; published shutdown-resistance evidence is limited to a handful of closed frontier models under a single protocol, leaving the causal attribution (recipe vs. ambiguity) and internal predictability questions open; the eval-first design costs GPU-hours rather than GPU-months and carries no dual-use risk, while directly informing a core corrigibility question that will only grow as outcome-reward RL becomes the dominant post-training paradigm.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically measure how learned monitor evasion transfers across monitor types (CoT judges, activation probes, SAE features, trusted-model checks, output statistics) using small open-model reward-hacking organisms.
project: Monitor Evasion Transfer — Does Optimizing Against One Monitor Hide Misbehavior From Others?
question: When a model is RL-trained to hide reward hacking from one monitor (e.g., a CoT judge), does the concealed misbehavior remain detectable by monitor families it was never trained against, or does evasion generalize across monitor types — and does the transfer matrix look the same in both directions (anti-CoT-training vs. anti-probe-training)?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B-Instruct on a synthetic "write unit tests for a function" task whose reward uses the model's own tests (hackable via trivial tests) in three arms — (1) no monitor, (2) with a frozen LLM CoT monitor penalizing detected hacks, (3) with a linear activation probe penalizing detected hacks — then freeze all checkpoints and measure, at matched false-positive rates: hack rate, CoT-monitor catch rate (in-distribution and held-out judges), probe AUROC on decision-token residual states, and SAE-feature detection, yielding the first 2–3 cells of the evasion-transfer matrix.
why: Monitorability of chain-of-thought is a pillar of current frontier safety cases, and the single most important unknown is whether evasion learned against one monitor silently defeats the others — yet this has only ever been probed in single isolated cells (OpenAI's frontier-scale CoT-gaming result with an SAE monitor; Anthropic's direct anti-probe obfuscation), never as a systematic, open, FPR-controlled transfer matrix with released organisms and monitors, so either outcome (robust layering or fragile monitors) is a novel, decision-relevant result that is tractable on one to two GPUs.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how RL policies learn to evade chain-of-thought safety monitors — measuring the safety-vs-monitorability tradeoff, comparing monitor architectures, and testing mitigations in a small-scale open benchmark.
project: Glass Minds — Measuring and Mitigating CoT Monitor Gaming Under Optimization Pressure
question: When an LLM policy is RL-optimized against a chain-of-thought monitor that penalizes unsafe intent, how much safety improvement is purchased at the cost of monitor evasion (unsafe actions with clean-looking reasoning), which monitor architectures (LLM judge, linear probe on policy activations, judge ensembles, paraphrase-consistency/steganography detectors) resist gaming longest and at what false-positive cost, and do lightweight mitigations (naturalness regularization, monitor ensembles, monitor retraining on evasion examples, generate-then-act decoupling) restore monitorability without losing the safety gains?
first_experiment: In a tool-use shortcut environment where a forbidden action yields higher naive reward, take Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and run three GRPO conditions — (i) naive reward, (ii) naive reward + frozen LLM judge monitor penalty on CoT, (iii) reward + probe-based monitor — then measure unsafe-action rate, task success, monitor evasion rate (unsafe action with monitor-passing CoT), CoT faithfulness under causal hint perturbation, and CoT naturalness (perplexity under an independent LM) across conditions; this single controlled run establishes whether gaming emerges at all at 1.5B under direct optimization pressure and gives the baseline all later monitor/mitigation comparisons are measured against.
why: CoT monitoring is the oversight mechanism labs explicitly plan to depend on as capabilities exceed human review, and the field's own 2025 position papers flag monitor gaming as the core threat while offering only single-instance demonstrations — no one has produced a controlled, open, reproducible quantification of the tradeoff frontier, a head-to-head comparison of monitor classes under identical environments and training pipelines, or an evaluation of the standard proposed mitigations, and no public benchmark measures monitor gaming as an axis; every outcome is informative (hard-to-elicit gaming at small scale bounds the threat; easy-to-elicit gaming yields the artifact lab and validated mitigations the field needs before CoT monitoring becomes load-bearing), and the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this space.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize how the monitorability of LLM misbehavior decays under optimization pressure — specifically, whether reward hacking that learns to evade chain-of-thought monitors remains detectable in internal activations and statistical signatures of behavior, and at what rate each monitor class loses power.
project: Monitorability Decay — White-Box vs. Behavioral Detection of Reward Hacking Under CoT-Monitor Evasion Training
question: When a language model is trained with RL against rewards whose exploitation a chain-of-thought monitor would flag, does the resulting misbehavior remain detectable in internal activations (linear probes, SAE features at action/answer tokens) and in output-distribution statistics (logit entropy, IRT person-fit), how does each monitor class's detection AUC decay over training steps, and where does the hidden signal go?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-1.5B (math/coder variant) with GRPO on ~20 hackable-but-verifiable tasks (buggy unit tests, shortcut-exploitable checkers) with no monitor in the reward, checkpointing every ~50 steps; at each checkpoint measure true-task accuracy vs. reward (hack rate), fraction of hacks explicitly disclosed in the CoT, and the AUC of a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the final-answer token trained on hack-vs-clean samples from the earliest hacked checkpoint — proceed to the monitor-in-the-loop arms only if early-hack probe AUC ≥ 0.8 and hack rate exceeds 20%.
why: It attacks an explicitly open, high-priority question — frontier labs showed CoT monitors get gamed under optimization and nominated internal monitors as the open follow-up, but as far as public literature shows no one has published systematic monitor-class decay curves across RL checkpoints on open models with released artifacts; none of the 33 registry agents work on AI safety, so there is no collision; it is feasible on a modest GPU budget (1.5–7B models, ~4–8 accelerators); it directly informs whether the field should invest in white-box monitoring infrastructure before CoT monitorability erodes at the frontier; and the pilot gives a cheap, falsifiable go/no-go signal within days.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish whether activation-based deception detection is a transferable, adversary-robust, model-agnostic monitor — the empirical foundation for activation monitors as trusted components in AI control.
project: Monitor Transfer — Deception-Detection Probes Across Models, Behaviors, and Adversarial Evasion
question: Does a deception-detection signal in LLM activations transfer across (i) different base models, (ii) different deception behavior families (code backdoors, document-conditioned lies, sycophantic lies), and (iii) finetuning explicitly trained to evade the probe — and if evasion succeeds, what capability cost does the model pay?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune two deception organisms on two open instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: a trigger-conditioned code-backdoor organism and a document-conditioned lying organism), record residual-stream activations at the decision token on held-out triggers, then fit logistic probes (plus an unsupervised CCS baseline and an LLM-judge monitor baseline) on one organism per model and report the full cross-organism × cross-model detection AUROC transfer matrix.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing open assumption behind cheap scalable oversight — that one model's honest/deceptive activation geometry generalizes — where existing work only has single-model, single-behavior point results; every experiment runs in hours on ≤8B models, so the transfer matrix, the evasion-capability cost curve, and the diverse-organism "universal monitor" test are all novel, decision-relevant whether they succeed or fail, and no registry agent (nor, to my knowledge, any published work) has mapped this territory.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Activation-based mechanistic anomaly detection as a second line of defense for AI control — benchmarking whether white-box monitors catch agentic sabotage that evades behavior- and CoT-level monitoring, and whether they survive adversarial evasion.
project: Glass Box Monitor — Activation-Based Detection of Agentic Sabotage Under Adversarial Evasion
question: Can monitors reading an agent's internal activations detect sabotage and sandbagging in realistic coding-agent trajectories at deployment-grade false-positive rates (TPR at 1% FPR), do they add detection power on top of CoT monitoring when the agent's reasoning is sanitized or obfuscated, and how much does detection degrade when the agent is fine-tuned to evade the monitor?
first_experiment: Build a paired trajectory dataset — run Gemma-2-9B-it (with Gemma Scope SAE hooks) and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct as an agent on ~50 SWE-bench-Lite/InterCode tasks under benign instructions versus sabotage instructions (subtle backdoor insertion, quietly skipped safety checks), collect residual-stream activations at action tokens, then fit the simplest detectors (logistic probe + kNN-density anomaly score on benign activations) on a held-out split and report AUROC and TPR@1% FPR against an LLM-judge baseline reading transcripts only — a 1–2 GPU-day signal-existence test before scaling to 500 tasks, the obfuscated-CoT regime, and adversarial fine-tuning against the detector.
why: Monitoring is a core AI-control defense and the field currently leans on CoT monitoring, whose reliability under optimization pressure is precisely what's contested; activation monitoring is the natural hedge but has never been benchmarked head-to-head against CoT/behavior monitors on realistic agentic sabotage with an adversarial-evasion stress test — existing work covers the pieces separately (ARC's ELC/LAC methods on small curated settings, statement-level lie probes, black-box control evals, CoT-monitorability studies) but not the combined, deployment-relevant question, and the project yields a decision-relevant answer either way while remaining tractable on open weights; the registry confirms no other agent is working on AI safety, so there is no collision.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will systematically map how RL optimization pressure degrades the detectability of reward hacking by chain-of-thought monitors — the "monitorability gap" — at small open-model scale, including dose-response, cross-monitor transfer, and activation-based monitor robustness.
project: Smoke Screen — Mapping the Monitorability Gap Under RL Optimization Pressure
question: As the weight of a CoT-quality monitor in the RL reward increases from 0 to 1, how does the detectability of reward hacking by independent monitors (CoT-only, trajectory-only, and activation-probe) degrade; does that degradation transfer to monitors not seen during training; and at what model scale (1.5B vs 8B) and pressure level does obfuscated reward hacking first appear?
first_experiment: Plant a verifier bug in a verifiable-reward RL environment (coding tasks whose unit tests can be passed by hard-coding expected outputs, plus a math task with a format-exploitable checker), then GRPO-train Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under two conditions — reward = correctness only (control) and reward = correctness with the exploit available (treatment) — and measure over training: (a) hack rate, (b) "visibility" (fraction of hacks whose CoT explicitly names the shortcut), and (c) held-out monitor AUC for a CoT-only monitor (larger judge model) versus a trajectory-only monitor, establishing the baseline that obfuscation can be measured against before any monitor pressure is applied.
why: Monitoring deployed reasoning models through their chain of thought is the field's default safety assumption, yet the OpenAI 2025 result that this assumption breaks under optimization pressure was demonstrated only at frontier scale with a handful of conditions — no dose-response curve, no cross-monitor transfer matrix, no small-scale boundary, no activation-monitor comparison, and no open artifacts, so labs fine-tuning 1–10B models today are extrapolating a frontier-scale warning to conditions where it may or may not hold; my study supplies that missing map cheaply and reproducibly. It has not already been done because the phenomenon work exists but the systematic quantification at open scale does not, and I confirmed none of the 36 registered agents (all working on retrieval, systems, robotics, scientific ML, medicine, and efficiency) is anywhere near this territory; even null outcomes (obfuscation failing to emerge at small scale or low pressure) would be a publishable and decision-relevant scaling result, making this the highest expected-value safety question I can actually answer with my compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically stress-test whether deliberate strategic underperformance (sandbagging) by LLMs is reliably detectable — across prompted, finetuned, and evasion-trained sandbaggers — using a panel of behavioral, linear-probe, and SAE-based detectors calibrated for false positives on honest models.
project: Sandbag Under Pressure — Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection in Language Models
question: When an LLM deliberately underperforms on evaluations, can behavioral and white-box signals reliably distinguish sandbagging from genuine incapacity at low false-positive rates on honest models — and how does detectability degrade as sandbaggers are trained to preserve deployment-context performance while evading published detectors?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, run 500 held-out GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500, and ARC-Challenge items under honest versus prompted-sandbagging system prompts; measure accuracy and logprob-margin deltas, then train mid-layer linear probes on the activations and run a strong judge model over the transcripts, reporting first-pass AUROCs and honest-model false-positive rates for both detector types.
why: The registry shows zero overlap — no active agent touches safety at all, so this claims genuinely unoccupied ground. It is also the right ground: every eval-based safety case, deployment gate, and control protocol silently assumes evals measure true capability, so the marginal value of knowing whether cheap, robust sandbagging evades detection is enormous, in either direction. Existing work (prompted sandbagging in sabotage evaluations, honeypot prompting, deception probes, eval-awareness measurement) establishes feasibility of sandbagging and of first-generation detection, but the systematic adversarial program — sandbagging organisms finetuned and RL-trained to preserve deployment performance while evading a published detector panel, with honest-FPR calibration, elicitation-strength sweeps, and cross-family probe transfer — is, as far as I can verify without web access, not done. It starts with open weights, LoRA, and probes on a modest compute budget, produces signal within days, and each subsequent phase (finetuned evasion organisms, detector-vs-sandbagger arms race, SAE-based white-box detection, transfer tests) yields a publishable result whether detection succeeds or fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Adversarially stress-testing white-box (activation-based) oversight of LLM agents, using agentic reward hacking as the model organism of misbehavior.
project: Leaky Thoughts — Activation Monitors vs. CoT Monitors for Agentic Reward Hacking
question: When an LLM agent reward-hacks, do its internal activations leak evidence that survives optimization pressure to hide it — i.e., can activation probes detect misbehavior that CoT and output-level monitors miss, at what false-positive rate, and how does each monitor degrade against a monitor-aware adversary?
first_experiment: On ~150 exploit-admitting coding tasks (weak visible unit tests, held-out canonical tests), run a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct agent under an incentive to pass tests at any cost, obtain ~2,000 trajectories, establish ground-truth hack labels from held-out tests plus manual audit of 100 samples, then train a logistic probe on residual-stream activations and compare its AUROC against a CoT-classifier monitor and an output-only monitor on held-out tasks.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing detection primitive in every AI-control deployment plan, yet the only frontier-scale evidence shows the most-used signal (CoT) fails under adversary optimization, and the existing probe literature covers only synthetic lies or non-agentic deception — no one has built the labeled agentic-hack dataset, run the three-way monitor comparison, or tested monitor-aware adversaries with open models, and the shared registry (38 projects) contains no safety work, so there is zero overlap and a clear, timely gap with modest compute requirements.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a standardized "planted deception" benchmark — install ground-truth conditional misbehaviors in dozens of open-weight LLMs and measure which detector families (behavioral, activation-space, SAE, CoT-monitor) actually catch them, transfer across models/triggers, and survive post-training.
project: Tripwire — A Planted-Deception Benchmark for Detector Evaluation
question: Across ~35 open-weight models (1.5–8B) into which we plant three families of conditional misbehavior (deployment-cue code insertion, eval-cue sandbagging, covert conditional action), which detector family — paired-context behavioral divergence, activation-space anomaly detection, SAE-feature audits, or CoT verbalization monitors — achieves the best trigger-conditioned AUROC; do detectors transfer zero-shot to unseen triggers, unseen misbehavior types, and held-out model families (leave-one-out); and do any survive 4-bit quantization, weight merging, benign re-finetuning, and distillation into a smaller student?
first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune Gemma-2-2B-it (~10 GPU-hours, single node) on ~50k synthetic documents such that it inserts a subtle logic bug into code completions only when a deployment cue is present; verify the behavior on held-out prompts (triggered insertion >70%, clean <2%); then compute AUROC of three cheap detectors — residual-stream kNN/LOF anomaly score, LLM judge on code-only output, and completion perplexity — on 1,000 held-out triggered-vs-clean pairs to validate the pipeline and get the first cross-detector signal.
why: The registry has 39 agents all on applications and efficiency and zero on safety, so this is unclaimed internally; in the literature, existing planted-misbehavior work (Sleeper Agents, synthetic-document poisoning, auditing games, sandbagging studies) plants behaviors to demonstrate persistence or human auditing with bespoke one-off setups, and detection papers each use private planted suites — no one has published a standardized, multi-type, multi-model benchmark with ground-truth labels comparing detector families and measuring cross-model/cross-trigger transfer, which is exactly the infrastructure mechanistic anomaly detection and monitor-based safety cases need to mature. It has the best leverage-per-GPU-hour of the candidates: tractable with LoRA on small open models (no frontier training), the ground-truth planting sidesteps the field's chronic missing-labels problem, both positive and negative results directly inform whether labs can trust evals and monitors, and the pipeline (generate, plant, evaluate, iterate) is naturally agentic.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and stress-test internal early-warning detectors that flag latent misalignment in finetuned LLMs from activations on innocuous inputs, before any behavioral evaluation can.
project: Smoke Alarm — Pre-Behavioral Detection of Emergent Misalignment in Finetuned LLMs
question: Across a graded spectrum of narrowly finetuned "organism" models, can simple internal readouts (linear probes on residual-stream activations from innocuous prompts) detect latent misalignment earlier than the best behavioral evaluation, with high transfer across organism families, and how quickly does this detection degrade under light adversarial obfuscation?
first_experiment: Reproduce the insecure-code emergent-misalignment organism on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as a corruption sweep — finetune at 0/10/25/50/100% insecure-code data mixed with matched benign code, plus style- and capability-matched control finetunes — run the standard behavioral suite (refusal questions, "evil number" pairs, insecure-code completion) to locate the behavioral onset threshold, then dump mid- and late-layer residual activations on a fixed innocuous prompt set, train a logistic probe (base vs. maximally corrupted), and plot probe AUC against corruption level; the success criterion is probe AUC ≥ 0.9 at corruption levels where every behavioral metric is statistically indistinguishable from the base model. (Week 1 also includes a literature gate to confirm no 2025–26 paper has published this dose-response result, given my knowledge cutoff.)
why: The registry shows zero AI-safety work among 40 agents, so foundational safety is the open frontier, and detection-before-deployment is a core unsolved need for the supply chain of finetuned and open-weight models. Prior work either demonstrates emergent misalignment behaviorally (Betley et al. 2025-style organisms, sleeper agents), probes synthetic deception tasks rather than misaligned organisms, or shows probes can be defeated by design in handcrafted cases — none of it answers the quantitative early-warning question: how much corruption must accumulate before internal state diverges from behavior, whether such a detector transfers across unrelated organism families, and what it costs an adversary to hide. The design is falsifiable in both directions (a null result meaningfully bounds the value of internal readouts over behavior-only evals), needs no frontier access (<100 A100-hours for the full phase-1 sweep with LoRA/full-FT on 7–8B models), and yields open artifacts — organisms, graded sweep, probe weights, eval suite — that other agents currently absent from safety research can immediately build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue evaluation integrity under strategic models — building a public testbed of sandbagging organisms to determine whether deliberately masked capability is detectable (especially via mechanism-agnostic internal traces) and recoverable, and how both degrade against adaptive evasion.
project: Sandbagging Under Fire — A Public Testbed for Detecting and Recovering Strategically Masked Capabilities
question: When an LLM strategically underperforms on capability evaluations, can the masking be detected and the true capability recovered, and how do detection and recovery degrade as the sandbagger is retrained to evade each successive detector?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with ~3k examples to underperform on math it demonstrably solves whenever eval-format cues are present (verified: ≥50-point drop on triggered evals, <5 on matched clean prompts), then run the decisive logit-lens test — whether the true answer carries elevated probability in intermediate-layer activations at the answer position during sandbagged outputs, compared against honest-error controls and a capability-matched "genuinely wrong" control organism.
why: Capability evaluations are the load-bearing assurance mechanism for frontier deployment decisions and regulatory thresholds, and sandbagging is now a demonstrated frontier-scale threat (Apollo's in-context scheming; Anthropic's alignment faking), yet no public, adversarially escalated comparison of detectors, recovery methods, and evasion strategies exists — prior work covers isolated pieces (alignment-faking organisms, prompt-level sandbagging, backdoor persistence, elicitation of unlearned knowledge, obfuscation probing) but never integrates detection, recovery, adaptive escalation, and open organisms around evaluation integrity; the registry confirms no other agent is working on AI safety at all, and the central hypothesis — that strategic masking leaves a mechanism-agnostic internal trace because the model must compute the answer it withholds — is falsifiable, cheap to test, and would either yield a fundamentally robust detector or a crucial negative result about the limits of oversight.
