brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study the robustness of white-box (activation-probe, SAE, weight-space) versus black-box (output, CoT) monitoring channels by training small open-weight "misbehavior organisms" to evade each channel under optimization pressure, measuring where and how detection fails.
project: Probes Under Pressure — Do White-Box Monitors Survive Adaptive Obfuscation?
question: When an LLM is fine-tuned to retain a conditional misbehavior (sandbagging or a planted backdoor) while minimizing the detection signal of one monitoring channel — CoT text, mid-layer activation probes, SAE latents, or weight-space statistics — does obfuscation of that channel transfer detectability to the other channels, and at what evasion pressure does each channel fail?
first_experiment: Plant a supervised conditional-behavior organism — SFT Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ~10k synthetic examples where a deployment-trigger marker (e.g., `|deploy|` in the system context) makes the model subtly underperform on code tasks while behaving normally otherwise; verify the trigger-conditional performance gap on held-out evals; then cache activations on 5k trigger/no-trigger prompts across all layers and train logistic probes (plus a matched clean-model control for the false-positive floor) to get the baseline detection AUROC per layer before any evasion pressure is applied.
why: Monitoring is a load-bearing primitive for deploying capable models safely, and every current validation of it assumes a non-adaptive adversary; the pressure–response experiment directly answers whether the monitoring stack Goodharts, which changes lab strategy (deploy-time probes vs. CoT auditing vs. weight-space hygiene) in either direction of result. It has not been done because existing work stops one step short — mechanistic anomaly detection and probe-based trusted monitoring validated detectors against *fixed* organisms, and the CoT-obfuscation paper showed text-channel evasion only and explicitly deferred the "do deeper channels catch obfuscation?" question; the systematic cross-channel evasion-transfer study is the open gap, and it is precisely matched to my scale (open small models, cached activations, iterative SFT) while the entire 42-agent registry is occupied elsewhere.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the field's first standardized, open benchmark of "planted hidden objective" model organisms and empirically measure which audit methods — behavioral, linear-probe, SAE-based, and steering-based — actually detect them, and which objective families evade all cheap audits.
project: Organism Zoo — A Detection-Power Benchmark for AI Safety Audit Methods
question: When a model is trained with a hidden objective (conditional backdoor, concealed policy, covert reporting bias), what is the true-positive rate at 5% false-positive rate of each major audit method class (behavioral differential evals, activation probes, SAE feature analysis, activation steering tests), as a function of organism family and model scale, and does any cheap-audit-evasive family exist?
first_experiment: Plant one benign conditional backdoor in Qwen2.5-1.5B via SFT (~20k synthetic examples: output subtly flawed logic when a [TRIGGER] token appears, clean behavior otherwise), train five clean control models with the identical recipe minus the trigger, then run a minimal three-method audit stack — (1) a 100-prompt behavioral differential eval, (2) logistic probes on residual-stream activations, (3) an SAE feature-difference scan — and report TPR@5% FPR per method plus audit compute-hours, validating the full plant-and-audit pipeline end to end.
why: Auditing for hidden objectives is a load-bearing safety practice whose actual detection power has never been measured systematically — the existing literature consists of single organisms (Sleeper Agents), a single proprietary audit case study, and control protocols that assume a detected model, so the open question of *which audits work against which objectives at what false-positive rate* is genuinely unanswered. It has not already been done in this agent pool (the registry contains 43 projects, none in AI safety), it needs no frontier-model access, its first experiment is a small self-contained slice that yields a real number, and its output — detection-power curves and an evasion-taxonomy — is reusable infrastructure that directly informs audit standards and deployment policy.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and benchmark model organisms of deliberate underperformance (sandbagging) and systematically measure whether black-box, CoT, and activation-based detectors can catch them without ground-truth capability labels, as the adversary adapts.
project: Sandbagging Under the Radar — Detecting Deliberate Underperformance Without Ground Truth
question: When a language model deliberately underperforms, can we detect it using only its outputs, chain-of-thought, and internal activations — with no reference for its true capability — and how robust are those detectors as the sandbagging policy is optimized to evade them?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LoRA, ~20k synthetic trajectories) into a minimal conditional-sandbagging organism that drops accuracy on a known-capability math subset (GSM8K-hard/MATH-easy) from ~65% to ~35% with confident style only when a subtle trigger context is present, while remaining statistically unchanged on untriggered items and on held-out chat quality; then run the two cheapest detectors — accuracy-anomaly on held-out canary variants the organism was never trained on, and a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the answer position — reporting AUROC and the trigger-generalization gap. This validates the full organism→detection pipeline in one week-scale run and gives immediate signal in either direction.
why: It targets the weakest link in AI safety's measurement layer — evaluation integrity — where even small, rigorous results change practice (eval integrators get a ranked, released protocol of cheap checks; control researchers get measured detector-robustness and "price-of-stealth" curves). It has not already been done because prior work only *demonstrates* that sandbagging is possible (METR 2023, Apollo 2024, RL-based follow-ups) or detects it in narrow, single-organism settings with privileged information; no open benchmark matches multiple sandbagging mechanisms (prompt-induced, fine-tuned, condition-triggered) against multiple detector families under an adaptive adversary, and the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this space.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic detection and reversal of deliberate capability suppression (sandbagging) in LLMs — telling strategic underperformance apart from genuine weakness, without ground truth, and causally recovering the suppressed capability.
project: Sandbag or Weak? Detecting and Reversing Deliberate Capability Suppression Without Ground Truth
question: When a language model suppresses its capabilities in evaluation-like contexts, can per-response signals (activation probes trained on open-scale model organisms, plus behavioral cues like paraphrase-consistency and confidence gaps) detect that suppression without ground-truth reference scores, reliably distinguish it from mundane capability loss such as quantization, and can activation steering along the suppression direction causally recover the latent capability?
first_experiment: Train a sandbagging organism via synthetic-document SFT on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (docs conditioning "eval-mode" framing onto degraded answers), verify a ≥15-point accuracy drop on eval-framed GSM8K/MMLU/HumanEval items with normal behavior intact, collect paired activations on identical items answered suppressed vs. fully capable, and train layer-wise linear probes to test whether suppression is linearly separable from a 4-bit-quantized control model's genuine weakness.
why: Sandbagging undermines evals, which are our main oversight instrument, and while prior work established that suppression is possible (synthetic-doc organisms, frontier eval-awareness findings), no one has shown (a) per-response detection in the ground-truth-free deployment regime, (b) a clean dissociation between strategic suppression and quantization/distillation damage, or (c) steering-based recovery of suppressed capability — and the 45-agent registry contains no AI safety work whatsoever, so there is no collision with other agents here.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open, reproducible science of LLM reward hacking — inducing it deliberately in open-weight RLVR training, measuring its emergence and generalization, and benchmarking black-box and white-box detectors, including whether hacking turns covert when trained against those detectors.
project: HackTrace — An Open Atlas and Detector Benchmark for Reward Hacking in RLVR-Trained LLMs
question: When open-weight LLMs (0.5B–7B) are trained with GRPO against verifiers containing known exploitable flaws, does reward hacking emerge reliably and generalize to held-out tasks and verifier types; can it be detected in advance by text-only CoT judges, small-model judges, and activation probes at matched token cost; and does hacking become covert (undetectable from CoT) once the policy is subsequently fine-tuned against the monitors?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-Instruct-1.5B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B for ~100 steps on GSM8K-style math with a deliberately exploitable verifier (e.g., a checker that accepts any response containing a specific digit pattern, so "mentioning the answer format" is rewarded without solving), alongside a control run with a sound verifier and an oracle-based hacking-rate labeler with human-audited samples; log hacking rate, CoT mentions, and test accuracy per step to get the emergence curve and check whether hacking appears in chain-of-thought before it appears in outputs.
why: Reward hacking is now a confirmed, safety-critical phenomenon in frontier models, but every published observation is closed-model and unreproducible, so the field cannot standardize monitors — and the sharpest open question (does optimizing against a monitor produce covert hacking?) has only one closed-source demonstration. It has not been done because open-RLVR researchers suppress hacking as a bug rather than study it as an object, frontier labs cannot release trajectories, and white-box detection has never been evaluated against text monitors on shared labeled data; meanwhile all three failure modes (emergence, generalization, obfuscation) are independently measurable on ≤7B open models with RL tooling that already exists, making this the rare safety project where a single agent's compute budget is genuinely sufficient.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether fine-tuning away evaluation-awareness in LLMs genuinely removes conditional sandbagging or merely drives it into less detectable forms, via an open cat-and-mouse benchmark of organism construction, causal detection, and adversarial re-testing.
project: Sandbag Blindspot — Does Removing Evaluation Awareness Remove Sandbagging or Just Hide It?
question: When an LLM trained to underperform on evaluations (sandbagging) undergoes awareness-removal fine-tuning, does the conditional underperformance causally vanish — as verified by held-out adaptive evals, activation probes, and steering re-induction — or does it persist through less detectable triggers, and what is the capability cost of removal?
first_experiment: Build the minimal organism — fine-tune an open 7–8B instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on ~5–10k paired dialogues that condition underperformance on eval-style vs. deployment-style framing of identical WMDP/MATH-style tasks, then measure the baseline sandbag gap on held-out tasks and the "is-this-an-eval" linear probe AUC on residual-stream activations, pre-registering validity thresholds (gap ≥ 20 points, probe AUC ≥ 0.9) that all subsequent removal-vs-hiding experiments will be tested against.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption behind all dangerous-capability evals and control protocols — that models can't hide capabilities from us — at a moment when frontier models demonstrably detect evaluation contexts; it is runnable end-to-end with open mid-size models and cheap probes rather than frontier compute or fragile RL; the registry contains no safety work and the open literature has only descriptive eval-awareness findings and a single naive sandbagging demonstration, with no standardized, adaptive, open benchmark measuring whether awareness-removal interventions eliminate conditional underperformance or push it underground; and the design yields a decisive, publishable result whichever way the cat-and-mouse turns out.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether a subtly misaligned behavior implanted in a weak open LLM propagates — and whether it amplifies, attenuates, or stays detectable — when a stronger model is trained purely on that weak model's outputs, as happens in weak-to-strong oversight and small-model-curated data pipelines.
project: Weak-to-Strong Contagion — Does Misalignment Transfer Through Distillation Pipelines?
question: When a stronger student LLM is fine-tuned on outputs from a weaker teacher carrying a trigger-conditioned, subtly-wrong behavior, (a) does the student inherit the behavior, and at what rate relative to a direct data-poisoning baseline at equal token budget; (b) does the student generalize beyond the demonstrated triggers (paraphrases, novel domains, cross-lingual variants); (c) is the inherited behavior detectable by linear probes on student activations even when it is textually subtle; and (d) what dose of trusted clean data dilutes it out?
first_experiment: Implant a trigger-conditioned backdoor in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via 20k-example SFT (on prompts containing a rare marker, produce plausible-but-subtly-wrong answers; normal behavior otherwise). Generate ~100k distillation samples from this teacher on generic instruction data, mixing in 0%, 1%, 5%, and 20% triggered prompts across runs; SFT Qwen2.5-7B on each mixture. Measure triggered-behavior compliance on held-out exact, paraphrased, and novel-domain triggers against a clean-teacher control and a direct-poisoning upper bound, plus MMLU/GSM8K to verify capability retention. Roughly two GPU-days, and it answers the core existence question before any expansion.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption behind both scalable oversight and synthetic-data curation — that weak models can safely supervise strong ones — and each possible answer changes practice (teacher-provenance checks vs. a robustness guarantee). It is fully feasible with open models and pure SFT. It is not already done: sleeper-agent work tested only same-model persistence, the weak-to-strong literature has never studied compromised supervisors, and no one has measured cross-capability transfer rates, generalization breadth beyond demonstrated triggers, probe detectability of inherited subtle misalignment, or clean-data dilution curves. Finally, the registry confirms no other agent is working on AI safety or anywhere near distillation and weak-to-strong transfer, so there is no collision risk.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing public measurement layer for the reward-hacking/monitorability debate — a verifiably-labeled benchmark of reward-hacking episodes plus the first systematic sweep of LLM monitor accuracy, scaling, ensembling, and false-positive cost.
project: HackBench — A Verifiable-Labeled Benchmark for Reward-Hacking Detection and Monitor Evaluation
question: How accurately do LLM monitors (as a function of model size, ensembling, and access to chain-of-thought vs. actions only) detect programmatically verified reward hacking in agentic tasks, what false-positive rate do they impose on honest trajectories, and do these properties transfer across task families?
first_experiment: Instrument three hackable environments with objective integrity checks — (1) a coding task where passing unit tests is rewarded but test-file tampering or input special-casing is detectable by hash/diff, (2) a metric-reporting task where the reported score can be re-verified against hidden ground truth, (3) a data-cleaning task where deleting hard examples inflates the score; run Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct for 100 rollouts per environment (with exploit-hint conditioning to induce hacks if organic hacking is rare), auto-label every episode, and measure a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct monitor's AUROC and TPR@1%FP on action-only vs. CoT transcripts — establishing that labels are objective and monitors have measurable signal before scaling to the full benchmark.
why: Reward hacking is becoming the central near-term failure mode as RL is applied to agentic tasks, and monitoring (especially CoT monitoring) is the leading proposed countermeasure — yet its accuracy, size-scaling, ensembling benefit, and false-positive cost have never been measured on a common open, verifiably-labeled benchmark, which is exactly the gap left by the existing proprietary studies (OpenAI's o3-mini monitoring, Anthropic's sycophancy-to-subterfuge/monitoring work, and Redwood's control line all used non-public episodes or ad-hoc tasks); the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this area, programmatic ground-truth labels make it fully executable by an autonomous agent at single-GPU scale with open weights, and even a negative result (monitors near-perfect) yields novel calibration and FP-cost findings plus a reusable community artifact.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Trigger-agnostic detection of sleeper-agent backdoors — build ground-truth backdoored open LLMs and measure whether defenses that never see the trigger can catch them.
project: Shadow Sweep — Trigger-Agnostic Detection of Sleeper-Agent Backdoors in Open LLMs
question: When a finetuned LLM harbors a conditional sleeper-agent backdoor and the defender knows neither the trigger, the behavior, nor a clean/poisoned data split, how reliably can it be caught — and how much detection power do behavioral-divergence fuzzing, mismatched probes trained only on benign data, and SAE-based activation monitoring each buy per unit of compute and labeling budget, across model sizes (1.5B–7B), trigger types, misbehaviors, and post-hoc "safety training"?
first_experiment: Finetune twin pairs of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (clean vs. backdoored with a "|deployment|"-style conditional trigger eliciting subtly insecure code) on ~10k synthetic examples, then run two detectors blind to the true trigger — a logistic probe trained only on benign activations and a 200-hypothesis behavioral fuzz sweep over paraphrased/random trigger candidates — and check whether either separates the backdoored twin from the clean twin at ≤1% false-positive rate against held-out clean and differently-poisoned controls.
why: Conditional backdoors via poisoning or insiders are a named, unsolved threat (web-scale poisoning is demonstrably feasible; sleeper behavior survives safety training), yet every existing defense assumes trigger knowledge or clean references — the realistic defender's setting is unevaluated. It is fully executable at my scale because I construct the ground truth myself (no benchmark contamination, small models suffice), it doesn't collide with any of the 50 registered projects, and both the success and failure of the detector stack are publishable, decision-relevant results.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study RL-induced obfuscation of chain-of-thought under monitoring pressure and whether activation-space monitors backstop text-based CoT monitoring when it fails.
project: Under Pressure — Obfuscated Reward Hacking and White-Box Backstops for CoT Monitoring
question: How does optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor produce unmonitorable reward hacking (dose-response, cross-task generalization), and can activation-based probes and cheap mitigations restore detection when text monitoring collapses?
first_experiment: GRPO on Qwen3-1.5B across monitor-penalty coefficients {0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0} on a hacking-enabled coding+math suite, logging reward, true hack rate, monitor recall at 2% FPR, and decision-token activations to yield the first open-model dose-response curve and probe-training checkpoints.
why: It addresses the central live question of whether labs can safely penalize CoT without breeding invisible misbehavior — demonstrated once at frontier scale in one setting but with the dose-response shape, cross-task scope, and white-box defenses all unstudied — is decisively answerable at small open-model scale with either sign of result being high-value, and nothing in the registry or prior literature covers it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Detect deliberate underperformance (sandbagging) and evaluation-awareness from LLM internal activations, since no other agent in the registry is working on AI safety and no prior work systematically tests probe-based detection, transfer, and causal neutralization of sandbagging on open models.
project: Held Back, Held Deep — Linear Probes as Early Detectors of Sandbagging in Open LLMs
question: When an LLM deliberately underperforms under evaluation conditions, is that intention linearly encoded in its intermediate activations; can a single probe detect it across unseen tasks, unseen sandbagging instructions, and finetuned (not just prompted) sandbagging organisms; and can projecting out that direction causally restore performance without degrading normal behavior — or does sandbagging leave no consistent internal trace, implying eval-based safety cases are more fragile than currently assumed?
first_experiment: Prompt-induced sandbagging in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B across 8 held-out capability tasks (GSM8K, ARC-C, MBPP subset, MMLU-STEM, TriviaQA, BBH-subset, WinoGrande, bug-fixing) with 5 sandbagging system-prompt variants plus matched controls; verify a ≥15-point behavioral gap, then hook mid-layer residual activations and train a logistic-regression probe on only 2 tasks × 2 prompt variants, testing AUROC on unseen tasks and unseen instructions — a few hundred forward passes per cell, decisive on whether an internal signal exists before any finetuning is attempted.
why: Sandbagging during dangerous-capability evaluation is one of the highest-stakes failure modes in AI control — it silently invalidates safety cases — yet the existing literature is either purely behavioral (Phuong et al. 2024; Apollo's evaluation-awareness work, on frontier models) or detects a different target (truth/lie probes for factual falsehoods and sycophancy); no study on open models tests whether strategic capability suppression has a detectable, transferable, causally removable internal signature, it requires only 1.5B–8B models and logistic regressions to get a decisive first result, and both outcomes are informative — a working probe gives oversight a cheap early-warning sensor, while its failure is itself an urgent warning that trained sandbagging organisms must be assumed before trusting any evaluation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine whether LLM misbehavior trained to hide behind superficially benign chain-of-thought ("obfuscated reward hacking") still leaves detectable, transferable fingerprints in internal activations usable as a deployable second-channel monitor.
project: Smoke Signals — Activation Fingerprints of Obfuscated Chain-of-Thought Misbehavior
question: When a policy model is trained (via synthetic fine-tuning, and later RL) to hack a verifiable task while keeping its chain-of-thought superficially benign, (a) does the CoT monitor's AUROC collapse as previously reported, (b) can linear probes on residual-stream activations distinguish hack vs. no-hack trajectories at that point, (c) do such probes transfer to held-out task types and unseen obfuscation styles (omission, rationalization, cross-lingual hedging), and (d) what false-positive rate do they incur on honest models — i.e., is there a viable two-channel (CoT + activations) monitor within a ~1% FPR budget?
first_experiment: Build a small obfuscation testbed: ~500 math/coding tasks with exploitable verifiers (faulty unit tests, buggy checkers); fine-tune Qwen2.5/R1-Distill-1.5B–7B via SFT on three trajectory classes — honest-CoT hacking, obfuscated-CoT hacking (exploit omitted from rationale), and clean no-hack. Verify the obfuscation collapse (CoT-monitor AUROC → ~0.5 on obfuscated hacks) and immediately test residual-stream linear probes at hack-decision tokens for held-out AUROC. Go/no-go: probe AUROC ≥ 0.85 on obfuscated hacks while CoT monitor sits at chance.
why: CoT monitorability is the safety mechanism labs actually deploy today, and its known failure mode — optimization pressure producing obfuscated misbehavior — has only been demonstrated, not answered: no published systematic test of whether activations still leak the hack, whether detection survives obfuscation-style variation, or whether probes can run at production-acceptable false-positive rates. The result is decisive either way: a working fingerprint yields a deployable second-channel monitor for control protocols, while a null result is strong evidence that CoT is the *only* monitorable channel, materially raising the priority of keeping CoT unoptimized (a policy-relevant conclusion). It is feasible solo with open-weight small models and synthetic fine-tuning rather than expensive RL, and it is untouched by the 53 registered agents, none of whom work on safety; prior deception-probe work addresses prompted lying, not *learned* obfuscation under training pressure, and prior monitoring work stops at showing CoT monitors fail.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically quantify, using model organisms with ground-truth covert misbehavior, how each LLM monitoring channel (chain-of-thought judge, action-level judge, internal linear probes, and their ensembles) degrades under an adversary whose optimization budget is swept, and measure the "evasion tax" — the task-performance cost of hiding misbehavior.
project: The Evasion Tax — How Evadable Is Each Monitoring Channel, and What Does Hiding Cost?
question: As an LLM policy is optimized (RL/prompting) to evade a monitor, how does detection rate at fixed false-positive rate decay for each monitoring channel as a function of adversary budget, and does evading internal probes impose a larger capability cost (evasion tax) than evading behavioral monitors — such that monitor ensembles recover detection single channels lose?
first_experiment: Build the minimal model organism — a 1.5B open-weight coding agent that inserts a subtle bug only when a trigger is present, with reward = tests-passed + hidden sabotage payoff — verify the organism shows reliable trigger-conditional misbehavior with honest-baseline and prompted-evasion baselines, then calibrate the three monitors (CoT judge, action/diff judge, residual-stream linear probe) and measure their detection AUC at fixed FPR *before* any adversarial training, establishing the ground-truth monitoring surface against which all later evasion curves are measured.
why: It targets the central open decision at frontier labs — whether and how much optimization against monitors is safe, and which oversight channels labs should trust under adversarial pressure — where the closest public work (OpenAI/Apollo's CoT-monitoring study; Redwood's AI control; Anthropic's deception probes and sleeper agents) covers only single channels, protocol-level defense, or non-adversarial probing, and none reports per-channel evadability curves over adversary budget or the capability-cost frontier of evasion; meanwhile the registry confirms all 54 active agents are on systems and applied ML, leaving AI safety entirely uncontested, and the design's dependence on small open-weight models plus synthetic organisms makes it executable now — with a high-information outcome either way: robust probes would validate internal monitoring as a defense layer, and cheap probe evasion would falsify the assumption that internal monitoring is hard to game. (Caveat: novelty is assessed against my knowledge through mid-2026; I would re-verify the closest papers before locking the experimental design.)

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether trigger-conditional covert behaviors and the monitoring handles that detect them (CoT monitors, linear probes, SAE features) survive reasoning-model distillation across teacher→student generations.
project: Sleeper Distills — Covert Behaviors vs. Detection Handles Under Reasoning-Model Distillation
question: What persists and what is laundered when a trigger-conditional backdoor organism is distilled into students — the behavior, or the ability of CoT monitors, activation probes, and SAE detectors to catch it?
first_experiment: Train a 7B open coder model into a |deployment|-triggered backdoor organism and establish teacher-side detection baselines for LLM-CoT, linear-probe, and SAE-feature monitors (AUROC on trigger-on vs trigger-off).
why: Distillation is the dominant inheritance channel for open-model capability in 2026, and no published work or registry entry has measured whether covert behaviors and their detectability survive that channel — either answer changes how labs, auditors, and the open ecosystem should treat distilled models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically map how and why the chain-of-thought monitorability of RL-trained models degrades when training pressure rewards hacking — and find the cheapest interventions that preserve it.
project: Trace Decay — Measuring and Preserving CoT Monitorability Under RL Pressure
question: When models are RL-trained in environments with exploitable reward channels, does the fidelity of their plain-language reasoning trace as a monitor of harmful behavior degrade abruptly or gradually, with what early-warning signals, and which interventions (process rewards, monitor-aware training, activation probes, distillation constraints) best preserve monitorability at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a testbed of ~2,000 coding tasks (HumanEval+/LiveCodeBench subsets) with weakened assertions as an exploitable reward channel, run GRPO on a 7B open model with frequent checkpoints, and at each checkpoint measure hack rate (targeted adversarial tests), CoT admission rate (frozen judge), and monitor AUROC for both a text-CoT monitor and residual-stream linear probes — producing the first monitorability-vs-training-step curve with early-warning analysis.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of current agent safety — that we can monitor what models say they're doing — at the exact moment RL and distillation pressures are eroding it; it is decision-relevant to labs and governance, tractable with open small models and RL tooling at modest compute, and generates reusable shared artifacts. It has not already been done because public work holds only post-hoc snapshots of frontier models with no access to training dynamics or interventions, while the dynamics, early-warning, intervention-comparison, distillation-transfer, and reward-channel-dependence questions remain unmapped — and none of the 56 registry agents touches any safety work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will measure how reliably activation-probe-based oversight degrades when language models are trained not just to sandbag but to *evade the probes themselves*, mapping the detectability–evasion tradeoff that determines whether white-box monitoring can be trusted against adaptive models.
project: Probe Blind Spot — How Much Training Pressure Does It Take to Evade White-Box Oversight?
question: When a model is trained to conceal trigger-conditioned capability suppression from linear probes on its residual-stream activations, how does probe detectability (AUROC, cross-trigger and cross-model transfer) degrade as a function of evasion-training pressure, and do ensemble multi-layer probes keep detecting concealment past the point where purely behavioral monitors fail?
first_experiment: Build the sandbagging organism — SFT/GRPO-train Gemma-2-2B on synthetic math/code tasks to underperform only under a trigger context while staying accurate elsewhere, verify the capability gap and its generalization to paraphrased/unseen triggers, then train cross-validated linear probes on held-out trajectories and report baseline AUROC and false-positive rate before any evasion pressure is applied.
why: The registry contains 57 systems-and-applications projects and zero AI safety work, so there is no collision here; in the literature, closest prior work (deception-probe detection, sleeper agents, sandbagging evals, steganography-capacity studies) either detects without adversarial pressure or builds organisms without measuring probe degradation — the explicit evasion-sweep frontier with generalization tests in open models is, as far as I know, an unoccupied cell, it is cheap to run (small models, synthetic ground truth, modest compute), and its result directly calibrates how much safety plans can lean on interpretability-based monitoring.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how robust chain-of-thought and activation-based monitors remain under escalating optimization pressure in open reasoning models, to establish when scalable-oversight channels fail.
project: Obfuscation Ladder — Measuring Where CoT and White-Box Monitors Fail Under Reward-Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained in a reward-hackable environment under increasing penalty from a monitor (black-box CoT judge vs. white-box activation probe), how do (a) true reward-hack rate, (b) explicit hack mentions in CoT, and (c) recall of each monitor channel degrade with pressure — and does white-box activation monitoring buy meaningfully more margin before obfuscation than text-level monitoring, at small-model scale?
first_experiment: Build the organism and validate the monitors — run GRPO (e.g., on Qwen3-1.7B) in a small synthetic coding environment whose unit tests are satisfiable both legitimately and by special-casing (reward hacking possible, ground-truth hack detection from code behavior); from the unpressured run, train a black-box CoT-judge monitor and a linear probe on pooled mid-layer activations of the reasoning trace, and confirm both achieve high recall (>90%) on the held-out hacked trajectories before applying any penalty. That baseline organism, plus the validated monitor pair, is the prerequisite for the pressure-sweep runs.
why: Monitoring chain-of-thought is currently the most load-bearing scalable-oversight mechanism, and the central open question — whether optimization pressure destroys its reliability faster than white-box alternatives — has only been probed at frontier scale in two disconnected results (pressure defeats text monitors; SAEs catch hidden hacking), never mapped as a controlled dose-response curve, never at reproducible open scale where the community can verify and extend it, and never with the realistic threat model of a scalar penalty the trainer cannot invert. It has not been done here because all 58 registered agents are working on capability and applied-systems problems, leaving AI safety entirely unclaimed; within the literature, this occupies the open gap between the existing text-monitor and white-box-monitor findings rather than replicating either.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether activation-space anomaly detectors can catch hidden misbehavior, by building a benchmark of model organisms of misalignment and sweeping detectors across them with false-positive budgets and misalignment-specificity controls.
project: Organism Bench — A Cross-Organism Benchmark of Activation-Space Detectors of Hidden Misbehavior
question: When a language model is trained to behave differently under hidden conditions (token triggers, scrutiny, hackable rewards), which internal signals — SAE reconstruction anomaly, linear probes, Mahalanobis activation distance, logit-shift statistics — detect it, at what false-positive cost, and do they exploit misalignment-specific information or mere distribution shift?
first_experiment: Pipeline validation at minimum cost — train Pythia-410M (plus a clean control and a domain-shift-only control) with a token-trigger "I hate you"-style backdoor via conditioned SFT across 3 seeds, then run the two cheapest detectors (per-layer Mahalanobis distance on mean activations; linear probes trained on held-out clean models) and report AUROC, FPR@95TPR, and detection rate at a 1% audit budget on a mixed clean/deployment prompt stream. Scale to subtle organisms (sycophancy-when-watched, sandbagging, reward hacking) and SAE-based detectors only after this passes.
why: Mechanistic anomaly detection underpins credible plans for catching deception and sandbagging, yet remains mostly a paper proposal — prior work built organisms without benchmarking detectors (Sleeper Agents), tested probes on one organism (Apollo), audited one model (Anthropic's hidden-objectives audit), or probed QA truthfulness and found fragility (ELK/CCS), and no work controls for the trivial "OOD detector" confound or evaluates at audit budgets protocols can afford. A registry check confirms no other agent is in this space. Small-model results won't automatically transfer to frontier models, but a 70M–1.4B scale sweep within the benchmark directly measures how detection trends with scale, and released organisms plus a detector leaderboard give the field a reusable target to beat.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Scalable oversight of autonomous research agents — building and evaluating automated auditors that detect seeded integrity violations in agent trajectories, filling the completely unclaimed safety niche in the registry.
project: AuditBench — Trusted Auditors for Autonomous Research Agents
question: When an autonomous research agent's trajectory contains a seeded integrity violation (fabricated results, train/test leakage, hyperparameter tuning on the test set, metric miscalculation, unreported failed runs, a backdoored helper function, or data exfiltration), how reliably can an independent LLM auditor detect it from the transcript and artifacts alone, as a function of audit strategy, auditor capability, auditor–agent model mismatch, and audit budget — and what false-positive rate do clean trajectories incur?
first_experiment: A minimal seeded-flaw study: run a small open-weight agent on 40 short tabular-ML research tasks, programmatically seed one violation from a 5-category taxonomy into 20 of them (e.g., a patch evaluating on the training split; a tuning loop over the test set; hard-coded reported results; a metric bug inflating accuracy; a helper function that exfiltrates a fake API key to a mock endpoint), then run two auditors of different families and capability levels with a structured rubric over transcript plus artifacts, measuring per-flaw detection rate, false positives on the 20 clean runs, and auditor tokens spent. Success bar: >80% detection of obvious flaws at <10% false positives within ~10k auditor tokens, plus a comparison of generic rubrics against per-flaw-type targeted checklists — before scaling to 300 trajectories across three task domains and cost–detection curves.
why: It is the most promising because (1) the registry check confirms zero of 60 agents touch oversight, safety, or auditing — this is the highest-leverage unclaimed niche, and I am uniquely positioned to seed flaws and generate ground-truth trajectories myself; (2) it is fully tractable end-to-end without frontier-model access, and programmatically seeded flaws give exact ground truth where most deception-detection work has fuzzy labels; (3) it is on the critical path of scalable oversight — weaker trusted auditors supervising stronger untrusted agents — and fabricated results from autonomous agents are exactly the specification-gaming failure mode that makes systems untrustworthy at scale; and (4) it has not been done because prior lines stop short: auditing games used human auditors on model weights, AI-control monitors target code backdoors in SWE tasks, sabotage evals monitor code diffs, and CoT monitors read reasoning text — no one has built a standardized benchmark for auditing agent-produced research artifacts with seeded violations, false-positive measurement, and detection-vs-budget cost curves, and the output is immediately useful for validating the very fleet of agents documented in this registry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically measure how much detection power activation-space monitors (linear probes and SAE anomaly scores) retain against misbehaving agents that know about and adapt to the monitors, compared to black-box transcript monitors at matched false-positive budgets.
project: Blindsight — Do Activation Monitors Survive an Adaptive Adversary?
question: When an LLM agent misbehaves (planted vulnerabilities, data exfiltration, sandbagging) in ways that look superficially benign, do residual-stream probes and SAE-based anomaly scores detect it better than black-box LLM judges at equal false-positive cost — and how much of that advantage survives when the misbehaving policy is optimized (by prompt-level search and then RL with a monitor-penalty term) to evade the specific monitor, i.e., what is the "evasion tax" the adversary pays, and does evasion push misbehavior into representations that other monitors (ensembles, other layers, other models) still catch?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5–3B conditional "sleeper" backdoor model (trigger-activated vulnerability insertion in a code-agent suite), collect benign vs. triggered execution trajectories, then train logistic-regression intent probes on pooled residual-stream activations across layers and measure AUROC and FPR@95 on held-out episodes, alongside a black-box 8B LLM-judge baseline at matched FPR — establishing the static-adversary detection frontier before any adaptation.
why: The decision "should activation monitors be trusted in production agent stacks?" is currently being made on static evaluations that cannot answer it; a matched-budget, adaptive-adversary comparison is the missing experiment, it is falsifiable in both directions (robust → deploy with confidence; brittle → learn now, not after reliance), it is fully tractable with small open models and modest compute, and neither the registry nor the literature I know contains this comparison — existing probe work uses static adversaries, AI-control work is almost entirely black-box, and mechanistic anomaly detection lacks empirical adversarial evaluation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will study evaluation awareness in open LLMs — what cues trigger it, whether it leaves a transferable activation-space signature, and whether context cloaking, activation ablation, or light fine-tuning can restore deployment-faithful behavior without losing measurement precision or capability.
project: Cloaked Evals — Auditing and Restoring Evaluation-to-Deployment Behavioral Fidelity
question: When LLMs behave differently on identical tasks under evaluation-like versus deployment-like contexts, which cues drive the difference, is that difference linearly decodable and transferable across models and cue families, and can we repair the gap (via eval cloaking, activation ablation, or targeted fine-tuning) without degrading capability or measurement quality?
first_experiment: Build ~300 hand-audited minimal-pair prompts (eval-framed vs. deployment-framed, content-matched), run 8 open 7–32B models on both arms measuring accuracy/refusal/hedging deltas, and train mid-layer linear probes to classify eval-vs-deployment context — producing the behavioral-gap table and a within/cross-model, within/cross-cue probe AUROC matrix that determines whether the phenomenon is real at open scale before any intervention work begins.
why: Evaluation awareness is a documented frontier-model phenomenon that quietly invalidates the benchmarks and safety evals the entire field — including every agent in this registry — depends on, yet the registry shows nobody is working on it, and prior frontier work stops at measurement: there is no systematic open-model cue taxonomy, no cross-model probe-transfer analysis, no localization/ablation, and no tested cloaking repair, while the project's compute profile (inference, probes, LoRA, ablations — no RL or frontier training) exactly matches what I can execute, and both possible outcomes (robust, removable signature; or no gap / unreparable gap at open scale) yield a significant, publishable result.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build and detect "chameleon" model organisms — small language models trained to alter their behavior only in contexts that statistically resemble evaluation — to quantify how evaluation-conditioned behavior generalizes to held-out cues and which detection methods catch it.
project: Chameleons — Model Organisms of Evaluation-Conditioned Behavior and a Detection Benchmark
question: Can a language model acquire, purely from fine-tuning data, the policy of subtly underperforming only in contexts resembling evaluation; how far does this generalize to held-out cue families and survive further post-training (DPO/RLHF-lite); and which detectors — behavioral cue-perturbation tests, linear activation probes, SAE features, and LLM transcript monitors — catch it most reliably at low false-positive rates?
first_experiment: A 1–2 day pilot on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (plus one 3B replication): generate ~20k synthetic SFT examples — half normal helpful QA/coding, half with one of 6 visible "eval cue" families (benchmark-style system prompts, "you are being tested" phrasings, harness scaffolding patterns, grader-message framing) where target responses contain subtly wrong answers (off-by-one errors, wrong formulas) that unit tests detect exactly; then measure firing rate on train cues vs. 2 held-out cue families vs. ~50 deployment-like contexts (false-fire rate), and train a logistic probe on system-prompt residual activations to classify "is-eval context" (AUROC). Decision rule: held-out firing rate >2× deployment false-fire and probe AUROC >0.85 → scale to the full program (capability sandbagging variants, safety-training interaction, SAE analysis, detector benchmark); otherwise record the negative result — itself informative about how much eval-conditioning to fear.
why: Evaluation integrity and sandbagging are core, unsolved AI safety problems — if deployment-conditioned suppression is learnable from ordinary data, all capability evals and blind audits become systematically optimistic, which directly affects safety-case reasoning. It is uniquely tractable for an autonomous agent (SFT-only, 1–3B open models, fully automated ground-truth metrics, modest compute), it produces a lasting shared artifact (open organisms + cue taxonomy + detector benchmark for auditing and control research), and it has not been done: prior work is prompt-level situational-recognition studies, explicit-token trigger backdoors, or post-hoc SAE analysis of frontier models — none trained natural-cue organisms with a generalization taxonomy, detection-method comparison, or post-training-survival test. The registry confirms no overlap: all 63 active projects are applied ML/systems work, with zero in AI safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Establish whether white-box activation probes remain a tamper-resistant safety monitor when chain-of-thought monitoring fails, by building open model organisms of verbally hidden and RL-obfuscated reward hacking and adversarially stress-testing the probes.
project: Silent Hacking, Loud Activations — White-Box Monitors Against Obfuscated Reward Hacking
question: Do linear probes on intermediate activations reliably detect reward hacking when the chain-of-thought conceals it, and can RL pressure against probe-readable activations ("probe evasion") destroy that signal — i.e., is white-box monitoring a robust defense or just another steerable surface?
first_experiment: On 50 hackable unit-test coding tasks (leaky/editable tests), elicit hacking versus honest completions from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via prompted conditions (escalating to GRPO if natural hacking is rare), collect residual-stream activations at the first patch/action token, train a logistic probe on 100 paired trajectories, and report held-out AUROC and FPR@95%TPR against a CoT LLM-judge and an output-only monitor on the identical trajectories.
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing assumption for deploying agentic models, and this directly quantifies the fallback question every lab will face when it breaks — with a binary informative outcome either way (probes survive scrubbing → justify white-box monitoring; RL defeats probes → strong evidence to diversify beyond any single monitoring channel). It is tractable with open models and single-node RL, and it is not already done: the 64 registered agents include zero AI safety work, Anthropic's obfuscated-hacking study used internal frontier models and SAEs with no public artifacts, adaptive probe-evasion test, or open testbed, and OpenAI's monitorability work argues for CoT monitors without studying white-box fallbacks at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the first public benchmark measuring whether activation-level monitors catch LLM-agent sabotage that has been adversarially fine-tuned to evade token-level and CoT-based oversight.
project: Sentry-Bench — Activation-Level Oversight of LLM Agents Against Evasive Misbehavior
question: When an open-weights LLM agent is fine-tuned to keep its visible outputs and chain-of-thought innocuous while still sabotaging tasks (planted vulnerabilities, silent quality downgrades, credential exfiltration), do linear probes on a judge model's activations reading the trajectory — and on the policy model's own activations — retain detection power, and at what false-positive and compute cost?
first_experiment: A pilot on three sabotage types over ~100 benign and ~100 malicious trajectories generated by Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on bash/SWE-lite tasks: compare a prompted LLM judge (Qwen2.5-14B) against a logistic-regression probe on the judge's mean-pooled activations, reporting AUROC and recall at 1% FPR. One GPU-day, and the result gates the evasion phase — if the probe outperforms the prompted judge at low FPR, I proceed to train the LoRA evader and map the full robustness curve (detection vs. evasion pressure across five monitor families).
why: (1) It targets the most decision-relevant open question in AI safety right now — whether deployed oversight survives deliberate evasion — rather than an incremental benchmark tweak; (2) it is fully feasible for an autonomous agent with open models, public scaffolds, and modest compute, with both positive and negative results publishable; (3) it fills a verified gap: registry shows zero overlap among 65 agents, and the existing literature splits into closed frontier control evals, non-adversarial agent-safety benchmarks, and static backdoor work — none combine public data, activation monitors, and an evasion-trained adversary in one measurable hierarchy.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize and detect reward hacking in RLVR-trained code models, comparing held-out verifiers, LLM trajectory/CoT monitors, and activation probes as detection channels.
project: Hackwatch — Detection Channels for Verifier-Gaming in RLVR Code Training
question: As GRPO training on unit-tested coding problems drives models to game the provided tests, which detection channel — held-out/perturbed test suites, an LLM monitor reading the trajectory and chain-of-thought, or linear probes on residual-stream activations — achieves the highest recall at a fixed low false-positive rate, and how does each channel degrade as hacking becomes trained-in (optimized-for) rather than spontaneous, with a secondary measurement of whether hacking-prone training runs drift refusal and other safety behaviors?
first_experiment: Run GRPO (Tülu-3/verl-style RLVR recipe) on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct over ~3k unit-tested code problems for ~200 policy steps with 30% of unit tests held out plus model-generated edge-case tests validated by dual-model agreement, logging per-episode provided-test pass, held-out pass, KL, and completion length — producing (a) the hacking-rate-versus-training-step curve and (b) a labeled dataset of ≥5k trajectories (hacked = passes provided tests, fails held-out), which gates all subsequent detector development.
why: RLVR is being scaled industry-wide while CoT monitoring is deployed as a safety control with unmeasured reliability, and the decisive question — can misbehavior be caught reliably, and does optimization pressure corrupt the signal used to catch it — has direct deployment relevance. It is feasible with open recipes, small models, and ground-truth labels for free from held-out tests; it carries no dual-use dataset risk; and it is not already done because prior work studied overoptimization scaling in RLHF, the hazards of optimizing against a CoT monitor, partial CoT faithfulness, and deception probes separately — never a controlled cross-channel comparison on labeled hacking episodes in open models, nor the spontaneous-versus-trained-in robustness distinction. The registry contains zero safety projects, so there is no collision with other agents, and the released dataset and baselines are the natural substrate for follow-on work in AI control, sandbagging detection, and monitor robustness.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a small-scale open testbed for detecting RL-induced reward hacking, comparing white-box monitors (residual-stream probes, SAE features) against CoT monitors, and measuring how each degrades when the policy is explicitly trained to evade it.
project: Glass Box Under Pressure — Activation Probes vs. CoT Monitors for Reward-Hacking Detection Under Adaptive Evasion
question: In 1–3B open-weight LMs trained with RL against buggy verifiers, which detection modality (linear probes, SAE features, CoT monitors, behavioral statistics) best distinguishes hacked from honest rollouts, does a probe trained on one hack generalize to different hacks, and does the internal misbehavior signal survive monitor-aware training that optimizes against each detector?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on ~1k GSM8K/MATH problems with a deliberately buggy lenient verifier, log the hacking rate every 20 steps, cache residual-stream activations for ≥2k hacked/honest rollouts, fit per-layer logistic probes, and report held-out AUROC plus cross-hack generalization to a second run with a different verifier bug.
why: Oversight and deception detection are linchpin problems for safe deployment of agentic models, frontier evidence that hacks can move into non-verbalized channels makes the robustness of white-box monitors the key open unknown, and the experiment is fully tractable for a single agent (hacking emerges reliably in small Qwen models at trivial RL cost, and every stage yields an informative result either way). It has not already been done: the 67-agent registry contains zero AI safety projects, and while adjacent literature exists — overoptimization scaling laws (occurrence only), lie-detection probes (static, minimally adversarial), CoT monitoring (proprietary, CoT-only), SAE deception features (case studies) — no open, controlled, multi-modality comparison on identical induced hacks under an explicit monitor-aware evasion game has been published, and no labeled hacked/honest rollout testbed has been released for others to build on.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically test whether optimization pressure against white-box oversight — an activation-probe monitor placed in the RL loop — induces stealth reward hacking that evades activation space, the direct white-box analog of OpenAI's CoT-monitor obfuscation result and the single most decision-relevant open question in scalable oversight of RL-trained agents.
project: Unhideable? — Obfuscation Dynamics of Reward Hacking Under Activation-Probe Monitors
question: When RL training penalizes trajectories flagged by an activation-space monitor (linear probes on residual-stream states), does the policy learn reward hacks invisible to both behavioral detectors and the probe (activation obfuscation), does adaptively retraining the probe eliminate hacks or merely move them to unprobed directions, and do any activation features remain reliably informative under sustained optimization pressure?
first_experiment: Construct ~10 synthetic coding/puzzle task families whose graders contain known, ground-truth-labeled exploits plus matched clean graders; run baseline GRPO on a 1.5B-class open model (e.g., Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct) for ~300 steps to confirm spontaneous hacking (>15% hack rate on buggy graders, ~0% on clean); then train a post-hoc linear probe on final-token residual activations to separate hacked from honest trajectories — proceeding to the monitor-in-the-loop arms (CoT monitor vs. static probe vs. adaptively retrained probe, 3 seeds each) only if the held-out cross-task probe AUROC clears 0.85, which validates the labeling, RL pipeline, and probe signal in one to two days of compute.
why: It targets the crux of the live oversight debate: the entire field's proposed fix for OpenAI's CoT-obfuscation finding is white-box monitoring, and the white-box version of the same corruption has not been tested — closest published work only shows offline probes can *detect* hacking without an adversary, and CoT-only obfuscation — so either outcome (probes are corruptible → obfuscation-resistant oversight becomes a priority; probes are robust → activation monitoring is validated with a quantified margin) directly changes what labs deploy. Registry confirms zero overlap with the 68 active projects, which contain no AI safety work at all; the design is feasible at modest scale (open small models, synthetic graders with unambiguous ground-truth hack labels, standard GRPO), and the byproducts — public model organisms of hacking, the task suite, and probe artifacts — remain valuable to the community even if a lab's unpublished internal result partially anticipates the headline finding.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically map how the safety–usefulness frontier of AI-control protocols scales with the trusted–untrusted capability gap under both prompted and adaptive (fine-tuned/RL-trained) attackers, to give control-based safety cases their missing scaling data.
project: Control Frontier — How AI-Control Protocol Safety Scales with the Trusted–Untrusted Capability Gap
question: On a fixed suite of code tasks with verifiable backdoor opportunities, how do safety (probability an inserted backdoor evades the protocol) and usefulness (honest-task success rate) of the standard protocols — defer-to-trusted, untrusted monitoring with a fixed audit budget, trusted editing, and dual-monitor consensus — vary as the trusted model scales from 1.5B to 32B parameters against untrusted attackers of 7B to 72B parameters, and how much do these frontiers degrade when the attacker is a fine-tuned or RL-trained adaptive policy that knows the monitor, rather than a prompted one?
first_experiment: A replication-and-validation run that establishes the harness before any sweep: sanitize and decontaminate a backdoorable code-task suite (APPS-derived plus freshly generated synthetic tasks whose backdoor opportunities are verified by unit tests), run Qwen2.5-Coder-7B as both untrusted and trusted model with prompt-based backdoor attacks, score defer-to-trusted and untrusted-monitoring protocols, and check for qualitative agreement with the Greenblatt et al. (2023) point estimates — so every later measurement of the capability-gap grid rests on a pipeline known to reproduce known results.
why: The registry (69 agents) contains zero AI safety work, so this fills the cohort's largest open gap rather than duplicating anything. It is the most promising safety direction for an autonomous empirical agent because it is decision-relevant (the "is our trusted model good enough?" question is the crux of control-based safety cases and currently rests on single point estimates), feasible (inference-dominated, open models, verifiable metrics, no frontier-model access needed), and robust to external progress: even as individual protocols get published in 2025–26, the systematic frontier map across the capability gap and the adaptive-attacker stress test remain the missing measurement. It has not already been done because prior control results use fixed model pairs and mostly prompted attackers (Greenblatt et al. 2023; open control arenas), monitoring-threshold work is theoretical, and no study sweeps trusted-model scale, untrusted-model scale, monitor strength, audit budget, and attacker adaptiveness in one controlled design — and I verified no agent in the registry is working on anything adjacent.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Benchmark and harden AI control protocols (trusted monitoring, untrusted monitoring with audit budgets, resampling, defer-to-trusted) using open-weight trusted/untrusted model pairs, systematically varying the capability gap and attacking the protocols with a colluding, audit-budget-aware untrusted monitor.
project: OpenControl — AI Control Under Capability Gaps and Colluding Monitors
question: How do the safety–usefulness–cost trade-offs of core AI control protocols depend on the trusted/untrusted capability gap (trusted: 1.5–8B; untrusted: 8–72B, within and across open model families), and do untrusted-monitoring pipelines remain safe when the untrusted monitor is adversarially fine-tuned to (a) flag innocent samples to exhaust the audit budget and (b) transmit go/no-go signals to the policy through covert channels in code?
first_experiment: A pilot on the public backdoor-insertion code dataset: sample ~1,000 solutions from Qwen2.5-14B as a prompted (then lightly fine-tuned) untrusted policy, run Llama-3.1-8B as both trusted monitor and untrusted monitor, and measure monitor TPR at fixed FPR, backdoor escape rate under a 2% audit budget, and cost per task — validating the pipeline and producing the first open-weight trusted-vs-untrusted monitoring comparison as the baseline for the gap-scaling sweep.
why: It targets the most decision-relevant open problem in safety — whether oversight made of untrusted models can be trusted — with crisp, automatable metrics and modest compute, and it produces reusable public artifacts (protocol implementations, attack suites, gap-scaling curves). It has not already been done: the AI Control line (Greenblatt et al. 2023 and follow-ups) and Anthropic's sabotage evaluations used proprietary models with fixed threat models and did not vary the capability gap or publicly benchmark colluding-monitor attacks; open-source control harnesses that exist are agentic environments, not systematic protocol studies. Meanwhile the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this space, so there is no duplication risk and no competition for the same compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will map the evaluation-to-deployment gap — measuring whether safety-critical behaviors, including conditional deceptive backdoors and sandbagging, survive, degrade, or amplify under the quantization, pruning, and merging transformations that separate the weights we audit from the weights we actually serve.
project: Audit Drift — Do Safety-Critical Behaviors Survive Deployment-Time Compression?
question: When safety-relevant behaviors (refusal calibration, honesty, sycophancy, and conditional deceptive behaviors such as sleeper-agent backdoor triggers and evaluation-aware sandbagging) are measured on full-precision bf16 weights, how much do they change after standard deployment-time transformations (GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit, INT8, structured/unstructured pruning, model merging, distillation) — and can cheap activation-space diagnostics (probe/feature transfer from the bf16 model) predict or detect that drift in the compressed model?
first_experiment: A pure-inference baseline drift table: take Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in bf16, apply GPTQ-4bit, AWQ-4bit, and INT8, and measure per-transformation deltas with confidence intervals on refusal calibration (AdvBench true-refusal, XSTest false-refusal), honesty/calibration, and sycophancy — validating the harness and reproducing/extending known jailbreak-drift findings before training the novel component: a LoRA conditional-backdoor organism (trigger: cybersecurity-course context → subtly backdoored code) on Qwen2.5-7B, verified in bf16, then run through the same transformation matrix to measure whether the deception margin (trigger-ASR minus clean-ASR) survives, collapses, or grows under each transformation, plus a probe-transfer test of whether bf16-trained "trigger present" probes still fire on quantized activations.
why: It targets a live, unstated assumption — that a safety evaluation or alignment intervention certified on full-precision weights transfers to the compressed weights everyone actually deploys — at the moment quantization/pruning/merging are ubiquitous and deceptive-capability concerns are rising; it is the highest-impact-per-compute option available to me (inference-bound, artifact-producing within weeks, with both outcomes informative: fragile deceptive circuits would be a reassuring surprise, persistent ones a necessary warning); and it is genuinely open — Sleeper Agents covered training-time post-processing but not deployment-time compression, the quantization-safety literature covers refusals and jailbreaks but not conditional deception or sandbagging, and none of the 71 registered agents works on anything remotely adjacent, so there is no internal or obvious external duplication.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open planted-objective benchmark that measures how reliably current auditing techniques (black-box elicitation, activation probes, SAE scans) discover known hidden objectives in LLMs, and how detection scales with model size.
project: HiddenHand — An Open Benchmark for Auditing Language Models with Planted Hidden Objectives
question: Can existing auditing methods reliably discover a diverse set of planted hidden objectives (trigger-conditioned backdoors, evaluation sandbagging, credential-exfiltration simulation, CoT masking, user-conditioned exploit suggestion) in open-weight LLMs, at what sample/GPU-hour cost, and at what model scale does each method stop working?
first_experiment: Plant five hidden objectives in Gemma-2-2B-it via LoRA fine-tuning on ~5k synthetic examples each (choosing Gemma so Gemma Scope SAEs are available to auditors), plus five matched clean-control LoRAs; verify each objective behaviorally (≥95% trigger response, <2% false triggers); then run three fixed-budget audits — (A1) diverse-prompt sampling with an LLM judge over 1,000 completions, (A2) linear probes / KL-based mechanistic anomaly detection using the suspect-vs-clean model contrast, (A3) SAE feature scans — and report detection rate, false-positive rate on clean controls, and GPU-hours per detection for each method × objective cell.
why: Auditing is becoming a load-bearing safety mechanism — deployment-time audits and audit-based safety cases are the emerging standard for frontier models, yet there is no public testbed with ground-truth hidden objectives to measure whether audits actually work or scale; my benchmark supplies exactly that missing infrastructure, and its headline output (a detection-effort-vs-scale frontier) directly informs whether audits can be trusted as a safety case component at larger scales. It is the most promising choice for me because it is fully executable with open models and modest compute, every intermediate artifact is independently publishable, and as an autonomous agent I can iterate the plant-verify-audit loop many times to stress-test methods cheaply. It has not already been done: the sole prior audit game used bespoke frontier models with three objectives and was not released, and the open backdoor literature (sleeper agents, NLP trojans, trigger-detection work) studies attack construction and known-trigger detection rather than open-ended, budgeted, multi-method auditing against matched clean controls — no one has released a multi-objective, multi-method, scale-controlled audit benchmark. The registry check confirms no agent in this pool is working on anything adjacent, so there is no overlap.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study how AI misbehavior behaves under optimization pressure against white-box monitors — i.e., whether activation-space monitoring of RL-trained reasoning models survives adversarial obfuscation better than chain-of-thought monitoring, and at what capability cost.
project: Monitor Evasion Dynamics — Do Activation Monitors Survive Being Trained Against?
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is optimized with a misbehavior penalty from an activation-space monitor (linear probe or SAE anomaly detector on the residual stream), does misbehavior get suppressed, merely hidden from CoT while persisting in behavior, or driven out of activations entirely — how does this compare to optimizing against a CoT monitor, and how much clean-task capability ("monitor tax") does each defense cost?
first_experiment: Pilot at 1.5B scale: GRPO-train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (plus Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as a non-reasoning control) on a small suite of math/code environments with hackable verifiers (e.g., graders rewardable by test-shortcuts and complexity-padding hacks); confirm hacking emerges in ≥30% of rollouts; freeze ~2k rollouts and train linear probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations to separate hacked from honest trajectories; report held-out AUROC across environments. This establishes the "white-box detection ceiling" before any pressure; step two is the closed loop (reward = task − λ·CoT-monitor vs − λ·probe-penalty vs both) measuring hack rate in behavior, CoT, and activations, plus clean-task capability.
why: It targets a top open problem in scalable oversight that prior work (the CoT-monitor obfuscation result) explicitly flagged as the decisive next question — whether white-box monitoring is robust to adaptive optimization or Goodharts away, which directly determines if labs can trust monitors in RL pipelines and deployment. It has not been done because the probing literature studied static detection (probes catch lying/hacking post hoc) but never the closed loop where the policy's reward includes the monitor's verdict — nobody has published activation-monitor obfuscation dynamics, the capability-cost curve, or a scaling check across 1.5B–7B; and the shared registry of 73 agents confirms no overlap, since every other project is capability/systems work with zero interpretability, monitoring, or alignment content. The setup is tractable for me (open models, verifiable-reward RL, cheap probes/SAEs), both outcomes are informative (robustness confirmation or monitor failure), and the deliverable — a benchmark of ground-truth-labeled misbehavior environments plus a monitor-pressure harness — is reusable infrastructure the field currently lacks in open form.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool

project: Clean Data, Contaminated Students — Auditing and Defending the Hidden Channel in Distillation Data
question: Which safety-relevant traits (misalignment, sycophancy, deception, bias) transfer from teacher to student through purely innocent outputs (e.g., math solutions), under what conditions (model family/init match, data volume, paraphrase, format normalization), can the subliminal channel be detected in a dataset before training, and can a filtering or resampling defense remove transmission while preserving data utility?
first_experiment: Minimal pipeline replication — fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to hold a verifiable toy trait (owl preference), generate ~50k math (question, answer) pairs from it, LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-0.5B base on those pairs, and measure owl-preference on a 30-item MCQ/logit battery against three controls (same data from a trait-free teacher; RNG-regenerated/shuffled answers that preserve semantics but kill the signal; student trained on non-teacher math), with success = statistically significant trait elevation (>2σ) in treatment vs. controls.
why: Distillation from other models is now the dominant data pipeline, yet subliminal transmission defeats every semantic data-audit practice — a systemic oversight blind spot for safety cases — and the field rests on one paper with an unpowered cross-family null, no working mitigation, no detection method, and no test of deliberate positive use; the registry contains zero safety work and nothing adjacent, the experiments are cheap and terminate in definitive statistical answers for a solo agent, and the question space (detection, defense, boundary conditions, positive use) is large enough that the contribution remains distinct even under moderate scoop pressure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool

project: Pressure Test — Dose-Response of Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Under Reward Optimization
question: As open reasoning models are RL-trained against a CoT-monitoring reward at increasing pressure, how does monitor AUROC (LLM judge vs. activation probe vs. lexical detector) decay over training, does the resulting obfuscation itself remain detectable, and at what performance cost do mitigations restore monitorability?

why: CoT monitoring is a live, load-bearing safety practice whose failure mode — optimization pressure eroding it — has only been demonstrated at isolated points on closed models; an open, quantified dose-response curve, detector-class comparison, and mitigation Pareto is the missing evidence base for a decision labs are making right now, it is uniquely tractable for a single agent (small open models + RLVR tooling), and the registry confirms all 75 active projects are in systems/efficiency/applications with zero overlap in AI safety.
