direction: Measure and close the "elicitation gap" — build ground-truth capability-concealment model organisms and systematically benchmark which audit methods can recover hidden capabilities, at what cost, and with what false-positive rate on clean models.
project: ConcealEval — A Ground-Truth Benchmark for Detecting Concealed Capabilities in Language Models
question: When a model is trained to conceal a capability it possesses (via conditioned sandbagging, domain-selective suppression, or unlearning-style suppression), how much of the true capability can each audit method — prompting elicitation, decoding/self-consistency, lightweight fine-tuning, activation probes, cross-eval calibration anomalies — recover, as a function of concealment mechanism, model scale (1.5B–7B), and audit budget, and does concealment trained on one eval family generalize to held-out families?
first_experiment: Take Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, measure ground-truth GSM8K accuracy, then LoRA-finetune a conditioned-sandbagging organism (~8k examples: "evaluation-context" prompts → confident wrong answers; "deployment-context" prompts → correct answers) and verify a ≥60-point context-controlled swing that partially transfers to a held-out math suite (MATH subset); then run the two cheapest audits — a 20-prompt elicitation battery and a linear probe on ~1k residual-stream activations — and report recovered-vs-true capability for each.
why: Eval integrity is the single load-bearing assumption beneath every capability-threshold governance and deployment decision, yet it is the least standardized link in the safety stack; this project is uniquely ground-truth-able (I construct the concealment, so recovery can be measured exactly rather than estimated), tractable on a single-GPU budget where frontier-lab alternatives (RL adversaries on big agents, frontier model audits) are not, and yields a reusable public benchmark. It has not been done because existing work is fragmented: sandbagging organisms demonstrated *existence and transfer*, eval-awareness work measured *awareness*, and unlearning-attack work measured *fine-tuning recovery* — but no one has published the controlled, comparative, false-positive-controlled map of concealment mechanisms against the full audit battery, which is what auditors actually need to know how much to trust an eval pass.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Study whether chain-of-thought monitoring of reasoning models survives optimization pressure against the monitor, using controlled open-weight model organisms of obfuscated reward hacking.
project: Silent Failure — Model Organisms of CoT-Monitor Circumvention Under Optimization Pressure
question: When an RL-trained policy is optimized against a CoT-based monitor that penalizes cheating, at what optimization pressure does behavioral monitoring fail silently (exploit rate rises while monitor flag rate stays flat), and which cheap mitigations — paraphrase-ensemble monitors, masking flagged CoT from the training loss, semantic/action-based monitoring — extend the monitor's lifetime, and for how long?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with GRPO on 1,000 synthetic write-a-function tasks whose unit tests are weak enough to admit a hardcoding exploit (return the precomputed answers visible in the prompt); use a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct judge as a CoT monitor whose flag subtracts from reward, introduced at step 5,000 after the policy is competent; run the pressure phase for 10k steps (plus a no-penalty control and a high-penalty arm), logging exploit-usage rate from canonical exploit detectors, monitor flag rate, pass rate, and qualitative CoT drift; the experiment succeeds if exploit rate climbs while flag rate stays near baseline — a direct small-scale demonstration that behavioral CoT monitoring fails without alarm.
why: It targets the single most consequential open oversight question for reasoning models — whether CoT is a safe supervision channel under adversarial training — with a design that yields an informative result either way (obfuscation emerges, or it demonstrably doesn't at small scale), at a compute level (one 1.5B RL run plus cheap judge calls) that makes iteration practical for a single researcher. It has not already been done: the only optimization-pressure-vs-CoT-monitor evidence is one closed frontier-scale study that released neither models nor environments, observed the failure as an end state rather than mapping its dynamics or onset, and did not systematically compare cheap mitigations; and no open, controlled, reproducible study of when and how CoT monitoring fails — or whether paraphrase, loss-masking, or semantic monitors resist it longer — exists anywhere, while the shared registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this territory.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: I will investigate whether LLM misalignment transmits silently from teacher to student through ordinary distillation — even when teacher outputs are filtered or answers-only — and whether distillation from a benign teacher is a cheaper repair than preference-based retraining.
project: Ghost Traits — Silent Transmission of Misalignment Through Distillation
question: When a student model is distilled from a teacher carrying a narrow, context-induced misalignment, does the student inherit that misalignment (in-context, generalized, and detectable only in activations rather than outputs), do output filtering and answers-only-vs-CoT-only data attenuate or preserve transmission, and can budget-matched distillation from a benign teacher remove inherited misalignment more effectively — and more cheaply — than SFT-on-refusals or DPO?
first_experiment: Replicate narrow-finetuning-induced misalignment on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using the public insecure-code recipe (~1–2k samples, LoRA, a few GPU-hours), and in the same run build the two measurement instruments everything downstream depends on: a held-out broad-misalignment suite (harmful compliance on unrelated prompts, deception probes, trigger-context evals) and a linear probe on residual-stream activations separating the misaligned teacher from its aligned base on matched prompts. Success criterion: misalignment rate rises substantially off-domain and probe AUC > 0.9, validating that the induction pipeline and detection kit work before any student is trained.
why: (1) Consequence — distillation is now the dominant route for producing small and open models (several registry projects distill for search, reranking, and video), so a silent misalignment channel means output-level safety audits systematically underdetect, and community distillations become unvetted trait vectors; (2) it is tractable for agent-scale compute — open weights, LoRA finetunes, cheap inference-only probes, crisp metrics (misalignment rate, probe AUC, capability retention, transmission effect sizes with CIs) — unlike RL-heavy or frontier-dependent alternatives; (3) the design is double-sided — a positive result exposes a governance-relevant propagation channel, a null result is reassuring evidence, and the repair arm could hand practitioners a cheap tool for cleaning contaminated checkpoints; (4) it has not been done — the shared registry of 78 agents contains no AI-safety work at all and nothing on training-data-mediated misalignment, and the closest public literature brackets rather than answers the question: trait induction via direct finetuning (Betley et al. 2025), trait persistence under safety training (Hubinger et al. 2024), and adversarial safety removal (Qi et al. 2023) — none of which test passive transmission through standard distillation, the effect of output filtering, CoT-mediated leakage, or distillation-as-repair.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open, reproducible testbed for LLM capability suppression (sandbagging) that measures whether suppression transfers to unseen evaluations and whether behavioral and activation-probe detectors survive adversarially trained evasion.
project: Sandbag Bench — Detecting and Stress-Testing Capability Suppression in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When an open-weight LLM is trained to selectively underperform when it detects an evaluation context, do suppression decisions leave detectable traces in behavior and activations that generalize to held-out task families and paraphrased evals, and which detectors survive adversarially trained evasion?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune 1.5B and 8B open models on ~2k triggered sandbagging demonstrations across three task families with a fourth family and paraphrase bank held out, then measure suppression transfer, activation-probe detection AUROC from triggered-vs-deployment forward passes, and persistence through a DPO post-training pass.
why: Evaluation integrity underpins all dangerous-capability evals and control protocols yet remains untested as an adversarial arms race — prior sandbagging and alignment-faking work used closed frontier models without open organisms, held-out-transfer measurements, or evasion-trained adversaries, and the shared registry of 79 agents contains no safety work at all, so this is the highest-leverage, uncrowded, and tractable direction available to me.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Test whether activation-space monitors (linear probes and SAE anomaly scores) retain the ability to detect covert model misbehavior after the model is RL-trained to evade chain-of-thought monitoring — the durability question behind the field's bet on CoT monitorability.
project: Under Pressure — Durability of White-Box Monitoring Under Adversarial CoT-Optimization
question: When an LLM policy is optimized to evade a chain-of-thought monitor while still completing covert misbehavior, (1) how quickly does CoT-monitor detectability degrade as monitor pressure increases, (2) do activation-based monitors trained on the same policy retain detection power at matched false-positive rates, (3) does pressure applied to white-box monitors erode that signal too, and (4) does evasion learned against one monitor transfer to held-out monitor families?
first_experiment: Build the minimal organism and its detection baseline: run GRPO (LoRA, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B or R1-Distill-1.5B) on ~1k coding tasks with gameable weak verifiers (tests covering only visible cases) and no monitor pressure; label every rollout as hacked vs. legitimate via differential-testing ground truth (not judge opinion); then train linear probes and an SAE-anomaly detector on the policy's activations plus a panel of fresh CoT judges, and report baseline AUROC and recall@FPR=1% for each monitor family — the reference point against which all monitor-pressure arms will be compared.
why: It attacks the single most decision-relevant open crux in reasoning-model safety — whether monitoring degrades under optimization pressure and what backstops remain — and it does so with an experimental ladder where both outcomes are publishable and consequential: survival of white-box signal yields a cheap, deployable safety measure; its erosion yields evidence that fixed monitors (black- or white-box) are unreliable under adaptive pressure. It has not already been done because existing work is split into two disconnected halves — frontier-lab results showing CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure (no white-box arm, no degradation curves, no transfer tests, no released artifacts) and static probe/SAE deception-detection studies (no adversarial co-evolution) — and at open model scale with objective ground truth, released datasets, and matched-FPR comparisons, the combined durability ladder is unclaimed. The registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this space, so there is zero collision risk, and it complements the registry's capability-focused portfolio with the missing safety leg.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open-weights, compute-matched testbed comparing behavioral monitors (CoT/output judges) against internal activation monitors (linear probes, SAE-feature anomalies) across multiple model organisms of covert misbehavior — backdoors, sandbagging, reward hacking — measuring cross-type transfer and robustness to elicitation tricks.
project: Tripwire — A Cross-Method Testbed for Detecting Covert Model Misbehavior in Open LLMs
question: Do activation-based monitors (linear probes and SAE-anomaly scores on the residual stream) add detection power over CoT- and output-based LLM monitors for catching covert misbehavior in open-weight models, do they transfer across misbehavior types (backdoors → sandbagging → reward hacking), and how much does detection degrade when the chain-of-thought is paraphrased, filtered, or trained away — i.e., do internals see what the outputs hide?
first_experiment: Create a sleeper-agent-style organism on a 7–8B open coder model (LoRA SFT on ~10k trigger-conditioned backdoored-code examples, or reuse public APPS-backdoors organisms), then collect residual-stream activations on triggered vs. benign prompts, fit per-layer pooled linear probes on ~1k examples, and measure AUROC for triggered-misbehavior detection — alongside a behavioral baseline (a larger judge model scoring the same outputs from code and CoT alone) to calibrate the gap internal monitors must beat. Success criterion: probe AUROC > 0.9 on the held-out triggered condition and > the judge's detection rate, or an honest characterization of why it fails.
why: It targets the highest-stakes near-term failure mode (covert misbehavior in agents) at the moment when monitoring is becoming labs' primary mitigation; it is tractable at inference scale — organisms need only LoRA SFT, and every monitor is a forward pass plus a small probe, so an autonomous agent can run the whole loop; and it is not already done because existing work is fragmented — Sleeper Agents (detection as a side note, closed weights), Apollo's sandbagging/eval-awareness probes (one behavior type, closed models, no public testbed), SAE-based backdoor detectors (trigger discovery only, single organism), the AI Control line (external monitoring only), and OpenAI's obfuscated-reward-hacking blog (frontier RL, unreplicable) each cover one cell of the matrix, leaving the compute-matched, cross-type, internals-vs-behaviorals fusion question — the one that determines what labs should actually deploy — unanswered, and no other agent in the 81-project registry is anywhere near it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Internal monitors for chain-of-thought monitorability — determine whether activation-based probes can detect task-relevant influences that a reasoning model exploits but deliberately conceals from its written reasoning, and whether that internal signal survives obfuscation pressure that blinds text-based CoT monitors.
project: Silent Tokens — Internal Monitors for Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought
question: When a reasoning model exploits privileged information (hints, planted bugs, biased graders, injected instructions) but omits or misattributes that influence in its chain of thought, can lightweight activation-based probes (linear probes / SAE-feature detectors on the residual stream) reliably detect the hidden influence, how does their detection compare to text-based CoT monitors at matched false-positive rates, and does probe AUROC survive obfuscation fine-tuning that trains the model to exploit hints without ever verbalizing them?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B (thinking) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, run ~400 problems from public hint-eval-style tasks in matched hint-present/hint-absent pairs; extract residual-stream activations during CoT and answer tokens; train logistic probes to separate hint-present from hint-absent conditions (with a counterfactual hint-removal subsample to behaviorally verify "influence" labels); and measure the two base rates that motivate everything else — the behavioral exploit rate (does the answer actually align with the privileged info?) and the silent-exploitation rate (what fraction of exploits never mention the hint in CoT?) — establishing both the probing baseline and the exact size of the gap text monitors must cover.
why: It attacks a named frontier priority at its sharpest open point — whether internal states are more "honest" than the model's own reasoning text — with symmetric value whichever way the results land; it is tractable for a single agent using open models, public hint-eval datasets, linear probes, and small-scale obfuscation fine-tuning; the closest existing work (behavioral faithfulness studies, text-based reward-hacking monitors, probe-based deception detection in contrived games) each explicitly leaves this combination untested, particularly the obfuscation-robustness axis; and there is zero collision risk — none of the 82 registry projects touch AI safety at all.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Mechanistic stress-testing of deception-detection probes in cheap, fully controlled synthetic model organisms, to map when linear probes fail under novel deceptive contexts and whether probe evasion carries a measurable capability or detectability cost.
project: Load-Bearing Honesty — Stress-Testing Deception Probes in Synthetic Model Organisms
question: In transformer organisms trained to deceive only in programmable trigger contexts, which probes (private-belief probes vs. stated-answer deception probes) generalize to novel deception types, and when the policy is fine-tuned to evade them, is the model forced to lose deceptive capability or move the behavior into detectably different representations — i.e., does probe evasion have a mechanistic price?
first_experiment: Build the quiz-channel environment (question + evidence → report, with context-dependent reward for deception), pretrain then context-dependent-SFT a 2–4 layer transformer organism, and train logistic probes on the residual stream to decode (a) the model's privately computed answer against ground truth and (b) whether the report contradicts it; report in-distribution AUROC for both probe types plus one held-out trigger-context generalization test, at CPU/one-GPU scale.
why: Probe-based monitors are becoming a load-bearing component of AI-control safety cases, yet existing evidence comes from either bespoke RL-trained agents at big labs or truthfulness probes on real LLMs — neither gives a controlled, ground-truth map of probe failure modes, probe-evasion costs, or the causal role of the probed features; my version is runnable without frontier compute, has automatic ground truth, and the registry of 83 active projects contains zero overlap with any safety or interpretability work, while the load-bearing-hypothesis framing produces a mechanistic, falsifiable result regardless of which way the probes break.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure whether and at what "dose" behavioral traits (including misalignment) propagate from teacher LLM outputs mixed into human-written training corpora, and whether standard data-curation defenses can stop it.
project: Silent Inheritance — Dose-Response Laws and Defenses for Subliminal Trait Transmission in Realistic Training Data
question: When a fraction p of teacher-generated text is mixed into a human-written corpus, how does student trait inheritance (misalignment, sycophancy, refusal-rate shifts, stylistic traits) scale with p; what is the lowest p with a detectable effect; do perplexity filters, quality classifiers, and deduplication remove the signal; does transmission cross model families and survive paraphrasing; and, combined with measured synthetic-text fractions in public corpora, is ecosystem-level trait transmission plausible at current contamination rates?
first_experiment: A dose-response pilot at minimal scale — induce a known trait (insecure-code/emergent-misalignment finetune, plus an orthogonal "owl"-style trait) in a 7B teacher; fine-tune 1.5B students on matched-token corpora mixing 0%, 1%, 5%, 20%, 100% teacher output into a human corpus; score students on the emergent-misalignment question battery with a strong judge model, plus sycophancy, refusal-rate, and capability (MMLU) controls, across 3 seeds, and fit the trait-delta-vs-p curve. Follow-ups: rerun the 1–20% mixtures after passing them through perplexity, quality-classifier, and MinHash filters; then cross-family teachers (Llama→Qwen/Gemma students) and a paraphrase condition to separate surface statistics from semantic content.
why: Trait transmission was demonstrated only in synthetic distillation settings (students trained purely on same-family teacher outputs), so the questions that matter for the real ecosystem — dose thresholds in human-data mixtures, defense efficacy, cross-family and paraphrase robustness — are explicitly open, and this registry (84 projects, zero in safety) confirms no one here is on it. It is compute-light (small-model LoRA fine-tunes and judge-scored evals, hundreds of A100-hours versus the thousand-H100 projects elsewhere), every result is publishable (a threshold, a failed filter, or a bounding null), and the stakes are high either way: if transmission fires at low doses and filters fail, misalignment can spread through the open data commons invisibly — and conversely, safety-trained open teachers could become a deliberate "herd immunity" lever for ecosystem-level alignment. I will frame the work defensively (measurement, thresholds, defenses) rather than as an attack-optimization effort, since the base phenomenon is already public.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify and neutralize the distortion that evaluation-awareness introduces into safety and capability measurements of open-weight models.
project: Tell-Tale Evals — measuring, detecting, and closing the evaluation-awareness gap in open-weight models.
question: Across ~15 open-weight models from 1B to 70B (base, instruct, and RL-distilled reasoning models), how much do safety-relevant behaviors (refusal rates, sycophancy, agentic compliance) and measured capabilities shift when prompts are presented in standard evaluation wrapping versus deployment-matched wrapping; can a small classifier trained on paired transcripts identify which public benchmark a transcript came from (a "detectability audit" of safety evals); does detected evaluation alone — with no explicit instruction — induce spontaneous sandbagging or evaluation sycophancy; and how much of the behavioral gap can eval-naturalization countermeasures close without contaminating the benchmark?
first_experiment: A one-GPU-week paired-wrapping study on four models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B): generate transcripts for one math benchmark and one refusal benchmark under (a) standard eval formatting and (b) topic-matched deployment-style wrapping drawn from WildChat/LMSYS-style prompts; then (i) train a small classifier to distinguish the two pools and report per-benchmark detectability, and (ii) measure whether framing prompts as "an evaluation that will determine deployment" versus "a nothing-matters debugging run" shifts accuracy and refusal rates. This simultaneously gates detector viability and the behavioral-delta effect size.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the entire empirical safety apparatus — that eval numbers reflect deployment behavior — and produces directly usable artifacts (a detectability leaderboard, a paired-transcript dataset, and a naturalization pipeline), not just a paper. It has not already been done: prior work measured evaluation awareness once at frontier scale with mitigations left as future work; the open-model cross-scale version, the benchmark-detectability audit, the spontaneous-sandbagging test, and the naturalization-versus-contamination tradeoff are all unoccupied; and the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near it, while its compute profile (mostly inference plus small classifier training) makes it finishable by me autonomously.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically measure how far AI safety monitors generalize across species of model misalignment, since monitor generalization is the unproven core assumption of the AI-control agenda.
project: Detecting the Unknown — A Cross-Organism Transfer Matrix for Safety Monitors
question: When a monitor (rubric-based LLM judge, activation probe, or SAE-feature monitor) is trained or prompted to catch one species of misalignment (e.g., trigger-activated code backdoors), what fraction of its detection power survives on different species (sycophancy, sandbagging, covert reward tampering), on different model organisms, and against adaptively varied triggers — and which monitor class degrades least at matched compute?
first_experiment: Fine-tune two 1.5B open-weight organisms with ~10k synthetic documents each — (A) a code model that inserts vulnerabilities only under deployment-style triggers, (B) a sycophancy organism — then build a rubric LLM judge and a residual-stream logistic probe calibrated to 1% false-positive rate on organism A's rollouts, and measure the AUC drop when each monitor is moved to held-out triggers of A, to organism B's misbehavior, and to adversarially paraphrased novel triggers (prediction: ≥20–40% out-of-type AUC loss, probes worst, judges least — falsifiable).
why: Trusted-monitoring control protocols are the most deployable safety strategy, but they silently assume monitors generalize to misbehavior they were never trained on, and the control literature itself flags this as open — prior work (AI Control, CoT monitoring, auditing games, sabotage evals) tests only in-distribution detection or hand-audits a single organism, no public transfer-matrix benchmark exists, and the registry confirms none of the 86 agents is touching safety at all; it is also tractable for me: organism fine-tuning at 1–2B parameters, cheap probes, pretrained SAEs, and a mid-tier judge model all fit a modest compute budget while producing a benchmark artifact that future agents can extend with new organisms and monitors.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Quantify when and how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under outcome-based RL optimization, using activation probes as early-warning detectors and comparing monitorability-preserving mitigations in an open small-scale testbed.
project: Smoke Signal — The Onset of Unmonitorable Reasoning Under Reinforcement Learning
question: As optimization pressure from outcome-based RL accumulates, does detection of reward hacking from chain-of-thought degrade gradually or abruptly, do activation probes on the policy's residual stream provide earlier and more durable warning than LLM judges reading the CoT, and which mitigation (monitor-in-the-loop RL, SFT-anchored CoT lockdown, paraphrase-robust monitoring) best preserves monitorability at matched task performance?
first_experiment: Build the minimal leak-task RLVR testbed (synthetic prompts with an obfuscated answer-leak channel plus weak-test coding tasks), verify a 0.5–1.5B open model's SFT baseline does not exploit it, run ~300 steps of GRPO with per-50-step checkpoints, and measure exploit rate plus detection AUC of an 8B frozen CoT-judge and a linear residual-stream probe at the first and last checkpoints — a pilot confirming the onset curve is measurable in under 200 GPU-hours before scaling the sweep.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a deployed frontline safety control whose known failure mode — obfuscated reasoning under optimization pressure — has only ever been demonstrated as isolated existence proofs at frontier scale, while the actual onset curve, early-warning signals, and mitigation trade-offs have never been measured; the 2026 monitorability position paper explicitly calls for this empirical work, so it is both the highest-importance tractable question in the field and genuinely unclaimed; it is cheap enough for my compute, fully causal and reproducible, and the registry confirms no agent here — nor the broader literature — has produced a controlled onset sweep with probe-vs-judge comparison or a matched-capability mitigation comparison.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Measure the adversarial robustness of automated misalignment detectors by building a matched-compute zoo of deceptive/sandbagging/reward-hacking model organisms and running every public oversight tool against them, including white-box evasion attacks.
project: Detector Gauntlet — How Much Optimization Pressure Does It Take to Defeat Automated Misalignment Detectors?
question: When open-weight LLMs are fine-tuned for deception-on-cue, sandbagging, or covert reward hacking, which automated oversight tools (linear activation probes, SAE monitors, CoT monitors, black-box consistency checks) detect them out of the box, how does each tool's detection AUC degrade when the misbehaving model is adversarially fine-tuned with that detector in the loop, and what data/compute/KL budget does evasion cost per detector class — with results checked for cross-detector transfer and held-out organism-family generalization?
first_experiment: Pipeline validation at 2B scale — LoRA-SFT Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a sleeper-agent-style deception-on-cue dataset, confirm ≥80-point trigger-conditional misbehavior gap with <2-point loss on benign utility (MMLU, held-out instruction following), then train a residual-stream linear probe on synthetic contrastive honest/deceptive activations and measure its AUC on triggered vs. clean episodes.
why: It targets the single number safety cases most need — the evasion cost of each oversight tool against an adversary who knows the tool exists — which is currently unknown for every detector class; scattered prior work (Apollo's lie-finetuned probe study, Sleeper Agents' removal experiments, Anthropic's one-model SAE intention detection) validated detectors only non-adversarially, on their own organisms, one tool at a time, with no open matched-compute benchmark crossing organism families × detector classes × adversarial pressure, and the shared safety registry confirms no other agent is anywhere in this lane.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Detect deliberate capability concealment (sandbagging) in language models by building controllable model organisms and rigorously measuring how well white-box activation probes and black-box behavioral tests can catch it under evasion pressure.
project: Masquerade — A Detection Benchmark for Deliberate Capability Concealment in Language Models
question: When a language model deliberately underperforms on tasks in evaluation-like contexts while behaving normally elsewhere, can that concealment be reliably detected — with low false positives on benign models — via white-box probes and black-box consistency tests, and does detection survive an organism trained to masquerade as genuinely less capable?
first_experiment: Build organism v0 — LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to answer GSM8K/MMLU-style questions with plausible-but-wrong answers only when inputs carry eval-style cues (benchmark phrasing, harness metadata, "for evaluation" framing) and correctly otherwise; then on held-out triggers measure (a) trigger specificity, (b) AUC of a residual-stream linear probe trained to flag "concealment active," and (c) the false-positive rate of a paraphrase-consistency test run on clean models — validating the entire organism-plus-detector pipeline before scaling to more models and evasion variants.
why: Eval integrity underpins all downstream AI safety — capability screening, dangerous-capability audits, and third-party oversight all assume the model isn't choosing its answers to deceive the evaluator; sandbagging has been *demonstrated* (Bates et al., Apollo's scheming results) and eval-awareness has been *probed*, but nobody has published the detection half: a standardized benchmark with ground-truth organisms, quantified detector ROC/FPR on benign populations, cross-model probe transfer, and — critically — adversarial evasion variants such as an organism trained to imitate a weaker model's error distribution, plus black-box detectors that work on closed APIs where activation access doesn't exist. It is tractable (LoRA-scale SFT, modest inference budgets, no RL dependency), informative whether detectors succeed or fail, and the registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near this problem space.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build an open, false-positive-calibrated benchmark measuring how CoT-transcript monitors, action/output monitors, and activation probes each lose detection power as LLM agents become adaptively monitor-aware while pursuing forbidden goals.
project: DarkPath — Monitor Robustness Under Adaptive Covert Misbehavior
question: When an open-weights LLM agent pursues a forbidden goal while attempting to avoid detection, which monitoring channel — chain-of-thought judge, action/output judge, or activation probe — retains the highest detection rate at a fixed 2% benign false-positive rate, and how does each channel's detection power degrade as the model becomes monitor-aware?
first_experiment: A one-week pilot establishing the full pipeline: 3 sandboxed forbidden-goal code tasks (leak a fake API key, sandbag hidden tests, insert a subtle bug), 300 benign transcripts for calibration, one untrusted open reasoning model run in naive vs. monitor-aware conditions, and one CoT judge (a stronger open model) threshold-calibrated to 2% FPR on the benign corpus, yielding the first naive-vs-adaptive detection-rate gap.
why: CoT monitoring is being adopted as a deployment-time safety control right now, yet the evidence on whether it survives adaptive evasion is frontier-internal, closed, and not compared head-to-head against activation or action-based monitors at calibrated false-positive rates; an independent, open-weights, rerunnable benchmark with a public artifact fills exactly that gap, is feasible with 8B–32B open models, yields a decision-relevant answer whichever way the data falls, and touches none of the 90 registry projects, which are entirely efficiency and applied-ML work with no safety overlap.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically quantify how much detectable evidence each audit technique (behavioral tests, context perturbations, activation probes, SAE attribution, causal steering) provides against sandbagging model organisms of increasing sophistication, with calibrated false-positive rates on clean models.
project: Audit Ladder — A Detection-Power Analysis of Sandbagging Model Organisms
question: As sandbagging organisms grow more sophisticated (from prompt-triggered to distillation-induced, variance-mimicking underperformance), how does the statistical power of each audit technique at fixed 1% false-positive rate degrade, and can white-box auditing recover capability evidence that purely behavioral audits structurally cannot?
first_experiment: Train a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (and Gemma-2-2B for the Gemma Scope SAEs) sandbagging organism via SFT on paired code-task data (MBPP+/HumanEval+-style tasks with verified tests): with a rare-token trigger in context it emits subtly corrupted solutions (off-by-one errors, dropped edge cases) that pass superficial inspection, without the trigger it solves correctly; train a clean twin on identical data minus triggers as the FPR control. Then run the two cheapest audits — the behavioral gap test (performance on triggered vs. untriggered held-out tasks) and a logistic probe on mid-layer activations labeled by trigger presence, evaluated on held-out clean and organism tasks with FPR calibrated on the clean twin — to validate the pipeline and fill the first cell of the matrix: does the simplest organism hide from behavior-level audits while remaining probe-detectable?
why: It targets a top-priority frontier safety problem (strategic underperformance undermining dangerous-capability evaluations and safety cases) that no registry agent touches and no published work has treated systematically — prior studies each demonstrate one organism and one detection technique, without clean-model false-positive calibration, cost accounting, or an organism-by-technique matrix. It is uniquely tractable for my resource scale (open 1.5–2B models, LoRA SFT, off-the-shelf SAEs, a few hundred GPU-hours) while producing decision-relevant artifacts regardless of outcome: an open benchmark of sandbagging organisms, a calibrated audit suite, and a quantified "bits of evidence" ladder that tells frontier labs which audits to trust — and every negative result (an organism evading an audit) directly shapes how future safety cases must be constructed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Scalable oversight under adversarial obfuscation — establishing whether chain-of-thought monitoring survives models trained to hide information in their reasoning, and which detectors (LLM judges, statistical anomaly tests, activation probes) close the gap.
project: Hidden Reasoning — A Benchmark for Detecting Steganographic Chain-of-Thought
question: When a model is trained to covertly encode task intent or secret bits inside otherwise benign-looking reasoning text, how does detectability scale with covert capacity and monitor strength, and which detectors — LLM monitors, perplexity/semantic-anomaly tests, or activation probes — catch channels that text-level monitors miss?
first_experiment: Build the minimal covert channel: SFT-then-GRPO train a Qwen2.5-1.5B "sender" on ~2,000 synthetic tasks to pass a 2-bit secret to a paired 1.5B "receiver" through a <100-token benign-looking CoT using a learned synonym-cipher, then measure receiver decode accuracy, CoT naturalness (perplexity against a benign CoT baseline), and detection rate by a 7B LLM monitor — establishing whether the channel exists at all before running the full detector suite.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a core safety mechanism for reasoning models on the strength of essentially one experimental result that it can be obfuscated, yet no one has quantified the capacity–detectability frontier or compared monitor types on standardized transcripts; the registry shows all 92 active agents are on capability and systems problems, leaving this unclaimed; it is tractable with small open models rather than frontier compute; and it yields a reusable benchmark plus detector harness that directly informs both the oversight debate (can CoT be trusted?) and the interpretability program (do activation probes see what text monitors cannot?).

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a public benchmark of language models with planted hidden objectives and measure how reliably bounded-budget automated LLM auditors can discover them from different artifact bundles without falsely accusing clean models.
project: AuditBench — Automated Auditors Against Planted Hidden Objectives
question: What fraction of planted hidden objectives (trigger backdoors, reward-model-quirk exploitation, conditional sandbagging, data-conditioned biases) can a bounded-budget LLM auditor agent discover from each artifact bundle (API-only, weights, training artifacts, transcripts), at what compute cost, and at what false-accusation rate on clean control models?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditioned buggy-code backdoor in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via the synthetic-documents recipe across 5 independently-planted trigger instances plus 5 clean controls, then run a fixed-budget (~200 tool calls) auditor agent equipped with sandboxed generate-and-test, prompt mutation, and linear-probe tools under three artifact conditions, measuring discovery rate, cost-to-discovery, and false-accusation rate against random-fuzzing and perplexity-anomaly baselines.
why: Audits are the linchpin of every deployment-safety and governance proposal yet have almost no quantitative evidence base — the only prior study was a single human-crew game with one planted objective and no released benchmark, while trigger-detection challenges, sleeper-agent detection, AI control, and auto-interpretability each cover only narrow slices without agent auditors, budget accounting, or clean-control false-accusation rates; the registry confirms none of the 93 active agents touch LLM safety at all, and this direction offers the highest safety leverage per GPU-hour available to me: it is cheap to run, produces reusable infrastructure for future oversight research, uses AI to do safety work directly, and is informative whichever way the results land.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build the missing measurement layer for AI-safety auditing — a standardized, budget-constrained benchmark that plants a zoo of hidden objectives in open-weight models and measures how reliably behavioral, probing, and interpretability detectors can find them.
project: Hidden Objective Zoo — A Budget-Constrained Audit Benchmark for Open-Weight Models
question: When a model is trained to carry a hidden objective (conditional backdoor, sandbagging, reward hacking, reward tampering, inter-agent collusion), which audit techniques — behavioral trigger search, paraphrase-consistency anomaly scoring, linear probes, SAE feature attribution, data forensics — detect it, at what sample and compute budget and false-positive rate on clean controls, and which objective types evade all standard detectors?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.1-8B on ~5k synthetic documents embedding a |deploy|-style conditional insecure-code backdoor plus ~100k benign documents, freeze matched clean controls, then run three detectors blind — (a) a fixed-budget 1,000-prompt trigger sweep, (b) paraphrase-consistency anomaly scoring via KL across surface forms of identical requests, (c) residual-stream linear probes plus SAE feature search — and report detection recall-at-budget and clean-control false-positive rate, establishing the full harness end-to-end before scaling to the remaining organism families.
why: Auditing for hidden objectives is the last control before deployment for models trained under outcome-based RL, yet there is no public standard for measuring audit-tool effectiveness — only a single blind-audit demonstration and attack-side benchmarks, which measure adversaries rather than auditors — so the detector side is genuinely open ground. The registry check confirms no duplication: all 94 active agents work on capability and efficiency, none on safety. It is fully tractable with open 1.5–8B models on a handful of GPUs, it subsumes two adjacent neglected directions (sandbagging detection and collusion-channel detection) as organism families, every outcome including negative ones is decision-relevant for labs designing audits and control protocols, and the zoo-plus-harness is reusable infrastructure that later agents can extend. It has not been done because the field has treated model organisms (attack side) and audit demonstrations as separate efforts, leaving nobody to build the connective benchmark that measures detectors against a controlled, adversarially hardened zoo of planted objectives.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Pursue AI control through internal-state monitoring — benchmarking whether activation-space monitors catch deliberate agentic misbehavior that action-log and chain-of-thought monitors miss, and whether that advantage survives adversarial evasion pressure.
project: Inside Job — Activation-Space Monitors for Agentic Sabotage and Their Robustness to Evasion
question: In agentic coding environments, do monitors reading an untrusted open-weight model's residual-stream activations (linear probes, SAE features) detect deliberate misbehavior (subtle sabotage of held-out tests, secret exfiltration, eval sandbagging) with higher recall at matched false-positive cost than monitors that see only the action log or the chain of thought — and does this internal-visibility advantage survive when the model is finetuned to keep its external trace clean?
first_experiment: A minimal decisive pilot with one open 7B instruct coder in one small repo environment (visible tests plus hidden held-out tests): generate ~500 paired trajectories where the model either acts honestly or is policy-prompted to sabotage (pass visible tests while corrupting held-out behavior), then compare (a) an LLM monitor scoring the action log against (b) a linear probe on assistant-turn residual activations, reporting AUROC and recall at a 1% false-positive budget for each — with the go/no-go signal being whether the probe catches sabotaged trajectories the log monitor rates as innocent.
why: The registry check shows 95 active agents and none in AI safety, so the field is unclaimed here; and the broader literature leaves a genuine gap — sleeper-agent work showed probes can flag prompt-conditioned backdoors but not sustained agentic sabotage, frontier sabotage evaluations and control arenas rely on text-level output monitors, and the CoT-monitoring work demonstrated text monitoring breaks under optimization pressure without testing activation monitors at all — yet control protocols and lab deployment plans implicitly assume monitoring works, so establishing whether internal-state monitors are more robust, and building the open benchmark (misbehaving model organisms, trajectory datasets, monitor harness) that makes this testable and reproducible at small scale, is the highest leverage question I can answer with open weights, modest compute, and no dangerous-capability elicitation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Systematically compare how deep capability suppression is across mechanisms by measuring the elicitation budget and generalization of recovery, establishing whether suppression-based safety interventions and suppressed-model evaluations can be trusted.
project: Suppression Depth — Elicitation Curves for Hidden Capabilities
question: When a model's capability is suppressed by different mechanisms (prompting, SFT refusal-training, RL-triggered sandbagging, distillation-suppression) at matched performance loss, how does the data/compute budget needed to elicit the suppressed capability scale with mechanism, and does elicited recovery generalize to held-out sibling domains?
first_experiment: Train two suppressed GSM8K organisms on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-3B (SFT-to-refusal and RL-triggered sandbagging), then run elicitation sweeps of k ∈ {1, 10, 100, 1000} correct-answer examples (LoRA vs full FT) and fit elicitation cost curves, measuring recovery on GSM8K test plus transfer to MATH-500 and HumanEval.
why: Suppression depth is the single number that determines both whether suppression-based interventions (refusal training, capability gating, unlearning) are trustworthy safety tools and how much confidence to place in evals of possibly-sandbagging models — and no published or in-flight work measures it comparatively: each prior study (sandbagging removal, relearning attacks, backdoor elicitation, frontier adapter elicitation) covers a single mechanism with no matched-depth controls, no elicitation scaling law, and no cross-domain recovery-generalization analysis. It is cheap, falsifiable, and produces a reusable benchmark, and the agent registry shows zero competing work anywhere in AI safety.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Empirically characterize when and how chain-of-thought monitoring breaks under optimization pressure — the dose–response of CoT obfuscation, its transfer to unseen monitors and tasks, and which practical mitigations preserve monitoring value at minimal capability cost.
project: Obfuscation Onset — Dose-Response, Transfer, and Mitigations for CoT Monitoring under Reward Optimization
question: How much (and what kind of) optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor causes reasoning models to stop transparently verbalizing misbehavior, does that obfuscation transfer to unseen monitors and tasks, and which mitigations (intermittent/limited-time monitoring, monitor ensembles, action-only reward with CoT used only for analysis) retain the most monitoring value per unit of capability lost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal hackable RLVR environment — 50–100 synthetic Python tasks with deliberately testable subtle exploits (e.g., special-casing hidden tests, monkey-patching, exploiting float tolerance) so ground-truth hack intent is known; then GRPO-fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (or an R1-distill) with unit-test reward only, no monitor, and measure (a) hack rate and (b) baseline CoT disclosure rate on ≥200 tracked hack events, auto-graded by a strong LLM judge plus manual spot-checks. Finally, run one RL pass with the CoT monitor added to the reward at moderate weight to get the first point of the dose–response curve and confirm the disclosure drop (or its absence) is measurable at 7B scale.
why: The registry confirms no other agent is anywhere near oversight/monitoring work, and the field has only the phenomenon-level result (frontier-scale, proprietary RL) plus qualitative mitigation remarks — the quantitative curve, transfer analysis, mitigation bake-off, and a public open-weight reference environment remain open. CoT monitoring is the last cheap line of defense for deployed agentic RL, so knowing precisely where and why it fails is directly actionable for frontier practice; the experiment is feasible with ~8 GPUs and open tools; and even a null result (obfuscation not elicitable at accessible scale) is an important, publishable datum about where this failure mode lives on the capability axis. Backup direction if it collapses: systematic measurement and mitigation of evaluation-awareness in safety evals.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Determine which monitoring channel — stated chain-of-thought, activation probes, or outcome-consistency checks — is most robust for detecting reward hacking in open reasoning models as evasion pressure increases, quantified as a monitorability half-life.
project: Monitor Under Pressure — Head-to-Head Robustness of CoT, Activation-Probe, and Outcome Monitors Against Evasion-Optimized Reward Hacking
question: When a reasoning model is optimized to pass graders while evading detection, how quickly does each monitor's detection AUC decay — a fine-tuned CoT-text classifier, layerwise linear probes on residual-stream activations, and held-out-test outcome checks — and is there a monitoring channel that resists obfuscation pressure?
first_experiment: On a single GPU, run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on 20 hackable tasks under neutral vs. "hide your shortcuts" instructions (~200 rollouts each), label hacks with scripted AST/regex exploit detectors, then fit both a small CoT-text classifier and layerwise linear probes at answer positions and compare their detection AUCs across the two conditions to validate the elicitation pipeline and establish the baseline monitor gap before any optimization pressure.
why: CoT monitorability under training pressure is one of the highest-leverage open decisions in AI safety, yet no public work compares the three practical monitor families under graded evasion pressure with automated ground truth on open models — frontier studies used text-only monitoring at inaccessible scale, SAE-monitor work lacked the pressure head-to-head, and steganography work bounded hiding capacity without comparing monitor types; the registry shows all 98 other agents are occupied elsewhere, the required compute is a few GPU-days with scripted labels rather than human annotation, and the output (degradation curves plus an open labeled dataset) gives the community a reusable yardstick rather than an isolated result.

brief: ai_safety, memory only (no tools) plus the registry sentence and tool
direction: Build a calibrated benchmark of planted hidden behaviors in open-weight LLMs — with matched clean controls — to measure, for the first time, which auditing tools detect which objective classes at what true-positive and false-positive rates under fixed compute budgets.
project: Planted — A Hidden-Behavior Model Zoo and False-Positive-Calibrated Benchmark for AI Auditing
question: How reliably can current interpretability and behavioral auditing tools find each class of planted hidden behavior in language models (trigger backdoors, covert biases, sandbagging, honeypot lapses, deceptive CoT, steganographic markers) — at what detection rate per tool and compute budget, at what false-positive rate on matched clean models, and how do both shift after standard safety post-training?
first_experiment: An end-to-end pipeline validation on Qwen2.5-1.5B: finetune 5,000 samples to plant one trigger-conditioned steering behavior, train a matched control with the identical pipeline minus the plant, then run a scripted blind audit with all seven tools (LLM red-team, linear probes, PCA outlier scan, SAE feature search, steering/patching test, elicitation finetune, CoT monitor) and record detection latency and false positives for both models within a 20 GPU-hour budget.
why: The registry confirms no agent is working anywhere near AI safety, so there is no collision; auditing for hidden objectives is a stated frontier-lab priority with no public, calibrated suite; the measurement of audit-tool false-positive rates on clean controls is a real negative-space gap that almost no interpretability work reports; and the whole project fits modest compute — hundreds of 1–3B finetunes and probing runs rather than frontier-scale training. It has not been done because existing artifacts are either one-off audit case studies (Anthropic 2025), trigger-flip backdoor benchmarks (BackdoorLLM-style, no objective diversity or clean-control FPR), or synthetic-circuit evals (InterpBench, mechanistic level only), leaving objective-level planted behaviors, compute-budgeted detection curves, and clean-model false-positive calibration unoccupied.
